EU planning mission to train Lebanon’s army
- The EU plans to launch a mission to train Lebanon's army, focusing on border and maritime security, without replacing the UN peacekeeping force UNIFIL.
- UNIFIL's mandate ends December 31, 2026, amid ongoing regional conflicts involving Israel and Hezbollah.
- Several EU countries show interest in the mission, aiming for a formal launch decision in October, while peacekeepers remain deemed necessary by the UN.
AI generated
WICKLOW, Ireland - The EU said on Sept 1 it was looking to launch a mission to train the Lebanese army in the coming months - but said it would not replace the UN peacekeeping force.
The United Nations peacekeeping force in southern Lebanon, UNIFIL, has roughly 7,500 personnel from nearly 50 countries, and has been in place since 1978.
Its presence has not prevented repeated outbreaks of conflict, with southern Lebanon seeing successive wars between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah.
In August 2025, however, the UN Security Council, under US pressure, decided to end UNIFIL’s mandate on Dec 31, 2026.
“Ministers discussed our plans for a new EU mission to advise and train the country’s armed forces, including on border and maritime security,” EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas said, after a meeting of the bloc’s defence ministers in Ireland.
“The EU is not seeking to replace UNIFIL, we are investing in Lebanon‘s capacity to provide security for itself.”
Kallas said that “planning is progressing well” on the mission with some 10 countries expressing interest in participating.
She said the hope was to reach a formal decision to launch the mission in October.
UN chief Antonio Guterres has said that peacekeepers will be needed in Lebanon after the mandate of the current mission expires.
France and Italy have previously said they want to set up a multinational coalition to succeed the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon.
The country became embroiled in the Middle East war after Hezbollah fired rockets at Israel on March 2, prompting a widespread Israeli bombing campaign and ground invasion.
More than 4,300 people have been killed, though violence has decreased since a US-Iran deal and a Washington-sponsored framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel went into force. AFP

Rivers swell across UP, inundating over 11,300 hectares in five districts
LUCKNOW: Rivers in Uttar Pradesh reached or crossed danger levels at several monitoring stations as satellite data showed inundation of 11,358.49 hectares across five districts, highlighting the spread of flood conditions in the state. The affected districts are Ballia, Ghazipur, Gorakhpur, Mau and Deoria.The inundation figures were released by the Flood Management Information System Centre (FMISC) under the Uttar Pradesh irrigation department. Its satellite-based assessment, prepared using RISAT-1A MRS SAR data analysed by the National Remote Sensing Centre, showed major inundation in Ballia and Ghazipur and minor inundation in Gorakhpur, Mau and Deoria by Monday evening.Ballia reported flooding in 179 villages across 12 blocks, covering approximately 8,061.63 hectares. Ghazipur saw inundation in 87 villages across six blocks, covering 2,341.33 hectares. Deoria reported flooding in 18 villages across five blocks, Gorakhpur in 14 villages across three blocks, and Mau in 13 villages in one block.The combined assessment covered 311 villages in 27 blocks. The total submerged area was estimated at 11,358.49 hectares.
The FMISC clarified that the assessment includes riverine flooding, water accumulation in low-lying areas, rainfall-induced flooding and isolated waterlogged patches.According to the Central Water Commission’s readings available at 9 pm on Tuesday, water levels were at or above the danger mark at 11 monitoring stations in Uttar Pradesh. The situation was serious along the Ganga, Ghaghra and their tributaries in Budaun, Barabanki, Ballia, Mirzapur, Varanasi and Ghazipur.At Kachhla Bridge in Budaun, the Ganga was flowing at 162.43 m, exactly at the danger level. Its warning level is 161.80 m.In Barabanki, the Ghaghra at Elginbridge was flowing at 106.09 m, 2 cm above its danger mark of 106.07 m and more than a metre above the warning level of 105.07 m. The CWC forecast suggested that the river could rise further to 106.07 m by 9 am on Wednesday.The Sharda also known as Mahakali river at Kukea in Lakhimpur Kheri rose to 139.81 m, marginally above its danger level of 139.8 m and well above the warning level of 138.8 m.The Ghaghra was also above the danger mark at Turtipar in Ballia, where it stood at 64.08 m against a danger level of 64.01 m. The station recorded 22 mm rainfall during the day. The forecast, however, indicated a fall to 64 m by Wednesday morning.In Ballia, the Ganga was flowing at 59.37 m, nearly 1.75 m above its danger level of 57.615 m. The district accounted for the largest share of the inundated area recorded by the state’s FMISC.The most pronounced river-level exceedances in eastern Uttar Pradesh were recorded along the Ganga and its tributaries. At Tendui in Varanasi district, the Varuna was flowing at 71.35 m against a danger level of 70.21 m. The station recorded 43 mm rainfall.At Saidpur in Ghazipur, the Ganga stood at 67.52 m against a danger level of 67.19 m. The station recorded 68 mm rainfall. At the Ghazipur monitoring station, the river was flowing at 63.33 m, exceeding the danger level of 63.105 m. The level was rising and was forecast to reach 63.47 m by 8 am on Wednesday. The station recorded 63 mm rainfall.In Mirzapur, the Ganga was above the danger mark at Ahraura and Chunar. At Ahraura, the river stood at 74.75 m against a danger level of 74.30 m, though the trend was declining. At Chunar, it was flowing at 72.82 m against a danger level of 72.78 m.
At Narayanpur in Mirzapur, the Ganga was at 72.59 m, above the warning level of 71.41 metres but 21 cm below the danger mark of 72.41 m. The station recorded the highest rainfall among the locations shown in the CWC data, at 75.4 mm.The CWC data also recorded a high level at Chausa in neighbouring Bihar, where the Karamnasa was flowing at 61.86 m against a danger level of 60.39 m. The reading is significant for the downstream flood situation in eastern Uttar Pradesh.“The readings suggest that flood pressure is spread across multiple river systems rather than being confined to one stretch. While some stations showed a declining trend, water levels at several locations remained above danger marks, leaving riverbank settlements, agricultural fields, roads and embankments vulnerable,” said an official source.

Chinese President Xi arrives in Egypt for first visit in 10 years

Amer Solyman, Hussien Elkabany and Mohammad Sio
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Cairo on Tuesday evening for his first official visit to Egypt in 10 years.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi received Xi at Cairo International Airport, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
The two leaders are expected to discuss strengthening bilateral relations and implementing the countries’ comprehensive strategic partnership, as well as regional and international issues of mutual concern.
The Egyptian presidency said Tuesday that the visit would focus on implementing the comprehensive strategic partnership agreement signed by the two countries in 2014.
The talks will also include consultations on regional and international developments, according to the presidency.
In an article published Tuesday in Egyptian state-run newspapers Al-Ahram, Al-Akhbar and Al-Gomhouria, Xi said relations between China and Egypt were in their “best period in history” after 70 years of friendship.
He called for a deeper, comprehensive strategic partnership and expanded high-quality cooperation under China’s Belt and Road Initiative.
Xi also called for stronger cultural exchanges and closer China-Arab and China-Africa cooperation.
Sisi, in an article published by Al-Ahram, said Egypt and China agreed that an expansion of armed conflicts would not serve the interests of any regional or international party.
China’s Foreign Ministry announced last Wednesday that Xi would undertake a foreign tour from Aug. 30 to Sept. 3, according to the official Xinhua news agency.
Xi last visited Egypt in January 2016, his first visit to the country since becoming president.
During that visit, Xi met Sisi and attended a ceremony marking the 60th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries.
Sisi has visited China several times, most recently in May 2024.
Egypt and China established diplomatic relations in 1956, making Egypt the first Arab and African country to recognize the People’s Republic of China.
Beijing backed Cairo during the 1956 Suez Crisis, while Egypt supported China’s restoration of its seat at the UN in 1971.
The countries established a strategic partnership in 1999, which was elevated to a comprehensive strategic partnership in December 2014 during Sisi’s visit to Beijing.

Ukraine experts to advise Europe on plugging defence gaps
- Military experts from Ukraine, Britain, and EU countries will advise Europe on quickly addressing defence gaps amid threats from Russia.
- The initiative aims to bring top security minds together to find innovative solutions, leveraging Ukraine's battlefield experience.
- Europe faces challenges as the US reduces NATO support and hybrid attacks increase, highlighting the need for stronger defence capabilities.
AI generated
WICKLOW, Ireland - Military experts from Ukraine are to join a new initiative to advise European nations on how to swiftly plug gaps in the continent’s defences, the EU said on Sept 1.
The European Union’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said advisers from the war-torn country as well as from Britain and EU nations will come together from next week, as Europe seeks to shore up its defences in the face of an aggressive Russia.
“Europe is investing more in defence than ever, but spending alone is not automatically a guarantee for success,” Kallas told journalists, after a meeting of European Union defence ministers in Ireland.
“We have not been fast enough to cover the gaps in Europe’s conventional power within NATO,” she added, noting that most EU countries were also members of the North Atlantic alliance.
European countries started ramping up military budgets after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump has also piled pressure on Europe to spend more on defence as Washington signals it wants to step back from the continent to focus on other challenges such as China.
Kallas said the initiative will bring together “senior political and military leaders from several EU countries” as well as from Britain and Ukraine.
“The aim is to have some of the brightest minds on security and defence to come together and really provide out-of-the-box solutions,” she said.
Ukraine was included due to its battlefield experience, she added.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said his country had increasingly “found itself in the crosshairs of hybrid attackers” after an explosive-laden drone was found in August at Leipzig airport, a crucial military transport hub.
Meanwhile, the Pentagon, which has some 80,000 troops stationed in Europe, has told allies it is reducing the number of assets it makes available for NATO’s defence plans.
While Europe can already fill in some of the gaps Washington is leaving in NATO’s defence plans, key assets such as long-range missiles will take time to substitute. AFP

What has changed for Ukrainians since September 1: fuel and gas prices, salaries, military payments, and education
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:01:34 EEST
02:01:34 KST

What has changed for Ukrainians since September 1: fuel and gas prices, salaries, military payments, and education
Kyiv • UNN
In September, educators’ salaries and student scholarships are increasing, while military personnel are receiving payments under a new system. Gas prices and excise taxes remain unchanged.
With the beginning of autumn, a number of decisions concerning educators’ salaries, student scholarships, and the organization of education take effect in Ukraine. Some payments to military personnel are also already being calculated under the new system.
UNN has compiled the main changes that Ukrainians should take into account in September.
Fuel and gas: how prices are changing at the beginning of autumn
Automatic price increases for gasoline, diesel fuel, and autogas due to new excise duties will not take place on September 1, 2026. The current schedule for increasing the excise tax provides for the rates to change once a year.
In 2026, the excise duty amounts to €300.8 per 1,000 liters of gasoline, €253.8 per 1,000 liters of diesel fuel, and €198 per 1,000 liters of liquefied gas. The next increase is scheduled for January 1, 2027—to €329.9, €291.9, and €223, respectively.
At the same time, retail prices at gas stations may change independently of the tax calendar. At the end of August, the average price of A-95 gasoline in Ukraine was about UAH 80.07 per liter, diesel fuel cost UAH 91.53, and autogas cost UAH 43.07.
On September 1, some networks had already adjusted their prices: WOG, in particular, increased the price of A-95 gasoline by UAH 1 per liter. These changes are related to market conditions, purchase prices, exchange rates, and logistics, rather than to the introduction of a new excise rate specifically in September.
For household gas consumers, everything also remains unchanged. At Naftogaz of Ukraine Gas Supply Company, which serves the vast majority of households, the “Fixed” tariff plan is UAH 7.96 per cubic meter including VAT and is valid from May 1, 2026, to April 30, 2027. Therefore, based solely on the change of season, the company does not plan to revise gas prices for its customers.
Salaries and payments to military personnel: what is new as of September
The government has not introduced a separate general increase in the basic monetary allowance for military personnel specifically from September 1. At the same time, a new system of incentive and combat payments has been in effect since the summer, and military personnel will continue to receive them in the autumn. It applies both to contract soldiers and to mobilized personnel.
In particular, military personnel serving in the rear are entitled to an additional reward of UAH 10,000 per month. For direct participation in combat operations on the line of contact, UAH 100,000 per month is paid proportionally to the time spent performing the tasks. For carrying out tasks up to and including a platoon strongpoint, UAH 170,000 per month is provided; for a company strongpoint, UAH 70,000.
Payments for assault operations are calculated separately: UAH 20,000 per day for restoring positions deep within one’s own defense and UAH 40,000 per day for an assault on the line of contact or deep within the enemy’s defenses. The total amount of monthly combat payments is capped at UAH 460,000, excluding the basic monetary allowance and certain bonuses.
Education sector: changes for schools and higher education institutions
The most noticeable changes from September 1 concern education.
The official salaries of teaching and academic teaching staff are increasing by another 20%. The first stage of the increase—by 30%—took place on January 1, so in 2026 the total increase compared with 2025, according to the Ministry of Education and Science, amounts to 50%.
In addition, schools, state vocational, professional pre-higher, and higher education institutions, as well as inclusive resource centers, are switching to a new mechanism for determining official salaries. For school teachers, salaries including allowances and additional payments, according to the Ministry of Education and Science’s calculations, will range from UAH 16,600 to UAH 37,000 before taxes. For teaching and academic teaching staff at higher education institutions, they will range from UAH 17,000 to UAH 53,000. The specific amount depends on the position, length of service, qualifications, workload, academic degree, and other additional payments.
Another change for students is the doubling of academic scholarships. Starting September 1, the standard academic scholarship at vocational education institutions will increase from UAH 1,250 to UAH 2,500, at professional pre-higher education institutions — from UAH 1,510 to UAH 3,020, and at higher education institutions — from UAH 2,000 to UAH 4,000 per month. For specialties with an increased rate, the scholarship at higher education institutions will amount to UAH 5,100. Named government scholarships for university students will increase to UAH 8,000.
Also, starting September 1, 150 academic lyceums will begin piloting a new model of specialized upper secondary education. Students will have a wider choice of profiles, subjects, and courses, while lyceums will introduce individual educational pathways. The full-scale launch of specialized upper secondary education across the country is scheduled for September 1, 2027.
Social payments: who will receive more in September
No general increase in pensions or all state social benefits is planned from September 1, 2026. The main pension indexation this year took place on March 1. However, for some households, the amount of their subsidy changed following an automatic recalculation carried out by the Pension Fund in August.
The recalculation applies to families whose average monthly total income increased or decreased by more than 50%. If income has decreased significantly, the subsidy may increase; if it has increased, the payment may, conversely, become smaller. There is no need to contact the Pension Fund for this recalculation.
In addition, the "Schoolchild's Package" program continues in the new academic year. Families whose child is starting first grade in the 2026/2027 academic year in territory controlled by Ukraine may receive a one-time payment of UAH 5,000 for each first-grader. The funds may be spent on books, stationery, school supplies, children's clothing, and footwear. Applications are accepted until November 1, 2026, via "Diia" or a Pension Fund service center.

Germany blames Russia for Leipzig airport drone attack, orders Russian consulate closed
Germany's government on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on 4 August using an explosive-laden drone, and announced that it would shut down a Russian consulate among other measures against Moscow. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and EU chief Ursula von der Leyen vowed "full solidarity" with Berlin in response.
The German government on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month using a drone laden with explosives, and announced that it would shut down a Russian consulate among other measures against Moscow.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and EU chief Ursula von der Leyen vowed "full solidarity" with Berlin in response.
"NATO will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend all Allies against any threat – including malign actions like those seen in Leipzig and elsewhere across the Alliance," Rutte wrote on X following talks with Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Rutte said Berlin had put forward "clear" evidence of Moscow's role in the "hybrid attack" and welcomed the measures announced in response.
"Russia's attempts to intimidate us, to undermine our unity and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and will fail," he added.
The European Commission president, who likewise spoke with Merz, vowed to "keep the EU united despite these escalating and serious acts".
"I assured him that the EU stands in full solidarity with Germany in the face of this attack by Russia," von der Leyen wrote on X.
"The German government has taken strong measures. And the message is clear: hybrid attacks will not go without a clear response," she said, adding the bloc was preparing additional sanctions against Russia.

Petraeus urges UK to lead NATO military overhaul
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:00:46 BST
02:00:46 KST

Britain should become the first major Western country to reorganise its defence institutions around lessons emerging from the war in Ukraine and use that experience to help drive a wider transformation of NATO, General David Petraeus has told the House of Lords.
Delivering the Lord Speaker’s Lecture on 1 September, the retired four-star US Army general argued that the nature of warfare is changing quickly enough to require more than conventional modernisation programmes. Petraeus said Britain’s early recognition of the threat posed by Russia and its sustained support for Ukraine had demonstrated what he described as strategic clarity, giving the UK an opportunity to take a leading role in reshaping how Western militaries organise, train and equip themselves.
Petraeus said: “Britain now has an opportunity to demonstrate that same quality once again. Just as it helped lead the Alliance in recognizing the strategic implications of Russia’s aggression, it can now help lead the Alliance in recognizing the revolutionary implications that Ukraine holds for the future of warfare itself.”
He described Ukraine as “the defining military laboratory of the twenty-first century”, arguing that its importance lies not simply in individual technologies but in the way sensors, software, unmanned systems, electronic warfare, precision weapons and industrial adaptation are being combined. Petraeus said information is being collected, analysed and acted upon at unprecedented speed, while commercial innovation is moving directly onto the battlefield and software, hardware and operational methods are being adapted while fighting is underway.
He told peers: “Much of the discussion has understandably focused on individual technologies—unmanned systems, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare, cyber capabilities, precision strike, battle management systems, and others. Each matters. But the principal lesson is larger: the very concept of warfare is changing.”
Petraeus said Britain’s Strategic Defence Review and Defence Investment Plan showed an appreciation of the changes taking place, pointing to their focus on unmanned and autonomous systems, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare, industrial resilience, procurement reform and accelerated innovation. He cautioned, however, that those measures should be regarded as the beginning of a larger transformation rather than its completion.
He said: “The most consequential military transformations seldom begin with new equipment. They begin with new ideas. Additional resources will clearly be required in important areas, but the greatest obstacle to transformation is rarely money alone. More often, it is the difficulty of questioning long-established assumptions and overcoming institutional inertia.”
Petraeus continued: “And I believe the United Kingdom is unusually well positioned to do precisely that. Not because Britain is free of serious economic, fiscal, or political constraints—it plainly is not—but because, as we have seen in Ukraine, Britain has demonstrated the capacity to recognize strategic reality early and act decisively.”
He added: “That now presents Britain with another opportunity: to become the first major Western nation to organize its defence institutions around the new concept of warfare that Ukraine has been pioneering—and, in doing so, to help lead the transformation of NATO itself.”
Petraeus said NATO itself would also have to change, including the operational headquarters responsible for commanding Alliance forces. He argued that NATO needs a common understanding of the emerging concept of warfare before individual nations can reorganise their forces effectively around it.
He said: “NATO must now summon that spirit again, with far greater urgency, by developing a common understanding of the new concept of warfare and the institutional transformation that must follow.” Referring to NATO’s operational headquarters, he added: “Those headquarters will have to think, organize, and operate differently if they are to lead this transformation successfully.”
Petraeus said the process could not be limited to another incremental modernisation programme, calling instead for changes to force structure, professional military education, training, procurement, personnel policy, industrial engagement and the way battlefield lessons are identified and incorporated.
He said: “The question is not whether this transformation will occur. It is already underway—most visibly in Ukraine, but also in Russia, the Middle East, and elsewhere. The question is whether we will lead it—or be forced to catch up to those who do.”

A large unusual fish caught in the floodwaters of the Gandak basin being examined by locals at Valmikinagar in West Champaran
BETTIAH: Unidentified and unusual fish swept into the Gandak river and its floodplains by floodwaters from Nepal have prompted the Bihar govt to issue a safety advisory, asking residents of West Champaran and Gopalganj not to consume or trade in such fish until their identity and safety are confirmed.The fisheries division of the dairy, fisheries and animal resources department issued the caution on Tuesday after unusual fish were found in local water bodies and low-lying areas across the flood-hit Gandak basin.Floodwaters from Nepal have entered the Gandak system, inundating several areas of West Champaran and Gopalganj. The department said fish can be swept away from ponds, rivers and other water bodies during floods and carried over considerable distances. During this movement, they may come into contact with contaminated drains, dead animals and other pollutants, raising the risk of contamination by bacteria, viruses and fungi.“Do not consume any unidentified or unusual-looking fish. Until confirmation by the concerned department, an unfamiliar fish should not be considered fit for consumption,” the advisory said.Residents have also been asked not to buy or sell unfamiliar fish caught from floodwaters or assume an unusual-looking species is safe merely because it resembles a commonly eaten fish.
Anyone developing vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dizziness or breathing difficulty after consuming such fish has been advised to seek immediate medical attention.Wildlife Trust of India director Sameer Kumar Sinha said most fish swept into the Gandak in Bihar following the Nepal floods are believed to be ‘Bagarius bagarius’, commonly known as the goonch catfish and locally called “Gochita”.
He said the large freshwater catfish is found in fast-flowing rivers of India, Nepal and parts of Southeast Asia. The carnivorous species feeds on smaller fish, crabs and other aquatic organisms and often hides among rocks in deep stretches with strong currents.Sinha said local communities consume the fish, but it spoils quickly after death and may pose health risks if eaten after deterioration. He urged people to follow the Bihar govt advisory and exercise caution. The species is listed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) as threatened.

China’s Xi makes first visit to Egypt in a decade, amid regional turmoil
Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Cairo for his first visit in a decade, marking 70 years of diplomatic relations and aiming to bolster economic cooperation amid regional crises.
China President Xi Jinping has made his first visit to Egypt since 2016, coinciding with the 70th anniversary of diplomatic ties between the two countries.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi received Xi in Cairo on Tuesday, having made eight visits to China since taking office in 2014.
Presidential spokesman Ambassador Mohamed el-Shennawy said Xi’s visit aimed at strengthening bilateral relations between the two countries and to follow up on the implementation of a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Agreement signed between the two countries in 2014.
“The visit will also include consultations on a number of regional and international issues of mutual interest,” he said.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs last week described relations with Egypt as being at their best state in history, and that Xi’s visit would set the direction of future ties.
Economic trade boom
Trade relations between the two countries also appear strong. China is Egypt’s largest trading partner in non-petroleum goods, with bilateral trade reaching nearly $20.7bn by the end of 2025, according to the State Information Service (SIS).

Chinese investments in Egypt are focused mainly in the Suez Canal area, a key passageway for trade between China and Europe. He said the joint Egypt-China Eagles of Civilisation air exercises, which began on August 22 in Egypt, aimed at showing how the Chinese Air Force is capable of operating far from its borders.

Russia’s new ad campaign uses teen slang to urge teens to back out of arson and sabotage jobs
Public service ads discouraging teenagers from committing arson and sabotage have appeared in St. Petersburg. Facebook users noticed one such banner, a rotating digital display.
The banners feature portraits of smiling teenagers alongside captions: “Coolly bailed on torching a relay cabinet and didn’t get 10 years for arson,” “Fearlessly ditched torching a cell tower and didn’t get 10 years for sabotage,” and “Quietly slipped off a handler’s hook and didn’t get 15 years for a bombing.”
The images are all advertisements for Vykhod31 (“Exit 31”), a project recently launched under the government’s Obyasnyaem.rf initiative. According to the project’s website, Vykhod31 was created “in response to increasingly frequent attempts to lure young Russians into committing arson, bombings, and other acts of terrorism.”
The project takes its name from Article 31 of Russia’s Criminal Code, which covers voluntary abandonment of a crime. State media, senators (1, 2), and lawmakers from the outgoing State Duma and from regional legislatures (1, 2, 3) are already promoting it.
Russia’s state news agency RIA Novosti said the project “combined outdoor advertising, posters, TV commercials, and social media content.” Among other things, the materials are meant to teach teenagers that “real law enforcement officers will never contact you on messaging apps from an unknown number.” The project’s website also publishes recommendations for teenagers and their parents, along with the stories of children who were sent to prison in arson and sabotage cases.
Arson attacks on railroad relay cabinets, cell towers, and other infrastructure have occurred regularly across Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Teenagers are often implicated in these cases: the youngest detainee was 11. Criminal liability for terrorism and sabotage offenses begins at age 14.
As of May 2026, the independent Russian news outlet Mediazona had counted at least 240 teenagers detained in Russia on terrorism or sabotage charges since the war began. In most cases — 205 of them — the teenagers’ actions were attributed to a desire for easy money from side jobs. Six were duped into committing arson by scammers, and five said they opposed the war. The motive was unclear in the remaining cases.
In an extensive review of these cases, the outlet said teenagers find arson jobs advertised online. The postings are often framed as insurance fraud or other “shady” schemes, but they are placed by Ukrainian and Russian security services. Human rights activists have also said that provocateurs from the security services may be involved in these cases.

Private equity’s London takeover spree goes on – and the politicians ignore it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:56:59 UTC
01:56:59 KST

The UK is in the business of “reindustrialising”, says the prime minister. If we are, an increasing portion of the activity will be under foreign ownership. Tuesday brought yet another overseas private equity swoop on a FTSE 250 industrial firm.
This time it’s the Macclesfield-based Bodycote, which describes itself as “the world’s largest service provider of heat treatment and specialist metallurgical technologies” – think, for example, processes and coatings to toughen jet engine blades. The buyer is the US buyout firm Veritas for £1.65bn or 940p a share, or £1.85bn including debt. Unless, that is, the rival bidder, CVC, a European private equity firm, comes back for another bite, which the market clearly thinks is a possibility because Bodycote’s shares closed at 955p.
The shame is that one cannot call 940p a stunning price. The valuation “does not appear particularly generous on a take-out basis”, said an analyst at the investment bank RBC, noting that it’s only 25% above the pre-bid level and the implied earnings valuation is merely in line with Bodycote’s 10-year average.
Indeed, nine-tenths of the “reasons for recommendation” section of Bodycote’s announcement sounded like an argument for doing the opposite. The passage started by saying how well the medium-term “optimise, perform, grow” strategy adopted in late 2024 was going. The plan was designed to find efficiencies and shift towards the expanding aerospace and defence sectors in pursuit of enviable financial metrics, including 20%-plus operating margins and a return on capital employed of 15 to 20% through the cycle. Good progress has been made, say the directors.
On the way, there has been enough spare cash for £120m of share buy-backs while maintaining a 38-year record of growing or maintaining the dividend. And the board is “confident in the ongoing execution” of the strategy, with “the majority of remaining improvements under Bodycote’s control”.
It was only in the last sentence that the company also said it was “mindful of increasing structural challenges in certain automotive and industrial markets together with macroeconomic uncertainties which create meaningful risk to delivery of Bodycote’s medium term financial targets”.
In other words, everything is going splendidly apart from a couple of risks – the sectoral one that the strategy is addressing, and the vague “macroeconomic uncertainty” that is a normal state of affairs for most companies. As a reason for accepting a bid at a mere 25% premium, it’s not terribly convincing.
In Bodycote’s defence, one might say the takeover price could yet improve if CVC, which said it was considering its position, comes back. More depressingly, one suspects Bodycote simply lives in that unloved sub-£5bn capitalisation part of the stock market that suffers from lack of attention and lack of regular inward capital flows. It is harder to fight for independence if the unspoken market pressure is to accept a bid for the sake of certainty.
The mini-tragedy in this case is that there was a wake-up call of sorts for investors when Apollo, yet another US private equity outfit, expressed an interest in bidding at 885p in the spring before walking away. The net result, though, is that Bodycote’s 54 years of London stock market life will come to an end one way or another. The company joins a long list of departees this year, which on Tuesday alone also took in telecoms company Gamma Communications for £1.1bn and the Scottish energy firm Capricorn for £292m.
Bodycote can still prosper under private equity ownership, of course. But a leading UK-based global specialist in its field, with 130 sites across 22 countries and 4,000 employees, is yet another bad one for the London market to lose.
The remedies for this rate of exodus have been trawled over in this column many times – and none are easy. But the process surely starts with recognition among politicians that “selling the family silver” – the title of a recent Peel Hunt report that calculated 150-plus bids for UK companies with a market value of more than £100m since the start of 2023 – may not be in the UK’s long-term economic interests. As ever, there was barely a squeak out of Westminster.

Western Sanctions and Ukrainian Drone Strikes Push Russian Oil Production to Lowest Since 2009

Western Sanctions and Ukrainian Drone Strikes Push Russian Oil Production to Lowest Since 2009
Russia has downgraded its oil production forecast for 2026 to a 17-year low, reflecting the escalating economic and infrastructural toll of the invasion of Ukraine, Reuters reported on September 1, citing a government draft forecast.
Moscow has reduced its crude production estimates for the 2026–2029 period by 16 million to 20 million tons compared to its previous May outlook.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Following Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, Moscow even banned aviation fuel exports and began importing Jet A-1 fuel for its aircraft. Shadow fleet tankers recently delivered 70,000 metric tons of fuel from South Korea and Egypt to cover shortages for Russian warplanes and drones.
The internal projections, which are slated to be finalized in late September for federal budget drafting, highlight the compounding impact of Western sanctions and intensified Ukrainian drone strikes on the country’s energy sector.
In its base-case scenario, the Russian government expects domestic crude oil production to decline by 17.2 million metric tons this year, dropping to 494.2 million tons, or 9.88 million barrels per day, Reuters wrote. This marks the lowest output level for the world’s third-largest producer since 2009. While production is projected to slightly recover to 500 million tons in 2027, the draft indicates that output will remain suppressed below 2025 levels through at least 2029.
The downward revision follows severe disruptions to Russia’s domestic fuel supply chain. According to Reuters, sustained Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries—coupled with existing European Union import bans—have significantly bottlenecked fuel production, triggering widespread gasoline shortages across Russia.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak publicly acknowledged the output drop earlier this year, though he attributed the decline to unplanned refinery maintenance rather than battlefield impacts.
To mitigate domestic shortages, Moscow has been forced to implement an export ban on diesel while restricting overseas sales of gasoline and jet fuel. As a result, the government forecast seen by Reuters projects total refined fuel exports will plunge by 27.3 million tons this year to just 98.5 million tons.
Conversely, the inability to process fuel domestically has forced an increase in raw crude exports, primarily bound for buyers in China and India. The draft forecast indicates crude exports will temporarily swell to 244.7 million tons this year before facing a sharp decline in subsequent years.
Ukrainian drones had recently struck Russia’s Ust-Luga port on the Baltic Sea, sparking a fire at the major energy resource export hub. The Leningrad region facility is a critical terminus for Russian crude oil and petroleum products, including shipments loaded onto Moscow’s shadow fleet tankers.

Israel’s newest submarine INS Drakon heads home from Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:56:43 UTC
01:56:43 KST

Israel’s sixth submarine, INS Drakon, has begun its voyage from Germany to Israel and is expected to arrive within weeks, the IDF and Defense Ministry announced Tuesday.
A send-off ceremony was held this week at the TKMS shipyard in Kiel, marking the end of years of joint Israeli-German planning and construction and the start of the submarine’s journey home.
INS Drakon is the third and final submarine in the Dolphin-class AIP series purchased by the Defense Ministry for the Israeli Navy. According to the IDF, it incorporates advanced technologies designed to expand the Navy’s operational flexibility, range and endurance for years to come.
The Israeli flag was raised aboard the submarine at the ceremony, formally marking the start of its voyage to Israel.
Its departure was accompanied by a large-scale security operation led by the Defense Ministry’s Security Department together with German security forces. A state ceremony is planned at Haifa Naval Base once the submarine arrives.
Israeli Navy commander Vice Adm. Eyal Harel said the Drakon, together with three future Dakar-class submarines, would form a central part of the future of Israel’s submarine fleet.
“They will bring more advanced capabilities, greater operational range, longer endurance on missions and significant operational power,” Harel said.
He added that the submarine’s crews would operate “covertly, in the dark and in silence, far from home,” often in circumstances in which only those on board would know what was happening around them and would bear responsibility for critical decisions.
The send-off ceremony was also attended by Rear Adm. Amir Chimney, head of the Israeli Navy’s Technology, Logistics and Material Command; Zeev Landau, head of the Defense Ministry’s Procurement Directorate; Israeli Ambassador to Germany Ron Prosor; German Navy chief Vice Adm. Jan Christian Kaack; and representatives of the Navy, Defense Ministry and TKMS.
Landau described the submarine as “the most advanced and complex weapons system in the IDF” and said its delivery reflected the strategic partnership between Israel and Germany.
He said the two countries were now discussing additional joint projects that could expand cooperation into new areas of development and production.
Prosor said the submarine’s delivery demonstrated the depth of ties between Jerusalem and Berlin and their cooperation in confronting shared strategic challenges.
TKMS CEO Oliver Burkhard said the Drakon’s departure marked the successful completion of a complex program built on years of trust, technological expertise and shared responsibility.
“Israel is an important partner for us in the maritime arena,” Burkhard said, adding that cooperation would continue with the future Dakar-class submarines.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who participated in the 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) in Bishkek, Kyrgyz Republic, presented a range of traditional Indian handicrafts, textiles, tea, musical instruments and literary works to leaders and dignitaries from Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan.The gifts showcased India's diverse cultural heritage while highlighting the country's longstanding cultural and diplomatic ties with Central Asia.
Gifts for Uzbekistan's president
Modi gifted president of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev a marble inlay decorative plate, featuring floral and foliate motifs in blue, green and red set into polished white marble. The craft is particularly associated with Agra in Uttar Pradesh and reflects generations of Indian artisan skill.
The Prime Minister also presented Mirziyoyev with two boxes of premium Kangra tea, Kangra First Flush Black Tea and Kangra Green Tea, housed in a carved wooden box. The tea represents the heritage of Kangra Valley in Himachal Pradesh, where cultivation dates back to the 19th century.Another gift was a sandalwood Shata Tantri Veena, popularly known as the Santoor, a many-stringed instrument associated with Jammu and Kashmir.
Its resemblance to Uzbekistan's traditional Chang was highlighted as a link between the musical traditions of the two countries.
Modi also presented Mirziyoyev with the original handwritten scoresheet of Uzbek Grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov from the 2025 FIDE World Cup final in Goa. Sindarov defeated China's Wei Yi to become the youngest FIDE World Cup champion and qualify for the 2026 Candidates Tournament.
Gifts for Uzbekistan's prime minister
Uzbekistan Prime Minister Abdulla Aripov received a marble inlay decorative plate, showcasing India's traditional stone-inlay craftsmanship and intricate floral designs.
He was also gifted a marble inlay casket with a Banarasi silk stole. The white marble casket carries floral patterns created with coloured stones, while the blue Banarasi silk stole features a paisley zari design, bringing together craft traditions from Agra and Varanasi.
Gift for the President's spouse
PM Modi gifted Uzbekistan president’s spouse and first lady Ziroat Mirziyoyeva, a marble inlay casket paired with a Banarasi silk stole, blending Agra’s stone craftsmanship with Varanasi’s weaving heritage. The floral marble work and blue paisley zari design reflected India’s artistic traditions.
Gift for the President's daughter
Modi gifted the daughter of Uzbekistan's president a fine silver brooch featuring a floral bouquet in an ornamental basket. The piece incorporates openwork, latticework, leaves, blossoms, green cabochons and clear stones.
For the prime minister of Kyrgyzstan, Modi presented a Dokra artwork depicting a pair of traditional musicians. The handcrafted pieces use India's traditional lost-wax metal-casting technique.Meanwhile, Kyrgyzstan's president was gifted a Ladakhi Tsug-dul blanket, a traditional woollen textile from Ladakh featuring geometric, floral and stylised motifs.
A 10-volume English translation of the Mahabharata by Bibek Debroy was also presented to the president.Together, the gifts showcased India's regional crafts, artistic traditions, literature and cultural heritage while underscoring the longstanding cultural affinities between India and Central Asia.

Faith in fakes: How anti-Russian hysteria is driving the EU’s drone hoax
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:54:05 UTC
01:54:05 KST

Faith in fakes: How anti-Russian hysteria is driving the EU’s drone hoax
Is it a bird? Is it a plane? Is it a well-timed ploy to ramp up defense spending? The late-autumn drone sighting hysteria that swept across Norway, Denmark, the Netherlands and Belgium, was used by the bloc to amplify and entrench an anti-Russia stance that has seen it throw hundreds of billions it cannot afford into weapons and a war its chosen side cannot win.
Tens of millions of Euro has since been spent on the back of a 'scare' that has been shown to have been irrational, exuberant and driven by vested interests.
The most bizarre national security scare in recent European history began at Copenhagen’s Kastrup Airport on September 2 last year. According to Denmark’s Frihedsbrevet news site, an airport employee told her supervisors that she saw two drones approach the area “stealthily,” adding that “they are big. They are not toys.”
The airport was temporarily shut down, and within hours, reports of a similar drone incursion came in from Oslo, Norway.
“I can only say that this is in my eyes a serious attack on Danish critical infrastructure,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said at the time. “I cannot in any way deny that it is Russia.” Her Norwegian counterpart, Gahr Store, came to a similar conclusion. “Russia has violated Norwegian airspace on three occasions this spring and summer,” he claimed. “We cannot determine whether this was done intentionally or due to navigation errors. Regardless of the cause, this is not acceptable.”
“It is clear we are witnessing a pattern of persistent contestation at our borders,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said. “Our critical infrastructure is at risk. And Europe will respond to this threat with strength and determination.”
Open-source investigators insisted that the sightings were a hoax from the outset. Sleuths on the Metabunk forums concluded that the ‘drone’ seen at Kastrup Airport in the above footage was actually a small single-engine plane. FlightRadar24 data showed one such plane – a Socata TB-20 Trinidad – passing over the airport’s main runway twice at the time of the sighting.
Where were drones spotted?
Nevertheless, panic spread across northern Europe as drones were supposedly spotted at the following airports, military bases, and infrastructure sites in the following days and weeks:
- September 23: Aalborg Airport, Denmark
- September 24: Aalborg Airport, Billund Airport, Sonderborg, Esbjerg and Skrydstrup airports, Denmark
- September 25: Billund Airport, Denmark; Thyssenkrupp factory, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany; University Medical Center, Kiel, Germany; Bundeswehr base, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Germany
September 26: Karup Air Base, Skrydstrup Air Base, Jutland Dragoon Regiment base, Denmark
- September 27: Orland Main Air Station, Norway
- September 28: Bronnoysund Airport, Norway; Borris Camp, Denmark
- October 2: Munich Airport, Germany; Elsenborn-Butgenbach Air Base, Belgium
- October 3: Munich Airport, Germany
- October 31: Berlin-Brandenburg Airport, Germany
- November 2: Bremen Airport, Germany; Kleine Brogel Air Base, Belgium
- November 6: Gothenburg Airport, Sweden; Brussels Airport, Antwerp Port, Belgium
- November 9: Liege Airport, Doel Nuclear Power Plant, Belgium
- November 22: Volkel Air Base, Netherlands
- December 1: In the Irish Sea off Dublin, during Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s arrival by plane
Police across northern Europe received thousands of additional drone reports from civilians. In Denmark alone, nearly 6,000 reports of suspected drones were filed.
Did the drones even exist?
Not only is there no proof that Russia was connected with these sightings, there is no evidence that any drones were present at all. No wreckage has been recovered, no perpetrators have been identified, and no footage of the drones exists, except for the video from Copenhagen that apparently shows a light aircraft.
Despite being certain that Denmark was under “hybrid attack,” Mette Frederiksen acknowledged in late September that there could be an “alternate explanation” for the sightings. Six months later, six government sources told Denmark’s TV2 that they don’t “have any technical evidence to support that Denmark was subjected to a hybrid attack with drones.” Frihedsbrevet’s sources came to a similar conclusion, with the airport employee who reported the initial sighting admitting that she could have been mistaken.
Airport management still insist that drones were present in the area on September 22, but police have not acknowledged any drones, only “reports” of drones.
Danish troops reportedly opened fire on a drone over Borris Camp on September 28. According to an investigation by TV2, the only aircraft operating in the area at the time was a turboprop passenger plane. The Danish military, if TV2’s reporting is correct, nearly shot down a civilian aircraft over a false alarm.
After interviewing witnesses and reviewing surveillance footage, Norwegian police closed their investigation on November 6, stating that they were “unable to confirm or deny whether drones were actually observed on the night of September 23.”
German police have not been able to confirm any drone activity; Dutch officials have identified no threat, with internal documents stating that there was “no indication of sabotage or attacks on vital objects.” Dutch and Belgian authorities have found no credible basis for panic, with Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken issuing a half-apology last month for attempting to pass off a video of a police helicopter as evidence of nefarious aerial activity.
Did they just lie?
Out of every country involved, Denmark’s leaders were most insistent that Russia was behind the spate of sightings. Frederiksen, Defense Minister Troels Lund Poulsen, and Justice Minister Peter Hummelgaard all described the incidents as “attacks,” despite nothing being attacked and no attackers being present.
“I consider it a new reality that Denmark and Europe are under more violent and frequent hybrid attacks,” Frederiksen said in a televised address on September 25. “And even though the authorities cannot conclude who is behind the hybrid attacks…there is primarily one country that poses a threat to Europe's security – and that is Russia.”
The flood of tips and reports from the public can be written off either as mass hysteria, or – more charitably – as a natural reaction from Europeans primed by their politicians and media to believe that Russia is planning an all-out war on the continent. As for why Frederiksen would stoke this fear, however, some clues can be found in her actions.
At the time, Denmark was just over a year into an historic rearmament program. After a €5.4 billion military budget hike in 2024, Frederiksen announced last February that defense spending would be increased from 2.4% to 3% of GDP by 2030 (since increased to 3.5%). By late 2025, Denmark had purchased hundreds of armored combat vehicles, signed contracts for new air defense systems, increased annual conscription numbers, and, for the first time in its history, introduced compulsory military service for women.
Denmark, she said last February, needs to undergo a “massive rearmament,” because “We don’t know what [Russian President Vladimir Putin] is planning, but we know that he and Russia are in the process of rearming.”
Frederiksen referenced this rearmament again in her September address, declaring that “the events of recent days only emphasize how important it is.”
Denmark held the EU’s rotating presidency at the time, and Frederiksen added that the alleged drone threat would be made front and center when EU leaders met in Copenhagen the following week, and that she would push for “the establishment of an actual drone wall.”
The EU’s drone wall
Frederiksen kept her word. Published on October 16, the European Commission’s ‘Defense Readiness Roadmap’ stated that a ‘European Drone Defense Initiative’ – the so-called “drone wall” comprising sensors and interceptors – would be operational along the bloc’s eastern borders with Russia and Belarus by 2027.
🚨🇪🇺 “We need to act now”Ursula von der Leyen now wants to build a “Drone Wall” on the Eastern Flank of Europe to protect from the alleged Russian Aggression. pic.twitter.com/UAGH93fKRc
— Concerned Citizen (@BGatesIsaPyscho) October 1, 2025
Drones continued to dominate the agenda at a European Council summit in Brussels in December. “The European Council strongly condemns all recent hybrid attacks against the European Union and its Member States,” read a statement released after the meeting. “In the light of Russia’s and Belarus’ intensified hybrid campaign, it calls for accelerated efforts to strengthen resilience, protect critical infrastructure, and…decisively ramp up Europe’s defense readiness by 2030.”
None of this is to suggest that Denmark orchestrated the drone panic to justify its remilitarization, or to sell the EU’s “drone wall.” Both initiatives were already underway at the time. Instead, it illustrates how Danish and EU officials saw an opportunity not to let a crisis go to waste, and kept the drone threat alive even as their own police forces, to put it mildly, struggled to substantiate it.
Belgium's very own drone crisis
Frederiksen wasn’t the only national leader who saw an opportunity amid the panic. Remember Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken? After police hotlines were flooded with more than 550 reports of drones between September and December, Francken bypassed the standard bidding process to authorize the purchase of €50 million worth of drone detection and jamming systems.
An investigation by Belgium’s VRT broadcaster has since found that none of the reports of drones were credible, and Francken has been hammered by the opposition for sharing an image of a ‘drone’ over Brussels Airport that turned out to be a police helicopter. VRT found that the defense ministry ignored warnings from Belgium’s Inspectorate of Finance and purchased detection antennas at an inflated price, and Francken is now the subject of an inquiry by the Brussels Public Prosecutor's Office.
The debacle is reminiscent of the Agusta-Dassault affair. During the 1980s, defense contractors Agusta and Dassault paid the equivalent of €4 million in bribes to secure no-bid contracts for AW109 transport helicopters and electronic warfare equipment. Once exposed, the scandal led to the criminal conviction of Belgian Defense Minister Guy Coeme and Foreign Minister and NATO Secretary General Willy Claes.
So did Russian drones spook the EU?
Nearly eight months after the first ‘drones’ were spotted over Copenhagen, the crisis is still being milked across Europe. In early May, long after the threat had been debunked in Denmark, Norway, Belgium, and the Netherlands, the Dutch defense ministry announced that it would acquire approximately 900 “electro-optical aiming devices” for use against UAVs, “without prior announcement due to the urgency of a crisis situation.”
Questioned by the Belgian parliament in April, Francken insisted that there is “no other plausible explanation” for the reports other than Russian drones, and that the only way to prove or disprove this is to invest in drone defense technology. “As long as you don’t have the means to detect and neutralize drones, it stands to reason that you cannot immediately produce physical evidence,” he told lawmakers.
The Dutch and Belgians aren’t letting a lack of evidence stop them from pursuing the defense deals that they wanted from this crisis, and the EU is unlikely to step in and pump the brakes.
The EU's censorious and paranoid media industry is the perfect environment for fake news to fester, as long as it suits the bloc. Remember, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's claims of “GPS jamming” hitting her plane on a trip to Bulgaria last September, and how, despite it being roundly debunked within days, it has been allowed to fester to serve her political agenda.
Anti-Russian hysteria is the animating political force in the EU, and the bloc’s leaders clearly aren’t going to let police and media investigations, or common sense, put a stop to the show.

Swinney sticks with pledge to cap prices on basic foods in Scotland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:52:44 UTC
01:52:44 KST

John Swinney insisted on Tuesday he still planned to introduce a legally binding price cap on bread, milk and other essential food items in Scotland despite fierce opposition from farming and business groups.
Unveiling the Scottish National party’s programme for government – the equivalent to the king’s speech – the first minister said he wanted to give “families greater peace of mind at a time of rising prices”.
Swinney also announced commitments to restructure local government and NHS boards, introduce a misogyny bill to crack down on violence against women and girls, and set a £2 price limit on bus fares in the west of Scotland. He confirmed his government would pilot a minimum income for artists.
But the proposals to limit essential food and drink prices have faced intense criticism from industry groups, which have described the policy as “unnecessary” and a “potty gimmick”.
On Monday, 23 food, drink and farming organisations published an open letter arguing that markets were already working to deliver the best possible prices and a cap could increase the cost of household goods.
“Scots benefit from western Europe’s most affordable grocery and food supply market,” the letter read. “A statutory cap would not address the root causes of elevated food prices: rising production, refrigeration, and distribution costs. Supply chain shocks after Covid and conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have pushed up fertiliser, fuel and energy costs.”
The SNP committed to introducing price controls by the end of the year in a manifesto published before Holyrood elections in May, framing the scheme as a health measure. Similar initiatives have been implemented in Hungary and Croatia and the UK government encouraged supermarkets to consider voluntary price caps on foodstuffs in May.
The Scottish government did not specify which essentials would be covered by the law in a consultation paper published on Tuesday, although Swinney has said that between 20 and 50 products would be included, such as rice, cheese and eggs. Any limit would cover only retailers that make more than half of their annual turnover from groceries, have more than 250 employees and make more than £250m a year.
“It is our ambition, and intention, to put more money in families’ pockets, building on what is already the most generous cost of living support package anywhere in the UK,” Swinney told Holyrood on Tuesday. “Today we have also begun a formal consultation on the legislation that will introduce a legal price ceiling on a basket of essential food items, giving families greater peace of mind at a time of rising prices.”
There is uncertainty over whether any price cap on food and drink essentials would even be legal. The Scottish government is planning to introduce the policy under devolved health powers. But critics say it would clash with post-Brexit internal UK market rules to stop regulatory divergence between England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
Scotland is facing growing pressure on its finances. The Scottish government estimated last year that there would be a near-£5bn gap in its finances by the end of the decade, with experts warning that difficult choices await over how to fund healthcare, schools and other parts of the public sector.
In his five-year programme for government, Swinney announced a major change to the structure of NHS Scotland, reducing the number of health boards from 14 to two. He described the shake-up as “the most significant structural reform of our NHS in the devolution era”.

Germany blames Russia for attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
Berlin says it will shut down a Russian consulate and take other actions, citing ‘hybrid attacks’ by Moscow
The German government on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month using a drone laden with explosives, and announced that it would shut down a Russian consulate among other measures against Moscow.
The drone was found near a Ukrainian plane on the evening of August 4, and the device was defused. German officials said at the time that the incident posed a new level of danger.
Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption across Europe with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilising European nations.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said on Tuesday that authorities found elements such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonator that are “known to us from other Russian hybrid operations and its war against Ukraine”.
He said that the device pointed to “a high degree of technical expertise” and painstaking planning, but that the execution of the plan appears to have been left to “low-level” agents.
Dobrindt told reporters in Berlin that intelligence points to “people being involved who acted on behalf of Russian state entities”, though he did not specify which ones.

EU will never recognize occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:50:00 UTC
01:50:00 KST

EU will never recognize occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian
EU Ambassador to the United Nations Stavros Lambrinidis said this during a General Assembly debate on the situation in Ukraine’s temporarily occupied territories, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“Crimea, Donetsk, Kherson, Luhansk and Zaporizhzhia are Ukraine. The European Union will never recognize as lawful any attempt by Russia to annex Ukrainian territory. We do not recognize the forced Russification of people and their communities, nor the results of any illegal so-called elections organized by the Russian occupation administration in the temporarily occupied territory of Ukraine,” Lambrinidis said.
He said Russia’s occupation was aimed not only at controlling territory but also at destroying the daily lives, rights and identity of Ukrainians living under Russian rule. Despite being denied access, the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine have documented Russia’s actions in the occupied territories, he added.
“Russia’s goal is clear: it seeks to alter the demographic composition of the territories it occupies, including through the forced transfer and deportation of civilians, including children. This is illegal. It is shameless. And it is disgraceful,” Lambrinidis said.
He reaffirmed that the EU would continue providing political, financial, economic, military and diplomatic support to Ukraine as it exercises its inherent right to self-defense, while addressing humanitarian needs and supporting diplomatic efforts to end the war.
Russia must end its “illegal war of aggression and occupation” of Ukraine, accept an immediate, unconditional and comprehensive ceasefire, and engage in negotiations aimed at achieving a just and lasting peace in accordance with international law and the UN Charter, Lambrinidis said.
He also called on Russia and Belarus to end the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children, which the UN Commission of Inquiry has found to constitute war crimes. He urged an end to the illegal adoption of Ukrainian children and called for the immediate, safe and unconditional return of all children unlawfully deported or forcibly transferred from Ukraine.
Read also: Around 6,000 Ukrainian Civilians May Be in Temporarily Occupied Kherson Region – Lubinets
Lambrinidis further called for the release of political prisoners and civilians arbitrarily detained by Russia and for stronger international monitoring of human rights and humanitarian conditions in the occupied territories. He urged Russia to provide UN human rights mechanisms with immediate and unhindered access, including to places of detention.
Lambrinidis delivered the statement on behalf of the EU and its member states. North Macedonia, Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine, Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Liechtenstein, Andorra and Monaco also joined the statement.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, the UN General Assembly is debating the situation in Ukraine’s territories temporarily occupied by Russia. The issue has been on the Assembly’s agenda since 2019 and covers the political, security, humanitarian and human rights consequences of Russia’s occupation.

====================================================================================================

SCO challenges West as diverse group of nations pursues multipolar future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:49:51 UTC
01:49:51 KST

The summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, which represents almost half of the world’s population, ended with an aim to signal the rise of a global powerhouse challenging the West. Yet the SCO's diversity also revealed significant disagreements and divergent interests.
The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), a diverse group aiming to balance the West’s global influence, has called for a more representative and fairer multipolar world order as its summit in Kyrgyzstan ended on Tuesday with a run of headlines.
The 25th gathering of the 10 members — China, India, Iran, Pakistan, Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan — brought together regional leaders as “dialogue partners” from Central Asia, the Caspian region, the Middle East and wider Asia in a broad forum of meetings to address a rapidly changing multipolar world, even amid significant disagreements and often diverging interests.
The Iran war and Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine defined the summit’s focus, with disruptions in global supply lines and emerging alternatives through Central Asia and the Caspian, as well as the rapid geopolitical shockwaves and realignments they have generated.
In a surprise moment with global impact, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Russian President Vladimir Putin directly, on live television, to end his war against Ukraine.
"Every single day spent in war pushes humanity backwards, ” Modi said unexpectedly to a visibly tense Putin. “We need to move from endless war to the end of war, to the end of hostilities.”
“This is very important for all of humanity," Modi added.
"We have to move in that direction, which is also essential for the welfare of humanity. It is humanity’s call to resolve all issues peacefully as soon as possible," the Indian premier told the Russian president.
"This is India’s message — the message from the land of Gandhi, the land of Buddha: a message of peace, a message of humanity."
Putin did not reply to Modi, but in a speech later at the summit said that "today, 1 September, is the day World War II began."
"We must do everything to exclude from world practice any provocation of armed conflicts," Putin added. Russia’s war in Ukraine is now longer than World War II in duration.
In another snub for the Kremlin, a bilateral meeting between Putin and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping produced no progress on a Siberian natural gas pipeline that Moscow urgently needs as the country’s infrastructure and economy reel from continuous Ukrainian strikes on key energy targets across Russia.
The Russian president however received the public gratitude of his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian, who thanked Putin "for your positions at every stage.”
Putin said that Russia is providing Iran with assistance and “supplying the needed goods,” and that “Russia stands in solidarity with the people of Iran, who are defending their interests. He further said he "admires their courage and steadfastness” in their fight against the US and Israel.
"Today we are experiencing an erosion of the foundations upon which international order is built," Pezeshkian said.
"If such actions are met with no effective response from the international community, what state can be certain that its sovereignty and security will be protected in the future against the use of force?"
The Iranian delegation pushed for maximum results at the SCO summit, with Pezeshkian also meeting his Azerbaijani, Indian and Pakistani counterparts, while Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met his counterparts from China, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Russia.
China and Turkey laud multilateralism
China, which sees the SCO as an alternative to Western-aligned organisations like the G7, has recently shown it wants to expand the organisation's scope and influence, while Russia and Iran joined the summit to build relations with non-Western partners and seek support and recognition.
In his speech at the summit, China’s Xi said the SCO should “foster an environment of universal security,” while criticising “hegemony, unilateralism, and protectionism” which run “counter to the tide of history.”
Xi further urged the SCO leaders and partners to “shoulder the responsibility of the times,” as multipolarity is an “irreversible trend” and that “dominance by just one or several countries, or bloc politics are not true multilateralism.”
Turkey, which holds partner status within the SCO, also seeks to use the platform to strengthen its position in the region, viewing its partnership in the organisation as part of a balanced foreign policy that maintains its traditional ties with the West through NATO while strengthening its influence in Eurasia.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told the summit that the SCO is “a rising star in every field” and that with its “3.5 billion people and $35 trillion in gross domestic product (it) is an indispensable element of a multipolar order."
Calling the SCO a “complement to the UN,” Erdoğan said the organisation “has a structure that aligns with our multidimensional foreign policy centred on regional ownership,” adding that “as Türkiye, we are taking responsibility for resolving conflicts around us through dialogue and diplomacy.”
Erdoğan highlighted one of the new thrusts of the SCO summit participants: alternative transport and energy corridors, as the war with Iran disrupted traditional avenues.
"We believe that the organisation can play a role not only in ensuring peace and stability, but also in establishing uninterrupted and secure transportation corridors, which are vital for the prosperity of our peoples, and in areas such as energy supply security," the Turkish president said.
Billions in Central Asia and Caucasus projects
The leaders of Central Asia and the South Caucasus pushed relentlessly during the summit to maximise the economic opportunities for their regions as the Iran war and wider Middle East disruptions place them at the forefront of new global trade and connectivity solutions.
Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Premier Nikol Pashinyan held a new round of their peace talks in Bishkek, with Aliyev saying “the South Caucasus is becoming a zone of peace.”
Pashinyan said transport corridors and regional connectivity are now developing toward the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP).
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev told the summit that trade among SCO countries has reached $1 trillion and that much more remains to unlock the full potential of cooperation and resource use.
Uzbekistan's President Shavkat Mirziyoyev proposed establishing a bank for inter-regional projects, natural resource management, digital services and healthcare.
Mirziyoyev agreed with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to raise bilateral trade from $18 billion in 2025 to $30 billion in the coming years through a portfolio of joint investment projects and industrial cooperation.
"The existence of multiple centres of political influence is an important condition for advancing a political pluralism on the international stage," Tajikistan's President Emomali Rahmon said.
New security centre approved
Away from the diplomacy, the summit closed Kyrgyzstan's year as chair with a package of institutional decisions. Leaders signed the Bishkek Declaration and a protocol amending the SCO's Founding Charter, which Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev said would create the basis for a more flexible bloc.
On security, members approved the rules for a Universal Centre for Countering Security Challenges based in Tashkent and an anti-drug centre in Dushanbe.
A unit to fight transnational organised crime will open in Bishkek under that centre, the first permanent SCO body on Kyrgyz soil.
Members also agreed to complete consultations "in the shortest possible time" on a long-discussed SCO development bank, with a view to signing its founding document, although they concluded no deal in Bishkek.
Leaders adopted further documents on artificial intelligence, climate, energy and information security, a declaration on nuclear safety, and a decision to develop cooperation with the African Union.
Kyrgyzstan said it held around 200 events during its chairmanship, more than 50 of them in the country itself, and marked the anniversary by naming a 4,050-metre peak in the Ala-Archa range "SCO Peak".
Pakistan now takes the chairmanship and will host the next summit in Islamabad.

IRGC commander thought dead in Israeli strike reportedly plans Asian sabotage- report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:49:21 UTC
01:49:21 KST

Brig.-Gen. Rahman Moghaddam, the commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)'s special operations unit, Unit 4000, began planning operations in the Strait of Malacca and the Bangka Strait, two waterways essential to global trade, and ports in Indonesia and China, Iran International reported on Tuesday, citing several informed sources.
Moghaddam was previously believed to have been killed during Israeli strikes on March 4. The day after reports of his death were published by Israeli media, two drones were launched by Iran towards Azerbaijan. The strikes were reported by CNN to be in retaliation for Moghaddam's killing in an attack believed to have been carried out from Azerbaijani territory.
Informed sources have told Iran International that Moghaddam survived the attack and commands Unit 4000, heading a unit responsible for assassinations and sabotage operations against Iran's opponents outside its borders.
IRGC recruits operatives in East Asia
The IRGC began recruiting non-Iranian operatives long ago to facilitate maritime terrorism operations in East Asia, allowing it to deny responsibility if operations were exposed, according to Iran International.
Moghaddam sought to recruit non-Iranian Shi'ite operatives in Thailand through Seyed Momen Saketicha, a senior figure in the Thai Shi'ite community. Saketicha participated in negotiations with Hamas in Tehran two years ago over the release of 31 Thai hostages held in Gaza.
Iran attempted to pressure Thailand into removing 40,000 Thai workers from Israel in exchange for the hostages' release.
In addition to attempting to recruit Thai operatives, Unit 4000 focused its attention on Indonesia, with Moghaddam using two Indonesian clerics to help recruitment, according to Iran International's report.
Three Unit 4000 recruits from Indonesia have been allegedly hired to carry out maritime sabotage operations in East Asia.
Iran threatens to expand war into Indian Ocean, Mediterranean Sea
Two months ago, Mohsen Rezaei, adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told CNN that if the war and US naval blockade were not lifted, Iran would expand the war into the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea.
IRGC Quds Force commander Brig.-Gen. Esmail Qaani said in a televised interview that the IRGC had additional maritime targets beyond the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb.
The Strait of Malacca has been repeatedly raised in discussions of the oil trade in recent months. As the shortest maritime route between Middle Eastern energy exporters and East Asian markets, roughly 29% of global seaborne oil trade passed through the strait during the first half of 2025.
Disruptions in Hormuz and Malacca would put pressure on two major energy supply routes from the Middle East to Asia.
While the Bangka Strait, located between Sumatra and Indonesia's Bangka Island, does not have the same global importance as Malacca, it forms part of the region's shipping network. An interruption there could intensify pressure caused by any potential disruption in Malacca.
Iran's target list also includes Tanjung Priok Port in Indonesia and the Ningbo Zhoushan and Shanghai ports in China, according to Iran International.
Hezbollah member Pando Yudahvinata, who was expelled from an Indonesian university before traveling to Tehran and being recruited by security organizations, is one of the three operatives the IRGC has hired, Iran International wrote. Yudahvinata was responsible for a failed suicide attack against the Israeli Embassy in Bangkok 32 years ago. His name has also been linked to a series of bombings in Sri Lanka.
He and two other Indonesian citizens, Ardianta Mutoha and Mohammad Hossein, traveled to Tehran for training to prepare for covert operations at ports and waterways in East Asia, according to the report.
