Third consecutive cut: Bank of Israel lowers interest rates to 3.25%, following economic review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:49:19 UTC
01:49:19 KST

The Bank of Israel (BoI)'s Monetary Committee cut the interest rate by 0.25% to 3.25% on Tuesday.
This comes amid a backdrop of a relatively moderate inflation rate and rapidly growing gross domestic product (GDP) in recent months and constitutes the third consecutive interest rate reduction in the past 12 months.
While uncertainty in the economy remains high, Israel’s risk premium continued to remain at levels similar to those prevailing before the October 7 massacre, and the shekel’s exchange rate with key global currencies remained without significant change.
The committee’s policy focuses on price stability, support for economic activity, and market stability, BoI said.
“The interest rate path will be determined according to developments in inflation, economic activity, geopolitical uncertainty, and fiscal developments,” BoI noted.
Israel’s Consumer Price Index remained unchanged in June and rose by 0.3% in July. Inflation over the past 12 months stood at 1.5% in July, below the midpoint of BoI’s target. According to forecasters’ assessments and one-year-ahead expectations from most sources, inflation is expected to remain near the midpoint of BoI’s target range in the coming months.
Shekel relatively stable in global monetary trade
Since the last decision to cut Israel’s interest rate in July, the shekel appreciated by 0.6% against the US dollar, depreciated by 1% against the euro, and depreciated by 0.1% in effective nominal terms.
BoI’s Monetary Committee estimated that the inflation environment will continue to be affected by geopolitical developments and energy prices, the risk premium and exchange rate, demand developments and supply constraints, alongside fiscal developments.
Israel’s Central Bureau of Statistics’ national accounts data for the second quarter of 2026 indicate a growth of 15.4% in annual terms compared with the first quarter of the year, and an increase of 6.2% as compared with the fourth quarter of 2025.
This, together with revisions to previous CBS data, narrowed the gap from the long-term growth trend to approximately 0.8%.
Israel's economy sees ramifications of war with Iran after Operation Roaring Lion
Growth in the second quarter of 2026 was affected by rapid growth in all GDP components and partly reflects recovery from the damage in the first quarter against the onset of Operation Roaring Lion, which began when Israel carried out intense airstrikes on Tehran on February 28.
However, excluding the activity of Israeli companies abroad, GDP in the second quarter was 3.8% higher than in the fourth quarter of 2025.
The labor market in Israel continues to be tight, according to BoI data, with a slight increase in participation rates and broad unemployment.
In July, employment rates for Israelis aged 25-64 stood at 78.9%, and the participation rate stood at 81.3%. The rate of those temporarily absent due to reserve military service remained stable at 0.5%. The broad unemployment rate among the 25-64 age group stood at 3.2%, similar to before the operation began, and the job vacancy rate rose slightly to 4.5%.
Additionally, the rate of nominal wage increases in the second quarter stood at 6.2% compared with the previous year, largely influenced by increases in minimum wage and in the public sector, while wages in the private sector, excluding hi-tech businesses, rose by 5.4% from March to May.
However, geopolitical tensions, including war with Iran, led to a surge in energy prices and disruptions in supply chains. The price of a barrel of Brent oil rose by about 25% to $90, and European gas prices reached their peak since the outbreak of Operation Roaring Lion.
Within Israel’s housing market, the availability of apartments for sale remained stable, data showed.
BoI said that a summary of the monetary discussions held by the committee will be published on September 15, and the next interest rate decision will be published on October 21, less than a week before the slated Knesset elections on October 27.

"Write down what I am telling you: the prime minister will receive a pardon as long as there is no judicial reform, as long as there is not even the slightest change to the Supreme Court justices and their powers. And that is the painful truth."
Following the broadcast of the recordings by N12, Gotliv published a post on X/Twitter directly responding to the remarks.
She wrote that her “tremendous dedication” to the prime minister and the right-wing government had always been immense, and that she had even “thrown herself on the grenade” for them.

The German government said on Tuesday it assessed that Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport this month and ordered a series of measures in response, including the closure of a Russian cultural center in Berlin.
"We assume that Germany is the target of further hybrid attacks by Russia," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said in a statement to the media.
"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the offenses and intelligence findings establish Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," he said.
Standing alongside Dobrindt, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany did not view Leipzig as an isolated incident.
"It fits into a broader pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe," he said.
Wadephul said Germany's response would include closing Russia's consulate general in Bonn and terminating its agreement with the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
"Germany remains secure, and Germany will defend itself against adversaries who seek to create insecurity," Wadephul said. "We will not allow Russia's attacks to divide or intimidate us in our social cohesion."
Responding to Germany's announcement, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Moscow would respond to what she called Berlin's "anti-Russian action," according to Interfax news agency. She did not elaborate.
The Russian Embassy in Berlin had previously dismissed such accusations as "fabricated provocation" and as "a new wave of anti-Russian hysteria in Germany."
EU countries express solidarity with Germany
Germany and Europe more widely face a serious threat from such "hybrid" actions, the interior minister said. "These actions target critical infrastructure, defense companies and support for Ukraine."
Germany will also push within the European Union for additional sanctions listings and travel restrictions on Russian nationals, while increasing pressure on Russia's "shadow fleet," Wadephul said.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she would discuss the attack on Wednesday with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, and EU foreign ministers would prepare a joint response.
"Looking forward to discussing collective countermeasures at the Gymnich meeting in Ireland tonight and tomorrow," Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said on X/Twitter. "Full solidarity with Germany."
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement that Britain stood with Germany and that any Russian attempts to undermine support for Ukraine were "doomed to fail."
Wadephul said Germany would "continue its civilian and military support for Ukraine and will resolutely continue its solidarity with Ukraine in its defense against Russia's war of aggression."

California Legislature passes SB 1387, advancing recognition of Jewish identity as ethnicity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:49:09 UTC
01:49:09 KST

The California Legislature gave final approval to Senate Bill 1387, placing the state on the verge of becoming the first in the nation to formally recognize Jewish identity as an ethnicity alongside its religious classification in state law on Monday.
During the final hours of the legislative session, the Assembly overwhelmingly passed the measure with a 62-0 vote, followed shortly by the Senate concurring on a 38-0 vote. The bill now heads to Governor Gavin Newsom’s desk, where it awaits a signature or veto ahead of the September 30 deadline.
Authored by Sen. Henry Stern (D-Sherman Oaks) and sponsored by the advocacy group Jewish California, SB 1387 requires state agencies collecting demographic data on ancestry or ethnic origin to include a separate category for Jewish identity.
Proponents emphasize that the shift will ensure Jewish Californians are accurately represented in state datasets tracking hate crimes, public health metrics, and educational outcomes.
Advocates point to data from the Pew Research Center’s 2020 study of American Jews, which revealed that 52% of respondents view ancestry as essential to their Jewish identity and 55% point to culture, while only 36% define it purely through religion.
California's data collection historically hasn't reflected its multifaceted identity
Despite this multifaceted identity, California’s institutional data collection systems have historically lacked a mechanism to reflect it.
“SB 1387 makes sure that we are seen and included when the state counts ethnic communities, a national first,” said David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California. “Good data makes good policy, and this bill means hate crime reports, health surveys, and education data will finally reflect who we actually are.”
Bocarsly also credited Stern’s leadership, the backing of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, and the coalition of 59 Jewish organizations that championed the legislation.
Under the bill’s provisions, participation will be entirely voluntary for individuals, and the new demographic option will be added without altering or removing existing religious data categories.
Data to remain strictly aggregate to address privacy concerns
To address privacy concerns, the legislation mandates that all published data remain strictly aggregate and explicitly prohibits using the collected information to establish individual registries or for law enforcement and immigration enforcement purposes.
The statutory requirements are scheduled to take effect in January, 2029, with the first formal reports slated for publication beginning January, 2030.
The landmark legislation underscores California’s role in setting potential precedents for state-level demographic accounting.
With SB 1387’s passage, all six bills sponsored by Jewish California during this legislative cycle now sit awaiting final action from Newsom, alongside measures establishing 100-foot safe zones around houses of worship, enhancing K-12 protections against antisemitism, reforming voter guides to exclude hate speech, combating campus disruptions, and securing care for Holocaust survivors.

What do the Altalena and the Heritage Ministry have to do with the approaching elections? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:49:05 UTC
01:49:05 KST

On the night between Sunday and Monday last week, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Heritage Minister Amichai Eliahu (both from Otzma Yehudit) announced that the remains of the Altalena – an Irgun ship which had brought weapons and immigrants from France to Israel, and on June 22, 1948, had been shelled by the IDF off the shore of Tel Aviv – had been found complete at a depth of 503 meters, 27 kilometers from the shore.
In July 1949, the Israeli Navy had towed what remained of the damaged ship 24 km. off the coast of Jaffa.
The Altalena was originally a 4,500-ton American World War II tank landing craft, converted by the Irgun to carry around 930 immigrants (most of them holocaust survivors) and Irgun personnel, and 4,500 tons of armaments, originally meant for Irgun fighters, and after the establishment of the state on May 15, 1948, to be shared with the newly founded IDF.
The Altalena departed from Marseilles in France on June 11 – 10 days after Irgun leader Menachem Begin signed an agreement with one of prime minister David Ben-Gurion’s assistants, Yisrael Galili, to disband the Irgun and integrate its fighters into the newly founded IDF.
At the time, Begin claimed that he had tried to put off the departure of the Altalena from France, but was ignored by the Irgun people there, and that after it had been sunk (at Ben-Gurion’s order), had done everything in his power to prevent civil war from breaking out, especially after it became known that 16 Irgun members and three IDF soldiers had been killed during the event.
The Altalena reached the shore of Kfar Vitkin, north of Tel Aviv, on the evening of June 20. The immigrants were all taken off the ship, and local members of Irgun managed to unload around 40% of the arms on board.
But then, due to disagreements with the IDF that deteriorated into mutual shooting, the ship departed for Tel Aviv on June 21 – with Begin on board.
On June 22, after the disagreements were not resolved, Ben-Gurion ordered the shelling of the ship. When the ship began to burn, and after everyone else was evacuated, Begin agreed to jump into the water.
From Ben-Gurion’s point of view, the whole affair happened because now that the State of Israel had been officially declared, there was to be only one sovereign power in it, which was to hold a complete monopoly over the holding and use of arms. There were to be no militias in Israel.
This assertion had practical ramifications for both the Irgun and the Palmah (the separately run, elite combined strike forces established several years earlier within the Hagana), both of which were finally obliged to give up their arms and separate command systems, and integrate fully into the IDF.
Ben-Gurion and Begin's relationship
In addition, Ben-Gurion did not trust Begin, and feared that he might instigate a revolt against his newly formed government. The order to shell the Altalena came after all other efforts to get the Irgun to surrender failed.
Begin believed that Ben-Gurion’s goal was to kill him, and that this was the main reason he had decided to shell the Altalena with him on board.
Though Begin accepted the sovereignty of Ben-Gurion’s government, he was divided with him over most policy issues, and suspected that the members of the Irgun and Lehi would continue to be discriminated against in the Mapai-governed state (as they were, to a certain extent).
And what does all this have to do with the approaching elections?
Though it is unclear what exactly is meant by “heritage” in the name of the Heritage Ministry, established as a separate ministry after the 2022 elections – whether it has to do with the heritage of the State of Israel as a whole, including its Arab citizens, only with the heritage of its Jewish population, or only with the heritage of specific sections of the Jewish population – Ben-Gvir and Eliyahu had no qualms about getting the Heritage Ministry to deal with this particular issue.
Most likely, Ben-Gvir did not have the elections in mind when he instructed Eliyahu to start searching for the exact location of the Altalena about a year after Israel’s 37th government was formed.
However, he did believe that the whole affair was part of the heritage of the Israeli Right, and that pulling the Altalena out of the sea and putting it on display on land would help give this feeling a concrete dimension, while pointing a scolding finger at the Left.
This issue has already been picked up by right-wing circles and Channel 14, and hurled in the direction of the “just not Bibi” camp, in connection with the approaching elections.
Furthermore, Ben-Gvir and Eliyahu had no qualms about embracing an issue with which the Likud is more directly connected historically than the Kahanist Otzma Yehudit.
Their decision to announce the finding of the Altalena by means of the Otzma Yehudit spokesperson around two months before the elections, and later on to hold a press conference at the Irgun Museum in Tel-Aviv, without involving Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in advance, was undoubtedly connected to the growing tensions between Ben-Gvir and Netanyahu.
These tensions are primarily over the latter’s statements that his goal is to form a “wide Zionist government” after the elections, and his efforts to get Otzma Yehudit to run again together with Religious Zionism’s leader, Bezalel Smotrich, in the coming elections.
Netanyahu managed to delay Otzma Yehudit’s press conference by half an hour by giving a separate photographed statement on the finding of the Altalena outside the hall where the press conference was to be held. His statement was directed at the voters, from a different perspective than that of Ben-Gvir and Eliyahu.
He stated that, “I undertake to extract [the Altalena] from the bottom of the sea so that it will serve as a concrete symbol for our generation and also for future generations: a concrete symbol to one simple command – never to a fraternal war!”
Netanyahu was obviously alluding to Begin’s efforts back in June 1948 to prevent his followers from instigating a civil war in reaction to the sinking of the Altalena.
However, it is doubtful whether the Altalena will ever be lifted from the bottom of the sea; first of all, because such a project cannot be performed by Israel on its own, and will cost tens or even hundreds of millions of shekels.
The Heritage Ministry required the services of a special Italian vessel equipped with specialized sensors and advanced survey systems for a single day, at the cost of one million shekels, just to find the Altalena. Furthermore, marine experts believe that the Altalena is likely to fall apart if moved due to corrosion.
Given the many real and urgent issues in almost all spheres of Israel’s existence and its citizens’ lives that ought to be dealt with in the election campaign, the Altalena affair is little more than a red herring within this context.
The writer has written journalistic and academic articles, as well as several books, on international relations, Zionism, Israeli politics, and parliamentarism. From 1994 to 2010, she worked at the Knesset Library and the Knesset Research and Information Center.

Abdel Raouf Arnaout, Sahin Demir, and Lina Altawell
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
- Israeli restrictions are ‘form of pressure’ to stop schools relying on teachers from West Bank, Richard Zananiri tells Anadolu
A Christian school official in occupied East Jerusalem said Tuesday that a strike by Palestinian private schools, including Christian schools, will continue as around 40% of teachers and staff remain without Israeli permits to enter the city.
Richard Zananiri, director-general of Al-Mutran School in East Jerusalem, told Anadolu that Israeli authorities issued some permits late Monday night, but not all of them.
He said private schools had taken a unified position to continue the strike until all teachers and staff receive permits, stressing that schools could not operate normally while part of their staff remained unable to reach their workplaces.
Zananiri described Israel’s failure to issue entry permits to teachers as a “purely political measure” aimed at separating the occupied West Bank from East Jerusalem.
“Students, parents and teachers had been waiting for the start of the new school year, including the return of school movement, the ringing of the bell and the morning lineup, but the lack of permits prevented that,” Zananiri said.
He said the permit issue is not new, noting that the same problem happened last December and caused schools to declare a strike.
“Teachers coming from the occupied West Bank need permits to cross Israeli checkpoints and enter Jerusalem,” he added, describing the restrictions as “a form of pressure on us to stop relying on teachers from the West Bank.”
“Those teachers are part of Jerusalem’s education system, especially amid shortages in some specializations, with around 25% to 30% of teachers at Al-Mutran School coming from the occupied West Bank,” he added.
He noted that Jerusalem schools as a whole have around 120,000 students.
Earlier Tuesday, private schools in occupied East Jerusalem, including Christian schools, began a strike as the new academic year started, protesting Israeli restrictions on teachers and staff living in the West Bank.
Israel requires Palestinians in the occupied West Bank to obtain special permits to enter occupied East Jerusalem, including for work, education, medical treatment and worship.
Jerusalem’s schools fall into three main categories: private schools, most of which are Christian; schools run by the Islamic Waqf Department; and schools affiliated with the Israeli municipality and Education Ministry.
In January 2026, the Knesset passed a law banning the employment of teachers who obtained their academic degrees from institutions affiliated with the Palestinian Authority in the Israeli education system.
According to a previous report by Haaretz, the law directly affects the availability of teachers in occupied East Jerusalem, where around 6,700 teachers work in the Arab education system, at least 60% of whom hold bachelor’s degrees from Palestinian academic institutions.

It ‘hurts,’ Messi says, as he ends international career
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01

Lionel Messi on Monday said he was retiring from international soccer after leading Argentina to a second successive FIFA World Cup final in July.
The 39-year-old forward who won the World Cup in 2022 and dragged his nation to the final in the US only to lose to Spain, said the decision had been painful.
“It was a decision that hurt and still hurts deep in my soul but I understand that it is the right time,” Messi wrote on Instagram.
Photo: Reuters
“I swear I always gave everything, not just in the last few years when we won everything but before that too, and I always fought and gave my all for this shirt,” he added.
Messi led Argentina to World Cup glory four years ago by winning the final against France in a penalty shoot-out in Doha, but his side lost 1-0 to a superior Spain side in the final in East Rutherford, New Jersey.
Following the death of his father, Jorge Messi, last month, Lionel Messi had said he had “serious doubts” about continuing to play soccer of any sort for “much longer.”
“I don’t know what I’ll do without you, I don’t know how to go on. I just played football, and now I have serious doubts about continuing to do so for much longer,” he said then.
Lionel Messi’s contract with Major League Soccer club Inter Miami runs until the end of the 2028 season.
In this year’s finals, Lionel Messi inspired Argentina to another final by scoring eight goals and provided two assists in the dramatic late comeback against England in the semi-finals.
However, the dream of lifting the trophy again proved one match too far as the South Americans lost to Spain in the MetLife Stadium.
Lionel Messi was pictured in tears after receiving his loser’s medal.
He said afterward that the pain of defeat was “immense” and that it would “take a long time for this wound to heal.”
In his statement on Monday, the eight-time Ballon d’Or winner said it was time for a new generation of Argentina players to take up the torch.
“I love, I loved and I will always love being on the national team,” he wrote. “I gave everything I had, I have nothing more to give, and besides, there are some very talented young players coming up behind me who deserve to be there.”
Argentine President Javier Milei simply posted on social media: “Thank you very much, incredible man.”
First called up in 2005 by Jose Nestor Pekerman as an 18-year-old, Lionel Messi would go on to play 207 times for Argentina and become the country’s leading scorer, with 125 goals.
He also won two Copa Americas in 2021 and 2024 during his 21-year international career.
Yet, prior to the trophy-laden later years, Lionel Messi did not hold the place in Argentine hearts reserved for other national idols such as Diego Maradona or Pope Francis.
After moving to Catalonia at 13 to join Barcelona, Lionel Messi could have represented Spain, but chose Argentina.
His long-time teammate Angel Di Maria, also a 2022 world champion, on Monday paid homage to Lionel Messi for this choice and his impact on the national team.
“We will be forever grateful to you for being Argentinian and for having taken Argentina to the top of the world,” Di Maria said.

GlobalWafers acclaims new tech

GlobalWafers Co (環球晶圓), the world’s third-largest silicon wafer supplier, said yesterday that advanced packaging wafers are expected to make a substantial revenue contribution this year following limited contribution last year, driven by their production ramp-up.
The company started delivering samples of 310x310mm square silicon wafers to customers for verification earlier this year, with the products designed for panel-level packaging applications and expected to enter volume production this year. GlobalWafers also produced a prototype of a larger 510x510mm wafer, it said.
“Silicon wafers, or wafers made on other materials, are playing an increasingly important role in semiconductor [production] as technology evolves generation by generation,” GlobalWafers chairwoman Doris Hsu (徐秀蘭) said.
Photo: CNA
“Wafers not only serve as the substrate for building dies and micro devices... They could also play a role in advanced packaging,” Hsu said.
A part of GlobalWafers’ revenue this year would come from advanced packaging wafers, she said.
In addition to square silicon wafers, silicon carbide wafers and transparent silicon carbide wafers are options for advanced packaging applications, Hsu said.
“The overall sentiment is exceptionally positive,” Hsu said.
The company has created a comprehensive range of wafers tailored for 3D packaging applications, including specialized silicon on insulator (SOI) wafers for silicon photonics, as well as wafers for devices, interposers and carriers. GlobalWafers supplies 12-inch SOI wafers to make high-end optical waveguides for silicon photonics, it said.
Hsu is optimistic about the global semiconductor wafer industry, saying the industry should grow at a double-digit percentage each year over the next two years as chipmakers expand capacity amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
“It is not just the beginning of another new cycle. AI is driving a structural shift in silicon and other semiconductor segments, leading to a stronger demand for semiconductors beyond silicon,” she said.
The growth also stems from wafer price hikes, she said.
GlobalWafers has concluded price negotiations with some customers and signed long-term supply agreements, and the trend is moving toward a “positive” direction, she added.
GlobalWafers said utilization rates are high across its production lines, reflecting strong order momentum. Customers are willing to secure capacity years in advance, the company said.
GlobalWafers in July secured a 10-year supply agreement with Micron Technology Inc, along with US$500 million in strategic funding from the US memory maker.

EDITORIAL: Taiwan grows its future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:47:01 UTC
01:47:01 KST

Taiwan is betting heavily on artificial intelligence (AI) as a pillar of its competitiveness. President William Lai’s (賴清德) administration plans to spend more than NT$40 billion (US$1.26 billion) next year on 10 major AI projects and train at least 500,000 AI professionals by 2040.
The ambition goes beyond expanding AI applications across industries. The government wants to boost Taiwan’s technological sovereignty and resilience by developing capabilities including sovereign AI and low Earth orbit satellite communications.
Lai spoke about the kind of adaptability Taiwan needs on Monday as he met with the VIS Mars robotics team. After Turkish customs detained the team’s equipment on their way to a tournament in Istanbul, the students borrowed tools to build a replacement robot from discarded parts, with which they won four matches.
Fostering talent in emerging technologies could do far more for Taiwan than simply make it more competitive. It could help diversify an economy heavily dependent on semiconductors while giving Taiwan greater control over technologies that would shape its economy and national security.
The AI industry is entering a period of rapid expansion as businesses and governments pour money into data centers, AI models and computing infrastructure. Gartner projects that revenue from AI-processing semiconductors would grow at a 26.8 percent compound annual rate through 2030, driven by demand for AI accelerators. The expansion is moving beyond AI training into inference, agentic AI and AI-enabled devices, all of which require substantial computing power.
Taiwan is well positioned to benefit. It accounts for more than 60 percent of global foundry revenue and more than 90 percent of leading-edge chip manufacturing, making it indispensable to the semiconductor supply chain. Its electronics industry is a major producer of AI servers and related equipment. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co in July said that demand related to AI remained “extremely robust” and projected its revenue for this year to grow by about 40 percent in US dollar terms.
However, manufacturing the hardware that powers AI should be only the beginning. Taiwan should cultivate the software engineers, researchers and entrepreneurs capable of developing the platforms and applications that run on that hardware. Building those capabilities domestically would allow Taiwan to capture more of the value generated by the AI boom while creating a more complete and resilient technology ecosystem.
There is a significant national security dividend. A strong domestic AI industry would reduce Taiwan’s reliance on foreign technology in areas that could become critical during a crisis. Domestically developed AI could help the military analyze intelligence, identify threats, improve surveillance and accelerate battlefield decisionmaking. It could assist researchers and defense companies in developing more effective weapons systems and strategies.
That matters because a conflict with China would place extraordinary demands on Taiwan’s ability to process information quickly and operate independently. AI cannot replace human judgement, but the ability to rapidly analyze enormous quantities of data and identify patterns could give Taiwan valuable time to respond to threats. Building that capability at home would make it less vulnerable to disruption or restrictions due to foreign technology.
Taiwan has long dreamed of creating its own Silicon Valley. The rise of AI makes that goal more plausible than it has been in decades. Taiwan already possesses many of the ingredients: world-class semiconductor manufacturing, a sophisticated electronics industry, strong universities and an increasingly ambitious technology sector. The missing piece is a deeper ecosystem connecting hardware with software, research, start-ups and investment.
If Taiwan can grow that ecosystem, it could attract some of the world’s best AI students, researchers and engineers, while giving talented Taiwanese more reason to remain at home rather than taking their expertise abroad. More talent would generate more innovation, which would attract more investment and create more opportunities for talent — a cycle that could transform Taiwan from a place that makes the chips powering the AI revolution into a place that helps create the revolution itself.
Taiwan has already demonstrated that it can become indispensable to the world’s technology industry. The next challenge is to ensure that its greatest technological strength is not simply making the machinery of the future, but developing the people and ideas that would determine how that machinery is used.
If Taiwan succeeds, its AI strategy could become much more than an economic diversification project: it could improve the nation’s technological independence, deepen its global importance and give it another tool with which to defend its future.

Questions still left unanswered over ‘Taiwan Pavilion’ name change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:47:00 UTC
01:47:00 KST

The name “Taiwan” is to appear at South Korea’s Gwangju Biennale when it opens on Saturday, after months of objections from Taiwanese artists and government agencies over an attempted name change.
China Pavilion personnel halted installation and left the venue on Friday, after China’s Ambassador to South Korea Dai Bing (戴兵) objected to the restoration of the “Taiwan Pavilion” name. As of Monday, the Chinese side was reportedly preparing to withdraw, although its formal withdrawal had not been completed.
The pavilion dispute began on June 10, when the ministry and participating artists said organizers had changed “Taiwan Pavilion” to “NTMoFA Pavilion,” referring to the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Culture
The government demanded that the original name be restored. The disagreement attracted wider attention in Taiwanese and South Korean media after it became public on Aug. 15.
Taiwanese artist Su Hui-yu (蘇匯宇), who is participating in the biennale, told the Taipei Times he believed Chinese pressure was behind the change.
“Everyone knows,” Su said, adding that he had never encountered such an extreme case in an art setting.
Photo: CNA
The Gwangju Biennale Foundation did not clearly explain why “Taiwan” was dropped. It said in its press release on Aug. 19 that NTMoFA had joined as an institutional participant and was therefore identified by its institutional name, rejecting allegations of “political censorship.”
The Ministry of Culture disputed this, saying it applied as the “Taiwan Pavilion” in January but the foundation suddenly proposed NTMoFA in June. Asked by a local broadcaster, Gwangju MBC, whether considerations involving China influenced the decision, the foundation said it “could not answer.”
Gwangju Biennale CEO Yoon Beom-mo told another local broadcaster, KBC, that “working-level staff” changed the name, adding that the foundation later had to consider “international and diplomatic issues” after Taiwan protested.
Photo: Euronews
After continued objections, an official at the foundation told the Taipei Times on Aug. 26 that the foundation had agreed to use “Taiwan” at the venue.
Gwangju Mayor Min Hyung-bae, who also chairs the foundation, criticized its handling of the dispute during the livestreamed city government meeting — seen by the Taipei Times — on Aug. 26, asking: “Why should politics intervene in art?”
He called the controversy “very shameful for Gwangju.”
Dai met Min the following day and expressed regret over the decision, South Korean media reported.
CHINA’S INTERVENTION
First held in 1995 and held every two years, the Gwangju Biennale this year features 27 pavilions representing 16 countries and 11 institutions. Taiwan used the name “Taiwan” at previous editions with no comparable dispute reported.
Questions remain over why the foundation resisted the name for months. Min’s criticism indicates that the decision did not originate with the foundation’s chairman.
The Seoul Shinmun reported that the foundation’s staffing problems and disrupted continuity might also have contributed, with mostly short-term employees and “only two contract workers handling 27 countries and institutions.”
Hankook Ilbo also reported suspicions that organizers resisted Taiwan’s objections because of Chinese pressure, while Taiwan’s venue — the National Asian Culture Center — also faced criticism for delaying installation.
PRESSURE ON INTERNATIONAL STAGE
The issue extends beyond Taiwan-South Korea relations. Beijing has long pressured international companies and cultural institutions over how they refer to Taiwan.
Gwangju is also closely associated with South Korea’s democracy movement and progressive politics, which made an apparent restriction on Taiwan’s name particularly jarring to Taiwanese artists and their supporters.
And with the Nov. 28 local elections three months away, another international dispute over Taiwan’s name could again become a domestic political issue.
Ahead of Taiwan’s 2018 local elections, the Dominican Republic, Burkina Faso and El Salvador severed diplomatic ties, reducing its allies from 20 to 17 within four months and fueling criticism of the Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) administration amid the “Han wave” led by Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜).
Attention now turns to whether China completes its withdrawal and the “Taiwan Pavilion” name remains throughout the biennale, which runs through Nov. 15.
The city government on Sunday apologized for its inadequate handling of the dispute. It said the pavilion name was a matter of artistic expression and did not represent recognition of Taiwan as a state, while affirming that its respect for South Korea’s “one China” policy remained unchanged. Broadcaster KBS reported that Min had visited the Chinese Embassy shortly before the apology.
As of Monday, the foundation confirmed to the Taipei Times that “Taiwan Pavilion” would remain in use, while the Chinese side was still withdrawing from the biennale.

Manufacturing growth hit 5-year high in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:59 UTC
01:46:59 KST

Growth in Taiwan’s manufacturing sector hit its fastest pace in five years last month, driven by the biggest rise in new orders and production since August 2021 as well as continued growth in employment, the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research (CIER, 中華經濟研究院) said yesterday.
However, supplier delivery time increased and inventory expansion slowed due to supply bottlenecks and rising cost pressures, the institute said.
CIER’s seasonally adjusted manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI) rose to 62.5 from 61.5 in July, the 11th consecutive month of expansion and the fastest expansion since August 2021, while the future outlook subindex increased 0.7 percentage points to 65.2, the eighth consecutive month of expansion, the institute said in a report.
Photo: EPA
The PMI results, based on a monthly survey of companies in six major industries, are measured on a scale of 0 to 100, with readings above 50 indicating growth in factory activity and below 50 indicating decline.
Last month, manufacturing activity expanded in all six major industries, with the electronics and optical devices industry registering the largest expansion, followed by the electricity and machinery equipment industry, the chemicals and biotechnology industry, the basic raw materials industry, the food and textiles industry and the transportation equipment industry, the report said.
For the next six months, only firms in the transportation equipment industry gave a conservative outlook, while companies in the other major industries all expressed optimism amid continued strong demand for artificial intelligence (AI) servers, data centers, high-end computer chips, advanced semiconductor specialty chemicals and high-speed optical communications, as well as rising investment in liquefied natural gas-related infrastructure, it said.
Services activity remained elevated last month, despite its rate of expansion slowing from July, a separate survey showed.
The nonmanufacturing index (NMI) remained in expansion mode for the 18th month in a row, although it edged down 1.7 percentage points to 55.6, which the institute attributed to the slowing momentum in business activity, new orders and employment.
The institute said that all eight major service industries’ NMIs and their outlooks for the next six months showed expansion, indicating that the non-manufacturing sector still has broad support.
However, business prospects among service industries varied, as the accommodation and food service industry and the construction and real-estate industry are affected by seasonal demand and government policies, and the finance and insurance industry is tied to sentiment in financial markets, the institute said.
The retail, wholesale, logistics and warehousing, and communication and broadcasting industries would leverage their exposure to AI-related business, it added.

NFL keen for Australia game to become an annual fixture in ‘strategic’ market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:58 UTC
01:46:58 KST

The NFL is looking to bring a game to Australia every season as part of its international strategy and sees the nation as a strategic growth market for football, a senior executive said yesterday.
Australia hosts its first NFL game at the 100,000-seat Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) on Friday next week with the LA Rams opening their season against the San Francisco 49ers in the first of a record nine-game international schedule across seven countries.
The MCG game is part of a multiyear contract with Australia’s Victoria state, which includes two confirmed games over four years and the option for a third.
Photo: Christopher Trim-Imagn Images
The timing of the second one is still to be decided, but Gerrit Meier, managing director and head of NFL International, said the league’s preference would be for annual games in Australia, much as the UK has had for most of the past two decades.
“I think that would be the plan, right?” Meier said in a video call from New York.
“Overall, we’re working off the hypothesis that we need to make a commitment to a market... We believe that at least one game per year should be something that we should be having in the markets that we commit to,” he said. “And maybe over time, as we have, maybe, greater inventory, then maybe you play two games [per season] or so.”
The longer-term scheduling of NFL games in Australia had to consider the players’ experience, whether the clubs saw value in the journey and how satisfied the hosts would be with the economic impact, Meier said.
“The teams coming back, they need to be healthy. They need to have a great experience. It needs to be a great game because in the end it counts. It’s not an exhibition game,” he said.
The Victorian government’s bid for the NFL games works out to about A$10 million to A$15 million (US$7.15 million to US$10.72 million) per game, Melbourne’s the Age reported.
Government officials have declined to disclose the cost, but see the games as a huge opportunity to showcase the state and expect “significant economic returns” on the investment.
The first game in Melbourne starts at 10:35am to suit the US TV audience, but the MCG is expected to be packed to near capacity.
Nearly half of the crowd would travel from other Australian states or from overseas, including about 10,000 US-based fans, the NFL said.
The league believed the idea of a regular season-opening game in Australia was “very, very special,” but would need conversations with the state government’s tourism arm, Visit Victoria, and the Australian Football League (AFL), Meier said.
The AFL is the governing body for professional Australian rules football, the most popular winter sport in the nation’s southern states. Multiple AFL games are played almost every week at the MCG through to the end of this month.
“We’re going to sit with the larger region and city and [ask] what all of you thought. Was it good? Was it not good? Would you want to have us back?” Meier said. “And ... we want to see how the grass is holding up. We want to kind of see how the overall setup has been working.”
The NFL set up a local office for Australia and New Zealand in 2022 and opened its second international academy on the Gold Coast in 2024, having launched the first in England in 2019.
Australian punters are common in NFL teams, and Philadelphia Eagles offensive tackle Jordan Mailata last year became the country’s first to win a Super Bowl as a participating player.
In a few years operating in Australia, the NFL’s perception of the nation’s potential had changed, Meier said.
“It’s kind of moved from being an interesting market to actually being a strategic growth market,” he said. “We have a fast-growing fan base... The game itself is just a catalyst.”

HKers have no crime to repent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:58 UTC
01:46:58 KST

On Friday last week, Chow Hang-tung (鄒幸彤), former leader of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, appeared before a Hong Kong court for what was supposed to be a mitigation hearing.
Chow had already been found guilty, together with the now-disbanded alliance and its former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan (李卓人), of inciting subversion of state power. Now came the familiar ritual before sentencing: The convicted tell the court why leniency is warranted.
However, Chow did not believe she had done anything wrong, saying: “We should not spend a single day in prison.”
It would be easy to describe what followed as defiance, but she was refusing something more fundamental: the moral premise upon which leniency would be granted.
The court could find her guilty. It could imprison her, but it could not make her agree that what she had done deserved punishment.
During her oral submission, Chow said she and her fellow defendants believe dictatorship is wrong and democracy is right. Judge Alex Lee Wan-tang (李運騰) said that the court was not punishing them simply for holding beliefs, but for acting on them.
When Chow argued that a belief never acted upon was hardly a belief, Lee replied: “Then it depends on whether your belief is permitted by law.”
There, in a single exchange, was Hong Kong’s new reality: A belief in democracy may be tolerated — until it is acted upon.
The case was never merely about Chow. In her written statement, she said: “This is my sincere belief. And it is not mine alone — the 30 years of candlelight in Victoria Park have already proved that.”
For 30 years, Hong Kongers gathered in Victoria Park to commemorate the Tiananmen Massacre of June 4, 1989. Parents brought children. Friends gathered after work. People carried candles to mourn people they had never known and demanded accountability for what happened that year in Beijing.
I was born and raised in Hong Kong. To people of my generation, the June 4 vigil was not some clandestine conspiracy against the state. It was the collective conscience of millions.
Year after year, Victoria Park became a sea of candlelight — a declaration that even if something could not be remembered openly on the other side of the border, it would be remembered there.
Legally, the millions who attended the vigils were not defendants, but if the cause pursued by the alliance was criminal, what does that say about those who stood with it for 30 years? Were we wrong to light those candles? To remember the dead? To believe that dictatorship is wrong and democracy is right?
That is why Chow’s refusal to seek leniency matters. The state was passing judgement not merely on former leaders of the alliance, but on all Hong Kongers who shared Chow’s beliefs.
Chow was answering for more than herself. The state can prohibit the vigil. It can imprison the organizers it, but it cannot retrospectively extinguish those candles. Power over the present is not ownership of the past.
I do not remember those candlelit nights as a crime. I do not believe the people sitting quietly in Victoria Park were criminals. I will not allow a judgement to tell me that they were.
Chow could not bring the vigil back or overturn the verdict, but she could refuse to surrender the meaning of what had happened. She could refuse to repent on our behalf. And she did.
“What we did was open and honorable. Our consciences are clear. We have no crime to repent,” she said.
John Cheng is a retired businessman from Hong Kong living in Taiwan.

====================================================================================================

Burnham’s ambitious plans need room to breathe – and Westminster suffocates change | Rafael Behr
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:58 UTC
01:46:58 KST

Nothing stays fresh for long in parliament and no one sounds normal. The air, thick with convention, suffocates originality, tuning every voice to the same Westminster pitch. The need to escape that climate is one reason why Andy Burnham quit his Commons seat to run for mayor of Greater Manchester. Or that is how he tells the story.
Returning after nearly a decade away, the prime minister says he wants to throw open the windows, let in some air. He thinks devolution can cultivate a healthier political culture. He intends to rebalance England’s centre of gravity with a power base in the new No 10 North.
The timing of Burnham’s arrival in Downing Street, just before the summer recess, suited those arguments. He replaced Keir Starmer, then promptly went on tour, posting chatty videos on social media, appearing as the antidote to a stuffy predecessor who, perhaps unfairly, had come to be seen as the archetypal Westminster mechanoid. Starmer, who today announced his intention to stand down as an MP, may find his authentic voice on the outside.
Meanwhile, Burnham has to bring his free-range prime minister act into the battery farm of the Commons. His mandate and legislative programme are inherited from the Starmer era. He is stuck with the same squeezed budgets in the same sluggish economy imperilled by the same turbulent global climate. His room for fiscal manoeuvre is constrained by Labour’s 2024 manifesto prohibition on broad-based tax rises and by the bond market’s punitive vigilance towards anything that looks like undisciplined spending.
In such conditions, politics is reduced to a zero-sum competition for scarce resources. Every promise made to satisfy the needs of one department or constituency contains an undeclared threat to deprive someone else.
Starmer’s leadership was ruined by many things, but few were as crippling as his failure to grapple with those dilemmas. He wouldn’t pick sides between irreconcilable demands within his cabinet. When his own ministers couldn’t read his political instincts or decrypt his priorities, the public had no chance. It was a recipe for paralysis, delivering a congealed gruel of continuity to voters who thought they had ordered piping hot change.
Determination not to repeat that mistake has shaped Burnham’s approach from his first moments in office. He declared a moral mission – the elimination of rough sleeping – before even crossing the threshold of No 10. He followed it up with emblematic policies to demonstrate that regime change brought a new focus on the cost of living.
No one in Downing Street pretends that capping bus fares or cutting VAT on fuel bills is enough to win affection from a sceptical public. The function of modest retail policies is to show that Labour, renewed by fresh leadership, has snapped out of despondency and started listening. A bounce in opinion polls suggests it is working.
But the transition from small-change symbols to big-ticket policy choices is not easy.
It is especially hard if the prime minister is conflict averse and prone to flights of empathic urgency. That is the hazard flagged by Burnham’s critics, based on observation of his career as a minister in the New Labour government and later as Manchester mayor. They are traits that generate spontaneous promises that later have to be diluted or retracted.
In June, Burnham got himself into just such a tangle over a commitment to compensate “Waspi women” who feel they were mistreated by the Department for Work and Pensions when their retirement age was raised. In May, he told a campaigner for party finance reform that he supported the principle of a cap on donations to guard against big money exerting undue influence in politics. A cap has been proposed as an amendment to the representation of the people bill, currently on its way through parliament. But the government, following trade union lobbying, is not backing the move.
The learning curve for any new prime minister is brutally steep.
Things that seem obvious from outside No 10 are revealed to be fearsomely complex. What seems compelling on the campaign trail can feel like a ruinous drain on time and political capital in government. The road is especially hard to navigate for those who arrive midterm, scrambling over unfinished and unpopular business bequeathed by an ousted predecessor.
The retreat from plans to free up prison capacity by releasing offenders early is a revealing case. Burnham understandably doesn’t want his first months in office marred by a parade of stories about villains walking free. But swerving unfriendly headlines isn’t a plan for reforming the justice system or growing its shrivelled budget.
Likewise, the prime minister’s appearance in Kyiv to celebrate Ukraine’s independence day, while important as a display of solidarity with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, came with no account of the sacrifices Britain faces as the price of ramping up its own defences against Russian aggression.
No one is better briefed on that challenge than the chancellor. As defence secretary, John Healey resigned from Starmer’s government in protest at the former prime minister’s reluctance to boost military spending. Relocated to the Treasury, he finds himself managing a downgrade in rearmament expectations ahead of the autumn budget.
The seasonal migration of politics back to parliament threatens a sudden narrowing of Burnham’s options. The prime minister has a theory to counter that threat. His argument is that devolution, as well as bringing fresh air to politics, spurs economic growth.
Loosening the dead hand of Whitehall control over public services is supposed to promote innovation and efficiency. A more responsive government, attuned to local market conditions, will unlock investment.
Assuming that can work, the mechanism is slow. Burnham accepts that it is a 10-year plan. The opposition calculates that the fiscal walls will close in on Labour a lot faster than that.
Kemi Badenoch thinks the economy is the issue that will rehabilitate Tory fortunes. To sharpen her attack on that front, she has sacked her shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, for insufficient pugnacity with the Treasury brief. His replacement, Andrew Griffith, is deemed more dynamic, a quality he once displayed in cheerleading for Liz Truss’s disastrous 2022 “mini-budget”.
In Badenoch’s view, Burnham is a “people-pleaser” who lacks the resolve to whip his MPs behind tough budget choices. He will rely on tax rises to pay for policies that the left see as essential maintenance to the social safety net and the right decry as profligate subsidy for fecklessness. The impossibility of feeding Labour’s big-government appetite with hands shackled by the 2024 manifesto will force the prime minister to seek his own mandate with an early election.
It is a plausible scenario. It is also unclear how the Tories get match fit on that timetable when they are running third in national polls. Badenoch’s personal ratings aren’t so bad, but she lacks insight into the reasons why so many voters think her party is unfit to govern. Discounting Griffith’s contamination by the Truss project when appointing a shadow chancellor is a symptom of that blind spot.
The Tories are flattered into feeling relevant by a sympathetic press and the constitutional crutch of official opposition status. In parliamentary arithmetic, the Conservatives still eclipse Reform UK.
Badenoch welcomes the enclosure of politics in the Commons chamber as much as the Labour leader resists it. The theatre of ritual combat is more her style than his. But the prime minister’s judgment is better in thinking voters are turned off by the whole spectacle. Burnham’s fresh manner has breathed life into a government that was expiring. It will take a different order of political skill to dispel the older miasma of cumulative failure that hangs heavy over Westminster.
- 
  Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

Forbidden planet: Was Pluto’s demotion a big mistake?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:56 UTC
01:46:56 KST

Twenty years ago, Pluto got demoted. After a vote by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in August 2006, Pluto was relegated from major planet to dwarf planet status. Our solar system dropped from nine planets to eight. At the time, many scientists were unhappy with the decision. Two decades on, the debate is, if anything, even more polarized.
“The definition of a planet they created, you can’t use it at all,” said Philip Metzger, the director of the Stephen W. Hawking Center for Microgravity Research and Education at the University of Central Florida. “It makes the definition of a planet completely non-useful in science.”
Metzger is one of a number of scientists and lay people who consider Pluto’s demotion a big mistake.
Illustration: Mountain People
For some, Pluto’s downgraded status is the source of their affection for the ex-planet.
“Pluto represents the underdog that so many people root for, the small kid on the block that is being picked on,” said Kevin Schindler, historian at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona, where Pluto was discovered in 1930.
For others, the IAU’s decision, and the way it was taken, is central to the debate.
“My being involved with advocating for Pluto started on the day of the vote,” writer, actor and amateur astronomer Laurel Kornfeld said. “I was like: Wait a minute, this is wrong.”
When we meet on Zoom she is wearing a T-shirt that says: “Pluto Resistance, 20 years: 2006-2026.”
The campaign to reinstate Pluto — with its passionate advocates, ongoing debates, occasional protests and petitions — seems to be largely confined to the US.
“It is more of an issue in the United States,” Metzger said. “This was the one we discovered.”
So, the planet’s demotion was a source of wounded pride?
“I’ll admit there was some of that — among the public, not the scientists,” he said.
More recently, the campaign has taken on a populist tinge, with NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman telling a congressional committee in April that he was in favor of a rethink.
“I am very much in the camp of Make Pluto a Planet Again,” he said.
The event that sparked the IAU’s 2006 vote was the discovery of a distant celestial body that would come to be called Eris. Eris was out in the Kuiper Belt, beyond Neptune — where Pluto also resides. It was roughly the same size as Pluto (less volume, but more mass). If Pluto was a planet, the argument went, then so was Eris. And if Eris was not a planet, how could Pluto continue to be one?
Eris and Pluto were by no means alone in the Kuiper Belt. Other smaller bodies were discovered around the same time, including Haumea, Makemake and Sedna. Were these also planets? There were likely many more similar objects still to be found. How would schoolchildren manage a planetary roster that might number in the hundreds?
In search of a solution, the IAU came up with a three-point definition of a planet: It must orbit the sun; it must have sufficient mass to pull itself into a round shape; and it must have “cleared its neighborhood” — meaning it must gravitationally dominate the area in which it orbits. Nothing beyond Neptune that we knew about qualified; Pluto was out.
It was the last point in particular that upset a lot of Pluto advocates, because a body’s ability to clear its neighborhood depends a lot on the neighborhood.
“One of the biggest flaws with the IAU definition is that you can have the same object in two different orbits,” Kornfeld said. “In one, it’s considered a planet, and in the other, it’s not considered a planet.”
If the Earth were towed out to Pluto’s position, the planetary scientist Alan Stern argued, it would not be able to clear its zone either, and would no longer meet the IAU definition of a planet.
“You could even have small asteroids, that are too small to be round, clearing an orbit if they’re close to a star,” Metzger said. “It just goes to show that orbit clearing isn’t really that meaningful of a category.”
To its detractors, the IAU definition seemed crafted with a specific intent.
“A reason was invented to exclude Pluto,” Kornfeld said.
Pluto’s demotion created two opposing scientific teams: the so-called geophysical camp, which believes the physical properties of a celestial body should count toward its planethood; and the dynamicists, who are more concerned with the position a body occupies, its surroundings and its direction of travel. You could characterize the split as planetary scientists vs astronomers. Many planetary scientists, including Metzger, simply do not use the IAU definition.
When the New Horizons spacecraft made its flyby of Pluto in 2015, the geophysical camp seized what it saw as an advantage. Pluto definitely had the geophysical makings of a planet, they maintained. It had mountains, evidence of recent geological activity, and water ice hills floating on frozen nitrogen. It might even be able to support life. How could that not be a planet?
Those agitating for Pluto’s planetary status do not, by and large, recognize any problems stemming from reinstatement. They welcome a definition broad enough to take in hundreds of new planets, as taxing as that might be for children and their wallcharts.
“The more the merrier,” said Paul Byrne, associate professor of earth, environmental and planetary sciences at Washington University in St Louis. “There are 1,025 official Pokemon species, and I’ve never heard a kid say that’s too many.”
Those against Pluto’s reinstatement say the problem is not with a larger number of planets, per se, but with a primarily geophysical definition that would encompass, among other bodies, planetary moons, including our moon.
“I have no problem with having a larger number of planets,” astronomer Mike Brown said over e-mail. “My argument is simply that we decided long ago that the moon is not a planet and that also precludes Pluto.”
Brown is often described as The Man Who Killed Pluto, because he led the team that discovered Eris back in 2005, setting the whole de-planetization in motion. It is a title he leans into: He even wrote a book called How I Killed Pluto and Why It Had It Coming.
Brown often says that the moon is bigger than Pluto; it is round and has a complex geophysical history, and would certainly meet the criteria for a planet if you excluded any requirement concerning orbit. What he is saying is: If Pluto is a planet, so is the moon.
“I don’t have an issue with calling the moon a planet,” Byrne said. “Because I can be a brother and a husband at the same time, and it doesn’t require that I be one or the other. And so I don’t see why the moon can’t be a satellite and a planet.”
For the outsider, this debate can often seem mired in political, even procedural questions, with Plutonians contending that the IAU vote was incorrectly conducted and therefore void.
“You could make the argument that they never officially voted on a planet, because they didn’t follow the procedure that was required,” Metzger said.
Brown denied there was anything political about the decision.
“The only people who complain about the voting procedure were the ones who didn’t like the outcome,” he said.
So the question remains: Why does any of this matter?
“It was almost like a coup,” Kornfeld said. “And as a result, kids are learning less. They’re learning eight planets, and that’s it.”
For Metzger, the planetary definition excluding Pluto is based on an outmoded notion of the solar system.
“They were creating a reactionary view towards an orderly cosmos, rather than the more modern scientific view where it’s chaotic,” he said. “The second problem was that I think they misread the room. The public of today is not the public of the 1800s. They’re perfectly happy understanding a dynamic, chaotic cosmos, and we missed the opportunity to teach that.”
Pluto’s nature has always been elusive. In 1915, the astronomer Percival Lowell published calculations based on peculiarities in the orbits of Uranus and Neptune, predicting the existence of a new, ninth planet, which he called Planet X, with a mass somewhere between Earth’s and Neptune’s. In 1930, the long search for Planet X bore fruit: The new body, discovered at the observatory that bore Lowell’s name, was christened Pluto.
Gradually, however, it became clear that whatever Pluto was, it was not Planet X. It did not seem anywhere near large enough to account for irregularities in Neptune’s orbit. Scientists offered theories to explain why Pluto looked so small, but the truth was, it was small — even smaller than the moon. Only in 1992 did we learn that Lowell’s calculations were based on an overestimation of Neptune’s mass. There was no Planet X.
Pluto’s reputation as an underdog, the picked-on kid, might stem from the 2006 vote, but one could argue it was punching above its weight for years. How would they have voted on Pluto’s planetary status if they had known the truth in 1930? And will it take another vote to satisfy Pluto’s defenders?
“People have locked in,” Metzger said. “We would have a less useful vote today than we did back in the 2006 timeframe. So we don’t want another vote. What we want is for people to recognize that voting was a mistake, and we’re not going to do that any more. We’re going to go back to the scientific method.”
As part of its relentless pursuit of hegemony, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and its People’s Liberation Army (PLA) are now sustaining two regional wars while threatening further arms races that shift the global balance of power in order for the CCP to advance its ultimate objective. Russia’s and Iran’s war efforts are being materially supported by Chinese supplies of drone components and missile fuels. So far in 2026, such Chinese support has enabled a 60 percent increase in civilian casualties in Ukraine caused by long-range Russian weapons such as missiles and drones from January to June 2026 compared with the same

Egypt denies reports of Suez Canal ownership transfer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:54 UTC
01:46:54 KST

Breadcrumb
Egyptian government denies reports of transfer, exchange of Suez Canal for debt relief
An Egyptian businessman and finance expert has triggered controversy after suggesting a proposal for a ‘swap’ that includes the Suez Canal in a bid to eliminate domestic debt.
Hassan Heikal, who is also an advisor to the Egyptian cabinet, caused a stir after mentioning the Suez Canal as a state asset that could be involved in a swap, prompting the government to intervene and issue a statement denying it had any intention to transfer ownership of the canal to relieve debt.
The cabinet said in the statement, issued on Saturday, that the reports suggesting that ownership of some state assets could be transferred to the Central Bank of Egypt in exchange for settling part of the country’s domestic debt reflected “a purely personal vision of its author”.
The statement added that the proposal did not represent government policy or an initiative adopted by the authorities, and that the idea had been considered but relevant bodies had concluded it was not possible to implement and therefore it was not included as part of the government’s public debt management policies.
Growing controversy
The government reaction comes just two days after the proposal generated a widespread public response and became a major talking point in Egypt.
It also came at the same time a historic debt, owed by the National Media Authority (known as Maspero) to the National Investment Bank, was settled.
Heikal described the settlement as a smaller-scale model of what a solution could look like for the state as a whole.
He mentioned his proposal again in a series of posts on X, citing what he described as the “small swap – Maspero”, as well as arrangements involving electricity and petroleum companies and the Ministry of Finance.
Heikal said the state had eliminated Maspero’s debts through an asset swap, involving mainly land, while transferring the debt to the National Investment Bank. This enabled the authority to rid itself of its debt burden, while the bank received assets in exchange for the debt.
He added that that example could be applied on a broader national level in an effort to ease the country’s crippling debt crisis.
The idea was first floated by Heikal in January, where he suggested that a fund should be created into which state assets would be consolidated, followed by an exchange of those assets for domestic debt after the debt had been transferred to the Central Bank.
Heikal’s proposal is based on the view that the central problem facing the Egyptian economy is not simply the size of its debt, but the cost of servicing it.
He said debt servicing consumes between 50 percent and 60 percent of state revenues, arguing that high interest payments are squeezing the public budget and limiting the government’s ability to spend on citizens, whether on education, universal health insurance, subsidies or wages.
He further argued that transferring the assets and debt could free the budget from a substantial part of the interest burden, thereby creating room for the state to spend on services that citizens directly experience.
According to the latest published official data, domestic debt stands at 1.057tn Egyptian pounds (about $219bn) as of the end of June 2025.
Many economists and politicians have criticised Heikal’s proposal, stating that it would mean that more money would need to be printed.
The proposal further divided opinions because it reignited conversations from 2022 over amendments to the Suez Canal Authority law and the creation of a fund affiliated with the authority that would have powers to sell, lease and exploit its assets. The controversy ended at the time with the government denying any intention to sell the canal itself.

Finland’s ‘happy education model’ opens in Kaohsiung
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:50 UTC
01:46:50 KST

The Kaohsiung Finland International School (KSFIS) would serve as an important link between Kaohsiung and Finland while providing an excellent educational environment for families, Finland Trade Center Director Lauri Raunio said yesterday.
The Finnish school, the first of its kind in East Asia, held its opening ceremony at Kaohsiung’s Cianjin Elementary School.
It occupies a separate building within the elementary school, with private entrances and controlled access to and from its campus.
Photo: CNA
Finnish education is known for its “happy education model,” which features fewer tests and aims to encourage students to learn through hands-on experiences, Raunio said.
KSFIS was established as the number of Finnish citizens and other foreign workers in Taiwan steadily increases, the Finnish representative to Taiwan said.
The trade office visited multiple locations before settling on Kaohsiung, primarily because of the city’s transition from traditional heavy industries to a high-tech center, as well as the growing number of foreigners settling in the city, he said.
Raunio thanked the Kaohsiung Education Bureau for its assistance throughout the process to establish the school.
The Kaohsiung City Government said the growth of the semiconductor, artificial intelligence and other advanced manufacturing industries would require more international talent and students from diverse educational backgrounds.
KSFIS would not only deepen educational exchanges between Kaohsiung and Finland, but would also provide international families in Taiwan with more educational options, the bureau said.
Kaohsiung City Government Deputy Secretary-General Chang Chia-hsiing (張家興) said the municipal government’s efforts to internationalize the city include attracting high-quality international education.
Education Bureau Deputy Director Liu Ching-wen (劉靜文) said Cianjin Elementary School is sharing resources while ensuring that its existing buildings continue to serve their original purposes, adding that the different educational systems would provide more opportunities for exchange.
KSFIS provides education from kindergarten through high school, with English as the primary language of instruction. It is dedicated to delivering the Finnish educational approach and pursuing candidacy for the International Baccalaureate (IB) program.
The school plans to establish a teacher training center focused on Finnish educational methodology, as well as a Quantum Computing and AI Education Incubation Center.
The centers will work with tech firms and industries in the city to incorporate ethical values into everyday school life and foster socially responsible future talent capable of understanding issues from an international perspective.

MND report flags PLA efforts to boost Taiwan landing capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:46:49 UTC
01:46:49 KST

The Ministry of National Defense’s (MND) 2026 report on China’s military power, submitted to the Legislative Yuan on Monday, places greater emphasis than last year’s report on the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) efforts to strengthen its capabilities for a potential landing operation on Taiwan, according to an analyst.
Chieh Chung (揭仲), an adjunct associate research fellow at Taiwan’s government-funded Institute for National Defense and Security Research (INDSR), said the report suggested that improving joint island-landing capabilities and completing military transformation had become the PLA’s priorities for force development over the coming years.
"Those efforts do not appear to have been significantly affected by the gaps in the PLA’s chain of command caused by [Chinese President] Xi Jinping’s (習近平) large-scale purge of senior military officials," he said.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of National Defense
In the report’s "weapons acquisition" section, the PLA Ground Force (PLAGF) is described as upgrading and modifying the Z-20 utility helicopter and developing unmanned transport helicopters, while the Air Force is replacing existing equipment with new airborne infantry fighting vehicles, transport vehicles and mortar carriers, Chieh said.
Meanwhile, the "military training" section says PLA Army Aviation helicopter units are conducting fuel and ammunition resupply operations using offshore platforms, he said.
These developments are closely linked to the PLA’s efforts in recent years to transform its joint island-landing capabilities, Chieh said.
Under the concept envisioned after the transformation, the first wave of attacking forces would consist primarily of troops transported by aircraft and helicopters into Taiwan’s main island, allowing them to bypass Taiwan’s coastal defenses, including drones, unmanned surface vessels and anti-ship missiles, he said.
The weapons acquisition section also says the PLA Navy will build the Type 076 amphibious assault ship and new types of amphibious landing barges, including self-elevating amphibious landing barges and "water-bridge" amphibious landing vessels, Chieh said.
The landing barges are designed to address major shortcomings in the PLA’s existing "pierless unloading" equipment, including its inability to cross the Taiwan Strait and operate effectively under Taiwan’s maritime conditions, he said.
They would allow follow-on waves of troops and supplies to be rapidly brought ashore even if Taiwan’s ports had been destroyed and rendered unusable, making the equipment critical to the PLA’s efforts to improve its joint island-landing capabilities, Chieh said.
Beyond frontline combat units, the report contains new material on PLA efforts to enhance joint island-landing capabilities through military space, cyberspace, information support and logistics equipment, Chieh said.
For the first time, China’s military space forces are said to be planning to deploy low-Earth orbit communications satellite constellations, including Guowang and Qianfan, and develop fourth-generation BeiDou navigation satellites to help prevent the PLA’s communications and navigation from being disrupted by Taiwan or the U.S. after a landing, he said.
The cyberspace forces are also focusing on AI-based deepfake technology to strengthen hybrid warfare capabilities and deploying mobile electronic warfare and reconnaissance vehicles to bolster the offensive and defensive capabilities of PLA landing forces.
The branch also plans to acquire new network, space- ground networking and information-fusion equipment to enhance their mobile cyberwarfare capabilities, Chieh said.
Meanwhile, joint logistics and support forces are focusing on battlefield medical evacuation and treatment, as many casualties in a cross-strait operation would occur outside mainland China, either on Taiwan or in surrounding waters.
Although the 2026 report provides a more detailed account of the PLA’s measures to improve its joint island- landing capabilities, it also notes that the PLA’s capabilities in conducting such operations remain inadequate at this stage.
Chieh said that while the ministry’s assessment was consistent with the current situation, "the report as a whole nevertheless shows that the PLA is accelerating preparations for a potential armed invasion of Taiwan."
He estimated that the various programs could be completed in stages between 2030 and 2035.
