Q&A: What Has Emerged From the Trial of a Businessman Charged in the Murder of a Maltese Journalist?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:51:00 UTC
22:51:00 KST

OCCRP: Daphne Caruana Galizia is said to have coined a phrase that has been picked up by anti-corruption activists: “Malta is not a normal country." Are there any aspects of this trial that bring the phrase to mind now that the lawyers have made their final arguments, and the jury will soon reach its verdict?
Julian Bonnici: The political shadow over the case is a long one. Keith Schembri, the former chief of staff to Malta's ex-prime minister spent close to four days in the witness box, and has been accused throughout the trial of being the real mastermind. He denies it, and little hard evidence for it has been put before the jury.
The trial has also laid out defendant Yorgen Fenech's web of contacts across Malta's political elite: his WhatsApp exchanges with Schembri, with former Prime Minister Joseph Muscat, with regulatory heads, and with the deputy police commissioner who once headed the investigation into the murder.
A lot of people know that Caruana Galizia was Malta’s most prominent investigative journalist and anti-corruption activist. Who is Yorgen Fenech, and what is the prosecution alleging motivated him to commission her murder?
Fenech is 44, and the heir to the Tumas Group, one of Malta's largest business empires. He was a director, and remains a shareholder, of ElectroGas, the consortium that won the contract to build and run Malta's new gas power station, a deal underwritten by a state guarantee of more than 400 million euros ($460 million).
He was also, though nobody knew it at the time, the owner of 17 Black, a Dubai company. Leaked documents later showed 17 Black listed as an intended source of payments into two Panama companies opened for Schembri and the then energy minister, Konrad Mizzi.
Fenech, Schembri and Mizzi were charged in 2025 with corruption and money laundering in connection with 17 Black. Those proceedings are ongoing.
The prosecution's case alleges Fenech was motivated to commission Caruana Galizia’s murder, because she was closing in on details about that alleged corruption. She first named 17 Black in February 2017, and hinted at Fenech's ownership in the comments beneath the article. Eight days later, the company changed its name. She also received a large leak of ElectroGas material that year.
Fenech and his defense team reject that motive entirely.
But he is not accused of carrying out her assasination by himself. How many people were allegedly involved in her killing?
Five men have already been convicted. Vince Muscat, a convicted hitman who turned state witness, admitted in 2021 to his part in planning the killing, surveilling Caruana Galizia, and acting as a spotter. He got 15 years in prison. Alfred and George Degiorgio, who placed and detonated the bomb, pleaded guilty in 2022 and got 40 years each. Robert Agius and Jamie Vella were sentenced to life in 2025 for supplying the bomb.
Melvin Theuma, the confessed middleman who says he brokered the killing on Fenech's behalf, received a presidential pardon in exchange for providing evidence.
Fenech is the latest to face trial over the murder, charged with complicity and criminal association. The prosecution has cast him as the man who commissioned and paid for it.
Jurors have been presented with covert recordings of Fenech made by Melvin Theuma, who confessed to acting as the middleman to arrange Caruana Galizia’s killing. What did Theuma’s testimony allegedly reveal?
Theuma gave the jury the full narrative arc of the murder, starting weeks before the 2017 general election was called on May 1 that year. He insisted throughout that Fenech ordered and paid for the killing.
Fenech confirmed under oath that he handed Theuma 450,000 euros ($520,000) after the murder, money that funded the legal defense of Alfred and George Degiorgio. Fenech's position is that he was being blackmailed.
Theuma broke down in the box describing the murder and apologized to Caruana Galizia's sons.
The recordings land hard. Fenech's voice is on them, and the prosecution says several of his remarks point to his own involvement. It built its closing address around them, with him saying things like: "Our power is the money" and "What am I going to do, tell the judge I killed her?"
Fenech's defense team is alleging that Keith Schembri was the true mastermind of the killing, not their client. The last line she wrote, in a blog post about Keith Schembri on the day she died was: “There are crooks everywhere you look now. The situation is desperate." Who is he and how credible do you see this allegation?
Schembri was chief of staff to Prime Minister Joseph Muscat from 2013 until November 2019, which in practice made him one of the most powerful people in the country. He owned Tillgate, one of the two Panamanian companies that listed 17 Black as its target client.
He resigned in November 2019, hours before he was arrested in connection with the murder. He was questioned and released without charge, and now faces separate criminal proceedings over leaks in the investigation.
Fenech conceded under cross-examination that Schembri never told him directly that he had ordered the killing, and that his source for that allegation was Theuma. During his four days of testimony, Schembri denied it flatly.
Schembri's credibility is not for me to decide. But there are open questions about whether the investigation into him was adequate. His mobile phone was suspiciously missing when he was arrested in 2019 and never recovered, and actions of investigators in this regard raise a lot of questions. Testimony has revealed that he leaked state intelligence secrets regarding the case to the plotters. He was allegedly involved in attempting to secure bail for the hitmen, and also allegedly wrote a note attempting to instruct Fenech how to frame another man for the killing.
Charles Mercieca, one of Fenech's lawyers, called Schembri "l-id moħbija" — the hidden hand.
The charges against Yorgen Fenech are based on a magisterial inquiry prepared and submitted to Malta’s attorney general. Under the country’s legal system, magisterial inquiries are not made public. Have previously unknown details emerged so far at the trial that provide insights into what the magisterial inquiry found or alleges?
A great deal, and this is the underrated public-interest function of the trial.
Magisterial inquiries in Malta are not published. Fragments have leaked over the years, and a 2024 court decree restricted what could be discussed publicly. So for six years the country argued about this case on the basis of partial material.
The trial has put the underlying evidence into open court. The Theuma recordings were played folio by folio rather than quoted second-hand, with the transcripts read into the record. Fenech's own police statements to Superintendent Kurt Zahra, taken over two days in November 2019, were played to jurors. Europol forensic experts gave evidence on the device extractions. Police witnesses set out what was seized, and where.
It is the closest thing Malta has had to a public audit of the investigation, and of the state's alleged involvement in the murder.
A 2019-2021 independent public inquiry into the circumstances of Caruana Galizia’s murder found no proof that the government ordered the bombing. But it said the state did not do what it could to prevent it. It alleged officials actively campaigned to isolate and dehumanize her, making her a vulnerable target, and that there was a “web of corruption” between top government officials and big business, which Caruana Galizia was working to expose. As someone covering the same issues she did, how do you find protections for journalists in Malta nearly a decade after her murder?
The public inquiry's recommendations have still not been fully implemented. That remains the most fundamental issue for the media in Malta.
Safety will always be a concern in a country where the government treats journalists as hostile actors. But the larger problem is structural. The government continues to introduce legislation that undermines the work of journalists, activists, citizens, and independent institutions. In the last two years alone, it has restricted the ability of private citizens to request magisterial inquiries, and passed a law granting a legal amnesty to accused tax evaders and money launderers.

What’s changing in Russia this September? ‘Spiritual and Moral Culture’ classes in schools, the digital ruble, and mandatory camel registration.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:50:53 UTC
22:50:53 KST

What’s changing in Russia this September? ‘Spiritual and Moral Culture’ classes in schools, the digital ruble, and mandatory camel registration.
High schoolers are starting to study social studies from a textbook edited by Medvedev, while fifth-graders begin a new course called “Spiritual and Moral Culture of Russia.” Some schools will now offer Arabic as a second foreign language, and behavior grades will be introduced for students in grades two through eight, though not every school will adopt the practice.
Adult Russians will be able to use the digital ruble, legally buy cryptocurrency on an exchange (though only in small amounts), ban themselves from gambling through the Gosuslugi portal, and take a mortgage payment holiday if they have more than one child. They’ll also be allowed to work up to 240 overtime hours a year, double the previous limit of 120, and buy gasoline that doesn’t meet the usual environmental standards at gas stations. And anyone keeping more than 10 chickens or ostriches — or even a single deer or camel — will now have to register the animals.

Breadcrumb
After Israel recognition, Somaliland president to make first US visit
Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi is expected to travel to Washington in the coming days as Hargeisa seeks US recognition following Israel’s decision to recognise the territory.
Israel’s KAN broadcaster first reported the development amid reports that Somaliland hopes to leverage Israel’s recognition of its independence to encourage the US to follow suit.
The broadcaster cited a source who said Abdullahi, better known as Irro, hopes to meet US President Donald Trump.
The reported visit is likely to renew questions over Somaliland’s efforts to secure broader international recognition, more than three decades after the territory declared independence from Somalia in 1991.
Currently Israel is the only country in the world to recognise Somaliland's independence.
However, US recognition has yet to be confirmed. Irro recently met with a US military delegation led by Claude K. Tudor Jr, commander of US Special Operations Command Africa (SOCAFRICA), to discuss expanding security cooperation and shared strategic interests in the Horn of Africa.
According to a statement issued by the Somaliland Presidency, the talks focused on maritime security in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, counterterrorism cooperation and wider regional security challenges.
Somali media have reported however that the US has no plans to establish a military base in Somaliland, citing comments by Dagvin Anderson, commander of US Africa Command (AFRICOM).
Anderson reiterated Washington’s longstanding recognition of Somalia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and rejected suggestions that the US was disengaging from Somalia or recognising Somaliland's self-declared independence.
Washington’s support for Somalia’s sovereignty was further underscored by a US State Department report submitted to Congress in June, titled “Potential Areas for Improved US Engagement with Somaliland”. The report stated that Somaliland was part of the Federal Republic of Somalia.
“Within that framework, the US maintains a positive, constructive relationship with Somaliland and continues to explore additional opportunities for engagement with Somaliland authorities,” the report said.
However, it also reaffirmed “the sovereignty and territorial integrity” of Somalia.
“Somaliland authorities have encouraged US investment in minerals and outlined priorities in infrastructure, trade, and economic growth,” the report added.
“However, regional security concerns and the dispute over Somaliland’s status, including its refusal to cooperate with national authorities, present challenges for investment, banking, and trade.”
The US position contrasts with that of its ally Israel, which recognised Somaliland in December 2025, paving the way for a swift rapprochement between the two governments.
In June, Irro made a visit to Israel, where he was received by President Isaac Herzog and Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana.

HEGTA, Iran Tour Operators Association to expand tourism cooperation
TEHRAN – Tourism Group of the Social Security Organization (HEGTA) and the Iranian Tour Operators Association have agreed to expand cooperation in domestic and international tourism markets, develop new tourism products and make greater use of HEGTA’s accommodation and rail transport capacities.
The agreement was reached on Tuesday when the two sides also agreed to establish a joint working group to identify target markets and develop pilot tourism products.
Key areas of cooperation include developing combined train, accommodation and tourism packages, developing the existing tourism health-care chain, examining markets in Central Asian countries, jointly participating in domestic and international roadshows, designing short-term practical training courses and assessing opportunities to expand accommodation facilities in line with market demand.
Akbar Ghamkhar, chairman of the Iran Tour Operators Association, said the tourism market offered several areas for cooperation with HEGTA, including pent-up demand for travel in the post-war period, health and pilgrimage tourism, rail tourism, Central Asian markets, and leisure travel programs for government employees and retirees.
He also emphasized the use of HEGTA’s accommodation and rail networks to develop new travel packages.
Ghamkhar said closer links among different players in the health tourism chain, combined with the capabilities of professional tour operators, could help expand inbound tourism.
Referring to the success of 37 members of the association in receiving export awards last year, he described the achievement as an opportunity to expand international tourism markets. He also called for joint participation in roadshows, specialized practical training programs and the provision of accommodation incentives.
Alireza Tabesh, HEGTA’s chief executive, for his part, welcomed the proposals and said the Iran Tour Operators Association had considerable experience and knowledge of tourism markets that could be used to develop the holding’s international markets.
He pointed to the capacities of HEGTA and its subsidiaries in accommodation, rail transportation, tourism, training and investment, stressing the need for practical and economically viable cooperation between the two organizations.
“HEGTA has considerable capacities, while the Tour Operators Association understands the market and has experience in marketing and selling tourism products,” Tabesh said. “If these two capacities are brought together, new products can be designed and offered to the market.”
The meeting concluded with an agreement to establish a joint working group aimed to examine target markets and design at least three joint tourism products on a pilot basis, preparing them for implementation and sale.

The Rs 2.05 crore question: Can Meta be blamed for what its glasses record?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:46:37 UTC
22:46:37 KST

Secretly filmed by Meta glasses: Why a Delhi man is demanding Rs 2.05 crore (Reuters image)
A Delhi man has sent a legal notice to an Instagram creator and Meta Platforms after he was allegedly harassed and covertly filmed at a café using Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses.The footage was subsequently posted on Instagram and viewed more than 4.19 lakh times.He has demanded that the video be removed, an apology issued and ₹2.05 crore paid in damages.But the notice, issued on August 24, goes beyond the actions of the creator. It seeks to hold Meta responsible in two capacities: as the owner of Instagram, which allegedly continued to host the reel after receiving complaints, and as the technology company behind the design and marketing of the camera-equipped glasses used to record it.The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), which provided the victim pro bono legal assistance, says this is, to its knowledge, among the first legal actions in India to directly raise the liability of a smart-glasses maker for harm allegedly enabled by its product design.The case has not been decided by a court yet and the claims in the notice, so far, remain allegations. The man, whose identity has been withheld and who is referred to as X, is represented by advocate Apar Gupta.
So, what allegedly happened?
According to IFF, X was sitting alone at a Costa Coffee outlet in Delhi’s Khan Market on July 24 when a stranger, who eventually turned out to be a creator, approached him.The creator allegedly pestered and insulted him with unsolicited questions and remarks and followed him inside the café. X complained to the staff and eventually moved to another seating area to get away from the unpleasant situation thrust upon him.What he did not know, IFF says, was that the encounter was allegedly being recorded through Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses. One or more of the creator’s associates also allegedly filmed the exchange from other angles without his knowledge or consent.The footage was posted as an Instagram reel on July 26. By August 6, according to IFF, it had received more than 4.19 lakh views, approximately 15,700 likes and over 500 comments.X reported both the video and the account to Instagram on July 27. According to IFF, the reporting menu offered no category specifically covering invasion of privacy or non-consensual recording. The victim, therefore, selected “bullying or harassment”.He also submitted a separate complaint to Meta’s grievance officer for India under “Privacy violation — sharing of personal information or representation without consent.”Instagram subsequently informed him that the reported material doesn’t go against its “Community Standards”, according to IFF.
Why has Meta been named?
The most significant part of the notice concerns the glasses themselves.Developed by Meta in partnership with eyewear company EssilorLuxottica, Ray-Ban Meta glasses resemble conventional eyewear but allow users to take photographs and record videos hands-free. They were launched in India in May 2025 at a starting price of ₹29,900.The glasses have a small white capture LED on the front that indicates when the camera is being used. The notice argues that this warning is inadequate because it can easily be missed by someone who does not know that the glasses contain a camera.“The recording indicator on the said devices is inadequate and easily overlooked, and the harm that eventuated to our client is due to a design that is foreseeably enabled,” the notice states.It argues that Meta “owed and breached a duty of care” to X and was negligent in contributing to the alleged intrusion into his privacy.Crucially, the notice argues that this liability arises from Meta’s own product-design and marketing decisions and is therefore separate from its role as an online intermediary.
Section 79 of the Information Technology Act provides conditional protection to online intermediaries against liability for content posted by third parties. The notice contends that such protection cannot extend to a negligence claim arising from Meta’s own product design.That argument has not yet been tested in court.The Delhi dispute could now test a different question: whether a company that makes wearable cameras has a responsibility not merely to indicate that recording is taking place, but to ensure that an unsuspecting bystander can reasonably understand that they are being filmed.To know more, subscribe and read the full story on TOI+ —Secretly filmed by Meta glasses: Why a Delhi man is demanding Rs 2.05 crore

Beyond the Mecca Agreement: The emerging architecture of regional security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:46:25 UTC
22:46:25 KST

Dr. Khaled Mohammed Batarfi is an Assistant Professor at Al-Faisal University in Saudi Arabia.
The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan on Aug. 7, 2026 may eventually be remembered less for the three countries that founded it than for the security architecture it set in motion.
Its most striking provision is straightforward: an armed attack against one member is to be regarded as an attack against all. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has compared the principle technically to Article 5 of the NATO Treaty. Yet reducing the Mecca Agreement to an "Islamic NATO" would be misleading. NATO emerged from the particular strategic circumstances of post-war Europe, under American leadership and against an identifiable adversary. The Mecca Agreement has emerged from a very different environment: a multipolar region in which states increasingly seek greater strategic autonomy while maintaining multiple, sometimes competing, international partnerships.
The agreement is therefore better understood not as the finished product of a new military bloc, but as the possible foundation of a new model of regional security.
Its three founders bring exceptionally complementary assets to the table. Saudi Arabia contributes economic weight, political influence and a strategic location connecting the Gulf, Red Sea and wider Arab world. Türkiye brings one of the region's largest and most experienced armed forces, NATO experience and an increasingly sophisticated defense industry. Pakistan contributes a large, battle-tested military establishment, extensive strategic experience and, uniquely among Muslim-majority states, nuclear weapons. But military capabilities alone do not make an alliance. The real test begins after the signing ceremony.
The immediate challenge for the Mecca Agreement is institutionalization. Türkiye has already indicated that the agreement will establish high-level political and military coordination involving foreign and defense ministers and senior military commanders. Plans also envisage joint exercises across land, sea and air, cooperation in cyber capabilities, unmanned systems, electronic warfare and artificial intelligence, and greater integration in defense production and technology transfer. A secretariat is expected to be established in Saudi Arabia. These details matter more than dramatic comparisons with NATO.
Collective defense becomes credible only when political commitments are supported by mechanisms capable of implementing them. The three countries will eventually have to address intelligence sharing, command and control, interoperability, contingency planning, air and missile defense, logistics, maritime security and the procedures governing consultation during a crisis. Most importantly, they must clarify what constitutes an attack triggering collective action and what form that action might take.
An alliance does not necessarily require every member to enter every war fought by another member. Political support, intelligence, logistics, weapons, air defense, naval deployment or direct military intervention represent very different levels of commitment. The credibility of the Mecca Agreement will depend on whether its members can develop sufficient clarity without surrendering the strategic flexibility that made the agreement politically possible in the first place. That is particularly important because Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan do not have identical threat perceptions.
Pakistan’s security priorities are heavily influenced by its relationship with India. Türkiye’s strategic concerns extend from Syria and Iraq to the Eastern Mediterranean and Black Sea. Saudi Arabia’s immediate security environment includes the Gulf, Yemen, the Red Sea and threats from missiles, drones and non-state actors. The strength of the agreement will therefore lie not in pretending that these interests are identical, but in determining where they converge.
The next question is whether three will become four or eventually considerably more. Egypt is the most obvious candidate.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has publicly raised the possibility of Egyptian participation, while Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has described Cairo as a natural partner. Egypt already participates with Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan in the emerging four-country consultation framework known as the R4. Strategically, Egyptian participation would significantly change the character of the agreement.
Egypt controls the Suez Canal and sits at the junction of the Mediterranean, Red Sea, Africa and Arab Middle East. It possesses the Arab world’s largest population and one of its largest military establishments. Its accession would also transform the Mecca Agreement from a trilateral arrangement linking three major non-contiguous powers into a security framework containing two of the central Arab states.
Yet Cairo has reasons for caution. Egypt has traditionally guarded its freedom of action and maintains important relationships with the US, Europe and other regional actors. Joining a collective-defense treaty carries obligations substantially greater than participating in political consultation or joint exercises.
Beyond Egypt, several Arab states could develop closer relationships with the new framework. Gulf countries such as Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain, together with Jordan, already maintain substantial defense relationships with one or more of the three founders. But enlargement need not follow a NATO-style process in which every partner becomes a full treaty member. The Mecca framework could instead develop in concentric circles. At its center would be states accepting the collective-defense commitment. Around them could emerge associate partners participating in military exercises, maritime security, intelligence cooperation or air and missile defense. A wider circle could involve defense-industrial cooperation, training, counterterrorism and strategic consultation. This may ultimately prove more effective than rapid expansion.
The success of the Mecca Agreement should not be measured primarily by how many flags are added to it, but by how much genuine political and military integration develops beneath those flags.
Any significant change in the regional balance inevitably generates reactions. But it would be premature to assume that the Mecca Agreement will automatically produce an opposing formal alliance. The Middle East today is not organized into two clearly defined camps.
Iran is the most obvious state whose strategic calculations will be affected. Yet the founders have repeatedly emphasized that the agreement is defensive and is not directed against Iran or any particular country. This distinction should not be dismissed as diplomatic language. Saudi Arabia has an interest in maintaining deterrence while preserving channels with Tehran, and neither Türkiye nor Pakistan has an interest in turning a collective-defense arrangement into a sectarian Sunni-Shia confrontation. If Tehran eventually perceives the agreement as threatening, its response is also unlikely to reproduce the Mecca structure. Iran historically relies on a combination of its own missile and military capabilities, bilateral relationships and networks of aligned armed actors. Its counterbalancing strategy may therefore remain asymmetric rather than treaty-based.
A second strategic reaction could develop around Israel. Israel will inevitably examine the implications of deeper military coordination among Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan, particularly if the arrangement expands into air defense, missile capabilities, advanced weapons production and intelligence cooperation. But here again, automatic bloc formation should not be assumed. Türkiye and Israel have profound political disagreements. Saudi Arabia has its own strategic calculations. Pakistan does not recognize Israel. Egypt and Jordan, if associated with the agreement, already have peace treaties with it. These differences illustrate why the emerging regional order cannot easily be divided into two military camps.
India represents another important variable. New Delhi has already indicated that it is assessing the implications of the Mecca Agreement for its national security and regional stability. Pakistan’s membership naturally gives India reason to examine the agreement carefully. But Saudi Arabia simultaneously maintains an important strategic and economic partnership with India, and Riyadh has little interest in importing the India-Pakistan confrontation into its broader foreign policy.
This points towards a larger conclusion: the most likely response to the Mecca Agreement may not be the creation of a rival alliance at all. Instead, regional and international powers are likely to hedge. States will strengthen some partnerships while preserving others. They will cooperate with one country on energy, another on security, another on technology and perhaps another on diplomacy. The result will be overlapping networks rather than a new bipolar Middle East.
Perhaps the most consequential question surrounding the agreement is what it says about the future American role in the region. It would be easy – but mistaken – to interpret the Mecca Agreement simply as evidence that Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan are moving away from the US.
All three retain substantial relationships with Washington. Türkiye remains a NATO member. Saudi-American defense cooperation remains extensive, while Pakistan has a long and complicated history of military cooperation with the US. Turkish officials have explicitly stated that the new agreement is intended to complement existing alliances rather than replace them.
US President Donald Trump’s reaction is particularly significant. Writing on Truth Social on August 16, Trump said he was “very happy” to see Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan sign the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. He described it as a “BIG, BOLD, AND IMPORTANT FIRST STEP” and presented it positively as evidence of countries in the region assuming greater responsibility for their own defense. The significance of Trump’s statement goes beyond its enthusiastic language. It provides a clear indication of presidential-level American political approval of the new arrangement. It also challenges the assumption that Washington must necessarily regard greater regional strategic autonomy as a threat to American influence.
On the contrary, an architecture in which capable regional partners assume a greater share of responsibility for their own defense can complement rather than replace their strategic relationships with the US. What is changing, therefore, is something subtler.
For decades, much of the regional security architecture rested on an implicit division of labor: local states maintained their national forces, but the ultimate strategic guarantee came from an external great power, principally the US. That model has been under increasing pressure.
Regional governments have experienced wars, attacks on infrastructure, disruptions to maritime routes and uncertainty about the timing and extent of outside intervention. At the same time, countries such as Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan have developed greater indigenous military, technological and diplomatic capabilities. The logical consequence is not necessarily the departure of America. It is the diversification of security.
Indeed, Trump’s response suggests that the emerging order need not be understood as post-American, but rather as less dependent on America – with Washington itself prepared to welcome greater regional responsibility for collective security.
Regional powers increasingly want strong relationships with Washington without total dependence on Washington. They also seek economic ties with China, diplomatic engagement with Russia and Europe, and stronger security partnerships among themselves. The Mecca Agreement fits this emerging pattern.
The greatest danger to the agreement may therefore come not from an opposing alliance but from disagreements within its own strategic geography.
A future India-Pakistan confrontation would test Saudi and Turkish interpretations of collective defense. A confrontation involving Türkiye in Syria or elsewhere could raise similar questions in Islamabad and Riyadh. Renewed attacks against Saudi territory by non-state actors would force the members to determine whether proxy warfare qualifies as an armed attack under the agreement.
Iran presents another test. The members share an interest in preventing attacks against their territory and in deterring destabilizing behavior, but they also share an interest in avoiding a major regional war.
Israel could become an even more complex issue. The Palestinian question generates considerable convergence among the three societies and governments, but their diplomatic and strategic relationships with Israel are far from identical. These are not arguments against the agreement. They are the normal problems that arise when political declarations become security institutions.
Indeed, managing these differences may become one of the Mecca Agreement's most valuable functions. An alliance is not merely a mechanism for fighting together. Properly designed, it is also a mechanism through which states consult one another, restrain escalation and prevent the security decisions of one member from unexpectedly dragging others into conflict.
The Mecca Agreement therefore should not be judged by whether it becomes another NATO. It probably will not – and does not need to. Its historical significance could lie elsewhere.
The emerging international order increasingly gives middle and regional powers greater room to organize their own security arrangements. Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan are large enough to influence their respective regions, but none can independently construct a stable security order stretching from South Asia through the Gulf and Red Sea to the Mediterranean. Together, however, they create an unusual strategic bridge.
If Egypt eventually joins, and if other Arab and Muslim states develop structured relationships around the agreement, that bridge could become the foundation of something substantially larger: not a rigid military bloc and certainly not a sectarian alliance, but a network of regional deterrence.
Such an arrangement would neither eliminate American influence nor necessarily challenge Western alliances. Trump’s welcoming reaction reinforces that distinction. Greater regional self-reliance and continued strategic partnership with Washington need not be contradictory objectives.
Instead, the agreement could reflect a transition from a system in which regional security was overwhelmingly guaranteed from outside to one in which regional states assume a greater share of responsibility themselves. That distinction may ultimately prove to be the most important consequence of the Mecca Agreement.
The geopolitical question after the Mecca Agreement is therefore not simply who will join. It is whether the agreement can reconcile collective security with strategic autonomy; whether it can deter aggression without creating new confrontation; and whether states with different interests can build enough common ground to manage an increasingly fragmented regional order. If it succeeds, the Mecca Agreement may represent something more consequential than the birth of another alliance. It may mark the beginning of a regional security architecture in which outside powers remain important—but are no longer indispensable to every equation.

Second drone brigade in two months: Ukraine is forming the 446th Unmanned Systems Brigade

22:46:16 KST

Ukraine's Armed Forces are forming the 446th Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade, which is recruiting servicemembers while formation continues, MilitaryLand reported. The new unit joins a force that hit 32,485 Russian personnel over the summer alone, the Unmanned Systems Forces (SBS) reported on 1 September.
Ukraine is facing a shortage of military personnel, yet the Armed Forces are forming their second separate unmanned systems brigade this year. The force's commander wants unmanned systems covering the entire front at tactical, operational, and strategic depths.
What is known about the 446th Brigade
Military personnel from other units can apply for a transfer through Army+, according to MilitaryLand.
The first of the two was the 445th Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade Chata, whose formation became known in July. Both units are recruiting for posts running from operators of ground robots, FPV, bomber, and interceptor drones to psychological-support officers, analysts, and accountants, Militarnyi reported.
The deployment of such units is part of the Ukrainian Armed Forces' broader effort to increase the number of unmanned systems in the military. Ukrainian drones accounted for about 96% of Russian casualties in March—33,988 of roughly 35,000 killed or severely wounded—Zelenskyy said in April.
Why Ukraine is turning to drones
The expansion of unmanned systems brigades is part of a broader effort initiated by Robert Brovdi, callsign Madyar, to increase the role of the SBS within Ukraine's Defense Forces, Militarnyi notes.
Brovdi told Reuters in June that he wants to raise the drone forces from about 2.5% of Ukraine's armed forces to 5%, a goal he first stated publicly in September 2025. At that share, the drone units accounted for roughly a third of Russian losses over the previous 12 months, according to figures the force gave Reuters, which said it could not verify them independently.
Then Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Oleksandr Syrskyi described unmanned systems as one of the key factors shaping modern warfare. Current Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapatyi stated that one of his priorities is the development and scaling of the unmanned component.
Overall, the SBS struck 58,465 targets in August, its own tally for 1–31 August shows.

Israeli media have reported that Netanyahu’s eldest son spent much of the previous several years living in the Miami area, where his reportedly lavish lifestyle and state-funded security detail repeatedly came under scrutiny in Israel amid the ongoing genocidal war in Gaza.
His extended stay abroad drew criticism following the outbreak of the war after Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack, according to The Times of Israel, with critics in Israel questioning why the prime minister’s son remained overseas while hundreds of thousands of Israelis were serving as military reservists.
Meanwhile, the reported visit by Shin Bet chief David Zini, a controversial far-right figure who reportedly opposed ending the nearly three-year Gaza war, would mark his first foreign trip since taking over as head of Israel’s internal security agency in October 2025.
His predecessor, Ronen Bar, announced his resignation last June after weeks of tensions with Netanyahu.

Kazakh president says Astana ready to advance transport initiatives across SCO
Unknown

2026-09-01

Burc Eruygur
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said Tuesday that his country is ready to help advance transport initiatives across the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), describing geographical connectivity among member states as a strategic advantage.
“Kazakhstan is ready to facilitate the promotion of transport initiatives throughout the Shanghai Cooperation Organization,” Tokayev said in an address to the organization’s Council of Heads of State meeting in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek.
Tokayev said Kazakhstan attaches “great importance” to integrating the Belt and Road Initiative, the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, the North-South Corridor and the “promising trade routes between Central and South Asia.”
He also proposed developing and adopting an SCO “Strategy for Transport Connectivity” through 2035.
Tokayev described the SCO as a “truly successful, influential, sought-after international structure,” saying it represents a unique combination of countries that are “diverse in essence but united in spirit.”
He said that amid the emergence of a new architecture of international relations, the SCO is taking on “particular significance,” expressing confidence that the results of the meeting would contribute to further strengthening the organization’s international standing, “enhance its effectiveness and shape clear strategic interests in a changing global reality.”
The Kazakh president also proposed holding an SCO ministerial conference on strategic stability, whose agenda could include reducing military risks, containing a new arms race and preventing dangerous incidents.
“Of particular concern is the fact that the consequences of armed conflicts are already extending beyond the immediate combat zones, affecting international markets, commercial shipping, and the stability of energy and transport links,” Tokayev said.
He added that these developments have significantly increased the risk of “cross-border crisis spillover,” while the fight against terrorism, extremism and separatism remains a priority for SCO cooperation.
“These threats are increasingly intertwined with transnational crime, drug trafficking, illegal arms trafficking, and cyber threats,” he added.

Former U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer Steps Down From Parliament. Read His Full Statement Here

Keir Starmer, who resigned as Britain's Prime Minister in June, announced Tuesday he will also be stepping down from Parliament to focus on international affairs.
Speaking to Camden New Journal, Starmer—who led the Labour Party to a landslide victory in 2024—said it had “been a huge honor and privilege” to serve as the Member of Parliament (MP) for Holborn and St. Pancras in North London for the past 11 years.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham paid tribute to Starmer during his first address to parliament since taking over leadership of the nation, crediting Starmer for securing one of Labour's "best victories" and creating a "platform to change this country for the better."
A by-election will now take place to replace Starmer as MP, with details to be finalized on the contenders and exact date.
Shortly after the news broke, Starmer shared a statement via social media, further explaining the reasons behind his departure.
You can read his words in full, below:
“Over the summer, I have had time to reflect and consider my future. I have decided that now is the right time to step down as MP for Holborn and St Pancras and hand the baton over to a successor.
It’s been an honor and privilege to represent the best constituency in the country since taking over from the great Frank Dobson 11 years ago. But it is now time to step aside and focus on other issues: international affairs including defense, security, trade and technology in a fast changing world. I will also continue working with others as I have done over many decades to tackle violence against women and girls.
As I do that, I will always remain immensely proud to have represented the place Vic, the kids and I call home.
I look back with pride on what my constituency team and I have delivered in Holborn and St Pancras since 2015 and I thank all those who I was privileged to work with on so many issues of local concern: affordable housing projects, delivering first class education and tackling youth violence through our Camden Youth Safety Taskforce.
I want to thank my CLP team who have always stood firmly by me, and given me the support I needed as I stood for Leader of the Labour Party and then as I took my Party from political, moral and financial ruin to an historic landslide election win in 2024 and two years as Prime Minister when we stabilised the economy, rebuilt our public services, invested record amounts in our defense and security, began lifting hundreds of thousands of children out of poverty and transformed Britain’s reputation with international partners.
I want to thank my constituency staff who, throughout all those 11 years, have worked tirelessly on casework and helped me do my utmost to serve the people of Holborn and St Pancras. I could not have done this job without them.
There will now be a process to appoint my successor ahead of a by-election. Whoever is lucky enough to become the Labour candidate here will have my full support and backing and I will continue to give my full support to the Prime Minister and this Labour government.”
Starmer's final months at Downing Street
Starmer announced his resignation as Prime Minister and head of the Labour Party in June following months of scrutiny over his leadership.
The one-time lawyer initially fought against calls from within his own party to step down over his handling of the appointment of Peter Mandelson, the former British ambassador to the U.S. who held a yearslong correspondence with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
After it was revealed in April that Mandelson had failed the security vetting in January 2025, only for his appointment as ambassador to go ahead the following month anyway on account of the Foreign Office overruling the decision, Starmer faced tough questions in parliament. Starmer denied having prior knowledge of the failed vetting process, telling parliament that “a deliberate decision was taken to withhold that material” from him.
Starmer weathered the storm, but faced renewed calls to step down in May, after Labour's poor performance in local polls.
Amid a flurry of ministerial resignations from his Cabinet, speculation grew as to who could might potentially challenge and replace Starmer. When Burnham—who had been open about his desire to launch a leadership challenge—cleared his own path back to Westminster through winning the Makerfield by-election, Starmer announced his departure.
Starmer endured a splintered relationship with Trump towards the end
Soon after Trump returned to the White House in early 2025, Starmer paid a visit to Washington, D.C., and presented the U.S. President with an invitation from King Charles for a second historic state visit to the U.K.
Downing Street later secured one of the first international agreements with Washington following Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs, marking the early success of the relationship between the two world leaders.
Trump and Starmer’s partnership was further strengthened when the President traveled to the U.K. in September, as the pair went on to sign a "groundbreaking" billion-dollar U.K.-U.S. Tech Prosperity Deal.
But cracks started to appear earlier this year, as Starmer was among the European leaders to staunchly oppose Trump’s threats to annex Greenland. Another disagreement occurred when Trump downplayed NATO’s contributions in the war in Afghanistan, prompting a public rebuke from Starmer.
Relations further splintered when Trump repeatedly lambasted Starmer for refusing to actively involve the U.K. in the Iran war.
“He ruins relationships. We are very surprised. This is not Winston Churchill that we're dealing with,” Trump said of Starmer in March.
Weeks later, the British Prime Minister admitted he was “fed up” with the President’s war in Iran and the detrimental financial impact it was having on the U.K.

From ghost launching to broligarchy: The tech terms defining the current digital era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:43:26 UTC
22:43:26 KST

As the digital landscape evolves, more new tech terms have surfaced, covering everything from the overwhelming presence of AI to the rising power of tech bros.
The last few years have seen the digital sphere expand considerably, supported by the rapid progress in cloud, artificial intelligence and next-gen interfaces. This has led to new tech terms popping up faster than we can keep up.
The inclusion of digitally-native Gen Z employees in the workforce has also supported this shift, calling for catchier tech terms across the digital and corporate landscape.
These are some of our favourite tech terms that you never knew you needed to know.
Ghost launch
Ghost-launching is when a product or startup is quietly released into the market without any kind of hype, public announcements, marketing campaigns or build-up.
This is mainly done to be able to judge real-life consumer behaviour quietly, without any pressure, by letting the product sit on an app store, website, or platform like Product Hunt and assess organic traction.
In many cases, it is also done to monitor real-world performance and usage for glitches without the pressure of a massive audience.
By eliminating the psychological fear of failure, it can also help founders avoid the perfection trap by endlessly delaying a project and forcing them to ship what is ready.
However, on the flip side, a ghost launch can also result in total silence, invisibility and user indifference.
Broligarchy
Broligarchy refers to a small group of extremely rich and powerful men, or tech bros, like Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg and Peter Thiel, who essentially use their immense wealth to gain political power.
Instead of just hiring lobbyists, these leaders usually take direct roles or build closer ties with key political figures to influence regulations, gain funding or acquire other lucrative contracts.
For example, Elon Musk spent hundreds of millions of dollars supporting the US presidential campaign and also acted briefly as the senior advisor to the President and de facto head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).
Similarly, Peter Thiel has been credited with launching Vice President JD Vance’s political career, while his data mining company Palantir secured billions worth of defence and government contracts.
AI-horning
AI-horning refers to AI features being present in anything and everything you use or want to do online these days. This starts from Google’s AI overview while searching to Instagram’s AI images and Spotify’s AI DJ.
This has extended to businesses that do not really need AI, including it just to hop onto the bandwagon and objectively making their services worse, more expensive and more confusing for consumers.
Some examples include confusing and incomplete navigation features that lead you to the middle of nowhere, along with chatbots that never seem to answer your actual questions while plying you with automated, templated nonsense.
Quit shaming
Have you ever tried to cancel a subscription and been hit with an endless wave of pages asking you increasingly desperate questions about why exactly you are going and what they can do to make you stay?
Congrats — you have just been quit-shamed.
Most of us know the rising frustration of having to click "no" for every offer a platform throws at you to not cancel: pauses, discounts, a bundle offer and so much more.
Having to call someone in order to cancel a subscription instead of simply clicking on an unsubscribe button has sadly become all too common now.
Algospeak
As more social media and digital platforms impose stricter content and censorship rules, algospeak has seen a distinct rise in the last few months.
This is essentially a way of self-censorship to avoid being banned or shadow-banned, where online creators and users use safe or coded language to bypass strict automated content filters. This can be substitute words and alternate spellings but can also be emojis in some cases.
For example, saying "unalive" instead of die, "seggs" instead of sex, "pew pew" for a gun or firearm and "leg booty" for the LGBTQ+ community.
While this can help bypass content rules in the short term, it highlights a deeper and more fundamental problem in how these automated filters identify explicit or banned content.
Subscription Creep
Another occurrence that may seem all too familiar now is subscription creep.
This is the gradual, stealthy accumulation of tiny monthly software and subscription fees that quietly drain your bank account on the backend until you suddenly realise you are paying dozens of euros for services and tools you never use.
This has been made far worse by subscriptions being added to a growing list of services that you do need, so you are left with no choice but to cough up. Think video doorbells, fitness trackers, printers, gaming consoles and so much more, which all quickly add up.
Enshittification
Sadly, we have all come across some form of enshittification or the other in recent years. This is the gradual, deliberate breakdown in the quality of a digital platform or service over time as they prioritise higher profits.
One example is social media platforms with feeds shifting away from content posted by actual friends and family towards more intrusive tracking, targeted ads and algorithm clickbait.
Similarly, several search engines now prioritise paid advertisements over relevant results, while online marketplaces promote sponsored listings that can crowd out genuine product options.
This can even extend to smart hardware like printers, tractors and other appliances, which may receive software updates that introduce subscription paywalls or block third-party repairs.

11 EU States Push to End Foreign Policy Vetoes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:42:00 UTC
22:42:00 KST

Eleven European Union countries are pushing to end what they call “obstructive” vetoes in the bloc’s foreign policy, urging the EU to explore replacing unanimity with qualified majority voting.
Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Romania, Spain and Sweden signed a joint letter addressed to EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, Euronews reported on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The Union’s culture of consensus is an important source of its legitimacy. Therefore, we continue to strive for consensus wherever possible,” the countries wrote.
“But we must also ensure that this culture of consensus fosters common action rather than preventing it – otherwise we will have legitimacy but no strength.”
Under current EU rules, foreign policy decisions generally require the unanimous approval of all 27 member states, meaning a single country can block a decision supported by the other 26.
The signatories argue that the EU needs to act faster and more effectively in response to growing strategic competition, instability and challenges to the rules-based international order.
5 principles for EU foreign policy
The countries proposed five principles to improve the bloc’s decision-making:
- uphold sincere cooperation and mutual solidarity
- increase the use of constructive abstentions instead of vetoes
- avoid linking foreign policy decisions to substantially unrelated issues
- explore options under EU treaties to move from unanimity to qualified majority voting
- require “substantiated vital reasons” to block such a move
What Changed in Russia’s Drone War in Ukraine?
“The legal framework for all five principles is already in place. It is solely up to us to put them into action and thus advance our foreign policy,” the letter said.
The proposal could involve activating the so-called passerelle clause under Article 31 of the EU treaties, allowing a shift from unanimity to qualified majority voting in certain foreign policy areas.
Supporters argue that the change would speed up decision-making and prevent individual countries from using vetoes to extract concessions. Critics say it could weaken democratic legitimacy, while smaller EU states view the veto as an important safeguard for their national interests.
The proposal itself faces a major obstacle: moving from unanimity to qualified majority voting would require unanimity, meaning countries opposed to the reform could potentially block it.
The push has gained momentum following the defeat of former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, whose government repeatedly used Hungary’s veto to obstruct EU decisions.
Germany and France have also discussed a plan to strengthen Kallas’ role while placing her under the direct supervision of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The road to Dunesday: Euronews Culture's massive Fall movie preview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:40:52 UTC
22:40:52 KST

The road to Dunesday: Euronews Culture's massive Fall movie preview
There's still plenty of cinematic goodness to look forward to in the last four months of 2026. Here are our picks for the hotly awaited movies you won't want to miss.
Summer blockbuster season is over and that can only mean one thing: it’s time to look ahead to this year’s slate of fall movies.
That and everyone is going to start stocking up on pumpkin spice everything. Good luck and don't overdo it. Or do - we don't give a frappe.
Considering we’ve already had eight months full of cinematic goodness - from horror hits Obsession and Backrooms to literal epics - and a box-office shattering summer courtesy of Spider-Man: Brand New Day, 2026 is looking like it's going to be one for the books. Especially since the last four months of the year are mighty promising, all leading to a single day in December when both of 2026’s biggest blockbusters open simultaneously...
Until then, it’s an extremely compelling but very crowded release schedule... With that in mind, Euronews Culture is making it a little easier for you by selecting the films that should be on your radar between September and December. Release dates vary throughout Europe, so we’ve ordered the picks as chronologically as possible. And if you don’t see this year’s Palme d’Or winner Fjord or the majestic Fatherland below, it’s because they've already been released in certain European territories and we’ve covered them already. You’re welcome.
Without further ado, these are the hotly awaited titles coming to the screen this fall that you won’t want to miss.
SEPTEMBER
Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger
While the Madferit lot are waiting for new tour dates in 2027, they’ll have a documentary about the Oasis Live ‘25 reunion tour to keep them happy. It opens at this year’s Venice Film Festival and has been billed as “an unapologetically uplifting account of the biggest musical event of 2025, capturing the experience and emotions of the band and their fans across the world.” It hits cinemas this month and will stream exclusively on Disney+ later this year.
Practical Magic 2
It’s been nearly 30 years since Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman played witchy siblings Sally and Gillian... Now they’re back, alongside returning cast members Dianne Wiest and Stockard Channing, as well as newbies Joey King, Lee Pace and Maisie Williams. This time, they’re wrestling with a multi-generational curse haunting the family lineage. As a sizeable bonus, the sequel is directed by the wonderful Susanne Bier (Open Hearts, In A Better World, The Night Manager) - so we’re expecting big things. Witch-ful thinking?
Resident Evil
Being a video game fan is a tough gig when it comes to film adaptations, and we’ve already had seven Resident Evil films since 2002... All of which range from averge to piss poor. None, however, have been co-written and directed by Zach Cregger, the man behind Barbarian and last year’s underwear-soiling Weapons. Billed as a (much-needed) new take on the franchise, we’re curious to see whether Cregger’s leap from indie scares to franchise frights may break the console-to-theatre curse.
Primetime
What a time to be Robert Pattinson. This year, he’s been a hapless groom-to-be in The Drama, a sniveling suitor in The Odyssey, and he’s capping off the year as a power-hungry plotter in Dune: Part Three. Before that, he’s playing Chris Hansen, the host of the morally questionable reality TV series To Catch a Predator. He’ll be directed by documentarian Lance Oppenheim, marking his narrative-feature debut after Some Kind of Heaven and Spermworld. The trailer looks promising - and gives off Nightcrawler vibes... Could an Oscar nomination be coming for R-Patz?
OCTOBER
Verity
The Hathayear continues... After Mother Mary, The Devil Wears Prada 2, The Odyssey and The End Of Oak Street, Anne Hathaway stars in her fifth feature of 2026. She plays a famous author whose unfinished book series brings a struggling writer (Dakota Johnson) into her home... And closer to her hubby (Josh Hartnett). Verity is the adaptation of the novel by Colleen Hoover (“It Ends With Us”), which has been described as a “gothic, psychosexual thriller in the vein of Rebecca and Gone Girl.” Sounds mighty promising... If you choose to ignore the trainwreck that was 2024’s It Ends With Us. Let’s hope Verity doesn’t derail a stellar year for its leading lady.
Digger
Will Digger be the film that finally bags Tom Cruise an Oscar? The first trailer for Alejandro González Iñárritu’s hotly anticipated new film has given audiences a first look at Cruise’s most transformative and least recognisable role since Tropic Thunder. He stars as Digger Rockwell, a powerful Texas oil man who “embarks on a frantic mission to prove that he is humanity’s saviour before the disaster he’s unleashed destroys everything”. The satirical tone recalls Dr. Strangelove, and it certainly looks like Cruise is taking one of the biggest swings of his career, looking to remind audiences that he’s more than just a running-jumping-fighting action star.
The Social Reckoning
The timing of this sequel’s release couldn’t be more opportune. Following recent headlines regarding Meta’s landmark billion dollar settlement and Mark Zuckerberg’s vile plan to replace his staff with AI, we get a very timely companion piece to David Fincher’s Oscar-winning The Social Network. Jeremy Strong takes over from Jesse Eisenberg as the Facebook founder in Aaron Sorkin’s film about Zuckerberg’s continuing woes. Strong certainly has that vacant / "Is he human?" / "Probably a soulless droid" stare down... The Social Reckoning focuses on whistleblower Frances Haugen (Oscar-winning Anora star Mikey Madison), who went public about Facebook’s algorithmic wrongdoings and active promotion of false information. Here’s hoping Sorkin can deliver another exhilarating screenplay and that he live up to Fincher’s superb work behind the camera.
Klara And The Sun
Based on Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel of the same name, Klara And The Sun is Taika Waititi’s bid to get back into Hollywood’s good books, following the back-to-back disappointments of Thor: Love And Thunder and Next Goal Wins. Set in a dystopian future, Jenna Ortega plays Klara, a solar-powered companion android yearning to bond with Josie (Mia Tharia), the sick girl for whom she was purchased. Let’s see if Waititi can harness his humour to work in favour of the source material, and that the big screen adaptation track record when it comes to Ishiguro’s works doesn’t get its first blemish.
Minotaur
Following its Grand Prix win at Cannes this year, Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur gets a staggered European release across October and November. Based on the 1969 French film La Femme Infidèle by Claude Chabrol, the story is set in 2022 and follows an affluent Russian business executive who discovers his wife’s infidelity and sets out to kill her younger lover. Echoes from Cannes have been overwhelmingly positive, with praise directed not only at Zvyagintsev but also at Iris Lebedeva and Dmitriy Mazurov, who play the couple navigating betrayal and corruption in Putin’s Russia.
Ali G: Who Iz I?
Does anyone care about Ali G anymore? Sacha Baron Cohen seems to think so, having unretired his Channel 4 / Ali G Indahouse (2002) character for a new mockumentary. Shot in secret and marking Baron Cohen’s directorial debut, Ali G: Who Iz I? has already faced considerable backlash even before its release. The painfully unfunny trailer has led many campaigners to try to get the film pulled from cinemas. They argue that the “outdated” and “racist” stereotypes don’t cut it, even if they are presented as satire. Time will tell whether the film is any good, but it’s bound to be one of the most talked about releases of October. Just maybe not in a good way.
Clayface
One of 2026’s big Halloween releases is, rather surprisingly, a DC Comics movie. Directed by James Watkins (Eden Lake, Speak No Evil) from a screenplay by the ever-reliable Mike Flanagan, Clayface gives us the origin story of the Batman villain with a gloopy face. It sees a famous young actor who is left horribly disfigured and turns to a scientist (Naomi Achie) so she can perform a cutting-edge skin treatment to return him to his former self. The side effects look gnarly. The creepy trailers show that Watkins and Co. have committed to body horror (clap clap clap), and certain sequences already look like they’ll leave audiences squirming in their seats. A certain LITERAL eye-opening scene on board an airplane looks set to churn a fair few stomachs.
Hope
A police chief, a rookie cop and a group of hunters try to track down and kill a mysterious kaiju-style creature that's laying waste to a Korean village. What’s not to love? South Korean writer-director Na Hong-Jin’s highly anticipated creature-feature comes 10 years since his horror gem The Wailing, and the reception at Cannes was mixed. Messy and saddled with sub-par VFX for some; unhinged and high-octane for others. Oh, and both Michael Fassbender and Alicia Vikander turn up to play two of the creatures. Colour us intrigued.
Wicker
Another Halloween release this year looks mighty promising: a comedic fairytale starring Olivia Coleman as a fisherwoman ostracised by a rigid medieval farming town. Faced with crippling isolation, she commissions herself a husband made out of wicker (Alexander Skarsgård). As you do. Based on a short story by Ursula Wills-Jones, this atypical romance directed by Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer seems to tick all the boxes. Coleman doing comedy? Tick. A weird, satirical and vulgar folk tale featuring a husband who’s “strong as a tree and just as hard” and plenty of F-bombs? Tick. Skarsgård playing bedworthy basketry who the townspeople want to climb like a tree? Tick. Prepare for this one to unlock a few subconscious kinks.
NOVEMBER
Godzilla Minus Zero
This sequel to 2023’s Oscar-winning hit Godzilla Minus One continues its predecessor’s story, with Japanese writer / director Takashi Yamazaki returning to hopefully deliver another impressive kaiju spectacle. Considering Minus One was one of the best Godzilla films ever made – an impressive feat considering there have been 39 by our calculations – there's every reason to believe Yamazaki will deliver the goods once more. Minus Zero is also Japan’s first-ever production to be filmed for IMAX, and the synopsis sounds... appropriate: “War reduced Japan to zero, and Godzilla plunged it into minus. Two years have passed since then, and the country has faced agonizing struggles to achieve recovery and finally reclaim its daily life. Just as humanity managed to cling to a hard-won peace, a new threat strikes, crushing hope in an instant. There is no third time. Everything ends here.” Bring the noise.
Wild Horse Nine
Following the multi-award-winning The Banshees of Inisherin, Martin McDonagh is back with another black comedy which seems to hark back to his very own In Bruges. Out with two bickering hitmen in Belgium and in with a squabbling pair of CIA agents (John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell) stirring shit up on Easter Island prior to the 1973 Chilean coup. The ensemble piece is Venice-bound and features the likes of Steve Buscemi, Parker Posey, Mariana di Girolamo and the great and powerful Tom Waits. This one can’t come soon enough.
Ebenezer
Marketed as both a twisted reimagining of “A Christmas Carol” from horror director Ti West (The Innkeepers, the X trilogy) and Johnny Depp’s big screen comeback, Ebenezer could be either a bold Christmas Gothic or a reheated Dickensian dud. A lot depends on whether audiences will welcome Depp back. While initial reactions to his prosthetic-caked transformation as Ebenezer Scrooge have been positive, the ghosts of his past have not been forgotten by some. Open minds and all that, but the far-too-meta trailer lays it on mighty thick: “He brought us Jack Sparrow, Edward Scissorhands and the Mad Hatter. This November, the master of misfits returns.” This is then followed by Depp whispering: “It’s good to be back.” We’ll see quite how good soon enough.
Paper Tiger
James Gray’s latest New York family saga is an 80s set crime story which seems perfectly fitted for the director behind Little Odessa, The Yards and We Own The Night. Paper Tiger follows two brothers who get caught up in a scheme involving the Russian mafia, and their dealings threaten not only their sibling bond but the whole suburban family unit. Starring Adam Driver, Miles Teller and Scarlett Johansson, this could be the A-lister packed film that finally gives Gray his overdue award recognition. Quite how The Lost City of Z and Armageddon Time didn’t bag him at least a Golden Baldie nomination, we’ll never know.
The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth
Quentin Tarantino didn’t want this to be his tenth and final film, according to the arbitrary rules that he’s set himself. Still, he wrote a sequel to Once Upon A Time In Hollywood centering on Brad Pitt’s stunt man Cliff Booth, and passed the project over to none other than David Fincher. On the plus side, this means we get another Fincher-Pitt team-up, following Se7en, Fight Club and The Curious Case of Benjamin Button. On the minus front, do we really need more? Once Upon A Time In Hollywood wasn’t QT’s best... Plus, there's the niggling question: Can Tarantino's voice and Fincher’s sensibility gel to make a winning combination? We’ll find out end of November, before the movie goes to streaming via Netflix on 23 December.
DECEMBER
La Bola Negra
Straddling the months of November and December when it comes to release dates in Europe, La Bola Negra was one of Cannes' most talked-about titles. Directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, this queer epic - inspired by the unfinished work of the same name by Spanish poet and playwright Federico García Lorca - earned both filmmakers the joint Best Director Palme alongside Paweł Pawlikowski for Fatherland. If it’s anywhere near as masterful as the latter, audiences are in for a treat. Spanning from Spain in the early 1930s to queer persecution during the turmoil of the civil war up until the 21st century, this sprawling epic could very well end up as the contender to beat when it comes to Best International Feature at next year's Oscars.
Ink
The opening film of this year’s Venice Film Festival is Danny Boyle’s Ink, which will hit select theatres in December and January, before streaming on Netflix early next year. Boyle’s Lido debut is a bio-drama adapted by James Graham from his 2017 stage play, about the early days of Rupert Murdoch amid the news mogul’s acquisition of The Sun. It stars Guy Pearce as the Australian newspaper magnate, Jack O’Connell as tabloid editor Larry Lamb, and Claire Foy as a fictional reporter. The synopsis, which promises a scathing and timely examination of the state of news reporting, states: “An explosive cinematic rollercoaster about a group of visionaries and misfits who had an idea for a new kind of news – one that would give the people what they wanted and would change the face of the world we live in today.” Since Boyle’s previous biographical drama, 2015’s Steve Jobs, led to numerous award nominations, we wouldn’t be surprised if Ink becomes a big contender throughout awards season.
Avengers: Doomsday
It’s been a rough five years for the world’s biggest movie franchise. The MCU has had more misses than hits in its post-Endgame era, and everyone was ready to be done with the overstuffed multiverse shenanigans. But apparently, superhero fatigue hasn’t peaked, judging by the record-breaking showing of Spider-Man: Brand New Day – which is now a bigger box office hit than Titanic. Still, the end of this year is truly make-or-break time for Marvel, who are leaving nothing to chance and going balls to the wall with what promises to be their biggest crossover epic yet. Everyone’s in for the ride: returning Endgame directors the Russo Brothers; the supposedly MCU retired Chris Evans and Robert Downey Jr.; The Fantastic Four; The Thunderbolts; the OG X-Men... It’s going to be one half of 2026’s biggest blockbuster extravaganza, and you just know it’ll obliterate the global box office. Records have already been broken, as pre-ticket sales have surpassed $35 million. You read correctly: even four months before its release, Doomsday has smashed advance sales records. Whether it lives up to the hype or becomes a cultural event like Endgame remains to be seen. What’s certain is that this adventure isn’t just about battling Doctor Doom; it’s the MCU’s fight to reclaim its title and prove it's still worth our time.
Dune: Part Three
If Avengers: Doomsday is one half of 2026’s massive blockbuster hoopla, the second is the third chapter of Denis Villeneuve’s Dune saga. Both films come out on the exact same day (18 December), leading many to predict a Barbenheimer-style double-bill event dubbed Dunesday. We’ll be indulging in this bladder-punishing day at the talkies come December, but truth be told, we’re far more excited about Dune: Part Three. It concludes the trilogy of adaptations of Frank Herbert’s Dune and is based on "Dune Messiah", in which emperor Paul Atreides’ holy war is getting waaay out of hand. Everyone’s back for the final chapter, including previously deceased Duncan Idaho (Jason Momoa) and some new faces (the ubiquitous Robert Pattison, Isaach de Bankolé, and Anya Taylor-Joy graduating from cameo to full-time player). Considering both Dune and Dune: Part Two were top-notch, this concluding chapter could very well make Villeneuve’s trilogy one for the ages. Only one question remains: Which out of Doomsday or Dune: Part Three will outgross the other at the box office?
There we have it. Which films are you most looking forward to? For up-to-date reviews of the latest film releases, head to Euronews Culture's Film of the Week section, and check out our picks for the Best Movies of 2026... So Far.

‘Worst yet to come’ as Hong Kong schools cut record 126 Primary One classes
Contraction hits Kwai Tsing hardest, where nearly half the district’s 31 primary schools forced to trim Primary One intake
Hong Kong public schools have slashed a record 126 Primary One classes for the 2026-27 academic year amid a shrinking student population, prompting a sector leader to warn that the “worst is yet to come”.
According to the latest Primary School Profiles, the total number of Primary One classes across public schools dropped from 1,558 in 2025-26 to 1,432 in 2026-27, representing a net decrease of 8 per cent.
The guide covers more than 500 local primary institutions and is compiled by the Committee on Home-School Co-operation to help parents select schools for their children.
The contraction hit Kwai Tsing the hardest, where nearly half the district’s 31 primary schools – 14 campuses – were forced to trim their Primary One intake. Tuen Mun and Eastern districts followed, each losing 13 classes.
The latest profiles of more than 500 primary institutions serve as reference materials for parents selecting schools for their children.
