‘Demonic oppression’ and ‘girly convos’: the podcast wooing young women back to Christianity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
12:00:58 UTC
21:00:58 KST

At first glance, the crowd gathering outside a music venue in Red Bank, New Jersey, could have passed for a group of sorority rush hopefuls – or Ella Langley fans on their way to the country star’s show. Most of them were under the age of 30. They wore cowboy boots, maxi sundresses and soft, bouncy blowouts, scrolling on their phones outside the doors as they waited for friends to arrive.
But one accessory gave them away: the Bibles they toted. These women were there to pray.
Specifically, they were there to see the Girls Gone Bible tour. Hosted by two “Bible-thumping bombshells” (per the Daily Mail), the Girls Gone Bible podcast is often sold as the conservative woman’s answer to Alex Cooper’s secular, sexual Call Her Daddy franchise. The hosts have “girly convo[s]” about some of the same issues you might hear on Call Her Daddy: dating dos and don’ts, going sober-curious, or battling insecurities. But Cooper never invited an Eastern Orthodox priest on to explain why the Greek church “makes manly men” or blamed the attention economy on Satan himself.
Since debuting in 2023, Girls Gone Bible has become a brand all its own, with more than 1 million followers on Instagram and ranking 42nd for the religion and spirituality genre on Spotify. Its Revival tour began in April, bringing evenings of music, prayer and religious testimony to the east coast, as well as Alabama, Tennessee and California.
Girls Gone Bible hosts Angela Halili, 30, and Arielle Reitsma, 36, call themselves “two imperfect girls serving an absolutely perfect God”, though neither grew up very religious or married into the faith. In fact, neither host is married, earning them relatability points among listeners who are still stuck in the dating scene. Both are relatively new Christians who spent their early careers as working actors in Los Angeles, a city usually depicted by conservatives as a den of sin. To that point: Reitsma played a character called “Slutty Girl” in the jukebox musical film Rock of Ages; Halili once appeared in a Marilyn Manson music video.
Both converted in moments of personal crisis. Halili told the Christian publication Relevant that her anxiety and alcoholism stemmed from the pressures of working in the industry, and she first “met” God in 2019 when she started praying to help her through an anxiety attack. Reitsma, meanwhile, walked into a church “on a whim” after a rough breakup and “found peace like [she’d] never known”.
The success of the podcast led to guest stints on Fox News segments about gen Z seeking faith. They opened Donald Trump’s “victory rally” the day before his 2025 inauguration with a prayer that included the lines “in the life of President Donald Trump, as it is in heaven” and “President Trump … we declare that no weapon formed against you will prosper.”
This association with the ascendant Christian right, of course, makes them Maga figures. But unlike podcasters in the conservative-aligned womanosphere who regularly toe the party line when it comes to topics such as immigration, abortion or birth control, Halili and Reitsma prefer a more lobotomized hang. Speaking softly, with matching vocal fry, they dispense vague platitudes about “healing” and soothe listeners with promises they are not alone in their struggles. They stay away from explicitly political messages in the same way that a pastor’s wife would not want to offend a congregant while making small talk during a post-service coffee hour.
It’s easy to fall into the Girls Gone Bible universe. Episode titles promise juicy discussions of topics that matter to young women: “Codependency and People-Pleasing”, “Overcoming an Eating Disorder”, “Honest Convo About Anxiety”. The hosts remind listeners that they are still figuring all of this out, too. It’s a welcoming space.
Kelsey Hanson Woodruff, a scholar of American religious history and postdoctoral fellow at Wesleyan University, said that this come-as-you-are branding has deep roots in evangelism. “Evangelical Christians love a conversion story,” Woodruff said. “It can provide a lot of credibility to someone’s authentic Christian experience.”
“They’re not shoving their opinions down people’s throats like some of these other podcasts [such as] Andrew Tate and all that stuff,” Alicia Reicis, a 30-year-old stay-at-home mom told me before the show.
The hosts’ everygirl approachability belies their mission to woo women back into a faith that increasingly preaches their oppression. Adult women under 30 are rejecting organized religion at record rates; a study released this April found that 40% of female respondents claimed no affiliation – up from 29% in 2013. This is probably due in part to the very visible rise of Christian nationalism tied to Trump’s administration. (The secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth, brought a pastor who does not believe in a woman’s right to vote to speak at the Pentagon; the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, has invoked terms like “spiritual warfare” and “malevolent forces” in speeches.)
Despite this, Girls Gone Bible has found success with women who seem able to compartmentalize. Every woman I spoke to at the show declined to talk politics, or how they feel about the hosts supporting Trump. “I don’t really have a full opinion on that,” Reicis told me before politely excusing herself.
Outside the venue, Genesis Gesualdo texted her friend who was running late. Gesualdo, 33, works at a salvage yard, which she called “a man’s job”. She told me that she had converted to Christianity less than a week ago because she felt she had strayed from a more modest lifestyle. “I wasn’t walking with him [Jesus], I didn’t obey him,” she said. “The way I dressed was provocative.” Gesualdo came to the event wearing a floor-length floral skirt. She said she was looking forward to “rejoicing”.
I couldn’t know the political leanings of every person in attendance. Yes, there were a lot of women sporting what’s become known as “Republican face” – heavy makeup, plumped lips, fake tans – but there were others I would not feel comfortable pegging as such. I lost track counting the number of full-arm tattoo sleeves I saw; I watched a young woman hit her vape while waiting in the concessions line.
I wondered if these fans – maybe new converts themselves – would soon find themselves evolving into what the hosts consider to be “godly” women: conservative in appearance, faith and political ideology. “One of the tactics of the Christian right is to narrow the definition of what it means to be a Christian,” Woodruff said. “[Girls Gone Bible] may not talk directly about policies, but they may put forth a certain definition of what it means to be a Christian woman, which is inherently political.”
Girls Gone Bible touts a regressive ideal of femininity, encouraging women to be “modest” and abstain from sex before marriage, which Halili once called “demonic oppression”. Harsh, but both women often insist that they’re not trying to shame anyone for prior transgressions – after all, both have pasts of their own. And their audience is perhaps already comfortable with the idea of celibacy. More young women, religious or not, are going “boy sober”, as voluntary abstinence is sometimes called on social media, due to their dismal dating pool and past bad experiences with men.
In fact, Girls Gone Bible’s message about dating gets very close to pop feminism. “It’s been genuinely the greatest joy of my life to enter into complete purity,” Halili said on a recent episode taped after she returned from a trip to Miami, a party city synonymous with bikinis and bottle service. “Living a life where I’m not seeking that sort of validation from men, for men to think that I am hot or to think that I’m sexy.”
At the New Jersey tour stop, Halili continued preaching girl power. “Marriage isn’t the reward,” she said, as groups of friends cheered and nodded along from their seats. Then she veered back: “Jesus’s presence in your marriage is the reward.”
Melissa, a 58-year-old woman grabbing a drink at an Italian restaurant before the show, told me that she wanted to bring her son in hopes of finding him “a Christian girl”. He couldn’t make it; she brought her hairdresser instead. Two college friends, Grace Colucci and Taylor Garvey, might have been just who Melissa was looking for in a potential set-up. Both are 22, and first encountered Girls Gone Bible through TikTok clips. Colucci has never had a boyfriend, but she still appreciates the hosts’ dating advice. “They just make [abstinence] so normalized,” Colucci said. “It’s very inspirational and it makes you feel good.”
But Colucci and Garvey were most interested in what Halili and Reitsma say about their mental health struggles. Halili has spoken extensively about living with OCD and disordered eating; for Reitsma, it was suicidal ideation. Colucci listens to their podcasts on stress and burnout. “What they go through is similar to us, and they’re good at [talking about it] in a way that’s fun and easy to learn from. It’s not too heavy.”
At the top of the show, Halili and Reitsma led a group singalong of worship music. When the pianist riffed that the “power in the name” of Jesus is “stronger than depression”, the crowd burst into the loudest cheers I heard all night.
It makes sense that members of the most depressed and isolated generation in history would gravitate toward this subject matter. In her book Esther’s Army: The Christian Women Who Power the American Right, sociologist Katie Gaddini calls this audience “a post-pandemic female populace eager to hear ‘the truth’”. A recent Pew survey found that 44% of 18- to 29-year-olds listen to “religious audio programs”, which they overwhelmingly digest as podcasts (as opposed to radio programs). Thirty-nine per cent of Americans of all ages who consume this content say they listen for “life advice or guidance”.
A young woman who posted on the subreddit r/Christianity seeking recommendations for podcasts geared toward “girls in their 20s” received this answer from another user: “Girls Gone Bible may not be the most theologically deep but they are a good starting place … Treat them [like] a source of relatability (a lot of their topics are highly relatable).”
Evangelicals have long touted the Bible as a cure for mental anguish, and many pastors view depression as a spiritual attack. Reitsma told the audience she “met Jesus on the bathroom floor” during a time in which “everything in the world was telling me to end [her] life”. She explained needing “healing beyond what medication can fix”, meaning antidepressants. She quickly added, “there’s nothing wrong with medications,” but this felt like a concession.
In general, the hosts speak of burnout without addressing the economic forces behind their generation’s collective exhaustion and despair. They detail their mental health struggles, but fall short of interrogating the institutional roadblocks women face when they do try to get help. The intended takeaway: Jesus alone will cure you.
The night ended with Halili praying for “sexual sinners” (that’s anyone who has sex outside of marriage) and women struggling with infertility. Reitsma hugged audience members who lined up at the foot of the stage. Women cried, holding up their Bibles. Some wore newly purchased tour merch, sweatshirts with phrases such as “Keep the Faith” and “Thank You Jesus.” They would bring home a sense of validation: they were not alone in their pain.
The tour has two more stops remaining, both in Florida in September, but there was something about the New Jersey show that especially delighted the hosts: it wasn’t happening in the Bible belt, or even a red state. “I feel such a hunger in here tonight,” Halili said. “It must be the east coast in ya.” Clearly, they believe their message is spreading.

Echoes of cold war as US accused of meddling in another Brazilian election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
12:00:57 UTC
21:00:57 KST

The year was 1962 and the Kennedy administration was desperate to swing Brazil’s congressional elections against its leftwing president, João Goulart, as a way of countering the supposed communist threat sweeping a region the US considered its back yard.
Historians say that in the lead-up to the vote, the CIA and the Department of State secretly channelled millions of dollars to opposition candidates and a group tasked with spreading rightwing propaganda and stirring up unrest.
“There was a very heavy-handed intervention here by the US government,” said Chico Rubens Paiva, a political activist whose congressman grandfather Rubens Paiva investigated Washington’s meddling during a 1963 parliamentary inquiry into the conspiracy.
More than six decades later, Paiva, whose grandfather was murdered by the US-backed dictatorship that seized power in 1964, is among those who fear history is repeating itself on the eve of Brazil’s 2026 presidential election.
October’s vote will pit the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Donald Trump ally who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a military coup.
Polls suggest a tight race and Trump and his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, have been accused of trying to tip the scales in Bolsonaro’s favour by launching an overt campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure against Lula.
The US measures include imposing 25% tariffs on most Brazilian imports and designating Brazil’s biggest crime groups – Rio’s Red Command and São Paulo’s First Command of the Capital – as foreign terrorist organisations. Brazilian officials suspect this is partly designed to boost Bolsonaro by making Lula look soft on crime.
In July, Lula said two Trump officials had been denied entry visas because they planned “to meddle in Brazil’s elections”. Brazilian officials believe the pair, who reportedly planned to meet Flávio Bolsonaro, intended to sow doubt about the reliability of Brazil’s internationally respected voting system – something the Bolsonaros have sought to do repeatedly. Soon after, the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to Washington was revoked.
Celso Rocha de Barros, a political scientist and podcast pundit, voiced bewilderment that US interference – which he considered the election’s most urgent theme – was not getting more coverage in mainstream media.
“The greatest superpower in human history is explicitly backing a candidate in our election and is strangling the Brazilian economy in order to help him [win],” Barros claimed. “We cannot pretend that this isn’t happening and treat this like a normal election … the Brazilian economy is under attack.”
Trump’s tactics have echoes of Washington’s cold war-era attempt to manipulate Brazilian politics in the lead-up to the 1964 coup, which ushered in two decades of authoritarian rule in which hundreds of people were killed or disappeared.
Back then, the CIA helped finance the Brazilian Institute for Democratic Action, which, according to the historians Lilia Schwarcz and Heloisa Starling, illegally poured money into the campaigns of hundreds of lawmakers and eight gubernatorial candidates. “The objective was strategic: to create a strong opposition in congress, block government initiatives and prepare the way for a coup d’état,” Schwarcz and Starling argued in their book Brazil: A Biography.
Another US-funded group, the Research and Social Studies Institute, was used to disrupt Goulart’s government by bankrolling anti-communist propaganda and anti-government protests. James N Green, a Brown University historian who has written a book about the period, said: “The intention [was] getting rid of Goulart [and] opening the door to the military coming to power.”
Green sees parallels between Trump’s use of tariffs to sabotage Lula’s campaign and how in the early 60s Washington sought to enfeeble Goulart’s government by funding his opponents and cutting off loans. Then, as now, the US government was “bent on doing everything possible to weaken the government” in Brazil.
But Barros sees one key difference between the two US gambits. “[The 1962 campaign] was done covertly, precisely because the CIA knew there would be real public anger in Brazil if people knew the US was bankrolling candidates. So they did it secretly,” he said. “Today, this is being done openly – and on an incomparably larger scale.”
The Department of State rejected claims the US was seeking to meddle in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” an official said in a statement.
“We respect the Brazilian people and whatever government that they choose freely through free and fair elections in Brazil. We’ve respected and dealt with governments from both sides of the spectrum in Brazil, and had very successful relationships with them.”
Last year Trump was accused of meddling in the politics of neighbouring Argentina after he threw his weight behind its rightwing president, Javier Milei, on the eve of crucial midterm elections. Milei recently attended Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign launch in Brazil, using his speech to lambaste Lula as a “thief”.
Green believes two strategic objectives lie behind the Brazilian pressure campaign being waged by Trump and by Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, who has made toppling Cuba’s communist government a personal project.
Firstly, it is designed to weaken and delegitimise Lula’s government, making it harder for Brazil, Latin America’s largest democracy, to challenge the US economic asphyxiation campaign against Cuba.
Secondly, it is about “neutralising” leftwing forces in Latin America more generally and boosting the right in the hope of helping to elect even more Trump-aligned leaders. Since 2023, a succession of radical rightwing populists have won power in Argentina and Chile, Costa Rica and Colombia. In reference to Trump’s tangerine complexion, this has been nicknamed Latin America’s “orange wave”.
Paiva, 38, believes US interference is intended to have a similar effect to the abduction of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro – strengthening “American dominance” in a region it considers a US sphere of influence.
Maduro’s removal in January allowed the US to impose a pliant successor, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has started opening up the South American country to US oil and mining firms. Paiva believes Bolsonaro’s election will “serve the same purpose: putting people into power who will serve their interests”.
He fears that as election day draws near, US social media companies could enter the fray, potentially giving Bolsonaro another lift. “Any kind of change to the algorithm has a brutal impact in the way information reaches people,” warned Paiva, who is running for a seat in congress in the election for the centre-left Brazilian Socialist party. He highlighted “the scary lurch the Silicon Valley bros” had taken into Trump’s camp during his second term.
Barros is convinced the US aims to help elect Flávio Bolsonaro, “because Flávio will give them everything they want”, he said. “Flávio will make a rare earths deal no other president would. Flávio will let American big techs do whatever they like in Brazil. Flávio will reduce economic relations with China as much as he can.” He noted that Bolsonaro supporters attended rallies carrying US flags.
Barros believes the campaign’s real driving force is not Trump but Rubio, who hopes to bolster a possible 2028 presidential run by showing voters he has “delivered the whole of Latin America to American interests”.
“The fact is, this is an election between Lula and Marco Rubio,” Barros said.

‘They take the water, the springs dry up’: fear as Guatemalan goldmine plan is revived
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
12:00:57 UTC
21:00:57 KST

In the community of La Lima in Guatemala, Elda Dinora Ramírez, 58, looks towards a small well at the back of her home. Dusty wooden planks lie across the opening, concealing the faint gleam of water far below. “The well is drying up again,” she says.
Ramírez’s home lies less than a mile from Era Dorada – a goldmining project acquired by the Canadian multinational Aura Minerals in January 2025. After years of inactivity, the project was reactivated this year when the Guatemalan government granted Aura a construction licence.
Exploration began in 1997 under the then-owners Entre Mares, a subsidiary of Goldcorp, and the project has faced a significant backlash throughout its 29-year history.
“Until all this started happening, we had a happy and peaceful life here,” says Ramírez. “There was no talk of mining; everything was calm.”
After initial excavation began in 2007, residents such as Ramírez reported water shortages. They blamed the mine for pumping out large quantities of geothermal water that was filling the tunnels during excavation.
“The machines they use draw from deep down; they take all the water and the springs dry up,” she says.
Although the mine’s development was suspended in 2013 due to unfavourable market conditions, the project site continued to have water extracted in subsequent years.
With operations temporarily halted, locals around the mine reported that water levels in their wells began to recover. Then known as Cerro Blanco, the project was sold by Goldcorp to the Vancouver-based Bluestone Resources in 2017. In 2021, Bluestone announced a controversial plan to convert the project into an open-pit mine.
A year later, a community referendum in nearby Asunción Mita rejected the project, with 88% of voters opposing it.
“It was a great victory for the people,” says Yony Barrera, 51, owner of a hardware store in Asunción Mita and vice-president of an activist group campaigning against the mine.
In 2024, Guatemala’s new government annulled the environmental licence for Bluestone’s proposed open-pit mine, just months after it had been approved by the previous administration. But activists feared that work on the project would not remain dormant for ever.
“I knew it wouldn’t be over,” says Barrera. “This will only stop when they take the gold.”
Today, the mining site hums with life once again. Heavy vehicles judder past the rusted coils of barbed wire that mark the site’s borders, clouds of dust rising in their wake. Workers in hard hats and navy-blue overalls gather around the entrance.
The company predicts an annual production of 111,000 ounces of gold in the first four years of operation. In a statement, Aura says industrial operations have not yet begun, although construction and site preparation work are under way, and that vegetation clearance is authorised under its licence and is being carried out within limits set by the project’s EIA.
“They are advancing a lot, and very quickly,” says Arnulfo Díaz, 43. “At the same time, we are advancing towards our own destruction.”
Díaz worked on the project in 2008 as part of the excavation team under Entre Mares, where he says he sustained an injury that left him deaf in his right ear. He fears the project’s return may bring wider consequences for his community.
“Our fear is that we will lose everyday access to water,” he says. “Where are we going to go?”
Ramírez says the effects are already being felt. As well as her well drying up since the project was reactivated in January, her fruit trees are losing their harvest to drought and her livestock are suffering from respiratory illness she attributes to dust from the mine.
“When I lie down at night I start to think: there is no hope left,” she says.
Aura Minerals says measures are being taken to suppress dust at the site and monitoring has so far shown that the work has had no impact on air quality.
Aura says it is approaching the project with a renewed focus on sustainability, pledging to develop it as an underground mine after more than 1,000 hours of dialogue with local communities. In a company statement, Aura’s president and chief executive, Rodrigo Barbosa, points to plans for a water-purification plant and the use of 100% recycled water.
“This ensures we not only do no harm, but go beyond and create positive value for the communities and environment,” he says.
Aura says it will recycle water used in the industrial process in a closed-loop system with no discharge and treat excess natural water from the mine to a drinkable standard for local communities. The company also points to continuous water-quality monitoring upstream and downstream of the operation and says hydrogeological studies and monitoring show no evidence of reduced water availability for local communities.
But activists claim that the environmental guardrails in place, designed to limit the project’s harmful impact, fall short of what is required.
According to Era Dorada’s opponents, the project continues to operate under a widely criticised Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), which was approved in 2007.
A 2023 report commissioned by the Central American Alliance Against Mining (Acafremin) says experts from Guatemala’s ministry of environment and natural resources rejected the EIA in 2004 and 2005, but the ministry replaced them in 2007, and the new head of the unit approved the EIA shortly afterwards.
Julio González, of the Guatemalan environmental organisation Madre Selva, and other activists say these changes are evidence of past corruption and have criticised the EIA for failing to account for key environmental considerations, such as the safe disposal of cyanide – a highly toxic chemical commonly used to separate gold from rock.
A 2022 report by Steven Emerman, a geophysicist and independent mining expert, recommended that all of the mine’s permits be revoked.
In its statement, Aura says the current underground project falls within the scope of the original EIA and its active environmental licence, which it describes as being fully valid and adequate for the operation. Aura confirms it plans to use cyanide in the Era Dorada project, but says the mine is designed to manage it in line with relevant standards, with the process operating in a closed-circuit system and a detoxification stage at the end of the process to neutralise cyanide in the solution.
The mine is in the protected biological corridor of the Ostúa dry forest, and environmentalists fear that inadequate governance could expose crucial ecosystems to contamination by heavy metals. Aura says the project is not located in an area with legal restrictions, and claims to have plans in place to maintain the ecological integrity of the surroundings.
Scientists also warn that geothermal water discharged during tunnel excavation carries high levels of arsenic. A 2019 study by a biologist, Cidia Cortes, reported elevated arsenic levels at points on the Ostúa River where the mine discharged geothermal water.
The company says, however, that arsenic occurs naturally at higher than normal levels in the region and that all of the water pumped from the underground workings is treated to reduce arsenic. Era Dorada also says it is investing to upgrade treatment to improve water to drinkable standards.
The Ostúa River feeds into Lake Güija, a protected site that straddles the Guatemala-El Salvador border. Here, communities fear that reactivating the mining project could jeopardise their livelihoods.
“We have eight children,” says Mirna Margarita, 58, who lives in the lakeside community of Cuevitas. “We fished just to sustain them and put them through school.”
Looking out over the blue waters of Lake Güija, she leans back on a lopsided sofa. “These times are very worrying, with all this contamination that could come to us.”
Her husband, Maximiliano Pérez, 59, who has fished all of his life, sits opposite her. “It worries us greatly that the mine might become active again and start working, with how much we stand to lose,” he says. “We look at the lake like a mother – she is what gives us our food.”
Amid ongoing uncertainty, many who live close to the mine share concerns about the future. Pedro Arrieta, 55, is a baker from Asunción Mita. He sits in his family home, where a small plate of home-cooked pastries is passed around the room. “What mining brings is contamination, corruption and death,” he says.
A collection of family photos is arranged on the wall behind him. Generations of faces look out from within the gold-rimmed frames. “What are we going to leave to our next generation?” he asks.

Microscopic brain vesicles reveal unique genetic markers for Alzheimer’s and frontotemporal dementia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
12:00:33 UTC
21:00:33 KST

A recent study indicates that microscopic, lipid-bound particles originating from the brain carry distinct genetic signatures depending on the type of dementia a person has. By analyzing these tiny packages, researchers identified specific regulatory molecules that differ between Alzheimer’s disease and various forms of frontotemporal dementia. These findings, published in Brain Communications, suggest a potential new avenue for early and accurate diagnosis of neurodegenerative conditions.
Dementia is an umbrella term for conditions characterized by memory loss and cognitive decline, affecting millions of people worldwide. Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause, followed by frontotemporal dementia, which typically strikes at a younger age. In their early stages, these two diseases often share overlapping symptoms, making it difficult for doctors to tell them apart clinically.
Accurate diagnosis is a pressing need because new therapeutic drugs are entering the market. “New treatments for dementia can only help patients if we can accurately diagnose the type of dementia early, with misdiagnosis impacting the success of patient treatment and the ability to test new drugs in clinical trials,” Gemma Lace, associate dean and researcher at the University of Salford’s School of Science, Engineering & Environment, told PsyPost.
To find early biological markers, scientists are looking at small extracellular vesicles, which are tiny, lipid-bound bubbles released by cells to communicate with one another. “Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) are fascinating structures that have only quite recently been implicated in neurodegenerative diseases, in particular, in the brain regional ‘spread’ of pathogenesis,” Lace said.
“Most studies have not explored brain sEV cargoes given the challenges associated with tissue access, yet the brain is the primary site of damage in dementia,” Lace added. “We were curious to know whether sEV cargoes varied between different sub-types of dementia given the research understanding around differential disease pathways, and if this variation could shed further light on disease process and/or have diagnostic value.”
Because these microscopic packages can cross the blood-brain barrier and enter the bloodstream, they offer a window into what is happening inside the brain. Past work has shown that looking at bodily fluids can yield clues about brain health; for example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2026 found that blood tests could accurately identify Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia by looking at disease-linked proteins.
Inside these vesicles, cells pack various types of cargo, including microRNAs. MicroRNAs are short strands of genetic material that help control how genes are expressed, often by turning certain genetic instructions off. Previous research provides evidence that these molecules play a role in brain diseases. A study covered by PsyPost in 2024 demonstrated that specific microRNAs are altered in both the blood and brain tissue of those with Alzheimer’s pathology.
In neurodegenerative diseases, toxic proteins build up in the brain. Normally, the body uses cellular recycling systems, known as autophagy, to clear away these toxic accumulations. The authors of the new study suspected that different forms of dementia might involve unique disruptions to these recycling pathways. By examining the microRNA packed into brain-derived vesicles, they aimed to see if they could differentiate Alzheimer’s disease from frontotemporal dementia and its specific genetic variants.
The research, led by Joseph Morgan of the University of Salford, utilized post-mortem brain tissue from the frontal lobes of 25 individuals. The sample included five people who had Alzheimer’s disease, fifteen people with different genetic mutations that cause frontotemporal dementia, and five older adults without any clinical dementia diagnosis. For the molecular tests, the researchers analyzed a subset of three samples from each diagnostic group.
First, the research team isolated the small extracellular vesicles directly from the frozen brain tissue. They then chemically treated the samples to strip away any genetic material stuck to the outside of the bubbles, ensuring they were only measuring the cargo safely sealed inside. After extracting the microRNAs, the scientists used a laboratory technique that amplifies genetic material to measure the levels of seven specific microRNAs known to regulate cellular recycling.
The researchers found distinct differences between the groups. A microRNA called miR-224-5p was detected at much higher levels in the vesicles of individuals with Alzheimer’s disease and those with a specific tau-related mutation for frontotemporal dementia. Specifically, this molecule showed an absolute fold increase of over 4 times in Alzheimer’s samples and over 7 times in the tau-mutation samples, compared to the healthy brains.
Another target, miR-106a-3p, was elevated in the Alzheimer’s disease samples compared to the control group and all the frontotemporal dementia subgroups. After the scientists applied strict statistical adjustments to account for multiple comparisons, however, these specific group-to-group differences for miR-106a-3p were not statistically significant.
To get a broader picture, the team also mapped the entire microRNA landscape of the vesicles using genetic sequencing. This exploratory analysis identified unique panels of altered microRNAs for each disease type. For instance, a molecule named miR-26a-2-3p was elevated in Alzheimer’s disease samples when compared to the healthy controls. It was also elevated in the Alzheimer’s samples when compared directly to all three genetic forms of frontotemporal dementia.
“Our study has identified that different subtypes of dementia, that have similar symptoms, have different biological fingerprints within tiny brain vesicles,” Lace noted. “This is very exciting with respect to developing new methods of early and accurate diagnosis.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. “This was a relatively small study given post-mortem human brain tissue is challenging to secure, with sample volumes available being limited,” Lace explained. “This meant we had to be very selective around the experiments we need to get the most meaningful data, and there were many things we were unable to explore due to the amount of tissue available to us.”
Because the sample sizes were small, there is an increased chance of missing subtle but real biological differences. The healthy control group was also older on average than the individuals in the disease groups, introducing an age difference that could potentially influence the types of microRNA found in the brain.
The results provide a snapshot of the brain after death, meaning post-mortem tissue degradation could have affected the stability of the genetic material. Furthermore, the exact microRNA signatures found directly in brain tissue may not perfectly match what is floating in a patient’s bloodstream or saliva. The brain is highly complex and made up of diverse, non-uniform tissue and cell types, so a sample from the frontal lobe may not represent the entire organ.
Future research will need to validate these candidate markers in much larger groups of patients, and scientists plan to test whether these same microRNA signatures can be reliably detected in more easily accessible bodily fluids. “It would be great to explore whether these brain sEV biomarker variations are detectable in peripheral tissues such as blood which is an accessible fluid for diagnostic use,” Lace said.
The study, “Distinct brain extracellular vesicle microRNA profiles differ in frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer’s disease,” was authored by Joseph Morgan, Toby Aarons, Arijit Mukhopadhyay, and Gemma Lace.

Finland's slow economic recovery has yet to translate into a meaningful rise in jobs.

Consent and the Formation of Preferences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

I visit your house and admire an ornament on your bookshelf. You say you’d like me to have it as a gift. If I thank you and take it with me when I leave, it seems I’ve done nothing wrong. It was yours, but you gave it to me.
You have a serious illness. Untreated, it will leave you physically incapacitated and often cognitively exhausted to the extent that you won’t be able to work. There’s an experimental surgery available, but it’s very risky: It might cure you completely, but it might kill you. You decide to have the surgery. You book it, show up on the day, and sign the consent form. If the surgeon then starts to operate, it seems they do nothing wrong. It’s your body, but you’ve requested they operate on it.
Of course, if I had forced you to give me the ornament as a gift by threatening you with violence if you hadn’t, I would do wrong by taking it. And similarly, if the surgeon knows your family threatened to cut you off completely if you didn’t sign the consent form, they do wrong by starting to operate. Coerced consent is not effective; it doesn’t release others from the duties they have not to take your property or interfere with your body.
But there is another way in which consent can seem ineffective that is more mysterious. Suppose you offer me the ornament as a gift because you have extremely altruistic preferences—you always wish others to have what they want to have. And suppose you have those preferences because of strong pressure from the unjust society in which you live or from the bullying family in which you were raised. Perhaps you belong to a social grouping whose members are severely sanctioned if they seek anything for themselves, or your family punished you whenever you sought something for your own enjoyment. Then, even if the resulting preferences are genuinely your own—you attest to having them, your other behavior supports that, and you reflectively endorse them—it seems that when you offer me the ornament on the basis of these self-denying preferences, it is still wrong for me to take it. Perhaps not as wrong as it would have been had you not offered it to me at all; and surely not as wrong as it would have been had I threatened you with physical violence should you not offer me it. But wrong, nonetheless.
Or suppose you consent to the risky surgery because you were raised in a society in which the dominant ideology teaches you that only productive lives are valuable and that you can only be productive by doing the sort of work you will be unable to do if your illness progresses unchecked. Suppose this view is everywhere around you from novels and films and television to political discussions and school lessons and your parents’ teachings. Then again, we might feel that the consent you have given is not completely effective and, should the surgeon proceed with the surgery, they will not have acted well.
Such cases, which in different areas of study go by the names of false consciousness or adaptive preferences or deformed desires, are mysterious because the consent is based on your genuine preferences, and the content of those preferences is not in itself troubling: After all, formed in another way, altruistic preferences can be deeply admirable. And you are surely permitted to almost exclusively value productivity in your own life, even if that’s absolutely not how you should value the lives of others.
If the preferences are genuine and their content untroubling, it must be the history of these preferences that renders any consent based on them less than fully effective. But of course, it cannot be just that they were formed in part under the influence of something outside of you—that’s true of nearly all your preferences! Instead, it must be the nature of the external influences. It’s natural to think that what is crucial here is that the external source applies strong pressure, that it is a social source of pressure, and that it arises from injustice. Why it must be all of these is an interesting and difficult question—what of nonsocial sources of pressure? What of pressure imposed by a just society? But these aren’t my questions. I’m interested in why some preferences formed as a result of unjust social pressure can ground effective consent while others can’t. My contention is that it is the precise mechanism by which the preferences are formed under this unjust social pressure that holds the key.
Now, there are a great many mechanisms by which we form our preferences. Some come from rather thoughtlessly mimicking others—we are often mimetic creatures. Some come from a post hoc rationalization of decisions between options we take to be on a par—what social psychologists call choice-induced preferences. Sometimes we come to prefer that which we think we might be able to get, and we disprefer that which we know is impossible—Nietzsche’s amor fati. In the case of the ornament from above, it might be that the altruistic preferences were formed as a self-preservation mechanism: If you genuinely have the preferences your society demands of you, rather than simply pretending you do, you won’t slip up and act in ways that will attract punishment or sanction. In the example of the surgery, the impoverished information environment your society has created leads you to form the belief that an unproductive life is objectively without value, and you then transfer that belief about objective value into a subjective preference. When preferences are formed via these latter two mechanisms, we tend to think that consent based on them is less than fully effective.
And yet there are mechanisms by which preferences might be formed under unjust social pressures that can ground effective consent. Consider, for example, the following case: Holt has never wanted children. Nonetheless, the society in which they live sanctions and punishes childless people in a hundred different ways from social stigma to material consequences, and Holt’s partner has piled on further pressures to make Holt have a child with them. Despite all these pressures, Holt still doesn’t want a child but nonetheless agrees to have one to avoid these various sanctions and punishments. It proves to be a transformative experience for them. Raising their child makes them value aspects of being a parent in ways that they didn’t value before. Their time with the child leads them to conceive of the activities of raising a child differently from how they conceived of them before: Where once they conceived of certain imaginative play as dull and repetitive, they come to see it as part of forming shared bonds; where once they conceived of checking the child’s behavior as authoritarian and confrontational, they come to see it as the process of helping the child discover who they are and how they want to be. Compare this with Iris Murdoch’s famous example of M. and her attitude towards her daughter-in-law D. When she first meets her, M. finds D. to be “a good-hearted girl, but while not exactly common yet certainly unpolished and lacking in dignity and refinement”; but later, after she reflects more carefully upon D.’s nature, “D. is discovered not to be vulgar but refreshingly simple, not undignified but spontaneous, not noisy but gay.” In Holt’s case and in M.’s, the key is attention: By becoming a parent, Holt’s attention is by necessity focused on the business of raising a child, and their attention leads them to conceive of certain aspects of that activity differently and that, in turn, changes their preferences. In M.’s case, Murdoch is keen to emphasize that it is extended attention to the memory of D. that effects the change.
Holt’s preferences are formed under pressure that is exerted by an unjust society and within a relationship in which they are treated unjustly. Nonetheless, the preferences so formed may ground consent because they were formed via a specific mechanism, namely, the mechanism of attending to the object of the preference.
Why the difference? If Holt later consents to have another child, their consent will be fully effective. Why is this different from the case of the ornament above, where you formed your altruistic preferences because having self-directed ones risked punishment, or the case of the surgery above, where you came to disvalue a life without work because the information your society fed you made you think such a life is objectively not valuable? The answer, I think, lies in the room these mechanisms leave you for the free exercise of agency. If I unjustly threaten severe sanctions should you not behave in line with certain preferences, I leave little room for you to determine for yourself whether or not to have those preferences. And if I unjustly create an information environment that gives you very strong evidence in favor of some claim about objective value, I might leave you space to freely exercise your agency, but I don’t leave you the resources you need to do so, such as access to alternative ways of thinking. Of course, I don’t thwart your free agency entirely, as I would if I were to install these preferences in you via involuntary hypnosis. But I leave much less space for it and many fewer resources to support it than if I were unjustly to force you into extended contact with the object of preference and leave you to make up your own mind. It is this, I think, that distinguishes the cases.
The post Consent and the Formation of Preferences first appeared on Blog of the APA.

Nepal floods: Mounting death toll and concern for women and girls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Nepal floods: Mounting death toll and concern for women and girls
As rescue efforts continue in Nepal, humanitarians are focused on how the recent deadly flash floods have impacted women and girls, as well as access to healthcare.
The death toll stands as just over 1,000, as of late Tuesday. Some 4,247 people remain missing, Jens Laerke, spokesperson for the UN aid coordination office OCHA, said earlier in the day, briefing reporters in Geneva.
The catastrophic flooding was trigged by a glacier collapse in the Himalayas on the border with China. Authorities there report that 16 people were confirmed killed and 546 are missing, he said.
‘Real and immediate’ risks remain
Nearly a week has passed since the flooding began, and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) is only now able to access hard-hit areas such as Rasuwa district.
“Search and rescue is still ongoing, and the monsoon hasn’t stopped” said Matt Baden, IFRC Operations Manager for the Nepal crisis response, speaking from Kathmandu.
“Blocked waterways remain at risk to further flooding, and threat of landslides is real and immediate.”
Meanwhile, people are returning to look for their homes and what is left of them.
Women and girls in need
As a result of the disaster, some 43,000 women and girls in Nepal now require immediate humanitarian assistance, according to UN Women.
Christine Arab, the agency’s Regional Director for Asia and the Pacific, said partners on the ground stress that women survivors are running out of food, while safe water is increasingly inaccessible and protection risks are growing.
They warn that women could be excluded from the decision-making around response and recovery.
Disaster highlights inequalities
She told journalists that many people who normally would receive humanitarian support—such as pregnant women, nursing mothers and persons with disabilities—have been “washed away” because they could not get to higher ground.
“And this is what happens when a disaster meets inequality: the people already left behind are often the first to be swept away,” she said, speaking from Bangkok.
Prior to the floods, women and girls in Rasuwa district were already spending hours a day travelling long distances to collect water.
“Now, these women are telling us that access to safe water has been cut off altogether, following the destruction of water systems, roads, and bridges,” she said.
Women’s role in recovery
The top official added that food is the most urgent priority for women in the worst-affected areas.
Moreover, disasters also bring increased risks of gender-based violence, exploitation, and trafficking, while damaged infrastructure and communications can make it harder for survivors to seek help and access protection services.
“The humanitarian response must recognize the experiences of women and girls,” she said. “It must reach them and it must include them as key drivers in Nepal’s recovery.”
Health access critical
Maintaining access to health services remains a priority, said Christian Lindmeier, spokesperson for the World Health Organization (WHO).
Six health facilities have suffered damage or destruction while two others cannot be reached, meaning that “people on the ground don't have a health facility available at the time of their biggest needs."
He stressed that “while immediate efforts remain focused on life-saving interventions…preventing secondary public health impacts is equally important.”
Mr. Lindmeier explained that flooding, displacement, overcrowding and stagnant water can increase the risk of disease outbreaks. In this regard, WHO is supporting surveillance in both affected and downstream areas to monitor the potential increase of dengue, scrub typhus, and other communicable diseases.
The UN agency has also supported the identification of priority medicines, diagnostic kits, and essential health commodities while also providing technical guidance, including with regard to infection prevention and the safe and dignified management of bodies.

Food aid cutback in the occupied West Bank as health fears grow in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01

21:00:00 KST

Food aid cutback in the occupied West Bank as health fears grow in Gaza
Lack of funding has forced the World Food Programme (WFP) to slash aid to families in the West Bank by half even though needs have more than doubled over the past two years.
“We’re running out of funding, and that means that from today, some 200,000 people will lose access to critical assistance,” Shaun Hughes, WFP country director for Palestine, told journalists in Geneva on Tuesday.
He said intensified settler violence and escalating Israeli military operations alongside severe movement restrictions, demolitions and widespread displacement “have eroded Palestinian livelihoods and contributed to increased food insecurity”.
Pushed to the brink
At the same time, a crippling economic crisis “is pushing people to breaking point”, with unemployment more than doubling and over a third of the population struggling to meet their basic needs.
“Food may be available in the markets, but people simply cannot afford it,” he said, speaking from London.
Today, nearly a million people across the West Bank – over a quarter of the population – are now food insecure, he said, adding that “two years ago, that figure was 11 per cent.”
Families ‘in a chokehold’
During recent visits to the territory, Mr. Hughes saw families that used to earn a living from the land “now forced from their homes, their livelihoods destroyed” and facing incredible injustice and hardship.
“They now find themselves in a chokehold, unable to move freely to access land or jobs and so unable to afford food for their families,” he said.
In response to journalists’ questions, he said that the West Bank was not traditionally considered to be experiencing a food crisis, but that increasing pressures were exacerbating food insecurity.
He added that the very small cash transfers that WFP provided – about 50 shekels per person per month (less than $20) – had become a “real lifeline” for many people and would now be cut off due to the funding shortfall.
Gaza: Don’t look away
Turning to the Gaza Strip, Mr. Hughes said that WFP was also forced to reduce its cash assistance to 75,000 families in July.
He stressed that the recent slight improvements in food security indicators reported last month “should not create a false sense of security” as two thirds of the population still face critical and emergency levels of hunger.
He warned that if humanitarian food aid does not continue, “up to 90 per cent of the population will face high levels of acute food insecurity by the end of this year.”
WFP requires $386 million to avoid any further reductions in assistance provided in Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months, he said, urging continued international support and solidarity.
“As global crises multiply and domestic fiscal interests take over, there is a real danger that the world’s attention moves on from Palestine, but the needs of Palestinians, both in the West Bank and in Gaza, have not moved on,” he said.
“Now is not the time to look away.”
Looming health crisis
From inside the Gaza Strip, the World Health Organization (WHO) representative in Occupied Palestinian Territory voiced concern about the security situation as airstrikes continued despite the ceasefire last October.
Dr. Renee van de Werdt was in Gaza City on Monday, where a nearby strike killed several people.
This was her sixth visit to the Strip, and she painted a grim picture of “endless piles of rubble” and “overcrowded” and flimsy tents.
‘Unacceptable’ water situation
She highlighted the catastrophic water situation in the enclave, noting that trucking is usually used in the immediate aftermath of disasters and crises.
“It is really unacceptable to see in Gaza, almost three years in, that these trucks are still the lifeline most Gazans depend on,” she said.
Contamination concerns
Dr. van de Werdt expressed grave concern over both the quantity and quality of water reaching the population. She said microbiological contamination has “almost tripled” since January due to the extremely limited testing capacity in the Strip.
“The laboratory capacities in Gaza remain very, very, very limited,” she said.
“We can only detect and track essential microbiological contaminants. We do not have the ability to detect and track other contaminants that are likely to be present in the water and in the environment."
Dr. Van de Weert said that the number of acute watery diarrhoea cases has nearly doubled from about 30,000 in March to more than 58,000 in August.
The water and sanitation situation is likely to worsen during the winter months, with sewage water flowing and emitting odours throughout densely populated areas.
Medical progress and challenges
In positive developments, WHO has noted a marked improvement in medical and clinical care in Gaza but this progress “has not been fast enough and also not equal”.
She estimated that more than 6,600 people require long-term care after having their limbs amputated, yet no prosthetic or artificial limbs “that would allow people, including many children, to walk and live in some dignity, have entered Gaza since May 2024.”
She said that as of July, only 12 per cent of people who have lost limbs since October 2023 had received prosthetics.
Dr. Van de Weert stressed the need to protect fragile health gains and prevent disease outbreaks “at all costs”.
“Unfortunately, we know what’s coming, but we still have time to prevent a public health disaster within this disaster,” she said.

At SCO summit In Kyrgyzstan, Guterres calls for more representative global governance

Unknown Publisher

At SCO summit In Kyrgyzstan, Guterres calls for more representative global governance
UN Secretary-General António Guterres on Tuesday urged leaders of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) to help reshape global governance for a changing world, arguing that a more multipolar international order can strengthen multilateralism, advance fairness and better serve developing countries.
Addressing the SCO summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, the Secretary-General said shifting global power dynamics present an opportunity to build more representative international institutions and a United Nations that works "at the service of all without double standards in line with the Charter."
The Shanghai Cooperation Organization is a Eurasian political, economic and security grouping founded in 2001 that today brings together 10 member States, including China, India, Pakistan, Russia and several Central Asian countries. It is one of the world's largest regional organizations by population and geographic scope.
‘A good thing’
“Our world is increasingly multipolar,” Mr. Guterres said. “That is a good thing and must be strengthened.”
He described multipolarity as “a condition for justice in global governance and international relations” and “the best support for effective multilateralism.”
The UN chief noted that while global power relations have evolved significantly, many international institutions continue to reflect the geopolitical realities of 1945.
“We must reform our multilateral institutions, including the United Nations and the Bretton Woods system, to reflect today's realities, and increase the representation and influence of developing countries to build a just world order,” he said.
He also praised the longstanding partnership between the UN and the SCO, describing the organization as “an important pillar of multilateralism.”
Four priorities for deeper cooperation
The Secretary-General outlined four areas where he believes cooperation between the UN and SCO can be strengthened.
1. Global security
Mr. Guterres voiced concern over continuing instability in the Middle East, warning that ceasefires and agreements are repeatedly being violated.
“I appeal for maximum restraint and for agreements and international law to be respected,” he said.
He stressed the need for “a peaceful, just and durable settlement” that would restore regional stability while safeguarding international navigational rights and freedoms, including around the Straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab.
Turning to Gaza, the Secretary-General said the ceasefire “must be respected” and called for the full implementation of the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict.
He also demanded the removal of obstacles hindering humanitarian assistance and renewed his call for an end to settler attacks and settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank.
“There will only be peace with a two-State solution,” he said, envisioning Israel and Palestine as “two independent, sovereign, democratic states” living side by side in peace and security, with Jerusalem/Al Quds serving as the capital of both.
On Ukraine, Mr. Guterres said that after more than four years of war, “it is high time for a full and immediate ceasefire.”
Such a step, he added, would open the way to negotiations towards “a just, lasting and comprehensive peace in line with international law.”
2. Financing for development
The Secretary-General called for reforms to the international financial system, arguing that developing countries continue to be burdened by unsustainable debt.
“We must reform the global financial architecture to introduce justice and equity and seriously address the debt that is strangling so many developing countries,” he said.
He also urged multilateral development banks to become “bigger, better and bolder” in supporting countries' development efforts.
3. Climate action
Warning that the world is on track to exceed the 1.5°C temperature limit, the UN chief called for rapid emissions cuts and a faster transition to renewable energy.
“Climate action requires climate justice,” he said, underscoring the need for substantially greater financial support for developing countries.
He also highlighted the importance of managing critical minerals responsibly and ensuring producing countries receive greater benefits from their natural resources.
“No more plundering,” he said.
4. Artificial intelligence
The Secretary-General said artificial intelligence must work for all countries, not just a few.
That, he stressed, will require effective guardrails and more inclusive governance mechanisms.
Meeting with Iranian President
On the margins of the summit, the Secretary-General also met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
According to a UN spokesperson, during the meeting, Mr. Guterres expressed concern over the devastating humanitarian and economic consequences of the conflict in Iran, across the region and beyond.
He stressed the urgent need to resolve the crisis through dialogue and negotiations, with full respect for international law, including international navigational rights and freedoms in and around the Strait of Hormuz.
The Secretary-General also reaffirmed the United Nations commitment to support diplomatic efforts aimed at achieving a comprehensive and durable solution.

Decades of war have left ‘depth and breadth’ of trauma across Afghanistan, UN finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Decades of war have left ‘depth and breadth’ of trauma across Afghanistan, UN finds
Victims of Afghanistan’s decades-long armed conflict continue to suffer profound physical, psychological, social and economic consequences, often without access to justice, reparation or formal acknowledgement of the harm done to them, according to a new UN report.
Afghanistan has endured over 40 years of continuous warfare, causing widespread death, displacement and destruction.
Between 2009 and 2021 – as fighting ground on between coalition and coalition-backed Government forces, the Taliban and other militants – the UN mission in the country (UNAMA) documented more than 40,000 civilians killed and more than 77,000 wounded caused by the conflict.
The report focuses on this period of conflict up to the Taliban takeover, interviewing almost 200 victims of armed conflict and their relatives.
Enduring harm
95 per cent of people interviewed experienced emotional or psychological harm, reporting depression, anxiety, memory loss, flashbacks and other trauma-related symptoms.
Nearly 60 per cent also experienced physical harm, with injuries continuing to affect them for months, years or even decades after the event.
Some victims continue to live with chronic pain and disabilities which they struggle to address due to financial barriers and/or lack of available healthcare in Afghanistan.
For some, their injuries prevented them from continuing their education and work, with serious economic consequences for them and their families. In some cases, relatives have also had to give up work or school to provide care.
Women widowed by the conflict face particular economic insecurity, as restrictions imposed by Afghanistan’s de facto authorities limit their access to employment.
No justice for the victims
Yet victims of the war have been unable to obtain justice.
More than half of those interviewed (55 per cent) had never attempted to seek compensation or any form of redress, often because they believe their concerns would not be taken seriously – or because they feared retaliation.
Among those who did try, 64 per cent reported that their efforts were unsuccessful. They cited bureaucratic obstacles, lack of response, perceived discrimination, and limited transparency when engaging with authorities or institutions.
When asked about their needs, victims identified financial compensation (81 per cent), access to justice (48 per cent) and personal security guarantees (47 per cent).
“The interviews we conducted highlight the depth and breadth of collective trauma that continues within Afghan society,” said Georgette Gagnon, a UNAMA official.
“Key to addressing the needs of victims is an acknowledgement of the harm done and a genuine commitment to putting victims’ voices and rights at the center,” she stressed.

Using High-Energy Laser, US Shoots Down Drones Near Mexico Border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

This week, the US Army used a high-energy multipurpose laser to shoot down three drones near the US-Mexico border, which official reports claimed were “posing a physical threat to US military personnel and CBP partners,” referring to Customs and Border Patrol.
The operation took place between the night of August 25 and the early morning of August 26 in the vicinity of the Rio Grande Valley in Texas and was led by the Joint Task Force Southern Border (JTF-SB), which operates under US Northern Command. Authorities confirmed that, during the operation, agents used technology derived from the Army’s High-Energy Multipurpose Laser (AMP-HEL) system, a military program focused on implementing high-energy lasers for new defense capabilities.
Available information suggests that this initiative began in September 2025, when AeroVironment, a company specializing in defense technology, delivered the first two functional prototypes of these laser-based weapons to the US Armed Forces. Two new, improved systems were delivered as the program was expanded in December of the same year. According to the manufacturer, this particular platform, called the Locust Laser Weapon System, is designed to be mounted on military vehicles, as the Army has done with the versions its received.
Operating at 20 kilowatts, the Locust system relies on an extremely concentrated beam of light that, in various phases, allows for the detection, tracking, illumination, damaging, or destruction of targets at a distance. Locust and other high-energy laser (HEL) systems typically use sensors, cameras, radars, or other means to locate an object. Once identified, the system focuses the light beam on the target with great precision, even when it is moving. It then uses an additional electrical energy charge to increase the beam’s power and convert it into heat. This ultimately damages or disables the drone, the exact outcomes depending on factors such as distance, exposure time, and the target’s characteristics.
In addition, Locust’s most recent versions—such as the one delivered to the military last December—include radar and command-and-control systems. These make it easier to integrate the weapon into a more complex mobile defense platform, rather than using it as a stand-alone device.
The exact location of the operation remains unknown. Nor is there any concrete information regarding the origin of the neutralized drones or the entities responsible for their operation. However, Curtis Taylor, commander of JTF-SB, suggested that the aircraft could be linked to criminal cells involved in drug trafficking and operations in Mexican territory.
“Cartel networks are increasingly employing unmanned aircraft systems to facilitate illicit human smuggling and actively spy on our personnel and law enforcement partners. By integrating layered countermeasures alongside advanced directed-energy capabilities like this laser system, we have made it clear that we will not tolerate hostile surveillance. We also greatly appreciate the support of our Mexican Army partners as we work together to combat this threat to the border region,” the major general stated in a press release.
The official statement also does not specify the exact models from the AMP-HEL program that were used in the operation. However, the international press has linked the action to the campaign against illegal immigration and drug cartels that President Donald Trump has been waging since he began his second term.
During his election campaign, Trump promised to combat both issues by implementing drastic measures, especially along the US-Mexico border. To that end, his administration has deployed a wide variety of technologies, HEL systems being just part of the growing toolkit.

Taiwan to launch shared senior housing program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
11:58:58 UTC
20:58:58 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan plans to launch a shared senior housing program as early as the third quarter, offering an alternative to living alone or moving into a residential care facility.
Health Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said Tuesday that the program will provide long-term care resources and National Health Insurance-covered home medical services at the shared residences. The goal is to help older adults remain in familiar communities as they age while receiving the care and medical support they need, according to CTEE and CNA.
Under the model, six to seven seniors will live in the same residence. Each person will have a private room, while common areas such as the living room and kitchen will be shared.
Long-term care workers will be stationed at the residences to provide assistance, while family members can also participate in caregiving. The arrangement is intended to reduce the need for relatives to provide care at home around the clock.
The program will initially focus on people who meet a specified level of disability. About 10 locations are expected to participate in the first stage, with priority given to areas where residential care facilities are unevenly distributed. These include metropolitan areas, where high land prices can make it difficult to establish large care facilities, and rural and remote communities with limited access to such services.
The program's funding model will draw on Japan’s experience. Costs will be covered through a combination of housing fees paid by residents and payments from the National Health Insurance and long-term care systems.
No standard fee has been set, as costs will vary depending on housing prices, building conditions, and the services provided at each location. Shih said costs in Taipei, for instance, could differ substantially from those in Taitung. However, shared housing for seniors who require long-term care is expected to cost less than retirement communities designed for healthy older adults.
The Ministry of Health and Welfare will run the pilot program for two years, with participating locations expected to begin operations in the third or fourth quarter of this year. The government plans to gradually expand the service.

Micron's Taiwan operations are also closely linked with other major technology companies. Mehrotra said the company works with TSMC on advanced packaging and the integration of memory and logic chips, while MediaTek and Asus are among its customers and partners.
He said closer cooperation across the semiconductor supply chain is becoming more important as AI systems increasingly depend on the integration of processors, memory, packaging, and other technologies. Taiwan's concentration of chipmakers, suppliers, and skilled workers makes it a key part of Micron's global manufacturing network, he said.
Mehrotra said Taiwan's importance to Micron extends beyond investment, pointing to its engineering talent, technical expertise, and capacity for innovation. He said those strengths will remain important as the company develops advanced memory products for the next generation of AI computing.
He also highlighted Micron employees' involvement in local disaster relief. More than 250 employees contributed over 7,000 hours to cleanup and recovery work following storm damage in Hualien, which he said reflected the company's deeper ties with Taiwan.
Mehrotra said Micron will continue expanding its role in Taiwan as global demand for AI memory grows. He said the company's Taiwan operations will remain an important base for supplying advanced memory products to customers worldwide.

China's revised defense mobilization law expands national wartime powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
11:58:28 UTC
20:58:28 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — China's revised National Defense Mobilization Law expands the government's ability to mobilize economic and social resources for national defense and broadens the grounds for state intervention in private property and economic development.
The revised law, China's first major overhaul of the legislation since it took effect in 2010, defines national defense mobilization as measures taken to respond to threats to national sovereignty, unification, territorial integrity, security, and development interests, per Liberty Times. It also requires the country to ensure a rapid transition from peacetime to wartime and convert economic and social resources into national defense capabilities. The revised law takes effect Oct. 1.
The law would allow China to more rapidly place personnel, transportation, communications, energy, medical services, and media resources under wartime controls once authorities declare a state of national defense mobilization. Chinese men aged 18 to 60 and women aged 18 to 55 would also be required to perform national defense duties under the law.
Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗), deputy executive director of Tunghai University's Center for China Studies, said the revision reflects China's broader effort to strengthen its ability to mobilize in response to national security threats and war, Liberty Times reported. He said it reflects a concept of “total mobilization” in which the military, economy, industry, manpower, and broader society would be mobilized to support wartime needs.
Yang Tai-yuan (楊太源), a researcher at Tamkang University’s Center for Advanced Technology, noted that the revised law newly includes the term “expropriation,” per RTI. The previous law used “requisition,” which implied that property would be returned after use or that other compensation would be provided, whereas expropriation involves a transfer of property rights.
“It is essentially giving them a blank check,” Yang said. Whether a company is state-owned, foreign-invested, or privately owned, he said, it could be expropriated or requisitioned if it operates in China and authorities consider such action necessary.
Shen Ming-shih (沈明室), a research fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, said the revised law adds “development interests” to the purposes of national defense mobilization, RTI reported. The term is broad and includes competition with other countries in technology, meaning mobilization is no longer limited to traditional security concerns such as war or regional conflict.
Shen said development interests could enable authorities to use national defense mobilization to ensure economic stability or control key areas of economic development, even outside wartime. The provision gives China greater flexibility to cite economic, industrial, or technological development as grounds for mobilization, he said.

11:58:23 UTC
20:58:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Semiconductor equipment maker Skytech Inc. announced Tuesday that an advanced-process laboratory jointly established with TSMC has begun operations.
The facility will serve as a base for developing and testing new technologies, particularly those related to thin-film deposition. Research and joint development are planned in three areas, according to Investor.
The work will include thin-film deposition equipment for advanced semiconductor processes. The companies will seek to improve locally developed equipment to meet the requirements of next-generation wafer manufacturing.
Thin-film deposition technology and the materials used in the process play an important role in semiconductor production. The selection and combination of materials can affect the characteristics of semiconductor devices and production yields, according to Materialsnet.
Differences in yield rates at advanced process nodes are among the factors contributing to Taiwan's leading position in advanced semiconductor production. Developing and identifying materials for future processes is therefore an important area of research.
Another focus will be improving thin-film quality through adjustments to manufacturing methods. The work will target film uniformity, gap-filling capability, and electrical and physical properties.
The project will also involve screening and testing precursor materials. Precursors are chemicals used in chip manufacturing to provide the elements needed to form thin films, according to Passion Fine Technology and Verkita.
Skytech will evaluate new specialty gases and materials for next-generation processes. The company will assess their chemical stability and compliance with environmental standards during the early stages of research and development.
Skytech CEO Yi Chin-liang (易錦良) said the facility's opening marked an important milestone for the company. He said the project will support efforts to develop advanced semiconductor equipment domestically.

Study pinpoints cantons with shortage of paediatricians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
11:57:00 UTC
20:57:00 KST

Study pinpoints cantons with shortage of paediatricians
There is a shortage of paediatricians in Switzerland, but it is not equally severe everywhere. A new study shows why families in some cantons struggle to get appointments, while others are well catered for.
Nationwide, there is one paediatrician for around 1,600 children, the University of Bern announced on Tuesday. While in Geneva there is one full-time post for every 750 children, in cantons such as Appenzell Outer Rhodes the figure is 4,750 children per post, and in Obwalden it is 4,150.
The study identified the high proportion of part-time work (87%), a heavy administrative burden and rising expectations from parents as the reasons for the shortages. Furthermore, the density of paediatricians is higher in cantons where medical services are better remunerated.
For the study, published in the specialist journal Swiss Medical Weekly, practising members of the Swiss Paediatric Society were surveyed.
