Favorable attitudes toward diverse sexual practices predict higher sexual well-being in young adults
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
11:00:30 UTC
20:00:30 KST

Young adults who hold open, favorable views toward specific sexual practices tend to experience higher levels of sexual pleasure, satisfaction, self-esteem, and confidence. The research, published in Psychology & Sexuality, suggests that embracing diverse forms of sexual expression acts as a protective factor for overall sexual well-being. These outcomes support a shift away from traditional risk-based sex education toward models that emphasize personal agency and healthy development.
Public health frameworks have historically approached sexual health through a lens of risk reduction, focusing primarily on preventing disease and unintended pregnancies. This perspective often overlooks the emotional and psychological aspects of human sexuality. Contemporary health organizations now advocate for a holistic approach that includes sexual pleasure, autonomy, and mutual respect as core components of well-being.
Global health authorities advise conceptualizing sexual health beyond the mere absence of dysfunction. Comprehensive sexuality education is designed to equip young people with the knowledge and attitudes needed to foster healthy development. Interventions that incorporate positive components, like sexual pleasure, often show better outcomes in promoting safer sexual practices, such as consistent condom use.
In many Latin American countries, sexual education remains heavily influenced by conservative cultural and religious traditions. These environments frequently prioritize abstinence and moral restraint, which can inadvertently foster shame or anxiety surrounding sexual exploration. Seeking to understand how young people navigate these cultural messages, psychologists Ana Chamorro Coneo of Universidad del Norte, along with Dayana Restrepo of Universidad de la Costa and Ailed Marenco of Corporación Universitaria Reformada, initiated a new investigation.
The research team focused on “positive sexuality,” a psychological framework that evaluates how people experience and manage their sexual lives in fulfilling ways. This framework relies on four main pillars: sexual pleasure, sexual satisfaction, sexual self-efficacy, and sexual self-esteem. Sexual self-efficacy describes a person’s confidence in their ability to communicate desires and make informed decisions. Sexual self-esteem relates to an individual’s perception of their own worth in intimate settings.
The researchers aimed to determine if holding favorable attitudes toward specific acts, namely masturbation, oral sex, anal sex, and pornography, predicts higher scores across these four pillars. They sought to identify whether these specific attitudes offer a better indicator of healthy sexual functioning than general demographics or overall psychological well-being.
To explore these associations, the researchers surveyed 475 heterosexual university students in northern Colombia. The participants, who ranged in age from 18 to 35, completed anonymous online questionnaires assessing their demographic backgrounds, religious affiliations, and household income. Over half of the respondents reported being in a romantic relationship, and a similar proportion indicated that they had their first sexual intercourse before the age of 16.
The survey included a widely used metric to evaluate general psychological well-being over the preceding two weeks. This allowed the researchers to account for general mental health as a baseline factor. By establishing this baseline, the team could test whether attitudes toward sexual behaviors explain variations in positive sexuality above and beyond a person’s general emotional state.
The core of the survey asked participants to rate their attitudes toward masturbation, pornography, oral sex, and anal sex. A separate set of questions measured the frequency of their positive sexual experiences across the four domains of pleasure, satisfaction, self-efficacy, and self-esteem. The researchers then used statistical models to separate the influence of general well-being and demographics from the specific impact of sexual attitudes.
The statistical analysis revealed that baseline demographics and general well-being accounted for only a modest portion of the variation in positive sexuality. By contrast, individual attitudes toward specific sexual practices strongly predicted the respondents’ sexual well-being.
Participants who expressed positive views regarding masturbation, oral sex, and anal sex reported higher levels of sexual pleasure and satisfaction. These same individuals also exhibited greater sexual self-efficacy and self-esteem. The researchers noted that accepting attitudes toward masturbation consistently related to better outcomes across all four domains. This supports the idea that solo sexual exploration acts as a developmental tool for building bodily awareness and confidence.
Attitudes toward pornography were not statistically significant predictors of positive sexuality. Favorable views on pornography neither enhanced nor diminished the participants’ reported pleasure, satisfaction, self-efficacy, or self-esteem. The authors suggest that pornography consumption is highly context-dependent, and simply holding a liberal attitude toward it does not automatically translate to changes in personal sexual well-being.
Age emerged as a consistent predictor of positive sexuality. Older participants generally reported higher levels of pleasure, satisfaction, and confidence than their younger peers. The researchers attribute this trend to the natural accumulation of relational experience and emotional maturity that occurs throughout a person’s twenties.
The analysis also highlighted a persistent gender gap in the domain of sexual pleasure. Men reported higher levels of pleasure than women, a pattern that remained even after accounting for the participants’ sexual attitudes. This finding aligns with established research on the “pleasure gap” in heterosexual relationships, where traditional societal scripts prioritize male physical gratification while insufficiently addressing female sexual stimulation.
General psychological well-being was positively associated with sexual satisfaction, self-efficacy, and self-esteem, but it was not linked to sexual pleasure. The researchers suggest that pleasure is often situational and shaped by immediate physical dynamics and partner responsiveness. In contrast, satisfaction and self-esteem involve more reflective evaluations of a person’s overall life and perceived competence.
Contrary to expectations based on regional cultural norms, neither religious affiliation nor socioeconomic status predicted any dimension of positive sexuality. The researchers propose that modern young adults might separate their broader religious identities from their personal sexual values. This separation allows them to maintain religious affiliations without internalizing restrictive sexual morals.
The study relies on a cross-sectional design, meaning the researchers collected all data at a single point in time. This methodology cannot determine a strict cause-and-effect relationship between sexual attitudes and positive sexuality. It is possible that individuals who naturally experience high sexual satisfaction gradually develop more open attitudes as a result of their positive experiences.
The sample consisted entirely of heterosexual university students who had access to digital platforms, and nearly three-quarters of the respondents were women. This demographic profile limits the ability to generalize the results to older adults, sexual minorities, or individuals living in rural areas with less educational access. Future investigations should employ broader sampling techniques to capture a wider array of perspectives and life experiences.
Additionally, the study assessed positive sexuality purely as an individual psychological experience. Future research might explore how these attitudes influence relational dynamics, such as partner communication, mutual consent, and contraceptive negotiation. Expanding the focus to include interpersonal factors could provide a comprehensive view of how sexual attitudes shape intimate relationships.
The study, “Beyond risk: how attitudes towards oral sex, masturbation, and pornography correlate with positive sexuality in emerging adults,” was authored by Ana Chamorro Coneo, Dayana Restrepo, and Ailed Marenco.

Poland has granted Ukraine a permit to carry out work in the village of Laskow in the Chelm region, at the suspected burial site of Ukrainians killed in March 1944, First Deputy Culture Minister Ivan Verbytsky said.
"Poland has granted a permit for a Ukrainian expedition to conduct search work in the village of Laskow in the Chelm region, at the suspected burial site of Ukrainian civilian residents killed in March 1944," Verbytsky wrote on Facebook.
The permit was issued to the Dolia memorial search center, and the work will be carried out on behalf of the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINP), he said.
He said the permit is the result of agreements reached by the Ukrainian-Polish working group on dignified burials, which operates on the initiative of both countries’ culture ministries.
As previously reported, the remains of 42 people were found in early May 2025 at an exhumation site in the former village of Puzhnyky in Ternopil region. The bodies were reburied on Sept 6.
A joint Ukrainian-Polish expedition also carried out search and exhumation work in Lviv (Stari Zboishcha), uncovering a mass grave of World War II victims. The remains of fallen Polish Army soldiers were reburied in Mostyska, Lviv region, on Nov 14, 2025.
In addition, search work took place in late September 2025 at a suspected burial site of Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) fighters in the village of Jureczkowa in Poland’s Podkarpackie Voivodeship, though no graves were found there.
In mid-December 2025, the Ukrainian-Polish working group on historical memory set out plans for search and exhumation work in 2026, including searches and exhumations on the Ukrainian side in Uhly (completed), as well as in the former villages of Huta Pieniacka and Ostrivky, while similar work in Poland was planned in Sahryn and Laskow.
Search work in the village of Uhly in Rivne region, carried out jointly by the Ukrainian-Polish expedition, concluded on March 27, 2026, with no mass graves found.
Search work at the site of a mass grave of victims of the 1944 events in the village of Huta Pieniacka, Lviv region, concluded on June 18, uncovering a mass grave covering about 70 square meters, though exhumation of those buried there has been postponed to next year.
In late June, a new stage of searches began for the remains of residents of the former village of Puzhnyky (now within the village of Sadove, Koropets settlement community, Chortkiv district, Ternopil region) who died tragically in February 1945.
In July, research was to be carried out in the former villages of Ostrivky and Volya Ostrovetska (now within the Rivne rural community, Kovel district, Volyn region) aimed at exhuming and reburying the remains of residents of those villages who died in August 1943. During the exhumation work, the remains of 48 people were found in the former village of Volya Ostrovetska, and the remains of 6 people were found in the former village of Ostrivky. The remains of 55 former residents of Ostrivky and Volya Ostrovetska were reburied in Volyn region in late August.
In early August, the Polish side handed over a list of sites for further search and exhumation work in Ukraine.
On Aug 25, search and exhumation work began at Holoskivske Cemetery in Lviv to locate the remains of Polish soldiers killed in 1939.

TIRED
ANC won’t win awards. Bass-forward tuning might not suit you. Build quality feels a bit more plastic than premium. Not a vast upgrade of the Momentum 4. Feel slightly overpriced.
We’ve waited almost four years for a new pair of Sennheiser Momentum wireless over-ear headphones. That’s eons in a world where Sony, Apple, and Bowers & Wilkins have been busy launching stellar Bluetooth headphones like the Sony WH-1000XM6, Apple AirPods Max 2, and Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3.
Plenty has happened in the intervening years—not least, Sennheiser’s consumer division being sold to hearing aid company Sonova, which is currently looking to sell it on. Thankfully, the Momentum 5 is a hugely enjoyable pair of premium headphones with some unexpectedly good features, and not the product of a troubled homelife.
Battery Life for Life
Photograph: Chris Haslam
The Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless look good. They strike a middle ground between premium cans (AirPods Max 2, Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3) and more lightweight ones (Bose QuietComfort Headphones, Sony WH-1000XM5). The 10.3-ounce build is mainly plastic, and the ear cups are basic, but the denim trim on the top of the comfortable headband adds fun texture. They are not head turners like the Nothing Headphone (1), but they are still nice to look at, and come in blue denim (pictured), black, and white.
They are, however, very comfortable, with a great level of squish to the earpads. Massive ears (like mine) have room to flap, and the headband doesn’t add any uncomfortable pressure. No over-ear headphone is perfect to wear with glasses, but I happily wore these for hours. When temperatures hit 95 degrees Fahrenheit my ears got sweaty, but so did the rest of me, to be fair.
The Momentum 5 Wireless get up to 57 hours of battery with ANC on, according to Sennheiser. That’s almost double what the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 can do. It’s three hours shy of the older Momentum 4, and 13 hours less than the similarly priced Marshall Monitor III ANC.
I didn’t perform an exact test on the 57-hour battery claim, but it seems fairly accurate in my real-world use thus far. I have been using the Momentum 5 daily for the past month, and they are still at about 50 percent charge.
The more interesting story to me is that the battery can be easily replaced. Remove the left ear pad, unscrew four Phillips-head screws, lift the cover, and the battery can be unplugged and swapped out in seconds.
iFixit has been showing us how to replace batteries in electronics for years, but this is the first time I’ve seen a headphone brand actively encourage consumers to do it themselves. I think Sennheiser embracing our right to repair is worth celebrating, even if, at the time of publication, the replaceable battery isn't available for purchase.
Lively and Warm Sound
Photograph: Chris Haslam
The Momentum 5 Wireless supports SBC, AAC, aptX, aptX HD, aptX Lossless, and aptX Adaptive codecs, plus multipoint connectivity. Plug in using either the 3.5-millimeter jack or the USB-C port to get digital lossless audio (up to 24-bit/96 kHz).
The Sennheiser Smart Control Plus app is where you can customize ANC levels, transparency, an eight-band EQ, connection preferences, and Dolby Atmos. You can also save sound profiles based on your location, maxing out ANC when you hit the office, for instance.
Controls on the headphones themselves are touch controls on the right ear cup, and they work fine: as in, they didn’t annoy me. A tap pauses music, swipes adjust volume and skip tracks, while a double tap toggles between ANC and transparency modes.
Active Noise Cancellation comes via eight microphones, and it is good, verging on great. It works well on public transport, provides a cocoon in cafés, and gifts solitude in a shared office. If you’ve never used Sony or Bose ANC headphones, you’ll be delighted with the Momentum 5s, but if you’re switching from those two brands, you might find these a bit of a letdown. We’re talking small margins here, but the Momentum 5 just lacks that eerily quiet sealed-off feeling of the WH-1000XM6 or Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen).
Call quality is good too, and the wind-reducing mics kept my voice front and center, but it’s not the reason I’d buy these headphones.
I tested the Momentum 5 Wireless using the best and worst playback resolutions from Spotify—both over Wi-Fi and cellular. I also listened to Qobuz hi-resolution recordings and my own digital music library. And no matter what I played, the headphones offered me a smooth, refined, and expressive performance.
They’re not “high-fidelity” in the sense that the extreme edges of a recording are not exposed, and they happily make poor-quality output sound enjoyable. That said, you’ll get a bit more out of them by listening to higher-fidelity sources. And if you’re still playing the lowest-resolution audio playback on Spotify (or don’t even know what I am talking about), you don’t need to spend $399 on a pair of headphones.
Mixing it up between the pop of Olivia Rodrigo’s excellent new album, the twang of Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band, via Wu-Tang, and more of the Police than I’m comfortable admitting, the Sennheiser made every genre enjoyable to listen to and were totally agreeable. They’re not neutral, with plenty of relaxed warmth to the sound profile.
Photograph: Chris Haslam
Listening to the Sennheisers side by side with the B&W Px7 S3, I noticed a little lack in punch and drive by comparison. The opposite is true when listening to them against the AirPods Max 2, however, with the Sennheiser’s classy midrange cutting through the mix with real authority. This was also the case when comparing them with the now discontinued Momentum 3 Wireless from 2019 (although I wish Sennheiser would bring back the sumptuous leather earpads at least as an add-on).
They are bass-forward, though, and anyone leaning toward acoustic or classical would do well to tweak the EQ via the app. The sound is clean overall, with a tight thump, although not a patch on the taut rumble from the more expensive AirPods Max.
Should You Buy Them?
The Momentum 5 Wireless are long overdue, but at $399, they face stiff competition from more mainstream competitors like Sony, Bose, Apple, and Bowers & Wilkins, all of whom have launched serious good over-ear headphones recently. This hasn’t left a lot of room for Sennheiser to compete in, but, sensibly, the brand hasn’t tried to win every battle.
The ANC is very good (but not spookily quiet), and the design is classy (but not indulgent). Sound is warm, expressive, and easy to enjoy for long periods of time, even if the bass might need taming in the EQ. But importantly, Sennheiser has created a headphone with superb battery life, easy wired and hi-res listening, an impressive codec list, and an easily replaceable battery you can swap yourself.
They are not the most exciting headphones in any one area, but they are comfortable, considered, likable, and impressively repairable.
Chris Haslam is an award-winning consumer technology journalist with over 20 years’ experience. As contributing editor for WIRED he specializes in audio, smart home, sustainability, and all things outdoors. ‘The work you do reflects your character’: How a Türkiye craftsman mastered mother-of-pearl inlay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:59:46 UTC
19:59:46 KST

At the end of a long day in the workshop, Mehmet Bulent Fistikci’s mentor would leave his apprentices with a lesson that had little to do with wood, wire or mother-of-pearl.
“My son, the work you do reflects your character. The cleaner your work, the cleaner your character will be.”
Decades later, the words of his late mentor, Hayri Akbay, still shape the way Fistikci approaches his craft.
For nearly 40 years, the Gaziantep-based craftsman has worked with walnut wood, thin strands of metal and shimmering pieces of mother-of-pearl, turning them into intricately decorated objects through a process that demands patience, precision and years of experience.
But his journey into the craft began almost by chance.
Born in 1976 and raised in Gaziantep, Fistikci first entered a workshop as a child.
One of his uncles was a carpenter. Fistikci recalls that his mother sent him to work with his uncle because he was constantly getting into trouble at home.
He spent several years there as an apprentice before another uncle introduced him to mother-of-pearl inlay.
“My mother told him, ‘Take him with you. He’s just sitting around doing nothing here again,’” Fistikci recalls.
His uncle took him by the hand to a mother-of-pearl workshop, where another coincidence helped determine the course of his life: the master’s son happened to be one of Fistikci’s primary school friends.
“He told his father, ‘He’s my primary school friend. Let him start working here.’ And I started there.”
On his first day, Fistikci learned how to make “kuncu”, a small brass decorative element used in the craft.
It was unusual for a new apprentice. At the time, he says, apprentices would normally have to wait at least three years before being allowed to work on it.
“I started doing it on my very first day.”
Fistikci spent 15 years in Hayri Akbay’s workshop, staying there until his mentor died.
The technical skills he acquired during those years were only one part of his apprenticeship. Just as important was the way Akbay conducted himself.
“I always looked up to his manner, the way he dressed and his attitude,” Fistikci says.
A mother-of-pearl workshop is filled with dust from cutting, carving and sanding wood, yet Fistikci remembers never seeing his mentor looking untidy.
“I never saw my mentor unshaved,” he says.
“Even though a mother-of-pearl workshop can be dusty and dirty, he always dressed very neatly.”
As a young apprentice, Fistikci wondered how his mentor stayed so immaculate while working in such an environment.
Over time, he came to understand that craftsmanship was not simply about producing an object. It was also about discipline and the character of the person making it.
“I always looked up to my mentor’s character, personality and the way he carried himself in the workshop.”
That philosophy remains visible in the painstaking way Fistikci works today.
From the Euphrates to the workshop
Mother-of-pearl inlay holds a distinctive place in Ottoman decorative arts. Among its best-known masters was [Sedefkar Mehmet Aga], who later became the architect of Istanbul’s Sultan Ahmed Mosque.
In the late 19th century, Sultan Abdulhamid II established a mother-of-pearl workshop at Yildiz Palace, helping sustain the craft within the imperial tradition. Geometric compositions and floral motifs, including tulips and carnations, became characteristic elements of the art.
Fistikci still works with many of those materials and motifs today.
One of the central materials he uses comes from freshwater mussel shells found along the Euphrates River.
During the heat of July, he explains, the shells wash up along the riverbanks, where they are collected.
“If we didn’t collect them, they would simply rot in nature,” he says.
“We make use of them without harming any living creatures.”
They break the shells, flatten them, and carefully shape them before using them as mother-of-pearl inlays.
“This is our original mother-of-pearl,” Fistikci says, holding up the material.
“The finest mother-of-pearl in Türkiye comes from the Euphrates River.”
His workshop also uses varieties originating farther afield, including abalone, commonly used in jewellery and decorative pieces, as well as pearl-bearing shells and red mother-of-pearl.
For Fistikci, their colours form nature’s own palette.
Black, green, red and iridescent surfaces eventually become tiny pieces within much larger geometric and floral compositions.
But before the mother-of-pearl can be placed, the wooden object itself has to take shape.
Fistikci begins with walnut wood, with carpenters and woodturners preparing the raw pieces before the design process begins.
The surface is divided into geometric forms, and the motif is drawn. Tulips and other flowers can form part of the composition, while names can also be incorporated alongside Ottoman numerals and Arabic, Turkish or Latin lettering.
Once the design is complete, a tool known as a “kesi” is used to open narrow channels for the metal wire.
Fistikci says his workshop commonly uses 0.80-millimetre brass wire, although aluminium, silver and alpaca wire can also be used.
The mother-of-pearl is then prepared by hand. Freshwater mussel shells are broken with pliers and flattened on both sides, with each fragment shaped by eye to match the space carved into the wood.
The pieces are then glued into place.
A day later, the surface is sanded until the wood, metal wire, and mother-of-pearl sit at exactly the same level.
The finished object may appear seamless, but the process behind it is anything but simple.
A craft passed from father to son
For Fistikci, preserving the craft has also meant bringing it into his own family.
His eldest son, Ali Fistikci, began working beside him at 10 years old. Today, Ali has spent years working as a master instructor at an Institute of Maturation, while his middle son, Hakan, works in the family workshop.
His youngest son, Cagri, who is still in high school, has also been trained by his father.
The sense of continuity extends beyond his sons.
Fistikci says he has worked with the same colleagues in his workshop for at least two decades.
“We’re like a family,” he says. “It’s the same team, and we’ve stayed together all these years.”
That continuity matters especially in a craft where knowledge has traditionally been passed directly from one pair of hands to another.
Fistikci himself learned by sitting beside a master. Now he occupies the other side of that relationship.
The boy who was once taken by the hand into a workshop now teaches his own children the craft he learned there.
Fistikci’s decades of work eventually brought wider recognition.
At the Usta Eller Bazaar, which brings together traditional crafts and masters from different cities, Fistikci was chosen to represent mother-of-pearl inlay.
There, he established a workshop and was allocated a 60-square-metre shop.
The recognition reached another level when he received an award in the presence of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
For Fistikci, the moment's significance was not financial.
“The material value is not what matters,” he says. “The emotional significance is beyond words.”
Receiving the award from the president, he adds, was “a great honour”.
“It was an indescribable feeling. I can’t put it into words.”
Yet nearly four decades after he first entered a workshop as a boy, Fistikci still returns to the lesson his mentor taught him there.
Amid walnut wood, brass wire and fragments of mother-of-pearl, Hayri Akbay’s words continue to shape both the objects Fistikci makes and the way he makes them:
“The work you do reflects your character.”

Russian Sailor Who Burned Serpukhov Missile Ship Reveals How He Pulled Off the Sabotage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:59:42 UTC
19:59:42 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Sailor Who Burned Serpukhov Missile Ship Reveals How He Pulled Off the Sabotage
A Russian Navy sailor secretly smuggled gasoline aboard his own missile ship, stole classified documents and then set fire to the vessel before fleeing Russia and eventually joining the Freedom of Russia Legion fighting alongside Ukraine, Sky News reported on August 31.
The sailor, identified by the call sign Goga, had served as a radio operator aboard the Serpukhov, a Russian Buyan-M-class missile corvette stationed in Kaliningrad and capable of launching Kalibr cruise missiles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The sabotage knocked the ship out of action for months, preventing it from being used to launch Kalibr missiles against Ukraine.
Goga told Sky News that he had opposed Russia’s full-scale invasion from the beginning despite serving in the Russian military.
“I was the only person on the ship who did not support the war,” he said.
Raised in a military family in Kaliningrad, Goga initially tried to convince fellow sailors that the invasion was wrong. His efforts eventually brought him to the attention of military prosecutors, who issued him an official warning.
He later attempted to leave the Russian Navy through official channels, but his resignation request was rejected.
“After I had exhausted every possible legal avenue for leaving the military, I no longer knew what to do or how to get myself discharged from service,” Goga said.
His situation became more urgent when rumors began circulating that several Russian vessels could soon be deployed for operations connected to the war against Ukraine.
Determined not to participate in attacks on Ukrainians, Goga contacted the Freedom of Russia Legion, a formation composed largely of Russian citizens fighting against Moscow’s forces.
After an extended verification process, a plan was developed for him to sabotage the Serpukhov and escape.
While continuing to serve aboard the ship, Goga gradually collected classified military documents and secretly carried containers of gasoline onto the vessel.
“I began bringing fuel into the communications compartment and pouring it onto the equipment,” he said.
Before starting the fire, Goga also removed sensitive documents from the ship.
“Before that, I gathered all the classified documents and took them with me,” he stated.
He then set a timer to ignite the fire, left the vessel carrying the files and took a taxi toward the Lithuanian border.
The blaze spread through the ship’s communications compartment, damaging critical electronics and putting the Serpukhov out of service for several months.
The damage deprived Russia of one platform capable of launching Kalibr cruise missiles during that period.
Goga later reached Ukraine and joined the Freedom of Russia Legion.
Previously, reports emerged that several damaged vessels belonging to Russia’s Black Sea Fleet have been spotted sheltering in bays around temporarily occupied Sevastopol, including a damaged missile boat concealed beneath camouflage netting.

Ukraine Converts US-Made Humvees Into Satellite-Controlled Unmanned Vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:59:13 UTC
19:59:13 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Converts US-Made Humvees Into Satellite-Controlled Unmanned Vehicles
Ukraine has begun deploying US-made HMMWVs converted into remotely operated ground vehicles, allowing military units to use existing vehicles for missions without placing a driver onboard.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Three modified HMMWVs equipped with the Ukrainian-developed Kaban remote-control system have already been delivered to military units, according to Defence Blog on August 31.
The vehicles were transferred to Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, the 429th Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment “Achilles,” and the 49th Brigade of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Developed by Ukrainian company Drone Fight Group, Kaban is designed to turn conventional military vehicles into remotely operated platforms rather than requiring the development of dedicated unmanned ground vehicles.
The system allows an operator to control the vehicle’s movement as well as its lights, infrared illumination, searchlights, two-way audio communications, and onboard computer systems from a remote location.
According to Defence Blog, Kaban uses satellite connectivity, potentially allowing operators to control vehicles at considerably greater distances than systems dependent on short-range radio links. The actual operating distance depends on network availability and mission conditions.
The control interface also incorporates a digital map for planning routes and placing navigation markers. Operators can manually correct the vehicle’s navigation if satellite positioning is disrupted by GPS jamming or spoofing, while a predicted trajectory display assists with maneuvering.
A built-in fail-safe automatically stops the vehicle if communication with the operator is lost.
“Our goal is not simply to make a vehicle drive remotely,” said David, the system’s lead developer. “We are building a system that gives an operator enough information and control to confidently perform real missions from a safer location.”
“That includes vehicle systems, navigation, communications, fail-safe behavior, and the ability to adapt the platform to different operational requirements.”
The technology is intended for missions including logistics, battlefield resupply, evacuation, and reconnaissance support where deploying a crew inside the vehicle would create additional risk. Drone Fight Group says the platform can also accommodate specialized equipment, including net launchers and systems for deploying drones.
In June, Ukraine also unveiled a remotely operated version of the Soviet-era BRDM-2 armored vehicle. The modernized BRDM-2M uses technology developed by Estonian company Telearmy, allowing operators to remotely control steering, braking, throttle, transmission, and weapon systems via mobile networks, satellite internet, or radio communications.

Germany eyes Algerian gas to diversify supply ahead of winter, FM Johann Wadephul says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:56:45 UTC
19:56:45 KST

The EU's top economy used to rely on cheap Russian gas but large deliveries stopped after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, dealing a heavy blow to German industry.
Germany is looking for gas deals with Algeria to diversify its supply, Berlin's foreign minister said in Algiers on Tuesday, where he joined a business delegation visiting the North African country.
"We need to diversify...We need long-term gas contracts," Johann Wadephul told German public broadcaster ZDF on the second day of his trip, as concerns grow in Germany that gas storage depots are only half full as autumn nears.
Wadephul said that he would meet with Energy Minister Mourad Adjal and that representatives of German companies looking for long-term contracts were travelling with him.
Noting Algerian deals with Spain and Italy, Wadephul said "I also hope that Germany will now be able to secure part of its gas supply here. That is our core interest."
The EU's top economy used to rely on cheap Russian gas but large deliveries stopped after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, dealing a heavy blow to German industry.
Berlin has since largely replaced Russian energy with Norwegian piped gas as well as American liquefied natural gas, though LNG prices are usually higher and more volatile than those from long-term piped gas deals.
The US-Israeli war on Iran has put further pressure on gas prices, leading to fears of a possible energy crunch this winter.
At the moment Germany's gas storage is just 53% full compared to an EU average of 65%, according to figures from the Aggregated Gas Storage Inventory.
"Since there is no prospect of a quick end to both crises it's clear that we need to diversify," Wadephul said. "We need more suppliers."
Following the gas crisis of 2022, the German government introduced mandatory minimum levels for gas storage in a bid to smooth out jumps in spot gas prices, with the state stepping in as a buyer if necessary.
The government has mandated that most gas storage facilities must be at least 80% full by 1 November.

The Danish foreign minister also met Syrian President Ahmed al Sharaa on Monday, with talks focusing on bilateral relations as well as cooperation on recovery and reconstruction to support stability in Syria.
Al Shaibani and Rasmussen previously met in Brussels in May, where they discussed expanding political and humanitarian cooperation and supporting stabilisation efforts in Syria.

Nepal flood: Death toll tops 1,000 as rescue continues
September 1, 2026
The death toll after a massive flash flood last week at the Himalayan border between Nepal and China has risen more than 1,000 people, local authorities said on Tuesday.
In Nepal, 987 deaths have already been reported, with almost 4,000 people still being unaccounted for. In China,16 deaths and 546 missing people have been reported.
The list of missing people includes some 800 foreign nationals.
Search and rescue teams are still carrying out operations despite difficult conditions and unstable terrain.
Search dogs are also taking part in the search efforts through mud, rocks and debris the flash floods left behind.
Roads were destroyed in places, cutting off access.
Efforts are also being made to locate the some 500 workers believed to be trapped inside the tunnels of twelve hydropower project tunnels, according to Nepalese authorities.
Climate change raises risk for region, PM says
The flash floods on August 28, started as a glacial collapse in the Himalayas triggered a powerful stream of rock, ice and meltwater into the valleys below.
The stream was so powerful that a seismic event of 5.2 magnitude was recorded.
Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah reacted to the disaster by emphasizing the need to fight climate change.
"This incident has indicated that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing with climate change," he posted on social media.
"Therefore, this region must be alert, and at the same time, it is time for us to strongly raise the issue of disasters caused by climate change before the international community."

How much should a dinosaur cost?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:52:41 UTC
19:52:41 KST

How much is a Tyrannosaurus rex worth? If you ask the person who bought “Gus,” one of the most complete T. rex skeletons ever found, last month, the answer is $50.1 million.
The price is eye-popping, but it underscores the rising value of dinosaur fossils—and the threat these prices pose to paleontologists.
Fossils didn't always command such steep prices. At least until the late 1990s, dinosaur skeletons didn’t cost more than $1 million, says Kirk Johnson, Sant director of the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History. “If you’re a paleontologist or a scientist, $1 million seems like a huge amount of money. So suddenly [$50 million], like, your brain explodes,” Johnson says. Still, it’s the consequence of dinosaur bones being treated—and sold—like fine art.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“Gus” is the most expensive dinosaur ever sold, but the previous record holder, “Apex” the Stegosaurus, sold for around $44.6 million in 2024. The first fossil sold at auction—and the first to sell for more than $1 million—was “Sue” the T. rex: in 1997 it sold to Chicago’s Field Museum for $8.3 million.
Each fossil is unique, says Craig Kissick, vice president of natural history at Heritage Auctions. Unlike more common collectables, such as coins or baseball cards, “there is not one dinosaur bone that is the same as another,” Kissick says. “Any collectible category that is not graded and commoditized is going to have its own unique set of rules.”
As a result, fossils are appraised based on what auctioneers know—the completeness of a fossil and the price that the last one sold for.
“If you talk to the auction houses and say, ‘What do you think this is worth?’ they’ll say, ‘I don’t know what it’s worth, but I can tell you how much it’s sold for,’” Johnson says. “When Apex the Stegosaurus sold for $44 million, Stegosauruses [became] worth $44 million.”
Who exactly buys these fossils is sometimes a mystery. Hedge fund billionaire Ken Griffin bought Apex and then loaned the dinosaur to the American Museum of Natural History in New York City. Another sold-at-auction specimen, the $32-million “Stan” the T. rex, disappeared from public view for years before reappearing at a natural history museum in Abu Dhabi.
“The people buying the expensive dinosaurs are not necessarily hardcore natural history collectors or museums. They’re hedge fund managers. They’re celebrities,” Kissick says. “If you’ve already got five homes and 10 cars, what’s next? Well, maybe a dinosaur.”
Like fine art, some economists believe fossils are more than unique collectibles and status symbols—they can be alternative investments. The benefit is that “their value may be less prone to volatility” compared to stocks, says Simon Condliffe, an economist at West Chester University. That said, they don’t appreciate the same way shares do. Comparing the prices of the most recently sold T. rexes to returns on the S&P 500 for the same period, “the S&P 500 wins comfortably,” Condliffe says.
Increasingly high fossil prices are a problem for paleontology, says Kristina Curry Rogers, a vertebrate paleontologist at Macalester College, because they “encourage the perception that dinosaur fossils are investment assets rather than irreplaceable pieces of our collective natural heritage.”
They also encourage fossil hunters—commercial paleontologists and hobbyists looking to turn a profit on dinosaur bones—no matter the cost to science.
Booming Commercial Paleontology
Fossil hunters aren’t a new phenomenon, Johnson says, and many work with museums, academics and collectors to find dinosaur bones ethically and legally. Cary Woodruff, curator of vertebrate paleontology at Frost Science in Miami, says he has a “wonderful relationship” with Jason Cooper, the paleontologist who found Apex, for example. Sue the T. rex was found during a commercial excavation trip, too.
“There have been so many amazing fossils that, frankly, just would not have been found” without commercial fossil hunters, Woodruff says. But the work isn’t charity. “A lot of them are very nice people, but in that simple respect of what they’re doing—digging to sell—they are not benefiting the scientific discipline,” Woodruff says.
Increasing payouts for fossils present an ethical problem, researchers say. They could incentivize poaching, illegally excavating fossils from federal land or fabricating information about a fossil to buyers.
“If you’re a land manager, you’re like, ‘I'm going to be watching for illegal digs now because there’s a $50-million dinosaur out there for somebody,’” Johnson says.
“As [we see] these higher and higher dollar values, we’re seeing more crimes,” says Woodruff, citing lawsuits and even the brandishing of weapons at dig sites. Rogers says she’s personally witnessed fossil poaching from active excavation sites—and later seen those fossils up for auction.
“I really think that, in a very short period of time, we will see someone killed in the United States over a dinosaur,” Woodruff says.
Are Private Fossils Lost to Science?
Some of the most expensive fossils are also some of the most complete ever found: Gus, Stan and Apex are among them, and access to them would help researchers understand of how their species looked, moved and evolved. Other dinosaurs are extremely rare finds, such as Archaeopteryx, of which just 14 fossils have ever been unearthed. Each specimen changes our knowledge of the animal, but at least one was hidden away for years before it could be studied.
In theory, scientific research can be done on privately owned fossils. But whether that research is worthwhile depends on who owns them and how they’re stored. The issue, Rogers says, “isn’t whether fossils are discovered. It’s whether, after discovery, their scientific value can be preserved for future generations.”
“When done right, amateur and commercial paleontologists add a great deal to the lexicon of our knowledge of the science,” Kissick says. “When we auction something, I don’t think it’s lost to science. I think it’s brought in front of the whole world.”
Certainly, many museums, such as the American Museum of Natural History, have accepted dinosaurs on loan from private collections. It makes the specimen available to the public, Johnson says, but this also amounts to a public institution storing an individual’s asset for them. “It’s certainly not unethical or illegal,” he says. “I just don’t think it’s very prudent.” And museums can bid for fossils at auction just like any other buyer, says Johnson—so long as it is within their budget, of course.
Auctions and acquisitions aren’t the only way these institutions obtain fossils: Museums have the legal right to excavate fossils on federal land, whereas commercial paleontologists don’t, for example.
But if a rare fossil that is important to science is being sold on the art market for an exorbitant price, the reality is simple: “Museums are not trying to buy these dinosaurs at this price rate,” Johnson says. “They can’t afford it.”

The brain, solved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:52:17 UTC
19:52:17 KST

It took years, an international consortium and a small army of volunteer proofreaders. That effort led to the first full map of every neuron and synapse in an animal brain—139,000 neurons, 50 million connections, none of them left unaccounted for. The animal brain being mapped? A fruit fly’s. In comparison, the human brain has upward of 86 billion neurons, connected by some 100 trillion synapses. It is easily one of the most complex objects we know—including the universe itself. In this special edition, Scientific American surveys that complexity—the everyday mechanics of a working brain, what keeps it healthy or lets it fail, and the odder mysteries scientists have yet to solve.
The brain, it turns out, is less a fixed organ than a system in constant negotiation with the rest of the body and the world around it. Sleep, for instance, isn’t downtime but active maintenance, when the brain flushes out cellular waste in ways that may help stave off dementia. That body-mind entanglement means that physical exercise may slow cognitive aging in the long run; synchronized movements such as dancing forge surprisingly deep connections between people. And new weight-loss drugs are exposing the neural circuitry behind hunger, pleasure and satiety and, in the process, complicating what we thought about food addiction.
But even a well-tended brain can falter, and nowhere is that more apparent than in people with Alzheimer’s. A more nuanced picture of the disease is now yielding a wider range of treatment strategies, including those that involve insulin and immune-modulating drugs. Some hope lies in prevention, as evidence suggests diet, exercise and social engagement may lower one’s risk. Meanwhile new blood-based biomarkers are offering better detection.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
If illness shows how memory can be lost, a parallel line of discovery is illuminating how it is built in the first place. The machinery switches on earlier than long assumed, as brain scans of infants reveal. Decades of work have now identified specific molecules that lock memories into place, with the search for others underway. And it turns out the act of forgetting may be less a flaw than a feature: everyday memory lapses are increasingly understood to be part of how learning happens.
Minds can be found everywhere in nature, often in places we’d never think to look for them—even without a brain to house them, clusters of cells no bigger than a speck can learn, remember and make surprisingly complex decisions. Consciousness itself can hide in unexpected places, too, with some patients in comas who seem entirely unresponsive revealing signs of a mind at work.
The search for awareness is now centered on machines, with the debate over artificial-intelligence sentience forcing scientists to take a hard look at what cognition and consciousness actually mean. The discourse is reshaping how we see other species as well. Growing evidence of even insects’ cognitive sophistication raises real ethical questions about how we should treat them.
The complexity of the mind guarantees that generations of scientists to come will be well occupied trying to understand it. But the tactics to help yours thrive are refreshingly unmysterious: whole foods, sleep, movement, friends. You don’t need to solve the brain to take good care of it.

Russia has no reason, plans or need to attack NATO countries, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko said Tuesday, specifically referring to the Baltic states.
“Why should Russia attack NATO, why? The Soviet Union recognised the independence of the Baltic states. And they left peacefully. Why attack them now?” Grushko told the Interfax news agency on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum.
He was responding to statements by European officials about possible Russian plans to attack a NATO member.
“There is no reason and no plans, none at all, to attack,” Grushko insisted.

Asked whether EU representatives had approached Moscow to discuss their concerns, Grushko said that “there is no real sentiment or desire on the part of Europeans that would be politically expressed as a political desire”, according to Interfax.

Investors tepid on Partners Group management reshuffle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:50:40 UTC
19:50:40 KST

Investors tepid on Partners Group management reshuffle
Swiss investment house Partners Group has reshuffled its top management after a slump in first-half earnings and warned of a weaker outlook for performance fees.
The Swiss private markets firm named veterans Roberto Cagnati and Juri Jenkner as co-chief executive officers, replacing David Layton, who will become chief investment officer. The shares slumped as much as 8.6%, bringing declines this year to almost 32%.
Partners Group, one of Europe’s largest alternative asset managers, has been struggling to emerge from a troubled period marked by a sustained share price decline, investor withdrawals and doubt over its valuation methods. Yet the firm reiterated its guidance for fundraising for this year on the back of record new assets in the first half.
Earlier this year, a wave of redemption requests hit Partners’ “evergreen” funds, which offer access to private markets with periodic withdrawals. The firm has been affected to a degree by the global decline in confidence over private markets.
“PG has announced a soft management reshuffle,” Pierre-Yves Gauthier, CEO and head of strategy at AlphaValue said. “This is intriguing. It may bring power back to Switzerland in contrast with Mr Layton running the firm from the US. The US is where the money is but also where the mess in evergreens started.”
Revenue fell 7% to CHF1.12 billion ($1.4 billion) in the six months to June from the same period last year, dragged down by a 39% decline in performance income. The alternative asset manager said that it was impacted by several sizeable exits that were “accelerated to capture market momentum.”
The firm said it now expects performance income to be around the range of 20% to 25% of total revenue for 2026, having previously said it expects between 25% and 40%. It said this was dependent “on the timing of select active direct exit processes.”
Citigroup analyst Nicholas Herman said he expects investors to react cautiously to the management change, and to the earnings coming in below consensus expectations. Profit decreased 13% to CHF502 million, below analyst estimates for CHF521 million.
Role Transition
The firm had previously signalled that Layton would transition into a different role.
Cagnati and Jenkner, who both joined the firm in 2004, “are highly experienced executives with a long history at Partners Group,” Chairman Steffen Meister said in a statement. “We are also pleased that after eight successful years as CEO, Dave is continuing in a key role in the firm.”
Despite the challenges evident in the past year, Partners has shown little sign of a radical change of course. In an interview with Bloomberg in June, Meister said there was “no need to change our strategy.”
The firm has reacted to recent turmoil by rotating long-term insiders into the top leadership team, rather than outside talent. Meister also commented on Layton’s move to the CIO role after holding the top executive job.
At “most companies, if that happens, the CEO would go on retirement or the competition or whatever,” he said on an earnings call. “That’s not PG style.”
At Partners, “successful key leaders in the firm, when they step back from their functions, they usually continue in other functions,” Meister said.
Cagnati has recently been head of portfolio solutions and chief risk officer. Jenkner is currently president and head of business development.
The firm, split between Zug in Switzerland and Denver in the US, has long been atypical of the private equity industry.
Partners downplays buyouts in favor of growing companies. The slogan “built differently to build differently” is emblazoned on its Baar, Switzerland headquarters while signage at the firm’s Colorado campus proclaims: “This Is Not Wall Street.”
Evergreen funds, which Partners Group pioneered in the early 2000s, have been central to its growth, and the centerpiece of its recent troubles. Those funds make up some 30% of all assets, with about $56 billion in evergreen funds as of year-end.
On the earnings call, Layton said that the firm had been “too concentrated” on certain segments. Partners is “working to build that diversification,” he said.
In July the company reported that across the group, clients added $16 billion in new commitments in the first half of the year, pushing assets under management to $186 billion.
Partners Group is considering paring back the overall sizes of its evergreen funds for wealthy investors, while broadly keeping its investment approach unchanged, Meister has said.
(Updates with shares. A previous version of this story was corrected to amend spelling of Jenkner’s name.)

julie blackmon’s midwest materials is a memory of the american landscape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:50:39 UTC
19:50:39 KST

In Julie Blackmon’s Midwest Materials, published in 2022 by Radius Books, is a series that both confirms and obscures the imagined life of the American suburb. In her photos, she moves through the landscape around her hometown in Springfield, Missouri, capturing moments that have all the trappings of childhood memory, but its meticulous colors, compositions, and staging render the stills closer to dreams than historical record.
Midwest Materials is Julie Blackmon’s third monograph published by Radius Books | image courtesy of Julie Blackmon and Haw Contemporary
The American Suburb as Muse
The ‘little boxes on the hillside, the little boxes made of ticky-tacky,’ as American folk singer Malvina Reynolds famously referred to American track-home suburbs in her 1962 song Little Boxes, has long captured the imagination of auteurs both in the States and abroad. Think Tim Burton’s Edward Scissorhands, Sam Mendes’s 2000 film American Beauty, or the hit television series Desperate Housewives, to name a few—they’re highly standardized rows of multi-bedroom homes have become their own stage for domestic drama. In Blackmon’s brightly colored, artfully composed images, she adds another narrative to the lore of the American landscape.
In the book foreword, art critic Leah Ollman draws the readers’ attention to the origins of the book’s title. The cover of Blackmon’s monograph comes from the image, called Midwest Materials as well, of children playing in front of a commercial building. They all face away from the camera, looking as though they are in the midst of playing a game of wall ball. In this image, the spheres hang in mid-air, paused as they ricochet off the side of the building. Ollman points out that the words ‘MIDWEST MATERIALS CO.,’ painted in a thick black san-serif against a creamy brick background, aptly describe how Blackmon manages to use people, places, and things from her home to materialize the energy of the place itself.
Throughout the book, Blackmon often returns to water as a site of relaxation and exploration. There are the scenic, moody images of lackadaisical days in River, where there is no land in sight—just floating docks, inner tubes, and adventures out into the blue. In Pool, an aquamarine swimming pool acts as a magnet for tots and tweens as they dot the composition. On the water-staining concrete image of Laying Out, you can almost feel the hot cement on your belly after crawling out of the chlorinated water. In these images, there’s a certain organized simplicity. The way that the kids fall upon the scene feels like sprinkles on top of a cake—it’s the rendering of a sweet memory. Even for those who have never been to the Midwestern region of the US, there’s a tender kinship here that knocks at the door that holds memories of summers with cousins, neighbors, and grade school classmates.
throughout the book, Blackmon often returns to water as a site of relaxation and exploration | image courtesy of Julie Blackmon and Haw Contemporary
Chairs, pianos, soccer balls
A hallmark of these photos is their sense of motion. Every space, whether it be a Costco, a living room with a piano, or a driveway, is a stage for actors to perform a domestic scene. In Costco, named for the wholesale grocer that’s famous for its low-cost bulk-buy offerings, children populate an open van as they dance, snooze, and explore an arrangement of name-brand vodka, a massive bag of sugar, and a near-child-sized bag of Doritos. Just off in the corner, an elongated group of shadows signals a group approaching the scene.
Similarly, New Chair features a bright red, bulbous armchair being unloaded from the back of a FedEx delivery truck. The chair that it’s presumably replacing—a mustard-colored lounger—sags in front of the garage with a handwritten ‘$20 OBO’ sign tacked to its front. As with almost all of her images, children, cats, and babies, captured in the middle of play and make-believe, frame the unloading of this recently arrived furniture. The scene is so familiar, with the saturation of it all makings something like a childhood memory feel like it was experienced just this afternoon.
every space, whether it be a Costco, a living room with a piano, or a driveway, is a stage for actors to perform a domestic scene | image courtesy of Julie Blackmon and Haw Contemporary
The portrait of home
In the end, Blackmon creates the portrait of a home that is at once hers, ours, and nobody’s. In the careful crafting of these familiar places, she offers these access points into adolescence that are almost hauntingly ubiquitous—being in water, play, exploration of the natural environment that borders a family home. Yet the perfection of the scene hints at the simulacrum of the composition, perhaps suggesting that the memory of place is just as real, if not more tangible and more meaningful, than the sum of its parts.
a hallmark of these photos is their sense of motion | image courtesy of Julie Blackmon and Haw Contemporary

This private island in the Venice Lagoon is on sale for €5.5m – and comes with a Napoleonic-era fort
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:48:13 UTC
19:48:13 KST

Ever dreamed of owning your own slice of Venice? This €5.5 million private island comes with lagoon views, boat moorings and has easy access to neighbouring islands of Murano, Burano and Torcello.
It’s one thing to get on the property ladder, but to own an entire island? Now we’re talking.
Tucked away in the idyllic Venetian Lagoon, famed for its calm, shallow waters that link to the Adriatic Sea, the island of Crevan is on the market for €5.5 million – and it comes with more than just a nice view.
Located around 7.5 kilometres from the bustle of mainland Venice, the 5,700 square metre private island offers lush vegetation, alongside sweeping views of neighbouring Venetian islands.
Boat owners will also be delighted to hear that the property features two boat moorings and a dockyard for easy sea access.
But perhaps its biggest selling point is its history.
The island is home to a restored Napoleonic-era fortress, which was later converted into a 215 square metre residence that has retained its original mid-20th-century layout. On offer at the sea-facing home are four bedrooms and three bathrooms.
“Crevan offers something increasingly rare in Venice,” Dimitri Corti, Founder and CEO of Lionard Luxury Real Estate, which is overseeing the sale of the property, told Euronews Travel.
“[It offers] the possibility of being extraordinarily close to the city while experiencing an almost complete sense of separation from it.
“Just a few kilometres from Venice, the island is a private fragment of the lagoon, accessible only by water or helicopter, surrounded by nature and overlooking Burano and Torcello.”
Referred to as “Venice’s most colourful island”, Burano’s technicolour homes reflect into the canal’s teal waters. This Venetian island is also known for its local lace and glassmaking techniques, with visitors able to try their hand at the crafts themselves at workshops.
Meanwhile, Torcello is home to just a dozen inhabitants. This quiet island is a short ACTV Vaporetto waterbus ride from Burano and offers a quaint place for visitors to discover the island’s unique finds rooted in local legends. This includes Attila’s throne; a mysterious marble seat in the centre of the square.
For Corti, what makes the island of Crevan “truly distinctive” is the “combination of landscape, privacy and history”. He added: “Owning Crevan does not simply mean owning a residence, but becoming the custodian of an entire island and of a small part of the Venetian Lagoon’s heritage.”

Kyiv, Odesa hardest hit in overnight Russian attack as 16 killed, 54 injured across Ukraine

Kyiv, Odesa hardest hit in overnight Russian attack as 16 killed, 54 injured across Ukraine
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
At least 16 people were killed and 54 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, according to local authorities.
The heaviest toll was reported in Kyiv and the surrounding oblast, where Russia’s fifth consecutive day of attacks killed at least 12 people and injured 21 others.
Six of those killed were Ukrainian Railways employees, who died when a ballistic missile struck railway facilities, the company said.
"Russia always plans its strikes in a way designed to cause maximum destruction to people’s lives," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Russia also heavily targeted Odesa Oblast, with the Air Force identifying it and Kyiv Oblast as the primary targets of the attack.
Residential, energy, and port infrastructure came under attack in Odesa Oblast, injuring one person, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) said. Two residential buildings, a sewing workshop, and the Orlivka international ferry crossing on the Romanian border were damaged, according to local authorities.
Later in the morning, another Russian strike caused a fire at a postal terminal that had already been damaged in a previous attack. The fire was extinguished, and no additional casualties were reported.
"Thousands of families were left without electricity, and work is underway to restore power as quickly as possible," Zelensky said, commenting on the attack in Odesa Oblast. "Russia deliberately damaged a border crossing with Romania, as well as export infrastructure."
Overall, Russia launched several types of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as 218 drones, around a third of which were jet-powered, the Air Force said.
Ukraine’s air defenses intercepted or suppressed 199 aerial targets, including five ballistic missiles, five Kalibr cruise missiles, two S8000 Banderol missiles, and 187 drones. Missile and drone strikes were recorded at 28 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at 10 others.
The attack was still ongoing when the Air Force published the figures at 8:32 a.m.
As of 12:30 p.m., strike and jet-powered drones were flying over Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, and Kharkiv oblasts.
Ukraine had intercepted all cruise missiles launched in the attack, most of the drones, and several ballistic and Banderol missiles, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat later said on Ukrainian television.
But Ukraine still needed more air defense capabilities, particularly missiles for Patriot systems capable of intercepting ballistic missiles, Ihnat added.
In Kherson, a Russian first-person view (FPV) drone struck a car, killing one person and setting the vehicle on fire, the DSNS said.
In Donetsk Oblast, one person was killed and nine others injured in Russian attacks, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
Six people, including a child, were injured in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
Five people were injured in Sumy Oblast, local authorities said.
Two people were killed and 12 injured in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Governor Ivan Fedorov said. The injured included four emergency workers whose vehicle was struck by a Russian drone while they were responding to a fire in the village of Kushuhum.
Russia also attacked Zhytomyr and Chernihiv oblasts, causing fires at an industrial facility and a warehouse in Zhytomyr Oblast and in two settlements in Chernihiv Oblast. No casualties were reported, the DSNS said.
"The number of victims of Russian terror directly depends on every new aid package. I am grateful to everyone helping Ukraine become more resilient," Zelensky said, urging partners to increase deliveries of anti-ballistic missiles to Ukraine.

UK long-term borrowing costs hit 28-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:44:36 UTC
19:44:36 KST

The chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s fiscal rules could be almost halved at his first budget if the current global bond sell-off persists into the autumn, economists say.
The UK’s long-term borrowing costs jumped to their highest level since early 1998 on Tuesday as investors dumped government bonds, betting on higher inflation.
The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 30-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, hit 5.89% at one point as London markets caught up with a sell-off that swept Japan and the US on Monday, a bank holiday in the UK.
Ten-year gilt yields were around 5.25%, their highest level since the 2008 global financial crisis.
Higher yields progressively increase the cost of financing the government’s debt. If sustained, these would pass through to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)’s forecasts for John Healey’s 28 October budget.
Deutsche Bank’s chief UK economist, Sanjay Raja, said that based on Tuesday’s yields, Healey’s headroom against the current budget rule would fall from £26bn at Rachel Reeves’s spring forecast to £13.8bn before covering any additional spending plans.
Almost all of the deterioration results from higher government interest costs. The OBR’s March forecast had gilt yields at 5.1% for this year. Gilt yields eased back a bit later on Tuesday – to 5.85% for the 30-year and 5.21% for the 10-year – but they are still well above the predicted level.
Raja suggested Healey would be likely to try to maintain headroom of at least £10bn to assuage market concerns about the government’s commitment to balancing the books. “£10bn to me is the floor. In a perfect world you would want to keep 15,” he said.
In addition to global forces, Raja said higher-than-expected growth in the UK in the first half of the year had also contributed to rising yields. “There are some good reasons,” he said.
The current budget rule is the promise that the government will match day-to-day spending with receipts and only borrow for longer-term projects.
Tuesday’s market moves underline the tricky global backdrop facing Andy Burnham’s government as he returns to Westminster promising to help consumers with the cost of living.
The OBR takes market expectations of future gilt yields during a two-week reference period in to account in its forecasts. It does not announce these dates in advance, but Raja suggested judging by the timing in previous years, the current tumultuous period may be included in its budget projections.
The bond sell-off was driven primarily by international factors. Japanese 10-year yields hit their highest level since the 1990s over expectations that the Bank of Japan would have to raise interest rates to control inflation.
Investors also appeared to be responding partly to higher oil prices, which were up 3.8% at nearly $94 a barrel after renewed hostilities between the US and Iran. Higher energy costs drive up inflation, potentially forcing central banks to respond.
As well as fretting about future price rises, bond investors also appear to be concerned about runaway deficits in the US, where the Trump administration has cut taxes and is having to hand back much of the revenue from swingeing trade tariffs.
The chief economist at the consultancy Capital Economics, Neil Shearing, said: “It’s been a perfect storm for the bond markets: we’ve had these fiscal concerns that have pushed up the long end of the curve, and now that’s being compounded by upward energy price pressure, pushing up interest rate expectations in the short term – and if you’re sitting in the Treasury, none of that is good news.”
Finance ministers and central bankers from the G20 major economies concluded their meeting in North Carolina to discuss the state of the global economy on Tuesday.
The US and Japan took the rare step of intervening jointly in global foreign exchange markets in August in an attempt to prop up the yen, but the Japanese currency subsequently resumed its slide.
Expectations of higher interest rates were also piqued by a speech on Friday by the Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, in which he said the US central bank would still have “work to do” if inflation did not return to target.
Before Warsh’s intervention, markets were betting on about a one-third probability of an increase in US rates in September, but that has risen to 70%.

Kazakhstan to introduce mandatory paid electronic entry permits for foreigners starting November 1. This will also affect Russians.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:42:30 UTC
19:42:30 KST

Kazakhstan to introduce mandatory paid electronic entry permits for foreigners starting November 1. This will also affect Russians.
Kazakhstan has begun phasing in paid electronic entry permits for foreigners who don’t need a visa, a requirement that will also apply to Russians. Serbia’s Foreign Ministry published details of the new entry rules.
The Electronic Travel Authorization, or ETA, will be issued through the QazETA digital platform, with applications required at least 72 hours before travel. The permit is valid for 180 calendar days and allows multiple entries during that period.
Obtaining the permit through QazETA is expected to cost 3,900 thousand tenge — about 730 rubles, or 7 euros. Applying at the border will cost twice as much, 7,800 thousand tenge, or roughly 1,460 rubles and 14 euros.
Here’s what is known about how the rollout will proceed:
- From August 25 to November 1, the system will run in test mode: foreigners will still be allowed into the country without a permit, though border guards will warn travelers that one will be required on their next entry
- Starting November 1, the permit will become mandatory for travelers arriving in Kazakhstan by plane
- Starting November 15, the requirement will extend to travelers crossing the external border of the Eurasian Economic Union by car or bus — meaning Kazakhstan’s borders with China, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan
- Starting November 30, it will extend to road crossings at the Eurasian Economic Union’s internal borders, including those with Russia and Kyrgyzstan
- Starting December 15, it will be mandatory for travelers arriving by train or sea.
Kazakhstan’s Internal Affairs Ministry disclosed plans to introduce paid electronic entry permits for citizens of visa-free countries in early August, when it published a draft of the corresponding resolution. The ministry reported that the permits would be rolled out between August and December 2026, though it did not specify the stages or the cost at the time.
Serbia and Kazakhstan maintain a visa-free arrangement, and Serbia’s Foreign Ministry did not clarify where it obtained its information about the stages of Kazakhstan’s permit rollout.
Kazakhstan, which Russians can currently enter without a visa or any permit, became a major destination for Russians fleeing the country after the start of the war and the mobilization that followed. Russians who spend more than 90 days there within a six-month period must obtain a temporary residence permit.

Finland unemployment rate remains highest in euro area
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:42:29 EEST
19:42:29 KST

Finland had the highest unemployment rate in the euro area in July, with 10.5% of its labour force out of work, Eurostat data published on Tuesday showed. The rate was unchanged from June and stood well above the euro-area average of 6.4%. Spain followed at 10.0%, while France recorded 8.3%.
Across the European Union, Finland also had the highest unemployment rate among countries with monthly data available. Sweden stood at 8.7%, while Greece recorded 7.9%.
The gap between Finland and most other EU economies has widened over the past two years. Finland's unemployment rate stood at 9.9% in July 2025 and has remained at 10.5% since April this year, according to Eurostat's seasonally adjusted series.
The number of unemployed people in Finland reached 302,000 in July, compared with 283,000 a year earlier. The country's unemployment rate has risen while the EU average has stayed close to 6%.
Finland moved ahead of Spain in the EU unemployment ranking in late 2025 after the two countries had recorded similar rates for much of the previous year. Spain's rate has since continued to fall, from 10.6% in July 2025 to 10.0% this July.
Finland also recorded one of the highest youth unemployment rates in the bloc. The rate for people under 25 stood at 23.4% in July, unchanged from June. Around 76,000 young people were unemployed. Sweden recorded 24.4%, while Spain stood at 22.9%.
The euro area's youth unemployment rate fell to 14.9% from 15.0% in June. Across the EU, the rate dropped to 15.1% from 15.6%.
Eurostat estimated that 11.264 million people were unemployed in the euro area in July and 13.516 million across the EU. Compared with July 2025, the number rose by 175,000 in the euro area and by 296,000 in the EU.
Finland's unemployment rate for men stood at 10.8% in July, while the rate for women was 10.1%. Both figures exceeded the corresponding euro-area rates of 6.2% for men and 6.6% for women.
Eurostat calculates unemployment under the International Labour Organisation definition. It counts people aged 15 to 74 who have no job, have sought work during the previous four weeks and are available to start work within two weeks.

DHAKA, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has approved a concessional loan of 175 million U.S. dollars to expand access to reliable and affordable electricity in Bangladesh's Chattogram Hill Tracts (CHT), helping boost livelihoods and support inclusive development in one of the country's most remote regions.
The project will extend and modernize power distribution networks across the CHT region, which is home to about 1.84 million people, more than half of whom belong to small ethnic communities, the Manila-based lender said in a statement on Tuesday.

In addition to the ADB financing, the project will receive a 2.72-million-dollar grant from an ADB trust fund.
Meanwhile, the Bangladeshi government will contribute 36.54 million dollars, and the Bangladesh Power Development Board, a statutory government organization, will provide 45.65 million dollars. ■

China's social security fund reports 13.22 pct investment return in 2025
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:41:50 CST
19:41:50 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- China's national social security fund posted an investment return of 13.22 percent in 2025, earning 390.67 billion yuan (about 57.61 billion U.S. dollars), according to an annual report released Tuesday.
The National Council for Social Security Fund (NCSSF), which manages the assets of the national social security fund, stated in its report that by the end of 2025, the total assets of the fund had reached 3.81 trillion yuan.
Since its inception, the fund has delivered an average annual return of 7.62 percent, with cumulative investment gains totaling 2.29 trillion yuan.
As a strategic reserve fund, it is designed to supplement and balance social security expenditures, particularly for old-age insurance, during periods of peak population aging.
In 2025, amid a complex market environment fraught with risks, the NCSSF closely tracked macroeconomic and capital market developments and proactively pursued dynamic asset allocation. This approach not only supported the steady development of domestic capital markets but also substantially boosted investment returns, an NCSSF official said.
The NCSSF also stepped up efforts to align with national strategies, optimized the structure of equity assets, and expanded allocations to real-economy investments, according to the official.
"We have consistently adhered to and refined our principles of long-term, value-oriented, and responsible investing, while managing investments prudently to fulfill our core responsibility of ensuring fund safety and preserving and enhancing its value," the official said.
After years of exploration and practice, the NCSSF has developed a comprehensive asset allocation framework that combines strategic asset allocation, tactical asset allocation, and asset rebalancing, the official added. ■

Thumann’s company, Donaustahl, supplies combat drones to Ukraine, according to the executive. He says he has been forced to live under round-the-clock protection after authorities uncovered an alleged Russian intelligence plan to poison him in 2025.
Authorities warned him shortly before Christmas that he could be in danger. “Yes, it comes from Russia. And yes, it is very serious — your life is at risk,” he said they told him. Within days, a suspected low-level operative had been detained.
Thumann said he had turned official addresses into surveillance-heavy “honeypots” — locations deliberately designed to lure hostile actors into a trap. “The low-level operatives were only there to find out where I was,” he added. “Then an assassination using poison was supposed to be carried out.”
The threat has upended his life. Thumann said he now lives at undisclosed locations with bodyguards, has not seen his family for months, and has prepared a will and advance health care directive in case he is killed.

Nepali rescuers built temporary bridges to reach remote areas and dug through the ruins of hydropower projects in the Himalayas to rescue close to 300 trapped workers, nearly a week after catastrophic floods left a trail of destruction across the country's towns and valleys.
