Apple's new CEO John Ternus makes AI top priority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:49:00 UTC
18:49:00 KST

Can new Apple CEO John Ternus fix the tech giant's AI woes?
September 1, 2026
On September 1, a new era begins at Apple as John Ternus becomes just the third man to hold the CEO role at the tech giant since 1997.
Ternus was announced as Tim Cook's successor back in April, bringing Cook's 15 years at the helm of one of the world's biggest companies to an end. Since then, Ternus, a leading hardware engineer at the company, has been working closely alongside Cook in preparation for the big job.
Just as Cook had when he took over from the iconic Steve Jobs, Ternus has big shoes to fill. Apple's share price has increased by more than 2,000% since Cook took over in 2011 and the company has sold more than 3.1 billion iPhones in that time.
Ternus faces a range of challenges at Apple, but his ability to keep the company at the top will hinge on how he reshapes its AI strategy.
Apple has struggled to successfully embrace the technology so far, with critics saying it has fallen far behind its rivals.
September 9: John Ternus makes public debut
Ternus will make his public debut as CEO at Apple's Autumn product launch event on September 9. Dubbed "Surprise and Shine," Ternus is expected to announce the company's first foldable iPhone as well as a new version of an AI-powered Siri, Apple's virtual assistant.
Francisco Jeronimo, VP for Data and Analytics at tech research group IDC, said Apple's forthcoming announcements were planned during Cook's time in charge and that it will be 2027 before the direction Ternus wants to take the company in becomes apparent.
"Of course, September 9 will be quite an important milestone for the company around foldables and around innovation," he told DW.
"But I don't think we have seen anything that could indicate that Apple is behaving in a different way or is showing a different kind of strategy because Tim Cook is not in the job anymore — yet."
Apple's huge AI challenge
What observers will be looking out for from Ternus on September 9 is the extent to which he focuses his remarks on AI.
While it was already undeniable when he was announced in April that the artificial intelligence boom would be pivotal to his time at the helm, it has become even clearer in the five months since the unveiling that the AI revolution is here to stay.
"It's becoming clear that AI is not a fad, is not something that will go away in the next two or three years," said Jeronimo. "It's something that will dictate the future of most tech companies and indeed all companies."
He reckons AI could be "the most consequential technology" for Apple because it could either help it maintain its lofty position or create a set of daunting challenges.
The biggest challenge he sees is that Apple doesn't "control" AI infrastructure the way it could previously in terms of designing and controlling both the hardware and software for its key products.
"Maybe that will be what John Ternus will be doing differently from Tim Cook, because at the moment, even if Apple built their own AI technology, the reality is that they still depend on someone else," he added.
Apple's reliance on other companies in the AI realm has led it into unfamiliar territory. It struck a deal with OpenAI in 2024 to integrate ChatGPT into the iPhone, but that has led to a bitter dispute between the companies. Apple sued OpenAI earlier this year, alleging that the AI company stole its trade secrets.
Earlier this year, it announced a deal with Google, whereby the search giant's Gemini models would be used for Apple's own AI models and its new AI-powered version of Siri.
"The risk for Apple is to become less relevant in a world where companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are leading in terms of technology, in terms of awareness, in terms of services and potentially in terms of hardware," said Jeronimo.
For decades, Apple's success has been built on its physical products, from the iPad to the iPhone.
"If devices from OpenAI become available, that could be very, very risky for Apple. They could completely disrupt the experience and the way we interact with technology. And if Apple is not on the front of that innovation, that is a big risk," he said.
A combination of Jobs and Cook?
Ternus' background as an engineer who worked on Apple's core products, as well as innovations such as the Apple Watch and AirPods, means he will be expected to lead the way on new AI-driven products for the company.
He also played a central role championing Apple's shift to designing its own chips instead of relying on external suppliers like Intel — precisely the kind of independence Apple would like to achieve when it comes to AI.
Jeronimo thinks Apple still has big advantages, given its massive volume of users as well as the company culture of having dominated innovation in tech for decades. He thinks if Apple can get to grips with AI under Ternus, it could lead to huge success: "What we will see in the next years will dictate whether Apple is on the right track or if they are really struggling."
For Ternus, the first task will be to simply fit smoothly and convincingly into a role that both Jobs and Cook undeniably made their own. "Steve Jobs was the guru of innovation and disruption and Tim Cook was the guru of execution," saidJeronimo.
"I think John Ternus can be a combination of both."

Occupied East Jerusalem private, Christian schools strike over Israeli restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:48:52 UTC
18:48:52 KST

Palestinian private schools, including Christian schools, in occupied East Jerusalem began a strike on Tuesday at the start of the new academic year in protest against Israeli restrictions preventing teachers and administrative staff from entering the city.
Private school administrators announced on Monday that classes would be suspended from Tuesday until further notice after Israeli authorities failed to renew entry permits for a large number of teachers and staff from the occupied West Bank.
They said classes would resume once Israeli authorities renew permits for all affected teachers and employees.
Christian schools in East Jerusalem separately announced the suspension of classes from Tuesday, saying Israel had failed to renew entry permits for more than 70 teachers and employees from the occupied West Bank, preventing them from reaching their schools.
Israel requires Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank to obtain special permits to enter occupied East Jerusalem, including for work, education, medical treatment and worship.
The new academic year began on Tuesday in Israel and East Jerusalem, with around 6,000 educational institutions receiving students, including 1,074 institutions serving the Arab community, where some 586,000 students are enrolled.
Since October 2023, Israel has restricted permits for Palestinian workers from the West Bank, including teachers.
In January, the Israeli Knesset passed legislation barring teachers who obtained academic degrees from institutions affiliated with the Palestinian Authority from working in the Israeli education system.
According to Israeli daily Haaretz, around 6,700 teachers work in East Jerusalem’s Palestinian education system, at least 60 percent of whom hold bachelor’s degrees from Palestine’s academic institutions.

U.S. Navy awards Boeing $12.7 million for MQ-25 drone upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:48:02 UTC
18:48:02 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Boeing a $12.7 million sole-source modification to upgrade electronic systems on the MQ-25 refueling drone.
- Work covers updated radio frequency and data storage components, plus security assessment corrections for the aircraft's mission computer, running through November 2029.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Boeing a $12.7 million contract modification to upgrade electronic components on the MQ-25 Stingray, the Navy’s first operational carrier-based drone, according to a Department of War contract announcement.
The modification covers non-recurring engineering and integration work on an updated Radio Frequency Blanker Unit and an Encrypted Mass Storage System with an embedded Data Transfer System, both components installed on the MQ-25. The Radio Frequency Blanker Unit shields the aircraft’s own transmissions from interfering with its onboard sensors, while the mass storage system secures data collected or transferred during flight. The modification also exercises a contract option covering deficiency analysis and corrections tied to security assessments of the MQ-25’s Mission Management System Computer, the aircraft’s central onboard computer.
Work under the modification will take place primarily in St. Louis, Missouri, which will handle 85 percent of the effort, with the remaining 15 percent performed in Fairborn, Ohio. The contract is expected to be completed by November 2029. Fiscal 2026 Navy research, development, test and evaluation funds covering the full $12.7 million will be obligated at the time of award. The contract was not competitively bid, and Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, is managing the award.
The MQ-25 is designed to extend the range of the Navy’s carrier air wing by refueling other aircraft in flight, a role currently filled by crewed F/A-18E/F Super Hornets flying dedicated tanker missions. Once fielded, the Stingray will be the first uncrewed aircraft to operate routinely from a U.S. aircraft carrier.
The program has moved through several milestones this year. The first production-representative MQ-25A completed its maiden flight on April 25 at Boeing’s facility at MidAmerica St. Louis Airport in Mascoutah, Illinois, after an earlier attempt on April 22 was aborted for undisclosed reasons. The roughly two-hour flight demonstrated the aircraft’s ability to autonomously taxi, take off, maneuver and land while responding to commands from the Unmanned Carrier Aviation Mission Control System MD-5 ground control station.
“The MQ-25A is not just an aircraft: it’s the first step in integrating unmanned aerial refueling onto the carrier deck, directly enabling our manned fighters to fly further and faster,” said Rear Adm. Tony Rossi, who oversees the Program Executive Office for Unmanned Aviation and Strike Weapons.
“The MQ-25A is the most complex autonomous system ever developed for the carrier environment, and this historic achievement advances us closer to safely integrating the Stingray into the carrier air wing,” said Dan Gillian, vice president and general manager of Boeing Air Dominance.
The aircraft completed a second test flight in July, which included cycling its landing gear up and down and testing a new software load intended to support future expansion of its flight envelope. Separately, deck-handling trials aboard the carrier USS George H.W. Bush confirmed the aircraft’s physical compatibility with carrier deck operations.
The Navy has previously said it plans to deliver nine MQ-25 aircraft for its test campaign, covering four Engineering Development Model airframes under an $805 million engineering and manufacturing development contract. Future test flights are expected to expand the aircraft’s flight envelope, certify its aerial refueling capability, and eventually transition testing to Naval Air Station Patuxent River for operational evaluation. The Navy has said it is targeting initial operational capability for the MQ-25 by 2027.

Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis Found Guilty of Tupac Shakur’s Murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:47:26 UTC
18:47:26 KST

Thirty years after rapper Tupac Shakur was killed in a Las Vegas drive-by shooting, a former gang leader has been found guilty of orchestrating his death.
A jury in Clark County, Nev., convicted Duane “Keffe D” Davis, 63, ex-head of Los Angeles street gang South Side Compton Crips, of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon, following a weekslong trial.
But prosecutors decided not to proceed with part of the charge about gang enhancement—an extra prison sentence added to a conviction when the crime is committed for the benefit of, or in connection with, a criminal gang—citing “witness logistics.”
Shakur’s murder in September 1996 at the age of 25 had left so many questions unanswered and has been the subject of conspiracies for years.
But the investigation into his death was revived after Davis published his memoir, Compton Street Legend, in 2019. In the memoir and during promotions, he outlined the role of the Crips in Shakur’s death. The Crips were feuding with the Mob Piru, which had ties to Shakur and his record label, Death Row Records.
Nevada law allows Davis to be charged with murder even if he did not pull the trigger.
Davis, who was arrested in 2023, could face life in prison. Clark County District Court Judge Carli Kierny ordered that Davis be held without bail and scheduled his sentencing on Oct. 13.
The former gang leader, however, said in court that he would appeal the conviction.
How the verdict was reached
The trial against Davis began on Aug. 17. More than two dozen witnesses testified before a panel of 16 jurors, four of whom are alternates. Jurors also watched footage about the fight that broke out a few hours before Shakur and Death Row Records co-founder Marion “Suge” Knight, who was riding with him, were shot by a man in a white Cadillac on Sept. 7, 1996, while Shakur’s car stopped at a red light.
Knight survived, but Shakur died six days later.
Throughout the trial, Davis's defense attorney, Michael Sanft, attempted to discredit the evidence against his client.
In his closing arguments, which lasted for more than an hour, Sanft argued that the prosecution lacked the physical evidence to connect Davis to the crime scene and to determine that Davis called the shots in Shakur’s death. He also claimed the investigation was compromised, and that the Compton Police Department, which probed the local gang rivalry that provided the backdrop for the shooting, was also shut down due to corruption.
“We’re not giving you everything,” Sanft told the jurors. “And you as jurors deserve everything—in terms of the full weight of the evidence in this case. We don’t have it.”
Sanft also repeatedly attacked Davis’ memoir, saying that his client did not even read the book and that his client was telling stories to make money.
“When you think about Mr. Davis's statements, they all conflict,” Sanft told the jurors. “They conflict with the book and they conflict with the facts. And the only thing that we have that we can agree on is that Tupac Shakur was shot and killed.”
But Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal emphasized the extent of evidence against Davis. Palal highlighted the defendant’s own statements over the years, in which he said he played an integral role in Shakur’s killing, including to documentary filmmakers, in his memoir, and to the police.
Davis told federal agents in 1998 that he had been in Las Vegas when Shakur was shot but denied knowing who killed him. The case lacked credible witnesses and the investigation stalled. But ten years later, when Davis was under threat of possible drug charges, he told police that he and his fellow Crips members looked for Shakur and Knight. Davis offered the information under a proffer agreement that he believed protected him from being prosecuted.
Prosecutors said that Shakur’s and Knight’s involvement in the beating of Davis’ nephew at the MGM Grand hotel and casino after a Mike Tyson bout prompted retaliation.
In the closing argument, Palal also played a recording of an interview where Davis urged purchases of his 2019 memoir to get the “real truth,” which counts as “textbook” admission of his statements.
“For nearly 18 years, Duane Davis has told the police, television, books, YouTube interviewers, anybody that will listen,” Palal said in his closing statement. “He has told you he is responsible for the murder of Tupac Shakur. Tell him you hear him. Find him guilty.”
The jury deliberated for less than three hours before reaching the verdict.
What are the reactions to the verdict?
The verdict comes two weeks before the 30th anniversary of Shakur’s death.
Footage from the courtroom shows that after the verdict was read, Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur, Tupac’s sister, wept while reaching for a person behind her. Some of Shakur’s other loved ones in the courtroom embraced each other, with one raising his fist in the air
But the reactions to the verdict were not limited to family members, as Shakur's 1996 killing became a defining moment of hip-hop culture's “gangsta” rap era—which reflected the violence pervasive in American inner cities that suffer from poverty.
Shakur fan Derrick Lee Stanton Jr. called the jury's conviction of Davis a “great moment” and “emotional.” But speaking to reporters outside, Stanton said that the case is “not done,” claiming that there are “more people that have to pay for the death of Tupac” as Duane is “not the lone soldier here.”

Spain records over 5,000 heat-related deaths between June and August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:47:22 UTC
18:47:22 KST

Spain registered more than 5,000 heat-related deaths from June to August, data from a public health institute showed on Tuesday, a record since the start of its statistics in 2015.
A string of exceptional summer heatwaves has been linked with thousands of excess deaths across Europe, with the continent's climate monitor reporting the hottest June-July on record for western Europe.
The 5,111 heat-related deaths in Spain from June to August recorded by the Carlos III Health Institute surpassed the previous high of 4,652 for the same period in 2022.
The estimate was also up from the 3,651 fatalities recorded during the same period last year and 1,977 for those three months in 2024.
The figures were estimated using data from Spain's Mortality Monitoring System (MoMo), which tracks daily mortality nationwide and compares it to historical trends.
It also incorporates external factors, such as weather data from the national weather agency AEMET, to assess likely causes of mortality spikes.
Although MoMo cannot confirm a direct cause between deaths and high temperatures, it provides the most reliable estimate of fatalities in which heat was likely a decisive factor.
Heart attacks and strokes are main reasons
Most heat-related excess deaths are due to heart attacks and strokes caused by the strain of trying to keep body temperatures stable.
Scientists have long warned that the climate crisis, driven by humanity's burning of fossil fuels, is making the extreme heat spells that have afflicted Europe longer, more intense and more frequent.
AEMET has said July was mainland Spain's joint-hottest month since the start of its records in 1961, while new temperature records tumbled across swathes of drought-hit Europe.
The heat and lack of moisture fostered ideal conditions for wildfires, with Spain suffering one of its worst such disasters in living memory in July, forcing the evacuation of tens of thousands of people just dozens of kilometres from Madrid.
Unusually high temperatures for September are set to bake Spain this week, with forecasts topping 40°C in the south and west of the country.

15-year-old newcomer Bruno makes the move to mainstream secondary school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:46:09 UTC
18:46:09 KST

Today is the first day back at school for hundreds of thousands of young Flemings. It’s also a new chapter for Bruno, who arrived in Belgium from Angola in 2024. After a year and a half in the reception programme for non-Dutch-speaking newcomers (OKAN), he is starting Year 3 at the Sint-Lucas School in Antwerp. “I’m going to study a new subject that I’m really keen to pursue: architecture and visual arts,” he told VRT.
15-year-old newcomer Bruno makes the move to mainstream secondary school
Bruno arrived in Belgium from Angola in December 2024. Since February last year, he has been attending reception classes, where young people who are new to the country take intensive Dutch courses and are prepared for the transition to mainstream education.
This first day at school has made Bruno a bit nervous: “I’m a bit worried about my Dutch. It really needs to improve. I’m afraid the teachers might not always understand me.”
His new school isn’t entirely unfamiliar. Last year, Bruno did a two-week work experience placement there to get to know the school and the course. Bruno is particularly looking forward to all the new things that lie ahead. “I’m looking forward to learning about new subjects and meeting new people.” There’s one subject in particular he’s really looking forward to: maths.
Still, saying goodbye to the OKAN classes triggers many emotions. “I am a bit sad, because I had lots of friends there and the teachers were really good at teaching. It really was like a second home to me. Going to a new school now is quite nerve-wracking,” says Bruno.
But Bruno remains determined. “Whenever I do something new, it’s a big step for me.” He’s highly motivated to learn. “I didn’t always feel like going to school, but I always feel like learning new things.” And despite his enthusiasm for this new adventure, he won’t forget his old school. “Of course I’m going to miss OKAN.”

Eurozone inflation jumps to 3.3% in August as energy prices surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:43:15 UTC
18:43:15 KST

Eurozone inflation rose sharply in August, as energy prices climbed by more than 14% compared with a year earlier, according to Eurostat.
Eurozone inflation climbed to 3.3% in August 2026, up from 2.9% in July, according to a flash estimate from Eurostat, the statistical office of the European Union.
The increase was largely driven by energy, as global oil and gas prices surged amid the war in Iran and disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Energy prices rose by 14.3% in the year to August, accelerating from 10.3% in July.
Leo Barincou, senior economist at Oxford Economics, said: "This was driven by a rebound in fuel prices following the renewed closure of the Strait of Hormuz, while underlying price pressures remained contained as services inflation came down. Inflation should remain well above target into next year, as higher gas and food prices put additional upward pressure on the index."
Food, alcohol and tobacco prices rose by 1.2%, unchanged from July.
Services inflation — a more persistent measure closely watched by the ECB — eased from 3.3% to 3.0%.
On a monthly basis, overall prices in the eurozone rose by 0.4% in August, with energy prices alone increasing by 2.9%.
At the same time, core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, edged down from 2.5% to 2.4%. This suggests that the rise in energy costs has not yet spread extensively to services and other prices.
Among eurozone members included in the August flash estimate, Lithuania recorded the highest inflation rate, at 5.8%, while Estonia had the lowest, at 1.3%.
Among the largest economies, inflation in France and Germany, at 2.7% and 2.9% respectively, remained below the eurozone headline rate. France, however, recorded a noticeable increase from 2.4% to 2.7%.
Spain stood out with inflation of 4.5%, well above the eurozone average, while Italy's rate reached 3.2%.
Eurozone inflation is considerably above the European Central Bank's 2% target. Markets expect the ECB to raise interest rates by 0.25 percentage points at its meeting on 10 September as policymakers seek to contain price pressures.
"With inflation still accelerating, the ECB is all but certain to hike at next week’s meeting, in line with our expectations," Barincou said.
"However, unlike markets, we think it is too early to pencil in a third hike, especially given that underlying price pressures remain contained for now," he added.

NATO jets scrambled after drones approach airspace of Latvia, Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:43:02 UTC
18:43:02 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
NATO fighter jets were scrambled after drones approached or entered the airspace of Latvia and Estonia overnight, according to local authorities cited by public broadcasters LRT and ERR on Tuesday.
In Latvia, a warning over a potential airspace threat was issued in the northeastern Aluksne municipality, prompting the NATO Baltic air-policing mission to scramble fighter jets, Latvia’s National Armed Forces said.
Residents were advised to remain indoors, close windows and doors and follow the “two-wall principle,” keeping two walls between themselves and the potential threat.
They were also told to call the emergency number 112 if they spotted a low-flying, suspicious or dangerous object.
The warning was lifted at 4.17 am local time (0117GMT).
About 90 minutes earlier, a lower-level yellow warning over a potential airspace threat had been issued in Latvia’s Ludza municipality. It was later canceled.
The incidents follow repeated airspace warnings in Latvia’s Latgale and Vidzeme regions this summer.
Foreign drones have also crashed and exploded in Latvia, with NATO fighter jets shooting down some of them.
The incidents were believed to involve drones used in the Russia-Ukraine war that approached or entered Latvian airspace.
In neighboring Estonia, Russian-launched drones briefly approached the town of Narva, while another crossed into Estonian airspace in the country’s southeast, according to ERR.
Estonian Air Force commander Brig. Gen. Riivo Valge said about 10 drones were detected near the border at around 2 am local time (2300GMT) while Ukraine was carrying out what he described as a large-scale drone attack against Russia.
At about 3 am local time (0000GMT), one drone turned toward Narva, prompting authorities to issue a public warning and activate ground-based air defenses. Fighter jets subsequently took off from Amari Air Base.
The drone later turned back toward Russia and did not enter Estonian airspace.
About 30 minutes later, another drone crossed into southeastern Estonia and flew for a time in the border area, Valge said.
Valge said its behavior was unpredictable, while more drones were detected just across the border in Russia.
The drone eventually left Estonian airspace without crashing, and the Estonian fighter jets did not have to open fire, Valge said.
The warning was lifted after the situation across the border calmed at around 5 am local time (0200GMT).
Valge said the situation was calm Tuesday and urged Estonians to focus on the start of the school year.

Two-seat Gripen F completes first flight
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:41:48 BST
18:41:48 KST

Saab has completed the first flight of the Gripen F, the two-seat version of the Gripen E fighter developed with Brazilian industry, beginning a flight-test programme that will progressively clear the aircraft across its operating envelope, according to the company.
Saab announced the milestone on 28 August, saying the aircraft took off from its airfield at Linköping in Sweden at 09:40 local time and remained airborne for 40 minutes. The flight was conducted by Saab chief test pilot Jakob Högberg and Brazilian Air Force test pilot Lieutenant Colonel Aviator Abdon de Rezende Vasconcelos, with the sortie used to verify the operation of the aircraft’s core systems and assess its initial flight performance.
Lars Tossman, head of Saab business area Aeronautics, said: “This first flight represents an important step forward for both Saab and the Brazilian Air Force. Seeing Gripen F take to the skies is particularly significant for all the Swedish and Brazilian teams whose years of engineering work have helped turn this aircraft into a reality. It is designed to accelerate pilot training while and enhancing operational performance in advanced combat missions.”
The first sortie moves Gripen F into the airborne phase of its test campaign. Saab said that, following initial production acceptance flights, testing will move into a progressive envelope expansion programme in which speed, altitude, G-load and angle of attack limits will be cleared in stages. Tactical capabilities and functions associated specifically with the rear cockpit of the two-seat aircraft will be assessed in parallel.
Gripen F was developed through cooperation between Sweden and Brazil under the Brazilian Gripen Programme, with Brazil acting as the launch customer for the two-seat variant. Saab said more than 350 Brazilian engineers, technicians and pilots have taken part in training connected with development, production, flight testing and maintenance of the aircraft, giving Brazilian industry and personnel a direct role in the programme.
The company said Brazil’s participation extended into co-development of the two-seat fighter rather than being limited to acquisition of completed aircraft. The Gripen F retains the two-seat configuration for training while Saab also intends the aircraft to support operational missions, with the rear cockpit and associated systems forming part of the dedicated test activity now beginning in Sweden.
The flight-test campaign will be conducted by Saab’s Flight Test Centre in Sweden. The aircraft will undergo further production acceptance activity before the programme moves through progressively more demanding flight conditions and evaluation of the systems associated with its two-seat configuration.
Once the planned flight-test work and acceptance procedures have been completed, Saab said the Gripen F will be prepared for delivery to the Brazilian Air Force. The 28 August flight therefore marks the beginning of the airborne test phase rather than completion of the aircraft’s development and acceptance programme.

Solar outpaces coal for the first time in China: How does Europe compare?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:40:54 UTC
18:40:54 KST

China has seen an explosive growth in its renewable installation, with coal's share in its energy mix edging down in recent years.
China's solar energy capacity has surpassed that of coal-fired power for the first time ever.
"As of the end of July this year, China's installed solar power capacity reached 1.286 billion kilowatts," China's National Energy Administration (NEA) said.
"For the first time, photovoltaic installed capacity surpassed coal-fired power, becoming the largest power source category in China," it added.
The country's coal-fired power installed capacity, the energy body said, stood at 1.285 billion kilowatts.
Solar generation rose 15.5 per cent in the first seven months of 2026 compared to the same period last year to 802.4 billion kilowatt-hours, about one-eighth of the country's total, the NEA said in another statement.
China, the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases that drive climate change, has pledged to peak carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060.
It did not detail in these statements what the total generation of coal-powered energy was for the first seven months of this year.
The NEA said China's installed solar power capacity and power generation "have maintained a steady trend of rapid growth," with it playing an "increasingly prominent role" in guaranteeing electricity supply and driving the energy transition.
Coal has been China's key power generation source for decades and a key driver of planet-warming emissions.
But the country's coal-fired power generation fell by nearly two per cent in 2025, despite rising energy demand in the world's largest emitter, data reviewed by the AFP news agency showed in February.
It marked the first decline in six years, with some analysts saying it was the first time on record that coal generation dropped at the same time as power demand rose.
China has seen an explosive growth in its renewable installation, with coal's share in its energy mix edging down in recent years.
The country installed a record 315 gigawatts of solar power and 119 gigawatts of wind power capacity last year, over 80 per cent of total newly installed power generation capacity, according to the China Electricity Council.
How does Europe compare to China on energy generation?
EU countries are trailing behind China when it comes to renewables, partly because China started their transition to clean energy much sooner. As an example, in 2023 China installed between 180 and 230 gigawatts of solar, compared to 58 gigawatts in all European countries combined.
China's ownership of clean technology parts and patents makes a big difference to how quickly and cheaply they can install, as well as cheaper labour.
China's energy grid is also more efficient at handling energy from multiple sources, where as Europe's grid has been called "outdated". Hybridisation has been recommended as a solution.

tamagotchi shrinks its classic digital pet into a wearable ring with LCD color screen

bandai turns tamagotchi into a wearable ring with color screen
Bandai shrinks the Tamagotchi into a ring-shaped device designed to be worn as an accessory. The Tamagotchi ring measures approximately 28 × 23 × 35 millimeters and places a color LCD screen inside a compact wearable form, allowing users to feed, care for, and play with the digital creature directly from their finger. The device is available in Japan in three color combinations: Pink & Pearl White, Light Blue & Metallic Gold, and Black & Metallic Silver. Bandai uses an aurora pearl finish for the pink version, while the other two models feature plated finishes.
Traditionally carried in a pocket, attached to a keychain, or suspended from a bag, the digital pet now occupies a more immediate position on the body. The format brings Tamagotchi closer to contemporary wearable technology, retaining the deliberately simple interaction that defined the original devices.
Despite its small scale, the Tamagotchi ring includes a color LCD display and supports the series’ familiar care and gameplay mechanics. Depending on how it is looked after, the digital creature can develop into more than 30 different Tamagotchi characters, with secret characters also appearing.
all images courtesy of Bandai
nostalgia meets the language of wearable technology
The ring is offered in sizes 10 and 14, with an included spacer allowing the fit to be adjusted. Each color also comes with a dedicated charger designed to display the device while it charges. A ball chain is included as well, suggesting that the object can move between ring and pendant-like accessory.
Bandai describes the Tamagotchi ring as the world’s smallest ring-shaped Tamagotchi device. Its LiPo battery is rechargeable through the included charger, while the compact body contains the screen and controls necessary for the familiar cycle of care.
The Tamagotchi ring tests what happens when a nostalgic digital object becomes wearable. Its appeal lies in this collision of scales: a tiny screen, a familiar virtual creature, and a piece of technology designed to remain attached to the hand.

Northrop gets $86M for security systems at nuclear missile bases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:39:44 UTC
18:39:44 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded Northrop Grumman an $86.1 million sole-source task order to maintain its Remote Visual Assessment missile silo monitoring system.
- Work covers four bases, Hill, F.E. Warren, Malmstrom and Minot, and is expected to run through September 2031.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded Northrop Grumman an $86.1 million task order to maintain the security cameras and sensors that watch over America’s nuclear missile silos.
The task order covers program management, maintenance, sustaining engineering and support services for the Remote Visual Assessment program, a ground-based camera and sensor network that monitors Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missile silos. The award falls under a broader ground subsystem support contract Northrop Grumman has held since 2021. The Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center at Hill Air Force Base, Utah, is the contracting activity.
Work under this task order will take place at Hill Air Force Base, along with F.E. Warren Air Force Base in Wyoming, Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, and Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota, the three installations that oversee the Air Force’s dispersed fields of Minuteman III silos across the northern United States. The contract is expected to run through September 2031.
The Remote Visual Assessment system lets Air Force personnel confirm what’s happening at a missile silo without physically traveling to the site, an important capability given how far apart individual silos sit across the missile fields. When a security sensor detects unusual activity at a silo, cameras tied into the RVA system let a missile alert facility crew visually verify the alert before dispatching a security response team, cutting down on unnecessary trips to remote locations.
The award was made as a sole-source acquisition, meaning the Air Force did not open the work to competitive bidding. Of the task order’s total value, $15.2 million in fiscal 2026 procurement funds was obligated at the time of award, with the remainder expected to be funded as the work progresses.

The incident formed part of a wider overnight airspace alert involving both Estonia and Latvia, with NATO fighter aircraft scrambled after drones entered the airspace of the two Alliance members. The information released so far does not identify the NATO aircraft involved in the response, their operating bases or how long the incursions lasted.
Estonia’s warning system was activated while the drone was approaching the country’s eastern border, allowing authorities to notify residents while military personnel monitored its movement. Narva sits directly on the Estonian-Russian frontier, separated from the Russian city of Ivangorod by the Narva River. The area is one of NATO’s easternmost borders and lies immediately alongside Russian territory.
The 1 September alert differed from routine interceptions in that the aircraft involved were drones associated with a strike against targets inside Russia rather than conventional crewed military aircraft.
The Estonian Defence Forces said the drones had been used in a Ukrainian attack against targets in Russia before flying close to the border, with at least one briefly entering Estonian airspace.
NATO aircraft were subsequently scrambled in response to the incursions affecting Estonia and Latvia, while Estonian authorities issued warnings to residents in the areas considered potentially affected.

WHO revises typhoid vaccine advice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:31:57 UTC
18:31:57 KST

NEW DELHI: Nearly 5 million typhoid cases were estimated in India in 2023, with children bearing much of the burden. Amid rising antibiotic resistance, the World Health Organization (WHO) has updated its guidance on typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV), recommending the first dose at 9-24 months in settings with high or very high typhoid incidence.A Lancet Regional Health – Southeast Asia study estimated 4.9 million cases, 7.3 lakh hospitalisations and 7,850 deaths from typhoid in India in 2023. About 6 lakh, or 82%, of hospitalisations were linked to fluoroquinolone-resistant typhoid.Children accounted for most estimated treated cases, with those aged 5-9 years accounting for 36%, followed by 10-14 years at 27% and 6 months to 4 years at 25%.“Given India’s very high typhoid burden and the emergence of drug-resistant Salmonella Typhi, including reports of carbapenem-resistant strains, routine introduction of TCV is justified and urgent. NTAGI’s 2022 recommendations and repeated cost-effectiveness analyses already support this,” said Dr Kamini Walia, senior scientist at ICMR.She said India could consider giving TCV at the existing 18-month vaccination visit, alongside the second measles-containing vaccine dose. “Even as a single dose without a booster, TCV is expected to have a significant impact on disease burden. A school-entry booster, particularly in high-burden urban areas, may be considered if surveillance shows waning protection,” she said.
WHO recommends TCV in settings with high or very high typhoid incidence, high case-fatality rates or a high burden of antimicrobial-resistant Salmonella Typhi. It also recommends catch-up vaccination when TCV is introduced, with children below 15 years potentially targeted depending on local disease burden and programme feasibility.On booster doses, WHO says countries with very high typhoid incidence should consider a booster around five years after the first dose given at 9-24 months. In high-incidence settings, a booster may be considered if there is evidence that protection is waning. Decisions should take into account disease burden, antimicrobial resistance, cost-effectiveness and feasibility.The updated advice comes amid growing concern over antibiotic-resistant typhoid, which can limit treatment options and increase reliance on more expensive injectable or last-resort drugs.
TCV is not a new WHO recommendation. The agency recommended its routine use in children in typhoid-endemic countries in 2017 and prequalified the first vaccine in 2018. The latest guidance updates recommendations based on newer evidence, including vaccination age, catch-up programmes and booster use.For India, the issue is particularly relevant. The study notes that the National Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation (NTAGI) recommended including TCV in the Universal Immunisation Programme in 2022.WHO also stresses that vaccination cannot replace basic measures such as safe water, sanitation, hygiene, food safety and timely diagnosis and treatment, which remain essential to controlling typhoid.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Ukraine’s War Chest Shrinks as Europe Mulls Gamble with Russia Billions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:30:43 UTC
18:30:43 KST

Europe’s grand €90 billion answer to Ukraine’s funding crisis survived for just eight months before Volodymyr Zelenskyy began proposing that part of next year’s allocation should be paid early.
Ukraine says it has already raided money earmarked for the second half of 2026 and is now staring down a €23.1 billion hole in its defense budget.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
That is why a letter from the foreign ministers of Sweden, Poland, Spain and the Netherlands has dragged Europe’s Russian-frozen-assets fight back onto the table. The four governments say the €90 billion package will be insufficient and want Commission experts to explore new uses for Russia’s immobilized assets.
Bringing some of the 2027 money forward could fill part of this year’s hole. It would also obviously leave Ukraine with less money next year. That is the approaching financial cliff: Ukraine could run short again during 2027, while the EU’s next seven-year budget only begins in 2028. European governments would have to improvise another financial bridge in the meantime.
The letter therefore returns to the €210 billion in frozen Russian assets, presenting them as the rope that could pull Ukraine back from the financial cliff edge. What’s new in the letter is that it acknowledges that a way must be found to share the responsibility and liability of using the money, so that Belgium is not left carrying the risk alone, the obstacle that stalled the plan in December.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, August 30, 2026
Until now, the Russian principal has largely been reserved for Ukraine’s eventual reconstruction. Sikorski argues that “it is better to use it to stop the aggression … rather than wait until the end of Russia’s aggression to spend it on reconstruction”.
There is a clear logic here. Money spent defending Ukraine today can preserve its cities, factories and power stations, leaving less for Europe to rebuild later.
Next year is arriving early
Ukraine says its defense ministry faces a $27 billion, or €23.1 billion, funding gap this year. The shortfall includes around €6 billion in advance payments for equipment due in early 2027.
Zelenskyy has suggested advancing part of the EU money scheduled for 2027, although the Commission says it has yet to receive a formal request.
What is interesting here is that front-loading fits a pattern. If you look across Europe’s funding mechanisms, each one finds a different way to turn tomorrow’s resources into weapons or budget support today.
In simple terms, each plan reaches into a different part of the future. The G7 loan brings forward the profits that Russia’s assets will generate over many years. The €90 billion package places the EU budget behind money borrowed from financial markets while waiting for Russian reparations. The proposed reparations loan would use the underlying Russian cash, leaving Euroclear with an EU promise to replace it. That final step explains why collective guarantees are important as Europe may have to provide the money if it ever has to be returned to Moscow.
The instruments are distinct, and the same euro has not literally been spent several times. Even so, Europe has addressed successive immediate crises by placing claims on future profits, budgets and reparations.
There’s nothing crazy about it. Governments borrow all the time because urgent bills can’t always wait for tomorrow’s tax money. But clever financial tricks don’t make the political gamble vanish; they simply push the costs down the road. And sooner or later, someone will have to shoulder the risk if the promised reparations or government funds fail to cover the bill.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Belgium holds the vault and the risk
That responsibility leads to Belgium. Around €210 billion of Russian central-bank assets are immobilized in the EU, with roughly €185 billion held by Euroclear in Brussels.
Belgium slammed the brakes on the earlier reparations-loan plan, fearing a legal nightmare: Russian lawsuits, massive damages claims or a sudden order to hand the money back. The plan effectively asked Belgian to carry the risk for Europe’s geopolitical experiment, but Brussels insisted that any potential liability had to be shared across the continent.
The previous Commission proposal already went some way to recognizing that problem. It envisaged national guarantees divided according to each country’s share of EU gross national income, with coverage eventually moving to the EU budget.
The catch was that governments still had to sign up voluntarily, raising fears that chunks of the plan could be left without cover. Belgium demanded ironclad protection against every legal and financial threat so that it wouldn’t be stuck picking up the tab.
The letter puts the issue back on the table but stops well short of a deal. It offers no figure for the loan, no clear guarantee plan and no fix for Belgium’s objections. The four governments can force the issue back onto the agenda, but turning it into a workable plan will still require the backing of Europe’s biggest economies.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Survival comes before reconstruction
Poland’s Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski makes a strong case for taking the gamble. “Russia will not get this money back until it pays reparations to Ukraine, so it is better to use it to stop the aggression, that is, to defend Ukraine, rather than wait until the end of Russia’s aggression to spend it on reconstruction,” he said.
The logic is to spend the money now on air defenses, ammunition and Ukrainian weapons factories, and Ukraine may save its cities, power stations, factories and territory from destruction. Every building and piece of infrastructure left standing could mean a smaller reconstruction bill later. A stronger Ukraine could also have a better hand when peace talks eventually begin.
Of course, nobody can put an exact price tag on the calculation. One euro spent on defense will not automatically wipe a fixed amount off the reconstruction bill. Ukraine will still need vast sums after the war, while the frozen Russian assets are limited. But the order matters. There can be no meaningful reconstruction if Ukraine does not survive as a sovereign, functioning country.

Subdivided-flat registration rate at 42.5% as ‘early bird’ phase deadline passes
Industry observers say ownership complications and low awareness have slowed landlords’ applications under new housing regulations
Property-ownership complications and low public awareness have slowed landlords’ registration of Hong Kong subdivided flats under new housing regulations, industry observers have said, after the government received only 42.5 per cent of the applications expected in the first phase.
Monday marked the deadline for the initial six-month “early bird” registration phase under the Basic Housing Unit Ordinance. Landlords who applied during this period were eligible for a waiver of HK$3,000 (US$382) in certification fees per subdivided flat for each of the first three years.
The legislation came into force in March to phase out substandard subdivided flats. The government estimates that about 80,000 flats across the city could be accredited, but only about 34,000 units were registered during the first six months.
Scott Leung Man-kwong, deputy chairman of the Legislative Council’s housing panel, described the 42.5 per cent application rate as acceptable but said the HK$3,000 discount was not a significant incentive for landlords to apply early.
“For inherited properties, sometimes the verification of legal ownership could delay the application,” he told a radio show on Tuesday.
“We’ve seen cases where a son inherited a flat from his father that is already subdivided. The tenants continued to pay rent and they did not process the legal transfer of the property. But now, with the application for basic housing units, they will have to do so.”

====================================================================================================

America has the power to defeat Iran. Why can’t it use it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:30:14 UTC
18:30:14 KST

America has the power to defeat Iran. Why can’t it use it?
The war against Iran, launched by the United States and Israel six months ago, was conceived as a lightning campaign against a weakened and already battered enemy.
As far as is currently known, the immediate trigger was the unrest that swept Iran in January, which appears to have convinced the Israeli and American leadership that the government in Tehran was teetering on the brink of collapse and required only a final push.
At the beginning of the campaign, Donald Trump confidently predicted that the war would last a month or six weeks, and sometimes suggested it could be over even sooner. Instead, it’s become one of the defining events of the 21st century and its long-term consequences may ultimately prove comparable to those of the September 11 attacks or Russia’s military operation in Ukraine, and perhaps even surpass them.
Among the most important consequences is the damage inflicted on the United States’ position as the principal guarantor of security for the Arab states of the Persian Gulf, a role Washington gradually assumed after the Second World War, initially alongside Britain and later largely on its own.
The war has exposed two fundamental weaknesses in that first, the United States has proved unable to protect the oil infrastructure and essential services of the Gulf monarchies from devastating attacks by a middle-ranking power such as Iran, and second, it has failed to guarantee freedom of commercial navigation in strategically important waters against attacks by Iran and its Houthi allies in Yemen.
This is important far beyond the military sphere where America’s role as the Gulf’s security guarantor, spectacularly demonstrated during Operation Desert Storm in 1990-91, became one of the foundations of the post-Cold War international order. It influenced not only the foreign policies of the Arab monarchies but their financial decisions, as they invested enormous sums in the United States partly because their relationship with Washington provided them with security.
The scale of the American commitment in 1990 illustrates how much has changed.
To defend Saudi Arabia and defeat Iraq, the United States concentrated about 540,000 troops in the region, roughly a quarter of the active-duty strength of the US armed forces at the time. Seven of the Army’s 18 active divisions and two of the Marine Corps’ three divisions participated, while six of America’s 15 aircraft carriers were deployed, along with approximately 1,600 of its 6,500 combat aircraft.
Desert Storm was ultimately an overwhelming American victory achieved at remarkably low human cost, but American planners didn’t know beforehand that casualties would be so limited. Pre-war estimates envisaged as many as 20,000 casualties, including 6,000 to 7,000 dead, but despite those projections and substantial opposition in Congress, President George H.W. Bush and his administration went ahead.
The contrast with today is amazing as the United States is no longer capable of assembling anything resembling its 1990 force in the Middle East. Around 50,000 American personnel have been deployed for the current operation against Iran, supported by approximately 300 aircraft and just over 20 warships, including two aircraft carriers.
Nor has Washington managed to mobilize its allies on anything approaching the same scale, while Britain alone contributed about 35,000 personnel to the campaign against Iraq in 1990, no American ally from outside the Middle East has made a comparable contribution to the present war.
There has therefore been a radical decline in the resources the leading Western power can mobilize to defend what it regards as vital global interests, as well as in its ability to draw upon allied military power.
Curiously, this has happened without a comparable decline in America’s share of global military expenditure, given the United States accounted for roughly 35-37% of world military spending in 1990 and around 33% in 2025. This discrepancy should encourage greater skepticism about attempts to measure military power simply by comparing defense budgets.
Yet resources are only part of the explanation as more important is Washington’s apparent inability to use effectively the formidable capabilities it still possesses.
The United States undoubtedly retains the technical capacity to inflict a crushing military defeat on Iran and overthrow its government through a sufficiently large joint military operation, even with substantially fewer forces than it deployed against Iraq in 1990, but the obstacle is the price.
Any decisive operation involving a substantial ground component would probably produce many thousands of American casualties, including hundreds, and more likely thousands, of deaths. The political system that accepted such risks in 1990 appears unwilling to accept them today.
The extraordinary effort mounted on April 5, 2026, to rescue the pilot of an F-15 shot down by Iran illustrates the problem, as the United States reportedly committed 176 aircraft to the rescue and lost three manned aircraft and two or three helicopters, representing some $300 million worth of equipment.
The determination to save individual servicemen is understandable, but a military cannot expend resources on that scale to prevent individual casualties while simultaneously fighting a major war intended to achieve decisive strategic objectives.
The same caution is visible elsewhere, seeing as American troops have been kept away from the most dangerous areas, while US warships have operated at considerable distances from the Iranian coast, reducing their effectiveness. Washington has also sought to minimize public attention to its casualties, despite their relatively small number, in marked contrast with its approach during the much more dangerous operations of the early 1990s.
Then there is the financial constraint. The 1990-91 Gulf campaign cost the US budget about $64 billion, or around $120 billion when indirect costs are included. Adjusted for inflation, that would exceed $300 billion today. By mid-July, the current operation against Iran had already cost approximately $37 billion. The total is now likely between $40 billion and $50 billion, even though the campaign has failed to produce the decisive result originally envisaged.
The lesson is therefore more complicated than the simple claim that American military power has disappeared because the United States retains enormous military and financial resources. What’s changed is its ability to concentrate those resources, mobilize allies, and accept the human and financial costs required to achieve decisive political objectives.
Desert Storm demonstrated what American military supremacy looked like at its height, but the war against Iran is revealing something very different, a superpower that can still inflict enormous damage, but increasingly struggles to convert its military superiority into the political outcomes it seeks.
This article was first published by the magazine Profile and was translated and edited by the RT team.

As Chinese chipmakers snap up local gear, self-sufficiency drive faces commercial test
Industry leaders caution that the semiconductor equipment sector must now transition from technical viability to commercial reliability
Chinese chipmakers are setting increasingly aggressive targets to source production equipment locally, adding pressure on domestic toolmakers to come up with machines that are reliable in the exacting environment of high-volume wafer production.
Several new wafer fabrication plants, or fabs, in the country were setting explicit localisation targets, according to Jie Chen, chairman of Britech Semiconductor Equipment (Shanghai) Corp, who spoke at an industry conference in eastern China’s Wuxi on Monday.
“One large customer here in Wuxi is aiming for 80 per cent localisation of equipment at its new fab,” Chen said.
However, industry leaders caution that the equipment sector must now transition from technical viability to commercial reliability, a shift Chen described as moving from a “zero-to-one” phase into a “2.0 era”.
“Making one machine is easy, but can five machines be the same as the first? What about 10, 50 or 100?” Chen said, noting that fabs required absolute consistency across multiple chambers and machines. He added that the industry’s “final exam” would come when Chinese toolmakers could win top overseas clients without home-turf advantage.

Dyson’s Next Act Is an Electric Toothbrush With a Camera
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Whenever Dyson enters a new product category, a ripple effect usually follows, with the buzz growing so loud that competitors are forced to react. The company did this with stick vacuums and premium hair dryers. Now it's aspiring to upend the oral care business.
On Tuesday, Dyson announced the CameraJet, a two-in-one electric toothbrush and flosser, to help you clean those pearly whites. It's not the company's first hybrid experiment (that would be the short-lived Dyson Zone air-purifying headphones), but as a pairing of two technologies, this makes far more practical sense—even if the word camera isn’t one you’d typically expect in the name of an oral device.
The CameraJet is an electric toothbrush with an embedded flosser that shoots liquid into the gaps between your teeth as you brush. How does the device know when the brush head is right above a gap that needs blasting? A built-in endoscope camera analyzes 28 images per second, shooting bursts of rinse as you move the device over your teeth.
Dyson calls this the Gap Optical Targeting system. The company says it’s powered by a macro-lens camera and a machine learning algorithm trained on 470,000 dental images that Dyson collected during the six years it spent developing the product. Dyson says the magic happens within 100 milliseconds—the camera sees the gap and flushes it with a mouth rinse, all while you brush normally.
The fluid jet itself has some interesting engineering. Dyson notes that it's a conical jet, which the company claims removes plaque more effectively than the “needle-type jets” used by competing stand-alone water flossers. Dyson says its cone-shaped jet of fluid can remove plaque over a wider area using less pressure, making the brush gentler on gums and enamel.
For testing this, Dyson created its own proxy plaque in collaboration with the National University of Singapore's Faculty of Dentistry. This allowed the designers to iterate and test the brush’s plaque-removing prowess in the lab without running a clinical trial after every minor change.
Right below the brush is a tank where the gadget stores 12.5 milliliters of alcohol-free mouth rinse. A diaphragm pump and pressure chamber ensure the jets shoot out no matter how you hold the brush, which Dyson claims gives the CameraJet an edge over its peers, which it says lose performance when tilted. A docking station refills the toothbrush with mouth rinse in three seconds with the touch of a button. It also recharges the CameraJet and gives it a nice resting place on your sink. There's a travel case for packing the whole thing up.
Finally, we get to the bristle brush head. Dyson says it's contoured precisely to reach a “greater proportion of the tooth's surface,” with firmer inner bristles and softer outer bristles. A radio-frequency identification (RFID) tag inside measures how many cleans it has completed, so you'll know exactly when to replace the brush head. There's also a softer version of the brush head for people with sensitive teeth and gums.
Don't forget the sonic oscillation! That's a normal part of an electric toothbrush, where it vibrates side to side to clean your teeth. Dyson's CameraJet uses variable sonic oscillation, which varies the angle of oscillation as you brush. The company says this design prevents the bristles from stalling under pressure.
All of this brings us to the CameraJet's biggest claim: that it “removes up to 69 percent more plaque than market-leading premium electric toothbrushes in hard-to-reach areas.” (Dyson's small print says this is based on laboratory tests in the brush-only variable mode in hard-to-reach areas.)
The CameraJet connects to your phone over Bluetooth (there's also Wi-Fi support), where it will show up in the MyDyson app. You don't need to open the MyDyson app to use the toothbrush. But if you do use the app, you can look through the brush’s camera in real time and watch the device shoot liquid into your tooth gaps. If you're worried about putting a camera in your bathroom, Dyson says not to worry; the camera is active only when you open the live view through the MyDyson app or when the brush is automatically scanning your teeth to find the places to shoot those rinsing jets. The company says it does not record or store images locally on the CameraJet or in the cloud.
If you decide to use the app, you can get personalized feedback, coverage mapping to make sure you're cleaning all your teeth, and even a guided cleaning mode. Also, if you don't want the CameraJet to shoot its jets automatically, you can use the manual jetting mode.
There are two more things you should consider before bringing this tech into your bathroom.
Dyson products command high prices, and the CameraJet will unsurprisingly cost you a pretty penny: $499. It comes in blue and pink, and each CameraJet comes with a refill dock, two regular brush heads, and a charging cable.
The final catch is that you cannot use any old toothpaste and mouth rinse. Dyson has a proprietary “non-foaming” toothpaste coming soon, which is crucial, because foam will block the camera. The “low-foaming” rinse is also specifically designed to work with the entire system. You'll be able to sign up for a Dyson subscription to get toothpaste, rinse, and replacement brush heads on a recurring basis. However, you can use any third-party rinses and toothpaste if they are sodium lauryl sulfate–free, as that substance causes foaming.
Around one in three adults in the US reports flossing daily, and multiple studies show that people often spend less than a minute brushing instead of the two minutes recommended by the American Dental Association. By combining brushing and flossing, Dyson is pitching that its product condenses two steps into one, though we'll have to see if its camera-equipped brush can successfully blast those jets into just the right spots.

Man cleared of plotting to kidnap princesses Amalia and Alexia
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A man has been cleared of plotting to kidnap princesses Amalia and Alexia, the eldest daughters of king Willem-Alexander and queen Máxima, after a court ruled he was suffering from a psychosis at the time.
Anne Romke van der H., 33, believed he was in a relationship with Amalia, 22, and fantasised about marrying her before living in the wilds in Poland with her and her 21-year-old sister.
He bought items from a hardware store designed to use as a survival kit, including knives, cooking equipment and two hatchets, one of which he inscribed with Alexia’s name.
The prosecution service said he intended to abduct or attack the two princesses if they were unwilling to go along with his plans.
But a court in The Hague ruled there was no evidence that van der H., from Groningen, was preparing an actual attack on Amalia and Alexia or intended to threaten them.
A psychiatric assessment found he was schizophrenic and had become obsessed with the royal family, particularly the two princesses.
He was found guilty of insulting six police officers and smashing a window, but the court did not impose a fine or punishment because he was in psychosis at the time.
The court said the offences were not severe enough to justify a compulsory treatment regime (tbs), but Van der H. told the judges at an earlier hearing that he was willing to undergo voluntary treatment.

Ukrainian Parliament will work in shelter during air-raid warnings – photos
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
12:27:00 EEST
18:27:00 KST

Ukrainian Parliament will work in shelter during air-raid warnings – photos
Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian Parliament) sessions are planned to continue in a shelter during air-raid warnings. Workstations for members of parliament have been set up in the basement, in the parliamentary conference hall and adjacent corridors.
Source: a statement by Ukrainian Parliament Speaker Ruslan Stefanchuk at a meeting with journalists, attended by an Ukrainska Pravda correspondent
Details: The Rada's administrative office has been developing a voting system outside the session hall since the beginning of the full-scale war, but there had been no need to use it until now, Stefanchuk noted. Given the increase in Russian attacks, MPs will be offered the option of continuing to work in the shelter.
Quote: "I want to immediately dispel some myths. People say that MPs will vote from unknown locations using unclear methods. The Rada's rules of procedure provide for two types of voting: using the electronic system and by show of hands. Voting by hand is not an option, because consideration of each document would take an indefinite amount of time. Therefore, we have developed an alternative electronic voting mechanism to preserve all procedural rules."
Details: Stefanchuk recalled the main provisions of the parliamentary rules of procedure. First, sessions must be held exclusively in the Rada building. Second, MPs may vote only in person.
The speaker stressed that "everything possible" has been done to ensure that every parliamentarian can vote in person in the shelter using the electronic system.
Currently, 368 workstations for MPs have been set up in the conference hall and adjacent corridors. As of 1 September, there are 392 MPs in the Rada. "We based our planning on maximum attendance during recent sessions. But we will find a way to accommodate the full composition of parliament in the shelter if necessary," Stefanchuk clarified.
After an air-raid warning is issued, MPs will have approximately 10 minutes to descend to the shelter and continue voting. After the all-clear is given, parliamentarians will return to work in the session hall. An online broadcast of the session from the shelter will be provided.
Viacheslav Shtuchnyi, head of the Rada's administrative office, explained that electronic voting will be carried out using QR codes placed on MPs' personal voting cards.
"For voting in the shelter, each MP's voting card will have a QR code that can be used to access the network. This is a closed network defined by the perimeter. If an MP leaves these boundaries, the connection will be lost and it will be impossible to continue voting. Since the card is personal, no one else will be able to access the system using that code," Shtuchnyi explained.
MPs will be able to vote using either their personal phones or work tablets.
The parliament speaker stressed that parliamentarians will test the new system over the coming week. A draft resolution will subsequently be adopted to formalise the mechanism.

U.S. Army boosts funding for new Kentucky TNT plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:26:37 UTC
18:26:37 KST

- The U.S. Army modified its TNT production facility contract with Paligen Aerospace & Defense, bringing the total value to $435 million.
- The Kentucky facility will be the first domestic TNT production site in the United States since the 1980s, targeted for completion around 2027.
The U.S. Army has ordered $30.8 million in additional work under a contract to build a domestic factory to manufacture TNT in Kentucky, bringing the deal’s total value to $435 million.
The modification, awarded to Paligen Aerospace & Defense LLC, based in Tampa, Florida, covers design, construction and commissioning work on the facility. Army Contracting Command in Rock Island, Illinois, is managing the contract, which is expected to run through February 15, 2029.
TNT is the primary explosive used to fill 155mm artillery shells, along with a range of other munitions from artillery rounds to aircraft bombs. The Army has described the facility as the first domestic TNT production site in the United States since the 1980s, when the Radford Army Ammunition Plant in Virginia halted TNT manufacturing. The Army originally awarded the $435 million contract in November 2024 to Paligen’s predecessor company, then known as REPKON USA, without competitive bidding.
The facility is being built at a commercial site in Graham, Kentucky. According to Paligen, the plant is designed to use automation, digitization and a new waste neutralization process, with construction and full operation targeted within 36 months of the original award, putting completion around early 2027. The award was funded in part through the 2024 Ukraine Supplemental appropriation.
Paligen Technologies, the parent company formed when REPKON USA rebranded in March 2026, has expanded significantly since the TNT contract was first awarded. The company acquired a 38-acre manufacturing facility in Garland, Texas, from General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems in March 2025, along with defense engineering firm McCormick Stevenson Corporation. Paligen now employs more than 400 people across facilities in Florida, Kentucky and Texas.
The push to rebuild domestic TNT capacity has gained added urgency since October 2025, when an explosion destroyed an Accurate Energetic Systems facility in Humphreys County, Tennessee, which had been supplying TNT to the Pentagon. The loss of that plant left the Army without any operating domestic TNT source while the Kentucky facility remains under construction.
The Army’s investment in domestic TNT production has come as the service has separately struggled to rebuild its broader artillery shell manufacturing base. ProPublica reported that General Dynamics failed to get two 155mm shell production lines in Mesquite, Texas, operating as planned before the Army shut the effort down, even as the company continued receiving other Army contracts totaling $2.5 billion since that shutdown.

Taiwan’s TSMC says 3DFabric can boost AI computing

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — TSMC’s 3DFabric platform can increase AI computing density and memory bandwidth while improving power delivery and cooling, TSMC Advanced Packaging R&D Director Chen Yen-ming (陳燕銘) said Tuesday.
Speaking at the Heterogeneous Integration Summit ahead of SEMICON Taiwan, Chen said AI is pushing chipmakers to find new ways to fit more computing power into smaller spaces, per CNA. He said better chip design alone is not enough, and companies also need to improve how chips are connected, powered, and cooled.
Chen said AI computing performance is improving fivefold each year, while AI models are also processing several times more tokens, or units of data. He said TSMC’s 3DFabric platform brings together several technologies, including CoWoS advanced packaging, to fit more computing power and memory into AI systems while improving data transfer and cooling.
For System on Integrated Chips, Chen said TSMC plans to reduce the connection spacing between parts of its A14 chips to 4.5 micrometers by 2029. TSMC is also applying its technology to high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI systems, with HBM4 base dies made using its N12 process expected to cut power consumption by more than 45% and increase bandwidth 2.5 times, CNA reported.
Chen said TSMC is also developing its Compact Universal Photonic Engine (COUPE), which connects electronic and optical components to move data more efficiently. TSMC plans to move COUPE closer to the main chip by placing it on an interposer, which Chen said can further improve power efficiency and reduce delays.
CoWoS packaging will also allow TSMC to fit more components into a single package as package sizes grow, Chen said. He said TSMC expects a CoWoS package that can support 24 HBM stacks and exceed 14 times the size of a standard reticle by 2029, while the number of AI computing transistors in a single package is projected to grow more than 48-fold from 2024 to 2029 and HBM bandwidth to increase 34-fold.

Iran, Kyrgyzstan review proposal for joint oil refinery construction
TEHRAN – In a significant move toward deepening energy and economic ties, Iran and Kyrgyzstan have agreed to jointly review a proposal for the construction of an oil refinery in Kyrgyzstan. The announcement came on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and Shanghai-Plus summit held in Kyrgyzstan on Monday.
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who met with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov on the summit's margins, confirmed that Tehran has reviewed the proposal positively and agreed to its principle. "Kyrgyzstan's proposal for the joint construction of a refinery in this country has been reviewed positively, and Iran agrees with the principle of this proposal," Pezeshkian stated.
Under the proposed framework, Iran would supply the crude oil required for the refinery, while the resulting petroleum products would be divided between the two nations. The Iranian president described this model of cooperation as a timely opportunity to elevate the level of economic and energy collaboration between the two countries.
The proposal comes at a critical juncture, as energy cooperation has been a central pillar of bilateral relations in recent years. Kyrgyzstan, which currently depends heavily on imports to meet its domestic oil and petroleum product needs, stands to benefit significantly from domestic refining capacity. If finalized, the partnership could expand beyond simple oil and product trade into joint investment, refining operations, technical and engineering services, and the marketing of petroleum products.
President Japarov welcomed the expansion of economic and energy cooperation with Iran and extended an invitation to capable Iranian companies active in oil exploration to bring their expertise to Kyrgyzstan. This invitation is expected to pave the way for a greater Iranian corporate presence in Kyrgyzstan's oil projects and the utilization of Iranian technical and engineering capabilities across various sectors of the Central Asian nation's petroleum industry.
Expanding bilateral economic ties
The refinery proposal is part of a broader push to strengthen economic relations between the two countries. In early August, Iran's Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, Seyyed Mohammad Atabak, met with Kyrgyzstan's Minister of Economy and Commerce, Sydykov Bakyt Tolomushevich. During that meeting, both sides emphasized the development of trade exchanges, joint investment, and the expansion of cooperation in industry, mining, energy, transport, and free zones.
The two ministers underscored the vast capacities for economic cooperation and stressed the importance of advancing trade and investment within the framework of regional agreements, including the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. They also discussed joint production for export to third-country markets, increased collaboration in the export of knowledge-based products, pharmaceuticals, and medical equipment, as well as expanded cooperation between free zones.
Mining, energy, and transit cooperation
In the mining and energy sector, Kyrgyzstan's mineral wealth was a key topic. Iran announced its readiness to cooperate in exploration, extraction, processing, provision of technical and engineering services, modernization of mining industries, and the transfer of technical knowledge.
On the transport and transit front, the two sides emphasized the activation of the Bandar Abbas–Osh railway route, the establishment of direct flights, the reduction of transit costs, and the completion of regional corridors. They also highlighted the importance of participating in China's "Belt and Road" initiative and utilizing Iran's strategic transit position to connect Kyrgyzstan to regional and international markets.
Banking and financial infrastructure
To facilitate this expanding economic partnership, both countries agreed on the development of banking, logistics, and transport infrastructure. Other key agreements included holding a joint banking committee, utilizing national currencies in bilateral transactions, establishing joint investment funds, and employing modern financing methods.
As Iran and Kyrgyzstan continue to build on their growing partnership, the proposed joint oil refinery stands as a potential flagship project—one that could redefine the contours of their economic and energy cooperation for years to come.
