Life after Maga: the group offering an ‘exit ramp’ for rightwingers questioning Trumpism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:00:05 UTC
18:00:05 KST

Stephania Messina kept birthing boys. In the Quiverfull conservative Christian church she belonged to outside Detroit, Michigan, that made her a community celebrity. Your quiver, as the church taught it, is your womb, meant to be filled with as many arrows – a metaphor for children – as you can shoot unto the Lord. She shot five. “They treated me like I was Mother Mary, like I was this gift to the church,” she said.
But while she was quickly pushed into leading worship and Bible study groups for women and children, she wasn’t permitted to talk about politics.
“It wasn’t my job to vote or to know who to vote for. I was just supposed to submit to my husband and do what he thought was necessary,” Messina said. “I was being indoctrinated into Christian nationalism.”
Messina quit her job, yielded to household voting, and took on home schooling and homesteading in a farmhouse, as part of an early 2010s precursor to the “Make America healthy again” (Maha) movement. When Donald Trump launched his first presidential campaign, he was suddenly “God’s chosen one” in the church, she said.
Though Messina was never a “red-hat wearing” Maga supporter, she didn’t start questioning the movement until the early days of the Covid pandemic. Trained as a respiratory therapist, she watched Trump reverse course daily – from claiming the Covid vaccine was good to questioning its effectiveness. Meanwhile, her pastor preached that Covid lockdowns were a “demonic deep-state attempt to keep people out of church”.
After a few other instances left her with doubts, she expanded her news sources beyond the church’s approved media, and then, she said: “The dam broke.” She sought mental health support and began to understand her years inside Maga as what she calls “a religious psychosis” built on fear, isolation and control. When she finally turned away from the church in 2021, she was cast as an outsider but felt the need to proclaim her Maga exit on social media: “I started speaking out to spread awareness. I was in so deep.” She felt alone. A few years later, she connected with the group Leaving Maga.
“Leaving Maga is about normalizing leaving,” said Messina. “And it’s especially important now, since I think the Maga [bubble] is bursting.”
Many Americans, like Messina, have drifted away from Trump in the past decade, but have done so quietly. Leaving Maga offers an exit ramp from Trump’s rightwing movement that has reshaped the Republican party and platformed political extremism. Launched in 2024, the movement turned non-profit is built on the premise that abandoning the Maga identity – and the community surrounding it – functions less like changing one’s mind and more like leaving a high-control religious group, fighting a disease or breaking an addiction. It requires not just rejecting a set of beliefs but rebuilding an entire structure of belonging and identity.
Leaving Maga has touched thousands, operating on multiple fronts: weekly support meetings for the friends and family of people still inside Maga, monthly in-person meet-ups for those who have already left, a nationwide billboard campaign built around invitation rather than confrontation and a budding media literacy program meant to help people recognize disinformation. The goal isn’t to start or win a debate – it’s to give people somewhere to land once they’re ready to leave on their own.
“There are more people than ever who are in Maga who are starting to have doubts and confusion,” said Rich Logis, who founded the group. “We’re trying to counter the toxicity of the Maga community by providing an exit ramp and a community where people can become what I call ‘a born-again human being’ and can reclaim their individuality, their empathy and their agency.”
How Leaving Maga works
Logis was drawn to Trump’s “burn it all down” energy in 2016, voting for him that year and in 2020. He spent nearly a decade as one of Maga’s most committed foot soldiers, writing the campaign’s call script for the first presidential election, helping register new voters for Trump, donating money and appearing on Fox News as a Maga pundit. But his decisive break from the movement came after the Uvalde school shooting in 2022 – he could no longer square his own values with the response he knew was coming from Trump supporters.
Months after the Texas shooting that claimed the lives of 19 children and two teachers, Logis published a public apology online for supporting Trump and hurting people with his actions and rhetoric. The response was overwhelming – people commended him and criticized him – leading him to start the movement. He figured others had also left Maga and wanted to repair the damage they caused.
“I had to go through a reckoning and acknowledge to myself that I had been culpable and complicit in assisting the president in dividing our country and amplifying conspiracy theories that resulted in unnecessary death, suffering and trauma,” Logis said.
He built Leaving Maga the way he poured into Maga years prior – by writing countless online posts, speaking out on social media and reaching out to others. On any given day, Logis is on Instagram Live explaining how and why he left and how others can do the same.
Maga leaders have defined the movement as one that calls for economic nationalism, secure borders, “America first” foreign policy and traditional conservative values, said Laura K Field, a political theorist and author of the book Furious Minds: The Making of the Maga New Right. “But an element of Maga that gets underestimated is its community-building dimension,” she said. “There’s a kind of appeal – a fascist and contrarian element, a deep religiosity to it – that unifies different parts of Maga, including the ordinary voters who aren’t DC beltway types, the elites, the high-powered Catholic intellectuals, or those in the manosphere, for example.”
Logis was one of those people who saw Maga as a community more than a political ideology. “I think that it’s where people find vindication and validation,” he said. “It’s where they feel seen and heard and respected and appreciated.”
But the glue holding the community together was “lies and falsehoods” and an “addiction to fear and rage” fueled by misinformation and disinformation, he said. “[In Maga], I had a dangerous belief in a ‘they’. A ‘they’ who were trying to abridge my rights and indoctrinate my children and take my guns and replace white people with brown people and foreigners.”
Logis argues that leaving Maga requires more than distancing yourself from the president; you have to actively renounce Maga’s underlying conspiracy theories and also commit to building democracy that understands “we as Americans agree on important issues more than we disagree.”
Logis and Messina describe leaving as a project of rebuilding empathy that Maga has deliberately suppressed. “As I began to listen to the people I had been told not to – the feminists, the people who they called ‘race baiters’, trans creators – my empathy came back,” Messina said. Logis put it similarly: leaving means you “no longer need to dehumanize and vilify and demonize those with whom we once disagreed”.
They also don’t try to change the minds of Maga supporters. The idea is to let those who are already questioning it know there is support on the other side. “It is my philosophy that I do not engage in debates with people who are in Maga,” Logis said. “I don’t try to bombard and inundate people with facts and with policy.”
Instead, he and other representatives for the organization spread the word through Instagram live streams and TikToks that receive thousands of likes. They go on cable news programs to speak out against the movement that once dominated their lives. One of the most effective methods is billboarding. Nearly 40 billboards have gone up in 27 states this year, with a simple message: “Having doubts? You’re not alone.” Logis said more than half a million visited the group’s website last year, and just as many have visited so far this year.
Through the website, people can sign up for a newsletter that shares testimonies about people’s journeys out of Maga, access a guide on how to talk to family members and friends still engaged in Trumpism and join online group chats and monthly meet-ups with others who have left.
Carter Brown, a former self-proclaimed tradwife who voted for Trump in 2020 and 2024, said Leaving Maga had helped her realize she needed to do more than just speak out online after leaving; she needed to help rebuild. “It has taken deconstructing my religion and the dogma of western theology and realizing that I wasn’t even living like Jesus,” Brown said.
She has changed her views on women’s rights, LGBTQ+ rights, capitalism and immigration. Brown said she now votes according to her new beliefs, volunteers with groups she harmed with her votes and has conversations with people she harmed. She also seeks friendship with people who have different lived experiences than her own.
Leaving Maga is growing, Logis said, as polls show Trump’s increasing unpopularity. In recent months, Logis has spoken with people who left after being fired during “department of government efficiency” (Doge) cuts. Others have been turned off by Trump’s broken promises on foreign policy and rising costs. Messina said the people she had met in Leaving Maga came from all kinds of backgrounds.
“We got into Maga for different reasons and got out for different reasons,” said Messina. “This is a space to learn other people’s stories and reckon with our own. Though the right knew how to capture us in its algorithms, I feel like the tide is turning.”
How the group supports friends and family of Maga supporters
Leaving Maga’s weekly online support group isn’t for people in Maga – it’s for the people who love them. That includes spouses, adult children, parents, siblings, friends and extended family who have watched someone close to them become “not the person who they once were”, said facilitator Julianna Forlano.
Forlano, a therapist, has worked with families of people with narcissistic personality disorder and in addiction recovery, and said the ruptures she sees every week aren’t really about ideology. “What’s happening in families and in marriages, and between mothers and daughters and fathers and sons has to do with behavior,” she said.
Forlano and her group borrow a framework used in addiction and recovery circles, treating the psychological grip of constant fear-based media and conspiracies like a disease. The mechanism is neurobiological, she said: people who consume a steady diet of fear narratives become fearful in general, adopt a “with us or against us” mentality and start treating loved ones as threats.
“The mind is functioning as a dopamine seeker,” she said, craving the next piece of alarming news the way an addicted brain craves its next hit. Forlano is careful to note that holding certain political beliefs doesn’t make someone diseased; the compulsive, threat-seeking pattern layered on top of those beliefs is what the group tries to address.
The stories members share reflect how the rupture disrupts daily life. One member married into a Latino family with her parents’ blessing, only to watch those same parents tell guests to “speak English” at her child’s birthday party and use slurs about mixed-race people; she has since decided her parents can no longer be part of their lives. Forlano said even conversations that start out ordinary can snap into political conflict without warning. “You could say something as simple as: ‘The tomatoes in my garden aren’t growing,’ and that person will respond by saying: ‘Well, climate change is a hoax,’” she said.
Instead of encouraging members to cut ties, or to keep engaging in the kind of fact-based debate Forlano believes is useless, the group teaches patience and creates a space for members to see they aren’t alone. Members are coached to “hold the door open”, staying present in case a loved one ever starts to notice cracks in what they have been told, without continuing to push, argue or send articles that only further entrench the divide.
The first step, Forlano said, was admitting that everything they have already tried hasn’t worked and to stop warring. Conflict often de-escalates once one party stops pushing back, she said. From there, the work isn’t about holding out hope that loved ones will turn on Trump and the movement he built; it’s about grief – mourning the relationship as it was, finding solidarity with others living through the same struggle and rebuilding a sense of self. Members stay in touch through group chats between sessions, trading techniques and support in real time.
“The supportive nature of the community has been healing,” Forlano said. “It helps people find their footing again.”
What life after Maga looks like
Coming out on “the other side” is different for each person leaving Maga. Logis now supports Democrats. Messina has gone further. “I consider myself a democratic socialist now 100%,” she said. “I’m a member of the DSA. So is my son.” She has become an outspoken supporter of Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan, and describes watching her husband and her 20-year-old son’s friend group all turn decisively against Trump within the past two years.
But that doesn’t mean everyone in her family has left Maga. Her mother, 64, voted for Trump twice and still struggles to fully let go of messaging that casts Democrats as enemies.
However, Messina has slowly had influence. She has talked to her mom about misogyny, intersectionality and the privilege that white women in Maga wield. “Now we’re working on Islamophobia because she can’t say Abdul El-Sayed without cringing because of these deeply ingrained biases,” Messina said. Their arguments used to end in screaming matches, but Messina has learned, slowly, not to cut her mother off. “Cutting them off completely just furthers the divides,” she said.
The group continues to grapple with questions about forgiveness and grace. How much grace does the rest of the country owe people who spent years amplifying conspiracy theories before denouncing Maga? Logis said Leaving Maga regularly receives hostile messages from people who see forgiveness as unearned. Logis understands the anger, he said, but argues that a movement built entirely around punishing defection offers no incentive for anyone else to leave.
“I am not asking anyone to like me. I’m not even asking for forgiveness,” said Messina. “I just hope that you’ll take what I have to say and believe it because I don’t have anything to gain except to hope that we can make a change.”

From milk to sausage rolls: how vending machines could help tackle UK ‘food deserts’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:00:03 UTC
18:00:03 KST

Fizzy drinks, packets of crisps and bars of chocolate: for decades, vending machines were known as a place to grab a quick snack.
Now one family of farmers is trying to change that by bringing vending machines offering fresh milk and local produce – including scotch eggs, sausage rolls and brownies – to villages and other rural locations.
Mark James, 70, and his sons Sam, 39, and Jacob, 36, first trialled vending machines as a way of selling their milk directly to consumers, giving themselves more control over the price they receive.
“For the first time ever, we’re price makers rather than price takers,” Mark says. “If we weren’t doing [the vending machine business], we’d have to think about giving up milk.”
Just under a third (30%) of the 4,500 litres of milk produced each day by the family’s herd of 130 dairy cows at Bodenham in Herefordshire is sold at their 17 Whole Moo World vending machines, located across Herefordshire and the neighbouring counties of Gloucestershire, Worcestershire and Shropshire. The remaining 70% is sold to a local milk processor.
When Whole Moo World took off, Jacob and Sam branched out into retailing cakes, sandwiches and other treats made by small local producers from vending machines. Their business, Tuckshop, now has 22 sites, mostly alongside the milk machines, and also allows them to sell empty glass bottles for milk.
Jacob says farmers are “waking up” to the advantages of selling directly to consumers, even if they do not have a suitable location or the funds needed to build their own farm shop.
He believes vending machines could be the answer for villages and small rural communities at risk of becoming “food deserts”, where lower-income households struggle to find fresh healthy food amid closures of local shops and poor public transport.
They also promise a more profitable way for squeezed farmers to reach customers directly and avoid expensive fees for intermediaries.
Dairy producers in Britain and beyond have suffered in recent years from a boom and bust price cycle, where the price of milk, a globally traded commodity, has been extremely volatile. Strong global demand for dairy has usually led to farmers increasing their herd size and upping production, followed by oversupply and a crash in the milk price.
Farmgate milk prices began to tumble again earlier this year, Mark says. “In August last year we were paid 44p a litre, and ever since the beginning of February it’s been down at 30p a litre.”
For many dairy farmers, including the Jameses, this price does not cover the cost of production. Margins in the industry have always been tight and UK supermarkets have traditionally used low milk prices to tempt shoppers through the door, and the milk processing sector is dominated by three main players – Arla, Müller and First Milk.
British supermarkets are currently charging between £1.20 and £1.30 for a two-pint, or 1.1-litre, bottle of milk.
Whole Moo World customers pay £1.50 for a litre of the family’s unhomogenised milk – where the cream has not been separated from the milk during processing – delivered into a refillable glass bottle, which customers can buy once in the vending machines and wash and reuse.
A litre of milkshake – with flavours including chocolate, strawberry, banana and specials such as mint choc and blueberry muffin – costs £2.90.
Mark James says customers are prepared to pay a small premium for milk that, he says, tastes creamier and is more environmentally friendly thanks to the use of glass bottles.
This is the Jameses’ second stint as dairy farmers. Mark took over his parents’ farm but quit milk production during the 2015 crisis, when low wholesale prices made it impossible to remain profitable.
The family subsequently diversified their business, farming beef cattle and opening holiday lets, but the rolling banks of their land did not make it particularly suited to growing arable crops.
The younger generation of the James family only supported a return to milk production if they ran the business differently.
“It is only through doing this [the vending machines] that I have any interest in being a dairy farmer,” Sam says.
It is not just the machines that make a difference: the mixed herd of dairy cows are milked by robots at a time of each cow’s choosing, freeing the family from 4am alarms and the labour-intensive nature of traditional milk production.
On the day the Guardian visited one vending machine located next to the Primrose Vale pick-your-own and farm shop on the outskirts of Cheltenham, there was a steady flow of customers who arrived to fill up their glass bottles from the machines.
“Our big issue is how to break the habit of [customers] picking milk up in a supermarket, and that is the difficulty because this means that someone is going to make a special trip to come here,” Mark says.
For this, finding the right location is vital. Placing the vending machines next to a farm shop has mutual benefits for both businesses, says Jon Henley, one of the managers at Primrose Vale.
“The machines seem to be bringing customers in 24/7, and then they see our strawberries and come back for the pick-your-own or the charging points [for electric vehicles]. It can also be helpful in winter when there isn’t much seasonal picking.”
The machines are also a novelty for children. “We come to pick berries and then get milk. The machine is fun for little ones,” says Emma Coulter, buying a bottle of milk with help from her three-year-old daughter, Bonnie.
Sam Carter-Campbell, who admits to treating himself to a strawberry milkshake as he drives around Gloucestershire for his job as an electrician, says: “I feel like I’m their best customer as I’m at the machine every day. I occasionally have a brownie, too, but sometimes I look and think, ‘I’d better not.’”
One customer, who gave her name as Vicky, describes the machines as a good idea, provided they are installed in the right places in pretty villages and do not become an “eyesore”.
The technology that powers vending machines has made significant advances in recent years, according to David Llewellyn, the chief executive of the Vending and Automated Retail Association.
“It’s no longer just a standalone mechanical machine, which you don’t have any control over. Now with cashless payments, telemetry and connected equipment, you can see what’s happening, what needs replenishing and it will maintain a range of different temperatures,” he says.
Machines stocked with fresh local produce have been available for consumers in France and Italy for some time, adds Llewellyn, while there is one machine for every 35 people in Japan. That compares with one for every 169 in the UK, where most are coffee and hot beverage outlets, usually found in factories and other workplaces.
Although the James family can now monitor their machines remotely, they still refill them with milk themselves, travelling to locations within a 30-mile radius of their farm. They plan to keep expanding and may have to take on staff to support the business.
“There is a new site we are looking at at the moment, a village of a couple of thousand people, where we think we could provide basic food like milk, eggs, cheese and sandwiches,” Jacob says. “We can do that fairly quickly. The place would support a a farm shop, but vending is much cheaper to install and run.”

From oil to orchids: how Vietnam made tourism its economic engine, what Iran must learn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:58:25 UTC
17:58:25 KST

From oil to orchids: how Vietnam made tourism its economic engine, what Iran must learn
TEHRAN- As a tourist-journalist who has visited many countries, my long journey through Vietnam in November 2024—from the dynamic streets of Ho Chi Minh City to the lantern-lit alleys of Hoi An, the imperial citadels of Hue, the bustling energy of Hanoi, and the emerald waters of Ha Long Bay—left me not just in awe of its beauty, but profoundly impressed by its strategic genius. Vietnam has done what few developing nations have achieved: it has transformed tourism from a peripheral activity into a central economic pillar, a veritable engine of national prosperity. For Iran, a nation rich in heritage but poor in tourism revenue, the lessons are urgent and actionable.
Vietnam’s economic transformation: the numbers that matter
Vietnam’s commitment to tourism is not rhetorical; it is quantified and ambitious. In 2025, the country welcomed nearly 21.2 million international visitors, a 20% surge that set a new record. Tourism receipts reached approximately $85 billion, contributing an estimated 6-8% of GDP annually during the 2021-2025 period. But this is merely the foundation. Under the recently signed Politburo Resolution No. 26-NQ/TW, Vietnam has set its sights on tourism contributing 10-12% of GDP by 2030, with total receipts targeted at $80-90 billion. By 2045, the sector is expected to account for 14-15% of GDP, with 70 million international visitors and a place among the world’s 30 most competitive tourism economies.
More tellingly, tourism’s spillover effects are immense. In the first half of 2026, despite global geopolitical tensions and inflationary pressures, Vietnam’s GDP grew 8.18% year-on-year, with services expanding by 8.09%. Retail sales of consumer goods and services reached VND 3,889.5 trillion, growing 12.9%, driven in large part by tourism recovery. The industry already supports approximately 2.3 million direct jobs and 3.5 million indirect jobs, with targets to reach 1.5 million accommodation rooms and a workforce capable of sustaining this growth.
Strategy pillars of Vietnam’s success
What I observed on the ground confirmed what the policy documents prescribe. Vietnam’s success rests on four interconnected pillars.
First, governance and political will. The Politburo resolution explicitly calls for tourism to generate “stronger spillover effects across other sectors, helping drive economic growth and innovation while promoting sustainable development.” This is not a ministerial afterthought; it is a national priority, signed by the Party General Secretary and State President. Implementation responsibilities are assigned across the political system—from the National Assembly to provincial Party organizations—ensuring coherence and accountability.
Second, infrastructure as a growth catalyst. Vietnam plans to develop three major tourism growth poles in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, and Da Nang, alongside 10 key tourism centres and 20 national tourism areas. Multimodal transport infrastructure—aviation, railways, inland waterways, seaports, and marinas—is being prioritized. During my cruise in Ha Long Bay, I saw firsthand how investment in modern vessels and passenger terminals enhances the visitor experience and extends stays, directly increasing per-capita spending.
Third, a shift from volume to value. The resolution marks a decisive move away from a tourism model focused primarily on visitor numbers towards one centred on quality, efficiency, higher added value, and distinctive experiences. Visa policies are being reformed with wider exemptions for key markets. Emerging models—the night-time economy, riverfront and coastal economies, and integrated tourism, cultural, sports, and entertainment complexes—are actively supported. Shopping tourism is being encouraged through research into value-added tax refund mechanisms. The goal is not just more tourists, but higher-spending, longer-staying visitors.
Fourth, digital and green transformation. Vietnam is establishing a national smart tourism ecosystem, including a national tourism database and digital platform. Big data and AI will be used in promotion and destination reputation management. Simultaneously, green tourism is being promoted through wastewater treatment, reduced plastic use, and circular-economy models. This dual focus on technology and sustainability positions Vietnam as a forward-looking, competitive destination.
A roadmap for Iran: what must change
For Iran, a country with 30 UNESCO World Heritage sites—more than Vietnam—and a civilization spanning millennia, the gap between potential and performance is stark. Iran's tourism sector currently contributes 5% of GDP, a fraction of what Vietnam achieves. Yet the opportunity is immense, and the lessons are clear.
First, elevate tourism to a national strategic priority. Iran lacks an equivalent to Vietnam’s Politburo resolution—a binding, high-level policy document that places tourism at the centre of economic diversification. Iran’s Supreme Leader and government must issue a similar directive, assigning clear responsibilities across ministries, provinces, and the private sector. Tourism must be treated not as a cultural sideline but as a spearhead economic sector, on par with oil and gas.
Second, invest massively in infrastructure. Iran needs an estimated 3,000 new four- and five-star hotels and a modernized aircraft fleet to compete globally. Vietnam’s target of 1.5 million accommodation rooms by 2030 should serve as a benchmark. Iran must prioritize multimodal transport—upgrading airports, expanding rail networks, and developing cruise terminals along the Caspian Sea and the Persian Gulf. Public-private partnerships, which Vietnam actively encourages for destination management and major projects, must be institutionalized in Iran.
Third, reform visa and entry policies. Iran’s visa regime remains cumbersome for many potential visitors. Vietnam is expanding visa exemptions and introducing more flexible policies for key markets. Iran should immediately implement visa-free access for citizens of major tourism-source countries, and adopt an electronic visa system to streamline entry. This alone could significantly boost arrivals.
Fourth, shift from quantity to quality. Iran must stop counting heads and start measuring value. The focus should be on attracting high-spending tourists—cultural heritage enthusiasts, wellness travellers, MICE (Meetings, Incentives, Conferences, Exhibitions) delegates, and luxury adventurers. Developing the night-time economy, shopping tourism (with VAT refunds), and integrated resort complexes would mirror Vietnam’s strategy and dramatically increase per-tourist expenditure.
Fifth, embrace digital and green transformation. Iran lags in digital tourism infrastructure. A national tourism database, AI-driven promotion, and digital booking platforms are essential. Simultaneously, Iran must invest in sustainable tourism—waste management, green transport, and heritage conservation—to protect its assets and appeal to the growing global market for responsible travel.
Sixth, develop human capital. Vietnam targets a tourism workforce of 2.3 million direct employees. Iran currently has only about 50,000 trained tourism professionals, whereas it needs at least 200,000 fluent in key languages. Investing in hospitality education and vocational training is not optional; it is foundational.
Conclusion: A window of opportunity
The first half of 2026 showed Vietnam’s resilience and diversified growth, with tourism, manufacturing, and domestic consumption driving an 8.18% GDP expansion. Iran, facing its own economic pressures, cannot afford to ignore this model. By adopting Vietnam's strategic focus—political will, infrastructure investment, visa reform, quality targeting, digital innovation, and human capital development—Iran could realistically generate $20 billion in annual tourism revenue and create 150,000 new jobs by 2030. More importantly, it would reduce its dependence on oil, diversify its economy, and project a more nuanced, welcoming image to the world.
My journey through Vietnam was a revelation—not just of natural beauty, but of national strategy. Iran has the heritage, the climate, and the geography. What it lacks is the resolve. The lesson from Hanoi to Ha Long Bay is unmistakable: tourism is not just about leisure; it is about livelihoods, growth, and national prosperity. Iran would do well to learn it.

U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation to President Donald Trump after several months of strained relations with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the news, which Newsmax later confirmed, citing three current and former U.S. Army officials.
According to Newsmax, Driscoll will leave his post by the end of this week.
Before his resignation, Driscoll met with Trump at the White House to discuss Army matters and submit his resignation. His family has already left the Secretary of the Army’s official residence.
According to the WSJ, disagreements between Driscoll and Hegseth centered on Army reforms, its readiness, and personnel decisions.
According to a source familiar with Driscoll’s decision, as reported by journalist Jennifer Griffin, the Secretary had raised concerns with the administration about Army transformation and readiness. Hegseth, however, blocked those efforts, including by firing generals responsible for implementing them.
Hegseth also threatened Driscoll with a formal investigation if he disclosed details of their disagreements to the press.
Last week, Driscoll attended the retirement ceremony for General Chris Donahue at Fort Bragg. According to a former official, he acted like someone who had already decided to leave the post. According to the WSJ, Donahue’s retirement was part of Hegseth’s campaign to reduce the number of U.S. generals and admirals by 10% and four-star positions by 20%.
Driscoll has served as Secretary of the Army since February 2025. He is an Iraq War veteran and a former Army Ranger officer. In 2020, Driscoll unsuccessfully ran for the U.S. House of Representatives in North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District.
He is also close to U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance, and one source suggested that after leaving office, he could help Vance with a potential 2028 presidential campaign.
As Secretary, Driscoll advocated for reforming military procurement and expanding the Army’s authority to repair its own equipment. He also emphasized using 3D printing to speed up parts production and military equipment repair.
The White House, meanwhile, praised Driscoll’s work. A White House spokesperson thanked him for his service and said that under his leadership, the Army had placed greater emphasis on readiness.

Russian drone and missile barrage kills at least 12 in Ukraine’s Kyiv
Russian attacks escalate as EU defence ministers meet in Ireland to discuss Ukraine air defence shortages.
At least 12 people have been killed and 21 wounded in a wave of Russian air attacks on Ukraine’s capital Kyiv and the surrounding region, authorities said.
“Kyiv region came under a massive attack by Russian missiles and strike drones tonight,” Kyiv regional military administration chief Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram on Tuesday.

- list 2 of 3Poland opens terror probe into fire at factory supplying Ukraine drones
- list 3 of 3US brings back Russia’s finance minister to G20 talks, angering Europe
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denounced “Russian terror” and said an Indian citizen was among the dead, calling on allies to boost Ukraine’s air defences.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least eight people were killed and five others, including two children, were injured during the overnight drone and missile attacks on the city.
Another four people were killed in the Kyiv region, Ukrainian prosecutors announced, saying a residential building was damaged in the suburb of Boryspil.
Zelenskyy said 50 people were evacuated from the building in Boryspil.
“Russia always plans its strikes specifically to cause as much destruction to people’s lives as possible, and it succeeds only when air defence capabilities are insufficient,” he said on social media.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it hit military and energy facilities in Kyiv and Odesa, as well as regions surrounding these cities overnight.
Ukraine’s border service also said Russian forces hit the ferry checkpoint at Orlivka on the border with Romania, a NATO member.

Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said Russia’s tactic of launching continuous waves of drones during the day was aimed at disrupting civilian life.
“Every time there’s an air raid siren, people have to evacuate certain commercial buildings and schools have to go underground. Ninety percent of Ukraine’s modern food storage has been destroyed, so grocery stores are having fewer supplies,” MacAlpine said.
Ukraine targets Russian port
In Russia, a Ukrainian drone attack caused a fire in the port area of Ust-Luga, a major export outlet in the northwest, and Moscow was repelling drones.
In the Samara region, a Ukrainian drone attack hit the town of Novokuibyshevsk, blowing out windows in an apartment building, Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said on Telegram.
Novokuibyshevsk and the surrounding area on the Volga River are home to a number of Russia’s major oil refineries run by the state oil company Rosneft.
The acting governor of Russia’s Belgorod region said a Ukrainian attack killed one person.
Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately attacking civilians.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s drone forces commander says it hit 54 Russian “shadow fleet” vessels in August to prevent oil sales funding Russia’s war in Ukraine.
EU meeting
The attacks come as European Union defence and foreign ministers gather in Ireland for talks on strengthening Ukraine’s air defences.
Ukraine faces a shortage of interceptor missiles, particularly United States-made Patriot systems used against ballistic threats.
Both sides have escalated long-range strikes in recent months, hitting infrastructure such as warehouses, businesses, and oil and port facilities, as well as ships, increasing civilian casualties.

Housing minister announces sites for 30,000 new homes by 2035

Housing minister announces sites for 30,000 new homes by 2035
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Housing minister Eleanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan has identified five new sites around the country to build 30,000 new homes by 2035.
The five urban locations in Friesland, Noord-Holland, Zuid-Holland and Limburg have been designated National Large-Scale Housing Locations (NGWs) as part of the cabinet’s plans to build 400,000 houses in the next 10 years.
Between 5,000 and 6,000 homes are planned at four of the sites in Haarlem, Deventer, Weert and Leeuwarden, while 8,000 houses are due to be built in Maastricht. All the sites apart from Haarlem are close to main railway stations.
The sites are the first to be identified by the current government under the NGW scheme, a €5 billion fund first announced in 2023 to speed up development in urban areas and relieve the pressure on housing.
It takes the total number of NGW areas to 26. However, last month plans to develop four sites nominated by the previous housing minister, Mona Keijzer, had to be put on hold because there was no money to build road and railway connections.
Boekholt-O’Sullivan said in a letter to parliament that the locations had been chosen because they could be easily connected to services such as water and electricity, allowing the areas to be developed quickly.
“In choosing these five new NGW locations we explicitly looked at locations where no extra measures are needed for availability to realise these homes,” she said. “That means we can use our joint efforts to realise new neighbourhoods at speed.”

Estonia's PPA urges caution over video claiming Russian riverbank work
Videos circulating on social media claim to show that Russia is reinforcing the bank of the River Narva, which borders Estonia, with crushed stone. The Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) said it continuously monitors developments on the eastern border.
In one video, a man claims the Russian authorities dumped several meters of crushed stone along the riverbank. In another clip, a woman says it is now difficult to access the riverbank to swim.
The activity is said to be taking place in the Vasknarva area near the entrance to Lake Peipus on Estonia's eastern border.
A person living in Vasknarva confirmed to ERR that they have heard noise coming from the other side of the border for several days. However, they do not have visual confirmation of what exactly is taking place on the other side of the river.
Deputy director general of the PPA for border guard affairs, Veiko Kommusaar, said the agency cannot comment on activities taking place on the other side of the state border or on the activities of another country's authorities.
Local residents have posted videos claiming that Russia is building gravel embankments along the Narva River near a border crossing with Estonia.
I don't know how reliable these videos are. I have followers from this region - what do you think? pic.twitter.com/bk42m6YshA
"However, we continuously monitor developments related to Estonia's security and border safety and cooperate with other security agencies to have a comprehensive overview of the situation," he told ERR.
The PPA recommends that viewers approach information circulating on social media critically.
"It is particularly important to exercise caution with content that is emotional, provocative or may be intended to create fear, anxiety or uncertainty among people. Before drawing conclusions, it is worth checking the origin of the information, seeking confirmation from reliable media outlets and following official information from the authorities," Kommusaar said.
He added that the PPA continuously monitors developments on the eastern border.
"We are aware of developments in the border area and continuously assess their possible impact on Estonia's security and border safety. If information or activity emerges that requires informing the people of Estonia or taking additional measures, we will notify the public through official channels," Kommusaar stressed.

NATO Submarine Rescue System conducts Exercise Flying Fish
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:55:36 BST
17:55:36 KST

NATO Submarine Rescue System conducts Exercise Flying Fish
The NATO submarine rescue system tests global RAF airlift capability in major exercise, keeping UK, France and Norway crews emergency ready.
The NATO Submarine Rescue System (NSRS) has taken part in an exercise to prove it can be flown, by the Royal Air Force, to anywhere in the world.
A tri-national government capability jointly owned by France, Norway and the UK, the NSRS is one of the world’s leading submarine rescue capabilities.
Developed to be fully air-mobile, this global capability can evacuate stricken submariners from a submarine disabled on the seabed at depths down to 610 metres.
With 350 tonnes of unique equipment that needs 27 lorries and several aircraft to mobilise, this exercise was key to proving the system can respond quickly.
An important part of the rapid response needed for a submarine emergency is transporting the system by road to an airport, which on this occasion was RAF Brize Norton.
A police escort was practised during the event, with every police force between Glasgow and Brize Norton used to provide a constant blue light presence to the convoy.
Once at Brize Norton, the Submarine Rescue Vehicle, effectively a mini-submarine, was loaded on a simulator with the exact dimensions and deck arrangement of a C-17A Globemaster. Some of the heaviest support equipment was also loaded onto a similar simulator for the A400M Atlas military transport aircraft.
This was the first use of the A400M Atlas for NSRS transport and means the aircraft can now be used by UK and NATO partner nations’ air forces for future mobilisation, enhancing the ability for rapid deployment of NSRS. Both loading events were conducted by the specialist RAF team at the Joint Air Delivery Test and Evaluation Unit.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP said:
  This is a piece of specialist equipment we hope never to have to use, but the ability to mobilise the NATO Submarine Rescue System at short notice to anywhere in the world is reassuring for the UK and our allies.
If a submarine is in trouble we will need to respond fast. Ensuring we have a tried and tested response is how we can be ready for any eventuality.
Captain Lyons RN, Operating Duty Holder for the NSRS, who witnessed the operation, said:
  Rescue of the crew from a stricken submarine will require numerous agencies to operate efficiently as one team, and this loading exercise on to a military aircraft is a vital aspect to maintain training and currency for our RAF colleagues.
I was delighted to see them maintain efficient and close control of this unique vehicle that is relied upon by so many nations.
The exercise tempo for all parts of the system is relentless, as it must provide assurance to all our partner nations that the NSRS remains rescue ready.
The NSRS is delivered on behalf of the Royal Navy, Marine Nationale, and Norwegian Navy by the DNE’s Submarine Delivery Group, with JFD Global as the service contractor.
Exercises like this help ensure the NSRS team remain qualified and provide assurance to our partner nations that the NSRS remains rescue ready.

In short:
Australian authorities are investigating reports a soldier who previously served in the Australian Defence Force has been killed in Ukraine.

What's next?
Authorities in Australia and Ukraine are yet to confirm details about his death.
Australian officials are investigating reports a former ADF soldier has been killed while fighting in Ukraine.
The soldier, known by the nickname "Mozzie the Aussie", had been serving as a volunteer and combat medic in the Ukrainian International Legion's Med Team Alpha.
The ABC has been asked not to report his full name out of privacy concerns for his family, but has confirmed the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is making inquiries with authorities in Ukraine.
His death has not been confirmed by any Australian or Ukrainian officials, but veteran and Shadow Minister for Defence Personnel, Phil Thompson, paid tribute to the former Australian soldier on social media.
In a statement, Mr Thompson remembered his friend as someone "who earned the respect of all who served alongside him".
"He was the kind of bloke who never hesitated to put others before himself. He was a good man, a great soldier, and someone his mates could always rely on when it mattered most,"
"Through his courage, skill and selfless commitment to others, Mozzie saved countless lives on the battlefield.
"My thoughts are with Mozzie's family, friends, and brothers in the battalion in both Australia and Ukraine as they mourn this terrible loss."
Former soldier went to Ukraine to help
Mr Thompson said "Mozzie" served in the Australian Army and was a member of the Townsville-based 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment.
He completed deployments to Papua New Guinea before travelling to fight in Ukraine.
In a video posted online by Med Team Alpha, a masked soldier identifying himself as "Mozzie from Australia" explained why he wanted to fight in Ukraine.
"I have a military background in Australia so a lot of the skills that I had wouldn't transfer over to other jobs," he said.
"So I thought Ukraine would be the perfect opportunity to help out the country as a whole and use my skills to a good use."
The Ukrainian Armed Forces has been contacted for comment.
According to Ukraine's Military Ombudsman, "around 16,000 foreign volunteers from at least 72 countries" are serving alongside Ukrainian forces.
In June, former ADF soldier Samuel Pedrazzini was killed while fighting on the front lines in Donetsk, in eastern Ukraine.
Melbourne man Oscar Jenkins, who was captured by Russian forces while serving in Ukraine's army in 2024, recently gave his first interview since being convicted in what the Australian government has slammed as a "sham trial".
Australian authorities say they have asked Ukraine to prioritise Jenkins in any future prisoner swap with Russia.

Japan's 10-year yield hits 3%, a first since 1996 as rate hikes dominate the G20
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:54:37 UTC
17:54:37 KST

Japan's 10-year government bond yield touched 3% on Tuesday for the first time since 1996, part of a deepening global sovereign debt sell-off, while US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent used the G20 finance meeting to press Tokyo for faster rate hikes.
The world's third-largest bond market crossed a line on Tuesday that it held for three decades, though the speed of the ascent is the more remarkable part.
The yields on Japanese 10-year bonds reached a level unseen since September 1996, driven by inflation, fiscal worries and near-certainty that the Bank of Japan will tighten this month, with that last expectation being actively encouraged from Washington at the G20 gathering in North Carolina.
The Japanese 10-year yield has more than tripled in two years and roughly doubled since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi took office last October on a platform of fiscal expansion perceived by concerned investors as reckless.
Shorter maturities are at extremes too, with the Japanese 5-year at a record high and the 2-year at a peak of over three decades as well.
The immediate driver is monetary policy as the BOJ's rate stands at 1%, a level last seen 31 years ago, reached through a slow sequence of hikes. Firstly, 0.5% to 0.75% last December, and then to 1% in June.
It meets on 17 and 18 September, with markets pricing an 80% to 90% chance of a further hike to 1.25% which would represent a 0.75% increase to Japan's benchmark rate in just nine months.
The bond sell-off is also not confined to Tokyo.
Global bond yields hit their highest since 2008, with a Bloomberg gauge of government debt rising for a fourth day to 3.72%, as climbing oil prices fuelled inflation concerns and Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole address boosted the probabilities of a US rate hike as well.
For instance, 30-year US Treasuries are currently enduring their worst run since 2006.
Washington's push for faster rate hikes in Tokyo
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spent the first day of the G20 meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, nudging Japan towards tighter monetary policy.
"I have information that the market doesn't have, and it's my belief that the Japanese government and the BOJ will do the things that will lead to a stronger yen," he stated publicly during the event.
When asked directly by reporters whether he meant higher interest rates, Bessent replied: "I think the market is pricing that in now."
A day earlier, the US Treasury Secretary had gone further by saying he expected the Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda "to do the right thing" on monetary policy.
According to the Japanese public broadcaster NHK, citing an interview with the US Treasury under secretary for international affairs, Erin Browne, Bessent told both Ueda and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama that Japan's next move should be a rate hike, and urged Tokyo to signal that it is putting public finances on a sustainable footing.
However, Katayama's account of the same meeting was narrower.
"We confirmed that an orderly yen exchange rate is essential for the stability of global financial markets, including those of the United States, and that the continued coordinated efforts of Japan and the United States contribute to achieving this shared objective," the Japanese finance minister told reporters.
Katayama said monetary policy did not come up at all, declined to say whether current yen levels are orderly, and had earlier described the joint intervention statement as one that "was a very strong one and still lives."
A senior finance ministry official was blunter, saying the Bank of Japan sets policy according to Japan's economy rather than what Washington tells it to do.
Ultimately, the currency is what Washington is watching.
The Japanese yen traded around 160 per dollar on Tuesday which is the level markets treat as the threshold for renewed intervention, up around 3% after weakening to its softest since the rare joint operation the US and Japan mounted in late July.
Bessent described recent moves as not disorderly, pointing away from a repeat of that intervention and towards rates as the preferred remedy.

China's Xi calls for universal security at SCO summit, hits out at ‘unilateralism’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:53:50 UTC
17:53:50 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
- Chinese president takes a swipe at trade protectionism, decoupling, calls on major countries to lead in upholding rule of law
 The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) should prioritize security and “foster an environment of universal security,” Chinese President Xi Jinping Tuesday told the bloc’s leaders at a summit in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek, hitting out at “hegemony, unilateralism, and protectionism.”
 
Stressing that the SCO should uphold dialogue and consultation, Xi called on the grouping to “improve governance in a fair and orderly manner,” according to state-run Xinhua News.
 
Bishkek is hosting a two-day summit of the Council of Heads of State of the SCO, a Eurasian bloc, that began Monday, marking the 25th anniversary of the organization.
 
Xi's statement came amid the Russia-Ukraine war, the US war with Iran, and the ongoing Israeli genocide in the Palestinian enclave of Gaza.
 
In addition to Xi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev are attending the summit. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are also attending.
 
“China sees the Shanghai Cooperation Organization as a priority area for high-quality joint construction of the Belt and Road and implementation of the Global Development Initiative,” Xi said.
 
He said China is ready to help build the SCO into an “important platform for implementing the Global Security Initiative.”
 
China is also willing to work with all parties to implement the Global Civilization Initiative, and supports the SCO in pursuing exemplary cooperation to implement the Global Governance Initiative, Xi added.
 
Emphasizing that the grouping should “lay a solid foundation for friendship across generations" and "usher in a future of shared prosperity," Xi announced that Beijing will establish a China-SCO basic education cooperation center.
Hegemony, unilateralism running 'counter to tide of history’
 
Addressing the "SCO Plus" meeting, Xi took a swipe at what he called “hegemony, unilateralism and protectionism.”
 
They run “counter to the tide of history,” said Xi, without specifying any country by name.
 
Urging the SCO to “shoulder the responsibility of the times,” Xi said multipolarity was an “irreversible trend” and “sovereign equality, mutual respect are the fundamental principles” for such a world.
 
The statement by Xi came amid the US-Iran war, as well as the Trump administration's unilateral tariffs on US trade partners.
 
“Multipolarity, independent development paths and democratization of international ties mark right path forward,” he said.
 
For a multipolar world, Xi emphasized that ensuring balance, order, and upholding the rule of law were “necessary.”
 
Pointing to the UN, Xi said authority and vitality of the world “need to be reinvigorated,” while calling on “major countries to lead in upholding rules and the rule of law, and jointly address global challenges.”
 
Stressing dialogue and consultation, Xi said that “dominance by just one or several countries, or bloc politics are not true multilateralism.”
 
“Protectionism and decoupling have no future,” Xi also said, adding that the SCO's mission is to “promote the global governance system in a more just and equitable direction.”

U.S.-led peace talks stalled this year as Ukraine refused Russian demands to cede territory and as Washington has become increasingly preoccupied with the conflict with Iran.

Agriculture Ministry estimates how much food prices could rise due to Russian attacks
Restructuring logistics following Russian strikes on food warehouses could increase food prices by no more than 2.5%.
Source: Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi
Details: Suppliers are switching to storing goods in smaller batches and delivering products directly from producers to shops. In this way, businesses are seeking to avoid losing large quantities of products at once in the event of another strike.
The new system requires more transport and could increase the cost of warehousing services. The Agriculture Ministry estimates that these additional costs should not lead to a sharp rise in prices.
As supply chains are restructured, shops may temporarily reduce the range of certain products they offer. The ministry stressed that this would not indicate a food shortage.

India, China Take Small Step Forward Toward Border Settlement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:51:00 UTC
17:51:00 KST

Top officials of India and China have agreed to work on identifying less contentious sections of their contested border for delimitation as part of a broader process toward resolving their longstanding boundary dispute.
A special group of negotiators will identify these less disputed parts of the border and delimit them, a joint statement released on August 26 said. The statement came a day after India’s National Security Adviser Ajit Doval met China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing for talks. Doval and Wang are the designated special representatives of their two countries for the boundary talks mechanism, which was established in 2003 to address the border dispute.
At the talks in Beijing, India and China also agreed to two new military hotlines in the eastern and middle sections of their border and two new meeting points for military commander-level interactions to immediately deal with any tensions that arise along their 3,500 km-long border. Officials of the two countries will meet next month to discuss issues related to trans-border rivers as they look to take their relationship forward after ties sank to a six-decade low during the June 2020 Galwan clash.
“The two sides agreed that any situation on the ground would be addressed promptly through existing diplomatic and military channels,” the statement, which listed eight outcomes, said. The emphasis was on stabilizing the border and ensuring that any tensions that surface are defused before they impact the larger relationship.
“The two sides discussed ways to improve understanding of LAC [Line of Actual Control, the de facto border] in appropriate areas, for better border management,” it said. This is a key outcome given that differing perceptions of where the border lies have been the principal source of friction between the countries.
There was agreement on maintaining peace and tranquility along the border and on creating “an atmosphere for healthy and steady development of bilateral relations,” the joint statement said. India has stated multiple times that peace on the border was a pre-requisite for progress in other areas of the China-India bilateral relationship, such as economic engagement.
The two countries said they were committed to finding a solution to their vexed boundary problem based on a 2005 pact that says the final agreement would be a “package settlement” that would cover the entire border – the western, middle, and eastern sections. The 2005 pact also provides for both countries to “safeguard due interests of their settled populations in the border areas.”
India has been particularly keen that the solution to border tensions with China be a comprehensive one, covering the entire stretch of the border rather than selected areas seen as easier to resolve. Moreover, some of these areas with easier resolution prospects are also ones where India holds a military advantage vis-a-vis China.
The joint statement was issued a day after the two countries put out separate readouts of their talks, which was taken as a sign that the two countries were far apart on key issues. The release of the joint statement has set at rest doubts that differences had outweighed points of agreement.
The China-India talks come against the backdrop of an increasingly unstable world order where the United States is seen as an inward-looking and unreliable partner. Previously, India had perceived the U.S. as a hedge against China’s growing assertiveness in Asia. India views China as its principal long-term adversary. However, New Delhi has been at the receiving end of Donald Trump’s tariffs and other punitive measures over the past year. Consequently, India is adopting an “America Plus” strategy that includes outreach to countries and groups like Japan, the European Union, Russia and China, said security affairs analyst C. Raja Mohan, in an article in the Foreign Affairs magazine.
C. Uday Bhaskar, a retired commodore of the Indian Navy and currently director at the Society for Policy Studies think tank in New Delhi, noted that a joint statement after talks between special representatives of India and China on border issues was “rare.” “This time, an eight-point text was actually agreed within 18 hours, which signals political intent at the highest level to lock in stability ahead of a packed fortnight,” he said in a recent opinion piece. The delay in issuing the eight-point document was symptomatic of what defines China-India relations currently — “deeply embedded wariness,” he added.
The Doval-Wang talks set the stage for the upcoming meetings between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at two summits over the coming fortnight: the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Summit at Bishkek on August 31-September 1 and the India-chaired meeting of the BRICS countries in New Delhi on September 12-13.
Xi is expected to travel to India for the BRICS meet, although Beijing has not announced the visit yet. It will be his first visit to India since 2019.
The move toward a rapprochement amid simmering tensions along the LAC triggered by the Galwan clashes began in 2024 with India and China announcing the pull back of troops from close proximity along border points in Eastern Ladakh, high up in the Himalayas. Indian and Chinese troops are now disengaged, i.e. no longer in close proximity to each other, but they are yet to move back to peacetime positions. This means that neither side has de-escalated deployment as yet.
Modi and Xi have met on two occasions since the disengagement of troops – in Kazan in Russia on the sidelines of the 2024 BRICS summit and on the margins of the China-hosted SCO summit in Tianjin last year.
Meanwhile, the two sides have acted to resume connectivity; travel woes have eased and airlines have resumed flights.
News reports suggest that India and China are exploring new ways to facilitate business-to-business exchanges with India aiming to attract Chinese investments. Some of these announcements could be made when Xi lands in New Delhi for the BRICS summit.
Earlier this year, India amended the rules allowing easier investment flows from China after tightening rules in 2020. India sees increased investments from China as a way to cut down its ballooning trade deficit with Beijing.
With a goal to become a developed economy by 2047, India is looking for investments, technology, and ways to boost its manufacturing. With Trump making the U.S. an unreliable partner and India looking at other partners to fill the void, China next door has emerged a real possibility.
“We are not in the 1991 world,” where there was only one superpower — the United States, Atul Aneja, a former correspondent of The Hindu in Beijing, told The Diplomat. “Today’s world is a multipolar world. There is China, Russia, and others. Power is fragmented and that is reflected in the change of character of global power system. In this scenario, India needs to engage with China,” he said.
India’s outreach to China comes against the backdrop of Beijing’s mounting military and economic support to India’s archrival, Pakistan, on many occasions. There is also concern in New Delhi over China’s propensity to weaponize supply chains, i.e., to stop export of key products that India’s economy is dependent on. Beijing’s sudden halt of fertilizer exports to India is a case in point.
While China is seeking increased access to India’s market for its electric vehicle (EV) manufacturers, news reports suggest that China is reluctant to transfer EV battery technology to Indian businesses. Indian companies are also reportedly struggling to obtain rare earth magnets from China, with restrictions first noticed in April 2025.
All this suggests India’s rapprochement with China isn’t likely to be smooth or straightforward. While it is in India’s national interests to seek out Chinese investments, Beijing would definitely seek a bigger footprint for its businesses in India. But it seems doubtful that Beijing would greenlight technology transfers or move to build up India, given that Delhi is a potential challenger to China’s Asian and global ambitions in the future.

Sweden rehearses mass military burials as part of largest defence drill in decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:49:12 UTC
17:49:12 KST

Real body bags, a priest reciting last rites to fictional soldiers, and cold-storage stress tests reveal just how far Sweden is willing to go to prepare its defence.
Sweden's armed forces have carried out a full-scale exercise in the logistics of burying fallen soldiers, part of a broader shift by the once-neutral Nordic country toward "total defence" planning since joining NATO in 2024.
The mortuary drill formed part of Aurora 26, Sweden's largest national military exercise since the 1990s, which ran from late April to mid-May 2026 and involved roughly 18,000 troops from 13 nations, according to the Swedish Armed Forces.
A peer-reviewed account published in the journal Frontiers in Psychiatry describes a mortuary affairs component using more than 500 mannequins and body bags representing fallen service members - a scale of drill not attempted in Sweden since the early 1950s.
More than 300 military personnel took part, alongside the Church of Sweden, the Swedish Tax Agency and the country's conscription agency.
The exercise tested the full chain of handling war dead: recovery, identification, notification of allied embassies and the International Committee of the Red Cross, and burial with military honours.
The commanding officer told researchers: "I am proud to have been part of this. The last time this was practiced was, I believe, in 1952, so I am proud to have contributed."
A military chaplain reflected on the visual impact, saying it made the abstract reality of war casualties suddenly concrete after seeing dozens of body bags lined up.
Defence trade outlet Defence24 reported it was the first time the process had been rehearsed jointly by every relevant institution.
Officials framed the planning as a matter of morale and institutional readiness rather than a prediction of casualties.
A military physician noted that after the exercise, personnel would need "a major adjustment" in how medical teams are resourced for mass-casualty scenarios, while another soldier told researchers the exercise gave them "a clearer understanding of the consequences of war."
Planning for the worst scenario
Separately from the exercise itself, the Church of Sweden, which remains the country's statutory burial authority, has long been instructed to plan for burial capacity equivalent to 5% of the national population, or roughly 500,000 people.
That figure is a Cold War-era civil defence benchmark covering both military and civilian deaths nationwide, not a forecast tied to Aurora 26 or any specific casualty estimate.
Asked about the planning, Jan-Olof Olsson of Sweden's civil defence agency told Le Monde it does not mean authorities expect that many victims, but that "to plan, we need an estimate."
The drill sits within a wider pattern of Baltic states and NATO's northern flank rehearsing worst-case scenarios as tensions with Russia persist. Aurora 26 also featured Ukrainian drone specialists training NATO troops in counter-drone tactics, and forces from the US, Netherlands, France, Poland and other allies operating across southern Sweden, Gotland and the Baltic Sea.
For a country that remained neutral through both World Wars and the Cold War and last deployed its military in 1814, the shift marks a significant psychological and institutional adjustment - one that mirrors similar measures in other countries in the region, including cross-border evacuation agreements signed by ten countries and Lithuania's mass-casualty hospital drills.

- Ukrainian drone attacks damaged several residential properties in the Samara Region in central Russia, Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said on Max.

- Two people suffered minor injuries in the drone attack on Samara Region and remain under medical observation, according to the latest reports.

- Authorities in Novokuybyshevsk declared a state of emergency following the drone attack.
- The Samara Region Prosecutor's Office said it is overseeing the rights of residents affected by the drone attack.

A look back at Estonia's presidential elections | Episode 7: Alar Karis, 2021
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:47:00 UTC
17:47:00 KST

A look back at Estonia's presidential elections | Episode 7: Alar Karis, 2021
Five years ago, Alar Karis emerged from a crowded field of potential candidates to win Estonia's presidency, backed by a cross-party search for a politically unaffiliated figure capable of securing broad support in the Riigikogu.
Kersti Kaljulaid, who became president in 2016, decided not to run in the 2021 presidential election.
"Good politics has no home. Today, the Riigikogu is not a home for good politics. And if you're one of the players on the field, then everything you say is simply part of the competition. But if you're a little removed from the field, you have an opportunity to comment on the game. And it seems to me that Estonian politics needs people like that as well," Kaljulaid told ETV's "Ringvaade" when asked why she no longer wanted to run for president.
During the first half of 2021, Riigikogu President Jüri Ratas was discussed as a possible presidential candidate. In June, Ratas announced that he did not intend to run for president.
Kallas and Ratas first approach Jüri Raidla
In July, attorney Jüri Raidla acknowledged that Prime Minister Kaja Kallas and Riigikogu President Jüri Ratas had jointly asked him to run for president. Raidla turned down the proposal, saying the president should be competent in foreign policy, an area in which he lacked expert knowledge.
In August, Jüri Luik said that although several political parties had approached him about becoming a presidential candidate, he would stick to his earlier plan to leave domestic politics and take up the post of Estonia's ambassador to NATO in September.
Other names floated as possible candidates included Henn Põlluaas, Tarmo Soomere, Kaimar Karu, Indrek Laul and several others. Of these, Soomere was perhaps the most seriously considered. He met with four Riigikogu parliamentary groups: Isamaa, the Social Democratic Party, the Reform Party and the Center Party.
The leaders of those parties met on August 6, after which Jüri Ratas said Soomere did not have enough support in the Riigikogu to be elected president, which would require 68 votes in favor. Soomere's lack of political experience, particularly in foreign policy, was cited as a weakness.
On August 17, Alar Karis, then director of the Estonian National Museum, acknowledged that Center Party Chairman Jüri Ratas had asked him to consider running for president. In addition to the Center Party, the leaders of the Reform Party, Isamaa and the Social Democratic Party supported the proposal. At the time, Kaja Kallas' first government, a coalition of the Reform Party and the Center Party, was in office. A day later, Karis agreed to become a presidential candidate.
On August 27, the Reform Party and Center Party's 59 members of the Riigikogu formally nominated Karis for president. Under their agreement, they were to support Karis through the end of the Electoral College process.
Isamaa and the Social Democratic Party left the decision on how to vote up to each of their members. About half of the MPs in each party's parliamentary group supported Karis.
The Riigikogu convened to elect the president on August 30. Alar Karis received 63 votes in the first round, five short of the number needed to be elected. As many as 16 unmarked ballots were cast. EKRE's 19 MPs, as well as Siim Kallas and Helir-Valdor Seeder, who were hospitalized, did not collect ballots. One MP who collected a ballot also did not cast it.
It was believed that some of the blank ballots in the secret vote came from Isamaa MPs, with several also coming from the ranks of the Social Democrats.
A day later, on August 31, the second round of the presidential election was held in the Riigikogu. The number of unmarked ballots fell from 16 the previous day to eight. The number of votes in favor of Karis rose to 72, exceeding the minimum of 68 required. Alar Karis was elected president of Estonia.
The new president took office on October 11. Alar Karis was 63 when he became president.
In March this year, public trust in the presidency rose to 76 percent, its highest level in three years. A nationwide Emor survey commissioned by the Government Office found that support for the president increased among both ethnic Estonian respondents and respondents of other ethnic backgrounds.
Everyone keen to avoid repeat of 2016 fiasco
Erkki Keldo, the Reform Party's secretary general at the time, said that in 2021 there was a clear determination to avoid a repeat of what happened in 2016 when a president could not be elected by either the Riigikogu or the Electoral College and the Riigikogu ultimately agreed to elect Kersti Kaljulaid.
"There was a clear desire to try to find a candidate right away in the Riigikogu who would not be seen as the candidate of any particular party," Keldo said.
Keldo said that because the Reform Party and Center Party were in government at the time, the search for a presidential candidate was led primarily by the parties' then-leaders, Kaja Kallas and Jüri Ratas, as well as the chairs of their parliamentary groups.
Ratas: Cooperation with Kallas was smooth
Jüri Ratas recalled that his cooperation with Kaja Kallas went very smoothly. "I rate it very highly. The cooperation with Kaja Kallas was very good and based on trust, both in finding a presidential candidate and in negotiations with the Riigikogu parliamentary groups, so that was important," Ratas said.
According to Keldo, it was difficult to secure opposition support for many of the candidates. For example, it became clear that it would not be possible to muster the 68 votes needed for Tarmo Soomere.
Ratas, who was also president of the Riigikogu at the time, said that when he proposed Karis as a possible candidate to the party leaders, he encountered no opposition to Karis.
Lauri Läänemets, the current leader of the Social Democratic Party who was a member of the party's parliamentary group at the time, also said the Social Democrats had no reason to oppose Karis because they had no prospect of putting forward a candidate who could attract broad support. "Besides, Karis was a pretty good candidate and there was no point in playing any games," Läänemets said.
Keldo said it was also important that Karis was not associated with any political party. "Alar Karis' name had come up before as well. We also had people who had worked with Alar many times before in various positions. Alar's strength was that he had served multiple terms as a university rector, had been auditor general and at the time he was head of the Estonian National Museum. He had held a great many positions in public life. It was important that he was clearly impartial and not associated with anyone," Keldo said.
Helir-Valdor Seeder, who was Isamaa's leader and parliamentary group chair at the time, said that because the president had to unite people and provide balance, they naturally sought someone who was not affiliated with any political force.
But what might explain why Alar Karis failed to secure the required 68 votes in the first round? "Because the vote is secret, politicians, particularly those in opposition, often like to play around a little and see whether the coalition's votes will actually hold. Once they saw that enough votes had been cast and that the coalition's votes were holding, the opposition and others also came on board in the second round and duly voted him in," Keldo said.
Ratas said that by the second round, members of the Riigikogu had recognized their responsibility to elect the president in parliament. "I suppose that in the first round, some members of the Riigikogu still wanted to test things out, play around a little and make things more interesting, but I think a sense of responsibility brought enough votes behind Karis," Ratas added.
Ratas said that because they were confident Karis had sufficient support in the Riigikogu, they did not undertake more extensive efforts to secure the support of Electoral College members.
--
