Andrey Gyurov launches presidential bid with Georgi Kandev
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:28:17 UTC
17:28:17 KST

Tuesday 1 September 2026 11:11
Tuesday, 1 September 2026, 11:11
Andrey Gyurov, left, and Georgi Kandev announced their candidacies for president and vice-president.
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Former caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev, who served as Interior Ministry Chief Secretary during his government, have formally entered Bulgaria’s presidential race. They announced their candidacies for president and vice-president outside the History Museum in their home town of Gotse Delchev.
“You all want to hear whether I will enter the race to become Bulgaria’s head of state, and the answer is yes, I will – and Georgi Kandev and I will do it together,” Gyurov said.
He went on to pose a series of questions: “Do we have a state that explains its decisions and knows how much those decisions cost? Do we have a state that does not make its citizens pay for poor planning, incompetence and dependence? Do we have a state that relies on those who are capable, rather than those who are loyal to those in power?”
Gyurov said the initiative committee nominating the pair was made up of citizens rather than representatives of a political party.
“No one sent us here and we owe nothing to anyone. We are working Bulgarian citizens and we have proved ourselves in the highest positions,” he said.
According to Gyurov, the two know Bulgaria from different perspectives: his own experience is in finance, the economy and academia, while Kandev’s is in law, security and the practical implementation of government decisions.
Kandev said he had chosen to stand alongside Gyurov because, from working with him, he knew him to be a man of integrity who loved Bulgaria.
“I know, and I can tell you, when a policy is actually being implemented. I have no hidden agenda. I was brought up to respect and uphold the law,” Kandev said.
The pair have set out four main priorities for their campaign: Bulgaria’s European path, economic competence, independence, and security and public order.
Among the first to address the event was internationally renowned scientist and philanthropist Prof. Minko Balkanski, who voiced his support for Gyurov and Kandev in a video message.
The presidential elections in Bulgaria will be held on October 25.

Lyulin Mountain – a step away from Sofia and now just a click away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:28:07 UTC
17:28:07 KST

Author
Yoan Kolev
News
Lyulin Mountain – a step away from Sofia and now just a click away
Tuesday 1 September 2026 09:53
Tuesday, 1 September 2026, 09:53
PHOTO Manastirska Koria Tourist Association
Font size
Ask someone to name the mountains around Sofia and chances are they will start – and perhaps finish – with Vitosha. Yet the Bulgarian capital, lying in the Sofia Valley, is surrounded by five: Vitosha, Plana, Sofia Mountain, Lyulin and Lozen Mountain.
For a big city, that is quite a privilege – five mountains within easy reach, offering fresh air, walking and hiking, or simply a chance to get away from the bustle of the capital.
The smaller mountains, however, have yet to become as accessible as Vitosha. Marked routes are few, convenient transport and parking are limited and, above all, there is not enough information about what they have to offer visitors.
PHOTO Facebook / Manastirska Koria Tourist Association
This is where the new initiative Lyulin Mountain – Preserving the Past to Build the Future comes in. Launched by the Manastirska Koria Tourist Association, it is putting Lyulin’s trails and lesser-known places on the map – and online – while a series of themed hikes will give people a chance to discover them for themselves.
And Lyulin has one obvious advantage: it is remarkably close. Stretching west of Sofia, the mountain is within easy reach of several neighbourhoods, with gentle trails suitable for families and people taking their first steps into hiking. There are approaches from Gorna Banya, Bankya, Malo Buchino, Golyamo Buchino, Marchaevo and Vladaya.
You do not necessarily need a car, either. Bus 103 at weekends and 803 on weekdays take visitors to the Vishna Zona Lyulin stop, virtually at the entrance to the mountain.
PHOTO Manastirska Koria Tourist Association
“Lyulin Mountain has a very rich history. There are monasteries here that form part of the historic ring of monasteries known as Sofia’s Holy Mountain,” Ivan Popov, chairman of the tourist association, told Radio Bulgaria.
“But the idea is also to take some of the pressure off Vitosha. We all know that when the weather is good, or when there is snow and children can ski and sledge, everyone heads there. Lyulin, too, has fresh air and pleasant places for walking, and we think more people should know about it.”
Supported by Sofia Municipality’s Europe Programme, the project is already taking shape on the ground. Its first step is a circular hiking route of about three hours, with QR codes along the way providing visitors with additional information.
PHOTO Manastirska Koria Tourist Association
The route begins at the Gorna Banya Monastery of Sts Cyril and Methodius, founded in the late 13th century and repeatedly destroyed during the period of Ottoman rule. From there, it leads almost entirely through woodland, past several chapels and, on the way back, through a rather different chapter of Lyulin’s history – a former anti-aircraft military base, now a ghost settlement, where more than 1,000 servicemen and their families once lived.
The abandoned base is also the starting point for a mountain-bike route aimed at intermediate riders. It finishes at Bonsovi Polyani, just five minutes from a car park and bus stop.
PHOTO Manastirska Koria Tourist Association
Finding your way around Lyulin is not always so straightforward, however. Poor trail marking remains one of the mountain’s main problems – one reason the first circular route was chosen in an area where the paths are already clearly marked.
And the project is not intended to exist only on maps and screens. Four organised hikes are planned for consecutive Sundays in late September and October, with the exact dates still to be announced.
PHOTO Manastirska Koria Tourist Association
“One will focus more on history and spirituality, while another will be about the former anti-aircraft base, with its history and photographs,” Popov says. “Our third walk will be an ‘eco patrol’. We’ll all have gloves and rubbish bags in our backpacks so we can collect what careless visitors have left behind. We want to set an example and say: ‘People, think when you’re out in the mountains and take your rubbish with you!’”
The fourth event will add a little competition to the programme – a speed ascent of Dupeevitsa Peak, with small prizes for the fastest participants. Each of the four hikes will be limited to around 35 people.
Lyulin lends itself well to this kind of exploration. It is a relatively low, sprawling mountain, with numerous peaks and viewpoints, while its generally mild weather makes sudden changes in conditions less common.
But the organisers are particularly keen to tempt younger people into discovering it. A dedicated app provides information about the mountain while turning exploration into something of a game: users can collect digital badges and points and exchange them at the mountain hut for a free drink or a slice of cake.
PHOTO Facebook / Manastirska Koria Tourist Association
The idea is simple – to get young people outdoors, even if the phone stays in their hand, and show them how much there is to discover in a mountain that lies practically on Sofia’s doorstep.
Editor: D. Semkovska
This publication was created by: Elizabeth Radkova

Russian drone struck a Ukrainian fire truck on its way to a house fire—four rescuers injured
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:28:00 UTC
17:28:00 KST

A Russian drone hit a fire truck driving to a call in the village of Kushuhum outside Zaporizhzhia on 1 September, injuring four rescuers, the head of Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ivan Fedorov, reported. The crew was on its way to a house fire that Russian shelling had started. The strike came hours after a countrywide Russian air assault overnight.
A drone hit the crew before they reached the fire
Fedorov said a Russian drone struck the State Emergency Service vehicle in Kushuhum as it drove to put out a fire. The truck took damage, and the crew was hurt. He said the men were under the supervision of medics.
The Main Directorate of the State Emergency Service in Zaporizhzhia Oblast confirmed the attack, and added that all four injured firefighters had been taken to hospital with injuries of differing severity. The directorate specified what the crew had been sent to: a fire in a detached house in the suburb, started by Russian shelling.
Over the past 24 hours, Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia city and district killed two people and injured eight, Fedorov said. Russian forces carried out strikes on 57 settlements across the region.
The night before: a countrywide strike
Overnight into 1 September, Russia attacked with ballistic and cruise missiles, anti-radar missiles, Banderol munitions, and 218 Shahed-type strike drones, about a third of them jet-powered, Ukraine's Air Force reported. By preliminary data, air defenses downed or suppressed 199 targets. Odesa and Kyiv oblasts were the main directions of the strike.
Russia killed 12 people across Ukraine, among them a citizen of India, and injured dozens, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Russia killed four people and injured 13 and damaged a five-story residential building, and 50 people were evacuated. Nearly 350 rescuers worked in Kyiv and the surrounding oblast alone.
Russia’s 6-day attack on Kyiv that started two days after CIA head’s visit to Moscow, culminates with massive ballistic missile strike on eve of school year
In Kyiv, a ballistic strike on Ukrzaliznytsia railway facilities killed seven people, six of them railway workers, and one more employee remains hospitalized. The capital's overall toll for the night stood at eight killed.
In Odesa Oblast, Russian drones, guided bombs, and missiles injured seven civilian men, four of whom went to hospital, and struck the Orlivka ferry crossing on the border with Romania again, the regional prosecutor's office found.
Ukraine has documented Russia striking the people who respond
As of May, Ukraine has documented 11,000 Russian first-person-view drone attacks on civilians, among them repeat strikes on the same spot once medics and firefighters arrive. Ukraine's UN envoy has built part of the case for expelling Russia from the Security Council on that practice.
Rescue workers in Zaporizhzhia have been caught that way before. After a strike on a Poltava Oblast gas site, Russia hit the crews who came to the fire. Firefighters in Chernihiv Oblast went to hospital mid-rescue. In Kryvyi Rih in August, a second Russian attack reached rescue workers thirty minutes after a drone strike on a shopping center, and a repeat strike killed a 20-year-old volunteer paramedic in Kyiv the same month.

Russia Wanted Its Own Starlink. Now Its Satellites Are Falling Before the Network Even Takes Off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:27:45 UTC
17:27:45 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Wanted Its Own Starlink. Now Its Satellites Are Falling Before the Network Even Takes Off
Russia’s planned alternative to Starlink is encountering severe operational setbacks, with satellites deployed in orbit losing altitude while newly launched units fail to reach their designated positions, French technology portal Numerama reported.
Moscow allocated 102.8 billion rubles ($1.3 billion) from its state budget for the "Rassvet " program. Commercial operations were set to launch in 2027, with plans to expand the constellation from 250 to 900 satellites in orbit by 2035.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Deploying the intended satellite group requires at least 18 Soyuz-2.1b rocket launches. However, Russia conducts only six to eight such launches per year.
On the night of August 15, the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck the Progress Space Center in Samara—the sole facility manufacturing the Soyuz-2.1b rockets used to place the Rassvet satellites into orbit.
Following claims that several hundred satellites would be in orbit by next year, the first spacecraft are already beginning to lose altitude earlier than anticipated. According to orbital tracking data, at least two satellites are losing altitude, while several others are unable to enter their assigned orbits.
As noted by the specialized website Russian Space Web, while the initial 16 launched satellites performed somewhat better—though one fell back in June—a July launch delivering another 16 spacecraft proved unsuccessful.
The goal was to place the satellites at an altitude of 800 kilometers, but several ended up below 500 kilometers, with some dropping below 400 kilometers.
Nine satellites began maneuvering to rise a few additional kilometers, while others appear to have stopped ascending and started falling. Currently, not a single satellite has managed to rise above 360 kilometers, while two have dropped below 300 kilometers on trajectories resembling a descent.
Even the spacecraft that continue to ascend remain significantly below the altitudes reached by the first group of satellites at the same phase of deployment.
Remaining at lower altitudes carries direct physical consequences. The lower a satellite travels, the higher the atmospheric drag it encounters, requiring it to burn more fuel to avoid falling and thereby shortening its operational lifespan. Consequently, even the spacecraft that stabilize at around 500 kilometers risk degrading much faster than originally anticipated.
With only 32 satellites in orbit and a portion of them barely reaching the required altitude, Rassvet remains far from becoming a fully functional network.
At present, Russia lacks the capacity to expand the satellite constellation to the 250 units planned for 2027, the report noted.
In early February, Starlink CEO Elon Musk deactivated devices not included on Ukrainian “whitelists,” following a request from Ukraine’s Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, which significantly weakened Russian command-and-control capabilities in several parts of the front.
Previously, reports emerged that Russian low-Earth-orbit satellites developed under the Rassvet program may already provide intermittent battlefield connectivity over Ukraine, creating an early-stage alternative to Starlink for Russian forces.

The Federal Protective Service has meanwhile expanded its priority-protection roster to include at least 10 senior military figures.
The mood among the Russian elite is even more pessimistic. Helmet required on scooters that can do more than 20km/h
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:23:59 UTC
17:23:59 KST

From 1 September, helmets are compulsory for riders of electric scooters capable of travelling at speeds exceeding 20 kilometres per hour. The regulation has been introduced by the Federal Mobility Ministry.
The helmet requirement does not depend on the speed at which a rider is travelling, but on the maximum speed the scooter is capable of reaching according to the manufacturer. The Royal Decree that enters force today states that the requirement applies to riders of “a motorised personal mobility device whose maximum speed, as determined by its design, exceeds 20 kilometres per hour”.
The rider may choose either a moped helmet or a cycling helmet that also protects the temples and the back of the head.
According to the Mobility Ministry, the measure is intended to improve road safety. “International studies and medical and accident statistics all point in the same direction: in serious and fatal accidents involving motorised vehicles, and in particular electric scooters, head and brain injuries are particularly common,” it states. Furthermore, the risk of serious injury increases as speed rises.
In Belgium, only electric scooters capable of travelling at a maximum speed of 25 kilometres per hour are permitted. The new compulsory helmet rule therefore applies to scooters with a design speed of between 20 and 25 kilometres per hour.
According to the government, one of the reasons why the requirement does not apply to all e-scooters is the desire not to discourage people from swapping their car for a (share) scooter for short journeys.
For share e-scooters, a helmet is not compulsory if the operator has limited the maximum speed to 20 kilometres per hour. According to the Mobility Ministry, this is often already the case in practice, and this speed limit is usually included in the operating licence.

Russia faces space setback in rapid deployment of Starlink analogue – ISW
Ukrinform reports, citing the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), that none of the 16 Rassvet satellites from the second batch launched on July 19 had reached the expected altitude of 550 kilometers above Earth as of August 31, according to satellite tracking data from N2YO.
Many of these satellites were at altitudes of between 300 and 400 kilometers, and at least two satellites were heading toward Earth’s atmosphere.
These altitudes are significantly below the planned operational altitude of 870 kilometers for the Rassvet satellites.

Overall, only 12 of the 16 Rassvet satellites launched on March 24 had reached the expected altitude of 550 kilometers as of July 31. They remained at that altitude as of August 31.
These 12 satellites provided Russian forces with two daily communication windows with ground terminals over Ukraine, each lasting up to 1.5 hours.

11 EU countries demand end to 'obstructive' vetoes on foreign policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:21:17 UTC
17:21:17 KST

Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Romania, Spain and Sweden are pushing to explore the idea of moving from unanimity to qualified majority in foreign policy.
A group of 11 European Union countries has joined forces to demand an end to the "obstructive" vetoes that have paralysed the bloc's external action in recent years, arguing that the principle of sincere cooperation must take precedence.
"The Union's culture of consensus is an important source of its legitimacy. Therefore, we continue to strive for consensus wherever possible," the countries say in a letter addressed to High Representative Kaja Kallas and seen by Euronews.
"But we must also ensure that this culture of consensus fosters common action rather than preventing it – otherwise we will have legitimacy but no strength."
Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Romania, Spain and Sweden signed the letter. Germany, the largest member state, has been leading callsto reform the bloc's foreign policy.
"The Union's external action faces a fundamentally changed landscape, shaped by strategic competition, growing instability and attempts to undermine the rules-based international order," they write in the document, also sent to those member states who did not sign.
"In this environment, the Union's ability to defend its values and interests hinges on whether it can mobilise its collective political, economic and diplomatic weight quickly and effectively."
Under EU rules, foreign policy is strictly governed by unanimity, which means one single country can, at any time, tie the hands of the other 26 member states.
This pattern played out repeatedly during the 16-year tenure of Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. Before losing power in April, Orbán regularly outraged his peers by using his veto power to extract concessions and advance his interests.
Earlier this year, he triggered an unprecedented crisis when he suddenly blocked a €90 billion loan for Ukraine, personally agreed by EU leaders, over an unrelated dispute with Kyiv involving the Druzhba oil pipeline.
Making the switch
Based on the lessons learned from the Orbán years, the signatories lay out five principles that, in their view, should guide and improve the bloc's common foreign policy:
- Uphold the principles of sincere cooperation and mutual solidarity
- Increase the use of constructive abstentions to replace vetoes
- Refrain from linking foreign policy decisions to "substantially unrelated" matters
- Explore options within the EU treaties to move from unanimity to qualified majority
- Provide "substantiated vital reasons" to block such a move
"The legal framework for all five principles is already in place. It is solely up to us to put them into action and thus advance our foreign policy," the letter says.
The idea of activating the so-called "passerelle clause" under Article 31 to switch from unanimity to qualified majority voting has been a long-running debate in Brussels that rose to prominence in the aftermath of Russia's war on Ukraine.
The switch could be done on a case-by-case basis, rather than all at once. (Germany, for example, resists using unanimity regarding trade with Israeli settlements.)
Proponents say it would speed up decision-making and avoid unnecessary vetoes, while opponents say it would undermine democratic legitimacy. Small member states consider the veto a useful last-resort tool to defend their views and interests against the heft of larger members. None of the Baltics signed up to the initiative.
The "passerelle clause" has been described as a Catch-22 because moving from unanimity to qualified majority would itself require unanimity, which means opponents would be certain to win the battle. The joint letter calls for "meaningful" consultations to address a potential dispute and reach a compromise.
The push to overhaul the EU's foreign policy has gained traction after Orbán's defeat, which many see as an invaluable window of opportunity that could be shut if Marine Le Pen, a staunch Eurosceptic, wins the French presidential election next year.
Germany and France have floated a plan that would strengthen the role of the High Representative, Kaja Kallas, but bring her under the direct supervision of the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.

Up to 70% of schools will provide in-person learning, shelters are available in 82%, and in kindergartens in 83% — how the academic year will begin
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
11:19:00 EEST
17:19:00 KST

Up to 70% of schools will provide in-person learning, shelters are available in 82%, and in kindergartens in 83% — how the academic year will begin
Kyiv • UNN
In Ukraine, more than 8,000 schools will operate in person, and more than 3.5 million students will begin their studies. The Ministry of Education and Science also announced changes to the New Ukrainian School reform and scholarships.
The Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine reported how the new school year is beginning in Ukraine, UNN writes.
How schools will operate
"More than 8,000 schools will operate in person, while another 2,211-plus will use a blended format. In 1,306 institutions, the educational process will be organized remotely," the Ministry of Education and Science reported.
The format, as indicated, is determined based on the security situation and the availability of shelters, so that children can remain in the Ukrainian education system regardless of their place of residence.
"More than 82% of schools operating in person have access to their own or another equipped shelter," the statement says.
Kindergartens
As of September 1, 11,622 preschool education institutions will operate in Ukraine: 9,301 in person, 1,111 in a blended format, and 1,210 remotely. This year, 712,987 children are beginning their studies in preschool education institutions
"All kindergartens operating in person or in a blended format have access to a shelter. (...) Currently, 83% have a shelter directly on the premises or within 100 meters," the Ministry of Education and Science reported.
It was noted that the first underground kindergarten built with state funds and co-financing from the local budget has already begun operating in the Kharkiv region.
Under the law, from September 1, 2026, the study of English in senior groups (for children aged 5–6) will become a mandatory component of the educational process in all preschool education institutions.
General secondary education
This year, more than 3.5 million students are beginning the school year at 11,940 schools. Among them are 243,398 first-graders
Of these, according to the Ministry of Social Policy, 148,065 are receiving a schoolchild's package.
The educational process is provided by more than 366,000 teachers.
The implementation of the New Ukrainian School reform continues. The assessment system has been simplified for students in grades 5–9. A teacher may record ongoing grades without being required to indicate result-group indices, and may assign one grade in a subject or integrated course for the semester. This reduces the workload on teachers while preserving the competency-based approach and teachers' academic freedom. In grades 7–9, the number of hours devoted to history and civic education is increasing, while approaches to organizing education are becoming more inclusive and barrier-free. At the same time, students who began upper secondary school under the program in effect before the NUS was introduced will be able to complete their studies under that same program.
Studying abroad
Ukrainian children living abroad also maintain ties with the national education system. There are 120 verified educational centers operating for them in different countries. In total, about 315,000 Ukrainian children study outside Ukraine. The updated state standards establish a Ukrainian studies component for them—the study of the Ukrainian language, literature, history, and other subjects that help maintain ties with their homeland and the Ukrainian education system.
Children from the temporarily occupied territories
Recognition of learning outcomes has been simplified for children and young people from the temporarily occupied territories. An application in any form can be submitted to a Ukrainian school in person or remotely. Results in most subjects will be credited automatically on the basis of an educational declaration, without additional assessment. Knowledge will need to be confirmed only in subjects belonging to the Ukrainian studies component, including the Ukrainian language and literature, the history of Ukraine, geography, law, and civic education.
Specialized upper secondary education
The transition to the third and most important stage of the NUS—the specialized upper secondary school—is beginning. From September 1, more than 10,500 tenth-grade students are beginning their studies at 150 pilot academic lyceums as part of the pilot program for the specialized upper secondary school.
From now on, upper secondary students will have more influence over their own education. They will be able to choose a track, subjects, and courses in line with their interests, abilities, and plans for the future, and study their chosen areas in greater depth. The specialized school will help teenagers explore different fields, better understand their own interests and abilities, and consciously plan their next educational step.
Career education advisers will work in pilot lyceums. They will help teenagers identify their strengths, better navigate educational opportunities, and plan an individual learning trajectory.
Before the pilot launch, the State Standard for Specialized Secondary Education and the standard educational program for grades 10–12 were approved. A total of 150 lyceums were selected, training for teachers and management teams was launched with the support of the World Bank, and a practical guide on organizing the work of an academic lyceum was prepared.
Throughout the school year, the lyceums will pilot new programs, profiles, and elective courses, develop individual educational trajectories, and test the work of career advisers. Feedback from students, parents, teachers, and institution heads will help improve the model before its nationwide implementation in 2027.
For teachers, specialized schools provide more space for author-designed courses, new work formats, and in-depth teaching of subjects. As stated, communities must form a capable network of lyceums, organize student transportation, prepare educational spaces, and ensure that institutions have teachers.
Update to the Defense of Ukraine subject
There are already 1,027 Defense of Ukraine centers in operation, with training reaching approximately 80% of upper-secondary students. At the centers, students learn tactical medicine, drone piloting, firearms training, and tactics.
Under the updated Defense of Ukraine program, 2,322 male and female teachers have upgraded their qualifications, including 426 male and female veterans. This year, UAH 500 million has been allocated to establish and further equip the centers, and another UAH 28.8 million to train teachers.
"Mriia"
"Mriia" is already used by 670,000 students, parents, and teachers in 4,600 schools across Ukraine.
Before the start of the school year, "Mriia" received new tools. The updated builder helps the administration of an educational institution automatically create a timetable taking into account the availability of teachers, classes, and classrooms. Students will be able to submit homework directly in the app, while teachers will be able to check it and record grades. Parents will have access to electronic certificates confirming a child's absence and to the history of changes in the average grade.
This autumn, "Mriia" will also launch a pilot of Ukraine's first national education gamification system. In the app for students at pilot schools, the Mriiky in-app currency, daily Kmitlyvky quizzes, and the Kramnychka rewards shop from partners will appear. Mriiky can be earned by completing quizzes and homework, viewing educational content, and performing other useful activities, and then exchanged for cinema tickets, master classes, tutoring sessions, certificates, and other development and leisure opportunities from partners.
The "Mriia.Extracurricular" section already offers more than 8,000 clubs and sections in sports, art, science and technology, music, dance, programming, scouting, and other areas. More than 350 schools have created their own clubs and groups in the system, so families can find additional activities in one place.
A separate area is "Mriia.Preschool," which is being piloted in 40 preschool education institutions in six regions of Ukraine. The new area helps simplify daily processes in kindergartens, reduce paperwork, and improve communication with parents.
Extracurricular education
In the 2026–2027 academic year, the systematic reboot of extracurricular education continues: updating the content and network of institutions, digitalization, and creating new opportunities for developing children's competences. The main focus is on access to quality extracurricular education, practical learning, STEM, national and patriotic education, and the opportunity to participate regardless of place of residence.
In 1,134 extracurricular education institutions, 51,053 clubs, sections, and creative associations operate. They bring together 769,981 participants, students, and learners, while classes are conducted by 14,252 teaching staff members.
The game "Falcon" ("Dzhura") is being updated: modern methodological approaches, safety standards, training requirements, practical training formats, and a network of regional training programs are being introduced. For the "Defence of Ukraine" centers, the Ministry of Education and Science has also developed rules for an all-Ukrainian competition with unified approaches to participation, assessment, and awarding.
In "Mriia. Extracurricular Activities," families can find more than 8,000 clubs and sections — sports, art and music, programming, science, technology, and scouting. More than 350 schools have already created their own clubs and groups in the system.
The Science Museum and the "KUBOID" Mathematics Museum continue to give children the opportunity to explore mathematics and the natural sciences through practical activities, while the traveling format brings interactive exhibits directly to communities. Children in Ukraine and abroad can independently join the Olympiad movement, open stages, Minor Academy of Sciences competitions, the GENIUS Olympiad, and other research and creative competitions.
Free meals
Approximately 3 million students in grades 1–11 at municipal schools who study in person or in a blended format will receive free hot meals. To this end, 2,023 school food-service facilities have already been modernized, while work is ongoing at another 272.
Professional and professional pre-higher education
Approximately 1,200 institutions of professional and professional pre-higher education help young people acquire the practical skills and professions needed by communities and the country's recovery. As part of the "100 Workshops" project, 200 workshops are already being renovated, and another 100 workshops, laboratories, and classrooms in colleges are planned for renovation.
Higher education
About one million higher-education students are beginning the new academic year, studying at different levels and in different formats.
This year, applicants submitted 1.2 million applications for first-year bachelor's and medical master's programs — the highest figure since the beginning of the full-scale war.
A total of 294,831 people were admitted to bachelor's and master's programs (preliminary data; the admissions campaign is ongoing). Of these, 98,564 were admitted on state-funded places. At the same time, 49,475 admissions were to specialties receiving special support — 50.2% of all state-funded admissions. Under Quota 2, 6,132 applicants from among internally displaced persons, residents of temporarily occupied territories, and residents of territories where active hostilities are taking place have already been admitted.
From September 1, financial support for student youth is being increased. From now on, academic scholarships for students at higher and professional pre-higher education institutions will double. Certain scholarships for winners of intellectual competitions and talented young artists are also being increased.
The academic grants program is continuing. For the first time, applicants to master's programs will receive state support of UAH 27,000 or UAH 40,000 per academic year. The grants will help fully or partially cover the cost of contract-based tuition for those who achieved the best results in the entrance examinations.
Universities determine their study schedules and formats independently, taking into account the security situation, the condition of the energy system, the specifics of their educational programs, and their own infrastructure.

Denmark reopens Syria embassy after 14-year closure: state media

SANA said that Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen, accompanied by Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani, reopened the outpost "after a 14-year-long break".

In July of 2025, Britain re-established full diplomatic relations with Syria more than a decade after cutting ties.
And in March that year, Germany officially reopened its embassy in Damascus during a visit by its foreign minister, two months after Spain raised its flag at its embassy, also in the presence of its visiting top diplomat.
Turkey and Qatar, key allies of Syria's new authorities, were the first to reopen their missions in Damascus after Assad's toppling.

Could 4+4 make 1 in Libya? UN-backed agreement looks to unite rival camps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:16:10 UTC
17:16:10 KST

Could 4+4 make 1 in Libya? UN-backed agreement looks to unite rival camps
After 15 years of civil war, a new UN-backed 4+4 agreement looks to unite Libya’s rival factions and pave the way for national elections within two years.
Representatives of Libya’s rival political camps recently signed a landmark agreement in Tripoli, drafting a roadmap that could see presidential and legislative elections within 24 months.
Mediated by the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL), the “4+4 committee” agreement attempts to resolve recurring legal and institutional disputes that have crippled the nation since 2011.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4What’s behind the US deal to seize control of Venezuelan oil reserves?
- list 2 of 4Rival Libya factions sign deal to hold national elections within two years
- list 3 of 4‘Opening a new chapter’: Syria reopens embassy in Libya after talks
- list 4 of 4Pan Am 103: What to know as alleged Lockerbie bombmaker faces US trial
However, in a country plagued by deep mistrust, shifting alliances, and entrenched armed factions, the path from a signed document to a unified government remains fraught with challenges.
Decades of division
Libya has been in a near-perpetual state of instability since a 2011 uprising toppled and killed longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi.
Initially, the country showed political promise, but divisions slowly arose in the rebel camp, chiefly between factions controlling the east and west.
In August 2012, the National Transitional Council officially handed over power to the newly elected General National Congress in what remains the country’s first and only peaceful transfer of power following national elections.
That fragile democratic momentum, however, quickly disintegrated into armed conflict. In May 2014, renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar took control of Benghazi and still controls the east of Libya.
A divisive election later that year prompted some newly announced MPs to form the House of Representatives and relocate to the eastern city of Tobruk under Haftar’s military protection.
The political divide turned into open warfare in April 2019 when Haftar launched an unsuccessful 14-month offensive to capture the capital Tripoli, where the United Nations-recognised Government of National Accord (GNA) was based.
By June 2020, the front lines stabilised near the strategic central city of Sirte, leading to a formal ceasefire agreement later that year that froze military hostilities but left the underlying political fracture intact.
Rivals and rulers
This left Libya with two distinct authorities operating across its territory.
Tripoli is home to the internationally recognised GNA, headed by interim Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah. This western-based authority includes the High Council of State – an advisory legislative body currently led by Mohammed Takala – and the Presidential Council, chaired by Mohammad al-Manfi.
In Tobruk and Benghazi, political power centres on the House of Representatives, led by Speaker Aguila Saleh, which supports a parallel eastern administration. But primary control across eastern and southern Libya is exercised by the self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), commanded by Khalifa Haftar.
In recent years, Haftar’s son and LNA deputy commander, Saddam Haftar, has assumed a critical role within the eastern establishment, emerging as the heir apparent, a key military commander, and a central political negotiator.
Profiting from chaos
Despite the 2020 ceasefire, political reunification has remained elusive due to failed international initiatives and systemic economic competition. The 2015 UN-brokered Skhirat Agreement created the GNA.
But it also preserved rival legislative bodies, meaning institutional duplication and the country remaining divided between two powers.
A subsequent UN political track appointed Dbeibah to lead an interim executive in 2021, contingent on conducting national elections at the end of the year.
As part of this deal, Dbeibah agreed not to run, but the 2021 election collapsed just two days before the scheduled vote when he reneged on his pledge.
Global diplomatic push
Another key factor in this new agreement is the involvement of major powers. Under United States President Donald Trump, Washington has intensified efforts to broker a unification deal, led by White House adviser Massad Boulos and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Boulos has put forward an initiative offering US energy investments in Libya’s oil fields in exchange for a unified executive. Washington even proposed a power-sharing arrangement that could see Dbeibah remain as prime minister while Saddam Haftar served as president.
This diplomatic push coincides with an extensive international tour by Saddam Haftar, who has held high-level meetings across regional and Western capitals.
Haftar has held talks with French President Emmanuel Macron and engaged in direct diplomacy with key Arab leaders. Haftar also met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington to discuss institution unification.
Meanwhile, Qatar’s Minister of State Mohammed bin Abdulaziz al-Khulaifi met with Khalifa Haftar last Thursday during a visit to Benghazi.
Furthermore, regional dynamics have shifted as Turkiye has expanded military and technical cooperation with Saddam Haftar and eastern authorities.
Joint military drills between eastern and western forces in Sirte under US supervision further illustrate this evolving landscape.
A historic breakthrough?
The newly signed 4+4 agreement ultimately represents a deliberate attempt to balance power between east and west, analysts say.
The makeup of the committee in its eight members reflects this: Two are from the House of Representatives, two from the High Council of State, and two each from Dbeibah’s government and Haftar’s eastern command.
The agreement mandates presidential and parliamentary elections within 24 months under a single executive authority.
It also seems aimed at resolving the primary legal disputes that destroyed the 2021 vote by allowing dual citizens to contest the presidency – so long as the winner relinquishes foreign nationality before taking the oath of office.
Further, it permits military officers to run as candidates upon stepping down from official posts. Both of these legal changes would appear designed to pave the way for either Saddam or Khalifa Haftar, who are believed to have US nationalities and are commanders in the self-styled LNA, to have official government posts.
The deal also restructures the High National Elections Commission under new leadership and establishes rotating official sessions in Tripoli in the west, Benghazi in the east, and Sabha in the south.
Analyst Wissam Abdul Kabir argued that the direct involvement of armed factions distinguishes this pact from previous ones.
“I believe what makes it different is that for the first time, the agreement is signed between the active parties,” Abdul Kabir told Al Jazeera.
“In previous agreements, whether in Geneva in 2021 or the Skhirat agreement in 2015, the agreement was made between the two councils or between the legitimate or elected bodies whose ballot-box legitimacy has eroded over time.
“Therefore, the difference is that the agreement is approved, adopted, and signed by the active parties on the ground, and this is a fundamental point.”
Still, many in Libya view 4+4 as the latest in a series of failed peace initiatives.
High Council of State leader Mohammed Takala boycotted the ceremony, while Presidential Council head Mohammad al-Manfi openly criticised the procedural transparency and foreign involvement in the arrangement.
Mohammed Mahfouz, a political analyst, said the arrangement appears to be nothing more than an attempt by outside powers to cement the powers of Saddam Haftar and Dbeibah.
“The matter goes beyond being confined to the issue of candidacy conditions only. The most important framework is that we are facing a repeated scenario tried in 2015 in the Skhirat Agreement in Morocco, and after that in Tunis and Geneva in 2021,” Mahfouz told Al Jazeera.
“Back then, it was always said that these political agreements take place between active parties … but Libyans did not go to elections.”
Despite the promise of new elections, there is little hope that Libya’s current leaders will relinquish their power if they lose at the ballot box.
“Is it possible to believe the hypothesis that parties possessing power and money, and possessing today new legitimacy according to this agreement and greater authority, will simply accept to be removed from power after two years and lead us towards elections?” said Mahfouz.
“There is a firm conviction among everyone that whoever reaches power in Libya cannot budge an inch from it except by the rifle, unfortunately.”

Türkiye joins Artemis Accords, plans Moon mission for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:15:51 UTC
17:15:51 KST

Türkiye has become the 71st country to sign the Artemis Accords, joining the United States-led framework for peaceful and responsible space exploration as Ankara prepares to send a hybrid-propelled spacecraft to the Moon in early 2027.
Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacır announced the mission after a signing ceremony at NASA headquarters in Washington, D.C., describing the agreement as a new phase in Türkiye’s expanding space program. “We aim to establish a sustainable presence in space and take steps toward the peaceful use of space for the benefit of all humanity,” Kacır said, pointing to growing cooperation with the United States in satellite technologies and human spaceflight.
Launched by the U.S. in 2020, the Artemis Accords are based on the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. They set out non-binding principles for safe, transparent and sustainable space exploration. The framework covers transparency, the registration of space objects, scientific data sharing, preventing harmful interference between missions and assisting astronauts in emergencies. Although initially focused on the Moon, it is also intended to support future missions to Mars and other deep space destinations.
The ceremony was attended by Kacır, Türkiye Space Agency President Yusuf Kıraç, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Space and Environment Connor Tomlinson. Türkiye’s Ambassador to Washington Sedat Önal and the country’s first astronaut, Alper Gezeravcı, also attended.
Kacır said Türkiye’s lunar mission would take place in the first months of 2027. The spacecraft is expected to travel to lunar orbit, collect data and demonstrate Türkiye’s ability to reach the Moon.
The mission is part of Türkiye’s National Space Program, which identifies lunar exploration as a central objective. In 2024, Türkiye’s first astronaut, Alper Gezeravcı, made the journey to at the International Space Station aboard a SpaceX rocket, marking a milestone in the country’s relatively young but ambitious space program. Gezeravcı spent 18 days on the orbiting laboratory before returning to Earth.
Kacır also said construction had begun on a planned spaceport in Somalia. The facility is expected to strengthen Türkiye’s position in the global space economy and provide greater independence in launching missions.
Isaacman called Türkiye’s accession an “important milestone,” saying Ankara had presented a “bold vision” for its future in space. He said the United States and Türkiye shared a vision of returning astronauts to the lunar surface, referring to Artemis plans for a sustained human presence around the Moon and eventual missions to Mars.
NASA welcomed Türkiye’s accession in a social media post, saying: “Welcome to the Artemis Accords, Republic of Türkiye.”
The agreement places Türkiye within a growing coalition seeking common principles for the next era of lunar exploration as governments and space agencies prepare for more ambitious missions beyond Earth orbit.

Anger as BBC withdraws jobs promise for apprentices amid sweeping cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:14:30 UTC
17:14:30 KST

The BBC is facing internal anger after a group of apprentices were told they could no longer expect jobs they had been promised, as a result of the corporation’s sweeping cuts.
In a sign of the pressure the BBC is under to find savings, apprentices working with BBC News were told that “exceptional circumstances” meant the broadcaster could no longer stand by its pledge to find them permanent positions.
The Guardian understands that some had previously been repeatedly reassured that the job pledge would be honoured.
Insiders said it was a betrayal of the apprentices, who are often selected for coming from non-traditional backgrounds to increase the diversity of the BBC’s workforce. Many are from working-class backgrounds.
“They’ve all been told that their jobs have now been closed and there isn’t a permanent role at the end,” a source said. “For a place that prides itself on honesty and integrity, it feels pretty dishonest.”
Another said: “There are some fairly senior editors who are absolutely raging about what’s happening.”
The decision affects some of those currently finishing their apprenticeships, which cover graduates and school leavers. Some apprentices from previous years who were still waiting for a permanent post are also affected. About 20 apprentices appear to be affected overall.
The BBC is aiming to cut as many as 2,000 jobs as it seeks £500m in savings by 2028. Further details of those cuts are expected within weeks.
It is understood that during an emergency meeting at the end of August, the apprentices were told that the job cuts on the way meant it was unfair to guarantee them a job.
Their scheme has been extended until December to give them time to prepare, while apprentices from previous years still waiting for a job have also been given a grace period.
However, there has been an angry response from some inside the corporation who say a scheme that increases the BBC’s diversity and brings in younger voices should have been protected.
“How are we signalling there’s still a future of the BBC if we’re cutting all the people that we’ve promised jobs to,” said one. “For me, it says a lot about the people that have been protected. There’s just so much middle management.
“Morally, we should be investing in young people to come and work here. That just feels so obvious. How can we be chasing young audiences while cutting a young workforce?”
Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, said last week he had not fully understood the extent of the BBC’s financial woes when he took on the job earlier in the year.
The BBC is having to make the cuts as the value of the licence fee has fallen dramatically over the past decade as a result of price freezes. An increasing number of households are opting not to pay it.
The corporation has already announced 550 job cuts in news, nations and TV and radio content as part of the first stage in its savings plan. The BBC has about 21,500 full-time employees in total.
Brittin has said popular shows will have to be axed. The first major casualty was BBC Radio 4’s The World Tonight.
A BBC spokesperson said: “BBC News needs to make considerable savings, and we have previously announced roles will close across the division at all levels. As there are fewer positions, fewer apprentices have been able to secure permanent placements. We are exploring opportunities to retain individuals where possible.
“More broadly, we are committed to providing entry-level roles and training in the industry and will continue to run schemes that provide these opportunities at the start of people’s careers.”

Britons face ‘risk premium’ for energy as US-Israel war on Iran intensifies

Britons face ‘risk premium’ for energy as US-Israel war on Iran intensifies
A price cap increase is on the way, the latest blow to people already struggling with rising costs.
London, United Kingdom – Andrew, a 70-year-old retiree from the eastern English city of Norwich, had enrolled months ago in a fixed-rate energy plan for 18 months, learning from earlier price shocks caused by wars.
“I guess I saw this coming,” he told Al Jazeera.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4How has life changed for Iranians six months into the war?
- list 2 of 4Who are the economic winners and losers of the US-Israel war on Iran?
- list 3 of 4Petrol prices strain US households as oil giants Chevron, Exxon profits soar
- list 4 of 4Inside the UK’s ‘stressful’ cost of living crisis Burnham hopes to tackle
Days ago, Ofgem, the energy regulator for England, Scotland and Wales, announced a 4 percent increase of the energy price cap from October 1, 2026, a result of the sharp rise in wholesale gas prices due to the United States-Israel war on Iran.
“The situation doesn’t look any clearer … the fog of war is still there, and who knows when it will blow away,” said Andrew, who requested that his surname be withheld for privacy.
The end of his fixed-rate plan is not something he likes to think about.
“I don’t think there’s going to be clarity,” he said. “I can’t see that the current state of geopolitics will allow for any resolution. I’m starting to think, if it’s not one conflict zone, it will be another.”
According to Ofgem, 35 percent of households in England, Scotland and Wales are on similar, fixed-rate energy plans, and will not be immediately affected by the Ofgem price cap increase.
Most, however, will face higher bills in the winter, an added blow to a nation already struggling amid a continued cost-of-living crisis.
A household using a regular level of energy will pay about 60 pounds ($80) a year more.
The UK government, alongside the increase, announced a tax cut on monthly electricity bills as part of a wider effort to shield people from the increasingly stark economic impacts of the Iran war as winter approaches. The tax cut is noted to last until the end of the 2027 financial year, but both experts and everyday people are not so sure that costs will be under control by then.
While the move on tax gives people “room to breathe, it doesn’t fix the fundamentals”, Ahmed Tabaqchali, a non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told Al Jazeera.
“We are not going to see a return to normality as far as the Strait of Hormuz is concerned. One way or the other, whatever end-game with the US and Iran, there is now a change to the status quo,” said Tabaqchali, who has worked in capital markets for more than 25 years.
Volatility is not a temporary concern, he said.
“As long as the United Kingdom relies on energy imports, we are going to be impacted by geopolitics,” said Jack Burt, a PhD candidate at the University of Cambridge, researching novel forms of energy storage.
Before the Iran war, roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) passed through the Strait of Hormuz, the only route connecting the Gulf to the ocean. Iran shut the strategic waterway not long after the initial US-Israeli strikes on Tehran in late February, triggering a global energy crisis.
Shortly after those initial strikes, the UK House of Commons Library released a briefing noting that the Bank of England would likely scrap plans to lower interest rates, while predicting that household gas bills would increase.
“Higher energy costs are likely to result in the UK economic activity weakening,” the report said.
Ofgem’s move is the latest development in the ongoing energy crisis stemming from the war.
Wholesale prices have risen by 11 percent over the past three months, noted Ofgem, with Neil Kenward, the body’s director general for markets, underlining that “high international gas prices are continuing to drive energy costs in the UK”.
The price cap applies to gas and electricity, while the tax cut applies to electricity bills, meaning households that do not use gas will fare better than those that do.
A ‘risk premium’ for energy supply
While diplomatic efforts in the Gulf region have focused on keeping the Strait of Hormuz open, US attacks on Iran over the weekend – the first in a month – threaten continued destabilisation.
“The consumer is going to be paying a ‘risk premium’ for energy supply,” noted Burt.
Following the 2022 full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, when monthly energy bills hit all-time highs, the UK moved away from gas coming through Russian pipelines “and became much more reliant on other suppliers of liquid natural gas, mostly coming from the Middle East”, he said.
Ozan, 20, a business owner in northeast London, said that “it’s getting more and more difficult to absorb the rises” for small business owners.
“Ultimately, the customer is also suffering, leading to less disposable income, meaning less spending.”
Last week, the Centre for Economics and Business Research forecast that by the end of 2027, the average UK household’s real spending power will be reduced by 2,400 pounds ($3,200), as the prices of everyday goods continue to increase.
Ofgem’s price cap will be reviewed again in January, following a quarterly schedule. But experts are predicting a continued rise in prices, painting a bleak picture for the UK’s energy sector.

Indian consulate in UAE issues warning over biometric fraud targeting nationals
Unknown

2026-09-01

The advisory urged nationals not to share their passports, Emirates IDs, biometric data, including eye, face or fingerprint scans, or personal and financial credentials with unauthorised individuals or agencies under any circumstances.
NEW DELHI: The consulate general of India in Dubai has warned Indian nationals in the UAE, particularly blue-collar workers, against handing over biometric data. The warning advised the workers against unauthorised agents claiming to help with visa regularisation, Emergency Certificates, Exit Permits, Emirates IDs or employment, after reports of fraud involving the misuse of fingerprints and facial scans.In an advisory issued on Monday, the consulate said it had received information about individuals and agents allegedly exploiting Indians seeking assistance with immigration and documentation procedures. The fraudsters reportedly ask victims to provide fingerprints or face scans, which can then be used without their knowledge to conduct financial transactions, open bank accounts or obtain loans and credit cards in their names.The consulate cautioned that such misuse could leave victims liable for financial obligations or transactions they did not authorise. In some cases, those affected could also face multiple fines, travel bans and even imprisonment.The advisory urged nationals not to share their passports, Emirates IDs, biometric data, including eye, face or fingerprint scans, or personal and financial credentials with unauthorised individuals or agencies under any circumstances.
It also clarified that biometric information required for procedures such as exit permits, Emirates IDs or visa regularisation must be provided only at official UAE Government facilities or counters. People were specifically warned against submitting such information through private individuals, agents or third-party service providers claiming to be authorised by UAE authorities.The consulate also sought to dispel a potential source of confusion by stating that biometric information is not required for certain consular services.The advisory said the Consulate General of India in Dubai and the Embassy of India in Abu Dhabi "DO NOT require any fingerprint scan or face/eye scan from applicants for the issuance of a passport or emergency certificate."It warned that any person or agent demanding such information while claiming to represent the Indian Embassy or consulate would be engaging in fraudulent activity and should not be entertained.
Indians approached by unauthorised individuals seeking biometric data or Emirates IDs have been advised to contact the Pravasi Bharatiya Sahayata Kendra through the toll-free number 80046342, WhatsApp or SMS at 00971543090571, or email pbsk.dubai@mea.gov.in to verify credentials or seek assistance.
The consulate urged Indian nationals living in or visiting the UAE to exercise caution, independently verify the credentials of anyone offering immigration or documentation-related services, and report suspicious activity to the Indian consulate and the relevant UAE authorities.

Japan, US agree on need for continued coordination to stabilize yen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:12:27 UTC
17:12:27 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
 Japan and the US agreed that continued coordination is essential to ensuring orderly movements in the yen and maintaining global financial stability, Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said Monday.
Katayama met US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on the sidelines of a two-day Group of 20 finance ministers and central bank governors meeting in Asheville, North Carolina.
“We confirmed that an orderly yen exchange rate is essential for the stability of global financial markets, including those of the United States, and that the continued coordinated efforts of Japan and the United States contribute to achieving this shared objective,” she told reporters after the meeting.
The two officials also reaffirmed the significance of their countries’ recent joint intervention in the foreign exchange market, Katayama said.
The meeting came about a month after Japan and the US conducted their first coordinated yen-buying intervention since the 1998 Asian financial crisis.
The intervention was launched on July 31 after the yen weakened to a 40-year low near 164 against the dollar.
Japan spent a record 15.4 trillion yen ($96 billion) between late July and August to support its currency, according to data released by the Finance Ministry last week.
The move initially strengthened the yen, but the currency subsequently erased those gains and weakened beyond the psychologically important level of 160 against the dollar late last week.
Katayama declined to say whether the yen’s recent movements were orderly but stressed that Tokyo remained prepared to take decisive action against disorderly fluctuations.
The yen’s weakness has largely been driven by the wide interest-rate gap between Japan and the US. Although a weaker currency supports Japanese exporters, it also raises the cost of imported energy, food and raw materials, weighing on household consumption.
Ahead of the meeting, Bessent said he expected the Japanese government and the Bank of Japan to take further steps that would lead to a stronger yen.
A senior Japanese Finance Ministry official, however, said Bessent did not make a specific request during the roughly 30-minute meeting, according to Kyodo news.
Katayama also briefed Bessent on Japan’s efforts to balance economic growth with fiscal sustainability amid concerns over the country’s heavy public debt burden.

Shaun the Sheep hailed on latest list of storm names
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:10:12 UTC
17:10:12 KST

From a five-year-old weather enthusiast to a beloved animated sheep, the inspiration for the list of storm names for this autumn and winter is wide and varied.
Austen, Boelo and Chloe will be the first named storms of this winter, meteorologists have revealed, after more than 40,000 suggestions were submitted by the public.
The UK’s Met Office, in partnership with Ireland’s Met Éireann and the Dutch national weather forecasting service KNMI, released the list for the 2026-27 season on Monday.
People submitted names in honour of a much-loved labrador puppy, meteorological pioneers and Shaun the Sheep, from the animation Wallace and Gromit.
The Met Office said the purpose of naming storms was serious as it helped people take notice, prepare and stay safe in severe weather.
The organisations have been naming storms since 2015, with the list running from early September to the following August. It coincides with the start of meteorological autumn, when the likelihood of low-pressure systems and the potential for storms severe enough to be named increases.
In the last year, four names were used from the list, reaching the letter D with Storm Dave on 1 April, although the UK was also affected by a further three storms named by other European meteorological services: Benjamin, Claudia and Goretti.
The third name in this year’s list, Chloe, was selected by the Met Office after being put forward more than 120 times, including by the mother of a five-year weather enthusiast who is “fascinated by the weather” but can also “create a storm by herself” when she is tired.
The name Finn was suggested for a two-year-old boy described by his family as “wild and a force to be reckoned with”, while Ivy was nominated in honour of a nine-month-old labrador puppy affectionately known as “the absolute destructor”.
Shaun also joins the list after a public vote that was run as part of a collaboration with the British animation studio Aardman, which is behind Wallace and Gromit.
Holly Clements, the Met Office head of warnings and guidance, said: “For more than a decade, storm naming has helped us communicate the risks from severe weather more effectively. A named storm provides a clear focus for forecasts and warnings, helping more people understand the potential impacts and take action to protect themselves, their families and their property.”
Storms are given a name when they are deemed to have the potential to have a medium or high impact in the UK, Ireland or the Netherlands. Wind is the primary focus, although additional issues such as rain or snow are also considered.
This year’s names, and the countries they came from, are:

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tells Russia’s finance minister Russia won’t get economic relief until Ukraine war ends

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tells Russia’s finance minister Russia won’t get economic relief until Ukraine war ends
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Russia’s Finance Ministry head Anton Siluanov there would be no “economic relief” for Moscow until the Russia–Ukraine war ends, sources told Politico and Reuters.
The ministers’ meeting centered on US President Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Ukraine.
According to those sources, Bessent told Siluanov that the United States would withhold economic relief from Russia until the war ends, though it is not specified whether he meant an easing of sanctions. When the Russian minister “tried to discuss areas of interest,” Bessent cut him off, saying “nothing is possible until the war is over.”
Erin Browne, US Treasury undersecretary for international affairs, told Politico the meeting had been “productive,” with the two men discussing “Trump’s plan for peace and economic growth.” Bessent, she said, told Siluanov that “the war needs to end.”
Russia’s Finance Ministry, in a brief statement issued the evening of August 31, stated that the two sides had discussed “issues of Russian–American cooperation on the financial track,” as well as “cooperation issues” within the framework of the G20.
The Bessent-Siluanov meeting took place in Asheville, North Carolina, on the sidelines of a G20 summit of finance ministers and central bank governors. It was the first time Russia’s finance minister had attended a G20 summit since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Anton Siluanov’s visit had not been announced in advance.

Ukraine's Sanctions Czar Lands In Washington As Russia Bill Hits House Wall Over Tariff Fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:09:52 UTC
17:09:52 KST

WASHINGTON -- Ukraine's top sanctions official has arrived in Washington seeking to keep alive a sweeping sanctions bill that cleared the Senate with overwhelming bipartisan support but now faces a tougher test in the House of Representatives.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's sanctions commissioner, is scheduled to meet lawmakers as Kyiv presses Congress to advance the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
The legislation passed the Senate on August 7 by an 86-11 vote, reflecting rare bipartisan agreement.
But the bill has yet to receive a vote in the House, where Democrats have raised concerns about provisions that would give President Donald Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries that buy Russian oil and gas or help Moscow evade sanctions.
Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York said on August 31 that his caucus had not taken a position on the bill. Democrats are concerned the legislation could give Trump additional tariff and sanctions powers that his administration could use too broadly.
From Senate Landslide To House Uncertainty
The legislation is the product of more than a year of negotiations involving Congress, the White House, and Ukrainian officials.
It was championed by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, who reached an agreement with the Trump administration before his death in July. A bipartisan group of senators subsequently carried the measure forward.
The Senate version would impose sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, and their family members, as well as financial institutions and foreign entities supporting Moscow's war effort. It also targets Russia's so-called shadow fleet, vessels used to transport oil and circumvent Western restrictions.
The package extends the Iran Sanctions Act and includes measures targeting Iran's energy and weapons sectors.
The White House has backed the legislation, portraying it as another tool Trump could use to increase pressure on Moscow and push Russia toward negotiations.
The most contentious provision involves tariffs. Earlier versions of the bill contemplated tariffs as high as 500 percent. The Senate-passed version lowered the maximum to 100 percent and narrowed the measure to major purchasers of Russian oil or gas and countries involved in sanctions evasion.
China and India could face some of the greatest exposure because of their purchases of Russian energy.
Supporters argue that the provision is intended to give the White House leverage over countries that continue buying Russian energy rather than automatically trigger a sweeping trade war. Critics question how much discretion it would give Trump over when tariffs are imposed or lifted.
Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska is among those urging the House to act despite the disagreements.
"The Russian Sanctions bill passed 86-11. The House should vote on this ASAP," Bacon said on August 31. "Some are letting perfection be the enemy of good in the House. Congress must take clear action in support of Ukraine and in opposition to Putin, and do it now."
Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, a Democratic supporter of tougher measures against Moscow, called for congressional action on August 31 while criticizing the Trump administration's treatment of a senior Russian official.
"As Russia kills civilians in Ukraine, the White House hosts Putin's sanctioned finance minister on US soil," Shaheen said, referring to Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov's attendance at a G20 meeting in North Carolina on August 31. "The Trump Admin needs to pressure Putin and his cronies, not offer them a platform. With the House back in DC, it's time to pass Russia sanctions."
Ukraine Makes Its Case
Vlasiuk's visit comes as Ukraine seeks to keep lawmakers focused on Russia's ability to finance and sustain its war.
Kyiv has long argued that Russia's war effort depends heavily on revenue from energy exports and on networks of companies, financial institutions, and intermediaries that help Moscow circumvent sanctions.
Ukrainian officials have increasingly urged Western governments to target those networks rather than simply add individual Russian officials to sanctions lists.
Vlasiuk has also worked with European governments to coordinate sanctions against Russian weapons manufacturers and foreign suppliers supporting Russia's defense industry.
In August, he told RFE/RL that the Senate vote sent "a strong signal from the American people" that Russia must face a higher price for its aggression and that support for Ukraine remains strong.
"We now look forward to the bill's passage by the House and its final approval by Congress," Vlasiuk said.
Zelenskyy's Role
During his July visit to Washington, Zelenskyy met with senators and urged them to advance the sanctions package after months of congressional uncertainty. His intervention helped produce the 86-11 vote and demonstrated that support for additional pressure on Moscow could still cross party lines.
Senator Richard Blumenthal, one of the legislation's Democratic supporters, has argued that the measure could increase the economic cost of Russia's war and strengthen Washington's leverage in negotiations.
The Senate rejected an amendment that would have removed the provision concerning duties on countries purchasing Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas or facilitating sanctions evasion. The amendment failed 32-64 before the final bill passed 86-11.
That vote underscored the importance supporters place on the tariff mechanism as a way to make the sanctions more effective.
Blumenthal has said he offered to have Zelenskyy return to Washington to personally address House members, as he did with senators. As of August 31, however, it was unclear whether such a visit could take place in the coming weeks.
The Politics Of Delay
The immediate question is whether House leaders can preserve enough of the Senate coalition to bring the bill to the floor.
Speaker Mike Johnson has not committed to a vote, and the legislation is competing for attention with funding measures and other priorities as lawmakers return from their summer recess.
The House's narrow Republican majority makes bipartisan negotiations especially important.
For Ukraine, delay carries risks. Kyiv wants the focus to remain on Russia's war economy: its oil revenue, sanctions-evasion networks, and ability to sustain weapons production.
The Senate vote gave Kyiv evidence that bipartisan support for tougher Russia sanctions remains strong. But a prolonged House fight could turn that consensus into a broader argument over Trump's trade powers.
