Long-term UK borrowing costs at 28-year high as rising oil prices trigger global bond rout – business live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:53:32 UTC
16:53:32 KST

Longer-dated gilt yields have also surged, which means higher borrowing costs for Andy Burnham’s government.
The yield, or interest rate, on the 30-year gilt jumped 9 basis points to 5.88%, the highest since March 1998.
This comes as oil prices keep climbing, with Brent crude rising 1.7% to $92.1 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate is 1.9% higher at $87.35 a barrel.
Thomas Pugh, chief economist at the audit, tax and consulting firm RSM UK, said:
Gilt yields are up and it’s tempting to blame this on UK-specific factors. But government bond yields are surging across the world, especially in America. That doesn’t mean the UK is off the hook. We still have to pay a higher interest rate than similar countries, suggesting investors see us as a riskier place for their cash. That reflects a combination of political risk, low growth and sticky inflation.
The energy shock and the threat of rising inflation are important factors. Inflation expectations matter because inflation erodes the purchasing power of a bond’s fixed payments. When investors believe inflation could remain elevated, they demand a higher yield as compensation.
But there is much more to it than that, especially for longer-dated bonds. Governments are still spending as if interest rates were near zero and their economies were in crisis. The budget deficit in the UK is likely to be close to 4% of GDP this year and close to 6% in the US. At the same time, this borrowing is becoming increasingly hard to finance.
The UK will spend about 3.7% of national income just to pay the interest on its debt. In other words, we are borrowing more to help cover our interest bill increasing the risk of public debt rising further and prompting global investors to demand a higher risk premium.
There is also something of a credibility issue, he said.
Inflation has been above target in the UK and US for much of the past five years, raising questions about whether it will return sustainably to 2%. Meanwhile, various governments have not followed through on promises to bring deficits down. Lenders therefore have to factor the prospect of higher inflation and greater bond issuance into the price they are willing to pay.
The elephant in the room is the rise of economic populism. There is a logic to populism, whether it comes from the right or the left. Both versions tend to favour expansionary fiscal policy – tax cuts, higher spending or both – tolerate higher inflation and resist efforts by central banks to restore price stability. If such policies continue for long enough without a course correction, the risks of financial and currency instability increase. Global investors understand where such policies can lead.
Alongside the huge supply of government bonds, the private sector is also starting to borrow more. AI firms are expected to borrow about $500bn this year to build data centres – for comparison, the UK government will borrow about $160bn. That is increasing competition for capital and pushing yields higher. None of these factors look temporary, and so bond yields are rising to compensate.
The UK’s long-term borrowing costs jumped to their highest level since early 1998 on Tuesday as investors dumped government bonds, betting on higher inflation.
The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 30-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, hit 5.89% at one point, up 10 basis points, as London markets caught up with a sell-off that swept Japan and the US on Monday, a bank holiday in the UK.
Ten-year gilt yields rose 10bps to about 5.25%, their highest level since the 2008 global financial crisis, and are now at 5.21%.
The moves were partly triggered by higher oil prices, with Brent crude jumping over 2% to $92.42 a barrel, up nearly $2. Gold slid 1.8% to $4,370 an ounce, and stocks fell in Europe and on Wall Street. The Nasdaq slid 1.3% at the open.
The sell-off in government bond markets around the world carried on for a second day, as traders fretted about rising inflation risks and surging government spending.
Japan’s 10-year benchmark bond yield hit 3% for the first time since 1996. The 10-year US Treasury yield hit 4.78%, the highest level since early 2025.
Germany’s 10-year yield, the benchmark for the eurozone, hit 3.34% earlier on Tuesday, a fresh 15-year high.
Higher yields progressively increase the cost of financing the UK government’s debt. If sustained, these would pass through to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)’s forecasts for John Healey’s 28 October budget.
Deutsche Bank’s chief UK economist, Sanjay Raja, said that based on Tuesday’s yields, Healey’s headroom against the current budget rule would fall from £26bn at Rachel Reeves’s spring forecast, to £13.8bn before covering any additional spending plans.
Almost all of the deterioration results from higher government interest costs. The OBR’s March forecast had gilt yields at 5.1% for this year. Gilt yields eased back a bit later on Tuesday – to 5.85% for the 30-year and 5.21% for the 10-year – but they are still well above the predicted level.

Eurozone inflation jumps to three-year high, adding to expectations of ECB rate hike next week
Eurozone inflation jumped to a three-year high in August, as the war in the Middle East continued to push up energy costs.
The annual inflation rate rose to 3.3% last month, official data showed on Tuesday, up from 2.9% in July and well above the European Central Bank’s 2% target.
The statistics office Eurostat said energy prices jumped 14.3% in August after rising 10.3% in July.
The US war against Iran and the near-total closure of the strait of Hormuz, a key shipping passage for global oil and gas supplies, have sent global energy costs soaring.
Leo Barincou of Oxford Economics said:
Inflation should remain well above target into next year, as higher gas and food prices put additional upward pressure on the index.
The ECB is widely expected to raise interest rates again at its meeting on 10 September to bring inflation lower, after a first hike in June.
The bank’s chief, Christine Lagarde, warned in July that the energy shock from the conflict “could intensify further”.
Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, has remained largely stable in recent months.
In August it eased to 2.4 after accelerating slightly to 2.5 in July.

AstraZeneca’s share price is up a more modest 0.4%, after Britain’s biggest drugmaker released positive results from a late-stage drug trial.
AstraZeneca and the Hong Kong-based drug developer Hutchmed said that a phase III trial of a combination of their cancer drugs Tagrisso and Orpathys significantly improved progression-free survival for cancer patients, when given early for a type of lung cancer.
Cancer therapies make up nearly half of AstraZeneca’s sales and Tagrisso is one of its biggest-selling drugs, while Orpathys is being developed in partnership with Hutchmed. The British drugmaker has set a goal of $80bn in overall annual sales by 2030.
The drug combination was able to help patients in the trial live longer without their disease worsening compared with cases where Tagrisso alone was given as a first-line treatment for EGFR-mutated advanced non-small cell lung cancer to patients whose tumours showed moderate to high levels of the MET protein marker, the companies said.
The leading principal investigator of the trial, Yi-Long Wu, said:
By combining Orpathys with Tagrisso, we have observed a clear clinical benefit that could reshape primary treatment strategy for this distinct patient population.
Patients in the trial had not previously received treatment for their advanced lung cancer.

This has stoked inflation fears, leading to a sell-off in bond and equity markets.

The housing market remains sluggish, as 56,053 mortgages were approved for house purchase in July, marking the lowest monthly figure since January 2024, the Bank’s monthly report said. This compares with 58,215 mortgage approvals in June.
Over the past six months, monthly mortgage approvals for house purchases have averaged about 60,800, the central bank said.
Meanwhile the Bank’s remortgaging approvals figures, which capture remortgaging with a different lender, showed an increase to 34,500 in July, from 34,100 in June.
The figures came as Nationwide Building Society said the average price of a UK home rose by 0.2% month-on-month in August, following a 0.1% dip in July, revised lower from a 0.1% rise.
It was the first monthly increase since April, as buyers and sellers remained in a “holding pattern” before an expected increase in interest rates later this year. Markets are expecting a quarter-point rate hike from the Bank in November or December.
Across the UK, the average house price in August was £275,465 – up by 1.6% year on year.
Lucian Cook, head of residential research at property firm Savills, said underlying house price affordability has shown signs of gradually improving, but:
The increase in fixed rate mortgage costs we saw in mid-July has prevented that from translating into any improvement in activity in the market, leading to a third consecutive month of weak mortgage approvals.
And with more inflation to work its way through the system, it seems unlikely that we will see much of a sustained turnaround over the course of the remainder of the year.
Hina Bhudia, a partner at Knight Frank Finance, said:
Geopolitical tensions and elevated energy prices pushed mortgage rates higher during the summer, which has weighed on demand in the housing market.
Mark Harris, chief executive at mortgage broker SPF Private Clients, said:
On the ground, some lenders have been easing mortgage rates in recent days and weeks but swap rates, which underpin the pricing of mortgages, remain extremely volatile in response to tensions in the Middle East.

Sarah Coles, head of personal finance at AJ Bell, said:
Savers and investors tend to be highly motivated by a deadline, and from April 2027 savers under 65 will see their annual cash Isa allowance reduced from £20,000 to £12,000.
That means we can expect cash Isa enthusiasm to build again as the summer fades and the end of the tax year gets closer.

The UK government’s long-term borrowing costs jumped to their highest level since early 1998 on Tuesday as a global bond sell-off gathered pace, writes our economics editor Heather Stewart.
The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 30-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, hit 5.89% as traders fretted about a fresh increase in oil prices driving up inflation.

BISHKEK, September 1. /TASS/. Member states of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) advocate for reforming the international financial architecture, according to the Bishkek Declaration signed at the SCO summit on Tuesday.
"Member states support the reform of the international financial architecture aimed at increasing the representation and strengthening the role of developing countries in the governing bodies of international financial institutions, including the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Monetary Fund," the document states.

Fast-fashion giant Shein plunges 10% after stock market debut
Kyiv • UNN
Shein raised $1.7 billion during its IPO, but its shares fell 10% after debuting in Hong Kong. The company was valued at $26.3 billion.
Shares in fast-fashion retailer Shein fell 10 percent after its long-awaited trading debut in Hong Kong on Tuesday, after the company raised $1.7 billion in a high-profile initial public offering (IPO), UNN reports, citing AFP.
Details
The share offering came after the company's plans to list in New York and London were derailed by regulatory scrutiny, but in July it received approval from Chinese authorities to sell shares in the southern financial hub.
However, shortly after the opening, the shares fell to 43.72 Hong Kong dollars, compared with the listing price of 48.56 Hong Kong dollars.
The IPO valued the company at approximately $26.3 billion — significantly less than the nearly $100 billion raised during private funding rounds in 2022.
Shein, known for its ultra-low prices and rapid clothing deliveries, said the proceeds from the sale would be used to fund its technological capabilities and expand its international presence.
Between 2021 and 2022, the online retailer moved its headquarters to Singapore, which analysts believe was done to avoid increasing global scrutiny of Chinese companies.
By the end of 2025, its European customer base had grown to 156 million users on average per month, making it one of the largest e-commerce platforms on the continent alongside China's AliExpress and U.S. giant Amazon, which have 193 million and approximately 180 million users, respectively.
The company has been criticized for its environmental impact and allegations of human rights violations, and is also facing growing competition from low-cost e-commerce companies such as Temu and AliExpress.
Executive Chairman Donald Tang told AFP last year that the company has "zero tolerance" for forced labor.
Morningstar analyst Lorraine Tan noted in an August report that revenue growth had "approached the rates seen in the fast-fashion industry and will be below 10 percent in 2025."
She added that the decline in valuation "reflects waning investor interest in Shein shares."
The company has developed an impressive model that is difficult to replicate, said Ken Pucker, a sustainable-fashion expert at Tufts University.
But its unprecedented growth has also created problems related to "newly introduced taxes and tariffs, deteriorating sustainability, privacy and copyright metrics, as well as competition," he added.
"The timing is not ideal, given the company's slowing growth. Nevertheless, it has been trying to go public for about five years, and I assume many of its investors were eager to cash out," he added.
In 2025, Shein reported full-year net profit of $2.06 billion, but in the first three months of this year it posted a loss of $99 million after the United States ended the exemption from import duties for small parcels.

Ukrainian Independence Day marked in Milan with focus on countering Russian propaganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01

Ukrainian Independence Day marked in Milan with focus on countering Russian propaganda
One of the event’s organizers told Ukrinform.
Key topics included countering Russian propaganda in Italy, continued support for Ukraine, and the role of the Ukrainian community in helping Italians develop an objective understanding of the country.
Organized by the Ukrainian association UaMi, the event brought together Ukrainian and Italian diplomats, politicians, military personnel, civil society representatives, cultural figures and young people. The organizers described it as a space for Ukraine and Italy to meet around shared values of freedom, culture, memory and the right to choose their own future.
From left: Anna Gordon, Volodymyr Vorona, Iryna Molovytsia
Ukrainian Consul General in Milan Volodymyr Vorona took part in the event. In comments to Ukrinform, he stressed that Russian propaganda in Italy has deep roots and has been developing for decades.
“Russian propaganda in Italy has very deep roots dating back to the 1990s, when much of the information was presented from a pro-Russian perspective. After 2022, changing this was not easy, but in recent years we have seen a shift in the position of Italian media. Italians are beginning to understand that much of what they had heard previously was disinformation and propaganda,” Vorona said.
Volodymyr Vorona
According to the consul general, there have been cases in which Italians who had been exposed to one-sided information for years have “almost apologized” after learning the facts, realizing how deeply Russian propaganda had influenced their perception of Ukraine.
The diplomat believes that one effective way to counter it is to work directly with Italian audiences.
“Through educational and informational events like these, we can convey our truth. Today, I deliberately spoke exclusively in Italian to address Italians directly, and I began my speech with Kyivan Rus. The most effective cooperation is when, at events like these, we tell Italians the truth,” the consul general stressed.
UaMi representative and event organizer Anna Gordon also emphasized the need for continued engagement with foreign audiences.
“We have to work with foreign audiences, and here our audience is Italians. It is important to find common ground, introduce them to Ukrainian culture and traditions, explain our policies, and tell them every day about the situation in Ukraine. If we do not do this, Russian propaganda will prevail here,” she said.
Gordon was also recognized by the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine for her support of the military.
“For me, this means that my work was not in vain, that I made my contribution to Ukraine’s victory and did not stand on the sidelines. It motivates me to keep moving forward,” she said.
Another part of the program focused on the price of freedom and the people who have personally taken up the defense of Ukraine. Among the participants was Lieutenant Colonel Denys Demydko of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, who came from Ukraine with his wife. He had suffered a serious injury while defending his comrades during an enemy attack.
Denys Demydko
Asked about the so-called “war fatigue” in Europe, the serviceman stressed that Europeans have an opportunity to help stop Russian aggression without sending their own citizens to fight.
“Europe now has a unique opportunity to stop this war without directly being involved in it. There is no need to send your people — give us the opportunity to defend Ukraine. Support us economically, financially and morally, do business with Ukraine, and help develop our economy. Russia will not stop at Ukraine; it has plans to go further. Ukraine will stand — and Europe will be preserved,” Demydko said.
Addressing the Ukrainians currently living in Italy and other European countries, he urged them not to lose their identity and to use their voices to support Ukraine.
“Never forget that you are Ukrainians. Do not be ashamed to say so. Support Ukraine with your voice — attend rallies, organize panel discussions and forums. Do not give Russian propaganda a chance to seize Europe,” the serviceman stressed.
Another participant in the discussion was Yuri Previtali, an Italian who left his life in Italy behind after Russia launched its full-scale invasion and traveled to Ukraine, where he joined the military as a volunteer.
Yuri Previtali
According to him, his decision was driven primarily by his personal values and his rejection of a situation in which a stronger state attempts to subjugate another by force.
“My values motivated me. Ukrainians are defending their own home. I was young, in good physical shape, and understood that I could do something, so I decided to go to Ukraine and join the military as a volunteer,” Previtali said.
Addressing his fellow Italians who view the Russian-Ukrainian war as distant and unrelated to them, he stressed: “Ukraine is defending itself. And we, as civilians, have a moral obligation to help. No one is asking us to go and fight — Ukrainians are asking us to provide them with weapons and the necessary assistance so they can defend themselves.”
Read also: Stockholm activists organize car rally in support of Ukraine
Previtali also spoke about the creation of the STUR (Support for Ukrainian Resistance) association, which supports Italian and other foreign volunteers fighting alongside Ukraine. The organization provides them with food and protective equipment, offers psychological support before and after their time at the front, and supports the families of fallen volunteers. STUR was among the partners of the Milan event.
Previtali also has a personal connection to Ukraine: in 2023, he met a Ukrainian woman from Vinnytsia there, and the couple married in November 2025.
Ukrainian business potential in Italy was also discussed by entrepreneur Bohdan Hladchuk.
“Ukrainians are highly creative and dynamic in business, willing to experiment and quickly seek new opportunities. Therefore, there is enormous potential here for the development of Ukrainian business,” he said.
Bohdan Hladchuk, Andrii Andrikevych
The “La Nostra Indipendenza” program featured a series of thematic discussions ranging from Ukrainian culture, literature, sports and medicine to youth participation in shaping Ukraine’s future, Russian captivity and the stories of military personnel. A separate panel focused on Ukrainian civilians held captive by Russia and the families of prisoners of war.
Participants in the first discussion included Ukrainian Consul General in Milan Volodymyr Vorona, Member of the European Parliament Pierfrancesco Maran, Milan City Council Vice President Roberta Osculati, and, online, Ukraine’s Ambassador to Italy Ihor Brusylo.
The program also featured video addresses by Save Ukraine founder Mykola Kuleba, Italian politician Carlo Calenda, Ukrainian skeleton racer Vladyslav Heraskevych, and Hero of Ukraine Sviatoslav “Kalyna” Palamar, one of the commanders of the Azov Regiment and a defender of Mariupol and Azovstal.
Participants observed a minute of silence in memory of Ukrainian military personnel and civilians who were killed in Russia’s war against Ukraine, and also remembered those who remain in Russian captivity.
The cultural program included a screening of the Ukrainian film “Roses. Film-Cabaret” and a performance by the Lviv folk group Eteria, which presented Ukrainian folk songs and traditional melodies.
The organizers stressed that UaMi’s goal is to create platforms in Italy where Ukrainians and Italians can meet, exchange ideas, launch joint projects and build long-term ties between the two societies. They also seek to convey the truth about Ukraine, counter Russian propaganda and disinformation, and support Ukraine and Ukrainians in every possible way in their struggle for freedom and independence.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, a commemorative event highlighting Russia’s crimes against Ukraine was held in Lisbon.

Death toll from devastating floods in Nepal and China surpasses 1,000
Rescue efforts continue to focus on hydropower sites, where hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped.
The death toll from catastrophic flooding in Nepal and China has reached 1,019, and more than 4,400 people remain missing as rescue crews work to reach communities cut off by the disaster.
In an update on Tuesday, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) revised the number of deaths to 1,003 from 987, with 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreigners.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Nepal FM speaks to Al Jazeera on devastating floods
- list 2 of 3‘Nothing is usable’: Nepal residents return to flood-ravaged homes
- list 3 of 3Aftermath of the Nepal-China floods in 30 Photos
Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 people still missing, including 261 foreigners, in their most recent update on Sunday.
The disaster hit on August 26, beginning with a chain of events high in the Himalayas, when a glacial collapse sent large amounts of rock, ice, and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream.
Scientists studying satellite imagery said the collapse appears to have involved the failure of bedrock beneath a glacier.
Hundreds of workers are feared to be trapped in tunnels at several devastated hydropower stations in Nepal that have become the focus of rescue efforts.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah said 279 workers had been rescued from hydropower projects so far, where authorities had initially estimated that more than 900 people were missing.
More than 11,000 people have been rescued across the affected region, and power and communication lines have been restored in some areas, he added.
“Thousands of citizens have lost their homes, families, loved ones, and property,” Shah said on social media.
“The government understands the immense pain they are enduring. The path ahead is to support them through this suffering and help them return to normal life through rehabilitation.”
Rescue teams had managed to restore road networks to Nuwakot, one of the worst-affected districts, facilitating rescue operations and the distribution of relief material, Shah said.
Reporting from the disaster-hit village of Dhunge, Al Jazeera’s Jessica Washington said nothing was left of people’s homes and belongings.
“Residents here have been telling us that at least 250 homes were pushed into the floodwaters,” she said.
“The real number could be much more; only a few buildings are still standing in such a deep state of disrepair,” Washington added.
Aid arrives in Nepal
Police official Bipin Regmi said a search team recovered 24 bodies from a house in Betrabati village in Nuwakot district.
“We are reaching new areas and recovering bodies,” Regmi told the Reuters news agency.
Aid worth more than $42m has poured into the country after the disaster, Shah said, and the government expects the contributions to increase.
Neighbours India and China are helping with rescue efforts, including building Bailey bridges to reach remote affected areas.
Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud and rocks under lights in the dark of the night as workers watched.
Soldiers used torchlight in a big pit they had created to look for space to get into one tunnel.
There has been a boom in hydropower projects in Nepal since the turn of the century, as the mountainous country sought to take advantage of its Himalayan water resources to address chronic domestic power shortages and exploit prospects for selling electricity to its southern neighbour, India.
Hydropower projects in Nepal’s mountains need tunnels to carry water through the steep terrain, allowing developers to exploit the sharp elevation drop between Himalayan rivers and powerhouses to generate electricity.

Russia Returns Nuclear-Powered Cruiser Admiral Nakhimov to Navy Service After 27 Years of Repairs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:49:42 UTC
16:49:42 KST

Russia is preparing to bring back the nuclear-powered missile cruiser Admiral Nakhimov to the Russian Navy after nearly 27 years of repairs and modernization.
Russian media outlet Novye Izvestia reported on this.
It is expected to enter service with the Russian Navy by the end of 2026, following trials.
During the modernization, the cruiser received new radar systems, an AK-192M 130 mm naval gun mount, and new missile armament.
Instead of the 20 P-700 Granit anti-ship missiles, the vessel received vertical launching systems. These allow it to deploy Kalibr, Oniks, and hypersonic Zircon missiles.
According to Russian sources, the cruiser has 176 launch cells. Of these, 80 are intended for strike missiles, while another 96 are allocated for S-400 surface-to-air missiles.
Thus, following its modernization, Admiral Nakhimov is expected to combine the capabilities of a long-range strike missile carrier and a powerful air-defense vessel.
The cruiser can also operate Ka-27 or Ka-31 helicopters. The latter are equipped with a radar system that extends the detection range for airborne and surface targets and relays information to the ship’s weapon systems.
At the same time, Admiral Nakhimov is not designed to operate entirely on its own. Given its importance and size, the cruiser will require escort ships to protect it from underwater, surface, and airborne threats.
Russia may attach particular importance to its deployment in the Arctic. After returning to service with the Russian Navy, Admiral Nakhimov could become one of the fleet’s flagship assets.
Admiral Nakhimov is the third ship of the Project 1144 Orlan. It was laid down in 1983 at the Baltic Shipyard in Leningrad, launched in 1986, and commissioned into the Soviet Navy in 1988 under the name Kalinin.
In 1992, the ship was renamed in honor of Russian Admiral Pavel Nakhimov.
Project 1144 Orlan cruisers are large nuclear-powered missile ships designed to engage major surface targets, provide air and anti-submarine defense, and perform command functions.
Admiral Nakhimov belongs to Russia’s Northern Fleet, but has spent most of its service life undergoing repairs. Modernization work began back in 1999, with the active phase starting only in 2013 at the Sevmash facility in Severodvinsk.
The modernization was initially scheduled for completion in 2018, but the deadline was repeatedly postponed — first to 2020, then to 2021, 2022, 2024, and 2025. As of 2025, the total cost of the work had exceeded RUB 200 billion.
In 2024–2025, Admiral Nakhimov went to sea for trials after undergoing extensive repairs.

Emergency services were dispatched to the sites.
The all-clear was given in Kyiv at 10:35.

Canada’s ruling Liberals sweep special elections in boost to Mark Carney
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:42:50 UTC
16:42:50 KST

Canada’s ruling Liberal party has swept three byelections, a result that showed voters backing the prime minister, Mark Carney, after his face-off with Donald Trump.
The Canadian Press, Canada’s national news agency, projected Liberal victories in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord in Quebec, Beaches-East York in Toronto and North Vancouver-Capilano in British Columbia.
Carney said the results of Monday’s votes amounted to an endorsement of his government’s approach. “At this consequential time for Canada, voters have placed their trust in our government’s plan,” he said in a statement.
The Quebec result was the most dramatic shift. The Liberal candidate Daniel Gobeil was projected to win big in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, a district held by the opposition Conservatives since 2018. The region is home to aluminium producers, dairy farms and other industries caught in an escalating trade war with the US.
“This victory means we can maintain Canadian unity all across the country,” Gobeil said.
The other two seats were previously held by Liberals. In British Columbia, Carney’s former deputy chief of staff Braeden Caley won North Vancouver-Capilano.
The Liberal MP Hedy Fry told CBC: “The United States is getting a message tonight. Our leader has the support of the Canadian people.”
US-Canada trade talks collapsed on 21 August after the two sides failed to reach a deal, and Trump imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20bn of Canadian goods. Canada responded with plans for tariffs on US products.
Trump has escalated his attacks on Canada since the talks failed. He signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America”, and on Monday the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said Canada had limited leverage in the dispute because the US economy was roughly 13 times larger. Trump has repeatedly talked about making Canada the 51st state.
Meanwhile, Carney has accelerated efforts to deepen economic ties with Europe and other partners.
The Liberal sweep would bring Carney’s party to 173 seats in the 343-seat House of Commons, further strengthening its position.
The byelections were called after the MPs who previously held the three seats resigned from parliament earlier this year.
Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University, said the sweep showed Carney retaining strong support across regions, and he called the Quebec result the most significant. He said the easy win in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord probably reflected, in part, the popularity in Quebec of Carney’s decision “to pull the plug on trade negotiations with the White House”.
He said the Conservative collapse there was bad news for the party’s leader, Pierre Poilievre. The party had about 41% of the vote in last year’s federal elections but fell to about 13% and third place on Monday. “These numbers do look bad,” Béland said.
Carney won Canada’s election last year, fuelled by public anger over Trump’s annexation threats, and he has vowed to reduce Canada’s reliance on the US.

54-year-olds got the biggest pension boost last year
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:42:05 EEST
16:42:05 KST

For Finland's 54-year-olds, 2025 was a particularly good year for growing older, at least on paper. They accrued more new pension benefits than any other age group, thanks in part to the last hurrah of a more generous accrual rate.
Workers in their 50s accrued an average of 57 euros in new earnings-related pension benefits in 2025, according to an estimate by the Finnish Centre for Pensions (ETK).
It was the final year in which workers aged 53–62 accrued pension benefits at a rate of 1.7 percent, rather than the standard 1.5 percent.
The higher accrual rate meant that 54-year-olds, people born in 1971, gained the most, with their projected future pension increasing by 63 euros over the year.
ETK's estimate covers all earnings-related pension-insured people living in Finland who were not already retired.

Russia hits port export facilities in Ukraine's Odesa region, Kyiv says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01

16:40:40 KST

Russia hits port export facilities in Ukraine's Odesa region, Kyiv says
KYIV, Sept 1 - Russia attacked Ukraine's port infrastructure and a border crossing with Romania in the southern Black Sea region of Odesa overnight, Ukrainian officials said on Tuesday.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said the strike "deliberately damaged a border crossing point on the border with Romania, as well as export infrastructure."
Ukraine's emergency service said the attack had also targeted energy infrastructure and caused a fire at a residential building, where one person was hurt, without giving further details.
Ukrainian state energy firm Naftogaz said later on Tuesday that Russia had also attacked its Odesa combined heat and power plant with missiles and drones overnight.
"Part of the main and auxiliary equipment was damaged, and debris clearance is ongoing," the company said in a statement.
In recent months, Russia has sharply increased both the number and intensity of its drone strikes on export infrastructure in the Odesa region, home to Ukraine's main Black Sea ports as well as the major Danube river ports of Reni and Izmail.
Russian attacks have effectively blocked the seaports, which once handled 90% of the country's exports, forcing Kyiv to divert cargo through Danube river ports with lower capacity and to railway crossings on the western border.
The Ukrainian border service said on Tuesday that in the overnight strike, Russia had attacked and damaged a checkpoint for ferry services at Orlivka on the border with Romania.
"Processing of citizens and vehicles through this checkpoint has been temporarily suspended," the service said in a statement.
The Odesa region faced more than 300 air-raid alerts in August, lasting a combined 238 hours, according to a monitoring service.
Railway officials say constant air-raid alerts and attacks on facilities are significantly complicating their operations.
However, Ukrainian railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said it had increased grain deliveries to the Danube's ports for future exports. REUTERS

US Army Secretary Driscoll submits resignation: White House

Breadcrumb
US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll submits resignation: White House
The US Army's top civilian leader Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation, the White House confirmed Monday, following reports of tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Asked about a Wall Street Journal report that Driscoll had resigned, White House Principal Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly did not deny it.
"Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump's agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army," Kelly said.
She cited his "outstanding leadership" during US military operations, "restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more."
She added: "The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War."
A former law school classmate of Vice President JD Vance, Driscoll had reportedly benefited from their friendship within the administration, but clashed with Hegseth.
The most senior Democrat on the Senate's Armed Services Committee, Jack Reed, laid the departure's blame at the defense secretary's feet, saying, "I do not welcome Secretary Driscoll's resignation... It is far past time for President Trump to recognise the lasting harm that Pete Hegseth is inflicting on the Department of Defense."
An Army veteran who served in Iraq, Driscoll ran unsuccessfully for Congress in 2020 and later advised Trump's 2024 reelection campaign.
With the Iran war entering its seventh month, the resignation could effectively leave the Army without permanent civilian or uniformed leadership.
Hegseth fired Army Chief of Staff General Randy George in April and has yet to nominate a permanent successor.

White House unveils more details of Trump’s Venezuela oil deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:39:52 UTC
16:39:52 KST

White House unveils more details of Trump’s Venezuela oil deal
Venezuela’s interim president gives new US company 100-year rights to more than 17 oil fields.
The White House has revealed new details of United States President Donald Trump’s push to gain access to Venezuela’s oil industry, with a deal that will give the Pentagon a stake in roughly one-fifth of the country’s vast oil reserves.
According to a fact sheet released by the Trump administration late on Monday, the US is creating a private joint venture with North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt. NABEP is already the second-largest operator in Venezuela, behind Chevron.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump announces ‘biggest oil deal in world history’ with Venezuela
- list 2 of 3Delcy Rodriguez says Venezuela ‘retains sovereignty’ despite US oil deal
- list 3 of 3Trump says US will refill its petroleum reserves using Venezuelan oil
In a statement, Betancourt said Venezuela is “blessed with an abundance of natural resources, hardworking people and untapped potential”, adding that the deal will “unleash that potential to the great benefit of both Venezuelans and Americans”.
Betancourt’s company has agreed to put up $100bn in new oil infrastructure investments.
The deal will give the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital a 35 percent ownership stake in the company, the White House disclosed. The US will also be guaranteed a right to buy 20 percent of the output at cost, orchestrated through the State Department.
The agreement, which the White House said secures “our energy dominance for the next century”, was signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodriguez is giving the company 100-year rights over 17 oil fields with proven reserves of 65 billion barrels. Many of those fields were previously owned by Russian or Chinese firms, the White House said.
The White House said: “The majority of the incremental oil fields to be operated by NABEP were previously controlled or operated by Russian and Chinese firms, or by corrupt cronies of [former presidents Nicolas] Maduro and [Hugo] Chavez.”
The sweeping agreement has been met with scepticism from some analysts who say it will take years to revive Venezuela’s production, but Trump and his aides are pitching it as a chance to develop a new oil giant in the Western Hemisphere.
Trump has been pushing to boost oil production in Venezuela since the January military operation that captured then-President Maduro and his wife on US “narcoterrorism” and drug trafficking charges.
On Monday, Trump acknowledged that US consumers would not immediately see a change in petrol prices. Asked about a timeline at the White House, Trump said “it could be a little bit” for prices to fall, and he played down analyst predictions that it could take years.
“If it was two years, you know, that’s a short period of time,” he said.
Trump said the deal would provide a source to help refill the US’s strategic oil reserves, which have been drawn down as the war on Iran chokes global oil shipments. He added that Venezuela’s heavy oil would also go towards producing asphalt and other goods.

Israeli non-profits, companies expand education access in remote communities worldwide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:39:04 UTC
16:39:04 KST

As Israeli children return to their classrooms for the new school year, Israeli adults are traveling the world to expand education in communities where there is limited infrastructure or where disaster has disrupted the education system.
A pilot program launched six months ago by ConnectingMath, an Israeli nonprofit working to expand access to math education in developing countries, has become part of the school routine for some 800 students in grades one through six at eight rural schools in Kenya.
The program centers on a local teacher, Aaron, who travels with 20 tablets to a different school each day to teach math. School principals say that at the sound of his motorcycle on the dirt roads, the children run out to greet him.
Students work in pairs or groups of three on hundreds of activities that do not require internet access. Since the beginning of the year, they have completed over 100,000 activities.
“When we left Kenya in January, we weren’t sure the pilot could keep going with only remote support from us,” Shmulik London, co-founder of ConnectingMath, said.
“Six months later, we returned to find that the students and teachers had made it part of their school routine. Watching classrooms come alive around just 20 tablets showed us how, even with limited resources, the right educational approach can bring learning, and the joy of learning, to life.”
Early Starters International helps young children in disasters and crisis areas
Former Education Ministry employee Keren Gantz-Maya, who used to train kindergarten teachers, joined Early Starters International, which specializes in working with young children during emergencies and crises in Venezuela.
Early Starters International has six safe spaces in La Guaira and Caracas. Children take part in educational activities that help them return to interaction, play, and learning.
By mid-August, over 25 activities had taken place with over 946 attendees. The organization has also trained over 214 local teachers, educators, therapists, and other professionals to ensure that the community will be able to continue the work.
“When you meet children after a disaster like this, you can’t begin with learning in the conventional sense. First, you have to help restore a sense of safety, routine, and connection. We saw children who struggled to connect and play together during our first meeting. After we returned again and again, they were waiting for us, joining in and playing together,” Gantz-Maya said.
“That’s when you understand how a safe, consistent educational space can become an anchor for a child whose world has changed overnight,” she added.
RoboGroup partners with Ghana government to construct STEAM learning centers
In Ghana, Israeli company RoboGroup is partnering with the country’s Education Ministry to establish 20 science, technology, engineering, arts, and math (STEAM) learning centers nationwide.
The centers feature science, robotics, and programming labs, 3D printers, and digital manufacturing technologies, giving students opportunities to experiment, investigate, build, and code.
RoboGroup is also training local teachers and instructors to lead the programs in order to build educational capacity that can be locally sustained.
“Our partnership with the government of Ghana is a flagship education project in Africa,” Yoram Doitch, CEO of RoboGroup, said.
“Our mission is to give every child the opportunity to explore their curiosity and to help every teacher develop critical skills in ways that are accessible, engaging and meaningful.”
Gabriel Project Mumbai brings digital science labs to indigenous communities
Gabriel Project Mumbai (GPM) brings digital science labs to seven government schools in Maharashtra’s Palghar District, where more than 6,000 children from indigenous communities study with limited access to computers.
Fourteen teachers travel in pairs between the schools carrying Einstein Tablets, designed by Israeli company Fourier Education, which function as portable science labs.
They also carry additional tablets for math, computer studies, and other STEM subjects.
For some students, the program provides their first opportunity to conduct a science experiment or learn using digital technology.
“The children love science and conducting experiments,” GPM founder Israeli social entrepreneur Jacob Sztokman said. “Their eyes light up when an experiment helps them understand how the world works. In those moments, you can see their curiosity grow, and their love of learning come alive.”
The three nonprofit organizations and RoboGroup are members of the SID Israel community, the umbrella organization for Israel’s international development and humanitarian aid sector.
“For us, a new school year begins in a classroom, but for millions of children around the world, the basic conditions needed to learn cannot be taken for granted,” Ayelet Levin-Karp, CEO of SID Israel, said.
“Quality education can change the course of a life, open up new possibilities, and give children the tools to build a different future for themselves. It is inspiring to see members of the SID Israel community not only believe that every child, everywhere, deserves a genuine opportunity in life, but work every day, even in some of the world’s most challenging and remote places, to turn that belief into reality.”

Iran's Pezeshkian says Tehran will reciprocate if US honors interim deal commitments - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:39:00 UTC
16:39:00 KST

Iran will immediately reciprocate if the US returns to its commitments under an interim deal signed in June, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Tuesday at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Summit in Bishkek, the Iranian Student News Agency reported.
“I am stating clearly that if the US returns to its commitments under the Memorandum of Understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate," Pezeshkian was quoted as saying by state media.
Several world leaders are also at the summit, held in Kyrgyzstan's capital, including Russia's Vladimir Putin, India's Narendra Modi, China's Xi Jinping, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
Pezeshkian arrived in Kyrgyzstan with the message that Tehran was aiming for diplomacy over armed conflict with the United States, saying this during several sideline meetings with different leaders.
On Monday, he told Modi on the sidelines of the summit that continued war was in no one's interest, and that dialogue and cooperation were the way to resolve existing problems.
According to Iran's semi-official Mehr News, Pezeshkian met Azerbaijan President Ilham Aliyev, and his agenda also included meeting Kyrgyzstan's deputy cabinet chairman, several participating leaders, and the presidents of Kyrgyzstan, Russia, and Tajikistan on the sidelines of the summit.
When talking about previous agreements, Pezeshkian was referring to an interim deal signed in June between Tehran and Washington in efforts to end the war, which started with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. The deal quickly unraveled amid disagreements over its implementation.
Tehran has repeatedly said it will allow free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global oil supplies, only if Washington implements the terms of the agreement.
Pezeshkian's contact with Mojtaba Khamenei
Last month, Iran's semi-official Tasmin News Agency reported that Pezeshkian had met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei around the start of the president's third year in office in late July.
Pezeshkian has given differing accounts in recent weeks about his access to Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since he succeeded his father in the role in March.
On July 21, the president said interactions with the supreme leader were "increasing day by day", but in early August he said communicating with Khamenei was "very difficult."
The late July meeting covered military affairs and the economy, including securing resources, managing foreign exchange and energy use, and economic ties with foreign partners, according to state media.
In May, state media also reported that Pezeshkian had met Khamenei for several hours, in what was then the first publicly reported meeting between the two since Khamenei became supreme leader.
Khamenei was reportedly seriously injured in the February 28 strike that killed his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei, on the first day of the US-Israeli war on Iran. He had also generally kept a low public profile before becoming supreme leader.

As schools start in Israel, government pushes for teachers to move up north with NIS 60,000 grant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:38:49 UTC
16:38:49 KST

Teaching staff working in border communities will receive a NIS 60,000 grant as classes started nationwide on Tuesday. The grant is part of a plan to push for more educators to move to these areas, which were among the most hurt during the last almost three years of war.
The program, formulated by the Tnufa Directorate for the North, the Education Ministry, and the Finance Ministry, is part of the government’s push to rehabilitate northern Israel.
The grant is intended for teaching staff, both teachers and administrators, working in communities located up to 9 kilometers from the northern border, with the personnel allowed to live up to 30 km. from the border in order to apply for the grant.
Unique learning environment
Along with the release, two educators currently working in border communities shared their experiences of working in this area.
Ofra Erlich, who is originally from Tel Aviv and decided to move to Metula to work as a first- and second-grade teacher at Hanadiv School, explained that her main objective is to “establish something anew in the wake of the war, in the wake of the security situation, and mainly to give some kind of horizon and hope to these children, who didn’t choose anything from the situation they found themselves in.”
“In Tel Aviv, kids who hear ‘Lebanon’ think it’s some kind of monster. So in Metula, kids look at Lebanon and see clouds. That’s kind of my hope – to remind them that this war is something that, in the end, doesn’t have the same power in their eyes,” she explained about why she chose to move to Metula.
“We have 14 children in the class; it’s the dream of every teacher, and also of every child and parent,” she said. “And yet, first of all, we give these children an anchor. Before all the pedagogy, we come to give them an anchor and hope. Before we learn the alphabet – first of all, let’s be here, together.”
Yuval Sharon, who moved from her homeland to Shlomi to work as a kindergarten teacher focused on special education, said that moving to a border settlement is not a given, mainly because of the distance from home and the different security situation in these areas.
“I think it’s very important because not everyone wants to move there; it’s not easy. It’s living in a different reality than what I’m used to,” she said about the importance of going to northern Israeli areas to work as an educator.
What are the program's main objectives?
The government said it will place special emphasis on teachers in shortage subjects, including mathematics, English, computers, physics, biology, chemistry, and technological and therapeutic subjects, as well as kindergarten teachers and educational counseling.
“Within this framework, we are working together with the Education Ministry to encourage the absorption of new teachers who move to live in the north and join the education system in the Tnufa region settlements and provide a response to the boys and girls of the Galilee,” said Aviad Friedman, Head of the Tnufa North and Resurgence Directorate.
The outline is groundbreaking and is one of the drivers of growth in the communities along the conflict line. It allows us to attract new teaching staff and to ensure the persistence of teaching staff in the area,” added Dr. Orna Simhon, director of the Northern District at the Education Ministry.

The approved price also includes a component covering Bulgargaz’s costs for storing gas at the Chiren underground storage facility, in line with obligations under the Emergency Action Plan.

Iran has deployed defense systems in over 3,800 locations

16:38:37 KST

Speaking in a televised interview on Tuesday, Second Brigadier General Mohammad Sadeghian congratulated the establishment anniversary of Khatam al-Anbiya Air Defense Base and National Air Defense Day, emphasizing, “Air defense is undertaken major four missions throughout the country, including detection, reconnaissance, interception, and engagement of aerial targets.”
The main mission of air defense is to detect any flying object in the skies of the Islamic Republic of Iran and even beyond the country's skies, he said, adding, “After detecting, the identification phase is carried out and, if necessary, interception is caried out by fighter aircraft or engagement using missiles and defense systems.”
Ultimately, the defense mission is to prevent hostile aircraft from carrying out their mission and, if necessary, destroy it, General Sadeghian underlined.
Turning to the role of air defense in normal [no war] conditions, he said, "The defense mission is not limited to wartime conditions. Every passenger plane that intends to enter the country’s airspace or travel between different cities, as well as all types of helicopters and aircrafts that operate for various missions, including relief, operate within the framework of air defense coordination and permits."
He went on to say that that air defense forces are present in more than 3,800 locations in the country, many of these locations are stationed in hard-to-pass areas.
Iran is a country with diverse geographical features, and defense forces are stationed in deserts, coasts, islands, and highlands, General Sadeghian added.
The surveillance forces, equipped with special equipment, electro-optical systems, and state-of-the-art technologies, along with a radar network, monitor and control the country's skies and even beyond Iran's skies 24 hours a day.

QSL No. 9: 1948–1960 – BNR’s music groups

Throughout 2026, Radio Bulgaria is confirming listeners' reception reports with a new series of 12 QSL cards. Each card highlights a significant moment from the history of the Bulgarian National Radio (BNR) and Radio Bulgaria, which is celebrating its 90th anniversary this year. At the beginning of each month, we present the story behind the image featured on the latest card.
The Ninth QSL card of 2026 is dedicated to BNR’s music groups
From its very beginnings, BNR has attracted the country’s leading musical talent, paving the way for extensive recording and concert activities. Today, the Bulgarian National Radio (BNR) has six musical ensembles.
The history of the Bulgarian National Radio Symphony Orchestra (the first photo in the top row), founded in 1948, is marked by the names of distinguished professionals such as conductors Vasil Stefanov, Vasil Kazandzhiev, Alexander Vladigerov, Milen Nachev, Rosen Milanov and Emil Tabakov. The BNR Symphony Orchestra has toured extensively around the world, performed concerts in numerous countries, and made recordings for renowned international companies. Konstantin Ilievski has been its chief conductor since 2023.
Bulgarian National Radio Symphony Orchestra
PHOTO Ani Petrova
The main activity of the Bulgarian National Radio Big Band (the second photo in the top row), formed in 1960, is making recordings for the radio’s music archive. For many years, it was led by Vili Kazasyan. Under his leadership, the orchestra developed an extensive concert program and took part in numerous Bulgarian and international events. Today, the BNR Big Band is led by Antoni Donchev.
Bulgarian National Radio Big Band
PHOTO Ani Petrova
The Bulgarian National Radio Folk Orchestra (the third photo in the top row), founded in 1952 as part of what was then the Bulgarian National Radio Folk Song Ensemble, brings together some of the most renowned musicians in the genre. The BNR archive holds thousands of recordings of folk songs and instrumental melodies performed by the BNR Folk Orchestra. The orchestra’s soloists have included many of Bulgaria’s best-known folk performers, such as Yanka Roupkina, Nadka Karadzhova, Kalinka Valcheva, and many others. Today, the orchestra continues its long-standing tradition of preserving and promoting Bulgarian folklore under the direction of Dimitar Hristov.
Bulgarian National Radio Folk Orchestra
PHOTO Ani Petrova
The Bulgarian National Radio Mixed Choir (the third photo in the second row) has been in existence since 1952. The professional ensemble has a long-standing tradition of performing operatic and cantata-oratorio works. Its current conductor is Lyubomira Aleksandrova.
Bulgarian National Radio Mixed Choir
PHOTO Ani Petrova
The Bulgarian National Radio Children’s Choir (the middle photo in the bottom row) was established in 1960 by Academician Hristo Nedyalkov. Following his death, Venetsia Karamanova took over as conductor of the vocal ensemble. The Bulgarian National Radio Children’s Choir has won numerous awards in Bulgaria and abroad and has given hundreds of concerts both in the country and around the world. It is particularly popular in Japan.
Bulgarian National Radio Children’s Choir
PHOTO Anton Chalakov
The Radiokids Vocal Group (the first photo in the bottom row) is the youngest and most cheerful addition to the BNR family of musical ensembles. It was founded in 1990 at the initiative of its longtime conductor, Ilina Todorova, with the aim of recording children’s entertainment songs for BNR’s programs and music archive. Today, the talented girls and boys, aged between 6 and 13, perform under the direction of Olga Mentzel.
Radiokids Vocal Group
PHOTO Ani Petrova
The talent of BNR’s musical ensembles shines brightest in their joint projects. One example is the folk song “Prituri se Planinata”, performed by the Bulgarian National Radio Children’s Choir, the Bulgarian National Radio Symphony Orchestra, and the Bulgarian National Radio Folk Orchestra

“We Must Work to End Hostilities”: Modi Urges Putin to End War Against Ukraine
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for an immediate end to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine during a meeting with Russian leader Vladimir Putin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, according to News18.
Addressing the Russian leader, Modi emphasized that every day of war pushes humanity backward and stressed the necessity of moving from a prolonged state of fighting to establishing peace.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Indian prime minister said: "We must work toward ending military actions. We will continue to support peace negotiations between Ukraine and Russia. We must transition from an endless war to an end to the war. This is India's message. We need an end to the war, not an endless war."
This is not the first time Modi has raised the issue of ending Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in talks with Putin. According to The Moscow Times, similar calls have been voiced by other leaders as well. On July 25, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev spoke to Putin at a forum in Omsk, suggesting to freeze the situation and resume negotiations based on "Istanbul Agreements 2.0."

The Kazakh president emphasized that he receives many signals from Europe and the US and decided to share this position because people asked to pass these proposals along.
Ukraine previously transmitted a proposal to Russia to hold a face-to-face meeting between the two heads of state at the G7 summit to discuss a path to peace. The plan envisioned direct negotiations between Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Vladimir Putin in the presence of G7 leaders, including US President Donald Trump.
Russia failed to provide a clear diplomatic response to the initiative, and following the proposal, Russian forces launched a shelling attack against Ukraine, which officials in the presidential office viewed as the Kremlin’s actual response to the meeting offer.

Taiwan to develop fishing-ground forecasts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:38:00 UTC
16:38:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan will begin developing fishing-ground forecasts next year, UDN and CNA reported Tuesday.
The four-year project will draw on decades of Taiwan’s annual catch records. Fisheries Agency Director-General Wang Mao-cheng (王茂城) said Taiwan has some of the most comprehensive fishery catch data in the western and central Pacific.
The National Science and Technology Council will also contribute historical satellite imagery. The analysis will incorporate oceanographic information such as sea temperatures, ocean color, and seawater acidity.
By comparing the datasets, researchers aim to identify patterns in fish distribution and determine where fishing grounds are likely to form. The resulting forecasts will initially be provided to domestic fishing fleets.
The system is expected to help crews identify potential fishing grounds and reduce the time and effort needed to find productive areas at sea. Wang said the service could eventually be offered to international markets if the ocean-monitoring and fishing-ground data meet the requirements for commercial use.
Taiwan’s fishing industry generated about NT$96.5 billion (US$3.05 billion) in output last year. The broader industry chain was worth about NT$350 billion, Agriculture Minister Chen Chun-ji (陳駿季) said, underscoring the sector’s importance to Taiwan’s economy.
Other efforts are also underway to support the sector. Systematic surveys of marine areas and fishing grounds began this year to help crews locate fishing grounds in open waters more efficiently. Chen said international cooperation could further improve the accuracy and efficiency of the work, with potential partners including Australia and Pacific island countries.

Cho says four-month salary freeze will not affect work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:37:51 UTC
16:37:51 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said Tuesday that a four-month salary freeze would not affect how he performs his duties, while urging the legislature to complete government budget reviews within legal deadlines.
Speaking at an offshore wind farm completion ceremony in Taichung, Cho said government officials should carry out their responsibilities according to law rather than seek the approval of individual lawmakers. Financial pressure would not change how he performs his duties, CNA and UDN reported.
Cho said his main concern was whether the legislature could complete budget reviews on time so government policies and infrastructure projects could proceed as planned. He added that he would continue carrying out his duties according to what he considered lawful and fair.
SETN News reported that the opposition-controlled legislature approved the 2026 central government budget on Aug. 14 and voted 59-51 to freeze Cho's salary from September through December. The motion was proposed by KMT Legislator Weng Hsiao-ling (翁曉玲).
Weng said the measure was intended to pressure Cho to comply with laws and budget requirements passed by the legislature. Under the motion, the salary can be released after the Cabinet includes the required appropriations in its budget, countersigns the relevant laws, and submits a written report to the legislature's Internal Administration Committee for approval, per UDN.
Weng has criticized the Cabinet for not including funding required under legislation covering military pay and retirement benefits for police officers and firefighters. She has also accused Cho of failing to countersign and implement legislation passed by lawmakers.
The salary freeze took effect Monday, the first working day of September, and covers about NT$1.49 million (US$47,200) in pay over four months, per UDN. Cho said neither financial incentives nor financial pressure would influence how he carries out his responsibilities.

Taiwan-Singapore trade surges 94% in first half of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:37:06 UTC
16:37:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan-Singapore trade surged 94.1% year over year to NT$3.78 trillion (S$152 billion) in the first half of 2026, Representative to Singapore Tung Chen-yuan (童振源) said Monday.
Taiwan surpassed China and Malaysia in 2025 to become Singapore’s largest trading partner for the first time, with bilateral goods trade reaching NT$4.24 trillion, up 46% from a year earlier, per CNA. Tung said Taiwan is likely to retain its position as Singapore’s largest trading partner for a second consecutive year.
Singapore was also Taiwan’s largest source of foreign investment during the period, with approved investments totaling NT$169.2 billion, accounting for 60.1% of Taiwan’s total foreign investment. Taiwan’s investment in Singapore reached NT$33.23 billion, making it the third-largest destination for Taiwanese overseas investment.
The economic partnership agreement between Taiwan and Singapore, known as ASTEP, took effect in 2014 and covers goods, services, investment, government procurement, and e-commerce, CNA reported. The two sides also signed an updated agreement in December 2025 to prevent double taxation and tax evasion, lowering withholding tax ceilings and strengthening tax coordination to reduce uncertainty and double-taxation risks for cross-border investment.
AI, semiconductors, and related components accounted for about 85% of Taiwan’s exports to Singapore in 2025, while related products made up about 80% of Singapore’s exports to Taiwan. On July 29, the representative office helped Ennoconn Corp. and the Singapore Manufacturing Federation organize a semiconductor and AI forum attended by executives from Google, Arm Holdings, and Intel, as well as Singapore industry representatives.
The Diplomat noted that Taiwan and Singapore play different but complementary roles in the AI supply chain, with Taiwan dominant in advanced chip manufacturing and Singapore specializing in semiconductor equipment, materials, assembly, advanced packaging, and testing. Singapore’s non-oil domestic exports to Taiwan also rose about 37.4% in 2025, the strongest growth among its major trading partners.
More than 80% of Taiwanese offshore assets were previously concentrated in Hong Kong, but 60% to 70% are now managed in Singapore, amounting to approximately NT$10.32 trillion, per The Diplomat. Singapore’s political stability, relatively low tax burden, mature private banking system, and accessible residency pathways have helped make it a preferred alternative to Hong Kong.

Politico: US Treasury Secretary told the Russian minister that the war must end

Unknown Publisher

Politico: US Treasury Secretary told the Russian minister that the war must end
Kyiv • UNN
On the sidelines of the G20, Scott Bessent urged Anton Siluanov to end the war. European officials refused to be photographed with the Russian delegation.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov during talks in Asheville, United States, on the sidelines of the G20 meeting that the war must end. Politico reported this, citing Erin Brown, the U.S. deputy secretary of the Treasury for international affairs, UNN writes.
Details
"Secretary Bessent had a productive meeting with the Russian finance minister," Brown said. Bessent "conveyed to him that the war must end, and that we want to see a peaceful outcome," she said.
A Treasury official said they discussed "Trump's plan for peace and economic growth."
The Trump administration's decision to return Russia to the meeting of representatives of the world's leading economies has meanwhile caused new tensions with European allies, the publication writes, as they want to continue isolating Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
Siluanov was present on Monday, the first day of the G20 talks organized by the United States. It was on the sidelines of the meeting that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent held a one-on-one meeting with Siluanov.
However, European officials in Asheville opposed Siluanov's participation on Monday, and the decision to include the Russian official in the meeting caused an uproar during preparations for the participants' group photo.
Brown said the decision to include Russia was made by the White House. "We follow the White House protocol," she said.
Responding to reporters' questions on Monday about including Russia in the meeting, Trump defended the decision. "We like getting along with everybody," Trump told reporters. "One of the reasons for my success is that I get along with everybody," he added.
During the meeting with Siluanov, Bessent "made it clear that the United States would not provide economic assistance to Russia until the war in Ukraine ends," a source familiar with the meeting said. When the Russian finance minister "tried to discuss areas of interest that should be addressed, Secretary Bessent firmly interrupted him and said that nothing was possible until the war ended," the source said.
Russia's inclusion marked a sharp departure from how the United States handled such gatherings after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. During the Biden administration, U.S. officials joined their European counterparts in publicly protesting Moscow's participation in international economic forums. Then-Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen was among the Western officials who walked out of the 2022 G20 meeting when a Russian official began speaking.
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil told reporters that he had made it clear "that he would not pose for a group photo with the Russian finance minister," noting that there had been no such photos in recent years.
Klingbeil said he had coordinated his position with other European officials.
"The unified European approach ultimately meant that the group photo took place without the Russian finance minister and without the Russian delegation," he said.
A U.S. Treasury spokesperson declined to comment on the controversy surrounding the photograph. On Monday evening, the country's Treasury Department published a photograph that did not include the Russian official.
During the talks in Asheville, Klingbeil said, he took the opportunity to "tell the Russian finance minister directly" that the Russian government must stop its war against Ukraine.
U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the senior Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, sharply criticized the administration's decision to include Russia.
"The Trump administration should pressure Putin and his cronies, not offer them a platform," Shaheen said. She also called on the House of Representatives to consider a new package of sanctions against Russia, which the Senate passed by an overwhelming majority earlier this month.

Norway's new king takes oath before parliament after Harald's death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:30:58 UTC
16:30:58 KST

Norway's new king takes oath before parliament after Harald's death
OSLO, Sept 1 - King Haakon VIII of Norway took an oath before parliament on Tuesday following the death of his father, pledging to uphold the Nordic country's constitution and laws in the latest in a series of ceremonies marking the passing of the crown.
Haakon's father King Harald died on Friday at the age of 89. Since then, tens of thousands of Norwegians have streamed to the royal palace to lay flowers, drawings, candles and flags.
Many have praised Harald's warmth and sense of inclusiveness, while Haakon described him as a wonderful father in his first address to the nation as sovereign.
The monarchy remains broadly popular: 72% of Norwegians support it, while 20% favour a republic or another form of government, according to a Norstat poll for broadcaster NRK published on Tuesday, the first poll on the issue taken since Harald's death.
The previous Norstat poll, conducted in May, showed support for the monarchy at 64%.
CONSTITUTIONAL MONARCHY
Haakon was driven in an open-top black 1966 Lincoln Continental through Karl Johan avenue in central Oslo, lined by soldiers and well-wishers.
The 17-minute ceremony in the 169-seat chamber underlined Norway's status as a constitutional monarchy.
The king was invited in by the president of parliament, Masud Gharahkhani, the full cabinet and lawmakers, all dressed in black, to swear the oath of allegiance to Norway's 1814 constitution, with Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra by his side.
Haakon declared: "Norwegian parliament, I promise and swear to rule the Kingdom of Norway in accordance with its constitution and laws, so help me God the Almighty and All-knowing."
In response, Gharahkhani stressed that the late king Harald "brought forth values that underpin our liberal democracy".
"Compassion was the core of his message in good times and tough times," said Gharahkhani, who arrived in the Nordic country as a child as a refugee from Iran with his family.
QUEEN METTE-MARIT TRANSPLANT COMPLICATIONS
Haakon's wife, Queen Mette-Marit, 53, who is recovering from a lung transplant in June, was due to be at Haakon's side, like Queen Sonja was in 1991 when Harald took the oath.
But on Tuesday she cancelled due to complications following her transplant, her doctor said in a statement from the royal palace.
"It is not unusual with complications after a lung transplant. The queen has had complications on some occasions with the operation, including today," said Are Holm, a pulmonologist with Oslo University Hospital.
"As a result she must be put under observation throughout the day today."
In addition to Ingrid Alexandra, 22, Prince Sverre Magnus, 20, and their grandmother, Sonja, 89, also attended.
Haakon automatically became king the moment his father died. There will be no coronation, as Norway abolished the practice in 1908.
Large crowds gathered as members of the public began paying their respects at Harald's coffin, which is lying in state at the palace chapel until September 8.
His funeral will take place in Oslo on September 9, with heads of state from around the world invited to attend. REUTERS

“We still expect net inflows in the second half, but the pace will be somewhat slower than in the first half,” said Meng Lei, China equity strategist at UBS Securities, at UBS’s annual China A-share strategy conference in Shenzhen on Tuesday.
Foreign appetite for A shares – domestic shares of mainland companies denominated and traded in yuan – hit a record in the first half. Overseas holdings reached more than 4.4 trillion yuan (US$654 billion) by the second quarter, the highest level on record, according to Meng.
However, analysts said several macroeconomic headwinds were tempering foreign capital inflows into onshore bourses.

Climate Infrastructure at Human Scale: From Water Management to Urban Cooling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

Water management, air quality, and heat mitigation are usually planned through systems much larger than the spaces where people actually experience them. Drainage networks sit below the street. Air pollution is measured across entire cities. Yet these conditions are felt much closer to the body: while waiting for a bus in the sun, walking through a flooded street, crossing an exposed plaza, or looking for somewhere to sit when the air itself feels difficult to breathe.
Heat makes this question especially urgent. As cities become warmer, streets, parks, transit areas, and other public spaces are increasingly becoming sites where design can reduce exposure through shade, planting, airflow, and water. For architecture, that brings part of climate adaptation into the spaces people use every day.

Microsoft’s email services were gradually recovering Tuesday after a technical issue disrupted access to Exchange Online and several other Microsoft 365 services worldwide.
The US technology company said mailbox connectivity had returned to expected service levels following the deployment of mitigation measures, although work to fully restore search functionality was continuing.
Users began reporting problems Monday with signing in, sending and receiving emails, searching mailbox content and completing other email-related operations.
Microsoft initially said it had identified a common failure pattern involving authentication and protocol connectivity within Exchange Online, its cloud-based email and calendar service.
The company later traced the disruption to an issue involving a core authentication configuration used by several internal services within the Exchange Online infrastructure.
Microsoft engineers conducted manual tests on individual servers before expanding remedial measures across the affected infrastructure.
“We continue to see gradual improvements to the service as our mitigation actions are applied,” the company said in an update.
It warned that users could continue to experience varying levels of disruption and email delays while recovery efforts continued.
Microsoft also said the authentication issue affected services beyond Exchange Online. Reports indicated that OneDrive for Business, SharePoint Online, Teams, Microsoft Purview and Microsoft Defender XDR were among the services experiencing disruption.
Outage-monitoring platform Downdetector recorded thousands of user reports at the height of the disruption, although its figures reflect reports submitted by users and do not represent the total number of people affected.
