Attorney-General says Hanson should reflect on behaviour after political violence claim
In short:
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has called on Senator Pauline Hanson to reflect on her own behaviour after she accused the prime minister of inciting political violence.
Anthony Albanese labelled the One Nation leader "dangerous, divisive and downright dishonest" at a Labor state conference in Queensland on Sunday.
What's next?
Politically motivated violence, threats and harassment are on the rise in Australia, with ASIO boss Mike Burgess previously warning it was "flashing red".
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has called on Pauline Hanson to reflect on her own behaviour and her party's ideology after the One Nation leader accused the prime minister of inciting political violence.
On Monday, Senator Hanson said Anthony Albanese had "crossed a line" during a Queensland Labor conference speech in which he labelled hard-right political parties "dangerous, divisive and downright dishonest".
"We simply must defeat them. We owe it to history," Mr Albanese said.
"They'll say anything and do anything to win votes. Bend any facts. Peddle misinformation and disinformation. Turn Australian against Australian. Parties like One Nation have no serious answers to our problems."
Senator Hanson on social media said the prime minister's speech went too far and the comments incited political violence.
She later told the ABC Mr Albanese's treatment of her made her feel unsafe.
"What he's doing is putting me in a position of threats against me now that I have to have federal police protection whenever I'm out here, meeting people," she said.
"It's a shame. He's caused this. I don't want it. I want to feel safe in my own country."
While Ms Rowland said it was becoming increasingly dangerous to be a high-profile female politician in Australia, she said Senator Hanson should reflect on how her own rhetoric was "encouraging" extreme behaviour.
"I don't wish any politician any ill will, irrespective of their political persuasion, but I think sometimes when comments like this are made, one needs to look at oneself and one's behaviour and the kinds of standards that they accept into their own party and their own ideology," she said.
"When you go on and you entertain some of the individuals whom she has been entertaining, who are not only convicted criminals, when you admit that you have a party that has been infiltrated by extremists and neo-Nazis, this is exactly the kind of danger to which politicians are being put in this country."
In a post to social media on Tuesday, Senator Hanson labelled Ms Rowland's comments slanderous and demanded an apology.
"No minister, especially the Attorney-General and first law officer of the country, should suggest there is any justification for threats against Australians because of the political party they support," she wrote.
Asked about the prime minister's comments, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said Mr Albanese must also be held accountable for his own "divisive and dangerous" behaviour.
"He divided Australians by race on the Voice, and what he has failed to do on many things, including with Islamic extremism, is he has failed to deal with dangerous situations," he said.
Hanson claim disingenuous, expert says
Associate professor Josh Roose, a leading expert on political violence and extremism at Deakin University, said alleging Mr Albanese's speech was particularly dangerous or divisive was a "step too far" but acknowledged threats against politicians were at an "all-time high."
"There should be zero tolerance for threats or violence against elected politicians," he said.
"However, weaponising statements that clearly aren't necessarily intended to incite violence and claiming victimhood … is disingenuous."
He said Senator Hanson appeared to be taking the opportunity to "claim victimhood" which could then be used as "political capital" and said the senator was in no position to take a higher moral ground.
"She has been well known for her political stunts over a prolonged period of time, not least of which wearing a burqa in parliament, which could be said was nothing other than an attempt to raise the political temperature," he said.
"Her rhetoric is divisive and designed to speak directly to her potential constituency."
In 2024, the senator was found to have breached the Racial Discrimination Act because of a social media post telling Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi to "piss off back to Pakistan".
One Nation MP Malcolm Roberts had also made a series of false and divisive claims, including that the COVID-19 vaccination dramatically increased miscarriage rates.
He has been criticised for sharing on his social media an image of an antisemitic mural, which he described as "the most powerful pic I've ever seen".
Last weekend, Ms Hanson put a nail into a prop coffin labelled net zero while attending a farmer rally in regional Victoria and later buried it.
The Australian Federal Police would not disclose the specifics of Senator Hanson's protection arrangement or whether there had been additional threats to her safety.
"The AFP does not comment on the protection of Parliamentarians and High Office Holders," a spokeswoman said in a statement.
Rising threats against politicians
Politically motivated violence, threats and harassment are on the rise in Australia, with ASIO boss Mike Burgess previously warning it is "flashing red".
A 2025 survey of federal politicians and their staff found 85 per cent had to deal with constituents behaving in a violent, threatening or volatile manner.
Last year, the AFP set up specialised strike teams to target extremist activity, including the sharp rise in political violence.
AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett said threats against parliamentarians had doubled over the past three years.
The AFP spent a record $523 million in protecting politicians and government buildings in 2024-25.
"Through the election period that was an enormous exercise for the AFP and a huge responsibility to protect parliamentarians and that was a success," she said in October.
"But the volume of threats remains concerning."
In 2024, police thwarted an alleged attempt to kill a NSW Labor MP, while other politicians who receive frequent threats had seen their security increased.
In June, Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie was identified for security upgrades at his home and electorate office.
Mr Albanese has repeatedly called for politicians and the public to "turn the temperature down".

German retail sales fell sharply in July, driven partly by a steep decline at petrol stations following the expiration of a fuel discount, official data showed Tuesday.
Retail sales decreased 3.4% from June, according to provisional figures from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).
Markets expected a monthly rise of 0.4% in July.
Petrol station sales plunged 9.1% after a fuel discount in effect during May and June expired.
Compared with July 2025, petrol station sales dropped 9.3%.

Online and mail-order sales declined 5.6% month-on-month and 0.8% from a year earlier.
Real sales of food products decreased more moderately, falling 0.8% from June and 0.3% compared with July 2025.
Overall retail sales were 2.5% lower than a year earlier.
Destatis revised the real monthly change for June to 0% from a previously reported decline of 0.7%.

The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) has become the world's largest regional association, bringing together countries whose combined population accounts for about half of the world's population, Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday.
“The SCO today is in fact the largest regional organization in the world, where half of the world's population lives,” Putin said at the organization's summit in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek.

The SCO was established in 2001 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan. It has since expanded to 10 full members, with India, Pakistan, Iran, and Belarus joining the organization.

The “best approach is to actually go in there and talk to him and make the argument as best as you can,” he said.
But Vance drew a clear distinction when it came to Fuentes, a far-right commentator with a long record of antisemitic statements.
“Obviously, I’m not going to go talk to a guy who’s attacked my wife or who said that Hitler was a good guy,” Vance said.
Vance also addressed what he called one of the “obvious elephants in the room”: increasing skepticism among younger Americans toward the relationship between the United States and Israel.
Rather than taking support for Israel for granted, he argued, advocates of the alliance need to explain its concrete benefits to the United States.
“What we have to do is articulate why this is in the best interest of the United States of America,” Vance said.
“I think it’s very, very important to talk about the concrete alignment of interest, and to hook the relationship on that,” he added.
The remarks came before an audience of conservative Jewish activists and donors, some of whom have been uneasy about Vance’s foreign policy instincts and his relationship with Carlson, whose commentary on Israel and Jewish issues has repeatedly drawn criticism from Jewish organizations and conservatives.
Vance’s comments suggested that his defense of the U.S.-Israel relationship rests less on appeals to tradition or sentiment than on a strategic argument: that the alliance must be explained to an increasingly skeptical generation in terms of tangible American interests.
At the same time, he defended a broader political strategy of engaging influential media figures even when their audiences or programs include views he rejects, arguing that entering those forums allows him to challenge those positions directly.
But his comments on Fuentes also marked a boundary to that approach, distinguishing between controversial figures with whom he is willing to debate and those he considers beyond the limits of legitimate engagement.

Ukrainians have begun taking out larger microloans: debt increased by 17%
Kyiv • UNN
Over six months, Ukrainians entered into 4.2 million microloan agreements. The average loan increased to UAH 9,200, while the debt rose to UAH 32.3 billion.
In the first half of 2026, Ukrainians entered into 4.2 million microloan agreements, approximately the same number as during the same period last year. However, the average loan amount increased from UAH 6,300 to UAH 9,200, while Ukrainians’ total debt grew by 17%. This is evidenced by data from the Opendatabot monitoring resource, reports UNN.
Details
"Microloans are no longer quite so micro. A total of 4.2 million agreements were signed in the first half of 2026—approximately the same number as last year. However, the average microloan amount increased noticeably: UAH 9,200 compared with UAH 6,300 a year earlier. In other words, we are taking out approximately the same number of loans, but the amounts are already larger," the post says.
According to the information provided, as of now, Ukrainians owe microfinance organizations UAH 32.3 billion. Since the beginning of the year, the amount of debt has increased by 17%, or UAH 4.7 billion.
"Meanwhile, MFIs are not complaining: the ten largest companies received UAH 12.8 billion in revenue over six months," the post says.
We would like to remind you
The NBU reports that banks expect demand for all types of loans to increase over the next 12 months. Growth is also projected in household mortgage lending.

On 15 June Somaliland’s president Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi opened an embassy in Israel with great fanfare. In December 2025 Israel had become the first country in the world to recognise this secessionist entity in northwestern Somalia. During a visit that lasted nearly a week, President Irro (as he is known) met with Israeli foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar and was also seen smiling alongside finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, a leading voice on the ethnonationalist far right. He visited the Knesset before meeting Binyamin Netanyahu to sign a declaration of strategic cooperation, whose contents have not been made public.
Somalia still considers Somaliland an integral part of its territory – but it has not had control of the region since 1991, when Somaliland declared independence amid violence after the fall of Mohamed Siad Barre’s regime. Since then the government in Hargeisa, its capital, has sought international recognition on historical grounds. First a British protectorate, then a colony, Somaliland was independent for just a few days in 1960 before merging with Somalia, which had gained independence from Italy.
Somaliland presents itself as an ‘exception’ : it is relatively stable and regularly holds elections, although the government tends towards authoritarianism, cracking down on protests. The government also highlights the territory’s strategic location on the Gulf of Aden.
Establishing official relations with Israel is part of Somaliland’s strategy for breaking out of diplomatic isolation. Hargeisa has support from conservative pro-Israel circles in the US who see Somaliland’s geostrategic value, especially for countering Chinese influence in Africa.

The search for an alternative to the dollar is on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:03:37 UTC
16:03:37 KST

On 31 July the US Treasury intervened massively in the markets to support the Japanese yen. ‘Washington’s historic intervention to prop up another nation’s currency stunned investors,’ the Financial Times wrote soon after. There hadn’t been such an intervention in nearly 30 years, so it was a clear sign of something badly amiss in the international monetary system (IMS). But why did it happen?
There are two answers. The first stems from immediate circumstances. For several years the yen’s value has been steadily declining because of the differential between the interest rate set by the Bank of Japan (1%) and those of other states, the US in particular (where rates are currently 3.5-3.75%). That’s all the encouragement investors need since it’s so easy to borrow in a cheap currency, invest the funds in one that offers a higher return, and pocket the difference. This operation is known as a carry trade. Because the yen is particularly cheap to borrow, it has long been a favourite for such speculation, and this has exerted further downward pressure on it. The yen’s gradual slide has made Japan’s imports more expensive, particularly hydrocarbons.
Rising oil prices caused by the war in Iran, combined with the dollar going above 164 yen – a level not seen in 40 years – eventually forced Tokyo to act. Since Japan needed to buy back its own currency to prop up its value, the White House feared it might try to raise funds by selling some of its holdings of US government debt – Japan is the biggest foreign holder. Large-scale selling would have pushed up (already historically high) US interest rates, something Washington was determined to avoid: 30-year borrowing costs are at levels unseen in nearly two decades. So the US Treasury stepped in to buy yen, thereby taking the world into bizarre new territory.

Things don’t look great for the US president. The war against Iran launched jointly with Israel was unpopular from the start. So what to do? He could hunker down and hope that a sporting event, a juicy news story or a hurricane will distract public attention from a war that, for the US, has not cost many lives (18 soldiers). Or he could raise the stakes of the coming election by conjuring up a monster that must be slain. Strategic consistency not being Trump’s strength, he is tacking between the two. One moment, everything is terrific thanks to his successes, which are the envy of the world; the next, beware the communist terrorists conspiring to destroy our beloved country.
Communist terrorists in the United States? Apparently so. They have even become the Republican Party’s great rallying cry. On the face of it, the murder of Brian Thompson, the CEO of a health insurance company in December 2024, the assassination of far-right influencer Charlie Kirk in September 2025 and two months later the election of socialist Zohran Mamdani as mayor of New York are disparate events that don’t portend the destruction of Wall Street or a new October Revolution. Macron, worst ever president?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:03:35 UTC
16:03:35 KST

Emmanuel Macron leaves the Élysée in eight months. And, in keeping with the political journalism tradition whereby last-minute criticism apparently makes up for a decade of deference, the brickbats are coming thick and fast. The Economist, having once regarded him as the ‘saviour of Europe’, now mocks a ‘lame duck’ president. Two Parisian courtiers have devoted a book to ‘the story of an exceptional man … who screwed things up in an exceptional way’. Alain Minc, mouthpiece of the liberal elite and once the president’s advisor, has called him ‘the Fifth Republic’s worst president’ (1).
As the Latin tag has it, Ingratis servire nefas – ‘There’s nothing to be gained from serving the ungrateful.’ And ungrateful they certainly are: since 2017 Macron has largely followed the recommendations of the Minc report (1994) and the commission chaired by Jacques Attali (2008), on which he served as deputy rapporteur. He has likewise followed the defence spending recommendations of the European Union and NATO.
More than any of his predecessors, Macron has stripped French diplomacy of the vestiges of independence that used to set it apart. Paris has adopted Kyiv’s Russia policy, Washington’s Venezuela policy, Abu Dhabi’s Iran policy and Berlin’s trade policy. It no longer has an Africa policy, since the Sahel states sent its army packing.
Macron has also completed the transformation of the state into a Committee of Private Safety, ensuring record dividends for shareholders (2). Of the EU’s 27 member states, France has become a haven for speculative funds that now control thousands of businesses, including some of the country’s most prestigious companies. The social security system no longer aspires to provide for each according to their needs, while resource-starved public services are turning into a nightmare for employees and users.
Macron has been the virtuoso exponent of the liberal, Atlanticist extreme centre. But he’s been playing out of time. A champion of globalisation and transcending traditional politics, he did not foresee either the former’s demise or the latter’s return. His supply-side strategy, discredited by the international resurgence of sovereignty and economic planning, has failed. Unemployment is on the rise, growth is stagnant. The trade deficit remains high, while almost half of France’s consumption-based carbon footprint consists of emissions generated abroad. The public finance deficit is used to justify France’s shortage of firefighters and firefighting aircraft.
As his country burned last month, Macron was photographed speeding across the water on a jet ski – a fitting image for a presidency ending with a headlong rush on two fronts. The first is Ukraine, which is intended to reunite his camp after his disastrous dissolution of the National Assembly in 2024 and give a boost to Europe’s defence industry in the name of strategic autonomy. But it comes with the risk of triggering massive German rearmament (see special report, in this issue) or even a confrontation with Russia.
The second is the erosion of civil liberties, which has been under way for several years, and has been reinforced by the recent appointment of a reactionary, François-Noël Buffet, as Defender of Rights, and government support for a presumption that police officers act in legitimate self-defence.
Five years ago, Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner for the 2027 presidential election said of Macron in Le Figaro, ‘Here’s a man who has suppressed freedoms … with unprecedented violence … And then he comes along and says Marine Le Pen is a threat to individual freedoms and democracy. It’s a joke.’
In May 2017 president-elect Macron said of Le Pen’s voters, ‘I will do everything to ensure that they no longer have any reason to vote for the extremes.’ Two terms later, we can see how well that’s turned out.

New alliances replace old certainties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:02:53 UTC
16:02:53 KST

On 7 August Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed a joint defence agreement in Mecca. It covers closer cooperation, intelligence sharing, joint military exercises and coordination between political and security officials to counter external threats. It also opens up the future prospect of greater collaboration in the defence industries, military technologies and cybersecurity.
The three countries have presented the pact as a strictly defensive alliance that is not targeted against any specific state. It chiefly reflects their desire to strengthen ties in response to the major shifts in the regional balance of power resulting from the US and Israel’s war against Iran and in the light of Tel Aviv’s expansionist ambitions.
The agreement is proof that the wider Middle East is entering a new phase of its history. This stems from the political and strategic upheavals that have occurred since 2023, which are reconfiguring power relations across a region shaped by war and the borders imposed in the early 20th century.
What looked like US disengagement under President Barack Obama (2009-17) – or at least the Middle East slipping down Washington’s priority list – contributed, after the outbreak of the Arab Spring in 2011, to the emergence of new regional configurations and economic relations.
Iran establishes dominance
Iran, pursuing an expansionist policy, established itself as the region’s major power. In 2012 its intervention in Syria temporarily saved the regime of its ally Bashar al-Assad. Its partial domination of Iraq had been enabled by the fall of Saddam Hussein in 2003 following the Anglo-American invasion. It had considerable strategic depth thanks to its political and military presence in Lebanon through Hizbullah and its support for the Houthi movement in northern Yemen. The 2015 nuclear deal brokered by the Obama administration and European governments subsequently consolidated its pre-eminent position. (…)

So here we are: Germany is a Western power just like any other. And its ruling class, freed from the historical scruples that stopped it asserting its dominance over Europe (except through fiscal austerity and trade surpluses), once again feels called to pursue a genuinely national ambition: to build ‘the strongest conventional army in Europe’. Friedrich Merz declared this a priority in his first speech to the Bundestag as chancellor in May 2025.
This Bundeswehr, soon ‘ready for war’, as defence minister Boris Pistorius is so fond of saying, will serve a triple objective, at once economic, military and strategic: reviving a faltering industrial base; protecting Europe’s northern and eastern reaches against Russia; and, with Washington’s blessing, securing German leadership of NATO in Europe.
‘We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace either,’ Merz has said. The proof: Germany’s $114bn of defence spending in 2025 means it has the world’s fourth largest military budget, behind only the US ($954bn), China ($336bn) and Russia ($190bn). Drawing on financial resources unmatched in Europe, Berlin will have spent more on armaments by the end of the decade than London and Paris combined.
This combination of economic and conventional military supremacy is destabilising the European security architecture created at the end of the cold war and exposing an imbalance that neither the façade of European integration nor the fiction of the ‘Franco-German couple’ can conceal any longer. True, bound by its international commitments, Germany is still dependent for strategic deterrence on US nuclear capabilities and, if the partnership initiated by Emmanuel Macron bears fruit, those of France. But the era when the Federal Republic was confined to the role of a ‘civilian power’ with no military autonomy is coming to an end.

To accelerate rearmament, Germany’s federal government has stepped up military procurement, but without any real strategic direction or effective political oversight. The country’s leading arms manufacturer, Rheinmetall, has emerged as the main beneficiary of an increasingly opaque and poorly controlled defence policy.
When the Atlantic asked Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger in March why governments should spend millions on tanks when the Ukrainians have mastered cheap drone technology, he was withering: ‘This is not the technology of Lockheed Martin, General Dynamics or Rheinmetall … It’s Ukrainian housewives. They have 3D printers in the kitchen and they produce parts for drones. This is not innovation.’ This response is indicative of Papperger’s self-assurance and ambition to compete with US giants several times his company’s size.
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the ‘historic turning point’ declared days later by Chancellor Olaf Scholz and the Bundestag’s vote to amend the constitutional debt brake, thereby enabling unlimited defence spending, have been a windfall for the conglomerate. And its chief executive’s satisfaction is growing in line with military expenditure, which is set to triple between 2022 and 2029, from €50.4bn a year to €153bn. Since 2022 Berlin has ordered 200 Leopard 2 tanks and 550 Boxer armoured personnel carriers; Rheinmetall supplies key components for both. Internal military projections envisage quantities five times higher in the years ahead.

Coming two days after the collapse of the €100bn Franco-German Future Combat Air System (FCAS) project over long-running leadership and workshare disputes between Airbus and Dassault, the ILA was an opportunity for Berlin to show that its determination to accelerate the militarisation of German industry remains unchanged. Meanwhile, Mercedes-Benz has formed a partnership with the Munich startup Tytan Technologies to develop drones, another example of how Berlin’s plans for €750bn in military expenditure by 2030 are encouraging struggling automotive firms to move into defence.
Three years after then chancellor Olaf Scholz announced a Zeitenwende (historical turning point) in late February 2022, the new CDU/CSU-SPD ‘grand coalition’ led by Merz has agreed to create a €500bn infrastructure fund and exempted large portions of military spending from the ‘debt-brake’ rule embedded in Germany’s constitution.

Menzel told us, ‘We were all proud of it.’
For the five years up to the conversion, the factory was under the ownership of French multinational Alstom; today it is operated by the Franco-German group KNDS. Some 300-400 workers – out of the 700 who work at the factory – are now manufacturing parts for Leopard 2 main battle tanks and Puma infantry fighting vehicles, both of which have been supplied to Ukraine. Menzel has worked at the factory for 20 years and his parents also worked there. He was a union representative during the Alstom era. ‘I think the transition was easier for me than for others because, as a rep, I took part in the negotiations and I knew what was coming.’
In 2024 Menzel, a member of the IG Metall union, was summoned to a meeting with the heads of Alstom and KNDS in Frankfurt. ‘It was already a done deal. They told us, “We’re going to close down. But there’s someone here who can offer you a new opportunity.” And for me, from that day on, the matter was settled.’ Only a small proportion of the population protested.
In early 2025 then chancellor Olaf Scholz visited Görlitz accompanied by the KNDS COO in Germany, Florian Hohenwarter. It was a high-profile visit for the town, which has a population of 56,000 and is still marked by the privatisations and mass unemployment of the 1990s. Just off the high street there are shuttered shops covered in graffiti. 07:02:43 UTC
16:02:43 KST

The cultural world doesn’t hold back when describing its predicament, which it calls brutal and destructive as well as stressful. The talk is of an existential threat, a plan to remake civilisation, democracy in peril.
It’s true that culture is under sustained attack, in terms of its funding and its freedom: in France, politicians are deprogramming events and public bodies cutting budgets. The culture ministry has part-frozen funding for 28 of the country’s top cultural institutions. The growing concentration of ownership in book publishing, the press and broadcast media has provoked outcries. There are calls to ‘switch off Bolloré’ (a major media owner) to avoid the danger of a ‘fascist takeover of the collective imagination’. While the growing influence of private patronage arouses less concern, cuts in the publicly funded arts, which are gradually becoming the new normal in the name of the need for realism, are seen as evidence of democratic backsliding.
Clearly, those employed in the cultural sector are afraid, not only for their working conditions but also, inseparably, as citizens. A new kind of coalition is forming, bringing together the whole spectrum of ‘leftwing sympathies’, to use an appealingly vague term. The culture war era is here.
The expression ‘culture war’ is now ubiquitous and has largely replaced the once-common notion of ‘hegemony’, borrowed from the philosopher and co-founder of the Italian Communist Party, Antonio Gramsci. The far right took up that concept in the early 1980s – notably influenced by the efforts of theorist Alain de Benoist – calmly reappropriating it for their own needs.
Power in the realm of ideas
Rightwing Gramscism, as de Benoist called it, was a kind of political marketing that depended on an oxymoron. Power is won first in the realm of ideas. Nothing to argue with there. But with Gramsci, things are a bit more complicated. As he wrote in his Prison Notebooks, (…)

Artificial intelligence and the left
Unknown

2026-09-01
07:02:42 UTC
16:02:42 KST

The great emancipations of the past were won on the bloodied cobblestones of the barricades. Today, they begin in the gloom of shopping centre car parks.
In July 2024, in the tiny Lancashire town of Ormskirk, Parkingeye, a British parking enforcement firm, fined Loren Cole £60. Armed with ChatGPT, the 37-year-old chef contested the charge. He beat the company in court, billed it for his time – and walked away with £462 including interest and fees.
Lancashire was Marx’s cotton country, where workers first ‘deposited’ their skill into machinery, only to watch it return as an alien power. Two centuries later an artificial intelligence (AI) model – a machine trained on humanity’s accumulated knowledge – helped one man claw back a piece of his life from another petty leviathan.
Cole is part of an army in the shadows: tenants fighting absentee landlords, migrants defending themselves against officialdom, healthcare patients challenging insurers. Revolutionary politics this isn’t. But to dismiss it entirely would be a mistake.
Many on the left have already delivered their verdict: AI means planetwide plagiarism, a climate disaster, a speculative bubble – something to be resisted, paused and socialised. They fail to see that AI is also the biggest opportunity the left has been handed in a century.
‘What can I do for you today?’
The threat is obvious: AI offers a frictionless synthetic agency that pacifies every revolutionary impulse with ‘What else can I do for you today?’ But a left that dismisses the attraction of AI as false consciousness writes its own obituary. If oppression can be contested one prompt at a time, why bother with the left at all?
Alas, Comrade ChatGPT is also a snitch. Cole’s victory over Parkingeye almost certainly became feedstock for AI models: a deposit, in the old Lancashire manner. The model inherits Cole’s cunning and compounds it. His neighbours inherit nothing: their prompt rebellions must (…)

France's winegrowers head north
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:02:40 UTC
16:02:40 KST

Just outside Latour-de-France, northwest of Perpignan, was a pile of freshly uprooted vines, one of many to be found in the Roussillon. The department of Pyrénées-Orientales is one of France’s poorest. Thirty years ago it had 50,000 hectares of vineyards. In early 2026, there were only 13,000 left, and 2,000 more are to be uprooted in the next few months. There are no plans for what to do with the abandoned land.
It’s not just in the Roussillon that panic prevails. In response to a global overproduction crisis, France’s vineyards shrank by 6% between 2003 and 2025. The Bordeaux region cut its red wine output by two thirds between 2016 and 2024. Consumption has been falling since the 1950s: today only 10% of French people drink wine daily, and half of those are over 55.
The climate crisis has made things worse by raising production costs, especially for vineyards in southern France. Between 2021 and 2025, Pyrénées-Orientales had very little precipitation; in 2023 there was only 246mm of rain, putting the department on the lower threshold of the ‘semi-arid’ category. After a respite in the winter of 2025-26, this July was the third driest on record, with less than 1mm of precipitation in the Perpignan area. Water usage restrictions revived memories of villages requiring tanker deliveries in 2023 and 2024.
The vines are dying from lack of water, yet the varieties grown locally are some of Europe’s most drought-resistant. At the height of the drought, the Estagel cooperative’s concrete tanks, built to store wines such as Muscat de Rivesaltes but sitting empty, were used to hold water reserves for the fire service. Every summer in recent years has brought huge wildfires: this July 5,000 hectares burned in the Trévillach area; last August 15,000 hectares were destroyed in the Corbières.

Palestine weekly: Israel’s rightwing campaigns on anti-Palestinian abuses
Israeli ministers escalate campaign rhetoric with AI ads as Gaza strikes widen ahead of tight October election.
Ahead of an October election in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc is behind in the polls, far-right Israeli ministers have turned the machinery of occupation into campaign material over the last week – not merely as policy, but as the message itself.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, whose face already appears on campaign billboards across the occupied West Bank, released an AI-generated ad warning that he would do to the Negev and Galilee – areas with large Palestinian populations inside Israel – what he has done to the occupied West Bank by building Jewish settlements there under the slogan “Ahmed is right to be afraid”.

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir responded with his own AI video depicting overweight Palestinian prisoners entering Israeli jails on an assembly line and emerging emaciated and crying. He also published a video of himself berating Palestinian women prisoners and separately planted an Israeli flag on seized United Nations agency for Palestinian refugee (UNRWA) facilities in occupied East Jerusalem.
These were not rhetorical excesses divorced from policy; each echoed recent broader government actions or pressure this week – from seizing a UN facility to a hardening right-wing push for a post-election ground operation to reoccupy Gaza City rather than proceed with Hamas’s disarmament. As the campaign rhetoric intensified, illegal outposts multiplied, demolitions and evictions continued across the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and Gaza’s death toll widened again beyond the narrower “targeted assassination” framing to include farmers, delivery workers, fishermen and children.
Gaza’s killings returns to its old shape
Following a brief lull leading up to talks with the Trump-appointed Board of Peace, Israel had framed a return to Gaza strikes around targeting individually named “commanders” of Hamas, though this in practice also included figures from Gaza’s police force.
This week, such pretenses were set aside as the toll widened again to Gaza’s general population. A drone killed three members of the Abdin family while they farmed land in al-Qarara on August 28. Another man was reportedly killed the next day, August 29, near Deir el-Balah. Separate strikes killed at least four people working as delivery drivers or riding electric bikes, and a quadcopter dropped a bomb on children collecting water near a road junction in Gaza City’s historic Tuffah neighborhood.
On August 30, a strike near a bakery west of Deir el-Balah killed Husam Osama Nasir and three-year-old Tim Said Mahmoud Hamdan. On August 31, two Palestinians were killed and several wounded following an Israeli airstrike targeting the entrance of a residential building near the Municipality Park in Gaza City.
Hospitals were hit as well. A drone struck a medicine warehouse inside al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital in Deir el-Balah on August 29, wounding three. Hospital officials also reported that cancer medicines had run out entirely after a strike damaged the hospital’s water tanks and laboratory equipment.
Beyond the daily strikes, Israeli journalist Amir Bohbot reported in Walla News that Israel’s military leadership now views a ground operation to reoccupy Gaza City as “unavoidable”. The plan, presented by the chief of the Israeli miltary’s Southern Command which oversees military operations on the Gaza border, would involve evacuating residents to new “humanitarian zones” but is timed for after the October election.
Gaza’s Ministry of Health reported 32 additional deaths last week, bringing the toll since the October “ceasefire” to at least 1,320 by August 31, and the cumulative death toll since October 2023 to 73,456. Some 58 percent of Gaza’s population still faces “critical or catastrophic” shelter conditions, according to the latest humanitarian situation report from the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
A widening map of settler violence
In the West Bank, meanwhile, settlers’ efforts to forcefully remove Palestinians from their own homes as part of the ongoing pogrom there continued, including in al-Mughayyir, a village northeast of Ramallah, which soldiers and masked settlers jointly raided on the evening of August 30.
Soldiers shot four residents, sealing the village’s only entrance while settlers besieged a home and loaded stolen property onto a pickup truck.
Beyond al-Mughayyir and Qusra – where Israeli authorities erected three new metal roadblocks encircling the Ras al-Ain hilltop on August 27 – settler violence spanned dozens of incidents this week, according to reports by the Palestinian news agency Wafa and OCHA. In al-Karmel, south of Hebron, soldiers opened fire on a vehicle carrying women home from a wedding on August 27, wounding Sanaa Abu Aram, Doaa al-Hroush and 14-year-old Lana al-Hroush.
In Beita, south of Nablus, settlers attacked and ransacked homes on August 30; Israeli NGO B’Tselem said such vandalism is “routine” and “carried out with the full backing of the Israeli authorities”, with soldiers sometimes participating and other times simply standing by.
Late on August 30, two Palestinians were killed and one detained in an Israeli raid on Nablus city. Elsewhere, among a litany of other incidents in the occupied West Bank, settlers set fire to a grove in Turmus Ayya north of Ramallah, assaulted a former Bethlehem governor, beat two elderly sisters picking figs in Silwad, abducted a British protective-presence activist in Masafer Yatta and stripped gates from Palestinian farmland southeast of Bethlehem, according to Wafa and reports from local activists.
Land seizures, outposts and demolitions
All the while, the Israeli state accelerated the land seizures that Smotrich is now campaigning on. Israel issued a military order seizing land around al-Bireh on the outskirts of Ramallah to encircle the nearby Psagot settlement – illegal under international law – with a “security route”. This is one of 46 such buffer-zone orders issued since October 2023, according to maps and documents shared by the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.
In Nahalin, west of Bethlehem, settlers leveled land to expand Beitar Illit under what a local source said was the direct supervision of the settlement administration. Similar work began near al-Minya to convert an outpost into a full settlement, according to Wafa.
Separately, the Israeli monitoring group Peace Now reported that settlers have established at least 26 new outposts specifically within Area B – nominally under full or partial Palestinian civil administration – over the past two and a half years, with more than 100sq km (39sq miles) now under settler control across Areas A and B combined.
As illegal Israeli outposts were built or expanded, demolitions of Palestinian homes continued. On August 31, Israeli forces demolished two homes in Nablus city and began large-scale demolitions in the al-Saqi area of Birzeit, north of Ramallah, according to Wafa. The commission reported 80 Israeli demolition operations in July alone.
At Qusra, dozens of settlers stormed the besieged area again on August 29, attacking a home under construction with stones. When soldiers arrived some 40 minutes later, they detained and beat the Palestinian residents rather than the settlers, who left without being arrested. Offering rare condemnation of settler violence, Netanyahu called the attackers a “handful of rioters” – but made no mention of the lack of arrests of marauding settlers in the area.

Raygun told her that the worst that could happen is that the whole world could laugh at her.
"She was like, 'Do you think that's reasonable?'"

Raygun didn't get a single vote from any of the judges at the Olympics during her rounds.

"Sometimes this all feels like a really wild dream," Raygun says in a voiceover at the start of the doco.
"It just still feels surreal to me.
"It's like I've been charged with some crime."
She reveals she's given up her job in academia, leaving things open-ended as to what comes next for her.

Almost half of terrorism arrests in Great Britain since 9/11 have been in past year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:00:48 UTC
16:00:48 KST

Almost half of all terrorism arrests in Great Britain since the 9/11 attacks on the twin towers in 2001 have come in the past year, official data shows.
There have been 6,539 arrests for terror-related activity in Great Britain since the 2001 attacks and 3,021 of those arrests were in the year ending 31 March 2026, according to the Home Office.
The increase coincides with the proscription of Palestine Action, which came into effect on 5 July last year and has led to thousands of arrests of people for allegedly supporting the direct action protest group, the first such group to be banned under the Terrorism Act.
The ban, which has been criticised by UN experts, NGOs, a former director of public prosecutions and a former director of the security services, is the subject of a continuing legal challenge, which will next be heard at the UK supreme court on 4 November.
Ruth Ehrlich, the director of external relations at Liberty, which intervened in the legal challenge, said: “The staggering increase in arrests over the past year is the clearest indicator that the UK’s counter-terror laws are not fit for purpose.
“The government’s current definition of terrorism is so wide-ranging it captures behaviour most people would never consider terrorism. When it’s not clear what counts as terrorism, public trust collapses and without trust, counter-terror laws simply won’t work.
“This data underscores the urgent need to update the current definition of terrorism to enable current and future governments to uphold their duty to safeguard the public whilst protecting people’s rights and preventing overreach.”
The proscription led to a mass civil disobedience campaign with most of those arrested at demonstrations organised by Defend Our Juries (DOJ), where they held up placards saying: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”
Terrorism-related arrests were up 1,434% in the year ending 31 March compared with the previous 12 months. There was also a 3,761% increase in women and girls arrested and a 2,306% increase in arrests of those aged 30 and over. Earlier, this year, Raj Chada, the head of criminal defence at the law firm Hodge Jones and Allen, said: “The most common terrorist in the UK at present is a pensioner at a silent vigil holding a placard.”
DOJ says the number of arrests relating to support for Palestine Action, which targets UK entities it claims to be complicit in Israeli genocide against Palestinians, has since risen to more than 3,600, which would be over half of the arrests since 9/11.
About 2,500 people have been charged under section 13 of the Terrorism Act, which prohibits showing support for a terrorism group and carries a maximum sentence of six months in prison. DOJ says at least 50 people have been charged under section 12, which concerns inviting support for a banned group, must be heard by a jury and carries a maximum sentence of 14 years.
A DOJ spokesperson said: “These shocking statistics expose the true nature of how the British government uses terror laws. Since July 2025, thousands of peaceful protesters have been arrested under the Terrorism Act for quietly expressing opposition to genocide and standing with those who have taken direct action against it. By doing this, the government has shown that they are not using these laws to protect the public – rather to silence those who speak and act against genocide.”
In June, four Palestine Action activists became the first defendants convicted of property damage whose offending – during a 2024 raid on a factory near Bristol owned by the Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit – was deemed by a judge post-conviction to have a “terrorist connection”.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “Showing support for a proscribed organisation is against the law. Decisions to arrest are operational matters for the police and are taken on the basis of the facts and circumstances of each case.”

Thinktank reports epidemic of loneliness among England’s ‘disconnected’ young
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:00:48 UTC
16:00:48 KST

The number of young people with no close friends has risen fivefold since 2014 as a result of growing up in a “bleak world” dominated by austerity, the pandemic and social media.
New research paints a sobering picture of how 11- to 24-year-olds in England are increasingly lonely, isolated and “disconnected” from themselves, peers and wider society.
“Young people in England are becoming dramatically more isolated from one another, with one in 20 now reporting that they have no close friends at all, up from one in 100 in 2014,” according to a report by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) thinktank called “the loneliest generation”.
Among the same age group to which that friendlessness applied – 16- to 21-year-olds – the proportion with at least three close friends also fell significantly. The number saying they had that many friends fell from 85% in 2012-14 to 72% in 2023-25, IPPR found.
The report rejected the idea that today’s generation was less resilient than its predecessors. Instead, it said youth club closures, unaffordable housing, the popularity of TikTok and a loss of self-esteem among young people had contributed to a recent sharp decline in their mental wellbeing.
Young people’s relationships also appeared less strong than before. The proportion of 14- and 15-year-olds who were completely or very happy with their friendships fell from 86% to 76% between the periods 2012-14 and 2023-25.
“The foundations of a good adolescence have eroded. A generation are coming of age in the shadow of a digital childhood, a pandemic and the erosion of the services and spaces that once helped them navigate the journey to adulthood,” the report said.
At the same time, young people’s transition to adulthood had been blocked and their childhood prolonged. “The traditional indicators of early adulthood are all happening much later, leaving young people in a longer, hollower and more precarious adolescence,” said IPPR.
According to the report, buying and renting a house had become harder, with the average age of a first-time buyer now 34 and nearly one in five young people spending half of their income on rent.
The reduced number of 16- to 24-year-olds starting an apprenticeship and the growth of “Neets” – young adults who are not in education, employment or training – was also deemed to be preventing them from becoming independent adults.
“Ever more young people are stuck in limbo: they are no longer children and yet are unable to access adult life,” the report added.
“Kids aren’t snowflakes. This is a rational response to a bleak world we have left for them”, said Avnee Morjaria, an associate director with the thinktank.
“We have stripped away too many of the places, services and routes into adulthood that help young people build confidence, connection and hope,” she said.
The IPPR based its findings on interviews with 150 young people and analysis of official data, including the National Centre for Social Research’s Understanding Society dataset.
Big changes in politics, society and technology have resulted in many young people feeling “disconnected from themselves. They no longer feel they have the support they need to realise their big ambitions. When they reflect on their lives, they conclude they have little control over what happens next,” said the IPPR report.
Disconnection was said to be reflected in the rise of doomscrolling – “a fundamentally solitary activity [that] has become the daily pastime of a generation”.
The report said young people’s disconnection with society was illustrated by their belief that health, education and support services were not set up to serve their needs.
The IPPR report added: “Today’s disconnection is the result of political choices made by adults in the name of neoliberalism. Our young people have grown up in a country reshaped by ideology that professes that ‘there is no such thing as society’.
“The disconnection young people describe can trace its origins back to a shift away from collectivism and towards the privatisation and marketisation of public services and assets, the adoption of identity politics over the politics of inclusion and a deference to unaccountable tech oligarchs.”
The IPPR’s findings echoed research carried out last December by Prof Eamon McCrory, the chief executive of the Anna Freud mental health charity in London, which blamed “social thinning” – the loss of in-person social interaction between adolescents – as a primary driver of the pronounced rise in anxiety, depression, self-harm and other mental health problems among young people, especially girls and young women.
“A profound thinning in the real-world social ecology – the social relationships, spaces and infrastructures – that once supported adolescent development” was as important in explaining the collapse in young people’s mental health as their immersion in digital technology, he argued.
Andy Bell, the chief executive of the Centre for Mental Health thinktank, said that the IPPR report presented “a very worrying picture about young people’s experiences of growing up in Britain today. Isolation and loneliness are toxic to our mental and physical health and young people feel increasingly alone”.

Beveridge revisited: Simon Callow film celebrates the radical co-founder of Britain’s welfare state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:00:48 UTC
16:00:48 KST

A new film that addresses issues fundamental to the new prime minister’s declared mission will star Simon Callow as a historical British political figure.
The hero of The Man With the Plan is William Beveridge, who helped to lay the foundations of the postwar welfare state. It shows that the Liberal peer was much more radical than is usually assumed – and certainly far more so than Churchill anticipated when he asked Beveridge to draw up a report into the future of Britain’s fragmented social insurance and national health system after the second world war.
Despite its misleadingly dull title, Social Insurance and Allied Services, Beveridge’s report caused a sensation: on the day it was published in 1942, a mile-long queue formed outside the government’s stationery office in Kingsway, central London. More than 650,000 copies were sold.
Now The Man With the Plan is about to tour the country – with a viewing on the eve of the Labour Party conference in Liverpool – to be shown mainly in small venues including libraries and community centres.
It was written and directed by Christine Edzard, who, with Olivier Stockman, the film’s producer, runs Sands Films Studio in Rotherhithe in London, where the film was shot. It is the home of the film studio; the Sands Films Cinema Club, which organises public screenings; a music room which hosts live events and concerts; and an acclaimed collection of period costumes. Edzard and Stockman’s previous films include Little Dorrit, As You Like It and, in 2018, an adaptation of Czech classic The Good Soldier Schwejk.
In The Man With the Plan, a young student called Flea, played by newcomer Sophie Jenkin, embarks on a journey and comes across Beveridge’s “five giants”: want, disease, squalor (voiced by Miriam Margolyes), idleness and ignorance. Puzzled by sceptics and opponents of the plan, she confronts a landlord, a skiver, some journalists (portrayed as sheep), politicians and city traders as well as the devil (played by a seductive Alan Cox).
Participants in the film include campaigning standup comedian Mark Thomas and Sir Michael Marmot, professor of epidemiology and public health at University College London. Beveridge’s words are spoken verbatim by actor Simon Callow. Prevention of ill health may begin with health centres, says Beveridge, but it also “spreads into problems of sanitation, housing, nutrition. One of the main efforts should be directed to improving housing – there lies the scope for raising standards of living and improving health and defeating the giant squalor.”
Beveridge continues: “A satisfactory scheme of social insurance also assumes the maintenance of employment and the prevention of mass unemployment: the giant idleness.”
During her travels, Flea faces fierce opposition to a “living wage”, defence spending, the role of the private sector in the NHS, and the privatisation of public utilities. Beveridge’s opponents mock his ambition to abolish want, and the need for an economic policy to maintain productive employment.
A sneering choir sings: “Minimum wages cause unemployment … minimum wages cause inflation … minimum wages cause spiralling prices … What of the nation’s debt? Think of the national debt! What of our defence spending? Defence from what?” A narrator intervenes to remind viewers that “the state is the people. The state is not some dictator or Google or Amazon – or ‘they’. The state is you. You!”
Flea asks Marmot whether he thinks Beveridge’s plan could be possible today. He replies: “Not just possible today, but necessary, vital, today. We have to address the causes of the causes – and they reside in those five giants of Beveridge. So we need social action, we need to rediscover the public good.”
For many people, probably most, this is utopian. But, as this film shows, the charge of utopianism should not be used as an excuse for political leaders simply to reject all his ambitious aims, as successive governments have done. Andy Burnham take note.

Nimbys can’t stand in the way of Labour’s legacy: a 21st-century new town boom | Polly Toynbee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:00:47 UTC
16:00:47 KST

New towns will again be a lasting Labour legacy, just as in the eras of Clement Attlee and Harold Wilson. Those monuments to optimism, created in the mid-20th century by pulling down slums and building better, will be joined by seven more in an attempt to ease the housing crisis.
Enfield has been the exemplar, its proposed 21,000-home new town enthusiastically backed by its previous Labour council, which was struggling with 3,000 families expensively dumped into miserable temporary accommodation, and, I’m told, 7,000 on the waiting list. But in May’s elections, the great anti-Labour storm brought in a regime resisting the new town in every way it can. A minority Conservative group, propped up by the Greens (yes, Tory-backing Greens), informed the government that it was “withdrawing”. Both parties had run on an anti-new town campaign.
Enfield council’s Tory leader, Alessandro Georgiou, gave me this quote, but no interview: “We were elected on a clear mandate to protect Enfield’s green belt, and we have honoured that commitment by formally withdrawing from the new town process.” But there is no “process”, as it was never in a council’s power to block a new town.
Devolution and localism? Only so far. Major infrastructure of national importance can’t, won’t and shouldn’t be stopped by local nimbys. Extending the grid, new power generation, waste recycling, transport by rail, air or ports, reservoirs and water treatment would never happen without planning from above. Building a new town falls under the regional control of the mayor, who has oversight of the interests of a far wider population. The London mayor, Sadiq Khan, is faced with a desperate housing shortage. He has the say-so here, and strongly supports new town plans for Enfield and Thamesmead. But pleading the interests of unhoused people rather than the voters in their patch will get councillors unseated, which is why they’re always brandishing alternative plans for building elsewhere, not here.
Enfield is the perfect borough for a new town, with excellent rail connections. Opponents protest that it is green belt land, but that’s not how much of it feels. Step out at Crews Hill station and all around is a cluster of glasshouses and garden centres, an unplanned sprawl. There is some charm in its haphazardness, but it is exactly what the government calls “grey belt” – technically green belt, but concreted over, one way or another. Chase Park, the other part of the plan, is described in government plans as “low-quality agricultural land”.
I was taken round by Ergin Erbil, who was the Labour council leader until he was defeated in May. He understands housing need: he has just moved into a privately rented two-bedroom flat with his wife and children. “I’ve a degree, a reasonable job, but we’ll never afford to buy,” he tells me. He agrees with Khan’s office: when the mayor and the then housing minister Steve Reed last year proposed cutting the affordable housing quota for fast-tracked developments from 35% to 20%, one official said: “20% of something is better than 35% of nothing.”
Local campaigners call Enfield London’s “green lungs”. But do golfing greens really count? Weirdly unnatural and often closed to the public, they are estimated to swallow billions of litres of water a year in England. The new town would mean building 5,500 homes over an area including Crews Hill golf club, to great protest from its members, who each pay up to £1,980 a year. Enfield has five other golf courses, part of a London “golf belt”.
Weighing some green belt loss against gaining 21,000 homes goes to the heart of political values. Enfield’s Green councillors made their choice: by protesting against the new town, they gave the council to the Conservatives.
New towns were always mocked by Tories for their New Jerusalem optimism. But the housing minister, Matthew Pennycook, tells me he has been speaking to planners from the last wave who can warn him of things they got wrong, and steer him towards what worked best. Don’t build them around the car, but rather public transport. Don’t build suburban garden cities when only high-density housing guarantees a big enough community to support frequent buses, busy shops, schools, clinics, leisure and new enterprises. Lack of civic planning failed to build enough housing for decades, while covering the countryside with isolated clumps of executive homes.
And these planners have proved themselves: after the contemptuous snobbery that greeted its birth almost 60 years ago, Milton Keynes has recently been declared one of the UK’s best places to live.
- 
  Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

kengo kuma honored with andrée putman lifetime achievement award 2027

Kengo Kuma will receive the Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award at the 2027 Créateurs Design Awards ceremony in Paris. Presented on January 16th, 2027, at the Shangri-La Paris, the award recognizes Kuma’s more than three-decade-long career and his continued exploration of the relationship between architecture and nature, material, and Japanese tradition.
Born in Yokohama in 1954, Kuma founded Kengo Kuma & Associates in Tokyo in 1990 before opening a Paris office in 2008. Over the years, his practice has developed an extensive international portfolio, ranging from the V&A Dundeein Scotland to the Japan National Stadium in Tokyo. His recent projects also include the Saint-Denis Pleyel station in Paris, completed in 2024.
‘In my design practice, I consider myself a long-distance runner. I believe the most important thing is to keep running over the long term with a single goal in mind: achieving harmony between humans and nature. Writing is also a vital part of this journey; the ideas that come to me while running often take the form of essays and books. More than anything, I am honored that the Lifetime Achievement Award recognizes the entirety of everything I do,’says Kengo Kuma.
ARCHITECTURE BETWEEN TRADITION AND THE NATURAL WORLD
The announcement frames the Japanese architect’s work around a question that has remained central to his practice: how architecture might restore a relationship between people and the natural world. The Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award acknowledges the broader trajectory of that pursuit across architecture, writing, teaching, and design.
Alongside his architectural practice, Kuma has served as a professor at the University of Tokyo since 2009. His work continues to move between contemporary construction and references to Japanese architectural traditions, with an emphasis on material expression and the relationship between buildings and their surroundings.
‘For more than three decades, Kengo Kuma has asked how architecture can restore the relationship between people and the natural world, and he has answered on every continent. Our members chose to honor not a single building but the entirety of that pursuit, in the spirit of dialogue between tradition and modernity that Andrée Putman herself embodied,’ says Yuri Xavier, Co-Founder of the Créateurs Design Awards.

More than 1.2 million Flemish children and young people are returning to school this morning.
In pre-school education (mainstream and special needs), there were around 256,900 registered pupils last year. In primary education the figure was 456,400 pupils. Secondary education (mainstream and special) counted 501,900 pupils. For this year it’s too early to provide accurate figures.
For 170,000 members of the teaching staff, too, the new 2026–2027 school year begins today. They have been busy with the preparations for some time now.
Minister Demir appeals to parents and grandparents
On social media site Facebook Flemish Education Minister Zuhal Demir (Flemish nationalist N-VA) has wished everyone a happy new school year. It will be a challenging school year, given the many changes being introduced.
“We are still giving young people a good foundation. But we need to do better. And we are doing everything we can to get back on the right track,” she writes.
Demir’s main appeal is for people to work together. “It reminds me of the famous words of the late John F. Kennedy: ‘Ask not what your country can do for you – ask what you can do for your country.’"
“In that same spirit, I would like to ask parents, grandparents, businesses and everyone who cares deeply about education: don’t just ask what education can do for your children, but also what you can do for our education system.”
What are the changes?
Nursery and primary schools must introduce nearly 1,000 new minimum learning goals (what pupils must know and be able to do) over the next four years.
In Year 2, separate language classes will be introduced for non-Dutch-speaking newcomers.
In secondary education, staff training days have been abolished and there will also be fewer assessment days.
Today is already a full school day, and this will also be the case for the last day of term.
In future every school must have a behavioural expert on the staff to help create a calmer environment and establish routines in and around the classroom.

Times Square stabbing in NYC leaves 1 dead, assailant killed
September 1, 2026
A woman with two kitchen knives fatally stabbed one person and wounded another in New York City's popular Times Square on Monday before police shot and killed her, officials said.
The knife attack occurred just before 4:30 pm near a police substation outside One Times Square, the building known for hosting the city's annual New Year's Eve ball drop.
What do we know about the Times Square knife attack?
New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said the 49-year-old suspect from the borough of Queens pulled the knives from a shopping bag and stabbed a 68-year-old man in the abdomen as he exited a subway station with his wife. She then attacked a 32-year-old woman, stabbing her in the abdomen. Both victims were hospitalized, with the young woman dying of her wounds. The older man is currently in stable condition, police said.
Officers surrounded the suspect and attempted to get her to drop the knives before deploying a Taser, which also failed to stop her, according to Tisch.
The suspect reportedly told officers, "I'm not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you," before advancing toward them with the knives raised.
Multiple officers then opened fire, with bystander video showing her falling to the ground, where officers handcuffed her and administered first aid. She was later pronounced dead.
What did the authorities say?
"This was an extraordinarily dangerous situation unfolding in the heart of Times Square, the crossroads of the world," Tisch said.
She added the attack was random and unprovoked.
Tisch said the suspect had a documented history of mental health contacts with police, including incidents in 2018 and 2019, but no prior arrests.
Investigators do not believe the attack was terrorism-related, and police have not released the victims' identities pending notification of family.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani, told a news conference, "We know that those families' lives have been shattered by what took place today, and we will continue to hold them close as the hours and days and weeks continue from this moment."
Both Mamdani and Tisch credited the responding officers, saying their actions likely prevented further casualties.
The incident marks the second fatal stabbing in Times Square this year, following a similar attack in May, even as the New York City's overall homicide rate has dropped sharply to one of its lowest totals in decades.

Swiss trade with Cuba stifled by fears of US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Swiss trade with Cuba stifled by fears of US sanctions
The Cuban economy is in tatters. And Swiss companies are finding it harder than ever to do business with the island. Bank transfers are becoming increasingly difficult, as financial institutions are wary of US sanctions.
Trade between Cuba and Switzerland now amounts to just a few million Swiss francs, and Switzerland’s main exports to Havana are paper and cardboard. While revenue stood at over CHF2.7 million ($3.4 million) in 2025, this amounted to barely CHF1 million in the first half of 2026.
Revenue from Swiss watch exports shrank from CHF1.4 million in 2025 to just over CHF357,000 in the first half of 2026. Meanwhile, Swiss pharmaceutical exports have fallen to just four figures: exports in this sector came to just under CHF9,000 from January to June 2026.
According to the Swiss-Cuban Chamber of Commerce (SwissCubanCham), this is not due to a lack of business interest. “When a Swiss company does business with Cuba, bank orders, invoices or guarantees can be issued by state banks. But the company almost never manages to collect the payments,” explains Ursin Mirer, president of SwissCubanCham. It often fails because payments cannot actually be processed.
One of the problems lies in Cuba’s state-dominated economic system and the chronic shortage of foreign currency. This is why Cuban entities are regularly unable to settle their debts to foreign companies.
However, it is also due to the United States tightening its long-standing sanctions against Cuba last year. Financial service providers in Europe and Latin America are therefore looking to minimise their risk by carrying out as few transactions as possible with countries affected by US sanctions. This is referred to as de-risking: financial service providers tend to reduce or terminate business relationships if they are considered to be at potential risk of sanctions. This apparently goes so far that a Swiss businessman or businesswoman might even travel to Havana with a suitcase full of cash to pay local partners.
Consequently, fewer Swiss companies are interested in economic relations with Cuba. This has become evident to SwissCubanCham. “Today we have only around 40 member companies, compared with 60 or 70 a few years ago. The companies don’t feel protected,” Mirer says.
When Cuba becomes a banking risk: the case of Swiss tour operators
One example of a Swiss company that specialises in Cuba and is grappling with difficulties is Caribbean Tours, a Zurich-based tour operator that has specialised in trips to Cuba for the past 26 years. “In recent years, we brought around 15,000 tourists to Cuba every year. Today, there are practically none left, resulting in a complete collapse in our turnover,” explains owner Reto Rüfenacht.
But Rüfenacht is not only facing problems in his direct business dealings with Cuba. He is also experiencing a knock-on effect from international financial controls and US secondary sanctions.
Caribbean Tours supplies holiday packages to major European tour operators such as DERTOUR Group and Kuoni. According to Rüfenacht, however, the risk associated with Cuba also affects activities that have no direct connection to the island. “Every one of our bank transfers is automatically linked to Cuba by the banks’ control systems, even when they involve completely different destinations such as Mexico or Belize,” he says.
To be able to pay its local partners on the island, the company therefore sometimes has to resort to unusual solutions. “European customers pay us in Swiss francs in Switzerland, but to get the funds to Cuba, at the moment I sometimes take the cash with me in my suitcase,” Rüfenacht explains. “The money has to arrive directly on the island so that we can pay for local services, tour guides and hotels.”
European companies also under pressure
European companies doing business with Cuba face the same problems. “The United States claims territorial jurisdiction as soon as a transaction has a link to its financial system,” explains Cedric Ryngaert, professor of public international law at Utrecht University. “The mere involvement of an American correspondent bank handling clearing in US dollars may be sufficient. This can cause a European transaction to fall under US jurisdiction.”
More
Cuban diplomats eye Switzerland in bid to ease US economic pressure
To protect European companies, there is the Blocking Statute, an EU regulation that prohibits European companies from complying with extraterritorial US sanctions. In practice, however, the effectiveness of this regulation is limited.
“The Blocking Statute does not work perfectly,” Ryngaert explains. “It prohibits European companies from complying with US sanctions. However, many banks still prefer to minimise risks, so they terminate or restrict certain business relationships to avoid potential consequences on the US market.”
According to Ryngaert, many financial institutions therefore attribute such decisions to general internal risk assessments, rather than openly stating that they are following US guidelines. The result is that, for many European companies doing business with Cuba, financial channels are becoming more complicated, more expensive and less secure.
When even Panama is no longer an option
For years, some Swiss companies have been trying to find alternative ways to process payments with Cuba. One of the key hubs was Panama, which historically played a significant role in Cuban financial transactions.
“It was still possible to work with certain banks and use Panama to transfer money to Cuba. Or, conversely, to send money from Cuba to Panama and subsequently receive payments via Spain or other countries,” explains Mirer of SwissCubanCham.
But this channel, too, is now effectively closed. With growing pressure from US sanctions and international financial controls, Panama’s banks have severely restricted or even ceased their activities relating to Cuba. “Today, it’s not possible to conduct business with Cuba via Panama. What used to be possible is now hardly possible at all,” Mirer says.
More
Switzerland closes a chapter on strengthening Cuban autonomy
A market without guarantees
To revitalise economic relations between Switzerland and Cuba, other structural conditions would need to be put in place. “First and foremost is legal certainty, followed by genuine protection for foreign companies and, finally, the question of currency,” Mirer explains.
Small to medium-sized Swiss businesses, which are less able to manage late payments and financial difficulties, have gradually reduced or ceased their activities. Those remaining are primarily international conglomerates such as Nestlé and Roche, or a handful of smaller companies that are persevering.
