In New York, amid protests and criticism of RSS, Bhagwat addressed concerns about exclusion; in Toronto, he explained how Hindu society should organise and lead internationally without imposing its beliefs.
“The word Hindu cannot be defined by any specific language, through any specific worship or through any living style,” he said. The dais reflected that wider outreach: former Alberta premier and federal cabinet minister Jason Kenney and Kashmir Singh Dhaliwal of the Khalsa Diwan Society joined Bhagwat, placing a senior Canadian political figure and a representative of a Sikh institution alongside the RSS chief at a gathering opposed by sections of the South Asian community.“We have to build our society in every country, all over the world, which is an exemplary society for the world,” Bhagwat said at the “Hindu Vishwa Bandhu — Embrace the World in Friendship” event. The programme in Vaughan, in the Greater Toronto Area, was organised by Canadian Hindus for Outreach, Relations and Dialogue.Presenting India’s global role as one based on service rather than power, Bhagwat said: “It became ‘vishwaguru’, not ‘mahashakti’.”
Whenever help had been sought during an international crisis, he said, India had not refused. “This is the tradition. This is the DNA of Bharat.”Bhagwat said the RSS organised Hindus “exactly for this purpose — and nothing else”, describing the purpose as developing individuals who would dedicate themselves to serving humanity.The RSS chief coupled the call for organisation with a message on civic responsibility. People connected with India but settled elsewhere, he said, “have to be honest, contributing citizens of that country”. At the same time, they should take to the world an outlook in which individuals, society and the environment could progress without harming one another.
He said this should be done through conduct rather than imposition. “We don’t force,” Bhagwat said. “We are the leaders who lead from within and lead by example.” He added: “Hindus respect all. Hindus accept all.”Going beyond the familiar expression “unity in diversity”, Bhagwat said Hindu tradition also recognised “diversities of unity”. Different identities, he argued, were expressions of an underlying oneness. “Diversity is never a problem for unity,” he said. “All the diversities are expressions of unity.”Bhagwat’s visit came despite demands from New Democratic Party and civil-society groups that he be denied entry to Canada. How prices in Tunisia have skyrocketed since the Arab Spring

How prices in Tunisia have skyrocketed since the Arab Spring
Al Jazeera tracked the cost of common food items and compared them with pre-revolution prices in 2010.
In Tunisia, the cost-of-living crisis has outlasted the government it once toppled.
On December 17, 2010, street vendor Mohamed Bouazizi set himself on fire in Sidi Bouzid following years of police harassment, setting off protests driven by unemployment, corruption, rising living costs and police brutality.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 48 migrants buried in Tunisia’s coastal town of Ben Guerdane
- list 2 of 4At least 12 dead, 54 injured as wildfires ravage northeastern Algeria
- list 3 of 4Qatar pledges support for efforts to end Libya’s political division
- list 4 of 4Tunisia swelters as power cuts disrupt water supplies
The movement, which became known as the Arab Spring, ultimately toppled longtime President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali and four other leaders around the Arab world.
Nearly 16 years later, however, Tunisians are still facing a cost-of-living crisis that some say is worse than ever.
To show how much everyday prices have changed, Al Jazeera tracked the cost of common food items and compared them with their 2010 prices.
Dinar has lost half its value against the dollar
In December 2010, one United States dollar bought 1.47 Tunisian dinars. Today it buys 2.93, meaning each dinar is only worth half (49 percent) the dollar value it was worth 15 years ago.
Tunisia buys much of its food abroad and pays for it in dollars and euros. A weaker dinar means each of those purchases costs more, and shoppers see it at the till.
The cost of daily essentials
Prices at the supermarket tell the story.
In 2010, eight Tunisian dinars bought 4kg (8.8lb) of tomatoes, half a kg (1.1lb) of chicken and a litre (34oz) of cooking oil. Today the same eight dinars buys less than half of that. The price of tomatoes has risen 113 percent; chicken, 118 percent; and cooking oil, 129 percent.
Prices of vegetables have climbed higher still. Carrots now cost 428 percent more (that is more than five times) than they did in 2010, potatoes 268 percent. Beef, already the most expensive item on the list, has risen 290 percent (nearly four times) to 52.5 dinars a kg – or about $18.
Rice, still tightly price-controlled, is the outlier at 10 percent higher.
Abdessattar*, 55, from El Jem, says that with the exception of subsidised goods, the increases are hard to miss. “You feel that 20, 30 or 40 dinars don’t buy much any more,” he tells Al Jazeera. Butter, cheese, cleaning products and school snacks have all risen in price since last year.
The graphic below sets average 2010 prices from the Tunisian monthly statistics bulletin against those recorded this week.
Tunisia has subsidised basic food items since 1970, when it established the General Compensation Fund (Caisse Generale de Compensation). The state holds prices for certain staples below market rate and pays producers and importers the difference.
Items have been removed from the list over the decades, however. In late 2022, the government agreed to gradually phase out universal food subsidies in favour of targeted cash transfers to secure an IMF loan, but President Kais Saied halted the implementation of these terms in 2023.
The result is a two-tier basket: Subsidised goods have kept their fixed prices, while unsubsidised food prices have surged.
‘The results were really, really disappointing’
Hamed el-Matri is an engineer and political activist who now lives in Qatar. He was in Tunisia during the 2010 uprising and says he was on its front lines.
El-Matri recalls how the uprising was driven by socioeconomic demands, including jobs, freedom and dignity.
“The expectations at the time were very high. But, when I see the situation today, or even across the last 15 years, the results were really, really disappointing,” he tells Al Jazeera.
El-Matri says the 15 years cannot be treated as one period. He describes 2011 to 2021 as “a stumbling democratic transition” and what followed as “a kind of populist totalitarian rule, with a very aggressive rhetoric but quite unclear policy”.
El-Matri says that over the past five years, economic systems in Tunisia have more than weakened, if not collapsed. He explains that investment has almost stopped, and the economy is not far from stagnation.
‘Public transport is no longer reliable’
Yassine*, 44, a father in Tunis, says preparing his children for the new school year has become a source of anxiety. Subsidised notebooks and other cheap school supplies have disappeared from shops, he says, and families are buying second-hand books and materials from one another instead.
Transport is another worry. “Public transport is no longer reliable, so we’re forced to use private transport. It has become a major worry for every Tunisian,” he says.
He points to cooking oil, which once cost one dinar per litre but is now sold only in a version costing five dinars a litre.
The strain shows at every occasion. During the recent Eid holidays, Yassine says, most people he knew could not celebrate properly, and many bought second-hand clothes.
‘People can no longer meet basic needs’
Hanen*, 45, a factory worker in Tunis, told Al Jazeera that prices have risen so fast that “people can no longer meet basic needs”. Red meat, which once sold for 20 dinars per kg, now costs 60 or more, she says, and the price of medicine climbs daily. Staples including canned tomatoes, sugar and cooking oil have all gone up sharply, along with fruit and vegetables. “The price hikes are extreme. It’s abnormal,” she says.
*Some names have been changed for anonymity.

Portugal: Kiala aims to bring Black authors from the margins to the heart of publishing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:34:25 UTC
15:34:25 KST

The imprint founded by Elga Fontes entered the market in May to tackle the lack of Black authors and show their work goes beyond racism, discrimination or suffering. In 2026 it will publish two books and already has its 2027 list agreed.
Kiala (source in Portuguese) was born from an idea that had been on Elga Fontes' mind for years: creating room in the Portuguese publishing market for Black authors. The imprint of the publishing house Vírgula d’Interrogação officially entered the market in May this year and intends to publish books exclusively by Black authors, but its founder rejects the notion that this amounts to setting up a closed-off space or a literary category of its own.
"Kiala is a word in Kimbundu [one of Angola's Bantu languages] that means to illuminate or bring light," explains Elga Fontes, who saw in the name a concise expression of what she wanted to build. The idea began to take shape about two years ago, when, then working as an editor at Vírgula d’Interrogação, she presented the project to Diana Almeida, the publishing director. After getting the green light, roughly two years of brand-building followed.
The need for the imprint arose in part from Elga Fontes' own experience as a reader and publishing professional. During her master's degree, she analysed the catalogue of a Portuguese publisher and found that, among the hundreds of books brought out in the three years she examined, only about 10% were by non‑white authors. Later she extended her analysis to other publishing groups and also followed the new releases announced by publishers with which she partners as a content creator.
The conclusion, she tells Euronews, was similar: "There was, and still is, a lack of space for books by Black authors." In Portugal, she adds, she is not aware of any formal study or platform that systematically tracks racial representation in the publishing market.
For Elga Fontes, the problem cannot be pinned on a single player in the process of getting a manuscript published, from editors, literary agents and critics to readers themselves and what they look for. The Portuguese market is small and fragile, publishers chase titles with commercial potential and social media tends to amplify books that already attract attention. At the same time, she believes, some readers are less open to works that stray from what is seen as the norm.
"There is no culprit. And Kiala is not intended as a criticism, it is meant as encouragement," she says.
An imprint to break out of the stereotype
One of the principles guiding Kiala is precisely to push back against the idea that literature by Black authors must necessarily be about racial experience. For the publisher and founder, talking about a single "Black experience" is reductive: Black people's lives are diverse, even if some are marked by common problems such as racism.
The imprint also wants to challenge the automatic link between Black authors and stories of pain. "With Kiala we also wanted to unsettle the notion that a Black person can only write about racism and suffering", she explains.
The problem, she adds, also lies in the way works are assessed. "We tend to see the creations of Black people as an exception, not as universal," she says. A white author can write about virtually any topic and have the quality of their work acknowledged regardless of the subject; for Black authors, she believes, that principle does not always hold.
That is why Kiala is not only looking for books centred on racial issues. Its first title, Feminismo na Periferia (source in Portuguese) by US writer, activist and cultural critic Mikki Kendall, "is a non‑fiction book that challenges a feminism presented as universal and addresses themes such as ethnicity, class, poverty and violence".
The second title, scheduled for November, will be The Death of Vivek Oji, by Akwaeke Emezi, who is from Nigeria. A celebrated novel, originally published in English in 2020, it explores identity, discovery and family and is also rooted in aspects of Nigerian society.
Several criteria shape the choice of titles. The team tries to understand "what conversation this book might spark or continue in Portugal" and what readers may find in it. "A good book is a book that never stops saying what it has to say. That is our guiding star when choosing our books. A book that has a lot to say," sums up Elga Fontes, pointing to this idea as one of the main selection criteria.
"Not every Black person gets published"
The imprint explicitly uses race as a criterion to tackle an inequality that Elga Fontes sees as very real, but not as a sufficient condition for publication.
"Our racial criterion is purely instrumental," she explains. "It is not a statement that Black authors form a homogeneous literary category that has to be confined to a single space."
Asked about the possibility that Kiala might end up pushing Black authors to the margins of the wider market, instead of fully integrating them into it, she rejects that interpretation.
"Kiala is present across the publishing market, as far as we can manage. We do not have just a Kiala bookshop, we do not have just a little corner where Black authors can be. Our aim and our work is precisely to bring in the voices of Black authors where they are not yet present, where they are scarcely represented, because Kiala is an imprint of 'affirmative action' created to correct a very real under‑representation in the publishing market," she argues.
For that reason, Kiala wants to be part of the traditional book market, rather than setting up a parallel circuit just for Black authors. The aim is "to normalise the idea of walking into a Portuguese bookshop and finding Black authors from different countries, in different genres and with different perspectives, without that being seen as something exceptional".
The imprint itself acknowledges that it may be seen as a niche publisher — or even as a racist publisher. "There are many possible perceptions, but it is not my job to police what people think of Kiala. My job is simply to publish books by Black authors," she stresses.
The same concern for representation extends to the team that produces the books. Proofreaders, translators, designers and other professionals must meet quality standards, but Kiala also seeks to bring in Black professionals. The founder believes such professionals do exist in Portugal, even if they "face more obstacles to entry, because there are in fact very few working actively with publishers".
Kiala is not the pioneer of this kind of project. Internationally, Elga Fontes mentions, for instance, New Beacon, a publisher and bookshop in the United Kingdom that only publishes Black authors. In Brazil there is Malê, which publishes Afro‑Brazilian literature. In the United States there is Black Classic Press, which focuses solely on classics of literature by Black authors. In the heart of Paris, Présence Africaine Editions, created in 1949 to provide thinkers, writers and researchers from Africa and the diaspora "with a sounding board" so that their literary and scientific work can benefit from better conditions of dissemination and accessibility across the world.
"Many people did this work long before Kiala existed. I believe Kiala exists because of that work and because of those people," says Elga Fontes.
Growing without losing sight of the mission
Kiala is still small for now. In 2026 two books will be published and, in 2027, the plan is to increase to three. The 2027 list is already closed and will consist entirely of fiction. For 2028, the publisher intends to bring out Portuguese authors.
The ambition, she explains, is not to become a big publisher at any cost, but to build a benchmark catalogue and show that it is possible to combine editorial quality, economic sustainability and "survive by betting on Black authors".
"Of course we would like to recoup the investment we make in our books," says Elga Fontes. "That alone would be ideal for us, as it would allow us to go on publishing more and more."
Among the main obstacles are distribution, production costs, the price of paper and the small size of the Portuguese market. The publisher also points to the cost of living and the country's reading habits as factors that make it particularly difficult for independent publishers to remain sustainable.
"As for reading habits, although they have grown considerably in recent years, Portugal remains one of the countries that read the least in Europe. That is why books have to be more expensive, because publishers need to be able to make a profit, to stay afloat, to pay workers, to pay for the production of books," she explains.
Despite the challenges, she sees one goal as more important than Kiala's own growth: reaching the point where the imprint is no longer needed.
"I would very much like Kiala's very premise to become obsolete, unnecessary, even absurd," she says. All it would take, she suggests, is for the imprint's work to encourage other publishers and publishing projects to invest more in Black authors.
Until then, Kiala will go on seeking out voices that, in its founder's view, still do not have enough space on Portuguese bookshop shelves. One absence that surprises her most is Octavia E. Butler, the African American author considered a major reference in science‑fiction literature, whose books have only begun to be published in Portugal in the past few years.
Ultimately, the aim is for Black authors to stop being an exception in bookshop catalogues. And for them to be read simply for what they write, whether it is about identity, fantasy, humour, science fiction, family or any other subject. "There are many books by Black authors that are not about racism, and thank goodness for that," concludes Elga Fontes.
Elga Fontes' reading suggestions
- Lendários, by Tracy Deonn, published by Desrotina in October 2022
- The Vanishing Half, by Brit Bennett, published by Alfaguara Portugal in June 2021
- A Cama Onde Elas Se Deitam, deFaridah Àbike-Íymídé, published by Desrotina in May 2024
- Finding Me, by Viola Davis, published by Cultura Editora in August 2024
- Irmãs Brown, by Talia Hibbert, series published by Desrotina

Ukraine updates: Russia hits Kyiv for sixth straight day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:34:00 UTC
15:34:00 KST

Ukraine: Russia threatens 'devastating' Baltic response
Published September 1, 2026last updated September 1, 2026
What you need to know
Follow this blog for the latest news on Russia's war in Ukraine on September 1, 2026.
- Russian strikes Kyiv, Odesa on first day of school year, killing at least 12
- EU ministers focus on Ukraine air defenses, military support at Ireland talks
- Drones trigger brief NATO response at Estonia's border with Russia
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google.
Vessels hit near Odesa: Russia Defense Ministry
Russia's military struck two cargo ships carrying military goods, the country's Defense Ministry said.
The vessels were hit in the port of Pivdennyi, near the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa, and in the Black Sea.
Russia, Ukraine hit each other's energy infrastructure
A Russian strike caused damage to a thermal power plant in the region of Odesa, southern Ukraine, state energy company Naftogaz said.
Elsewhere, Ukraine's military intelligence said that a strike by the Ukrainian army hit Russia's Novatek oil complex in the region of Leningrad.
Kyiv and Moscow have been exchanging blows in the past 24 hours, with energy infrastructure being targeted as part of the mutual strikes.
Russia threatens 'devastating' response amid Baltic tensions
Russia says it will "deliver a devastating response" to any hostile action against it in the Baltic region.
"In the event of a further escalation of the military-political situation in the Baltic region, it must be emphasized once again: Russia's response to the instigators of reckless anti-Russian ventures will be decisive. And they need to know this - it will be devastating for them," Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at her weekly briefing.
It's not exactly clear what she was referring to, but earlier in the day a fire broke out at Russia's Baltic port of Ust-Luga following a drone attack according to the regional governor.
Separately, NATO scrambled military aircraft due to a possible air threat in Latvia's airspace near the town of Ludza, close to the Russian border.
Russia sees no peace gains from Black Sea attack moratorium
Russia does not believe a moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea, a key grain shipping route, would bring a peaceful resolution to the war closer, Interfax quoted Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko as saying Tuesday.
Both sides have stepped up attacks in the Black Sea in recent months, driving global grain prices higher.
In mid-August, Ukraine reportedly conveyed an offer to Russia through a third party proposing that both sides halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea.
Monday, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said his country had prepared a plan to ensure the safe passage of grain through the Black Sea and was working on an agreement similar to the 2022 grain deal that would facilitate safe exports.
EU's Kallas says more interceptors needed to shield Ukrainian cities
On Tuesday, European Union defense ministers discussed Ukraine's shortage of interceptor missiles needed to protect cities and civilians.
"July and August have been the deadliest months for civilians in Ukraine," the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said on Tuesday about the deadly wave of strikes on Ukraine.
"Russia is really escalating, to hurt the people of Ukraine as much as possible, to break them," she said on the sidelines of a gathering of EU defense ministers in Wicklow in Ireland.
Against that backdrop, she said securing additional interceptors remains difficult because some countries face security pressures closer to home.
"We know that some of the countries have interceptors that will expire soon. So it would be very good if those would be given to Ukraine," Kallas said.
Beyond efforts to bolster air defenses, the EU is also working to unlock additional financial support for Ukraine's armed forces in the coming days.
Germany says response to drone find near Ukrainian plane will be measured
Germany's foreign minister said Berlin would respond in a measured way to the discovery of an explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.
Johann Wadephul said the government was coordinating its approach with NATO and European Union partners.
The case sparked widespread speculation that Russia was responsible, though Berlin has not publicly assigned blame.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pledged a clear-cut response.
Despite declining to publicly assign responsibility, Wadephul stressed Germany would not be deterred by the incident.
"Germany will not be intimidated in any way, and that will continue to be the fundamental stance of our policy," Wadephul said, adding that Berlin "stands side by side with our Ukrainian partner."
"Russia must know that Germany is a stabilizing force in Europe, one that is always prepared to negotiate, but which will not be intimidated in any way."
Ukraine says Russian missile and drone assault hits Kyiv, Odesa
Ukraine's air force said Russia struck at least 28 locations in overnight attacks that continued into Tuesday, with debris falling at several additional sites.
The attack targeted Kyiv and the Odesa region and involved ballistic, cruise and anti-radar missiles, along with more than 200 drones and decoys.
At least 11 people were killed in the capital region:
- Seven people were killed in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district; three others were wounded, including a child.
- One Indian citizen was reported among those killed
- One person was killed in the Holosiivskyi district after a building was hit and caught fire.
- Three people were killed and 12 were injured elsewhere in the Kyiv region.
In Odesa, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian strike "deliberately damaged a border crossing point on the border with Romania, as well as export infrastructure."
Ukraine reports August strikes on 54 Russian 'Shadow Fleet' ships
Russia and Ukraine are not only battling for dominance in the air with drones, but are also increasingly taking the drone war to the seas.
The commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert Brov, said Tuesday that his force struck 54 Russian "shadow fleet" vessels in August.
He did not immediately provide additional details.
Separately, Russia's state news agency Tass reported that Russia attacked "more than 150 seagoing vessels involved in military cargo deliveries for the Ukrainian army, as well as accompanying patrol boats, during the summer."
At least 70 of those attacks were recorded in August.
EU defense ministers meet in Ireland to discuss Ukraine air defenses
European Union defense ministers are gathering in Wicklow, south of Dublin, for talks that are expected to focus on bolstering Ukraine's air defenses.
Moscow has taken advantage of Ukraine's shortage of US-built air defense missiles to pummel the country, while Kyiv has hit back against Russian infrastructure with its own long-range drone strikes.
There is also concern over Russia's apparent move to ramp up operations in Europe.
The ministers are also expected to discuss the bloc's support for Ukraine, including the implementation of a €90 billion ($104 billion) loan for Kyiv.
The loan, approved in April, aims to assist Kyiv with its most urgent economic and military needs as it continues to fight against Russia's full-scale invasion.
The talks are also expected cover further military assistance and closer cooperation between Ukraine's and the EU's defense industries.
Ministers are also expected to discuss the growing role of space in modern defense strategy.
EU foreign ministers are due to arrive later on Tuesday ahead of separate talks on Wednesday focused on continued support for Ukraine.
NATO jets scrambled after drones briefly enter Estonian airspace
NATO military aircraft were scrambled overnight after drones flew close to Estonia's border and briefly entered Estonian airspace, the country's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.
The aircraft were launched from Amari Air Base, Tsahkna wrote in a post on social media.
"NATO reacted swiftly and exactly as planned. The Alliance is vigilant and ready to protect Allied territory," he added.
It was not immediately clear who launched the drones.
The incident highlights ongoing security concerns along NATO's eastern flank and is seen as a consequence of Russia's continuing war against Ukraine.
Russian strike on Kyiv railway depot kills 7
Russia targeted Ukraine's capital for a sixth day in a row, including a ballistic missile strike on a railway depot in Kyiv that killed seven people.
"The ballistic strike took the lives of 7 people, 6 of whom were our employees. 1 colleague is in hospital with injuries," Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, chief executive of Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine's state-owned railway network said, adding that "there is extensive destruction."
Emergency services said eight people were killed and five wounded in Kyiv, including three children, as fires broke out across several parts of the capital during the overnight attacks.
Elsewhere in the Kyiv region, one person was killed and nine others, including a child, were injured after missiles and drones struck an apartment building and a business facility in Boryspil.
The attacks marked the sixth consecutive day of Russian strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region.
Russia's Defense Ministry said it targeted military and energy facilities in Kyiv, Odesa, and nearby areas.
Across the border in Russia's Belgorod region, one person was killed in a Ukrainian attack, acting Governor Alexander Shuvayev said.
Welcome to our coverage
European defense ministers are meeting in Ireland today and are expected to hear from Ukraine's new acting defense minister, Yevgeniy Khmara.
He is likely to point to the latest wave of Russian attacks, now entering a sixth straight day, as Moscow continues its campaign against Kyiv and surrounding areas.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly argued that the sustained bombardment underscores the urgent need for additional air defense systems.
The meeting comes as several European countries are also strengthening their own military capabilities, partly in response to a growing number of drone-related incidents near their borders.
Overnight, Estonia reported a new drone incursion into its airspace, adding to concerns about regional security.
We'll be following these developments, along with other key events in Russia's war against Ukraine, throughout the day in this blog.

Ukraine: Russia threatens 'devastating' Baltic response
Published September 1, 2026last updated September 1, 2026
What you need to know
Follow this blog for the latest news on Russia's war in Ukraine on September 1, 2026.
- Russian strikes Kyiv, Odesa on first day of school year, killing at least 12
- EU ministers focus on Ukraine air defenses, military support at Ireland talks
- Drones trigger brief NATO response at Estonia's border with Russia
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google.
Vessels hit near Odesa: Russia Defense Ministry
Russia's military struck two cargo ships carrying military goods, the country's Defense Ministry said.
The vessels were hit in the port of Pivdennyi, near the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa, and in the Black Sea.
Russia, Ukraine hit each other's energy infrastructure
A Russian strike caused damage to a thermal power plant in the region of Odesa, southern Ukraine, state energy company Naftogaz said.
Elsewhere, Ukraine's military intelligence said that a strike by the Ukrainian army hit Russia's Novatek oil complex in the region of Leningrad.
Kyiv and Moscow have been exchanging blows in the past 24 hours, with energy infrastructure being targeted as part of the mutual strikes.
Russia threatens 'devastating' response amid Baltic tensions
Russia says it will "deliver a devastating response" to any hostile action against it in the Baltic region.
"In the event of a further escalation of the military-political situation in the Baltic region, it must be emphasized once again: Russia's response to the instigators of reckless anti-Russian ventures will be decisive. And they need to know this - it will be devastating for them," Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at her weekly briefing.
It's not exactly clear what she was referring to, but earlier in the day a fire broke out at Russia's Baltic port of Ust-Luga following a drone attack according to the regional governor.
Separately, NATO scrambled military aircraft due to a possible air threat in Latvia's airspace near the town of Ludza, close to the Russian border.
Russia sees no peace gains from Black Sea attack moratorium
Russia does not believe a moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea, a key grain shipping route, would bring a peaceful resolution to the war closer, Interfax quoted Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko as saying Tuesday.
Both sides have stepped up attacks in the Black Sea in recent months, driving global grain prices higher.
In mid-August, Ukraine reportedly conveyed an offer to Russia through a third party proposing that both sides halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea.
Monday, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said his country had prepared a plan to ensure the safe passage of grain through the Black Sea and was working on an agreement similar to the 2022 grain deal that would facilitate safe exports.
EU's Kallas says more interceptors needed to shield Ukrainian cities
On Tuesday, European Union defense ministers discussed Ukraine's shortage of interceptor missiles needed to protect cities and civilians.
"July and August have been the deadliest months for civilians in Ukraine," the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said on Tuesday about the deadly wave of strikes on Ukraine.
"Russia is really escalating, to hurt the people of Ukraine as much as possible, to break them," she said on the sidelines of a gathering of EU defense ministers in Wicklow in Ireland.
Against that backdrop, she said securing additional interceptors remains difficult because some countries face security pressures closer to home.
"We know that some of the countries have interceptors that will expire soon. So it would be very good if those would be given to Ukraine," Kallas said.
Beyond efforts to bolster air defenses, the EU is also working to unlock additional financial support for Ukraine's armed forces in the coming days.
Germany says response to drone find near Ukrainian plane will be measured
Germany's foreign minister said Berlin would respond in a measured way to the discovery of an explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.
Johann Wadephul said the government was coordinating its approach with NATO and European Union partners.
The case sparked widespread speculation that Russia was responsible, though Berlin has not publicly assigned blame.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pledged a clear-cut response.
Despite declining to publicly assign responsibility, Wadephul stressed Germany would not be deterred by the incident.
"Germany will not be intimidated in any way, and that will continue to be the fundamental stance of our policy," Wadephul said, adding that Berlin "stands side by side with our Ukrainian partner."
"Russia must know that Germany is a stabilizing force in Europe, one that is always prepared to negotiate, but which will not be intimidated in any way."
Ukraine says Russian missile and drone assault hits Kyiv, Odesa
Ukraine's air force said Russia struck at least 28 locations in overnight attacks that continued into Tuesday, with debris falling at several additional sites.
The attack targeted Kyiv and the Odesa region and involved ballistic, cruise and anti-radar missiles, along with more than 200 drones and decoys.
At least 11 people were killed in the capital region:
- Seven people were killed in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district; three others were wounded, including a child.
- One Indian citizen was reported among those killed
- One person was killed in the Holosiivskyi district after a building was hit and caught fire.
- Three people were killed and 12 were injured elsewhere in the Kyiv region.
In Odesa, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian strike "deliberately damaged a border crossing point on the border with Romania, as well as export infrastructure."
Ukraine reports August strikes on 54 Russian 'Shadow Fleet' ships
Russia and Ukraine are not only battling for dominance in the air with drones, but are also increasingly taking the drone war to the seas.
The commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert Brov, said Tuesday that his force struck 54 Russian "shadow fleet" vessels in August.
He did not immediately provide additional details.
Separately, Russia's state news agency Tass reported that Russia attacked "more than 150 seagoing vessels involved in military cargo deliveries for the Ukrainian army, as well as accompanying patrol boats, during the summer."
At least 70 of those attacks were recorded in August.
EU defense ministers meet in Ireland to discuss Ukraine air defenses
European Union defense ministers are gathering in Wicklow, south of Dublin, for talks that are expected to focus on bolstering Ukraine's air defenses.
Moscow has taken advantage of Ukraine's shortage of US-built air defense missiles to pummel the country, while Kyiv has hit back against Russian infrastructure with its own long-range drone strikes.
There is also concern over Russia's apparent move to ramp up operations in Europe.
The ministers are also expected to discuss the bloc's support for Ukraine, including the implementation of a €90 billion ($104 billion) loan for Kyiv.
The loan, approved in April, aims to assist Kyiv with its most urgent economic and military needs as it continues to fight against Russia's full-scale invasion.
The talks are also expected cover further military assistance and closer cooperation between Ukraine's and the EU's defense industries.
Ministers are also expected to discuss the growing role of space in modern defense strategy.
EU foreign ministers are due to arrive later on Tuesday ahead of separate talks on Wednesday focused on continued support for Ukraine.
NATO jets scrambled after drones briefly enter Estonian airspace
NATO military aircraft were scrambled overnight after drones flew close to Estonia's border and briefly entered Estonian airspace, the country's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.
The aircraft were launched from Amari Air Base, Tsahkna wrote in a post on social media.
"NATO reacted swiftly and exactly as planned. The Alliance is vigilant and ready to protect Allied territory," he added.
It was not immediately clear who launched the drones.
The incident highlights ongoing security concerns along NATO's eastern flank and is seen as a consequence of Russia's continuing war against Ukraine.
Russian strike on Kyiv railway depot kills 7
Russia targeted Ukraine's capital for a sixth day in a row, including a ballistic missile strike on a railway depot in Kyiv that killed seven people.
"The ballistic strike took the lives of 7 people, 6 of whom were our employees. 1 colleague is in hospital with injuries," Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, chief executive of Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine's state-owned railway network said, adding that "there is extensive destruction."
Emergency services said eight people were killed and five wounded in Kyiv, including three children, as fires broke out across several parts of the capital during the overnight attacks.
Elsewhere in the Kyiv region, one person was killed and nine others, including a child, were injured after missiles and drones struck an apartment building and a business facility in Boryspil.
The attacks marked the sixth consecutive day of Russian strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region.
Russia's Defense Ministry said it targeted military and energy facilities in Kyiv, Odesa, and nearby areas.
Across the border in Russia's Belgorod region, one person was killed in a Ukrainian attack, acting Governor Alexander Shuvayev said.
Welcome to our coverage
European defense ministers are meeting in Ireland today and are expected to hear from Ukraine's new acting defense minister, Yevgeniy Khmara.
He is likely to point to the latest wave of Russian attacks, now entering a sixth straight day, as Moscow continues its campaign against Kyiv and surrounding areas.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly argued that the sustained bombardment underscores the urgent need for additional air defense systems.
The meeting comes as several European countries are also strengthening their own military capabilities, partly in response to a growing number of drone-related incidents near their borders.
Overnight, Estonia reported a new drone incursion into its airspace, adding to concerns about regional security.
We'll be following these developments, along with other key events in Russia's war against Ukraine, throughout the day in this blog.

Source: Exilenova+ monitoring Telegram channel; Alexander Drozdenko, governor of Russia's Leningrad Oblast
Details: Drozdenko also claimed that Russian air defence had shot down 52 drones.
Ust-Luga is one of Russia's largest commercial seaports on the Baltic Sea. Significant volumes of strategic cargo, including oil, petroleum products, coal and mineral fertilisers, pass through the port.
The port handles about 700,000 barrels of oil per day, while Reuters reported that exports of petroleum products through Ust-Luga exceeded 32.8 million tonnes in 2025.

Background: Ukraine attacked Ust-Luga on 6 July and in March. The port suspended shipments following the March attack.

Speaking at the 26th SCO heads of state meeting in Bishkek, Pezeshkian said the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran on 13 June 2025 and 28 February 2026 were a clear aggression against the UN Charter and international law.
He said the aggression began with the assassination of the Leader, the killing of 168 students and teachers at a school in Minab, and an attack on a sports hall in Lamerd that killed and wounded 200 people on the first day of the 40-day war.
Iran, he said, imposed heavy strategic defeats on the United States and the occupying regime of Israel, forcing Washington to accept a ceasefire after failing to achieve any of its predetermined objectives.
Pezeshkian said nearly three months of talks mediated by Pakistan and Qatar led to the Islamabad memorandum of understanding on 18 June 2025. But U.S. commitment to a document bearing the American president's signature lasted less than two weeks.
"I say clearly: if the United States returns to its commitments in the memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate. Unlike America, my country has a brilliant record of honouring its international commitments and has always acted in accordance with the principles of international law," he said.
The president also proposed three economic initiatives for the SCO: deepening financial and banking cooperation, including wider use of national currencies and the establishment of an SCO bank; creating an SCO export insurance and investment union; and forming an SCO energy consortium.
He also proposed establishing an SCO strategic security studies centre and a parliamentary forum of SCO member states.
Pezeshkian said security and development are inseparable, and the organisation must address both security and economic dimensions simultaneously to play an effective role toward multilateralism.

Israeli forces demolish Palestinian Christian home, illegal settlers displace another family
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:32:31 UTC
15:32:31 KST

A senior Palestinian church affairs committee on Tuesday condemned the demolition of a Christian family’s home and the bulldozing of its farmland by Israeli occupation forces in the occupied West Bank.
The Presidential Higher Committee for Church Affairs said in a statement that Israeli forces demolished a home and razed agricultural land belonging to the Christian Abed family in the al-Saqi area of Birzeit, north of Ramallah.
In a separate incident, the Christian family of Bashir Naim Kouna was forced to leave its home in the village of Taybeh, east of Ramallah, following persistent threats and attacks by illegal Israeli settlers, the committee added.
The family had moved into the house only about a week earlier after spending more than $300,000 building and furnishing it over seven years, according to the Al-Baidar Organization for the Defense of Bedouin Rights.
The group said the house had all required municipal permits.
The church affairs committee described the demolition, land razing, and displacement as violations of international law and part of a policy aimed at seizing Palestinian land and imposing illegal settlement expansion by force.
It said attacks on the homes and lands of Palestinian Christians amount to “an attack on the entire Palestinian presence,” stressing that Christians are an integral part of the Palestinian people, history, and identity.
The committee said demolitions, land seizures, and forced displacement continue across the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, Masafer Yatta, the Jordan Valley, and the governorates of Nablus, Bethlehem, and Ramallah, as well as in Gaza.
It called on the international community to halt the violations and hold those responsible accountable.
Taybeh is the only remaining Palestinian town whose population is entirely Christian.
On August 11, the committee warned that Israeli attacks on Christian communities are threatening their deeply rooted presence in Palestine.
It said the assaults are “no longer isolated incidents” but part of an ongoing pattern involving settler violence, land confiscation, illegal settlement expansion, and restrictions on freedom of worship.
The committee also warned that Taybeh’s population is falling as growing numbers of Christian families had been forced to leave Palestine since 2023 amid escalating Israeli attacks.
Like other Palestinian towns in the occupied West Bank, Taybeh has faced escalating attacks by illegal Israeli settlers against Palestinians and their property, aimed at pressuring them to leave their land, particularly in areas adjacent to illegal settlements and settlement outposts.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,489,640 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:32:28 UTC
15:32:28 KST

Russia has lost around 1,489,640 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 31.
The figure includes 1,440 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,320 tanks, 25,257 armored combat vehicles, 142,332 vehicles and fuel tanks, 48,954 artillery systems, 2,079 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,597 air defense systems, 440 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 2,452 unmanned ground systems, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs).
The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Major developer faces liquidation as funding deadline brought forward

Bathla Group's collapse may be imminent as funding deadline brought forward
In short:
Hopes for an eleventh-hour cash injection into the crumbling Bathla Group are fading fast as some lenders take matters into their own hands.
The administrators have brought forward a deadline to the end of Tuesday to see if the business has any chance of survival.
What's next?
Administrators are preparing to shut down the company imminently if funding cannot be secured.
Hopes for crumbling property developer Bathla Group are deteriorating fast as a crucial deadline was brought forward while some lenders took action into their own hands.
Bathla's administrator, Teneo, has said it is preparing to shut down the company by the end of the day as hopes of securing $20 million in emergency funding fade away.
The realisation came after a meeting with lenders on Monday night failed to secure the commitment needed.
Teneo senior managing director Stephen Longley told Nine's Today Show: "We'll start planning at the end of the day for the wind down of the business," and said the situation was "very dire".
"We're running out of hope for a holistic solution to finish the 45 construction projects," he said.
"We've had intensive discussions with lenders, but I don't think we're going to get enough funding in place."
Mr Longley's latest comments were more pessimistic than yesterday, when he told ABC's The Business that he remained hopeful of securing a last-minute lifeline from lenders.
He also said, at a press conference on Monday, the property firm had "no cash", but could still complete at least 45 construction projects if it received more funding.
Human cost of financial collapse
Some of Bathla's 350 staff have not been paid for eight weeks while the developer has accumulated debts exceeding $3.2 billion.
Bathla's administration has left the fate of 200 building projects across NSW in jeopardy, with about 2,000 homes under construction and another 13,000 in its development pipeline.
Some private credit lenders have taken control of individual worksites and will be responsible for delivering particular projects.
The ABC understands a 312-apartment block development in Pemulwuy in Sydney's west is going ahead after the lender, PAG, made a commitment to continue paying contractors directly.
A manufacturing contractor who provided his first name, Moqvul, said that PAG had told him not to worry and continue working on the Pemulwuy site.
Mustafa, the owner of a kitchen joinery business, told the ABC he had received a written commitment from PAG, but it did not extend to any other Bathla sites.
He was also unsure what it meant for outstanding bills that his business was owed.
"No-one is giving us any clear image of where we are heading," Mustafa said.
"We are stressed. We owe the ATO, we owe the suppliers, we owe the workers."
Another contractor, Charbel, said the situation "didn't look good" and said he had four kids and was owed "a fair bit" of money from Bathla.
Administrators had tried tapping existing lenders for extra funds and late last week asked the New South Wales government for a $20 million lifeline to keep the business afloat.
However, the state government refused to offer any bailout money.
Teneo also said it had borrowed $1 million from its own head office so Bathla Group could afford to pay for vehicle registrations, petrol and "just to keep the lights on".
Its situation has also left questions around how home buyers will be impacted, including deposits.
Mr Longley said on Monday as many as 1,000 deposits could have been paid to the developer, and that some of those may have been used.
"Some of the contracts allow the deposits to be used by the business, deposits have been used as the contracts allow," he said.

‘The mountains are changing’: What the floods tell us about the future of India’s Himalayas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:30:46 UTC
15:30:46 KST

It has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floods swallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.
Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. The disaster unfolded when a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.
Among the 275 Indians missing at the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’s Isha Foundation spiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have been rescued as of Monday.
For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.
“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.
The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke to Dr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert on glacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.
What are the climate- or glacier-related risks emerging across the Himalayas?
“There are different forms of cryosphere and how they pose a hazard. In a layperson’s terms, the cryosphere is where water exists in solid form, for example a glacier. When it melts, it forms glacial lakes. If they have an outburst, they can cause damage downstream.
Another cryospheric component is glacier ice. This is what we’ve seen in Nepal, where a glacier detachment happened. The frontal part of the glacier detached from the main glacier and eventually led to a debris flow.
The third component is permafrost. They exist widely in the Himalayas, but there has not been much monitoring because it’s very difficult. Everything – these lakes, glaciers and permafrost – are all hazards. Unless they’re triggered, they would not cause damage.
With climate change, these grounds will go above zero degrees and will start to degrade. These would need very little … to mobilise debris. We might expect a higher frequency of debris flows in the future. We won’t know how they are getting conditioned, unless we have some monitoring stations and scientific investigation.
And given the Himalayas are very vast, monitoring every part of it becomes tricky. It can be the mountain ranges within India, or maybe outside India, eventually, which drains into the Indian subcontinent. That needs to be well studied.”
How big are the downstream risks for India?
“Right now, this is a gap in scientific studies; nothing [is] quantified yet. There is direct evidence of climate impacts, even in the Indian part of the Himalayas. The number of glacial lakes is increasing, the size of glacial lakes is increasing, the volume of glacial lakes is increasing, and glaciers are retreating. The risk exists because it might happen any time.”
Which parts of India are the most vulnerable?
“Everyone in the Himalayas, every Himalayan state has hazards. We can’t deny it. If you look at the eastern side, they have a lot of glacial lakes. They have already reached their maximum extent. Most full-grown lakes are about to reach their limits, like maximum extent. In the western Himalayas or even the central Himalayas, there’s a lot of scope for the lakes because they have not reached their full extent. As the glaciers would retreat, they would keep on growing.
We are still unsure when the status is going to change for any of these states. That’s a very, very difficult question, and I don’t think anyone [can] answer it at this moment without any scientific investigation.”
How would you describe India’s early warning systems and disaster preparedness?
“The National Disaster Management Authority is taking proactive steps now with the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) Risk Mitigation Programme to install early-warning systems.
Maybe an early warning system should be community-based. It should be for the people and by the people. It’s not always the scientist or the policymakers who can actually make this work at its full potential. We need to have local knowledge, involve the communities to make them more effective.”
How long will it take to have these systems in place?
“I have no idea because each of these organisations are working at their own pace. They have their own style of working. I’m sure it is going to happen soon. I can just comment on the areas where I know, and I’ve been in touch.”
Is prevention possible, or can it only minimise the damage?
“Prevention is possible, but it is very expensive: computationally, financially and manpower-wise. Minimising is also possible. It would require a lot of intervention in the high mountains, which is very difficult in those terrains.
We know that the mountains are changing and the hazard levels are increasing, so the only way forward is to minimise the exposure to the risk below. That means how much of the hazard is going to interact with the downstream. If something is in the path, we remove them.”
To support relief efforts in Nepal, you can contribute to the prime minister’s Disaster Relief Fund here.
What else we’re reading about
RSS in New York | Last weekend, Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat addressed Indian Americans at New York’s Madison Square Garden calling for global unity. The Quint reported that the newly formed group behind the event has RSS links. The visit was opposed by several diaspora groups that reject the RSS’ Hindu nationalist ideology and criticise its record on minority rights.
Books and backlash | A reading session organised in Ahmedabad after a private school was forced to drop books by Malala Yousafzai and Anne Frank was allegedly disrupted by a group affiliated with the rightwing Bajrang Dal. Three people have been arrested.
Indian cinema abroad | Two Indian films have been selected for the Busan International film festival, which begins on 6 October. Birds in the Dark, by Shashank Walia, explores an unexpected human connection while Tamil writer-director Sailesh Rathnakumar’s Selvi is set in the world of home-care workers.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Photographer Aashim Tyagi (@aashim), who once documented Art Deco architecture in Gujarat’s Balasinor, suggests a prehistoric side quest: “I was intrigued by the town’s reputation as the ‘Jurassic Park of India’ and a little digging led me to a dinosaur museum in neighbouring Raiyoli. It’s set amid open fields near one of Asia’s largest fossil beds where Rajasaurus narmadensis and a dozen other species once roamed. Much of the museum and the village’s paleontological preservation is owed to Aaliya Babi of Balasinor’s erstwhile royal family, earning her the nickname ‘Dinosaur Princess’. Balasinor and its dinosaur museum are a worthwhile detour from Ahmedabad or Baroda.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
176
India ranked 176th, second from the bottom, in the 2026 Environmental Performance Index, which evaluates countries on environmental health, climate change and ecosystem vitality. The country recorded negative values on air-quality indicators but showed an improvement on the index’s 10-year change metric. In 2022, when India had been ranked last, the central government had dismissed the EPI’s conclusions, saying it used “unscientific methods”.

Locals raise doubts about explosives factory to be built in western Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Locals raise doubts about explosives factory to be built in western Estonia
The state plans to build an explosives plant in Piirsalu in Lääne County, but residents in the village of Piirsalu feel decisions are being made over their heads.
The state plans to build an explosives plant in Piirsalu that would produce up to 1,200 tonnes of RDX a year and create 75 or more jobs.
The area is already home to a Defense Forces tactical training area and a Defense League shooting range. A Soviet missile base was once located here.
The local Lääne-Nigula government supported the building of the plant.
"The arrival of jobs has some impact in areas with a declining population. Since a sufficient number of better-paying jobs are expected there, that is quite an important argument," said Mayor Janno Randmaa.
Council Chairman Sven Köster, who lives in Piirsalu a couple of kilometres from the site of the planned plant, does not see the explosives plant as a threat.
"It will be a proper chemical plant that meets European standards. During the Soviet era, there were Soviet servicemen there – with their missile forces, they certainly caused more pollution," he said.
Piirsalu is a village away from the main highway, with no shop or school. But salmon live in the river, which is why it is a nature conservation area. Many locals are concerned about how the explosives plant will affect the natural environment and their quality of life.
Village elder Lea Lai asked what would happen if the drilled wells run dry. The village elder recalled a case in Salajõe village in Lääne County, where, after lengthy disputes, a peat producer built a drinking water system.
"It is assumed that the developer or the municipality will then dig us a new well. We know that Salajõe village did not get a well for ten years. They had to prove it, prove it, prove it," Lai said.
The Ministry of Defense said studies show this is not an issue.
"As part of this environmental study, we have also carried out a groundwater study. It shows that there should in fact be no impact on local wells. The plant would draw its water from deeper groundwater layers than the local wells," said Indrek Sirp, special adviser for defence industry development at the Ministry of Defense.
Rein Kruusmaa, a member of the Risti subdistrict council, said residents draw up development plans, but when development actually arrives, it happens over the heads of local people.
"The local government operates on the basis of its development plan. Unfortunately, none of the measures in the development plan are implemented. What gets implemented are the things brought here under pressure from developers. Be it a wind farm, large solar parks, or a defense industry park," he said.
Sirp said that Europe needs explosives for the production of ammunition. In addition, the plant would create the conditions for producing ammunition in Estonia.

Kengo Kuma to Receive the 2027 Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Japanese architect Kengo Kuma has been selected to receive the Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award at the 2027 Créateurs Design Awards (CDA). The award, one of two Legacy Awards presented by the organization, recognizes a career that has influenced architecture and the built environment across generations and geographic contexts. Kuma will receive the honor during the CDA Awards Ceremony, which will take place at the Shangri-La Paris on January 16, 2027.
Born in Yokohama in 1954, Kuma founded Kengo Kuma & Associates in Tokyo in 1990 and opened a Paris office in 2008. Across more than three decades of practice, his work has explored the relationship between architecture and nature, often drawing on Japanese architectural traditions and reinterpreting them through contemporary materials, construction methods, and spatial approaches.
Among Kuma's projects are the V&A Dundee in Scotland, the FRAC Marseille, and the Cité des Arts et de la Culture in Besançon. His practice was also involved in the design of the Japan National Stadium in Tokyo, built for the 2020 Summer Olympics, and the Saint-Denis Pleyel station in Paris, which was completed in 2024. His work has extended across cultural, civic, transportation, and institutional projects in Japan and internationally.
Related Article
Christian de Portzamparc to Receive the 2026 Créateurs Design Awards Lifetime Achievement Award
Alongside his architectural practice, Kuma has maintained an academic and research-oriented career. He has been a professor at the University of Tokyo since 2009 and has previously taught at Keio University, Columbia University, and the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His work has also been accompanied by a number of international recognitions, including the Wood Design Award and Global Award for Sustainable Architecture in 2016, the Japan Art Academy Prize and Imperial Prize in 2024, and the Prix Versailles for Best Museum and the 38th Louis I. Kahn Award in 2025.
 In my design practice, I consider myself a long-distance runner. I believe the most important thing is to keep running over the long term with a single goal in mind: achieving harmony between humans and nature. Writing is also a vital part of this journey; the ideas that come to me while running often take the form of essays and books. – Kengo Kuma
The Lifetime Achievement Award is named after French designer Andrée Putman and is selected by members of the Créateurs Design Association rather than through an open submission process. Previous recipients include Norman Foster, Tadao Ando, and Christian de Portzamparc. According to Yuri Xavier, Co-Founder of the Créateurs Design Awards, the decision recognizes Kuma's continued exploration of the relationship between tradition and contemporary architecture. The announcement of Kuma as the 2027 recipient coincides with the opening of submissions for the 2027 Créateurs Design Awards. Entries will be accepted from September 1 through October 31, 2026, across 15 categories covering architecture, interior design, product design, and art and culture.

UBS scores interim win on capital buffer rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:27:33 UTC
15:27:33 KST

UBS scores interim win on capital buffer rules
UBS bank notched up an interim victory in its multi-year struggle against Switzerland’s push to make it hold billions of extra dollars in capital.
The Zurich-based bank should be able to use convertible debt, known as AT1s, for as much as 50% of the extra requirement, provided that those instruments are reformed, lawmakers from the key Economic Affairs and Taxation Committee of the Senate said on Monday.
+How to tame UBS without making the bank toothless
Since the collapse of Credit Suisse more than three years ago, the Swiss government has been seeking ways to make its lone remaining global bank crisis-proof. A key plank of its reform agenda is a capital requirement hike of around $20 billion, intended to make sure that UBS’s foreign businesses can’t sink its domestic entity.
UBS executives have argued that the measure will make it uncompetitive. The bank has tacitly backed the AT1 measures as a potential compromise.
More
Credit Suisse AT1 bond ‘rip-off’ could cost Swiss taxpayer
The “committee has backed a materially softer approach,” said Joseph Dickerson and Theo Massing, analysts at Jefferies, in a note. “The result would enable UBS to have more flexibility around how it meets the Swiss government’s demand to back foreign subsidiaries.”
Soften impact
The bank didn’t immediately comment on the committee decision. The Swiss Bankers Association, a lobby group, said in a statement that it welcomed the reform proposals for AT1 instruments but rejected the stricter capital requirements.
The committee’s endorsement, if it makes it through a legislative process due to run until at least next year, would soften the impact of the extra capital requirement on the basis that debt funding is generally cheaper than pure equity.
+ Read about the fight between UBS and Swiss regulators
The committee voted 10-2 in favor of the 50% recommendation, with one abstention.
While the upper house committee’s stance will influence the debate ahead, it’s only one step in a lengthy legislative process. Lawmakers in the more left-leaning lower house could reverse some of the concessions to UBS.
The Social Democrats, the second-largest party in parliament, issued a statement on Monday criticising the committee’s stance. That signals a potentially harder fight as the political process continues.
Bonus pool reduced
The next stop is a vote on the upper house’s floor that’s set to take place during the chamber’s autumn session from September 14 to October 2.
AT1s were born in the aftermath of the global financial crisis as a way to increase a bank’s loss-absorbing capacity. UBS is a substantial player in AT1s globally, and the debt that it has issued accounts for about 7% of the $286 billion European market.
Debt investors generally expect lower returns on their capital than equity investors. Using less equity also helps the bank’s profitability metrics and can affect bonuses.
UBS should back all of the value of its foreign units, using the combination of equity and AT1 debt, the committee said. That meets the government’s initial demand – though the finance ministry has criticised the use of AT1s as not reliable as a means of absorbing losses in a crisis.
The lawmakers backed changes to the instruments that would enable them to kick in earlier in stress situations, addressing a key weakness of AT1 debt that emerged during Credit Suisse’s decline.
Under the proposal that lawmakers backed, UBS would face several obligations in case it falls below its minimum requirement for highest-quality equity capital, CET1. According to a draft distributed to journalists, the bank would be barred from paying dividends or making any share buybacks as well as from paying coupons on its AT1 bonds.
At the same time, the bonus pool would be reduced.
Erich Ettlin, the president of the committee, said on Monday that the solution would “serve Switzerland,” and “is no victory for UBS.”
More
Switzerland outlines stricter too-big-to-fail banking rules

Shein shares fall on Hong Kong debut as parcel duties and Iran costs bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:26:17 UTC
15:26:17 KST

Shein has listed in Hong Kong after failed attempts in New York and London, as US tariffs and rising shipping costs squeeze the fast-fashion giant's profits.
Shares in fast-fashion giant Shein fell as much as 10% on their trading debut on Hong Kong's stock market on Tuesday, before recovering some of their losses, following years of delay to the company's plans to list publicly and regulatory setbacks in Europe and in the US.
Shein's initial public offering opened on 24 August, with the final share price set a week later on 31 August. Trading began the following day, on Tuesday.
The gap reflects standard IPO process, as investors placed their orders over about a week, the banks running the deal then fixed the final price and decided who got shares, and trading opened a few business days later once the exchange gave the final go-ahead.
The listing marks the end of a long search for a stock market willing to take Shein after plans to list in New York and London stalled amid scrutiny over its Chinese supply chains, forcing the company to turn to Hong Kong instead.
New US and EU tariffs on low-cost parcels from China, along with rising shipping costs from the war in Iran, have contributed to Shein's swing from a $395 million (€340mn) profit to a $99 million (€85mn) loss in the first quarter of this year.
Shein raised about $1.7 billion (€1.46bn), pricing shares at HK$48.56 (€5.33) each, in one of the city's biggest share sales this year.
"Shein's Hong Kong listing marks a new starting point," said Leigh Gui, Shein's chief financial officer, in a short speech at its listing ceremony.
But in early trading, the shares fell to below HK$44 (€4.83) before losses narrowed.
Tariffs squeeze profits
Shein has built its appeal to customers on ultra-fast, affordable fashion, delivered from China to the West within days.
However, the end of "de minimis" tariff exemptions in the US and the European Union has raised duties on low-value parcels from China, including Shein's products. Higher logistics costs, driven partly by the war in Iran, have also squeezed the company's low-price business model and profitability.
Tariff costs have forced Shein to raise prices, "cutting into its main advantage," said Jacob Cooke, CEO of WPIC Marketing + Technologies.
Back to its roots
Shein, pronounced "she-in," earlier explored listing its shares in New York and London, and moved its headquarters from China to Singapore in 2021.
But increasingly strict scrutiny by Beijing and by regulators in the US and Europe led it to embrace its Chinese roots and switch to a Hong Kong listing.
Launched in 2012 in China, much of Shein's operations were in the southern province of Guangdong before it moved its corporate headquarters out of the country.
"Guangdong is Shein's roots, and the starting point of our journey," founder Sky Xu said in a speech in February.
Pivoting its focus back to China also highlighted the advantages Shein derives from a supply chain system that "only exists" in Guangdong, said William Ma of GROW Investment Group, referring to its small-batch, fast-response manufacturing model.
Shein has hit other roadblocks in expanding in Europe. In February, the EU launched a probe into the company with a focus on "illegal" products, including alleged child sexual abuse material.
In May, Shein acquired San Francisco-based eco-friendly clothing retailer Everlane, a move some analysts said was not the best fit.
Hong Kong's IPO boost
The company's market value was roughly $27 billion (€23.2bn) as it listed in Hong Kong, a fraction of its peak valuation a few years ago.
"Shein has probably missed its golden listing window due to the shift of momentum toward AI and tariffs, which can affect valuations and profitability," said Gary Ng, a senior economist for Asia Pacific at French bank Natixis.
Still, Shein's listing is welcome news for Hong Kong, as the Chinese territory makes increasing efforts to hold onto its role as a global financial hub following a downturn in 2023.
Hong Kong's stock exchange has had a strong year for IPOs, raising more than $40 billion (€34.4bn) so far.
There is also a backlog of companies seeking to list there, said Lorraine Tan at investment research firm Morningstar.

(China Economic Roundtable) China facilitates flow of resources to strengthen regional innovation systems
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
14:23:01 CST
15:23:01 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- China is stepping up efforts to facilitate the flow of innovation resources and strengthen regional innovation systems, said the guests on the latest episode of China Economic Roundtable, an all-media talk show hosted by Xinhua News Agency.
China has vowed to improve regional innovation systems during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The systems bring together government, businesses, universities and research institutes, allowing different regions to better leverage their respective strengths and helping move research findings from laboratories toward commercial applications.
China's three international sci-tech innovation centers are Beijing (Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei), Shanghai (Yangtze River Delta), and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area.
Facilitating the flow of innovation resources, such as talent, capital, and technology, is a central focus in efforts to strengthen regional innovation systems.
Yi Tong, a researcher with the Beijing Academy of Science and Technology, said at the roundtable that Beijing is taking multiple measures to facilitate the flow and allocation of innovation resources.
The capital city has established the country's first leading group for the integrated development of education, science and technology, and talent, and rolled out three-year action to promote the commercialization of scientific and technological achievements, according to Yi.
In Shanghai, the local authorities have launched a special initiative targeting technology companies, which helps smart technology companies connect with application scenarios, accelerate commercialization and drive development across the entire value chain, said Zha Hao, chairman and CEO of Shanghai Smartlogic Technology.
In the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, efforts are also underway to remove barriers to the cross-regional flow of innovation resources, said Zhang Zhengang, a professor at South China University of Technology.
The region is building innovation platforms to pool resources, forming a model in which Hong Kong contributes scientific research, Guangdong supports commercialization and the global market provides broader opportunities for application, Zhang noted. ■

TOKYO, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Japan's benchmark 10-year government bond yield spiked to 3 percent on Tuesday, a level unseen since October 1996, amid growing concerns over the country's deteriorating fiscal health.
The barometer of long-term interest rates crossed the key threshold a day after media reported that budget requests from Japanese government ministries and agencies for fiscal 2027 were set to hit a new high of about 143 trillion yen (around 894 billion U.S. dollars).
While the figure is not final, it underscores Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's drive to ramp up spending to boost the economy, despite the fiscal constraints facing the heavily indebted nation.
The recent uptrend in Japanese government bond yields also reflects growing market expectations that the Bank of Japan will raise interest rates at its policy meeting in September.
Higher bond yields will put further pressure on Japan's debt-servicing costs. With outstanding debt twice the size of its economy, Japan's fiscal health is the worst among advanced economies, Kyodo News said. ■

Gas from major north Australian fracking project begins flowing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
14:22:37 CST
15:22:37 KST

CANBERRA, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Gas from a major fracking project in Australia's Northern Territory (NT) on Tuesday began flowing into the electricity grid eight years after a local ban on fracking was lifted.
NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro on Tuesday cut the ribbon to mark the first flow of gas from the Beetaloo sub-basin, declaring that the project will deliver long-term economic benefits.
"This project means Territory gas powering Territory homes, businesses and industry," she said in a statement.
According to the NT government, the sub-basin located about 500 km southeast of Darwin is a world-class shale gas resource, with an estimated 430 trillion cubic feet of gas in place.
The beginning of production on Tuesday by the Sydney-based Tamboran Resources, the largest acreage holder in the basin, comes eight years after the NT government lifted a moratorium on fracking that was imposed in 2016.
Finocchiaro said on Tuesday that the NT government has signed long-term fixed-rate contracts for gas from the basin that will replace costly emergency gas arrangements.
"We have secured Beetaloo gas at a fixed price the government is extremely satisfied with, locked in for the next decade," she said.
"Putting downward pressure on energy prices over time, helping to curb price increases, while also reinforcing reliability is a major step forward for the Territory."
Australian Conservation Foundation Head of Advocacy Gavan McFadzean said in a statement that fracking the Beetaloo Basin could be the most destructive and irresponsible gas project ever proposed in Australia and called for the federal government to ensure that water resources are protected. ■

Details
The invaders also deployed 10,947 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,872 shellings of populated areas and the positions of the Defense Forces.
In the Sumy region, the enemy shelled the populated areas of Mala Korchakivka, Yastrubshchyna, Pysarivka, Kucherivka, Ulanove, and Bachivsk. In addition, the area of the populated locality of Korenok came under an air strike.

On the South Slobozhanskyi axis, Ukrainian units repelled 16 enemy attacks. The invaders attempted to advance near Starytsia and Vovchanski Khutory, as well as toward Chuhunivka, Khatnie, Mala Vovcha, Dovhenke, and Okhrimivka.
