Former economic crime chief to head discipline team at Hong Kong, Macau office
Hua Liebing’s appointment fills vacancy left last year and marks another change in HKMAO’s top ranks
A veteran mainland Chinese economic crime investigator and former police official has been appointed to lead the discipline inspection and supervision group at Beijing’s top office overseeing Hong Kong affairs.
Hua Liebing, a former director of the Ministry of Public Security’s economic crime investigation bureau, fills the vacancy at the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office (HKMAO) left by Geng Changyou, who stepped down last year to become secretary of Hebei province’s Commission for Discipline Inspection.
The new appointment was revealed on Tuesday when the office updated its organisation chart on its website.
It marked another change in the office’s top ranks following the selection of Zhang Dongmei, a former vice-president of the All-China Women’s Federation, as a deputy director in March.
Hua’s appointment brings the HKMAO’s senior leadership to seven members. They include Xia Baolong, who has led the office since 2020, and deputy director Zhou Ji, who also serves as the director of Beijing’s liaison office in Hong Kong.
The appointment came a day after a meeting of the HKMAO’s leading group for Communist Party building, which was also attended by members of the discipline inspection and supervision group.

Deep-sea team joins search for missing in Cyprus ferry disaster

Deep-sea team joins search for missing in Cyprus ferry disaster
NICOSIA, Sept 1 - A specialist team from Turkey equipped to search deep waters started work on Tuesday to pinpoint the wreckage of a ferry that capsized off northern Cyprus on Sunday, with 20 people still missing.
At least eight people died when the twin-hulled vessel started taking in water and overturned shortly after leaving the port of Kyrenia with 267 passengers and crew on board.
The Turkish navy rescue vessel has a remotely operated vehicle able to search the deep water where the ferry sank, about four nautical miles off the coast, minutes after setting off for the town of Tasucu in Turkey's Mersin province.
"Once the wreck is identified, salvage operations will begin at a significant depth of 500 metres (1,640 feet), and detailed search and investigation activities will be carried out ... using a remotely operated vehicle," said Major Ulas Cesur, commander of the TCG Isin.
Survivors who scrambled to safety by clinging to part of the overturned hull were picked up by boats. Footage posted on social media appeared to show people still inside one of the compartments as others perched on the tip of the boat waiting for help. Children are among those missing.
The cause of the disaster is under investigation, though Turkish Cypriot authorities said the vessel had a valid seaworthiness certificate.
Witnesses have said the ferry, a wide-bodied catamaran, was lurching violently before crashing into the water, the impact tearing open part of its bow.
On Monday, nine people connected to the vessel’s operations were remanded in custody for three days to assist police inquiries. REUTERS

US university students associate Israel with 'genocide' against Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01

15:18:55 KST

Mucahit Oktay
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
University students in the US state of New York increasingly identify the word "genocide" as their primary association with Israel, highlighting a shift in the nation's international standing among young Americans.
The military operations, seizures, and human rights violations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank have led many to question the nation's international legitimacy.
Interviews conducted at Manhattan-based New York University (NYU) and Columbia University revealed consistent primary associations among the youth.
Samuel, a student at NYU, told Anadolu that his first thought is the genocide Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is committing against the Palestinian people. He listed his top three associations as "Netanyahu, genocide and Palestine."
Another NYU student named Maddy, with a troubled expression reflecting on her face when the word Israel was mentioned, said the word that most strongly came to her mind was "genocide".
She characterized the association as "scary," explaining that her perception of Israel is that of a country utilizing its military power against those who are significantly weaker.
One group of students collecting aid for a university association declined to comment and withdrew from an interview once they learned the topic was Israel.
At Columbia University, a student named Rom responded to the question of what comes to mind with the phrase "Let's save the world," before adding: "Let's maintain peace."
The shifting perception follows a recent assessment by Naftali Bennett, former Israeli prime minister, regarding the country's public image in the US.
“For the first time since the establishment of the State of Israel, among the American public, Israel has become a negative brand,” Bennett said in a recent interview.
“If you ask an American student, ‘Israel — what comes to mind?’ They say genocide. That’s the situation,” Bennett said.
Drawing a comparison with how countries are commonly associated with symbols, he added: “You say Italy — ‘pasta, spaghetti.’ You say Israel — ‘baby killers.’”
According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, over 73,300 Palestinians have been killed and more than 174,200 injured since Israel launched its war on Gaza in October 2023.
Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant also face arrest warrants issued by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
South Africa initiated legal proceedings against Israel at the ICJ on Dec. 29, 2023, alleging violations of the 1948 Genocide Convention.

On 1 September — the day Ukraine marks Knowledge Day, when schoolchildren and students are meant to begin the new academic year — Russia launched a massive attack on Kyiv and its region with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones. Moscow used different types of its fast, deadly weapons, including ship-launched Kalibr, and hypersonic Zircon missiles, and jet-powered drones to target the Ukrainian capital.
This attack was the culmination of a 6-day assault on the capital and region that began on 27 August. It started two days after CIA Director John Ratcliffe arrived in Moscow on 25 August. US President Donald Trump announced that the visit was linked with US-initiated peace efforts to end the war against Ukraine. Throughout this 5-day period, air raid sirens sounded every hour in the capital and region, paralyzing life in Kyiv, according to Sky News.
As early as the day after the 5-day attack began, Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky stated that Russia had destroyed about 90% of the food logistics infrastructure of retail chains, according to UkrInform.
Russia injures three children and continues the attack
As a result of the "ballistic" attack on Kyiv and the region, hits from enemy missiles and strike drones were recorded at 28 locations, and debris from downed targets fell at 10 locations, according to the Air Force of Ukraine.
In addition, some enemy missiles did not reach their targets, and the locations of those missiles are being clarified.
"Unfortunately, as a result of the Russian attack, there are dead and injured. The attack continues, with more than ten Russian drones in the airspace," the military reported.
According to the Kyiv City Military Administration, civilian infrastructure was damaged in 5 of Kyiv's 10 districts — Holosiivskyi, Darnytskyi, Dniprovskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, and Solomianskyi.
"As a result of the attack, unfortunately, 8 people died. Another 7 people were injured, including 3 children," the Kyiv authorities said.
Railway workers are still receiving treatment and remain hospitalized
Russia struck a railway facility, a critical link in the country's logistics chain, as its airways have been closed since 2022.
Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, head of the board of Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways), stated that Russia carried out a targeted ballistic attack on Kyiv's railway infrastructure. Russia killed six railway workers.
According to him, another employee was injured and is in the hospital, where they are receiving the necessary care.
He added that dozens of employees managed to take shelter and survive the attack. They are now being helped to recover from what they experienced.
Pertsovskyi noted that the strike caused "extensive destruction," including the complete destruction of one workshop, and that efforts to extinguish fires at the facility were still ongoing.
He said that, due to the attack's consequences, movement was temporarily restricted on two railway sections, but it was later restored.
Earlier, a source close to the Russian president told The Economist that Vladimir Putin most likely regarded Ratcliffe's visit as a sign of American weakness. He already interpreted former CIA Head Bill Burns' meeting with Russian authorities in 2021 the same way, where he warned about the consequences of Russia's war against Ukraine. Three months after the meeting, Russia launched the full-scale invasion.

China’s solar power capacity surpasses coal for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:18:43 UTC
15:18:43 KST

People ride bikes on a street in Beijing, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (AP Photo)
China's installed solar energy capacity has surpassed that of coal-fired power for the first time, the national energy body said on Sept. 1, hailing the milestone.
China, the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases that drive climate change, has pledged to peak carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060.
"As of the end of July this year, China's installed solar power capacity reached 1.286 billion kilowatts," the National Energy Administration (NEA) said.
"For the first time, photovoltaic installed capacity surpassed coal-fired power, becoming the largest power source category in China," it added.
The country's coal-fired power installed capacity, the energy body said, stood at 1.285 billion kilowatts.
Coal has been China's key power generation source for decades and a key driver of its planet-warming emissions.
But the country's coal-fired power generation fell by nearly 2 percent in 2025, despite rising energy demand in the world's largest emitter, data showed in February.
China has seen an explosive growth in its renewable installation, with coal's share in its energy mix edging down in recent years.
The country installed a record 315 gigawatts of solar power and 119 gigawatts of wind power capacity last year, over 80 percent of total newly installed power generation capacity, according to the China Electricity Council.

EU Frets over Kyiv’s Defences, ‘Hybrid’ Threat From Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:18:18 UTC
15:18:18 KST

EU defense and foreign ministers gathering in Ireland from Tuesday will grapple with bolstering Ukraine’s air defenses amid growing worries over Russia’s campaign to destabilize Kyiv’s European backers.
Moscow has taken advantage of Ukraine running low on US-built air defense missiles to pummel the country, while Kyiv has hit back against Russian infrastructure with its own long-range strikes.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The Russian attacks on the Ukrainians are getting harsher and harsher,” an EU official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Defense ministers -- who meet Tuesday before foreign ministers hold talks Wednesday -- are expected to speak with Ukraine’s new acting defense minister Yevgeniy Khmara.
But there appears little they can do to massively increase the supply of desperately needed air interceptors to Ukraine -- beyond pressuring European countries that still have stockpiles and urging the likes of Japan and South Korea to share more.
While the Kremlin escalates its air campaign against Ukraine, there have been growing worries that Moscow is also looking to deflect from its battlefield troubles by ramping up operations in Europe.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said his country has increasingly “found itself in the crosshairs of hybrid attackers” after an explosive-laden drone was found in August at Leipzig airport, a crucial military transport hub.
Berlin hasn’t yet officially blamed Russia over the incident -- but the clear suggestion is that the finger of blame is pointing at Moscow.
6 Wounded, Including a Child, in Russian Strikes on Dnipropetrovsk Region
Fuelling the concerns over Russia’s intentions, CIA chief John Ratcliffe paid a surprise visit to Moscow last week, with US media reporting he warned Russia against attacking any NATO country.
EU officials insist they don’t see Moscow preparing for a military attack any time soon, but they are bracing for more incidents in the grey zone beneath open conflict.
“What we see is these hybrid and then not-so-hybrid attacks continuing and our assumption is that those will go on,” the EU official said.
While Merz said that those behind the incidents in Germany will “pay for them”, Europe has struggled to counter the low-level campaign of sabotage and interference it blames on Moscow.
- Sanctions, assets, reforms -
Beyond ramping up intelligence sharing and police cooperation, the EU sees bolstering support for Ukraine and hitting Moscow with sanctions as ways to raise the costs for the Kremlin.
Brussels has floated fresh plans to add 1,600 more firms and individuals to its already long list of Russians sanctioned over the war.
Meanwhile, discussion has resurfaced on whether the bloc should tap some 200 billion euros ($235 billion) of frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine.
A proposal to use the funds failed last year after opposition from Belgium, where the bulk of the assets are held, and the EU offered a 90-billion-euro loan to Kyiv off its own back.
But there is already a sense that the money might not last the two years it was intended for, and the EU may need to find a way, sooner or later, to use the immobilized Russian funds.
“As each day passes, the cost of the war is rising as Russia’s relentless attacks continue unabated,” the top diplomats of the Netherlands, Poland, Spain and Sweden wrote in a letter last week.
New British foreign minister Ed Miliband and Ukraine’s Andriy Sybiga will join their EU counterparts for a long-scheduled meeting in Ireland, where the bloc holds its rotating presidency.
But while crises rage around the globe from Ukraine to Iran, the EU ministers will also open a debate on reforming how the bloc runs its diplomacy as it seeks impact in an increasingly hostile world.
While some advocate overhauling the EU’s diplomatic service under foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, others say now is not the time for institutional reshuffling and that the 27 nations need to focus on better coordinating their positions.

====================================================================================================

India-Russia: A Changing Equation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:18:00 UTC
15:18:00 KST

On August 31, in Bishkek, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi did something that New Delhi has increasingly been willing to do in public: he told Vladimir Putin that the war in Ukraine needs to end.
Meeting the Russian president on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit, Modi said that every day the war continues is a setback for humanity and called for a move “from endless war to an end to the war, to a cessation of hostilities.” Putin thanked him and said Russia was moving towards peace, while maintaining Moscow’s longstanding position that any settlement must meet Russian conditions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
On the surface, this looks like a significant diplomatic intervention. It is also consistent with Modi’s increasingly familiar language on Ukraine: India supports dialogue, diplomacy and a negotiated settlement. But the problem with New Delhi is not what Modi says to Putin. It is what India does with Russia immediately before and after saying it.
Just one week before the Bishkek meeting, India’s External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar was in Moscow for two days of talks. On August 24, as Ukrainians were commemorating their independence day, India and Russia held the 27th session of their Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic and Cultural Cooperation. A week later, Modi and Putin reviewed progress across the full spectrum of the bilateral relationship, including economic ties, defense, energy, space and mobility, agreeing to continue strengthening what India officially calls its “Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership.” Modi also highlighted the importance of the upcoming BRICS summit on Sept. 12-13 in New Delhi, which Putin plans to attend.
Drone Attack Sparks Fire at Russia’s Key Baltic Oil Port of Ust-Luga
The juxtaposition is revealing. India is asking Russia to end the war while simultaneously working to make its partnership with Russia more commercially viable and less vulnerable to the consequences of the same war.
That does not make India’s diplomacy meaningless. Nor does it mean India has chosen Russia over the West. New Delhi is pursuing a familiar oath of “strategic autonomy,” keeping channels open to all major powers. But there is a growing gap between India’s rhetoric about ending the war and the practical direction of its relationship with Moscow.
Three areas make that gap particularly visible: energy, trade and transport connectivity.
Reliable energy trade – a two-way street
Energy remains at the heart of the India-Russia economic partnership. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, India emerged as the second-largest buyer of Russian crude oil after China. Washington’s tariff pressure subsequently placed renewed emphasis on India’s dependence on Russian energy and on the role of Russian oil revenues in financing Moscow’s war effort. The Trump administration sought to use India’s position vis-à-vis Russia as leverage in its broader trade negotiations with New Delhi in order to get concessions.
Indian purchases of Russian crude did temporarily decline, but the trend proved short-lived. The latest Kpler figures, reported by the Financial Times, point to a sharp reversal, with Indian purchases reaching record levels this summer. In June and July 2026, India imported more than 2.6 million barrels of Russian crude per day, accounting for more than half of its crude imports.
Yet, the more interesting development is that the energy relationship is becoming increasingly reciprocal. Faced with domestic fuel shortages following sustained Ukrainian attacks on its refineries, Russia has begun importing refined petroleum products from India. A 68,000-ton gasoline shipment from India recently reached Russia, with further Indian supplies expected.
This marks an important shift. Russia remains a crucial source of crude for India, but India is increasingly becoming a supplier of refined fuel to Russia. The relationship is being shaped not only by longstanding strategic ties, but also by the unintended economic consequences of the war itself. Ukraine’s campaign against Russian refining infrastructure is shaping a new form of interdependence within the India-Russia energy relationship.
Trade imbalance – and the financial settlement problem
Trade presents a different problem. India-Russia merchandise trade reached roughly $68.7 billion in 2024-25, but Indian exports accounted for only $4.88 billion. The imbalance is overwhelmingly driven by Russian exports of crude oil and petroleum products, fertilizers, coal, metals and other commodities.
For New Delhi, the challenge is therefore not simply to increase the volume of bilateral trade, but to change its composition. India wants to expand exports of pharmaceuticals, machinery, chemicals and food products, while encouraging greater Indian investment in Russia.
The trade imbalance also exposes a persistent weakness in the financial architecture of the relationship. Although India and Russia have pursued settlement in national currencies, Russia has accumulated substantial rupee earnings from its exports to India without sufficient Indian imports to recycle those funds. The Reserve Bank of India acknowledged the problem in March, saying it was working on additional ways for Russian counterparts to use accumulated rupees for Indian imports or investment.
The issue is therefore not the complete absence of a local-currency settlement mechanism, but its limited ability to solve a fundamentally unbalanced trade relationship. Without more Indian exports and investment, simply settling trade in rupees does not eliminate the surplus. Reaching the two countries’ declared $100 billion trade target by 2030 will therefore require not just more trade, but more balanced trade – and a more effective way of recycling the financial flows generated by Russian energy sales.
Making transit corridors commercially viable
The third challenge is connectivity. If India and Russia are serious about reaching their $100 billion trade target, they will need transport links that are faster, cheaper and less vulnerable to geopolitical disruption. The challenge is no longer simply to build alternative corridors, but to make them commercially viable.
The International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) remains the most established option, connecting India with Russia through Iran and the Caspian region. It provides an alternative to the Suez route and could reduce both transit times and costs. Its commercial success, however, depends on sufficient cargo volumes, streamlined customs procedures and reliable multimodal logistics.
The Chennai-Vladivostok Eastern Maritime Corridor offers a more direct maritime alternative, potentially reducing transit time from around 40 days to approximately 24. Its real value will depend on whether it can support two-way trade – carrying Russian energy and commodities to India while providing a competitive route for Indian pharmaceuticals, machinery, chemicals and food products to Russia.
The Northern Sea Route is the longer-term bet. It could deepen India’s access to Russia’s Arctic and Far Eastern economies, but remains commercially more challenging, requiring specialized vessels, polar navigation capabilities and supporting infrastructure.
The three corridors therefore face different tests: the INSTC needs scale, Chennai-Vladivostok needs two-way cargo, and the Northern Sea Route needs to prove its commercial viability. Their success will ultimately be measured not by the number of agreements signed, but by whether they can move goods reliably and competitively.
But their significance extends beyond transport economics.
All three are part of a broader effort to build alternatives to routes and financial systems that have become more vulnerable to geopolitical pressure. They are instruments for ensuring that India-Russia commerce can continue even as the international economic environment around Russia becomes more fragmented.
Empty rhetoric
The contradiction exposed in Bishkek is that India continues to talk about ending the war while building a stronger, more durable relationship with Russia designed to survive that exact war.
Modi told Putin that the world must move from “endless war” to “end of war.” Yet, around the same meeting, India was proactively deepening cooperation with Moscow in energy, trade, finance and connectivity – precisely the areas that can help Russia withstand the economic consequences of the war.
India is not responsible for ending a war it did not start. Nor is it wrong to pursue its own interests. But New Delhi is one of the few major powers with both enormous economic ties to Russia and direct access to Putin. It has leverage, and it has chosen not to use it in any meaningful way.
Instead, India is insulating its relationship with Russia from the war while asking Russia to end the war.
That is not pressure. It is accommodation – wrapped in the language of peace.

Flash estimate: Inflation in Estonia up 0.3% in August
Estonia's annual inflation fell to 1.3 percent in August, its lowest level since spring 2021, Statistics Estonia said.
The harmonized index of consumer prices (HICP) rose 0.3 percent between July and August, with housing and transport costs up but food and non‑alcoholic beverage prices falling.
The flash estimate, which includes tourist expenditures, will be refined once more detailed data on August prices are received.
Lauri Veski, Consumer Price Statistics Service Manager at Statistics Estonia, said the year‑on‑year increase has not been this low since the economy was recovering from the coronavirus pandemic.
"Compared with August 2025, the index was primarily influenced by the increase in housing‑related and transport costs, on the one hand, and by the fall in the prices of food and non‑alcoholic beverages, on the other hand," Veski said.
The consumer price index (CPI) uses weights reflecting the average expenditure structure of Estonian residents, while the HICP also takes into account tourist spending, naturally highest in Estonia in the summer months, and is comparable to international indices.
The CPI for August will be published on September 7, and the finalized HICP data on September 16, Statistics Estonia said.
More detailed information is available from Statistics Estonia here and here.

"Every day that the war continues, humanity is, in effect, set back a step, whilst every step towards peace gives all of humanity real hope for peace," Modi told Putin on the sidelines of the annual Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek.

Russian state media reported that Putin briefed Modi on developments in Russia's war against Ukraine.
India remains Russia's second-largest customer of fossil fuels, only behind China. Purchases of Russian oil from the two countries have helped replenish Moscow's budget since 2022.
Putin also met Chinese President Xi Jinping at the two-day SCO summit, though the Kremlin said their talks only "superficially" touched on the war in Ukraine and focused on bilateral ties.
Despite the rare public appeal to end the war, Modi called Putin "my friend" and praised growing economic ties between India and Russia.
In July, Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev also publicly called for Russia's war against Ukraine to be frozen, urging a return to peace negotiations. Russia and India will continue strengthening what India describes as their "Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership." Modi said he expects to host Putin in India for the BRICS summit on Sept. 12–13.

Joint monitoring teams comprising officials from the Electricity Distribution Corporation, Water Resources Department, Revenue Department, and Police will patrol day and night to prevent misuse.
Reaffirming the state’s legal entitlement to Cauvery water, the chief minister said Tamil Nadu would not compromise on its rights upheld by the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal and the Supreme Court’s 2018 verdict.

Farmers were urged to adopt medium-duration rice varieties and water-saving methods such as direct seeding.“Let us use water sparingly, ensure it reaches the end user, and make samba cultivation a success,” the chief minister appealed.

Death toll from Nepal-China floods tops 1,000, around 4,500 still missing

The death toll from catastrophic flooding in Nepal and China has surpassed 1,000 as rescue teams work to reach communities cut off by the disaster.
Nepal’s disaster agency said on Tuesday that 987 deaths had been recorded in the country, while Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths in Tibet in their latest update on Sunday.
The combined death toll now stands at 1,003, while 4,462 people remain missing across the two countries.
In Nepal, the number of missing people fell to 3,916 as rescue efforts entered their seventh day, while 546 people were reported missing in China.
Foreign nationals among missing
The missing in Nepal include 583 foreigners from more than 30 nationalities, according to the disaster authority.
China has reported 261 foreign nationals among those missing, according to state media.
Indians account for one of the largest groups of missing foreigners. New Delhi said 275 Indian citizens and 128 people of Indian origin were missing in Nepal.
The US State Department said on Sunday that 85 US citizens were missing.
Reports citing Nepal’s tourism board and foreign embassies said 62 Ukrainians, 51 Malaysians, 42 Australians and 33 British nationals were also missing.
Glacial collapse triggered floods
The disaster began on Wednesday with a chain of events high in the Himalayas, when a glacial collapse sent large amounts of rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream.
Scientists studying satellite imagery said the collapse appeared to involve the failure of bedrock beneath a glacier in the Himalayan region. The rockfall was powerful enough to register as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
In neighbouring India, authorities in Uttar Pradesh said they had recovered 17 bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal that were believed to belong to flood victims.
Indian authorities are working to identify the bodies, which have not been included in the overall death toll.

Washington to press G20 on light-touch AI regulation

(AP Photo)
Tech bosses including Elon Musk, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and OpenAI's Sam Altman are participating in a G20 meeting in North Carolina this week amid a global debate on how governments should address the dangers of artificial intelligence.
The meeting in Chapel Hill, home to the University of North Carolina, a leading U.S. research hub, takes place on Sept. 1-2 and will be attended by ministers from the world's leading economies, including Japan, Germany, France, India and South Korea.
The United States holds the rotating G20 presidency this year and is hosting a series of ministerial meetings ahead of a leaders' summit that President Donald Trump will convene on Dec. 14-15 at his Trump National Doral resort in Miami.
Washington has framed its host year around limiting regulatory burdens and promoting new technologies.
The Chapel Hill meeting is organized by White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who will attempt to get attendees to sign on to a commitment to light-touch AI regulation.
The meeting is spread over two days, with Musk joining by video call and Huang and Altman expected in person for fireside chats with Lutnick.
Google DeepMind boss Demis Hassabis will also participate, Kratsios in a post on X said.
According to a report published by Bloomberg and re-posted on social media by Kratsios, the U.S. will push something called the Carolina Principles, a policy where governments commit to avoid creating new regulatory bodies to regulate AI.
The meeting takes place just weeks after OpenAI revealed that testing of its AI models went seriously awry, when so-called AI agents, while operating without human supervision, went onto the internet and broke into the internal systems of Hugging Face, a kind of online library for AI software.
The incident is still causing major ructions in Silicon Valley, with some, including Microsoft founder Bill Gates, calling for the industry and officials to urgently come up with ways to govern the development of the sector.
In the fallout, Google's Hassabis in July called for the United States to create an organization that would test the most powerful AI systems before they can be released to the public.
The new regulatory body would be modeled on the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), the private watchdog that polices Wall Street brokerage houses under federal oversight.
The Trump administration is largely committed to a hands-off approach that would leave the industry to find ways to self-regulate, even as companies race furiously to stay ahead in AI despite the risks.
In a sign that his administration is loath to create any obstacle for the AI industry, Trump on Aug. 31 attacked opponents of artificial intelligence data centers, saying they would end up "backwards and poor" and were helping rival China.

What does Iceland’s “No” vote mean for the EU’s enlargement policy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:15:29 UTC
15:15:29 KST

Iceland won’t reopen EU membership negotiations after 58.2 percent voted against in Saturday’s referendum. Does this challenge whether the EU can still attract stable, wealthy democracies for reasons beyond finances?
On Saturday, Icelanders were called to the polls to vote on whether the country should resume negotiations to join the European Union. 52.8 per cent voted “No” and the government has no official mandate to go back to the negotiation table.
Unlike other candidate countries, where membership depends on deep institutional reforms, Iceland’s case is different. It is a wealthy, stable country that aligns closely with EU democratic values and principles.
“In the previous accession process, 27 of 35 negotiating chapters were opened and 11 were provisionally closed. Moreover, through the EEA and Schengen, Iceland already applies a substantial part of EU legislation and is deeply integrated into the Single Market”, said Christine Leuchtenmüller, Head of Regional Programme Nordic Countries at the Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung.
However, according to Leuchtenmüller, Saturday’s outcome “primarily reflect[s] Iceland’s particular political and economic circumstances” and should not “allow for broader conclusions about EU enlargement”.
Iceland's vote also questions the EU’s wider security outlook, especially as the bloc depends more on enlargement to boost its global influence and security. This approach has become more critical following Russia’s war in Ukraine, strained relations with Washington, and conflicts in the Middle East.
Reasons for accession
Accession negotiations with Iceland would have moved quickly as the island already implements much of EU law. “In the previous accession process, 27 of 35 negotiating chapters were opened and 11 were provisionally closed. Through the European Economic Area and Schengen, Iceland already applies a substantial part of EU legislation and is deeply integrated into the Single Market”, said Leuchtenmüller.
For PM Kristrún Frostadóttir’s government, reopening accession talks was a flagship initiative. The intention was to build a better security shield and economic anchor for Iceland. Reasons included economic pressures, such as inflation peaks of 10.2 per cent and interest rates at 9.25 per cent, and urgent security threats from Arctic instability and diplomatic frictions over Greenland. Adopting the euro and entering the EU Customs Union would have lowered living costs and helped its defence and sovereign interests.
“Icelanders did not vote against Europe; they voted against redundancy. When a country already has the single market, Schengen and open borders, the marginal value of a seat must outweigh shared control of its core resource”, said MEP Mika Aaltola from the European People’s Party (EPP) and shadow rapporteur in the European Parliament of the report on the EU’s diplomatic strategy and geopolitical cooperation in the Arctic.
Ukraine and Moldova also mainly consider EU membership a security choice. Russia’s invasion made EU accession key for Ukraine’s future, while Moldova faces Russian interference and pressure of its own. Both became official candidates in 2022, formally opened accession negotiations in 2024, and have since moved through the process in parallel.
Membership would give both countries access to the full EU single market and potentially billions in European funding for modernisation, infrastructure and, particularly for Ukraine, reconstruction.
Meanwhile, Montenegro and Albania are currently the frontrunners. Montenegro has been negotiating since 2012 and already opened all 33 policy areas, while Albania, a candidate since 2014, accelerated its negotiations in recent years. For both, membership promises greater investment and access to EU funding and markets. The accession process is also designed to drive domestic reforms, particularly on corruption, judicial independence and the rule of law.
Candidates Serbia, North Macedonia and Bosnia and Herzegovina also see membership as a route towards greater economic development and political stability, but their paths have been slower. Serbia has been negotiating with Brussels for more than a decade, but its relationship with Kosovo, concerns over democratic standards and its continued ties with Russia complicate progress.
North Macedonia faces obstacles such as disputes with neighbouring EU members, and Bosnia and Herzegovina still needs significant institutional and rule-of-law reforms. For all three, accession means access to a market of around 450 million people, greater investment and a stronger political position within Europe.
The most complicated cases are Georgia and Turkey. Georgia became an official candidate in 2023, but its accession process has stalled amid EU concerns over democratic backsliding and the direction of its government, despite strong historical public support for European integration. Turkey has been a candidate since 1999 and began negotiations in 2005, making it the longest-running candidate, but its talks have been frozen for years because of concerns over democracy, fundamental rights and the rule of law, as well as disputes involving Cyprus.
Does enlargement benefit the EU?
For the EU, enlargement matters most for security and geopolitical influence, particularly since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Bringing neighbouring countries closer to the bloc reduces border instability and limits the influence of powers such as Russia and China in Eastern Europe and the Western Balkans.
Ukraine and Moldova are particularly important to this strategy because of their position on the EU’s eastern flank. Integrating the Western Balkans would bring a region surrounded largely by EU member states more firmly into European political and security structures.
A larger bloc would also represent a bigger market and population and could strengthen Europe’s negotiating power on trade, foreign policy, energy and security at a time of growing competition between the United States, China and Russia.
On the economic side, new members would increase the size of the EU’s single market, creating new opportunities for trade and investment and helping connect European transport, energy and supply networks. The Western Balkans, for example, are important transit routes between different parts of the continent and could play a greater role in European energy and infrastructure networks.
Enlargement is also designed to promote democratic and institutional reforms in countries seeking membership. Candidates must meet EU standards on the rule of law, judicial independence, fundamental rights and the fight against corruption and organised crime before they can join.
This gives Brussels leverage to encourage reforms beyond its current borders and, in turn, can strengthen the EU’s own security by improving cooperation on issues such as migration, border management and cross-border crime.
How can a country join the EU?
EU membership is a merit-driven process that requires countries to align with EU values and legislation. Any country can apply to join the EU, but it must first meet the 1993 Copenhagen criteria. These include stable and democratic institutions; respect for the rule of law and human rights; a functioning market; and the ability to take on the obligations of membership, including implementing the full body of European law. Negotiations formally begin once these conditions are met. Then the EU Commission and the EU Council grant the country candidate status.
The Commission starts with a screening process to determine how well the candidate is prepared. Then it must implement EU law, and where necessary, make reforms across 35 policy areas (called “chapters”) divided into six thematic clusters. These include the fundamentals (such as justice, public administration, economic functioning, and fundamental rights), internal market, competitiveness, green agenda, agriculture and cohesion, and external relations. The last two chapters, "institutions” and "other issues", include matters which come up during the negotiations but are not covered by any other chapter.
Chapters are opened individually and provisionally closed once the Commission and the Council consider that the country has made sufficient progress and implemented enough reforms.
Once all chapters are concluded, the Commission decides whether the country is ready to become a member of the EU, followed by the Parliament and the EU Council’s final green light. Upon a positive decision, the member states and the candidate country sign and ratify the accession treaty.
Negotiations can take years, although the Commission wants to speed up the process, depending on the candidate’s reforms and political stability. They are also lengthy as each step requires unanimous agreement from all member states. Hungary, for example, has blocked Ukraine's progress for years, despite receiving candidate status in 2022.
Out of the seven candidate countries, Montenegro is the frontrunner, with all chapters opened and 18 provisionally closed. Albania has opened all chapters and closed three, followed by Serbia, which opened 22 chapters and closed two. Moldova and Ukraine opened the fundamentals and external relations chapters, while North Macedonia is still in the screening process. Negotiations with Turkey stalled in 2018.

designboom radar: exhibitions to see around the world this september
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:15:27 UTC
15:15:27 KST

September exhibitions from DESIGNBOOM RADAR
September brings a dense new season of exhibitions across art, architecture, and design, with major retrospectives arriving alongside immersive installations and more focused looks at individual practices. This month’s exhibition radar moves from the late legend Yayoi Kusama at the Stedelijk Museum and Remedios Varo at Louisiana to Maurizio Cattelan in Berlin, Do Ho Suh in Seoul, and Homo Faber’s return to Venice, while shows in Tokyo, Mumbai, Lisbon, and New York take on subjects ranging from artificial intelligence and contemporary habitation to craft, technology, and the natural world.
Some of the exhibitions highlighted in earlier radars and listings on our dedicated events guide remain on view, giving designboom readers more time to encounter them around the globe.
Wendell Castle: Living
At Friedman Benda‘s New York gallery, Wendell Castle: Living reconstructs the domestic world that furniture maker and sculptor Wendell Castle shared with ceramist and multimedia artist Nancy Jurs in Scottsville, New York. Curated by their daughter Alison Castle, the exhibition takes a 1973 House Beautiful feature on the couple’s home as its starting point, returning Castle’s furniture and Jurs’ ceramics to the kind of lived setting in which they originally appeared.
Several works photographed in the 1973 interior are being shown publicly for the first time in decades, alongside domestic objects that suggest a kitchen, bedroom, living room, and dining room. Early pieces including Castle’s Chaise Rocker from 1962 and Environment from 1972 sit with later works, tracing how his sculptural approach to furniture developed while keeping its relationship to everyday use in view.
name: Wendell Castle: Living
designer: Wendell Castle
 museum: Friedman Benda
 location: New York, USA
 dates: September 17th, 2026 — October 17th, 2026
Wendell Castle: Living, Friedman Benda | image courtesy Friedman Benda
do ho suh
Do Ho Suh’s largest exhibition to date brings together around 500 works spanning more than thirty years of practice at the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art in Seoul. Drawings, sculptures, videos, and installations trace his ongoing interest in home and migration, and in the ways memory and identity become attached to the spaces people inhabit. The exhibition reaches back to works from his student years in Seoul alongside major pieces and projects still in progress.
Early material appears in a section called Seed Bank, including drawings, records, and objects that would later develop into recurring ideas across Suh’s work. The exhibition also brings together architectural installations including ‘Small Gate’, the ‘Rubbing/Loving’ series, and ‘Perfect Home: London, Horsham, New York, Berlin, Providence, Seoul’, where translucent fabric reconstructs the ordinary details of homes the artist has lived in across different cities.
name: Do Ho Suh
 artist: Do Ho Suh
 museum: National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA)
 location: Seoul, Korea
 dates: August 27th, 2026 — February 9th, 2027
Do Ho Suh, Nest/s, 2024 Polyester, stainless steel, photo by Jeon Taeg Su © Do Ho Suh
Yayoi Kusama
A major retrospective for the legendary late artist Yayoi Kusama retrospective arrives at the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam, tracing more than seventy years of work from her early practice in Matsumoto through the experimental years she spent in New York and her later work in Tokyo. Painting, sculpture, drawing, fashion, collage, installation, and documentation of happenings come together to show how recurring ideas around repetition, infinity, and the dissolution of the self developed across her career.
The Amsterdam exhibition is the final stop of a European retrospective organized with Fondation Beyeler and Museum Ludwig. Alongside familiar works are historical pieces rarely seen in Europe and recent installations, including a new version of one of Kusama’s immersive environments, where patterns and reflections extend across the surrounding space.
name: Yayoi Kusama
 artist: Yayoi Kusama
 museum: Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam
 location: Amsterdam, Netherlands
 dates: September 11th, 2026 — January 17th, 2027
Yayoi Kusama with Yellow Tree / Living Room at the Aichi Triennale, 2010 | image courtesy Ota Fine Arts and David Zwirner © YAYOI KUSAMA
Remedios Varo
Louisiana Museum of Modern Art presents the first major museum exhibition in Europe devoted to Remedios Varo, bringing together more than 70 works from across the Spanish-Mexican surrealist’s career. Early paintings from Barcelona and Paris appear alongside works from her most productive years in Mexico during the 1950s and early 1960s, including rarely shown loans from museums and private collections.
Varo’s strange interiors and imaginary landscapes bring scientific inquiry into contact with mythology, mysticism, mechanics, and the occult. Paintings populated by hybrid creatures, travelers, and eccentric machines are joined by drawings, notebooks, and archival material, giving a broader view of the references and ideas behind her precisely constructed surrealist world.
name: Remedios Varo
 artist: Remedios Varo
 museum: Louisiana Museum of Modern Art
 location: Humlebæk, Denmark
 dates: September 18th, 2026 — January 10th, 2027
Still Life Reviving, 1963 © 2025 The Art Institute of Chicago / Art Resource, NY / Scala, Florence
Water Works: in the Flow of Making
Berlin-based collective raumlaborberlin brings Water Works: in the Flow of Making to TOTO GALLERY·MA in Tokyo, extending its long-running experiments around water, public space, and collective forms of urban life. The exhibition gathers earlier water-related projects alongside new work developed in Japan, where the group has been looking at Tokyo Bay as a space for architecture and everyday use beyond the city’s fixed ground.
A workshop with students from Shibaura Institute of Technology feeds directly into the show. Working with bamboo and inflatable dunnage bags, the group built floating structures and staged a performance from a barge in Tokyo Bay, testing how bodies, temporary construction, and maritime regulations might shape new ways of occupying the waterfront. Materials from the workshop return inside the gallery alongside documentation, studies of water circulation, and proposals for future waterfront environments.
name: Water Works: In the Flow of Making
designer: raumlaborberlin
 museum: TOTO GALLERY·MA
 location: Tokyo, Japan
 dates: September 10th, 2026 — November 29th, 2026
Bathing Culture (Göteborg, Sweden, 2014) © raumlaborberlin
Second Nature
Second Nature takes over all four floors of the Art House at Mumbai’s Nita Mukesh Ambani Cultural Centre, bringing together nine immersive installations by Random International, teamLab, A.A. Murakami, Simon Heijdens, and Es Devlin. Presented with experiential art platform Superblue for its first exhibition in Asia, the show looks at the increasingly blurred relationship between digital systems and the natural world.
Several of the works shift in response to visitors or their surroundings. Digital flowers bloom and disappear around moving bodies, weather data animates an indoor landscape, and motion-sensing installations change as people pass through them. Across the exhibition, technology becomes part of the environment itself, shaping how visitors move, look, and interact with each work.
name: Second Nature
 museum: Nita Mukesh Ambani Cultural Centre (NMACC)
 location: Mumbai, India
 dates: July 3rd, 2026 — January 10th, 2027
Nirvana: Fleeting Flowers, Radiance Within, Mumbai | image courtesy Superblue
john baldessari: sculptures
John Baldessari is best known for the deadpan collisions of image and language that shaped his approach to conceptual art, but sculpture ran through his practice as well. Sculptures at Sprüth Magers Los Angeles turns to this three-dimensional side of his work, bringing together projects that play with physical space, scale, and the expectations attached to familiar objects.
Among them is Beethoven’s Trumpet (With Ear) Opus #133 from 2007, an oversized ear and trumpet installation that transforms a visual joke into something visitors physically encounter in the room. Across the exhibition, Baldessari’s humor moves off the flat surface, using enlarged forms and spatial relationships to extend questions that occupied him throughout his career.
name: John Baldessari: Sculptures
artist: John Baldessari
 museum: Sprüth Magers
 location: Los Angeles, USA
 dates: September 11th, 2026 — October 24th, 2026
John Baldessari, Beethoven’s Trumpet; In One Ear & Out the Same Ear, Bonner Kunstverein, Bonn, 2007 | image by Reni Hansen
Learning from “Hōjōki”: Tiny Architecture Reweaves Life
Learning from ‘Hōjōki’: Tiny Architecture Reweaves Life at 21_21 DESIGN SIGHT begins with a 13th-century text about living in a ten-foot-square hut. Written by Kamo no Chomei, Hōjōki reflects on impermanence through the small dwelling he called home, and the exhibition uses that modest structure as a way to think again about contemporary habitation and the built environment.
Exhibition director Yoshiharu Tsukamoto brings together architects, designers, artists, and companies to reinterpret Chomei’s hut within the same nine-square-meter footprint. Their structures fill the galleries alongside research into the forms of living described in Hōjōki, turning the historic text into a series of physical propositions about how little space a life might need, and what that constraint can make visible.
name: Learning from ‘Hōjōki’: Tiny Architecture Reweaves Life
 museum: 21_21 DESIGN SIGHT
 location: Tokyo, Japan
 dates: August 28th, 2026 — January 11th, 2027
image © 21_21 Design Sight
Koo Jeong A: OUSSSMOS
Koo Jeong A brings three decades of work to Leeum Museum of Art for OUSSSMOS, her largest solo exhibition in Korea to date. The show draws together recurring elements from across her practice, including phosphorescence, skateparks, scent, and magnetism, tracing how she has used barely perceptible forces and large-scale installations to alter the way a space is sensed.
The exhibition extends beyond Leeum’s M2 gallery into the museum’s lobby and less expected spaces, with works appearing behind walls and among historical objects. These interventions lead into OUSSS, the conceptual universe Koo has developed across her practice, where familiar surroundings can shift through changes in light, smell, movement, and invisible fields.
name: Koo Jeong A: Ousssmos
artist: Koo Jeong A
 museum: Leeum Museum of Art
 location: Seoul, South Korea
 dates: September 5th, 2026 — December 27th, 2026

Maurizio Cattelan: NIGHT
Maurizio Cattelan takes over Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie with NIGHT, his first major solo exhibition in Germany and the presentation connected to the 2026 Preis der Nationalgalerie. Historical works including Him (2001) and Novecento (1997) appear alongside new commissions, bringing several of the artist’s recurring questions around authority, memory, and representation into the same space.
At the center is a new site-specific work developed for Mies van der Rohe’s glass-and-steel building. Cattelan uses the architecture itself as part of the exhibition, altering how visitors move through and gather within the museum while placing familiar works into a different physical and historical context.

Roy Lichtenstein Sweet Dreams, Baby!
Sweet Dreams, Baby! turns to Roy Lichtenstein’s printmaking, bringing together around fifty works made across five decades. Many are being shown publicly for the first time, including thirty-three prints recently given to Kunstmuseum Basel by the Roy Lichtenstein Foundation, alongside works already held in the museum’s collection.
The exhibition follows Lichtenstein from early experiments in the late 1940s through the comic-book imagery, Ben-Day dots, interiors, still lifes, and art-historical references that became central to his work. It also looks closely at the technical side of his practice, including collaborations with specialist print studios and works built through unusually complex combinations of lithography, woodcut, screen printing, and other processes.
name: Roy Lichtenstein Sweet Dreams, Baby!
artist: Roy Lichtenstein

Tatiana Trouvé: The Auxiliaries
Tatiana Trouvé brings new sculpture, drawing, and installation to Xavier Hufkens for The Auxiliaries, her first solo exhibition in Brussels. Spread across three levels of the gallery, the show moves through familiar strands of her practice: travel, memory, mapping, studio labor, and the way materials can carry traces of earlier uses. One installation resembles an improvised storage system cast in aluminum, while other works begin with objects gathered during the artist’s travels or with measurements of sound pollution around Paris.
The basement turns toward the often unseen materials that support sculptural production. Mattresses, blankets, lifting straps, silicone molds, pallets, and discarded fragments reappear as part of Trouvé’s Invisible Workers series, giving physical form to the movement and labor behind finished works. Upstairs, new drawings sit alongside her ongoing Les Dessouvenus series, extending the exhibition’s interest in things that shift between states, uses, and meanings.
name: Tatiana Trouvé: The Auxiliaries
 artist: Tatiana Trouvé
 museum: Xavier Hufkens
 location: Brussels, Belgium
 dates: September 10th, 2026 — October 31st, 2026

homo faber 2026: An Island of Light
Homo Faber returns to Venice for its fourth edition with An Island of Light, bringing the work of more than 500 artisans from over 70 countries to the Fondazione Giorgio Cini. Artistic director Es Devlin has shaped the biennial around the relationship between light, materials, and the human hand, arranging more than 700 objects across fifteen installations on San Giorgio Maggiore.
The exhibition takes its cue from the Venetian lagoon, treating each maker as an individual island within a wider landscape of craft. Water, mirrors, movement, and shifting light run through Devlin’s staging, while live demonstrations and workshops bring the processes behind the objects into view alongside the finished works.

Energies of IA
Energies of AI looks at artificial intelligence through the physical and social systems that keep it running. Curated by Antonio Somaini, the exhibition considers the electricity, water, critical minerals, computation, labor, and capital behind AI alongside the effects these technologies produce across culture and everyday life. Its setting at MAAT, partly housed within Lisbon’s former Tejo Power Station, gives that question of energy a particularly direct architectural context.
The exhibition brings together recent work by artists including Hito Steyerl, Kate Crawford and Vladan Joler, Trevor Paglen, Grégory Chatonsky, and Fabien Giraud. Several projects are being produced specifically for the show, addressing subjects such as the hidden labor used to train AI models, its material metabolism, machine learning, surveillance, and forms of psychological influence.

Tony Oursler: Between Technology and Spiritual Knowledge
Tony Oursler’s Between Technology and Spiritual Knowledge – Magic, Media, and Art brings together more than three decades of work at Tokyo Node, tracing his long-running interest in the spaces where technology, psychology, belief, and the paranormal begin to overlap. Video, sculpture, sound, light, and language appear throughout the exhibition, alongside subjects ranging from surveillance and data flows to magic, religion, conspiracy theories, and signals that remain invisible but shape daily life.
The show includes major works such as Private and Specular, as well as previously unrealized pieces and new site-specific installations created for Tokyo. Oursler also presents material from his own archive of roughly 3,000 objects and documents relating to science, magic, and unidentified phenomena, extending the exhibition beyond finished artworks into the research and visual culture that has fed his practice for decades.

Liu Wei: Speculation
For The Met’s 2026 Genesis Facade Commission, Beijing-based artist Liu Wei places four large-scale sculptures across the museum’s Fifth Avenue exterior. Titled Speculation, the installation centers on the recurring form of the human hand, using it as a familiar motif that shifts between bodily, architectural, and more fantastical associations.
The commission continues Liu’s interest in fragments drawn from urban environments, historical imagery, and the body, while responding directly to the scale of The Met’s facade. Shaped in part by his experience of rapid transformation in contemporary China, Speculation considers cycles of rupture and repair and marks Liu’s first major presentation in the United States.

Taryn Simon fills the Guggenheim’s rotunda with Father Country I Do Love You, a new body of work nearly a decade in the making. Forty-two interconnected works move across photography, text, video, and sculpture, tracing the life of an unnamed federal agent whose actions and omissions ripple outward into larger histories of power, justice, and national identity.
The project also brings Simon’s own family history into her practice for the first time. Dedicated to her father, who worked for the U.S. government and later manufactured arcade games, the exhibition folds fragments of his life into a wider narrative about America and the stories that remain partially hidden within institutions and personal memory.

War on words: Russia destroyed a third of Ukraine’s annual book production this summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:15:00 UTC
15:15:00 KST

Russia continues to devastate Ukraine’s cultural heritage. Attacks on the book market, already under threat from the war, have intensified recently – over the summer, a third of Ukrainian publishers’ annual output, including a large proportion of textbooks, was destroyed in warehouses or printing works. Industry representatives are warning of a collapse of the sector, which would deprive Ukraine of the right to speak with its own voice.
“The whole world should know what has happened here,” said Viktor Kruhlov, director of the Ranok publishing house, which specialises in children’s and educational literature, to RFI. The Russians attacked the company’s largest warehouse in Kharkiv on August 1.
“It was a deliberately planned attack on the bookshop,” noted Kruhlov, according to Reuters. “Two explosions followed one after the other, a few minutes apart. There were about fifty employees on the premises at the time, and it is a miracle that no one died. Everything melted as a result of the heat following both explosions,” RFI quoted him as saying.
It was the biggest blow to the Ukrainian publishing industry since the start of the war. In a 10,000-square-metre warehouse, where not only Ranok but also the KnyhoLand chain stored books, eight million books were destroyed in the fire caused by the attack.
Around a million of these were textbooks; Ranok prints roughly a third of the total number of these in Ukraine. Although the company has other warehouses, the one in Kharkiv was the largest and housed the majority of its output.
“We learnt that during the Second World War, the Nazis burnt thousands of books. Now the Russians are routinely destroying millions of Ukrainian books. It is a deliberate strategy to undermine Ukrainian culture and identity, because Russia refuses to accept a prosperous Ukraine,” added Kruhlov.
Systematic attacks
Russia is systematically targeting the Ukrainian publishing industry. It carried out its first such attacks as early as spring 2022, specifically in Kharkiv.
Further attacks followed, which intensified significantly in 2024. In May of that year, Moscow destroyed the Faktor-Druk printing works in Kharkiv, killing seven workers who were printing children’s books. The facility produced around a third of all books in Ukraine, according to the Ukrainian Publishers’ Association.
Last year, Russia extended its strikes to include warehouses in Kyiv and Dnipro, and its attacks on Ukrainian books reached their peak this summer. In July, it struck, amongst other targets, a warehouse belonging to the BookChef publishing house, destroying 800,000 copies – the majority of its stock. In the same month, it also destroyed two other warehouses, the office of a publishing house and a printing works in the capital.
The attack on Ranok in Kharkiv in early August was followed by further strikes; for example, in the middle of the month in Kyiv, several warehouses belonging to various companies were targeted once again, including BookChef’s backup warehouse, where 100,000 copies were reduced to ashes. The Počajna open-air book market in Kyiv was also targeted.
A third of the annual output was destroyed by fire
The attacks mentioned above are among the largest, but by no means an exhaustive list. The attacks over the last two months have caused losses to dozens of publishing houses and bookshops – whether through direct destruction or indirect consequences.
In July, the Russians destroyed 1.5 million copies and in August ten million, which represents roughly a third of Ukraine’s annual book production, reported Ukrayinska Pravda (UP).
The Ukrainian Publishers’ Association reports as many as thirteen million books destroyed over the summer and direct losses amounting to 1.2 billion hryvnias (roughly six hundred million korunas) – though, according to the association, the actual losses are significantly higher. The Ukrainian Book Institute estimates them to be in the billions of hryvnias.
The Ukrainian book market as a whole is, however, relatively small; according to the publishers’ association, its annual turnover is around seven to eight billion hryvnias, which is comparable to the turnover of a small shopping centre.
Hundreds of schools have also been affected, as nine per cent of new textbooks were destroyed shortly before the start of the school term. According to the Ukrainian Ministry of Education, this amounts to more than 1.2 million copies. In the case of some subjects, Russia has even destroyed the entire print run for the 2026–2027 academic year, according to Serhiy Babak, chair of the parliamentary committee on education, as reported by UP.
“Russia’s genocidal policy”
As well as book warehouses, printing works, bookshops and publishers’ offices, Moscow is also destroying Ukrainian libraries. The Ukrainian Ministry of Culture reports that, since the start of full-scale war, 228 libraries have been destroyed and 678 damaged as a result of Russian attacks. The actual damage, however, is likely to be greater, as the figures do not include damage in the occupied territories.
Attacks on libraries and book publishing in general form part of a wider Russian campaign aimed at destroying Ukrainian monuments and cultural heritage. The Ukrainian Ministry of Culture has recorded – in the unoccupied territories alone – thousands of such cases.
Ukrainian Minister of Education Andriy Butenko described the Russian attacks on bookshops and printing houses as an attempt to destroy the Ukrainian language, history and memory, “everything from which our children’s identity grows”. Similarly, Oleksandra Matviychuk, director of the human rights organisation Centre for Civil Liberties, which was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022, described the destruction of Ukrainian books as “part of Russia’s broader genocidal policy”.
“We know from history that the burning of libraries has accompanied genocides for centuries – as a means of erasing someone else’s identity. (Russian dictator Vladimir) Putin openly states that there is no Ukrainian nation, no Ukrainian language and no Ukrainian culture,” says Matvijčuková, alluding to Russia’s questioning of the existence of an independent Ukraine.
The Struggle for Survival
“One in three planned new releases either never sees the light of day or reaches shop shelves with a significant delay and in reduced print runs. All of this is accompanied by colossal additional costs for an industry that is already struggling to survive,” summarises the consequences of the Russian strikes, reports the UA News website.
Like other sectors of the Ukrainian economy – with the exception of the defence industry – the book sector is struggling as a result of the Russian war, even in the absence of direct attacks.
The cost of printing books has risen by around forty per cent over the last two years, and fewer and fewer Ukrainians can afford to buy them regularly, according to Reuters. Demand for books is so low that a number of bookshops have had to close this year, reports UP.
Russian raids on warehouses and printing works are further complicating the situation – the publishing houses affected will find it very difficult to replenish their stocks, as they have had to temporarily suspend operations, RFI adds. According to Reuters, it can take between six and eighteen months to produce books.
‘The right to speak with a Ukrainian voice’
The Publishers’ Association is therefore warning that the entire sector is on the brink of collapse, and is calling on the country’s leadership to convene the National Security Council and introduce support measures. These include state-subsidised loans, insurance to cover the cost of books, tax relief and subsidies for shop rent, as well as the resumption of state purchases for libraries, which were suspended in 2022.
The association also warns that if domestic publishers are unable to recover, they will be replaced by foreign companies, which would mean that the Ukrainian book market would lose not only books written in Ukrainian, but also support for Ukrainian authors, national values and identity.
A similar appeal was published by the Ukrainian Book Institute. “We are facing the risk of the collapse of the entire book ecosystem,” it states, calling on the international publishing community to support their Ukrainian colleagues and to cease cooperation with their Russian counterparts.
“Supporting Ukrainian publishers today is not just about preserving the industry. It is about defending Ukraine’s right to speak with its own voice and shape its own narrative on the world stage,” the institute added.
Article initially published on August 27, 2026, 06:00 (CEST).

New director of Ruhnu Primary School: This is the most wonderful schoolhouse in the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:15:00 UTC
15:15:00 KST

New director of Ruhnu Primary School: This is the most wonderful schoolhouse in the world
Starting this autumn, Heily Rikker will take up the position of director of Ruhnu Primary School. She said that a small school does not mean a small world, and that this school gives every opportunity to succeed anywhere.
Rikker explained that her mother is from Kihnu, while she considers herself a Pärnu native. "My roots are in Kihnu and I do have experience with small islands, but I've been visiting Ruhnu for 20 years. One of my very good friends moved to Ruhnu — she has since left — but you could say that since nature abhors a vacuum, I took over her Estonian‑language teacher position there last year."
She mentioned that she actually met her husband on Ruhnu as well. "For me, it's a magnetic place — not always romantic, perhaps — but all the people who end up there and whom life has brought into my path are so interesting and exciting, and usually those encounters turn into long‑lasting friendships."
"I dare say this is the most wonderful schoolhouse in the entire world," she emphasized, explaining that the school is located in an old parish house built in 1875. "Schooling was offered there from that time on, but in 2016 and 2017 the building was renovated and restored. So it's a slightly Swedish‑style, lovely house. I think it's not only the green and red wooden floors and Swedish wallpapers that make it special — it also has a warm, inviting energy. It's simply a pleasant place to be."
Rikker noted that they currently have the smallest school in Estonia. "Four students are in on‑site instruction and three are in home‑schooling," she said, adding that none of their students were born on Ruhnu. "One is from Tartu County, one from Viljandi County, and two from Pärnu County. The home‑schoolers as well — two from Pärnu County and one from Rapla County. You could say we accept students from all over Estonia."
At the moment, one child in the second grade and three children in the ninth grade attend on‑site classes. "Right now we've arranged it so that a lesson lasts 40 minutes, but very often there's a small break in between and the same subject continues — a longer, more flowing school lesson."

Commission warns of worsening health of Palestinian women detainees in Israeli jails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:14:21 UTC
15:14:21 KST

The health of several Palestinian women detainees in Israeli custody has deteriorated amid intensified raids, searches and punitive measures, the Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs said on Monday.
The Palestinian prisoners’ body said testimonies from women prisoners documented overcrowding, shortages of basic necessities, poor food and inadequate medical care in prisons and interrogation centres.
It said the conditions were taking an increasing physical and psychological toll on detainees.
Among them is Abeer Odeh from Tulkarem in the occupied West Bank, who suffers from asthma as well as problems affecting her oesophagus and back, according to the commission.
Odeh, who underwent surgery before her detention, said she was receiving only stomach medication despite needing further treatment.
She said prison authorities raided rooms holding women detainees at Damon Prison on August 17 and carried out another crackdown the following day, forcing prisoners out and confiscating clothes and personal belongings.
Detainees report medical concerns
The commission said Yasmine Shaaban from Jenin also requires treatment for a uterine condition.
Shaaban previously spent around nine years in Israeli prisons before being detained again in May 2025. She has since been issued five administrative detention orders, according to the commission.
It also reported that Nadine al-Daghamin from as-Samu, south of Hebron, suffers from a severe skin rash and allergies, while Shahd Adi from Beit Ummar has contracted scabies.
The commission said Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir entered Damon Prison on August 19, where he threatened Palestinian prisoners and spoke about measures imposed on them.
It also raised concerns over the health of 54-year-old Palestinian physician Dima Mohammed Amin, who was detained on August 18.
Amin experienced symptoms of a heart attack and underwent cardiac catheterisation, while also suffering from low blood sugar, unstable blood pressure, high cholesterol and dizziness, the commission said.
After a lawyer visited her at the Russian Compound interrogation centre, Amin described shortages of food and clothing, repeated searches, shouting and psychological pressure.
She also said women detainees were forcibly dragged from their cells and made to stand in a corner without being allowed to move.
The commission warned that Amin’s detention conditions posed further risks to her health and said she required continuous medical care.
Around 92 Palestinian women are currently held in Israeli prisons and detention centres, according to the commission.
Palestinian figures put the total number of Palestinians in Israeli prisons at around 9,400 as of early July, including more than 350 children, 3,244 administrative detainees and 1,320 people Israel classifies as “unlawful combatants”.

Ex-gang leader ‘Keffe D’ found guilty of killing rap legend Tupac Shakur
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01

Ex-gang leader Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis found guilty of murdering Tupac Shakur
Jury finds Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis, 63, guilty of murdering the chart-topping artist in the 1996 shooting.
Former gang leader found guilty of Tupac Shakur’s 1996 murder
A former gang leader accused of orchestrating the killing of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur in the United States in 1996 has been convicted of murder for his role in the long-unsolved crime.
A jury in Clark County, Nevada, deliberated for nearly three hours on Monday before finding Duane “Keffe D” Davis, 63, guilty of a single count of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon, capping an 11-day trial in a courtroom in the city of Las Vegas.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Suspect in rapper Tupac Shakur’s killing makes first court appearance in US
- list 2 of 4Who killed Tupac? What to know about the trial of Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis
- list 3 of 4‘Truth or fiction’: US trial of Tupac Shakur’s accused killer begins
- list 4 of 4Tupac Shakur murder trial begins thirty years after his death
Davis will face a maximum sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole at his sentencing on October 13. He told the judge “he plans to appeal this matter”.
Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang in Los Angeles, was accused of ordering the drive-by shooting that killed Shakur on September 7, 1996. Prosecutors said he was enraged because members of Shakur’s entourage had beaten his nephew at a Las Vegas casino hours earlier.
“Duane Davis, in the culture of gangs, could not let that stand,” prosecutor Binu Palal said during closing arguments. “So what did he do? He acquired a firearm, got his group together and went hunting for Mr Shakur.”
Shakur, who was in Las Vegas for a Mike Tyson heavyweight fight, was shot about two hours after the casino confrontation by a gunman in a white Cadillac that pulled up at a red light alongside the BMW in which the rapper was riding in the front passenger seat.
According to prosecutors, Davis handed the gun to someone sitting in the back seat of the Cadillac and ordered that person to shoot Shakur, who died six days later.
Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.
The driver of the BMW, Death Row Records cofounder Marion “Suge” Knight, was wounded.
The killing of Shakur, also known as 2Pac, has been one of the US’s most notorious cold cases, prompting endless debate among music fans over who did it and why.
The investigation into Shakur’s murder sputtered for decades because of a lack of evidence, but the case was revived when Davis’s memoirs were published in 2019. Davis has repeatedly boasted over the years of involvement in Shakur’s murder, in interviews with law enforcement and media and ultimately in his autobiography, Compton Street Legend.
He has since backtracked and pleaded not guilty to the murder charge.
Palal, the prosecutor, played clips from Davis’s various alleged confessions as part of his closing arguments.
Michael Sanft, Davis’s defence attorney, characterised his client’s confessions as fiction and lies partly designed to promote his book.
“You’re reading a book that is fiction and not fact,” Sanft told the jury. “But the state wants you to believe that this is somehow a confession, that he was there and present at the time of the shooting.”
Sanft said there was no evidence implicating Davis in Shakur’s murder other than his own statements.
In the run-up to the trial, Davis’s lawyers tried in vain to keep the book from being introduced as evidence, along with remarks he made in an interview with police in 2008.
Shakur, who was 25 when he was killed, was a key figure in a hip-hop rivalry pitting US East Coast rappers against West Coast artists.
Known for hits including “California Love” and “All Eyez on Me”, Shakur – the son of a Black Panther – was raised in Harlem and Baltimore, but became the epitome of California hip-hop when he signed with Los Angeles-based Death Row Records.

Oil prices jump as US, Iranian attacks stoke fears of escalation
