NASA delays Crew-13 launch after leak found on SpaceX Dragon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:33:37 UTC
14:33:37 KST

NASA delays Crew-13 launch after leak found on SpaceX Dragon
- Date:
- September 1, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA and SpaceX have delayed Crew-13 after finding an oxidizer leak in the Dragon spacecraft’s propulsion system during prelaunch preparations. Engineers are investigating the problem before the four-person crew can begin its journey to the International Space Station.
- Share:
NASA and SpaceX have delayed the planned launch of Crew-13 to the International Space Station after engineers discovered an oxidizer leak in the propulsion system of the mission's Dragon spacecraft.
The issue was found during routine spacecraft processing ahead of launch. An oxidizer is a chemical that helps fuel burn inside a rocket or spacecraft propulsion system, making it an essential part of the vehicle's ability to maneuver.
NASA and SpaceX teams are now carrying out additional testing and reviewing data from the spacecraft. Any repairs or other required work will be completed before Dragon is cleared to fly. NASA has not yet announced a new target launch date.
Four Astronauts Will Join Expedition 75
NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney will serve as commander and pilot of Crew-13, respectively.
They will fly alongside CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov, who will serve as mission specialists.
Once the crew reaches the International Space Station, the four astronauts will become part of Expedition 75, the station's long-duration crew responsible for research, maintenance, and other operations aboard the orbiting laboratory.
About two weeks before the flight, the Crew-13 astronauts will begin quarantine at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston. The precaution helps reduce the risk that crew members could become sick shortly before traveling to space.
Crew-13 Will Launch on Falcon 9
When the mission is cleared to proceed, Crew-13 will travel aboard SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft, which is designed to carry astronauts to and from orbit.
Dragon will launch on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. NASA and SpaceX will announce a new launch date once testing, data reviews, and any necessary work on the spacecraft have been completed.

Rotterdam medical students offer cash to jump training queues
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Medical students in Rotterdam are offering each other thousands of euros to move up the queue for the hospital training they need to qualify as doctors amid a shortage of spaces.
The bids – one as high as €2,000, according to news website NU.nl – after the lottery system for places at Erasmus MC left hundreds of students waiting months, some more than a year, to begin.
The medicine master’s is built mostly around clinical placements in hospital departments. Each department can take a limited number of trainees, so start dates are drawn by lottery, and pulling the short straw can cost the better part of a year.
This time the draw went badly for a lot of them. Of the roughly 380 students who entered, about a quarter can’t start until autumn 2027 and 35% not until 2028, NU.nl reported, citing an email sent to students.
Richer students paying ahead
 Students have bought and sold Rotterdam start dates before. Medisch Contact, a medical journal, documented the trade in 2020, when the medical faculty’s student council warned it let wealthier students buy their way ahead.
Erasmus MC told NU.nl it did not want money deciding who trains first, and said it would look at tightening the rules on swaps. It called the shortage of places temporary: extra students are graduating amid a switch to a new curriculum.
Students who wait longest can sometimes claim compensation from a university fund that covers study delays outside their control. The Netherlands is already facing a shortage of doctors, particularly neurologists.

Israeli forces raze West Bank homes as EU weighs ban on settlement goods
Pogroms in the occupied West Bank continue, with Israeli forces demolishing homes in Birzeit and Nablus, and settlers attacking Palestinians.
Israeli forces have demolished more Palestinian homes in the occupied West Bank, as settlers attacked residents of the village of Burqa in an escalation of violence ahead of Israeli elections in October.
The pogroms on Monday came as Ireland pushes for sanctions on goods from illegal Israeli settlements at an informal meeting of European Union ministers this week.

In the town of Birzet, north of Ramallah, Israeli soldiers demolished two residential buildings, saying they lacked the required building permits, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
In Nablus, Israeli forces used a bulldozer to raze a two-storey house and a three-storey building under construction.
And in Burqa, east of Ramallah, video verified by Al Jazeera showed a large group of settlers raiding the village and attacking Palestinians. One clip showed settlers and Palestinians throwing stones at each other.
Witnesses said the settlers entered the village from several directions on Monday night before assaulting residents, trying to set cars alight and stealing livestock.
The United Nations human rights office said last month that settler violence was at an “all-time high”, with new settlements approved and settlers and the Israeli army often acting together against Palestinian communities.
Settler violence and settlement expansion are on the agenda of a two-day meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland beginning on Tuesday.
Ireland, which holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU and has moved to ban settlement goods itself, wants member states to act together.
The talks are expected to build on discussions in Brussels in July, based on a confidential European Commission paper floating three options, including an import licensing system, prohibitive tariffs or an outright ban, according to Reuters news agency.
EU rules require goods from illegal West Bank settlements to be labelled as originating in the occupied territory rather than Israel. But the bloc has not banned trade with the settlements, leaving that to individual states.
Decisions on the policy have long been difficult for the 27 member countries, which are deeply divided over Israel and Palestine.
Neale Richmond, an Irish minister of state, said Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory and its failure to stop settler violence breached international law.
“We see certain EU politicians or European politicians supportive not just of the actions of settlers and settler violence, but of this Israeli government who are supporting them,” he said. “And we cannot be complicit in the actions of this Israeli government, which more broadly is genocidal.”

Factbox: Latest relief and rescue progress at mudslide-hit border port in China's Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:27:00 CST
14:27:00 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, causing heavy casualties and leaving many missing.
Chinese rescuers immediately launched an all-out effort to reach the mudslide-hit port area and search for the missing. Here is what we know about the deadly mudslide and the latest rescue and relief progress in China:
-- Sixteen people have been confirmed dead and 546 others remain missing after the mudslide struck the border port, according to the regional government's latest update.
A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries have been identified as unaccounted for.
-- An ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-mountain glacier in Nepal has been identified as the cause of the mudslide.
-- Memorial services were held on Tuesday in Gyirong to mourn the victims of the mudslide.
-- More than 2,000 personnel have joined the search and rescue operations, including those from the People's Liberation Army, the People's Armed Police Force and China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise. Despite difficulties such as high-altitude terrain, steep valleys and volatile weather, the rescue forces have been working around the clock to search for survivors, repair roads, set up communication base stations and restore power lines.
-- Rescuers are working round the clock to reopen a major highway leading to the Gyirong Port to facilitate the entry of key equipment, personnel and supplies into the disaster area. The G216, a national highway to the port, had been restored to within 1.1 kilometers of the port as of Monday noon.
-- On Monday afternoon, two Xinhua reporters arrived by helicopter at the core disaster-stricken area, near the border gate of the Gyirong Port. Their video footage captured scenes of knee-deep mud and powerful gusts that make it difficult to stand upright.
-- In the face of the tragic disaster, the Chinese side rejects malicious speculation that has no factual basis, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday at a news briefing in response to some foreign media's inappropriate remarks regarding the cause of the disaster.
-- China is making every effort to search for and rescue the missing at home and abroad, and is in close contact with foreign embassies in China to jointly conduct screening and aftermath handling for the missing foreign nationals, Guo said.
Noting that the Chinese government has provided Nepal with emergency cash assistance and humanitarian aid, Guo said that the first batch of 50 tonnes of relief supplies has already arrived in Kathmandu, and two rescue teams composed of Chinese tunnel rescue experts have rushed to the disaster-stricken areas in Nepal.
-- China has been providing Nepal with meteorological and hydrological data, conducted consultation among experts, and shared early-warning information. China will continue giving strong support to Nepal in its relief efforts and strengthen cooperation with Nepal on disaster prevention and control for the shared benefit of both peoples, Guo said. ■

Captain among nine held over deadly Turkish Cyprus ferry sinking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:26:53 UTC
14:26:53 KST

A deep-sea search-and-rescue vessel deployed by Türkiye on Sept. 1 joined efforts to recover the 20 people still missing after a passenger ferry capsized off Turkish Cyprus’ Kyrenia.
The TCG Işın began the extensive operation to locate the missing persons after the high-speed ferry sank on Aug. 30, 4 nautical miles off the port town of Kyrenia.
Authorities confirmed late on Aug. 31 that the disaster killed eight people, bringing the number of people still unaccounted for from 18 to 20.
A total of 241 of the 267 people aboard the Filo Jet, which was bound for Taşucu on the Turkish southern province of Mersin when it began taking on water, were rescued, authorities said. Almost all of those on board were Turkish or Turkish Cypriot nationals.
As the wreck lies at a depth of 514 meters, efforts by conventional divers and other vessels had been unable to reach it.
The operation therefore turned to a remotely operated mini-submarine capable of descending to depths of up to 3,000 meters, along with divers equipped with specialized pressure-resistant suits, to access the wreckage.
The immediate priority is to recover the bodies of those who may have become trapped inside the vessel after it sank.
Investigators will then focus on locating the ferry’s black box, which is expected to provide crucial information for determining the cause of the accident.
The remotely operated systems will also capture detailed images of the wreck, potentially providing investigators with important evidence about the circumstances surrounding the disaster.
Police detained the captain and 15 others following the accident.
Nine of them appeared in court in Kyrenia on charges of negligent homicide.
Addressing the court, the captain and crew members said the front section of the vessel had been torn open by the force of the waves, according to Türkiye’s state-run Anadolu Agency.
The captain was remanded in custody.
Some survivors said there had not been enough safety equipment for all passengers.
“Some people had to jump without lifebuoys or life jackets,” a young survivor, Efe Mültici, told CNN Türk. “It was literally a fight for survival.”
One of the victims was a police officer who had returned to the catamaran in an attempt to find life jackets for his wife and child, both of whom survived.
Turkish Cypriot officials said that it was likely “all those responsible” would be charged with gross negligence as the seaworthiness of the 26-year-old ferry was also questioned.
The owners and shareholders of the privately owned company operating the passenger vessel have also been ordered to appear in court.
The vessel was built in the 2000s by Iris Catamarans, a subsidiary of now-defunct French group Fountaine Pajot, company founder Jean-Francois Fountaine told AFP, saying he did not have any information on the accident.
The Turkish Coast Guard and military were assisting rescue teams from Turkish Cyprus, Prime Minister Ünal Üstel said, describing the incident as the worst maritime disaster in the island’s history.

BRASILIA, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Brazil on Monday reiterated its dissatisfaction with U.S. tariffs on Brazilian products, saying the tariffs were "unjustified and inconsistent" with international trade rules.
Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira and Development, Industry, Trade and Services Minister Marcio Elias Rosa expressed this position during a virtual meeting with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

In July, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative imposed a 25 percent surcharge on several Brazilian products after nearly a year of review. An additional 12.5 percent surcharge was later applied to more Brazilian goods. ■

China Focus: China's summer box office edges up as diverse slate lifts market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:26:48 CST
14:26:48 KST

by Xinhua writer Zhang Yunlong
BEIJING, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- China's 2026 summer movie season closed Monday with total box office revenue at nearly 12.5 billion yuan (1.84 billion U.S. dollars), up slightly from about 12 billion yuan a year earlier, marking a second consecutive year of growth for the June-August window, according to data from the China Film Administration.
Admissions rose to about 340 million, up from 321 million in 2025 and 284 million in 2024.
While these figures still fall well short of the 2023 summer season's record of 20.6 billion yuan in revenue and 504 million admissions, according to data from ticketing platform Maoyan, industry observers view the quality and diversity of this year's film slate as a bright spot after several sluggish seasons.
Lai Li, an analyst at Maoyan, said the season got off to a slow start but gained momentum as more films were released in its second half, with box office and admissions climbing steadily to post year-on-year growth in both metrics -- a sign of the market's resilience. Chen Jin, an analyst at data platform Beacon, said the summer box office results had boosted confidence for the film market's performance in the coming months, including the National Day and New Year holiday periods.
"Kung Fu Soccer," directed by Stephen Chow and released July 11, topped the season with 2.3 billion yuan. Three other films, namely restaurant-set war drama "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East" (1.9 billion yuan), animated fantasy "All Wishes Come True" (1.8 billion yuan) and Hollywood's "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" (1.5 billion yuan), each cleared 1 billion yuan.
Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" took in roughly 600 million yuan. Further down the chart, crime drama "V," war film "Crossing" and action thriller "The Furious" brought in 400 million, 290 million and 200 million yuan, respectively.
Animation studio Light Chaser's "Three Kingdoms: The Beginning," the first installment of a planned trilogy retelling the classical epic, earned just 90 million yuan but drew critical acclaim, suggesting a possible slow-burn following for the franchise.
In an interview with Xinhua, Rao Shuguang, president of the China Film Critics Association, said the season followed a "low-then-high" trajectory, with box office performance improving as it progressed. He singled out "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East" as the season's standout, calling it a major achievement for Chinese cinema and saying its expansion of genre and style, particularly in its more international approach to storytelling, offered new experience for how Chinese films can gain a stronger voice abroad.
Noting that this season's titles served a wider range of audience tastes, Rao said Chinese cinema is still undergoing "difficult structural adjustment" while adapting to the disruptive effects of new technologies such as AI, and needs to keep strengthening audience engagement to expand its market.
Directed and co-written by Wen Muye, "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East" follows a Chinese cook, Xu Fu, who travels to the Middle East to work in a Chinese restaurant and finds himself building a gathering place for people of different backgrounds as war breaks out around them. Rather than centering the story on soldiers or political leaders, the film follows cooks, restaurant workers and children whose lives are upended by conflict.
Wen has said this choice grew out of a simple contrast: war is cruel, while food represents happiness. Some Chinese commentators have framed the film as a marker of Chinese cinema's growing ability to compete for international narrative influence.
Mohamed Mazen, an Egyptian journalist who has lived in China for 17 years, said the film offered a distinctive perspective on war. Having grown up on Hollywood films centered on soldiers and larger-than-life heroes, he found its focus on ordinary people struggling to preserve a sense of normality amid violence to be a striking departure.
"All Wishes Come True," an animated fantasy-comedy, drew strong word-of-mouth acclaim by reimagining the eight Taoist immortals of Chinese folklore as flawed, striving individuals before their ascension, rather than as already-divine figures.
Unlike most tellings of the legend, director Mou Zhengyang said in an article published in People's Daily that he set out to show the immortals as ordinary people first -- figures with their own trades and flaws, prone to petty scheming and undermining one another, who become immortal only after learning to back each other up when it counts.
"Going it alone is fast. Going together goes further," Mou wrote of the group's arc. The approach has resonated with audiences. Mou cited one viewer's review that read, simply: "I walked out of the theater and decided to become a kinder person."
Chen Xuguang, director of Peking University's Institute of Film, Television and Theatre, said the film tapped into a familiar formula -- updating classical mythology in ways that invite contemporary parallels -- a strategy that worked for animated hits such as "Ne Zha 2" and "Nobody" last year.
He told Xinhua that the film's blend of folklore with a game-like narrative structure and visual style had also helped it connect with younger, more digitally native audiences. ■

China's PALLAS-1 rocket completes successful maiden flight
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:26:44 CST
14:26:44 KST

The PALLAS-1 Y1 carrier rocket blasts off from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwest China, Sept. 1, 2026. The rocket blasted off at 10:00 a.m. (Beijing Time) and performed normally throughout the flight. All test objectives were met, and the mission was a complete success. The mission marked the maiden flight of PALLAS-1. (Photo by Wang Jiangbo/Xinhua)
JIUQUAN, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- China on Tuesday successfully launched the PALLAS-1 Y1 carrier rocket into space from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwest China.
The rocket blasted off at 10:00 a.m. (Beijing Time) and performed normally throughout the flight, sending its payload into the designated orbit. All test objectives were met, and the mission was a complete success.
The mission marked the maiden flight of PALLAS-1, a medium-sized, two-stage liquid carrier rocket independently developed by Galactic Energy.
The rocket is 52 meters long and has a core-stage diameter of 3.35 meters, a liftoff mass of about 283 tonnes and a liftoff thrust of 350 tonnes. It can carry 5 to 7 tonnes to low Earth orbit.
"The rocket is designed to provide commercial satellite customers with an efficient, cost-friendly 'space express,'" a Galactic Energy executive said.
The rocket's main propulsion system uses the company's self-developed CQ-50 liquid oxygen-kerosene engines, with seven arranged in parallel on the first stage. The configuration is designed to meet recovery and reuse requirements while providing fault redundancy. Tests showed that the engines can throttle from 32 percent to 105 percent of rated thrust.
The company said the rocket also features an integrated structural and propulsion design, a bipropellant auxiliary propulsion system and multidimensional aerodynamic load-alleviation technology. It can also be fitted with an EROS-2 upper stage for greater mission flexibility. ■

China's photovoltaic power capacity overtakes coal-fired power for first time
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:26:28 CST
14:26:28 KST

An aerial drone photo taken on Aug. 27, 2026 shows a view of a photovoltaic power project in Sanxing Town of Shizhu County, southwest China's Chongqing. China's installed photovoltaic (PV) power capacity surpassed coal-fired power capacity for the first time, making PV the country's largest power source by installed capacity, the National Energy Administration said Tuesday. China's installed PV power capacity reached 1.286 billion kilowatts at the end of July, according to the administration. (Xinhua/Huang Wei)
BEIJING, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- China's installed photovoltaic (PV) power capacity surpassed coal-fired power capacity for the first time, making PV the country's largest power source by installed capacity, the National Energy Administration said Tuesday.
China's installed PV power capacity reached 1.286 billion kilowatts at the end of July, edging past coal-fired power capacity of 1.285 billion kilowatts, according to the administration.
"This marks a milestone in China's green and low-carbon energy transition," said Liu Zhiqiang, an expert from the China Electricity Council, adding that the country's new power system, with new energy as the mainstay, is taking shape at an accelerated pace.
By the end of July, PV power accounted for more than 30 percent of China's total installed power generation capacity. Measured by newly added capacity, the share rose to more than 40 percent in the first seven months, underscoring the rapid expansion of the PV sector.
China has built a complete PV industry chain covering research and development, design and integrated manufacturing. Technological advances, including repeated breakthroughs in PV conversion efficiency, have helped drive continuous upgrades and rapid cost reductions.
China's rapid development of PV power and other forms of new energy is also making a positive contribution globally.
With the world's largest and fastest-growing renewable energy system, the country supplies more than 80 percent of the PV modules and 70 percent of the wind power equipment around the world, assisting the green transition in many countries.
In particular, amid uncertainties in global supplies of energy and key raw materials, China's growing new energy capacity helped it meet domestic energy demand while contributing to the stability of global energy markets and supply chains, experts said. ■

EU considers military mission to replace UN peacekeepers in South Lebanon
Analysts say Israel could benefit when UNIFIL’s mandate expires on December 31.
With the nearly 50-year United Nations peacekeeping mandate in southern Lebanon set to expire at the end of 2026, proposals for a European Union mission to fill some part of the vacuum have attracted attention.
Lebanon, still under almost daily Israeli bombardment with a fifth of its territory occupied and about 335,000 people still displaced, is expected to be on the agenda during an EU defence and foreign ministers meeting in Ireland this week.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Israel continues attacks on Syria, Lebanon despite US push for diplomacy
- list 2 of 4Is Iran war diplomacy ramping up, as Qatar, Oman, Pakistan officials visit?
- list 3 of 4Israeli strike kills ‘newlywed’ woman in south Lebanon, wounds others
- list 4 of 4Video: Israeli strike kills newlywed woman in south Lebanon
The European External Action Service (EEAS), the EU’s diplomatic service, has circulated a proposal for a three-year military and civilian mission to advise and train the Lebanese armed forces (LAF) and the Internal Security Forces (ISF), Lebanon’s police, including in border and maritime security, an attempt, officials said, not to replace the UN peacekeeping force – known as UNIFIL – but to strengthen the Lebanese state.
But while the EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, told reporters in May that Europeans were willing to put together a mission to help the LAF, she questioned whether there was an appetite for an entirely new European mission to come in to fully replace UNIFIL’s mission.
A mandate with limitations
UNIFIL was created on March 19, 1978, days after Israel invaded southern Lebanon. Its mandate has been expanded several times since, most consequentially after the 2006 war between Israel and the Lebanese group Hezbollah when UN Security Council Resolution 1701 added the tasks of monitoring the ceasefire and supporting the LAF’s deployment in the south to UNIFIL’s mission.
However, UNIFIL was never given the power to enforce any of it. It could watch, report and accompany but not compel an Israeli withdrawal or disarm any armed group.
Yet it was Israel that was largely behind UNIFIL’s end after it accused the force of failing to prevent Hezbollah’s military build-up along the Israel-Lebanon border.
A new European force is unlikely to be tasked with confirming an Israeli withdrawal or disarming Hezbollah, said Raymond Murphy, a professor at the Irish Centre for Human Rights at the University of Galway who served as a UN peacekeeper with UNIFIL.
Its role would more likely be to monitor, he said, but with “sufficient capacity to use military force to protect itself and to carry out its mandate. For example, it would have freedom of movement and [the ability] to prevent the movement of arms in its area.”
Europe is not the only option under discussion.
The UN is running its own succession planning: One proposal would hand a residual role to the UN Truce Supervision Organisation, and in June, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres put three options to the Security Council with the number of soldiers ranging from 900 to 3,000, compared with UNIFIL’s roughly 7,000 in June.
Israel could benefit from a power vacuum
The risk of a temporary vacuum is “quite serious”, Lebanese political scientist Imad Salamey told Al Jazeera, partly because Israel could benefit.
Without an international force, he argued, Israel could pursue an arrangement in which the LAF is “compelled to coordinate” more directly with Israeli forces as the United States acts as an “intermediary or guarantor”, shifting the architecture from internationally supervised monitoring towards bilateral coordination between a Lebanese army and an army occupying Lebanese territory.
“Once UNIFIL disappears, the alternative arrangements created in its absence could become permanent and make the establishment of a successor force considerably more difficult,” Salamey said.
The US has mediated talks between Israel and Lebanon for months, but critics said those talks have done little to force Israel to abandon its attacks and its occupation of Lebanese territory.
And if a European force is deployed, Murphy does not expect that to change Israel’s position or bring about a pullback. That would make “life very difficult” for any prospective European deployment, he said.
“In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if they would create the equivalent of a new Blue Line [the demarcation line between Israel and Lebanon], 10km [6 miles] or so north of the old armistice line,” he said.
The problem may be in the framework, not the force
Israel and Lebanon agreed a framework in late June establishing so-called pilot zones, areas from which Israeli forces would withdraw and into which the LAF would deploy to assume security responsibility, including barring Hezbollah’s return.
Talks in Rome in early August ended without agreement on expanding the pilot zone model.
That is the political process any European mission would depend on, which is why the identity of the peacekeepers matters less than the terms of their presence.
Any force deployed without a comprehensive political agreement and a mandate acceptable to both sides “risks facing the same limitations that confronted UNIFIL”, Salamey said.
If Israel continues operations and keeps forces inside Lebanon while Hezbollah rejects the framework, European personnel could “quickly find their neutrality questioned by one side or the other”.
Absent reciprocal commitments, agreed rules and a realistic enforcement mechanism, swapping UNIFIL for a European mission “may simply reproduce UNIFIL’s difficulties under a different name”, he said.

'Sea change: Much of the world's economic GDP has moved to the Asia-Pacific region'

Unknown Publisher

'Sea change: Much of the world's economic GDP has moved to the Asia-Pacific region'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Rana Mitter, historian, author and ST Lee Chair in US-Asia Relations at the Harvard Kennedy School. He discusses the significance of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) as it pertains to the evolution of a changing international system, this as the bloc holds a summit in Kyrgyzstan's capital Bishkek.
Once largely a symbolic vehicle for China and Russia to signal their distance from a US-led order, the SCO is quickly becoming a forum in which Asian powers increasingly coordinate around the material foundations of security: energy, technology, infrastructure and trade.
Mitter's analysis resists the simple narrative of an emerging anti-Western bloc. India, in particular, illustrates a more fluid order in which major powers can participate in rival institutions while pursuing their own strategic interests. What is emerging, in his view, is therefore not necessarily a replacement for American hegemony led by China, but a more fragmented and transactional system shaped by the long-term movement of economic and demographic weight toward Asia.
Even a change of administration in Washington, Mitter argues, is unlikely to restore the unipolar order of previous decades. Bishkek thus offers a glimpse not simply of today's geopolitical alignments, but of a world whose economic and strategic center of gravity is steadily moving towards the Pacific.

Poland pivots to home-grown defence production as it builds Europe's biggest army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:20:53 UTC
14:20:53 KST

Poland pivots to home-grown defence production as it builds Europe's biggest army
WARSAW/GDANSK/PRAGUE, Sept 1 - As Poland builds Europe's biggest army, it is pivoting toward domestic and other central European defence companies to reduce reliance on far-flung suppliers unable to quickly ramp up deliveries, government officials and companies say.
Polish spending on defence procurement from domestic companies, including joint ventures with other central European companies, has risen nearly four-fold since 2022 to 30.4 billion zlotys ($8.15 billion) last year, according to Armaments Agency data analysed by Reuters.
While the Ukraine conflict has prompted higher defence spending across Europe, in Poland it's a top priority as the country shares a border with Ukraine and sees Russia as an existential threat, officials say.
"We're building the largest land army in Europe," Deputy State Assets Minister Konrad Golota told Reuters.
"The fact that something is used by our army and the fact that it's manufactured in Poland is becoming increasingly important."
State‑linked Polish defence firms have stepped up capital spending again in the past year, and more than a dozen government officials, companies and experts told Reuters that Warsaw's new push reflects a shift that creates opportunities for defence firms in the region.
This year, Poland is expected to spend around €53 billion ($61.45 billion) on core defence expenditures, the fourth-highest in the EU behind France, Italy and Germany, according to NATO data, up from €44 billion in 2025 and equal to around 4.7% of gross domestic product.
While big-ticket systems such as U.S.-made Patriot missile batteries, Abrams tanks and F-35 fighter jets remain important, Polish officials say expanding domestic and regional production of drones, ammunition and other frequently used equipment has become a priority.
REGIONAL SHIFT
Poland's strategy reflects a broader rethink across Europe as governments seek to rebuild defence industrial capacity after the war in Ukraine exposed how quickly modern conflicts can deplete ammunition stockpiles.
"This is not merely an investment to ensure we have a highly developed defence industry, which serves as a driving force for the Polish economy, but a matter of supply chain independence," Defence Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said.
"It ensures independent supplies to the front line should the need arise."
Until recently, defence firms in countries such as the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Hungary had a more limited presence in Poland, which relied heavily on state-owned producers such as PGZ and U.S. suppliers.
Now those companies see an opening.
Czech-based CSG, a major supplier of ammunition to Ukraine, signed a series of agreements in recent months to expand production in Poland.
These include a transfer of propellant production technology to PGZ subsidiary MESKO and an agreement with PGZ to expand production of drones, missiles, ammunition and armoured vehicles.
CSG's Polish unit has also acquired defence component maker Domar MS.
In August, CSG signed an agreement worth more than €100 million with PGZ unit Dezamet to supply components for 155 mm artillery ammunition and a separate €150 million contract with Huta Stalowa Wola for fighting vehicle equipment.
"Central Europe is undergoing a broader shift in how defence industrial capacity is built," CSG Polska Chief Executive Wojciech Grzonka told Reuters.
"Poland is a strategic market for CSG and one of the key directions for our long-term development and expansion of production capabilities."
'NEAR-SHORING' PIONEER'
Other defence groups are responding to Warsaw's push.
Polish arms maker Grupa Niewiadow, a Niewiadow PGM unit, is setting up 155 mm ammunition production with KNDS Ammo France, with output expected to reach 180,000 rounds annually from next year.
PGZ said in March it will partner with Estonia's Frankenburg Technologies to manufacture ultra‑short‑range air defence systems in Poland.
Zdenek Rod, a defence expert at CEVRO University in Prague, said Poland was emerging as a pioneer in efforts to "near-shore" military production within Europe.
"For years, supplies from the United States were a priority to ensure NATO interoperability," Rod said. "Now Poland is also trying to ensure resilience against global disruptions by turning more toward regional and European suppliers."
Polish officials also told Reuters they are discussing expanded industrial cooperation with countries including Slovakia and Hungary.
Germany's Rheinmetall said rising demand from Poland was one reason it was establishing production capacity there and developing a regional maintenance and repair hub for land combat systems.
"The demand generated by Poland's defence modernisation programme justifies establishing full-scale production sites there, which can be integrated into European supply chains and contribute to redundancy and resilience in the European defence industrial system," Rheinmetall said.
The Polish Armed Forces surpassed 220,000 personnel this year, one of Europe's biggest, and Poland, along with Estonia, is one of few NATO members that are close to their NATO commitment to spend 5% of GDP on defence by 2035. In another sign of its defence industry ambitions, Warsaw last month offered to jointly produce missiles for the Patriot air defence system with Ukraine and the United States.
"If you want to sell in Poland, you have to invest in Poland, you have to transfer technology, you have to work on joint projects with us," Deputy State Assets Minister Golota told Reuters.
"The more factories and know-how we have on our side, the better our defence is." REUTERS

Türkiye, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia agree first steps for defense alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have agreed to establish a secretariat in Saudi Arabia to oversee work under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
The body will initially be headed by a secretary-general from Pakistan for a three-year term, according to a joint statement issued after the pact’s first Strategic Political and Defense Committee meeting in Istanbul on Aug. 31.
The meeting brought together the foreign and defense ministers and military chiefs of the three countries.
“We formally adopted the first institutional decisions of the Mecca Defense Alliance,” Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said following the talks.
The three countries agreed to take further steps to institutionalize their cooperation, strengthen collective deterrence and support efforts to ease tensions and resolve regional crises peacefully, the statement said.
They will also seek to improve their defense capabilities and military interoperability through defense industry cooperation, joint technology development and joint production.
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the agreement in Mecca on Aug. 7.
The pact stipulates that an armed attack against one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all.

Two dead and one still unaccounted for in Grand Canyon flash floods, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:19:45 UTC
14:19:45 KST

Rescue efforts were hampered on Monday by more heavy rains that swept through the region, a natural part of the seasonal monsoon that frequently causes flash floods.
The number of people unaccounted for after a deadly flash flood hit part of the Grand Canyon has fallen to one as US Park Rangers said they had managed to make contact with over a dozen people who had been missing.
A monsoonal downpour that lashed the northern side of the huge canyon sent torrents of water, rock and debris down a popular hiking course on Saturday, washing out campgrounds in Bright Angel Canyon and around the historic Phantom Ranch.
Two men are known to have died in the sudden flood whose bodies were recovered as search and rescue teams moved in, amid fears that many more could have been swept away at one of the most popular and dramatic tourist spots in the United States.
But late on Monday, Dave Black of the National Park Service said nearly all those who were known to be in the canyon had now been found.
"There is one person unaccounted for that we know of right now," he told reporters in Grand Canyon Village, Arizona.
Black said 82 people had been rescued over Saturday and Sunday as a huge operation swung into gear and rangers had been canvassing the park's camping permit system to determine who might have been there when disaster struck.
"They've cross-checked between permits, license plates, any information they have, and talked to family members, made sure that they were out," he said.
Rescue efforts were hampered on Monday by more heavy rains that swept through the region, a natural part of the seasonal monsoon that frequently causes flash floods in the many creeks, gullies and washes that make up the arid landscape.
Black said better weather expected on Tuesday would help in the hunt for the one person still known to be missing, as well as any day hikers who may have been caught up in the flood. Day hikers do not require a permit to be in the canyon.
"We are still actively searching...we are absolutely holding out hope that that person is still alive," Black said.
Water pipeline damaged
The flooding damaged or destroyed 40% of the Transcanyon Waterline, a key water pipeline into Grand Canyon National Park, the park service said on Monday.
It announced water restrictions in its most visited area and a ban on wood and charcoal fires in areas where the lack of water might hamper firefighting efforts.
The 20-kilometre pipeline runs from the Roaring Springs source on the North Rim to the South Rim, providing drinking water and fire suppression, according to the park's website.
The flooding also resulted in "significant impacts to infrastructure," destroying footbridges and blocking hikers from crossing Bright Angel Creek, the park service said.
The Grand Canyon remained open to visitors, despite the tragedy. On Monday, dozens of people, many of them foreign tourists, huddled under umbrellas or wore rain ponchos as they stood on the South Rim snapping selfies and straining to make out the Colorado River far below.
Trails down into the canyon from the South Rim were also passable, but staff were warning of the potential dangers, with sudden squalls possible at any time.
The hike down into the wild belly of the canyon from one popular starting point takes many visitors around four hours, one staff member said, while the return journey would likely add another six.
Flash floods are common in Northern Arizona because the arid, sparsely vegetated environments there have little capacity to absorb rain, the park's website said, urging visitors to be especially cautious from July to mid-September.

The lame duck’s swan song: Why Trump’s final two years in office could be his most chaotic period yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:17:09 UTC
14:17:09 KST

In January, Trump will officially become a “lame duck” — a president serving out the second half of his term without the possibility of seeking reelection. Normally, that means a president’s influence begins to wane — but Trump’s case is different. He has already demonstrated a willingness to bypass Congress, test the limits of judicial constraints, and largely disregard public opinion, relying instead on an exceptionally loyal inner circle while running the federal government through executive orders. After the midterms — particularly if Republicans lose control of the House — Trump may feel even less compelled to heed the word of Congress or abide by established norms, potentially leading to further chaos both at home and abroad.
Thanks to America's system of term limits, the end of Donald Trump's political career is already coming into sight. However, the paradox is that this reality could make him more dangerous as the next two years develop. The less of a political future Trump has, the less incentive he has to safeguard his approval ratings or worry about the consequences of his decisions. In other words, the weaker he is as a politician, the freer he is as president.
A “diluted” Trump vs. the “pure” version
There is a striking contrast between Donald Trump’s first and second presidencies.
His inner circle during his first term consisted largely of technocrats pursuing an institutional approach to government. They saw Trump as a big child and themselves as the wise "adults in the room" who could keep the president under control. Inexperienced as he was, Trump listened to advisers even when they repeatedly blocked or sabotaged his initiatives. However, that did not save him from two impeachments — one over his abuse of power in his dealings with Volodymyr Zelensk, and the other after the events of January 6 (by which point most of his remaining political allies had abandoned him).
After miraculously surviving an assassination attempt in July 2024, Trump came to feel his own mortality while simultaneously claiming to be convinced that he had been spared for a revolutionary mission. “God saved me to make America great again,” he later declared.
During his second term, Trump stopped listening to anyone but himself and assembled his team primarily on the basis of personal political loyalty. In doing so, he sought to eliminate the managerial chaos, leaks, and inefficiency that had plagued his first term.
Today, almost no one can tell Donald Trump “no.” The traditional independence of the intelligence agencies has been eroded almost beyond recognition, and Trump openly demands that the Justice Department investigate his political opponents. Meanwhile, investigations into Trump himself — a regular feature of his first term in the White House — have become virtually unthinkable.
The Republican majority in Congress effectively withdrew from governing the country during the first year of “Trump 2.0.” Congress made permanent the tax cuts that will leave the country with trillions of dollars in additional debt and raised no objections when Trump launched a war with Iran despite his failure to consult the legislative branch. Finally, Trump blocked $400 billion in spending that had been approved by Congress, a clear violation of the Constitutional principle that places the government’s purse entirely in the hands of Congress.
The U.S. Supreme Court, despite its 6-3 majority of Republican appointees, has not always sided with Trump. For example, the court declined to abolish birthright citizenship and struck down most of the tariffs Trump imposed on imports from around the world. Still, even before his second term, the court recognized broad criminal immunity for presidents, sharply reducing the risk that Trump could later face prosecution over decisions and actions taken while in office.
Perhaps most importantly, under Trump 2.0 presidential power has been so openly transformed into personal enrichment that it borders on corruption — from the aircraft gifted to Trump by the Qatari government to the billions earned by his family through opaque deals during just the first year of his second term. There has also been unprecedented interference in private business, as when Trump demanded the resignation of Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan over his alleged ties to Chinese companies (even if, after Tan met with Trump at the White House and explained himself, the threat disappeared). In the end, the administration reached a deal under which the government would acquire nearly 10% of Intel in exchange for financial support.
Presidential power has, for the first time, been so openly transformed into personal enrichment that it borders on corruption
The New York Times editorial board has distilled these developments into a 12-point “autocracy index,” that covers everything from Trump's circumvention of the legislature and pursuit of political opponents to suppression of dissent and the use of power for personal gain. Still, elections have not been abolished, and independent centers of power have survived — precisely where Trump’s vulnerability begins.
The patriarch’s autumn
However weak Congress may appear, Republicans’ once-total submission to Trump has begun to weaken. They fear losing control of one or even both chambers in the midterm elections if they continue to back the president unquestioningly, and they have even dared to vote for a resolution calling for an end to the war with Iran.
As during Trump’s first term, the courts remain the most effective check on executive overreach. In addition to the Supreme Court rulings mentioned above, a series of decisions by lower courts has blocked key elements of Trump’s immigration and tariff policies from being adopted. The judiciary has also prevented Trump from firing a member of the Federal Reserve Board and restricted a number of political appointments at the Justice Department that were made in violation of proper procedures. As a result, Trump has discovered that, although the system of checks and balances has been significantly weakened, the president still cannot act with complete disregard for the will of the other branches of government.
Finally, public opinion has turned sharply against Trump. His already low approval rating continues to slide, with two-thirds of Americans saying they disapproved of his job performance as of mid-August. Democrats, despite being consumed by their own internal problems, have begun to recover in the polls.
The economy has traditionally been a Republican stronghold, with the party positioning itself as the champion of low taxes. But in an August Reuters/Ipsos poll, voters gave Democrats a narrow edge over Republicans on economic issues: 38% to 35%. At the same time, a majority said they trusted neither party to handle the economy.
Under the circumstances, Trump's endorsement is no longer a guarantee of victory in GOP primaries. Even if most of Trump's preferences prevail at the polls, as of August roughly a dozen Trump-backed candidates had lost their races to represent the party in Congressional and gubernatorial elections this November.
Endorsement no longer guarantees victory in Republican primaries
“Trump will naturally begin to lose influence, especially after the midterm elections,” an unnamed White House adviser acknowledged in an interview with Reuters. Meanwhile, presidential historian Douglas Brinkley told the agency that Trump’s leadership style is a “mess” that will not produce results, regardless of which party controls Congress following the mid-terms.
As summer draws to a close, current forecasts fairly confidently predict that Republicans will lose the House of Representatives, while it remains unclear which party will control the Senate. On Aug. 25, the prediction market Kalshi put the odds of Democrats taking the House at 86% while giving Republicans a 53% chance of retaining control of the Senate.
The outcome will play a key role in Trump’s ability to govern going forward. If the Republicans retain control of both chambers, the president will have another two years to pass legislation and confirm judges. Trump is already being called the de facto speaker of the House, and a Republican victory would only strengthen the president’s influence over Congress.
However, if Democrats take the House, they will be able to block most of Trump’s legislative agenda, and the budget will become the subject of constant bargaining. Democrats will also gain the power to investigate the administration, subpoena officials to testify at hearings, and demand documents. A Republican-controlled Senate, however, would allow Trump to continue pushing through appointments and blocking initiatives originating in the House.
If the Republicans lose control of both chambers, legislative gridlock will be compounded by serious difficulties in confirming administration officials and federal judges. Trump’s main tools will be executive orders, the power to veto legislation passed by Congress, and direct control of the federal bureaucracy. At the same time, a Democratic Congress will be able to use the budget, investigations, and legislation to constrain the White House. This is the scenario with the greatest potential for an open confrontation between the branches of government — and for Trump to test the limits of his own powers even further.
No holds barred
A weakening of Trump’s political position will not necessarily constrain him — quite the opposite. There are sound theoretical grounds for that conclusion.
In 2018, political scientist Marc Shehker published a study arguing that term limits create accountability problems for U.S. governors. This followed the 2016 examination by political scientist Philip Potter of the behavior of U.S. presidents in their final terms; he concluded that they were more ambitious than during their first terms, particularly in foreign policy. As Trump becomes a “lame duck,” his support is weakening and Republicans are becoming less afraid of him. Yet he still retains enormous power that he can exercise more or less unilaterally.
With no need to campaign for reelection, Trump may even feel free to ignore public opinion. At the height of his trade war with the wider world, he argued that American children would now have “two dolls instead of 30,” implying that voters had become accustomed to living far beyond their means. Trump was even more explicit when the war with Iran sent gasoline prices soaring and accelerated inflation: he called it “a small price” to pay for security.
With no need to campaign for reelection, Trump may ignore public opinion
A second presidential term creates an inherent imbalance: a president’s incentive to negotiate with Congress and remain responsive to voters can disappear before his ability to act unilaterally does. Trump appears to sense this. In their recently published book, Regime Change, journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan write that the president has grown less interested in the backlash to his policies. According to Swan, Trump “doesn’t care at all” about the outcome of the mid-term elections. Instead, he is focused on his legacy as a historical figure.
Whatever the outcome of the November elections, Trump will enter 2027 at the peak of his presidential power, with little incentive to seek compromise with either allies or opponents. Against a backdrop of economic troubles, an unpopular war with Iran, mass deportations, and new ideological battles at home, political tensions may only intensify.
Trump’s critics have often optimistically suggested that he had reached the limits of his reckless and dangerous behavior. Yet his political career has repeatedly demonstrated otherwise: Trump can still keep raising the stakes, turning his unpredictability into an ever greater threat for the country's stability.

Cancer and virus-free: Bats' longevity genes could hold clues for human health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:15:05 UTC
14:15:05 KST

Scientists are studying the mechanisms behind bats' immune systems to uncover what they could teach about human longevity.
Bats are the longest-lived mammals for their size and have the ability to adapt to viruses and boost their defences. Scientists are now trying to see whether humans can learn anything from bats’ ability to resist viruses and even prevent cancer.
A new study published in the journal Nature looked at what these animals can teach about longevity and fighting disease. The findings reveal that the bats' ability to slow ageing and tolerate viruses is genetically linked, suggesting that the same biological 'tricks' protect them from both infections and the decay of old age
“Bats have evolved this incredible fitness capacity, this incredible ability to deal with disease and this incredible ability to be able to prevent cancer,” said Juan Manuel Vazquez, author of the study at the University of California, Berkeley.
“That means that, by understanding how bats have evolved to do all these things that other mammals haven’t, we can find completely new and unexpected ways of dealing with the normal things that cause human diseases.”
For the study, Vazquez travelled to capture, biopsy and release different species of bats. He currently has cell cultures from 259 individuals representing 32 species.
He focused on those in the Myotis genus of bats, known for having some of the most extreme adaptations for longevity and disease resistance among mammals. In this group, the Myotis brandtii (Brandt’s bat) can live up to 42 years.
How bats resist ageing and cancer
By creating high-quality genetic maps for eight different species, the researchers identified the specific biological "tricks" these animals use to survive.
One of the most important findings is that long-lived bats have evolved ways to prevent cancer. For example, the little brown bat (Myotis lucifugus) has an enhanced ability to clear out damaged cells before they can cause harm.
An example of this is a specific immune factor called PKR, as most Myotis species have evolved extra copies of this gene to fight a wider range of viruses.
A different way of fighting viruses
Bats act as zoonotic reservoirs — animals that can carry viruses dangerous to humans without becoming ill themselves. Their ability to do this is a result of a specialised evolutionary strategy known as viral tolerance.
The research found that while most mammals use "resistance" to fight viruses by attempting to eliminate the pathogen, bats have evolved high levels of viral tolerance.
They have developed mechanisms to suppress the damaging inflammation and cellular stress that would normally kill other mammals, which allows the virus to live in their bodies.
For RNA viruses, responsible for human outbreaks such as the COVID-19 pandemic, bats tend to change the number of immune genes they have and evolve extra copies to broaden their defence.
What this means for human disease
Because bats have developed natural solutions to problems like cancer and cellular decay, they provide a roadmap for understanding how these same processes might be managed in humans, the researchers said.
Vazquez noted that bats evolved to live for a long time without getting diseases, which suggests we don't necessarily need to look at diseases of ageing and diseases of infection as completely separate fields.
“We can look at these bats and try to understand how, in the same way you can improve your immune system to fight off viruses, maybe you can improve your immune system so it doesn’t decline in old age,” he noted.
“Or maybe bats can help us find ways to fight off tumors so our immune system doesn’t get tired, and that can also help us deal with other stresses of life and not exhaust our immunity.”

====================================================================================================

More freedom, more order: The integration of migrants works better in countries where newcomers face fewer restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:14:33 UTC
14:14:33 KST

The number of migrants worldwide has reached 300 million, and despite growing anti-immigration sentiment and the rise to power of leaders promising to halt the influx of newcomers, neither the United States nor Europe has managed to significantly reduce their numbers. Migration will continue to grow as aging economies face increasingly severe labor shortages. The main challenge for governments is not so much to stop the flow as to integrate migrants effectively, avoiding social conflicts while reaping the economic benefits immigration brings. International experience varies, but numerous studies show that migration policies have been more successful in countries where migrants have equal access to the labor market and can participate in public life. The higher the employment rate among migrants and the fewer bureaucratic barriers they face, the better results migrant communities show when it comes to questions of crime and social exclusion.
In recent decades, almost all developed countries have been experiencing a severe demographic crisis caused by population aging. Combined with globalization, this has led to a growing influx of migrants into these countries. According to the UN, the number of migrants worldwide stands at around 300 million, double what it was in 1990 (although its share of the global population grew much more modestly, from 2.9% to 3.7%).
This growth has fueled a global wave of anti-immigration sentiment. Yet even politicians who come to power on the back of such rhetoric usually fail to stop the influx of migrants. Donald Trump, for example, only slightly reduced the number of legal migrants entering the United States during his first term, largely by cutting the number of refugees admitted through the UN resettlement program. And during Giorgia Meloni's tenure as Italy's prime minister, the number of migrants arriving in the country has only increased — Italy has even remained the leading destination for people entering Europe illegally.
Brexit, which took place against a backdrop of British discontent over migration, led European citizens to leave the country, but they were replaced by far more migrants from non-European countries. Russian authorities, meanwhile, are fueling anti-immigration hysteria while trying to replace laborers from post-Soviet countries with different migrants from farther afield.
Migration, of course, has an objective driver: growing demand for labor. And as long as that demand persists, migration will continue to grow. According to forecasts by the International Organization for Migration, the number of migrants worldwide will exceed 400 million by 2050. It is therefore essential to understand how best to manage migration while integrating newcomers.
By 2050, the number of migrants worldwide will exceed 400 million
As with measures aimed at restricting entry, attempts to integrate migrants often produce outcomes that run counter to the aims of government efforts.
Sweden, for example, is the world's most migrant-friendly country and has the highest score on the Migrant Integration Policy Index (MIPEX). Yet migrants in Sweden are still more likely to commit crimes than the native-born population; they earn less, pay less in taxes, and their children perform worse at school.
In Spain, by contrast, migrants account for a similar share of the population — just over 20% — while both the MIPEX score and spending on integration programs are lower. Yet the gap between migrants and the native population is also smaller across all indicators. Moreover, migration has reduced unemployment and crime in the country and boosted GDP per capita.
In Russia, meanwhile, a country that is extremely unwelcoming to newcomers and has a very low MIPEX score, migrants commit crimes significantly less often than the native population while having the same employment rate.
Research shows that three factors matter more than either spending on integration or the strictness of migration policy itself: migrants' access to the labor market, the composition of migration flows, and the ability of institutions to prevent discrimination against newcomers.
Access to the labor market
Employment is the main factor determining an individual's propensity to commit crime across all population groups. Unemployed people are more likely to turn to crime to survive — subsistence crimes, which typically include theft, squatting, or even prostitution. They are also more likely to become involved in criminal networks, which essentially serve as alternative forms of employment.
Even among employed people, peaks in criminal activity occur during periods when they are not working — namely, on holidays, when the rate of violent crime tends to increase, largely because of alcohol. Among unemployed people, by contrast, holidays have a much smaller effect on crime.
Around 60% of migrants worldwide moved in search of work. Since labor migrants generally have lower crime rates than the local population as a whole, an influx of labor migrants can even reduce the overall per-capita crime rate.
Crime rates among labor migrants are generally lower than among the local population
This largely explains the paradoxically low crime rate among migrants in Russia. The country accepts virtually no refugees, and the overwhelming majority of newcomers are labor migrants. Since 2014, Ukrainian refugees — following Russia's occupation of Crimea and parts of Ukraine's Donetsk and Luhansk regions — have been granted preferential residency arrangements allowing them to work immediately, access government services, and remain in the country indefinitely. They were also eligible for a simplified path to citizenship (meaning they have barely registered in official crime statistics as migrants).
There is considerable evidence that allowing migrants to work legally also improves their integration. A revealing comparison of two waves of immigration to Britain illustrates the point. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the country received asylum seekers who were mostly not allowed to work immediately, leading to an increase in property crime. By contrast, the wave of migration that followed the accession of 10 new countries to the EU consisted of people who immediately gained the right to work and, in turn, slightly reduced crime rates.
A similar situation emerged in Italy after Bulgaria and Romania joined the EU. Because citizens of those countries automatically acquired legal status, the incidence of “subsistence crimes” among them fell by half. The effect was particularly pronounced in the country's industrialized northern regions, while in the south, where migrants were often already working informally in agriculture, legalization had virtually no effect on crime rates.
The same pattern can be seen in the contrast between English-speaking countries — the UK, Canada, the U.S., Australia, Ireland, and New Zealand — and continental Europe. This is partly because the English-speaking countries are geographically distant from major conflict zones, making it more difficult for refugees to reach them unless they are resettled through the UN Refugee Agency's programs.
As a result, these people have already had their asylum claims approved and are granted the right to work immediately upon arrival. Consequently, in all these countries, the share of migrants among the prison population is lower than their share of the total population, while their children perform better on standardized tests than children of native-born residents.
In continental Europe, by contrast, refugees arrive directly across land borders or by sea, meaning they do not immediately gain the right to work. A report by the European Council on Refugees and Exiles notes that, although numerous European directives recognize the right to work as a fundamental human right and call for asylum seekers to be granted access to the labor market as soon as possible, many countries still impose various barriers until their applications are processed.
In some countries, refugees are housed for long periods in camps located in areas with high unemployment or are frequently transferred between accommodation centers, making it difficult to secure permanent employment. Elsewhere, authorities delay the issuance of documents, while employers themselves may be unsure whether they are allowed to hire asylum seekers whose applications have not yet been approved.
In many EU countries, migrants are allowed to work only in a limited range of sectors, mostly in low-skilled jobs. At the same time, many higher-skilled positions require a relevant degree and a certain level of proficiency in the local language, and their professional qualifications obtained abroad may not be recognized. As a result, for example, low-skilled migrants in Italy have a higher employment rate than Italians with a similar level of qualifications (65.0% versus 53.2%), while highly skilled migrants have a lower employment rate (69.0% versus 85.7%).
In Hungary, temporary residence permits are issued for just three months, meaning refugees must repeatedly have their documents verified at their place of work, increasing employers' administrative costs. In Greece, only 3% of refugees have managed to open bank accounts into which they can receive their salaries. In the Netherlands, of the 26,520 people who applied for asylum in 2021, only 590 were granted the right to work.
In eight EU countries, migrants from non-EU states have a higher employment rate than the native population: the Czech Republic, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg Malta, Poland, Portugal, Slovenia. Among these, Poland and the Czech Republic receive large numbers of Ukrainians who benefit from simplified work-permit procedures, while Portugal has an analagous arrangement for people from its former colonies.
In the United States, migrants have traditionally had lower crime rates, better health outcomes, and higher levels of academic achievement than native-born Americans, while by the third generation they tended to converge with — or even surpass — them on economic indicators. Even refugees had employment rates comparable to those of labor migrants.
However, in the 2010s, a surge of asylum seekers began crossing the U.S. border from four primary countries: Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala, and Venezuela. This influx was largely a legacy of U.S. intervention in these countries' politics during the Cold War, exacerbated by the flow of weapons into Latin America from the United States itself. Because these asylum seekers arrived in the U.S. directly rather than through the UN resettlement program, they were barred from working until their asylum claims were approved. Unsurprisingly, their integration outcomes were worse than for previous waves of newcomers, forcing the government to spend considerably more money to support them.
Restricting asylum seekers' right to work therefore has long-term negative economic effects. Until the restriction is lifted, refugees are forced to rely entirely on government support, thus becoming dependent on benefits. During this period, they remain disconnected from society because they are excluded from economic life, while their professional skills gradually deteriorate. As a result, their chances of finding employment after receiving work authorization fall by 15%.
Restricting asylum seekers' right to work has long-term negative economic effects
The phenomenon is not American in nature. In Germany, a court ruling reduced the length of time refugees had to wait for work authorization. This experience showed that people who had to wait an additional seven months for permission to work were 20 percentage points less likely to find employment than those who obtained the right earlier. The gap only disappeared ten years later, and researchers estimate that the EU lost €37.6 billion in GDP because refugees who arrived during the migration crisis triggered by the war in Syria faced restrictions on employment.
Which migrants arrive
In Sweden, refugees can work almost immediately after applying for asylum, although only in low-skilled jobs. Nevertheless, the country's integration outcomes are among the worst of any developed country.
A major factor is the composition of the migration flows arriving in Sweden. For decades, the country has accepted large numbers of refugees, most of them from the culturally distant Muslim world. The three main countries of origin for migrants in Sweden are Syria, Iraq, and Afghanistan. Sweden is now the European country with the highest number of refugees per capita.
Refugees, however, are the category of migrant that is hardest to integrate. Unlike economic migrants, who typically choose their destination in advance, prepare for the move, learn the language, and often already have useful contacts, in-demand skills, or a job offer, refugees are forced to leave their homes. They often lose their property, documents, professional networks, and the ability to make use of the human capital they have accumulated. They adapt much more slowly than labor migrants and people who move for family reunification, resulting in what researchers refer to as the “refugee gap.”
Refugees are the category of migrants that is hardest to integrate
While labor migrants move based on their skills and the needs of the labor market that attracts them, refugees go wherever they can find safety. Their integration is further complicated by the trauma they have experienced, prolonged uncertainty over their legal status, restrictions on access to the labor market while their applications are being processed, and administrative policies that place them in areas with limited economic opportunities and little or no diaspora support.
In Spain, the flow of humanitarian migrants today is comparable to that seen in Sweden at the peak of its refugee intake (although its relative size is significantly smaller given that Spain's population is five times as big). At the same time, 47% of migrants in Spain come from Latin America, with which Spain shares a language and similar culture. They can enter without a visa, are immediately allowed to work, and can apply for citizenship after just two years of residence. Another 27% come from other European countries, while only 18% come from Africa and 6% from Asia (including the Philippines, which was also once a Spanish colony). In short, historical, cultural, and linguistic ties make integration into Spanish society considerably easier for most migrants than the integration of Middle Eastern migrants in Sweden, despite the lower level of government spending.
Russia likewise has significant cultural and linguistic influence in Central Asia, as well as large diasporas from the region, making it easier for migrants from Central Asian countries to integrate into Russian society. Similarly, the U.S. has exerted influence across Latin America for centuries and is home to large Latin American diasporas. Poland and the Czech Republic have also achieved strong migrant integration outcomes because, historically, they have primarily received Ukrainians, who are culturally and linguistically similar and can take up employment immediately. Thus, even when a large influx of Ukrainian refugees arrived after the outbreak of the war, they were relatively easily integrated.
Cultural differences, however, do not account for the entire gap. The quality of the human capital that countries attract also matters. The U.S., for example, is geographically distant from most of the world's main migration routes, so reaching the country itself requires substantial resources. Its high wages consequently attract some of the most successful and highly educated migrants.
For example, Middle Eastern migrants in the U.S. are twice as likely as Americans overall to hold a bachelor's degree, and they earn slightly more. In Europe, by contrast, where many arrived as low-skilled guest workers, undocumented migrants, or refugees, they are among the most disadvantaged groups, with low incomes and high crime rates.
Similarly, Pakistani migrants in the U.S. have higher incomes and higher levels of education than the native-born population, while in Britain they have one of the lowest employment rates in the country. The colonial legacy plays a role: in the 1950s and 1960s, Britain itself brought in large numbers of workers from Pakistan to work in factories, and they later brought their families over.
A substantial part of the employment gap, however, is also explained by the fact that many Pakistani women, due to cultural traditions and discrimination, choose not to work and instead engage in unpaid domestic work, a common practice among diasporas from Muslim-majority countries across Europe.
The impact of discrimination
Finally, it also matters how prepared a country's institutions are to receive migrants. Even if a country attracts relatively well-off migrant groups and provides them with rapid access to the labor market, that alone is not enough. What matters is whether institutions allow migrants to compete with native-born residents on an equal footing.
The U.S., Canada, Australia, and New Zealand are countries built by migrants. They have accumulated experience with immigration and established diasporas that help newcomers integrate. European countries, by contrast, only became countries of immigration in the 20th century, having previously been countries of emigration. They are considerably more ethnically homogeneous and therefore have less experience and few longstanding institutions for integrating migrants.
A meta-analysis of 97 experiments examining hiring discrimination across nine developed countries — the U.S., Canada, France, Belgium, the UK, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, and Sweden — found that the highest levels of discrimination in the initial screening of résumés were recorded in France and Sweden, while the lowest were found in Germany, Norway, and the U.S. In Sweden and France, the groups facing the highest levels of discrimination were also those that make up a significant share of the migrant population: Black people and people from the Middle East.
France and Sweden have the highest levels of discrimination in screening résumés from applicants with “migrant” names
The poor results of Sweden's integration policy can therefore also be attributed to informal practices, such as screening out candidates with foreign-sounding names at the résumé stage. Even when the state is highly willing to fund social programs, migrants can face serious barriers as early as the search for their first job. And this is only one form of discrimination. The study's authors note that Germany has managed to build a system that limits bias in hiring, while discrimination remains widespread in the housing market.
Promoting formal integration also has a positive effect on other aspects of integration. The experience of Switzerland, where naturalization applications in some municipalities were decided by referendum, showed that immigrants who won their vote and obtained citizenship earned an average of $5,000 more per year over the following 15 years than otherwise similar immigrants who failed to gain similar support. The effect was particularly strong among the most marginalized groups — people from Turkey and the former Yugoslavia, as well as low-wage workers.
Thus, institutions that not only give migrants access to the labor market but also recognize them as equal members of the political community can generate long-term economic benefits and improve the prospects for successful integration.
