====================================================================================================

Only clear rules, command chain, can let IDF avoid internal conflict due to religion - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
03:13:47 UTC
12:13:47 KST

At least seven religious soldiers from the Givati Brigade’s Rotem Battalion were sent to military prison after refusing to board a Namer armored personnel carrier with a female paramedic during an operation in Gaza.
The soldiers argued that the cramped conditions inside the Namer violated the IDF’s Joint Service Order and understandings reached with religious-Zionist yeshivot. The IDF said religious soldiers are entitled to carry out operational activity in a gender-segregated framework, except in exceptional cases, and that the mission was canceled because of the refusal.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich backed the soldiers, saying they had insisted on their “right and duty” to serve while preserving their faith. “As the leader of religious Zionism,” he said, he could not sit idly by and would demand answers from the IDF.
The IDF also has questions to answer.
Religious-Zionist soldiers have paid a heavy price since the October 7 massacre. Hesder students and graduates have filled combat units and reserve units.
The army has to take their religious commitments seriously and honor the Joint Service Order and agreements with the yeshivot whose students serve in combat.
Integrating must allow one sector to serve alongside another, without expense
Integrating women must allow one sector to serve alongside another without coming at its expense, Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir said in June. The army should examine whether commanders respected the framework promised to religious soldiers and whether the female paramedic’s presence inside the Namer met the order’s exceptional-circumstances standard.
War wrecks carefully drawn arrangements. The October 7 massacre showed exactly what that means.
Col. Shemer Raviv, who at the time was commander of the Paran Brigade, came from the religious-Zionist world and studied at the Otzem Pre-military Torah Academy, founded in Atzmona by Rabbi Rafi Peretz. Raviv has described himself as a man of faith.
On October 7, his force encountered dozens of terrorists near Yated. A tank commanded by a woman reached the battle. Raviv climbed inside, joined the female crew and directed its fire. He later said he had fought alongside women in extremely difficult encounters and had seen female soldiers perform flawlessly.
That same day, female tank crews fought at Holit and Sufa, while male and female combat medics treated casualties under fire. During the war, female paramedics entered Gaza with male combat units. A female paramedic also spent a month in a Namer with observant soldiers after a rabbi ruled that saving lives permitted it.
These examples show that religious observance and mixed-gender service have already collided under the harshest conditions and been resolved.
When a soldier is bleeding in Gaza, nobody asks whether the medic is a man or a woman.
When mission leaves no alternative, the commander decides
Religious soldiers should receive the accommodations they were promised whenever the mission allows it. The army should make every reasonable effort to prevent unnecessary clashes over religious observance. When the mission leaves no realistic alternative, the commander gives the order and soldiers follow it.
Soldiers can raise religious objections. Commanders should listen and find a practical solution whenever one exists. The army’s rabbis should help resolve disputes before they explode inside an APC. The rules also need to be clear enough so that soldiers do not learn what they mean while already heading into Gaza.
Smotrich went too far
Civilian rabbis do not command IDF units. Neither do politicians.
This is where Smotrich went too far.
As a cabinet minister, he has every right to demand an explanation from the IDF and ask whether it broke commitments made to religious soldiers. Giving political backing to soldiers after they refused an operational order sends another message: Refuse first, and political protection may follow.
Apply that principle throughout the army: A religious soldier follows his rabbi; a secular reservist follows his political conscience; another soldier listens to an activist group; every community gets its own veto.
No army can operate that way.
Israel wants more religious soldiers in uniform, including haredim who distrust the military’s willingness to protect their way of life, while women are serving in more combat and medical roles.
That reality demands clear rules, common sense, and commanders who know the soldiers they lead.
The IDF should keep its promises to religious soldiers and respect the women who serve beside them. When an operational order is given, there must be no doubt about who commands the army.
Common sense, mutual trust, and clear lines of authority can make this work. Without them, the IDF risks losing some of its most committed religious soldiers while making haredi recruitment even more difficult than it already is.

US Homeland Security blasts ‘garbage’ NYT report claiming detainee torture
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has dismissed as “garbage” a New York Times report alleging torture and abuse of detained deportees, accusing the newspaper of spreading false claims about federal immigration enforcement.
In a report published on Sunday, the Times said it interviewed ten people deported from the US to Liberia and Equatorial Guinea, several of whom said they had no ties to the African countries. They alleged physical abuse, harsh restraints and degrading treatment while in the custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
In comments provided to the newspaper before publication, DHS disputed several of the allegations, saying detainees receive comprehensive medical care and rejecting claims that migrants were denied bathroom access or abused during deportation flights.
Following publication, the department went further, dismissing the report as another “hoax” and describing it as “garbage.”
Another day and another hoax about ICE detention from the @nytimes. The media is clearly desperate for these false allegations to be true.
NO ONE is being tortured, denied medical care, or beaten in ICE detention facilities. 
Make no mistake: this type of GARBAGE being peddled… https://t.co/C0B868THrr
“NO ONE is being tortured, denied medical care, or beaten in ICE detention facilities,” DHS said on X, adding that “the media is clearly desperate for these false allegations to be true.”
The department also accused such coverage of fueling hostility toward immigration officers. It said assaults on ICE personnel increased by more than 1,300% between 2024 and 2025, while death threats against officers and their families surged by 8,000%.
ICE has faced mounting scrutiny during US President Donald Trump’s second term as his administration has expanded arrests and deportations as part of what it has billed as the largest immigration crackdown in US history.
The campaign has triggered nationwide protests and legal challenges, with detainees and advocacy groups accusing ICE of excessive force, poor detention conditions, and inadequate medical care.
At least 52 people died in ICE custody during the first 500 days of Trump’s second term, according to a June report by Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights.
DHS has denied that abuses are systemic and has repeatedly accused politicians and media outlets of demonizing immigration enforcement, including by comparing ICE agents to historical secret police and other authoritarian organizations.

Kākāpō rising: 90 chicks swell population of the world’s heaviest parrot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
02:57:21 UTC
11:57:21 KST

The population of the world’s heaviest parrot, the kākāpō, has surpassed 300 birds for the first time in 75 years, after a record breeding season triggered by the mass fruiting of a native New Zealand tree.
Ninety chicks were officially added to the population of the critically endangered birds on 1 September, pushing the total to 325 – a record high since recovery efforts began.
“The last time the population is thought to have exceeded 300 birds may have been as long as 75 years ago,” said Deidre Vercoe, the conservation department’s kākāpō recovery operations manager.
“We had a four-year gap between breeding seasons, so it’s fantastic to finally see the population increase after all that time.”
Kākāpō, the world’s only nocturnal and flightless parrot, were once abundant across New Zealand. But their population plummeted after the introduction of predators such as cats and stoats. By the 1900s, they were nearly extinct.
A recovery programme was established in 1995 with a population of just 51 birds and has battled challenges with genetic diversity, infertility and poor chick hatching rates. There are three kākāpō breeding populations, all based on predator-free islands off the South Island.
Kākāpō breed only every two to four years when the native rimu trees produce large numbers of berries, so repopulation is slow. This year, after a four-year wait, a bountiful harvest of rimu berries prompted the birds to breed and produce a record number of chicks. 
  “In the early years of recovery, it took 16 years to produce that many chicks,” Vercoe said.
Kākāpō are thought to live between 60 and 80 years, can weigh up to 4kg and are famously entertaining. More than 100,000 people tuned in to watch a live stream of a kākāpō sleeping, eating and attending to her nest and chicks during breeding season.
The parrots have unusual mating rituals. Male birds gather in a “lek” to produce a distinctive booming sound, emitted from air sacs in their chests while sitting in a dugout bowl in the ground. The deep boom, which can travel up to 5km, sounds similar to a softly plucked cello string.
After choosing a partner and mating, females typically lay one to four eggs. The females become solely responsible for their eggs and hatched chicks for roughly six months.
At 150 days of age, the chicks are fledged and considered independent enough to be added to the total population. The youngest chick of the 2026 breeding season was female Awarua-A3, who hatched on 30 March.
Modelling indicated the next breeding season could occur as soon as 2028, Vercoe said.
“So, while we’ll take a moment to stop and reflect on this remarkable year, we’re already looking ahead to 2028 and preparing for what could come next.”

Ukrainian drones damage Russia’s Ust-Luga port, governor says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
02:55:06 UTC
11:55:06 KST

Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Ukrainian drones struck the Novatek-Ust-Luga complex at Russia’s Baltic Sea port in Leningrad Oblast early on Sept. 1, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR) confirmed.
The strike damaged key components of an oil-processing unit and other technological equipment, causing a large fire at the facility, according to HUR.
The operation was carried out jointly by HUR’s Active Operations Department, its Unmanned Systems Department, and other Ukrainian defense forces, the agency said.
Ust-Luga is one of Russia's largest and most important ports on the Baltic Sea and home to an oil terminal that serves as a major hub for the export of crude oil and petroleum products. Located west of St. Petersburg, far from Ukraine's border, the port plays an important role in generating revenue for the state budget.
Earlier, Leningrad Oblast Governor Alexander Drozdenko confirmed damage at the port. He claimed Russian air defenses had intercepted 38 drones across the region, including 17 near Ust-Luga.
Russian air defense reported downing dozens of drones over the region in the hours between Aug. 31 and Sept. 1, with 17 drones intercepted during the ongoing attack in the Ust-Luga port area. By 6 a.m. local time, Drozdenko said 38 drones had been destroyed over Leningrad Oblast and confirmed damage at the port.
Footage circulating on Telegram appeared to show a fire at the port. The extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
Separately, Samara Oblast was targeted by Ukrainian drones, according to local officials.
In Yekaterinburg, outdoor school ceremonies scheduled for Sept. 1 were canceled following the Aug. 31 drone attack. Similar restrictions were imposed in at least 16 Russian regions.
The Kyiv Independent cannot verify the claims made by Russian officials.
As Kyiv steps up its attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, the Ust-Luga port has repeatedly served as a target of attacks in recent months. The Ukrainian military carried out a series of deep strikes against the Ust-Luga port in March and April of this year.
The most recent reported attack on the facility occurred on Aug. 14, damaging two processing plants and sparking a fire, the General Staff confirmed.
Ukraine has been aging an increasingly successful deep strike campaign against Russian oil infrastructure, striking oil depots, disrupting production at major facilities, and in some cases halting operations indefinitely.
Ukraine's oil infrastructure attacks have mounted pressure on the Kremlin by aggravating a domestic fuel supply crisis that has already caused export bans, price hikes, and sales restrictions across Russia.

Massive Russian missile attack on Kiev, surrounding areas kills four
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
02:49:03 UTC
11:49:03 KST

A "massive" Russian missile and drone attack on Ukraine’s capital, Kiev, and its surrounding areas has killed at least four people and injured more than a dozen others, Ukrainian officials said.
The strikes landed as children were set to return to school following the summer holidays, prompting authorities to tighten security measures amid concerns over further Russian aerial attacks.
"Kiev region came under a massive attack by Russian missiles and strike drones tonight," Kiev regional military administration chief Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram.
"Sadly, 3 people were killed in the enemy attack on the capital," the city military administration said, reporting five wounded.
In Boryspil, east of Kiev, strikes damaged a commercial facility, leaving one person dead and another wounded, while eight more were injured when a residential building was struck.
Air defence strains
The Ukrainian Air Force warned that the threat of "ballistic weapons and other means of attack against Kiev and the region remains in effect," urging residents to stay inside shelters.
With the new school term starting Tuesday, regional authorities banned large gatherings in high-risk zones.
Kiev has faced sustained aerial pressure from Russian drone attacks, with jet-powered drones triggering up to a dozen daily air-raid alerts.
A weekend strike on an ammunition depot in the capital's suburbs killed 38 people.
Both sides have intensified long-range strikes targeting warehouses, commercial facilities, ports, and oil infrastructure.
Ukraine continues to face a deficit of interceptor missiles, particularly US-made Patriot systems required to counter ballistic threats.
Separately, a Ukrainian air attack damaged civilian facilities in Russia's Samara region along the Volga River—an area hosting major oil refineries—with regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev reporting no initial fatalities.

Australian home values fall for fifth consecutive month
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:47:12 CST
11:47:12 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Australia's median house price fell for a fifth consecutive month in August, with Sydney leading the downturn, according to data released on Tuesday.
Property data firm Cotality said that Australia's median dwelling value fell by 0.9 percent in August to 912,885 Australian dollars (about 654,415 U.S. dollars) following a decline of 0.7 percent in July.
Cotality said that the national median dwelling value has fallen for five consecutive months and is now 3.6 percent below the record-high set in March.
Across all capital cities, median values were down 1.1 percent in August and by 3.7 percent on a quarterly basis.
The report said that home values fell across 93 percent of capital city suburbs over the three months from June to August.
Sydney, Australia's most lucrative housing market, had the biggest downturn of any capital city, with the median home value in the city down 1.4 percent in August and by 7.1 percent since February.
"The combination of a sharp drop in demand and higher than average advertised stock levels is weighing more heavily on Australia's largest housing market," Tim Lawless, Cotality's Research Director, said in a media release.
Cotality noted that its quarterly estimate of national home sales was tracking 15.5 percent lower than at the same time in 2025 and 11.5 percent below the five-year average.
Over the four weeks to the end of August, capital city real estate listings were 24 percent higher than in 2025 and 8 percent above the five-year average. ■

Messi calls time on Argentina career
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:47:12 CST
11:47:12 KST

BUENOS AIRES, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Lionel Messi announced his retirement from international football on Monday after a trophy-laden career spanning more than two decades.
Messi, 39, made the announcement on social media, explaining that he made the decision two days after Argentina's World Cup final defeat to Spain in July.
"It was a decision that hurt - and still hurts deep down - but I understand that the time has come," he wrote.
He departs as Argentina's record holder for both appearances and goals, having played 207 games and scored 125 times, 21 of them at World Cups. Only long-time rival Cristiano Ronaldo has more international goals, with 146 for Portugal.
Messi briefly held the record for career World Cup goals during this year's tournament in the United States, Mexico and Canada, before being overtaken by France's Kylian Mbappe.
The announcement marks the second time that Messi has called an end to his international career. He briefly walked away from the national team in 2016 after Argentina lost three straight major finals, including that year's defeat to Chile in the Copa America final in which he missed an attempt in the penalty shootout.
A public push from Diego Maradona and Argentina's then-president Mauricio Macri helped bring him back.
The comeback paid off. Messi won his first major trophy with Argentina at the 2021 Copa America, then led the team to the World Cup title in Qatar in 2022 - when he won the Golden Ball award for the tournament's best player - before adding a second Copa America crown in 2024.
Messi's decision came less than a month after the death of his father, Jorge, in the family's hometown of Rosario.
"I always fought and left everything on the field for this jersey, to bring you joy and make you feel proud to be Argentine through football," Messi wrote, adding that he has "nothing left to give" at the international level and that a new generation of young players deserves the chance to represent the country.
He will continue playing for Inter Miami, where he continues to impress in the MLS, having scored four times in a 7-1 win over Montreal on Saturday. Messi did not say how much longer he plans to play at club level.
The Argentine Football Association paid tribute on Instagram, thanking Messi "for giving us the most beautiful journey of our lives" and calling his legacy something that "will remain forever etched" in the country's football history.
Messi closed his own statement by thanking supporters for backing him over 21 years.
"I leave with the peace of mind and pride of having given you - alongside my teammates - moments we once only dreamed of," he wrote.
Messi is an eight-time Ballon d'Or winner and is widely regarded, alongside Maradona and Pele, as one of the greatest players in the sport's history.
"He is pure history," Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni said of him during this year's World Cup. "A legend." ■

Tunisian President Kais Saied (1st R) meets with German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul (1st L) in Tunis, Tunisia, on Aug. 31, 2026. Tunisian President Kais Saied on Monday met with visiting German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul to discuss bilateral relations, economic cooperation and ways to further develop their partnership, according to a statement from the Tunisian presidency.(Tunisian Presidency/Handout via Xinhua)
TUNIS, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Tunisian President Kais Saied on Monday met with visiting German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul to discuss bilateral relations, economic cooperation and ways to further develop their partnership, according to a statement from the Tunisian presidency.
Saied reaffirmed Tunisia's commitment to enhancing cooperation with Germany, particularly in higher education, scientific research, vocational training, energy and technological innovation.
Saied called for a review of several existing agreements, including the partnership agreement between Tunisia and the European Union.
Earlier in the day, Tunisian Minister of Foreign Affairs Mohamed Ali Nafti and Wadephul co-chaired a bilateral working session.
Germany is one of Tunisia's major economic partners, according to a statement issued by the Tunisian Foreign Ministry.
Nafti reaffirmed Tunisia's commitment to creating favorable conditions to encourage more German tourists to visit his country.
The two sides signed several agreements and financing contracts worth nearly 100 million euros (about 116 million U.S. dollars), covering support for small and medium-sized enterprises, energy, environment, digital transitions, as well as regional development and employment. ■

Feature: Song's Shanghai stunner underscores UFC's deepening China commitment
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:47:10 CST
11:47:10 KST

by sportswriter Dong Yixing
SHANGHAI, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- A record crowd of 16,188 packed Shanghai's Oriental Sports Center on Saturday night, setting a new high for UFC Fight Night events in Asia.
The turnout, revealed by UFC senior vice president and head of Asia Kevin Chang at the post-fight press conference, surpassed the venue's previous single-event attendance record.
The milestone came as China's Song Yadong delivered the biggest victory of his UFC career, knocking out third-ranked Umar Nurmagomedov in the second round to thrust himself firmly into bantamweight title contention. The 28-year-old entered as an underdog against Nurmagomedov, whose only previous loss came against current champion Merab Dvalishvili.
Song's breakthrough performance came as Chang, speaking to Xinhua days before the event, had identified more Chinese fighters contending for championships as the organization's primary goal in the country over the next three to five years.
"We wanted to go where it makes sense to go," Chang said of the UFC's trajectory in China. "The progression to being recognized as a D Class event tells us that we are highly valued here."
The designation comes from Shanghai's official sports event brand recognition system, launched in 2021 to categorize events into three tiers: Premier events with global influence, Hallmark events, and Developing events. UFC Fight Night Shanghai was named last year in the D Class, which recognizes events with strong growth potential, alongside Formula E and the IRONMAN 70.3 triathlon.
While the category sits below marquee properties like Formula 1 and the Shanghai Masters, Chang said the recognition signals a transformation from niche combat sport to an officially endorsed part of Shanghai's sporting calendar.
"To be recognized as a top-tier sport alongside basketball, football, and other major properties is something we always dreamed of," he said. "I've been in China since 2011, and to see the progression from where we were then to where we are now - moving into the mainstream - is very exciting."
The Shanghai card featured eight Chinese fighters across the main and preliminary cards, evidence of a development pipeline that Chang said has been central to the UFC's China strategy since its inception.
When the organization first entered the market in 2011, Zhang Tiequan was its lone Chinese representative. "He was the pioneer and carried the torch," Chang recalled. "Then he passed it to Li Jingliang, who carried it for a few years. But it was still just one guy at a time."
The realization that a fighter competes only two or three times annually prompted investment in infrastructure: the UFC Performance Institute in Shanghai, the UFC Academy, and the Road to UFC tournament series, which provides a pathway for regional talent.
"China is too big and too important a market for us not to," Chang said of the investment.
Several Chinese fighters delivered notable performances Saturday. Sumudaerji earned a unanimous decision over 11th-ranked flyweight Alex Perez, while light heavyweight Liu Ce made an explosive UFC debut with a first-round knockout of Brazil's Levi Rodrigues Jr.
"We're no longer waiting for one or two Chinese athletes to compete while the whole country watches," Chang said. "We have Chinese athletes competing almost every week or every couple of weeks, at different stages of their careers."
The setback Saturday for Yan Xiaonan, who suffered a first-round stoppage loss to Brazil's Denise Gomes in the co-main event, underscored the level of competition in the promotion. The 37-year-old strawweight, ranked fourth entering the night, now faces a difficult path back to title contention.
Yet Chang pointed to Zhang Weili, who headlined UFC 300 alongside Yan in 2024, as the template for what Chinese fighters can achieve globally. "She started as a Chinese star but is now far beyond that," he said. "If you go to our headquarters in Las Vegas, her picture is on the wall."
"Song Yadong is on the cusp of that," Chang said before the fight. "He's already a global star because of his exciting style. Everyone wants to watch him fight, and he's fought the best in the world."
Song's victory positioned him as a genuine title challenger in one of the UFC's deepest divisions, a scenario Chang had anticipated.
The year's two China events in Macao and Shanghai reflect a deliberate geographic strategy that Chang said balances domestic accessibility with international appeal. "Shanghai at the moment draws more domestic tourists from all over China," he said, while noting that Macao "is perhaps a bit more international."
With only 42 events annually and roughly half held outside the United States, Chang acknowledged that satisfying Chinese fan appetite presents a logistical challenge.
"There's a finite number of places we can travel to, but far more demand than inventory," he said. "The fact that we've committed to two events in China this year, and that's quite a lot internationally."
Last year's Shanghai event sold out in one minute; this year's record crowd confirmed sustained momentum. For Chang, the metric that matters most extends beyond attendance figures.
"Our milestone is how many Chinese athletes we can turn into global stars," he said. "It starts with opportunities like the one this Saturday." ■

CANBERRA, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- The Australian government on Tuesday announced funding for athletes and officials from Pacific countries leading up to the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Xinhua Commentary: Forging ahead toward China-Egypt community with shared future in new era
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:46:58 CST
11:46:58 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- As China and Egypt mark the 70th anniversary of diplomatic ties, Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to Egypt is set to inject fresh impetus into bilateral relations and further advance the building of a China-Egypt community with a shared future in the new era.
The seven-decade journey of China-Egypt relations is a powerful testament to what solidarity and cooperation can achieve. Over the years, the two countries have steadily strengthened their ties despite shifts in the regional and global landscape, maintained close coordination on international affairs, supported each other on issues of mutual interest, and expanded practical cooperation, making their partnership a model of amity, solidarity and cooperation among developing countries.
That spirit of solidarity was evident from the very beginning of their diplomatic ties. In the early years of the People's Republic of China, Beijing supported Egypt's efforts to reclaim sovereignty over the Suez Canal. In 1971, Cairo voted in favor of restoring the People's Republic of China's lawful seat at the United Nations. The two peoples also stood together in the struggle against colonialism and hegemonism, laying a solid foundation for a friendship that has endured for seven decades.
In recent years, China-Egypt relations have been deepening under the guidance of the two heads of state and are now at their best in history. For over a decade, Xi and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi have met more than 10 times, providing strategic guidance for the continued expansion of bilateral cooperation.
In 2014, the two countries elevated their relationship to a comprehensive strategic partnership. During Xi's 2016 state visit to Egypt, the two sides agreed to align the Belt and Road Initiative with Egypt's development strategies. In 2024, Egypt became the first Arab country to include the goal of building a community with a shared future in a bilateral joint statement.
Anchored in the leaders' shared vision, China-Egypt cooperation has flourished across a range of fields including trade, investment, industry, energy, science and technology, and cultural exchange, delivering tangible benefits to people in both countries.
China has been Egypt's largest trading partner for over a decade, while landmark projects such as the China-Egypt TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone, the Benban Solar Park, the remote sensing MisrSat-2 satellite and the Government Data and Cloud Computing Center illustrate how bilateral cooperation has expanded into areas ranging from renewable energy and space technology to digital governance.
Cooperation has also extended beyond economics. Joint archaeological excavations in Luxor and exhibitions of Egyptian civilization in China have brought the histories and cultures of the two ancient civilizations closer to their peoples. Such exchanges have given the bilateral relationship a deeper human foundation.
The significance of China-Egypt ties also extends beyond the two countries. Egypt was the first Arab country to establish diplomatic relations with Beijing, making the China-Egypt relationship a starting point for China's ties with the Arab world. Over the years, the momentum of China-Arab cooperation has continued to grow, with Belt and Road projects creating new opportunities for development and improving livelihoods across the region.
China and Egypt have also worked closely in multilateral institutions, including the United Nations, the Group of 20, BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. By coordinating their positions and speaking up on issues of common concern, the two countries have contributed to a stronger voice for the Global South.
At a time of profound global change -- with economic recovery still fragile, unilateralism and hegemonism on the rise, and regional conflicts continuing to escalate -- it is more urgent than ever for Global South countries to stand together and pursue common progress.
For the Global South, China-Egypt cooperation carries a broader message. By pooling their strengths, expanding practical cooperation and supporting each other's development paths, Global South countries can create more opportunities for themselves and make a greater contribution to the world's shared development.
The upcoming visit by Xi will provide a new opportunity to carry this spirit forward. China will continue to work with Egypt and other partners across the Arab world to deepen mutually beneficial cooperation, uphold multilateralism, amplify the voice of developing countries and promote a more just and equitable international order. ■

TOKYO, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- The leaders of the Centrist Reform Alliance (CRA), the Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan (CDPJ) and Komeito decided at a meeting in parliament on Monday that the three Japanese opposition parties will not merge, local media reported.
According to Kyodo News, CRA leader Junya Ogawa said that he hopes to find "a new framework" to allow members to "restart" efforts to achieve a change of government.
CDPJ leader Shunichi Mizuoka said the party would resume discussions on how to counter the administration led by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Komeito head Toshiko Takeya said the party had previously sought to have its upper house lawmakers join the CRA and had prepared to align its local organizations following the merger. However, given the CDPJ's decision not to proceed with the merger, Komeito would not join the alliance on its own.
The CRA was established in January by the lower house lawmakers from the CDPJ and Komeito as a counterweight to the conservative-leaning Takaichi administration.
In the subsequent lower house election in February, however, the alliance won only 49 seats, far short of expectations. After the defeat, caution and opposition has grown among CDPJ and Komeito upper house members and local party organizations that had originally planned to join the CRA, leading to the ultimate cancellation of the three-party merger plan.
Koji Nakakita, professor at Japan's Chuo University, said that although the three-party merger did not come to fruition, it is just one stage in the long-term process of realignment among Japan's opposition parties. He added that the parties could continue cooperating and pursue realignment in other forms going forward. ■

TOKYO, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Capital spending by Japanese companies increased 1.6 percent in the second quarter of 2026 from a year earlier, government data showed Tuesday.
Investment by all non-financial sectors for purposes such as building plants and purchasing equipment stood at 13.03 trillion yen (about 82 billion U.S. dollars), the Ministry of Finance data showed.
Major sectors with higher capital spending during the April-June period included services and goods rental and leasing, while spending fell in the transport machinery and telecommunications equipment sectors.
Pretax profits climbed 24.6 percent to 44.67 trillion yen, up for the seventh straight quarter, while sales rose 5.9 percent to 393.94 trillion yen, according to the ministry.
The latest figures will be used to revise Japan's gross domestic product data for the April-June quarter, which showed the economy expanded at a weaker-than-expected annualized real rate of 1.1 percent. The Cabinet Office will release the revised GDP data next Tuesday. ■

SBS has cemented its place as Australia’s spiritual home of football, securing exclusive national rights to the FIFA World Cup 2030.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Celebrating its centenary year, the 2030 FIFA World Cup will be the most geographically diverse tournament in the competition’s history.
It will be the first in history to be played across six host nations — with the opening three matches taking place in Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay before the tournament moves to primary host countries Morocco, Portugal and Spain.
All six host nations will automatically qualify for the tournament.

Palfreyman said the "important partnership" reflects a "long-standing commitment to making the world’s biggest sporting moments accessible to all Australians".
The agreement follows a massively successful 2026 World Cup for SBS, with the tournament watched by more than 18 million viewers.
Delivering full matches and recaps in 30-minute, 12-minute and three-minute clips on SBS On Demand, SBS reached 209 million hours of consumption — with around 55 per cent being solely digital.
"SBS has always approached the FIFA World Cup as much more than a sporting event," said SBS director of sport Ken Shipp.

====================================================================================================

Column: 25 years of SCO and the rise of multipolarity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:46:18 CST
11:46:18 KST

by Maya Majueran
When the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) was founded in 2001, the international system was still largely dominated by a single center of power. For many developing countries, global governance appeared heavily shaped by Western institutions and priorities, leaving limited space for alternative voices and perspectives.
Today, the picture looks very different. The SCO has grown far beyond its original regional purpose. Its expansion reflects the rising confidence, influence, and strategic weight of the Global South in international affairs.
With member states and partners spanning much of Asia, the Middle East and Eurasia, the organization has become an important platform for developing countries to coordinate policies, deepen economic cooperation, and amplify their collective voice on the global stage.
What makes the SCO particularly significant is that it emerged at a time when many developing nations were seeking greater representation in global governance. For years, countries across the Global South have argued that international institutions often fail to reflect contemporary economic and geopolitical realities. The SCO offers an alternative space for dialogue and cooperation: one based on mutual respect, sovereign equality and consensus-building rather than bloc politics or ideological confrontation.
Beyond security cooperation, the SCO has steadily expanded its focus to sectors that include trade, connectivity, energy, digital development, cultural exchange and people-to-people ties. Through initiatives linking transport corridors, energy networks and regional markets, SCO members are working to enhance economic connectivity and create new opportunities for growth across some of the world's most dynamic regions.
Equally important, the SCO provides a platform for developing countries to collectively address shared challenges, from terrorism and regional security to food security, energy transition and sustainable development. As global power becomes more widely distributed, the organization is helping its members navigate an increasingly complex international environment while preserving strategic autonomy.
In many ways, the evolution of the SCO mirrors the broader rise of the Global South itself. It reflects a world in which emerging economies are no longer content to simply adapt to decisions made elsewhere. Instead, they are increasingly participating in shaping regional and global agendas, contributing new ideas, institutions and approaches to international cooperation.
The SCO's expansion is not about creating a new military bloc or replicating Cold War-style alliances. Rather, it reflects something the Global South has long sought: cooperation without coercion, dialogue without domination, and partnership without political conditionality.
Over the past 25 years, the SCO has expanded to a 27-nation family, bringing together countries with diverse cultures, political systems, economic models and historical experiences. That diversity is precisely what makes the SCO distinctive. Unlike Western-style alliances built around ideological conformity, the SCO demonstrates that cooperation can emerge despite differences rather than because of uniformity.
At the heart of this approach lies the Shanghai Spirit -- a philosophy grounded in mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diversity of civilizations and pursuit of common development.
For many nations across Asia, Africa, the Middle East, Latin America and beyond, this approach is especially appealing. For decades, developing countries often found themselves navigating partnerships that came with political conditions, governance prescriptions, or expectations of strategic alignment. The SCO offers a different model, one that emphasizes consultation rather than instruction and cooperation rather than pressure.
The SCO members do not agree on every issue, nor do they share identical strategic interests. Yet the SCO's ability to bring together countries with differing perspectives is one of its greatest strengths. It demonstrates that multilateralism does not require uniformity; it requires a willingness to engage, consult, and find common ground.
Meanwhile, the SCO's most important contribution is its approach to global governance. For many countries across the Global South, international institutions have too often been perceived as reflecting the interests of a limited number of powerful states. The SCO offers an alternative vision that emphasizes consultation, inclusiveness, and shared participation in international affairs.
By advocating extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, the organization seeks to create greater space for developing nations in global decision-making. Its support for sovereign equality, multilateralism, and opposition to unilateral measures resonates with countries that have long sought a stronger voice in shaping international rules and priorities.
The SCO has therefore evolved beyond its original regional role. It has become a platform through which countries of the Global South can express their priorities and aspirations with greater confidence. Its vision resonates because it emphasizes respect for diversity, common development and sovereign choice. For many nations, the goal is not to replace one center of power with another, but to build an international system where countries can pursue their own development paths without being forced into geopolitical rivalries.
After 25 years, the Shanghai Spirit is not a fading slogan. Its continued relevance lies in the fact that it answers a deep need shared across the Global South: the desire for partnerships based on equality, mutual respect, and common development rather than hierarchy and dependency.
At a time when the world appears increasingly divided by rivalry and competing blocs, the SCO demonstrates that cooperation remains possible. Its emphasis on consultation, mutual benefit and respect for diversity offers a different path -- one that expands opportunities rather than imposes choices.
For billions of people across the Global South, that vision is more than a diplomatic concept. It is a source of optimism about a more equitable, balanced and multipolar future.
Editor's note: Maya Majueran serves as the director of the Belt and Road Initiative Sri Lanka, an independent and pioneering organization with strong expertise in Belt and Road Initiative advice and support.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

Air threat alerts issued across eastern and southern Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
02:46:00 UTC
11:46:00 KST

EDF: Drone threat warning lifted across Estonia
NATO fighter jets scrambled in response to drones in Estonia's airspace early on Tuesday morning (September 1), the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) said. The threat warning has now ended.
Public warning messages about possible air threats were sent to residents in Lääne-Viru and Ida-Viru counties in eastern Estonia at around 3 a.m. on Tuesday morning, and later expanded to Tartu, Jõgeva, Viljandi, Valga, Võru and Põlva counties.
The messages told residents to "seek shelter if you spot a drone."
At 5:58 a.m., Taavi Laasik, head of the EDF's press department, confirmed to ERR that the drone threat warning had been lifted across Estonia. An update on the government's crisis communication website, kriis.ee, said the warning ended at 5.30 a.m.
Previous alerts have been issued when Ukrainian attack drones strayed off course, often due to GPS jamming, when attacking Russia's oil infrastructure on the Baltic coast.
Leningrad Oblast regional Governor Alexander Drozdenko said 38 drones had been destroyed over Leningrad Oblast, which borders Estonia, early on Tuesday morning and confirmed damage at the Port of Ust-Luga.
NATO jets scrambled
On Tuesday morning, residents in eastern Estonia reported hearing fighter jets overhead.
Col. Uku Arold, head of the EDF's Strategic Communications Department, told ERR that drones had breached Estonia's airspace and Turkish Air Force fighter jets stationed at Estonia's Ämari Air Base as part of NATO's rotation air defense mission were scrambled in response.
"There have been drones that moved parallel to Estonia's eastern border and also Latvia's eastern border and entered Estonia, which is why we have also sounded the alarm," Arold said.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) also said the drones had "entered Estonian airspace."
"NATO reacted swiftly and exactly as planned," he wrote on X. "The Alliance is vigilant and ready to protect Allied territory. Incidents like this are a direct consequence of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and underline the need to increase pressure on Russia to end its aggression."
An airspace alert was also issued in Latvia's eastern Alūksne district on Tuesday morning, and the Finnish Defense Forces restricted aviation and shipping in the eastern Gulf of Finland in response to possible drones.
Aerial threat – steps for informed action
The government's crisis website says residents need to "be alert!" when a potential aerial threat warning is issued.
"There is a possibility that drones or other dangerous aerial devices may end up in the region but there is no direct danger. For instance, a drone that will probably fly over the region and will not pose a direct threat to the population has strayed into or is entering the Estonian airspace," it says.

He said a vessel from Türkiye would arrive in the area on Tuesday to support the operations, adding that it has the capacity to operate at depths of around 1,000 meters (3,280 feet).
Erhurman said the identities of all eight people who died after the ship capsized had been determined and their families had been contacted.

Embassy officials visited injured survivors and provided accommodation, essential supplies, and airline tickets for those wishing to return to Türkiye.
Temporary travel documents are also being issued to survivors who lost their ID documents, while the bodies of those killed have been brought to Türkiye.
Relevant Turkish institutions have also been mobilized under embassy coordination to support survivors and their families. 
Investigation ongoing
Erhurman said an investigation into the disaster is also continuing, with nine people detained so far and legal proceedings underway.
Noting that numerous allegations have emerged, Erhurman stressed that the investigation would be done transparently.

Turkish deputy foreign minister visits injured survivors

Ozel arrived in the TRNC Sunday evening following the disaster and visited Dr. Burhan Nalbantoglu State Hospital in Lefkosa, where he met with TRNC Health Minister Hakan Dincyurek and was briefed by hospital officials about the condition of the injured.

VLADIVOSTOK, September 1. /TASS/. The 11th Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) begins in Russia’s Far Eastern city of Vladivostok on Tuesday. This year’s discussions will focus on ways to make economic development in the Far East tangible for its residents, starting from housing construction and urban development to new jobs, advanced technology and accessible infrastructure.
The main theme of the 2026 EEF is "The Far East: Development for the Benefit of People."
"The forum remains a key event for developing breakthrough solutions and signing major investment agreements that improve the lives of thousands of local residents. <...> It is largely thanks to the EEF that almost 3,000 investment projects worth a total of 14 trillion rubles [$162 billion] are being implemented in the broader region. Of these, 6.5 trillion rubles have already been invested, more than 1,100 enterprises have been launched, and over 180,000 jobs have been created," Russian Presidential Plenipotentiary Envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District Yury Trutnev said.
More than 70 sessions across five tracks will be held as part of the EEF business program. Participants will discuss the implementation of master plans for 25 cities, rental housing construction, demographic issues and personnel training, as well as new ways to attract private capital, including "people’s" bonds, digital financial assets, and the development of the Eastern Financial Center.
The future of the Far East will be discussed at the forum from more than just an economic perspective. A separate track will focus on data centers, robotics, unmanned vehicles, and the digitalization of public administration. Another will discuss goods deliveries to Russia’s northern territories, transport infrastructure, air links and the region’s energy independence.
President’s agenda
As always, Russian President Vladimir Putin will take part in the Eastern Economic Forum. On September 2, the head of state will hold a meeting on the development of the Far Eastern Federal District. In addition, Putin will inspect an interactive presentation on the region’s current development, after which new enterprises will be launched via video conference. Putin is also expected to hold a meeting with Primosky Region Governor Oleg Kozhemyako.
The forum’s central event, the plenary session, will be held on September 3. Apart from Putin, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, Mongolian Prime Minister Nyam-Osoryn Uchral, Myanmar’s Vice President Nyo Saw, and Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang will also address the session.
The Russian president is also scheduled to hold a number of bilateral meetings with the heads of foreign delegations.
"Far East Street"
"The Far East Street" will be one of the EEF’s main platforms, with 11 regions of Russia’s Far Eastern Federal District and federal ministries presenting investment projects, advanced technologies and solutions aimed at improving quality of life. As 2026 is the Year of Unity for the Peoples of Russia, special attention will be paid to the cultures and traditions of the peoples of the Far East. Forum guests will have an opportunity to learn about their crafts, cuisine and sports, as well as enjoy performances by artistic groups. The exhibition will run from September 1 to 4 for EEF participants and from September 5 to 7 for the general public.
During the forum, Vladivostok itself will host major cultural and sporting events. Guests will be able to visit exhibitions dedicated to the history of the Far East, Russian art and the culture of indigenous peoples, as well as attend concerts and tours of the city’s historic center. The cultural program will culminate in a gala show titled "Melodies of the Pacific" on September 5.
The sports program includes the 10th five-kilometer race on Russky Island, international tournaments in coastal rowing and mas-wrestling, as well as chess and tennis tournaments. One of the most unusual events will be a 68-kilometer ultramarathon swim along the Amur River involving athletes from Russia and China. The Amur Bay will host the EEF Parade of Sails, bringing together more than 1,000 yachtsmen and sailors.
EEF
The Eastern Economic Forum is taking place in Vladivostok from September 1 to 4 under the theme "The Far East: Development for the Benefit of People." The Roscongress Foundation is the organizer of the EEF, with TASS as its general information partner.

The meeting had not been announced in advance, and a Ukrainian government official said Kyiv had not been informed about it.
‘A quite troubling signal’
European officials expressed deep frustration over Washington’s reception of Siluanov.
Klingbeil publicly criticized the American hosts, saying that receiving the Russian minister as a normal guest sent a “quite troubling” signal while Russia continues its war and attacks on Ukrainian cities.
“I would have wanted greater clarity from the American side that he should not be received here as a normal guest,” Klingbeil told reporters.
He said he also confronted Siluanov directly during a plenary session, demanding that the Russian government end its war and reiterating Europe’s support for Ukraine.
Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski delivered an even sharper rebuke.
“We do not trust Russia. They lie constantly and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them,” Domanski said.
Klingbeil also said Europe was preparing another sanctions package against Russia and hoped Washington would join efforts to increase economic pressure on Moscow.
Transatlantic fault lines deepen
The surprise invitation marks a sharp reversal from previous US policy.
In April 2022, when Siluanov participated virtually in a Washington-hosted G20 meeting, then-US Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen joined officials from Britain, Canada and other Western partners in walking out as Russian representatives began speaking in protest against Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
Four years later, Washington invited Siluanov back into the room, leaving European officials to stage their own protest against the optics of Russia’s return.
White House spokesman Kush Desai defended the administration’s decision to engage Moscow, saying it “will never shy away from talking with the folks we need to talk to” in pursuit of an agreement to halt the bloodshed.
The confrontation unfolded concurrently as Russian President Vladimir Putin met Chinese President Xi Jinping and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Kyrgyzstan, highlighting Moscow’s parallel effort to deepen ties outside the West while testing whether diplomatic doors are reopening in Washington.

Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv kills at least eight

The strikes came as children were set to return to school after the summer holidays, and as officials tightened security measures during fears of further Russian strikes.

Ukraine faces a shortage of interceptor missiles, particularly US-made Patriot systems used against ballistic threats.

Labour’s new housing model comes from California’s backyards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
02:26:53 UTC
11:26:53 KST

Recently built homes are seen in a suburban neighborhood in California, where policies have helped drive new housing construction. | David McNew/Getty Images
LONDON — The U.K. reveled in California-style sunshine this summer. Now it wants to try the Golden State’s housebuilding policies.
Faced with a housing crisis successive governments have failed to address, Britain’s new administration under Prime Minister Andy Burnham is desperate to push up building rates and is looking west for answers.
A recent update to planning rules encourages adding homes above existing buildings and in gardens in England. The policy bears similarities to the “accessory dwelling units” (ADUs) that now make up a quarter of all new housing in California.
Advertisement
Experts think the tweaks could help the government stretch towards its target of building 1.5 million new homes before the next general election, but note the risk of a political backlash among local residents worried about their neighborhoods losing their character and green spaces and becoming overwhelmed.
“It could be significant and it’s certainly creative,” said Simon Creer from the Royal Town Planning Institute. “But it’s hard to say definitively what the increase in housing delivery could be, and whether it will be popular. There’s always a fundamental tension between the need for more homes and the potential local backlash about where those homes are and what they look like, which is why early, meaningful communication with communities matters.”
Indeed, planning changes around garden use during the previous Labour government in the 2000s led to public outrage about homes being demolished so speculators could cram properties into available land, as well as fears about destruction of green spaces. Labour was forced to intervene on what was dubbed “garden grabbing” as the 2010 election loomed, then the successor Conservative-Lib Dem administration was quick to change the rules.
Now the government has tweaked them again to fuel development on and around existing buildings, instructing planning committees via national guidance to favor upward extensions to homes and commercial buildings and filling gaps around houses.
The aim is densification: increasing the number of homes on a designated land mass.
“These changes are in line with our push for urban and suburban intensification, aiming to unlock private land and speed up small-scale construction alongside major transport-hub and grey-belt redevelopment,” said a government official who was granted anonymity to speak about the plans.
Advertisement
The official said the rules are designed to encourage “ADU-style” building, but help “safeguard residential gardens from inappropriate development” while retaining local government oversight.
The Cali formula
When it comes to finding gaps to slot homes into, California is the blueprint. The state that invented suburban sprawl has seen a surge in ADU home construction over the last 10 years to add more housing into already-developed neighborhoods — although it took aggressive government intervention to make it happen.
For decades, the state had laws on the books to encourage the building of ADUs, also dubbed casitas and granny flats. But cities implemented barriers including high fees, strict rules on size and lengthy reviews that stymied most new building.
Amid a housing shortage driving up home prices, California state lawmakers passed a series of new laws, starting in 2016, to strip away restrictions local governments were using to block construction.
Those behind the effort worked clandestinely at first. They didn’t want to provoke a backlash from residents fearing the plans would upend the suburban development pattern of a single-family home, spacious backyard and two-car garage — putting their property values at risk. Authors of the 2016 legislation changed the terminology for the buildings in state code from “second unit” to “accessory dwelling unit,” helping the new houses appear as part of an existing home’s footprint, rather than a separate development.
Over time, the effect of all the new laws not only made it simpler and less expensive for individual homeowners to build on their properties, but it also spurred the growth of a niche construction industry. Without having to wade through individual permitting rules, contractors could work across cities more easily, increasing their opportunities to drum up business.
Advertisement
“The goal here was to standardize the process across the board,” said Muhammad Alameldin, director of growth for California YIMBY, a pro-development organization that has supported the new state laws. “The theme is that if you own a piece of property, you should be able to build on that piece of property.”
The state’s effort on backyard homes is considered its most successful policy to increase homebuilding in recent memory. In 2018, fewer than 9,000 backyard homes were permitted in California, making up less than 8 percent of the state’s total production, according to an analysis of state data by researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, and shared with POLITICO. Last year, backyard home permits topped 32,000, representing a quarter of all homes approved in California, the analysis found.
Due to rising interest rates and high labor and materials costs slowing down construction, among other headwinds, it’s possible that housing construction in California would be declining without the boom in backyard homes.
Meanwhile, back across the pond
Labour in the U.K. wants a piece of that action as part of wider efforts to fuel building. But opponents are fueling dissent before a single new unit has even been approved.
The Conservatives have already sounded the alarm about “garden grabbing,” arguing the new rules will create a boom in one-bedroom flats to make up building targets, despite high demand for larger houses with sizable gardens for families.
“Britain needs more homes,” said Shadow Housing Minister Gareth Bacon. “But Labour’s top-down housing targets and density requirements will result in more blocks of flats being crammed into people’s gardens, rather than communities getting new family homes with gardens and parking spaces.”
Advertisement
Recent experience suggests a political war on the issue can be successful. A similar densification plan in the London borough of Croydon was implemented in 2019 and led to a boost in new homes. It was revoked in 2022 amid a public backlash over properties being demolished and replaced with low-rise flat blocks.
Government officials insist their policies will not cut across local government power to account for public concern, and will protect gardens via a series of caveats about maintaining the character of areas and ensuring transport routes and services are not overwhelmed.
“We have made changes which recognize that in many places, there is potential for more development to support thriving neighborhoods, improve access to jobs and services and make the best use of land within our towns and cities,” said a housing department spokesperson. “Our changes will help more homes be built where they are needed, while stopping unsuitable development.”
Other examples in the U.K. suggest a balance can be struck. Upward extension allowances in the London district of South Tottenham in 2013, which included strict rules on maintaining building character, led to a significant increase in residential space in that one small area.
“Making it easier for homeowners to build granny flats and loft extensions could make a big dent in England’s housing shortage,” said Sam Dumitru, Head of Policy at pro-building campaign group Britain Remade. “So long as politicians hold their nerve when the inevitable objections from angry neighbors rear their head.”

Cronulla Sharks captain Cameron McInnes wants his team to play their home elimination final at Shark Park, but says he would not be surprised if the NRL moved it to a bigger ground.
Shark Park has been deemed unfit for use in week two or three of the finals, but hosted week-one finals matches in 2022, 2023 and 2025.
What's next?
The NRL is unlikely to publicly confirm venues until after round 27 finishes this Sunday, and told clubs in the pre-season it had the discretion to determine where finals games were played.
Cameron McInnes would not be surprised to see the NRL deny Cronulla a home final at Shark Park, warning players were now used to head office making rule changes "at the drop of a hat".
Out of form on the eve of finals, the fifth-placed Sharks are nevertheless guaranteed to host a week-one elimination match against one of South Sydney, North Queensland or Newcastle.
But the finals suitability of dilapidated Shark Park, the NRL's lowest-capacity regular venue at 15,000 seats, has been a discussion point in recent years.
The NRL pockets ticket sales from finals games so would take a financial hit from hosting in the shire rather than the Sydney Football Stadium or Stadium Australia, which each have more than twice the capacity.
Shark Park has been deemed unfit for use in week two or three of the finals, but hosted week-one finals matches in 2022, 2023 and 2025.
The NRL is unlikely to publicly confirm venues until after round 27 finishes this Sunday, and told clubs in the pre-season it had the discretion to determine where finals games were played.
The possibility of playing elsewhere did not sit well with England-bound McInnes, who could be playing his last game at Shark Park against Melbourne this Saturday.
"I was under the impression the rule was if you earn a home semi, whether you're first or second, or fifth or sixth, you get to play it at your home. Our home is Shark Park," he said.
"I don't know if that was a rule change that they can just put in, but then again, the NRL changes rules all the time.
"Rule changes just happen at the drop of a hat now, don't they? So as a player, you just have to adapt."
The league most recently trialled a change to the kick-off rule in Melbourne's defeat of Brisbane last week, having introduced six-agains, 20/40 kicks, two-point field goals and captain's challenges since the start of the decade.
The NRL has also made less prominent changes to its trainer and interchange policies in that time, as well as reverting to one on-field referee per game.
"How much do you need to change? I understand at the end of the day, it's entertainment, I get it," McInnes said.
"But it's like someone's constantly sitting there going, 'The game's going really well, but now let's change something else'."
Inconsistency around ruck infringements was most dismaying to veteran McInnes, who sympathised with the league's match officials.
"When you bring that [six-again rule] in, I get it, to speed the game up and have the speeds to score long-range tries with fatigue, but it also creates an inconsistency in the game," he said.
"[It's] hard for the refs, isn't it? Because it's so subjective.
"If someone gets hit in the face and is offside, that's clear as day, but with the six-agains, it's just sort of a lottery."

US brings back Russia’s Siluanov to G20 finance talks, angering Europe
Russian foreign minister holds talks with US counterpart as European officials object to his return to G20 talks.
Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov has made a surprise appearance at United States-hosted G20 finance talks in North Carolina, sparking frustration and dismay among European ministers and officials.
Siluanov’s appearance at the talks in Asheville on Monday marks the first time the minister, who was appointed in 2011, has attended a G20 meeting in person since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

- list 2 of 3US plans to sanction another bank to keep economic pressure on Iran
- list 3 of 3War and heat: Why are wheat prices soaring?
He held a bilateral meeting with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, with Russia’s Ministry of Finance saying the two men discussed financial cooperation within the G20 framework.
A US official said the meeting focused on US President Donald Trump’s peace plan for Ukraine.
Asked about the invitation to Siluanov, Trump told reporters: “We like getting along with everybody. One of the reasons I’m so successful, I get along with everybody.”
European officials, however, criticised the move.
Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski said he was unhappy to see Moscow represented, although he recognised the right of G20 hosts to invite guests.
“We do not trust Russia. They lie constantly, and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them,” he told the Reuters news agency, stressing that Russia was the aggressor in its conflict with Ukraine.
“So for me, it would be very difficult to have any kind of conversation with Russia.”
‘Troubling’ signal
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said the US’s decision to welcome Siluanov sent a “signal I find troubling”.
He said he told Siluanov during a plenary session that Moscow had to end the war and “that we clearly support Ukraine”.
He also said Europe was preparing a further package of sanctions against Russia and hoped for close cooperation with Washington on the measures.
European ministers and central bankers also opposed appearing with Siluanov in the traditional G20 “family photo”, European officials said. The photograph was ultimately taken without the Russian minister.
Klingbeil said European officials, including European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, had discussed Russia’s involvement on Sunday and agreed that maintaining an avenue for dialogue could allow them to deliver a frank message to Moscow.
“However, the mere fact that the Russian finance minister is back – after, I believe, four G20 meetings without Russian participation – indicates an attempt at normalisation, and that makes it all the more important for us to push back,” he said.
Siluanov’s appearance marked a sharp contrast with the G20 meeting in Washington, DC, in April 2022, when his virtual participation prompted officials from Canada, the United Kingdom, the US, and the European Central Bank to walk out.
White House defends talks with Russia
Asked about Siluanov’s attendance, White House spokesman Kush Desai told the AFP news agency that the Trump administration had been working with Russia to push for a deal that “would stop the endless bloodshed that the president has really condemned”.
“The president and the administration will never shy away from talking with the folks we need to talk to, to further that,” he said. “That’s what we’re working on here at the G20.”
Separately, Reuters and AFP, citing sources familiar with the Washington-Moscow talks, said Bessent had made clear that the US would not provide Russia with economic relief until war in Ukraine was over.
Trump has pushed Moscow and Kyiv to reach a deal to halt the fighting, but an initial 28-point plan that largely adhered to Russia’s demands was criticised by Ukraine and European governments.
The US, which currently holds the rotating G20 presidency, did not invite South Africa, last year’s G20 host, to the gathering. Poland, which is not a permanent G20 member, was invited.
Certain reporters from major US newsrooms, including The New York Times and Bloomberg News, were not granted credentials to cover the gathering.
The decision was condemned by the National Press Club, which said that “no administration should be allowed to handpick the press corps that scrutinizes it”.
The two-day meeting comes as global debt levels have reached a record of nearly $353 trillion and the global economy faces an energy shock triggered by the US-Israel war on Iran. The talks also come amid rising tensions over China’s large trade surplus and uncertainty over the effects of a surge in artificial intelligence investment.

Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing to Visit Vietnam Soon, State Media Says

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
02:21:00 UTC
11:21:00 KST

Myanmar’s military-appointed president, Min Aung Hlaing, will soon visit Vietnam, his fourth visit to an ASEAN member state since taking office in April, Myanmar state media reported today.
According to a report in the Global New Light of Myanmar, the former general will travel to Vietnam “in the near future” at the invitation of To Lam, Vietnam’s president and the head of the Communist Party of Vietnam. In addition to meeting with Lam, he will also meet with Prime Minister Pham Minh Chinh and Tran Thanh Man, the head of the National Assembly, and “receive representatives from economic organizations.”
“During the visit, the President will hold cordial discussions and exchange views on further consolidation of the existing friendly relations… as well as cooperation across economic, cultural, and various other sectors,” the report stated.
The announcement, which has not yet been confirmed by Hanoi, comes shortly after Vietnamese Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung traveled to Myanmar last week, the first time that a Vietnamese foreign minister has visited the country since the 2021 coup. During talks with Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw, he “discussed boosting bilateral trade and investment, as well as mutual support on the international stage,” The Irrawaddy reported, citing state media.
Trung also met Lower House speaker Khin Yi and Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe, to whom he pledged “continued support for Myanmar at the U.N., ASEAN, and other international forums.” Trung also reportedly extended a formal invitation for Min Aung Hlaing to visit Hanoi.
The trip would be the former general’s fourth to an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member state since taking office as president in April, after visits to Laos in early July and Thailand last month and an upcoming trip to Cambodia in early September. He has also made state visits to India and China in June, and to Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan last month.
All of this reflects a concerted push by Min Aung Hlaing to consolidate Myanmar’s relationship with key partners. A top priority, which he mentioned in his inauguration speech in April, is to normalize relations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
Since late 2021, the 11-nation bloc has excluded the country from its summits over its failure to implement the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan. This plan calls for a cessation of violence, access to humanitarian aid, and inclusive dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
Min Aung Hlaing’s quasi-civilian government, which was formed after flawed multi-phase elections in December and January, has taken an increasingly defiant line toward ASEAN, dismissing the Five-Point Consensus as an unwarranted “interference” in its internal affairs and demanding its full readmission to the bloc.
At the same time, it has sought to engage directly with willing ASEAN member states, particularly Thailand, which has positioned itself as a bridge between Myanmar and ASEAN. During Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Bangkok last month, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul “reaffirmed” Thailand’s commitment “to supporting and continuing to work closely with Myanmar for Myanmar’s full and equal participation in ASEAN mechanisms and processes.”
The fact that all four of Myanmar’s mainland Southeast Asian neighbors have now extended invitations to Min Aung Hlaing to visit reflects a growing regional fatigue with the Myanmar conflict, and a belief that “calibrated reengagement” (in Thailand’s phrase) is the best way to manage the effects of the civil war, if not to resolve it.
It also reflects a continuing divergence between ASEAN’s mainland and maritime member states on how to deal with Myanmar. Over the past five years, the mainland states have favored more engagement than maritime nations such as Singapore, Indonesia, and Malaysia, which have advocated a more robust regional response to the military coup in Myanmar. Whether and to what extent Myanmar manages to make inroads into this camp, which is reportedly also growing with the protracted deadlock inside Myanmar, may become clear in the run-up to the next ASEAN summit in November.

New York cannot enforce state law demanding $75b. from fossil fuel companies, federal judge rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
02:14:43 UTC
11:14:43 KST

A federal judge ruled on Monday that New York cannot enforce a 2024 state law that sought to force fossil fuel companies to contribute $75 billion over 25 years into a fund to pay for damage caused by climate change.
Chief US District Judge Brenda Sannes in Syracuse, New York sided with 22 Republican state attorneys general, as well as industry groups including the US Chamber of Commerce, in finding the state measure preempted by federal law.
Sannes, an appointee of Democratic president Barack Obama, said the Clean Air Act, which gave the federal Environmental Protection Agency authority to regulate carbon-dioxide emissions, did not authorize states to adopt emissions compensation schemes such as New York's.
She said enforcing New York's Climate Change Superfund Act risked upsetting the balance between preventing global warming, "a project that necessarily requires national standards and global participation," and promoting economic growth, energy production, foreign policy interests and national security.
"The Climate Act conflicts with the overriding need for a uniform rule of decision on matters influencing national energy and environmental policy, and basic interests of federalism," she wrote.
West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey, a Republican who led the states' opposition, in a statement hailed the decision, calling the state law "a money grab by the elites in New York."
The office of New York Governor Kathy Hochul, a Democrat who signed the state law in December 2024, is reviewing the decision to determine possible next steps, spokesperson Ken Lovett said.
"Taxpayers shouldn’t have to foot the bill for damages caused by polluters," Lovett said.
New York demands fossil fuel companies contribute to climate change superfund
New York was the second US state to create an industry-financed "superfund" to address climate change. Vermont was the first state, and its law also faces legal challenges.
The New York law required fossil fuel companies to contribute $3 billion annually to the superfund starting in 2028, divided based on their greenhouse gas emissions between 2000 and 2018.
The law applied to companies that the state's Department of Environmental Conservation considered responsible for 1 billion tons of greenhouse gas emissions during that period. Money would have gone to build roads, water systems, sewage systems, and other infrastructure to protect communities and coastlines from weather events such as extreme heat and flooding.
In their February 2025 lawsuit, the Republican attorneys general called New York's law a politically motivated "overreach," which punished traditional energy companies that now comply with applicable laws. They said payouts from coal, oil and natural gas producers could wipe out thousands of jobs if the producers were forced to shut down.
The US Department of Justice under Republican President Donald Trump had filed a similar lawsuit last year and supported the state attorneys general in the case before Sannes.
The Environment and Climate Change portal is produced in cooperation with the Goldman Sonnenfeldt School of Sustainability and Climate Change at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev. The Jerusalem Post maintains all editorial decisions related to the content.

Suspect agreed to livestream mosque shooting, release manifesto

At first they only knew one of them was a woman in the Eastern time zone but later were able to identify Santiago.
