EU targets ChatGPT, Reddit, and Roblox under censorship law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
02:10:57 UTC
11:10:57 KST

EU targets ChatGPT, Reddit, and Roblox under censorship law
The EU has placed ChatGPT, Reddit, and Roblox under the strictest tier of its online regulations, giving the US-based services four months to comply with rules denounced by Washington and leading tech figures as censorship.
The European Commission on Monday designated ChatGPT a Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE), while Reddit and Roblox were classified as Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) under the Digital Services Act (DSA). All three reported at least 45 million average monthly users in the EU, crossing the threshold for heightened oversight.
They now have until the end of December to comply with additional requirements, including assessing and mitigating “systemic risks” linked to illegal content, minors, users’ physical and mental well-being, fundamental rights, elections, and public security. Violations of the DSA can carry fines of up to 6% of a company’s annual global turnover.
Brussels argues that the law makes powerful platforms safer and more accountable. Critics say its broad demands to police harmful content and mitigate vaguely defined societal risks pressure companies to suppress lawful speech to avoid punishment.
None of the three companies has publicly challenged the designation. OpenAI and Reddit said they were preparing to comply with the new requirements, while Roblox pledged to continue working “constructively” with Brussels.
The DSA and its competition-focused sister law, the Digital Markets Act (DMA), have become a major source of friction with Washington. US President Donald Trump has ordered officials to scrutinize EU digital rules that could force American companies to moderate content in ways that “undermine freedom of speech and political engagement.”
Vice President J.D. Vance has likewise accused Europe of retreating from free speech, telling the Munich Security Conference last year that “digital censorship” is being presented as a defense of democracy and warning that “free speech… is in retreat” across Europe.
X owner Elon Musk has been among the DSA’s fiercest critics. He accused the European Commission of offering X an “illegal secret deal” under which it could avoid punishment by “quietly” censoring speech, claiming that other platforms have accepted. Brussels denied the allegation.
Telegram founder Pavel Durov has similarly accused the EU of using the DSA to expand censorship. In April, he argued that Brussels is using sympathetic Soros-backed NGOs and media to justify increased online surveillance and restrictions, warning that these campaigns are being used to “take away what’s left of our freedoms.”

steel layered facade revives 1969 modernist city hall in czech republic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
02:10:54 UTC
11:10:54 KST

atelier gram reworks Přerov City Hall as an open civic facility
The reconstruction of Přerov City Hall by atelier gram transforms a closed administrative building completed in 1969 into an open, multifunctional civic facility. The project retains the original steel structure and reinforced-concrete panels while introducing new spatial, material, and technological layers to meet current requirements for energy efficiency, fire safety, user comfort, and long-term use. A new glazed staircase on the south facade becomes the main architectural intervention, connecting the building’s administrative functions with exhibition areas, informal meeting spaces, and publicly accessible destinations.
The existing building represents a particular period of modernist public architecture, characterised by functional planning and an inward-facing relationship with its surroundings. The reconstruction addresses the changing role of public administration by opening the building towards the T. G. M. square and incorporating functions that extend beyond municipal offices. The intervention establishes City Hall as a civic infrastructure in which circulation, meeting, exhibition, and administrative spaces are connected within a more accessible spatial framework.
all images © Maxime Delvaux
A glazed staircase opens the administration to the square
The new staircase is attached to the south façade facing the city square and forms the central organisational element of the reconstruction. Enclosed in glass, it provides a continuous vertical connection between the floors while making movement through the building visible from the public realm. The staircase accommodates exhibition areas and informal meeting spaces alongside its circulation function, bringing activities that would traditionally remain within internal corridors closer to the facade.
The intervention by czech design practice atelier gram establishes a diagonal public route through the building, beginning at the ground-floor reception and continuing upwards to the top floor, where the registry office and café are located. This circulation sequence provides a new connection between the square, the municipal offices, and the publicly accessible rooftop level.
The entrance hall extends the public square indoors
At ground level, a fully glazed entrance hall creates a direct visual and spatial connection with T. G. M. square. The transparent facade allows views through the building towards the backyard, establishing sightlines between the urban space and the interior. The ground floor consequently operates as an extension of the square, with the boundary between public space and municipal infrastructure becoming more permeable. At the opposite end of the building’s vertical sequence, the rooftop terrace and café form a lightweight pavilion with views across Přerov. The accessible roof becomes the endpoint of the public route established by the new staircase, introducing a civic destination above the administrative floors.
Inside, non-load-bearing partitions have been removed to create open floor plates organised around a stable central core. The arrangement allows workplaces to be reconfigured as requirements change, using lightweight partitions without altering the primary structure. This approach increases spatial flexibility while limiting the need for extensive structural intervention. The open-plan strategy also makes use of the existing modernist structural system. By retaining the principal load-bearing elements and reorganising the internal layout around them, the reconstruction combines adaptability with a comparatively economical construction approach.
Existing structure forms the basis for new material layers
The material strategy is based on retaining the valuable elements of the late-1960s building and adding new layers where necessary to address contemporary technical and environmental requirements. The original load-bearing steel frame and floor and ceiling slabs made from prefabricated reinforced-concrete PZD panels remain in place. These elements were cleaned, structurally assessed, and adapted for their new use. The original construction therefore remains legible within the renovated building, while new finishes and technical layers establish a contemporary architectural expression.
The steel skeleton of columns and beams continues to form the primary structural system. To satisfy current fire-resistance requirements, the individual steel elements have been enclosed with fire-protective plasterboard and finished with anodized aluminum sheeting. The treatment gives the exposed structure a consistent appearance while distinguishing the new finish from the original structural material. The existing reinforced-concrete floor panels have been supplemented with new floor build-ups designed to improve thermal and acoustic performance. These comprise thermal and impact-sound insulation, a leveling anhydrite screed, and a final polyurethane resin finish. The durable, easily maintained surface creates a continuous interior finish while maintaining the clarity of the existing structural grid.
facade combines modular rhythm with new performance layers
The renewed facade follows the original modular arrangement of alternating glazed and solid panels, retaining the proportions and rhythm of the 1969 building. New thermal insulation and contemporary window and door fillings improve the performance of the building envelope while maintaining its underlying composition. On the south-facing sections, expanded-metal shading elements are integrated into the facade to limit solar heat gain and reduce overheating. The shading also introduces a changing visual layer to the building. Its appearance varies according to daylight, time of day, and the viewer’s position, adding depth to the otherwise regular facade grid. On the west side, the original reinforced-concrete arcade elements within the passage have been preserved. Their surfaces were renewed with břízolit, a pebble-dash render consistent with the material character of the existing building. The treatment protects the concrete elements while maintaining their relationship with the surrounding public space.
The reconstruction of Přerov City Hall is consequently based on a combination of retention, adaptation, and addition. Its original steel frame, prefabricated concrete panels, facade rhythm, and arcade elements remain part of the building, while new circulation, glazing, shading, finishes, and technical systems address contemporary requirements. The project uses material and spatial interventions to shift the building from an inward-facing administrative structure towards a more accessible civic facility, while keeping its original structural logic visible.

Toxic haze from Indonesian fires chokes Malaysian Borneo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
02:06:01 UTC
11:06:01 KST

Toxic haze from Indonesian forest fires chokes Malaysian Borneo
Respiratory illnesses surge in Malaysia as hazardous air settles over Borneo in the region’s worst smoke crisis in a decade.
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Smoke from forest and peatland fires burning across Indonesia has pushed air quality in parts of Malaysian Borneo to hazardous levels, triggering a surge in respiratory illness and forcing the cancellation of outdoor Independence Day celebrations.
The smoke – drifting from fires in Kalimantan in the Indonesian portion of Borneo – has settled over the Malaysian state of Sarawak, located on the same island, for much of August. It has also reached peninsular Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4‘Everything is covered in ash’: Indonesia wildfires leave people in crisis
- list 2 of 4‘We can’t breathe’: Indonesians battle wildfire haze
- list 3 of 4Indonesia battles haze as wildfires rage across South Sumatra forests
- list 4 of 4Governments brace for historic El Nino impacts on global weather extremes
It is the region’s worst haze episode since 2015, when fires in Indonesia exposed tens of millions of people to toxic smoke and caused more than 500,000 people to suffer respiratory ailments.
On Tuesday, six areas in Sarawak recorded hazardous air quality, with readings above 300 on Malaysia’s Air Pollutant Index. Anything above 100 is considered unhealthy. In Kuching, the state capital, the index hit 407, while in Serian, a town close to the Kalimantan border, it hit 408.
Mia Emylia Hassan, 33, a mother of two in Kuching, said the smell of smoke was inescapable.
“The air here is very thick,” she said. “It smells like smoke, and it’s just white all over.” Visibility from her house, she said, had dropped to about a kilometre, or roughly half a mile. “We have not seen blue sky for over a month,” she said.
The haze arrived in early August, shortly after her 10-month-old daughter came home from the hospital after a lung infection. “She’s not healing properly because her lungs are still developing,” Hassan said. “She’s been on medication this whole month, and she has been coughing and vomiting.”
Twice, the family has had to rush the infant back to the emergency room because she could not breathe.
“It’s a mini heart attack for us every time,” Hassan said.
Asthma cases surge
Malaysia’s Ministry of Health has reported a sharp rise in illness nationwide. During the week of August 23 to 29, asthma cases climbed to 1,811, up from 219 the previous week, the ministry said on Saturday, while conjunctivitis cases also rose to 720, from 146.
In peninsular Malaysia, Karen-Michaela Tan, an asthma patient who lives near the capital, Kuala Lumpur, said she was “wheezing audibly” last week and feeling “breathless when climbing the stairs”. Air quality readings in her area were above 100 for most of the week and the 52-year-old said she needed two nebuliser treatments back to back to stop the wheezing, along with a heavy dose of steroids.
“Doctors are erring on the side of caution when it comes to asthma patients, choosing to up dosages rather than risk a patient being hospitalised for shortness of breath,” she said.
Her house is sealed, and two purifiers run continuously. Still, “I battle throat scratchiness and nasal dryness even with these measures,” she said.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), a regional bloc, has activated a Level 3 transboundary haze alert – its highest – for the southern part of the region. The alert signals a high risk of severe cross-border haze. ASEAN cited an increase in fire hotspots and prolonged dry weather, fuelled by an intensifying El Nino weather pattern.
The toxic smoke has forced Sarawak to cancel its outdoor Independence Day celebrations on Monday, and officials warned that more restrictions could follow. Douglas Uggah Embas, the deputy premier, said any area where readings cross 500 will be placed under a local emergency and all public and private offices will be closed. “Only essential services will be allowed to operate,” he added.
Schools, too, have been hit hard. Under Ministry of Education rules, outdoor activities are suspended when the index reaches 100, and schools must close at 200. On August 20 and 21, nearly 600 schools in and around Kuching shut, affecting some 200,000 primary and secondary students. And on August 28, 30 more schools in Sarawak closed, keeping more than 4,000 children at home.
This week, schools across the country are closed for the Independence Day holiday.
Youth sport has been affected, too, including in the capital. Yap Kai Jinn, 31, a coach at Square One Football, a Kuala Lumpur academy, said the club had cancelled all training sessions and matches since last week.
“Along with our parents, we decided that it is not healthy; it is not safe for our players to play under these conditions,” he said. “For now, we are looking for an enclosed area to do sessions, and for outdoor, we have to wait and hope that the weather gets better.”
Fires surge in West Kalimantan
The toll of the haze has been far heavier in Indonesia.
The country’s deputy health minister, Dante Saksono Harbuwono, told reporters on Monday that some 13,500 people were treated for respiratory infections in July and August, while about 5.5 million people on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra have been directly exposed to smoke.
Borneo is the world’s third-largest island and is divided between Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.
According to the Indonesian government, fires between January and July burned more than 200,000 hectares (about 494,000 acres), an area three times the size of Indonesia’s capital, Jakarta, across the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. Nearly 95,000 hectares (about 235,000 acres) burned in July alone.
And despite efforts to control the blazes, the fires continue to surge in parts of Indonesian Borneo.
Hotspots in West Kalimantan nearly doubled on Monday, rising by 3,553 to 7,377, while the number of active fires rose by 88 to 104, and visibility fell below a kilometre, said Berton Panjaitan, an official at Indonesia’s National Disaster Mitigation Agency. In Central Kalimantan, hotspots declined by 147 to 5,244, while fire spots increased by 16 to 72, he said.
Cities in Kalimantan have recorded hazardous air, too.
Readings in Palangkaraya in Central Kalimantan reached 780 on Monday on the air quality index used by IQAir, a Swiss company that monitors pollution data. Pontianak in West Kalimantan reached 593.
The fires are largely set on purpose, analysts say, with plantation companies and smallholders alike burning rainforest and carbon-rich peatland to clear ground for palm oil, farming, and pulp and paper production. The practice is illegal, and Indonesian police said last week that they had arrested 72 people suspected of setting recent fires.
Super El Nino
Researchers warned people in Southeast Asia to brace for a long fire season.
El Nino – the naturally occurring pattern that shifts winds, air pressure and rainfall worldwide – appears headed for “super” strength, said Helena Varkkey, a specialist on transboundary haze at Universiti Malaya.
In Southeast Asia, she said, “the intensifying El Nino means hotter and drier conditions”, so “any fires that happen will have a bigger and longer regional impact”.
Jayaprakash Muralitharan, a Malaysian atmospheric scientist, said the worst was still ahead.
Haze conditions are “going to be severe and longer, because the hot weather started much earlier last year”, he said. “El Nino came in and made conditions drier. Now you have the extreme drying of the peatland.”
And peat can make fires stubborn, he said. What looks extinguished on the surface can smoulder underground for weeks and flare up again, and nothing short of sustained rain will soak the soil enough to put it out.
Until the rains arrive, Muralitharan said, there is little to be done.
“Human intervention now is only a temporary solution. It would go on until end of September or October when the rain comes in. I hope that rain comes in by then.”

The Ukrainian military launched a total of 29 projectiles in the past 24 hours.

China’s top brokerages step up global push as overseas profits surge

China’s top brokerages step up global push as overseas profits surge
Citic, CICC and Guotai Haitong among those broadening cross-border deal-making and committing fresh capital to international arms as Beijing backs stronger investment banks
China’s leading brokerages are accelerating their push overseas, pouring billions of yuan into their international arms as cross-border deals expand and profits from overseas operations grow, according to their latest interim reports.
Citic Securities, one of China’s largest brokerages, saw revenue generated outside mainland China rise 45.5 per cent, year on year, to 15.86 billion yuan (US$2.4 billion) in the six months ended June, according to its interim report. The growth slightly outpaced the group’s 44.1 per cent increase in overall revenue.
Its international arm, Citic Securities International (CSI), generated US$2.32 billion in operating revenue and US$829 million in net profit during the period, up 56 per cent and 114 per cent, respectively, from a year earlier. Total assets reached US$91.43 billion, 60 per cent higher than a year earlier.
Citic also expanded cross-border deal-making, completing 44 overseas equity transactions worth US$4.22 billion, including two major Malaysian initial public offerings. The brokerage also handled 96 offshore bond transactions for Chinese issuers, as well as 28 global mergers and acquisitions that had a total value of US$22.88 billion and involved Chinese companies. Citic also completed deals across Southeast Asia and Europe, according to the report.
China International Capital Corporation (CICC) reported a similar trend. Its overseas revenue in the first half of 2026 saw a year-on-year increase of 45 per cent to 9.19 billion yuan from 6.34 billion yuan a year earlier, faster than the investment bank’s 39.2 per cent overall revenue growth, according to its interim report. Overseas operations accounted for about 35 per cent of its revenue, up from 34 per cent a year earlier.
Meanwhile, CICC sponsored 27 Hong Kong IPOs with an underwriting value of US$5.74 billion in the first half, compared with 13 deals worth US$2.87 billion a year earlier.
The total assets of CICC International, its offshore arm, stood at HK$448.6 billion at the end of June, while net profit saw a year-on-year rise of 65 per cent to HK$4.35 billion.

PRHI declined to reveal the nature of the disputed issue, citing its contractual obligations and commitment to author confidentiality.
NEW DELHI: Penguin Random House India on Monday said publication of Sonia Gandhi’s memoir in India had stalled after the publisher and the author’s representatives reached an “impasse over a particular issue.” The publisher also firmly denied that any external pressure had influenced the decision.Penguin India said the disagreement emerged during its normal editorial review of Belonging: A Journey of Love, which it had been keen to publish.The clarification came amid a growing political controversy over the memoir’s India publication, after Alfred A Knopf, the US-based imprint of Penguin Random House, announced that the book would be released worldwide on November 10. While Congress leaders have raised questions about possible governmental pressure and freedom of expression, Penguin India said the disagreement was strictly part of the editorial process.
“On some, they agreed to changes and on others, we accepted the author’s position. Unfortunately, and ultimately, an understanding could not be reached on a particular issue,” the publisher said.PRHI spokesperson Pallavi Narayan said the publishing house had been “really keen” to bring out the memoir, describing it as “a hard-won acquisition”.
“We feel it is important for us to correct certain misrepresentations regarding the forthcoming memoir 'Belonging'. This is a book that we at Penguin Random House India, were really keen on publishing as it was a hard-won acquisition,” Narayan said in an exclusive statement to PTI.The publisher said the manuscript had gone through its “normal editorial process”, during which several points were raised and discussed with the author’s representatives. Some proposed changes were accepted, while on other matters Penguin India accepted the author’s position.It was ultimately the unresolved issue that brought the publication process to a halt, according to PRHI. The author’s team subsequently informed the publisher that they did not wish to proceed with the publication, a decision the publishing house said it respected.At the same time, Penguin India rejected suggestions that the impasse was the result of intervention from outside the publishing process.“Since the content of the book is confidential and under embargo, there was no external pressure whatsoever,” the publisher said.PRHI declined to reveal the nature of the disputed issue, citing its contractual obligations and commitment to author confidentiality.“Since we are bound by an agreement, and author confidentiality is paramount to us, we will not divulge details of what led to the impasse,” the publisher said.The publishing house also defended its decision to scrutinise the manuscript, saying editorial assessment, questioning, fact-checking and recommendations were part of its responsibility as a publisher.“As publishers, it was its “responsibility and duty” to critically assess a manuscript, ask questions, make recommendations and exercise its independent editorial judgement,” Penguin India said.The controversy intensified after reports that Penguin India had backed out of publishing the memoir following disagreements over editorial changes. Former Rajasthan chief minister Ashok Gehlot alleged that pressure had been put on Penguin India to remove sections concerning Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the RSS and China’s occupation of Indian territory during the Modi government.
Former Madhya Pradesh chief minister Kamal Nath also questioned whether the publisher’s position had been influenced by pressure from elsewhere.Penguin India’s latest statement, however, maintains that no such external intervention took place and that the disagreement arose solely during the editorial process.The memoir is expected to offer a rare account of Gandhi’s life, covering her childhood in post-war Italy, her marriage into the Nehru-Gandhi family, the assassination of her husband and former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, and her subsequent entry into politics.While the international edition is scheduled for release on November 10, the status of its publication in India remains unresolved.

Britain’s Liberal Democrats get a new think tank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

LONDON — Britain’s Liberal Democrats are dreaming of a return to government. A new think tank wants to help.
The Britain Project — a newly formed group offering liberal policy ideas — will officially launch at the party’s conference in Brighton on September 21.
It comes as divisions on the right of British politics make the idea of a progressive pact involving the Liberal Democrats at the next election more likely, even as their poll ratings stagnate.
Advertisement
The think tank is not formally affiliated to Ed Davey’s party, but at least 50 of his 71 MPs attended a presentation promoting its work during one of their regular parliamentary meetings in July — with many indicating they want to get involved.
Tim Leunig, the group’s policy director, who recently became a Liberal Democrat peer in Britain’s unelected House of Lords, said: “We are here to help them.”
“But we’re also here to ask them tough questions because: who knows? They might be a minister one day, and then the civil service will ask them tough questions.”
While in public the Lib Dems refuse to countenance any future deal with Burnham’s Labour, in private their MPs are frank that the opinion polls — which anyone can read — point to the two parties’ combined seat totals being an obvious route to a post-election majority.
Luke Tryl, executive director of More in Common, a think tank which tracks public opinion, said the “ever more acrimonious” battle for the right now makes a pact between the Conservatives and Nigel Farage’s Reform UK “less likely.”
“The Burnham bounce and consolidation of the progressive left vote makes a Lib-Lab pact a more likely prospect,” he said.
Advertisement
“If the Lib Dems can demonstrate their traditional staying power and Burnham’s lead remains at the narrow end, the prospect of them holding the balance of power — and almost certainly choosing to favour Labour — becomes very real indeed,” he added.
Prepare for government
Talk of a coalition usually sends a shiver down a Lib Dem spine. The party was left with just eight MPs in 2015 after five years in government with the Conservatives.
The slow recovery from its 2015 nadir means that the vast majority of the party’s MPs were elected for the first time two years ago, so the party does not have a depth of parliamentary experience.
Britain’s Liberal Democrat party leader Ed Davey addresses supporters during a local election tour in Redhill, Surrey on May 6, 2026. | Justin Tallis/AFP via Getty Images
“We have a lot of people who haven’t spent the years that some people have spent thinking about policy,” Leunig,a civil servant for more than a decade who recently served as a government policy adviser across multiple departments, including under the Tories, said.
The Britain Project aims to provide “decent ideas that can be given to the civil service to implement” and ensure parliamentarians “understand what tough choices look like in government,” he added.
The Starmer administration — which collapsed after two years in government — was “caught like rabbits in a headlight” soon after entering Downing Street, he said.
Advertisement
Papers please
The Britain Project will also publish regular policy papers with a specific focus on economic growth and public services.
“We don’t want to try and be all things for all people at this stage,” said another person closely involved with the think tank, granted anonymity because they are not currently authorized to speak publicly. “We really want to focus on what are the really key issues for the country at the moment,” they added, citing the cost of living as a priority.
The think tank wants to show “you need a vibrant economy in order to be able to support social justice,” that person said, adding “liberalism endorses a national confidence” alongside being proudly internationalist.
Britain’s Chancellor of the Exchequer Rishi Sunak attends a virtual press conference inside 10 Downing Street in central London on March 3, 2021. | Tolga Akmen/AFP via Getty Images
“What we want is people who are specialists in their area who’ve done a lot of deep thinking,” the person added. “We can support them with research, but [they] will have a lot of experience themselves to draw on.”
Through the scrutiny of the policy process, Leunig says he is optimistic they’ll create ideas that are both acceptable to the public and can be implemented.
“I want us to be publishing things that people say: ‘Hey, that is worth thinking about,’” Leunig said, pointing out that he proposed the furlough scheme to stop mass unemployment when he was economic adviser to then Chancellor Rishi Sunak during the Covid-19 pandemic. “What I don’t want to be doing is just saying exactly what everybody else has said.”
Advertisement
Shoestring affair
The Britain Project is funded by individual donors. Though the group would not disclose names, it will not have a physical office to save money.
The Britain Project is set up as a not-for-profit company with an advisory board and a corporate board. While the advisory board won’t only have Lib Dem members, there will be a clear crossover with the party.
“We want to work with a range of people because it’s about the ideas. It’s not necessarily about the party membership,” the anonymous person quoted above said.
Tempting fate
Lib Dem parliamentarians have welcomed the Britain Project.
One peer, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said it should “help flesh out policies to fill the big gap between ‘worked out enough to do a press release and survive a question from POLITICO’ and ‘ready to put into action.’”
However, some MPs are nervous about giving the impression the party is already thinking about joining a governing coalition.
Advertisement
One Lib Dem MP warned it would be “absurd” to “think about what we would want to do and how we would work with coalition partners” as “any kind of preparation actually makes it less likely because we aren’t likely to attract Tory switchers if they think we’ll keep Labour in power.”
Ultimately, Leunig wants the new organization to offer “some degree of novelty” and have its ideas adopted by all parties.
“Just because you’re a party in the center, whatever that means, doesn’t mean you should be a soggy consensus,” he said.
Dan Bloom contributed reporting.
This story has been updated to correct the project’s status as a not-for-profit company.

Marine Le Pen’s risky economic gamble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

PARIS — Marine Le Pen’s bid to broaden her appeal beyond the far right is running into a familiar challenge: The promises that energize her core voters are precisely the ones that worry fiscal conservatives.
At the first debate ahead of next spring’s presidential election, the far-right veteran promised French voters an ambitious cost-cutting package she says would bring the country’s budget deficit under control.
But she also doubled down on her promise to roll back a key element of French President Emmanuel Macron’s pension reform and make it possible for workers to retire at 62.
Advertisement
“I can already hear what people are going to say … ‘It’s an additional deficit’,” she told the event last week, which was organized by Medef, France’s main business lobby. “It’s a choice we have to make as a society,” she added. “And I stand by it.”
As her campaign kicks off in earnest, many wonder whether the candidate for the far-right National Rally will revisit her economic platform to broaden her appeal, especially among business leaders and traditional center-right voters.
Instead, she made clear that fiscal discipline wouldn’t come at the expense of the promises she has made to her core voters.
Politically, that choice could cut both ways: Sticking with her pension promises may shore up support among her core voters, but make it harder for her to win over the moderate electorate she will likely need if she is to enter the Elysée.
France’s public finances leave little room for maneuver. Public debt has climbed to 117.5 percent of GDP while the budget deficit remains well above EU limits and borrowing costs have risen sharply.
At the Medef debate, Le Pen said she was in favor of a “golden rule” to keep budget deficits below 3 percent of GDP, similar to Germany’s debt brake.
Advertisement
She also said she would soon present a plan to cut some €125 billion in spending, including on budget items associated with migration, “useless” public agencies, and France’s contribution to the EU. Le Pen will present her detailed platform in the fall, but Jean-Philippe Tanguy, a member of Parliament for the National Rally, told POLITICO this would be accomplished in “less than five years.”
But Le Pen has yet to explain in detail how those savings would be achieved, and rivals are already questioning whether the numbers add up. “Marine Le Pen will ruin France,” Bruno Retailleau, a conservative candidate from Les Républicains, told reporters shortly after the Medef event.
Marine Le Pen and François Durvye visit the VivaTech technology startups and innovation fair at the Paris Expo Porte de Versailles, in Paris on June 19, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images
The tension has also surfaced inside her own camp. As Le Pen was outlining her economic agenda at the Medef event, news broke that François Durvye, one of her key economic advisers and a leading advocate of greater fiscal discipline, was leaving the campaign.
Internal cracks
Durvye, who has informally advised Le Pen for five years, has been credited with building bridges between her party and the business world. A former fund manager, he was a key voice in the party on economic issues.
But his push for more fiscal discipline and economically liberal policies ran against the instincts of the party’s old guard, which remained wedded to the party’s populist positions. He was also a special advisor to National Rally President Jordan Bardella, Le Pen’s protégé who was expected to take the campaign’s reins if Le Pen had been judged ineligible to run because of her guilty verdict for embezzlement of EU funds.
Bardella has been working to move the party toward the center on economic issues, including softening Le Pen’s pledge on the pension age — something that Durvye had been advocating for internally.
Advertisement
While Durvye declined to comment on the exact circumstances of his departure, he made clear privately and publicly that he did not feel able to defend the party’s latest positions to his business contacts.
“What was accomplished to break down the barriers between business representatives was quite significant,” Durvye told POLITICO, adding he had used his “freedom to leave.”
Le Pen, asked about his departure on French TV, said it was her “wish.”
Trust issues
With France among the countries hardest hit by a global surge in borrowing costs and under close watch from ratings agencies, fiscal issues are bound to play a major role in the campaign.
As the frontrunner, Le Pen’s proposals are coming under increasing scrutiny. Polls place her in first place at about 35 percent in the first round of France’s election, and well placed to beat her rivals in the runoff round.
In terms of her economic credentials, Le Pen has come a long way since 2017, when Macron crushed her during a debate performance, hammering her on a now-abandoned pledge to take France out of the eurozone.
Advertisement
In a poll by French research firm Odoxa published last week, 36 percent of respondents said they trusted Le Pen to implement sound economic policy if elected — the highest score among all presidential candidates tested.
But the results mask a more nuanced reality: The figure is largely driven up by support from National Rally voters, with centrists far less confident. Le Pen’s leading centrist rival, former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, had a broader base of support on the issue. That could prove decisive in the runoff, where two finalists have to woo voters who didn’t opt for them in the first round.
Bruno Jeanbart, the vice-president of polling firm Opinionway, who surveyed business leaders ahead of last week’s debate, said business-minded voters were still skeptical that the National Rally was up for the task when it comes to fixing France’s economy.
Le Pen’s return as a presidential candidate fuels that dynamic. Bardella and his allies had made a point of reaching out to economically liberal voters and “gave the impression that they might be more attuned to the expectations and challenges of the business world,” the pollster said.
By contrast, Le Pen has long been seen as defiant towards the world of business, railing at the global elites that meet in places like Davos and expressing sympathy with voters hurt by the ripple effects of globalization in France’s industrial heartlands.
When she unveils her full platform, expected next month, Le Pen will need to show centrist voters that she can make the numbers work.

What 248 books reveal about Kaja Kallas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

While actively running the EU’s foreign policy on the world’s most demanding issues, Kaja Kallas still finds time outside work to read about … more foreign policy.
The top EU diplomat and former Estonian prime minister frequently talks about her love of reading, citing her favorite authors in speeches and meeting with them privately to discuss their work. Since taking up her most recent post in December 2024, she has read at least 52 books she has shared publicly — all of which she has posted on her Instagram — most of them related to international affairs. In total, she has shared more than 200 titles since 2017.
“You know, my reading list is quite long,” said Kallas, who officially serves as the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy, at a press conference in January. “By the end, when I finish this job, I will be very smart,” she joked.
Advertisement
The collection closely tracks the subjects Kallas is most involved with in her role, evolving alongside her professional remit: 24 books on Russia and Ukraine, nine on China, and seven on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Further-flung regions pop up only rarely, with just three books on the rest of East Asia and none on South American politics beyond Venezuela.
“Reading books is a valuable advantage, especially as it is not so common nowadays,” an official from Kallas’ team told POLITICO. “The Middle East wars, Russia’s aggression and China’s growing influence are major geopolitical issues, so naturally they feature on the High Representative’s reading list.” Noting that she meets with ministers, officials, staff and experts daily and receives countless briefing papers, memos and other sources of information, “books are a nice addition on long-distance flights,” the official added.
The reading lists alone have not shaped the full contours of Kallas’ foreign policy, of course. But they provide a view into which political subjects Europe’s chief diplomat is interested in learning more about and where she goes looking for answers.
So, what does Kallas’ bookshelf reveal about the person shaping Europe’s diplomacy? To find out, POLITICO reviewed the 248 titles she has included on public reading lists since 2017 and spoke to 24 of the authors.
Noted bookworm
Kallas is not the only avid reader in Brussels, but few politicians talk about their love of literature quite as often. Since 2023, she has released reading lists twice a year on Instagram, and before that, she blogged about her latest reads monthly.
“I read a lot, but you’re always influenced by the books you’ve read most recently,” Kallas told POLITICO in 2025.
Political scientist Ivan Krastev, who co-authored 2019’s “The Light That Failed: A Reckoning” on why liberalism failed to spread in Eastern Europe, said Kallas had reached out to him after reading his book. She was trying to find a publisher to translate it into her native Estonian, he told POLITICO. The translation was eventually released in 2022.
Advertisement
While Kallas was prime minister, her government had similarly pushed for the translation of political scientist Mark Leonard’s “The Age of Unpeace: How Connectivity Causes Conflict,” which she said she would “often cite.”
“It’s interesting, particularly when a politician in a high position reads a book,” said Krastev. “They’re trying to make sense of their own experience” and “trying to answer some of the questions that [they] are struggling with.”
Indeed, Kallas’ book choices appear to closely reflect her scheduled diplomatic trips. Visiting Montenegro for the EU-Western Balkans Summit in June this year, the top diplomat had read the memoirs of Richard Holbrooke, architect of the 1995 Dayton Accords in Bosnia, and Martti Ahtisaari, the former Finnish president and mediator of the 1999 Kumanovo Agreement forcing Serbia’s withdrawal from Kosovo.
“A lot to learn also today, and actually a lot of parallels,” said Kallas of Holbrooke’s book in July.
Ahead of her trip to Sarajevo a month later, she then contacted former Swedish Prime Minister and High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina Carl Bildt about his 1998 book “Peace Journey: The Struggle for Peace in Bosnia,” a memoir about his work in the region.
“She sent me a text and said, ‘I’m reading your book, and I like it very much.’ And I said, ‘How on earth did you get hold of that one?'” Bildt told POLITICO, joking that the book was published nearly three decades ago. “She wanted to go down into the weeds of the history … and that could be useful.”
Advertisement
Earlier in the year, after the U.S. forcibly captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, Kallas picked up two books about the South American country, too: “Comandante: Hugo Chávez’s Venezuela” and “Things Are Never So Bad That They Can’t Get Worse: Inside the Collapse of Venezuela.”
“She is one of the best-read people I know,” said Marietje Schaake, a friend and former liberal MEP who served with Kallas in the European Parliament. “That depth has shaped her thinking and her career.”
What’s in the library?
Six of the authors who spoke to POLITICO for this article specifically cited Kallas’ hawkish stance on Moscow as echoing the messages in their books — perhaps unsurprising given Kallas warned of Russia’s threat to Europe back in 2021, during her first term as prime minister.
“What is happening in Ukraine right now is what I was reading about in our own history books,” she told Vogue Greece in 2023.
Sylvie Kauffmann, author of 2023’s “Blindsided” (Les aveuglés) — which argues that Germany and France failed to recognize the Russian threat — told POLITICO her book “confirms everything that Kallas thinks” about how others downplayed Moscow’s aggression.
Advertisement
Speaking to POLITICO about his 2018 book “Identity,” famed political philosopher of liberal democracy Francis Fukuyama said the work contained “a kind of ideological roadmap to be able to better explain what it is that … we’re fighting for.” Noting that Ukraine’s fight against Russia was one of the reasons he wrote it, Fukuyama then praised the chief diplomat’s support for the country.
Kallas has also read extensively on Israel-Palestine, a conflict on which her stance has attracted both attention and controversy in Brussels.
Far more critical of Israel than her peers in the European Commission, Kallas reportedly compared the situation on the ground to South Africa under apartheid during a closed-door meeting in June, causing Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar to sever contact.
Two of the authors on the subject who feature on Kallas’ reading lists told POLITICO her reported comparison mirrored the arguments made in their books, with 2024 Pulitzer Prize winner Nathan Thrall saying his “aim in writing [“A Day in the Life of Abed Salama: Anatomy of a Jerusalem Tragedy”] was to influence people like her.”
“The fact that she has come to the conclusion that Israel is practicing apartheid is most welcome as far as I’m concerned,” he said.
“I explain the aspects of apartheid, and I hope she’d see that her judgment is well founded,” echoed Michael Scott-Baumann, author of “Palestinians and Israelis: A Short History of Conflict.”
Advertisement
But not every author on Kallas’ lists approves of her foreign policy decisions when it comes to their topics of specialization.
Kim Ghattas, who wrote her book “Black Wave” on the Middle East, for example, said Kallas has been too passive on the Israeli-U.S. war with Iran. “That is not good policymaking. I would hope that reading books like mine can help prepare policymakers like her, specifically for moments like the one that we find ourselves in right now.”
Former U.S. National Security Adviser John Bolton, who has long advocated for regime change in Iran, said he, too, wished Kallas had become more involved — though in support of President Donald Trump’s military operation.
He also noted that Kallas’ blunt style risked further alienating the U.S. from the EU, with her comments advocating for the bloc’s sovereignty “giving [Trump] the excuse to do what he probably wants to do anyway.”
Criticism extended beyond the Middle East as well. Robert D. Kaplan, author of 1993’s “Balkan Ghosts” — which heavily influenced former U.S. President Bill Clinton’s initial reluctance to militarily intervene in the region, according to his biographers — told POLITICO that Kallas’ impolitic moments “may be things that she’ll come to partially regret over time.”
“When you get far quick, you tend to make mistakes. Because you’re confident, you’re even arrogant,” said Kaplan.
Booking ahead
It’s not all about world affairs and global diplomacy, though — some of Kallas’ more recent political predicaments lie a little closer to home.
Recent months have seen the top diplomat losing a turf war with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen over the bloc’s foreign policy, while her diplomatic service, the European External Action Service, has struggled to build consensus across a divided Europe.
So with the rentrée almost upon us in Brussels, there may be no better time for Kallas to get through a few more books — a strategy she has turned to previously.
Advertisement
While serving as prime minister, during a 2023 podcast, Kallas recalled how she once considered foreign policy to be her greatest political weakness — until she turned to books.
“It’s not my weakness anymore because I’ve read so much about this,” she said.
Perhaps this time it will be Brussels that sends her back to the stacks.

The Balearic Social Housing Model Receives the 2026 OBEL Award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Amid growing economic, political, and climatic instability, the 2026 OBEL Award highlights the need for architectural approaches that rethink both existing and emerging infrastructures. The title for this edition is "Systems' Hack," where "systems" are understood as interrelated mechanisms governed by shared rules and "hacking" is framed as a strategic intervention that seeks to alter how these mechanisms operate. Within this framework, the OBEL Foundation has announced the Balearic Social Housing Model as the winner of this year's award, while also announcing a new cycle in 2027 under the same topic. The Balearic Social Housing Model is recognized for "transforming the role of social housing administration in the Balearic Islands between 2019 and 2023," proposing new approaches in response to an acute housing shortage and a critically limited public rental housing stock in Spain.
The Balearic Social Housing Model was led by a partnership between Cris Ballester Parets, the Balearic government's former managing director of IBAVI (Instituto Balear de la Vivienda), and Carles Oliver Barceló, the head of IBAVI's technical department. They developed the project as a new model to increase the supply of public housing at scale and speed, without losing architectural, environmental or social qualities. The model completes a full housing-building cycle, rethinking how public housing for vulnerable communities can be commissioned, procured, designed, built and inhabited. It offers a systemic approach to public housing that goes beyond one particular material, architectural language or construction technique, entangling responses to real social, environmental and economic challenges.
In association with several architecture firms and external collaborators, they developed a research ecosystem and a significant portfolio of built social housing projects. The designs bring together local materials, circular construction practices, climate-responsive design and new approaches to public procurement and project delivery. According to the OBEL Foundation, the housing model's significance lies "in the way it connects public policy, architectural experimentation, environmental responsibility, local productive capacity, and dignified housing delivery as parts of one system." The jury, composed of Nathalie de Vries, Sumayya Vally, Aric Chen, Anne Marie Galmstrup, and Manuel and Francisco Aires Mateus, highlighted the project for using public administration as a space for experimentation and for using public procurement, investment, and management as tools for systemic change.
Related Article
“For Decades We Have Valued the New More than the Old”: In Dialogue with OBEL Award 2025 Winners HouseEurope!
 What makes the Balearic Social Housing Model remarkable is how innovative architecture can be found not just in design and material choice but also in procurement, policy and process. Public housing shortages are not unique to the Balearic Islands; the same structural pressure is playing out in cities and regions across the world. What this model offers is a framework wherein public institutions can adapt to their own context along with proof that public administration itself can become a genuine engine for change. — Nathalie de Vries, Chair of Jury, OBEL Award
The Balearic Social Housing Model rethinks how public housing is designed and delivered through six interconnected shifts. First, it moves from global supply chains to territorial resources, using a "Map of Resources" to prioritize local materials, climate, and industrial and human capacity, assessed by carbon impact, availability, performance, cost, and scalability, so that housing strengthens local industry rather than relying on standardized global systems. Second, it shifts from a passive client to an active public developer, with the administration building in-house technical capacity, redesigning procurement and competitions, and coordinating innovation across projects instead of simply commissioning the cheapest code-compliant design through rigid tender processes.
Third, it moves from mechanical dependence to climate-responsive architecture, using passive strategies such as orientation, thermal inertia, cross-ventilation, solar protection, and intermediate climatic spaces to cut emissions and household energy costs, addressing environmental and social vulnerability simultaneously. Fourth, it moves from the "dormitory model" to the democratic house, designing flexible, non-hierarchical spaces that adapt to changing household configurations over time. Fifth, it moves from short-term delivery to permanent public value, abandoning Spain's traditional VPO model, in which subsidized units were built for private sale, in favor of public rental housing that stays permanently in public hands. Finally, it moves from isolated projects to a collective learning system, with an in-house team tracking materials, costs, and performance across the whole program so that lessons, successes, and failures accumulate and inform future projects.
The project's creators, Cris Ballester and Carles Oliver, committed to dedicating part of the prize funds to expanding the international reach of the Balearic Social Housing Model. Carles Oliver renounced his personal share in favor of supporting emergency housing initiatives in the Balearic Islands. Separately, following this cycle of the awards, the OBEL Foundation jury decided to extend the "Systems' Hack" focus into 2027, to continue exploring how architecture can transform existing structures and act where those structures have failed altogether. For the first time, the jury will extend its annual focus to recognize another initiative in spring 2027, calling for projects that demonstrate architecture's ability to engage with systems at different scales and through different forms of intervention.

Bomb attacks by Mexican gangs on the rise, officials say

Bomb attacks by Mexican gangs on the rise, officials say
MEXICO CITY, Aug 31 - A recent spate of bomb attacks has swept across Mexico, from car bombs to drones rigged with explosives, exposing an escalation in cartel violence that local authorities say has intensified over the past three years.
The latest incident occurred on Sunday, when a suspected car bomb ripped through the central Mexican state of Zacatecas, injuring at least 11 people, including two police officers, while causing extensive damage to about 40 buildings, the state's governor, David Monreal, said on Monday.
The vehicle was abandoned outside the police headquarters in Ojocaliente, central Zacatecas.
Images on social media showed columns of fire and people, including children, running to escape the flames. Reuters was unable to verify the authenticity of the footage.
Initial reports suggest the attack was carried out by a criminal group in retaliation for the arrest of one of its members on Saturday, Monreal said at a press conference.
Sunday's explosion follows nearly a dozen similar incidents, some carried out using “mini drones” loaded with explosives, or landmines, and points to an evolution in the operations of criminal groups, Monreal said.
Such attacks have been on the rise in Zacatecas in recent years, the state's security head, Arturo Medina, said on Monday.
In 2024, just one such incident was registered, followed by six in 2025, with 10 so far this year, Medina said.
Medina did not specify the number of victims from these attacks.
“Organized crime is evolving; I don’t understand why people aren’t grasping the full extent of what’s happening in the country,” Monreal said.
Other states plagued by violence, including Michoacan, have seen similar attacks where criminal groups have used explosives to target security facilities, communities, or law enforcement.
Military personnel have been killed in these incidents. The Mexican central government has not commented on the issue. REUTERS

"Their plan that day was to commit mass murders not only at the mosque but to follow up at a local Jewish temple and finally at a predominantly African American high school there in town," he said.

Las Vegas Jury finds ex-gang leader Duane 'Keffe D' Davis guilty of Tupac Shakur murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
01:47:14 UTC
10:47:14 KST

A Las Vegas jury has found an ex-gang leader guilty of murder in a case accusing him of masterminding the drive-by killing of legendary hip-hop artist Tupac Shakur, bringing a decades-old cold case to a close.
Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, was charged in Nevada's Clark County with a single count of murder with a deadly weapon.
The jury reached a verdict in less than three hours.
Davis was accused of leading a group of men to kill Shakur, 25, who was one of rap's most commercially successful and influential artists, in retaliation for the beating of Davis' nephew.
Police had long suspected Davis but lacked sufficient evidence to charge him until he went public with his accounts in media interviews and a memoir, which alongside recordings of his confidential meetings with investigators formed the core of the prosecution's case.
Davis' defence lawyer argued his client's statements were mere bravado uncorroborated by independent evidence.
The 1996 casino dispute
During the trial, which began on August 17, prosecutors presented recorded conversations detailing how Davis became enraged after Shakur and his entourage assaulted his nephew at a Las Vegas casino on 7 September 1996.
Davis and three other men, including his nephew, searched for Shakur and Death Row Records executive Marion "Suge" Knight in a white Cadillac later that night.
Davis admitted passing a firearm to the back seat, from which one of two passengers opened fire when they pulled alongside Knight and Shakur's vehicle.
Prosecutors have not named the shooter, and the three other occupants of the vehicle have since died.
Under Nevada law, Davis faced murder charges as a co-conspirator despite not pulling the trigger himself.
Davis led the Southside Compton Crips, a Los Angeles street gang locked in conflict with the rival Mob Piru gang, which was associated with Shakur and Death Row Records.
Shakur's death marked a defining moment in hip-hop history during the height of the 1990s East Coast–West Coast rivalry.

Going big and going green can work together for Hong Kong mega-events
By building green standards into event infrastructure, Hong Kong can stay competitive as an event host and irresistible to global organisers
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Hong Kong’s mega-event economy is thriving. In a blog post last month, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po noted that in the first half of 2026, the city hosted more than 130 mega-events, drawing 1.75 million visitors and injecting roughly HK$5.8 billion (US$739.9 million) into the local economy.
These figures are the ongoing dividends of the government’s sustained policy and financial backing. This momentum is well-documented: in the last two years, the concerts of global A-listers such as Coldplay and Blackpink drew hundreds of thousands of fans and generated millions of dollars in ticket sales, while the 2025 Hong Kong Sevens delivered a HK$768 million boost.
While sold-out stadiums and economic gains capture the headlines, a lesser-known aspect of these mega-events is their commitment to environmental sustainability.
By introducing features such as a recycling leaderboard, Coldplay made going green fun, boosting LED wristband return rates to an impressive 94 per cent in Hong Kong and reducing their global tour emissions by 59 per cent compared to their previous tour.
These efforts reflect a shift across the event sector. Blackpink’s management company, YG Entertainment, introduced event-level carbon tracking, ensuring their 2026 Hong Kong concert conducted rigorous carbon accounting. The 2024 Paris Olympics halved its carbon footprint compared to previous Games.
As consumers and businesses increasingly value sustainability and extreme weather becomes more commonplace, greening Hong Kong’s mega-event economy should no longer be optional. A report by Our Hong Kong Foundation estimates that greening our mega-events could bring around HK$1 billion annually – all while reducing emissions.

BISHKEK, September 1. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin continues his visit to the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek. His agenda for Tuesday includes events related to the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and a marathon of bilateral meetings.
SCO summit
The SCO summit will officially begin on the morning of September 1 with a welcoming ceremony for the leaders of the organization’s member states hosted by Kyrgyzstan's President Sadyr Japarov. The leaders will then pose for a photo.
The summit will kick off with a Council of Heads of State meeting themed “25 years of the SCO: together for a stable world, development, and prosperity.” Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov told reporters that the leaders would review the organization's activities in the past 25 years and discuss efforts to further strengthen the SCO and expand cooperation in politics, security, the economy, and humanitarian ties. The SCO leaders will also exchange views on pressing international and regional issues, with a special focus on improving the organization’s effectiveness.
After the SCO session, a traditional SCO+ meeting will be held, bringing together the leaders of SCO observer countries, dialogue partners and guests invited by the chair. This time, the SCO member states - Russia, Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan - will be joined by Afghanistan, Mongolia, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Bahrain, Egypt, Cambodia, Qatar, Kuwait, Laos, the Maldives, Myanmar, Nepal, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Sri Lanka. The meeting will also be attended by the heads of several international organizations, including the United Nations, the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). The broader meeting will be held under the theme "The United Nations as the Key Element of a Fair World Order: The Contribution of SCO+ Countries to the Formation of a Multipolar World," Ushakov said.
The summit will conclude with the signing of more than 20 documents, the main one being the Bishkek Declaration, which will reflect consolidated approaches to pressing regional and international issues, including economic challenges. Another important document is a protocol to the 2002 SCO Charter, which will streamline the structure of the organization’s bodies. The Universal Center for Countering Security Challenges and Threats and the Anti-Drug Center will be added to them. A new "SCO partner" category will also be introduced, aimed at simplifying the organization’s structure by merging the existing observer and partner categories. In addition, a package of decisions on combating drug trafficking, international security, science, technology and logistics is expected to be signed, along with statements on energy efficiency, nuclear safety and security, and cooperation in emergency response.
International communication
Once the SCO summit is over, Putin will continue his series of meetings with other countries’ leaders. He is scheduled to hold talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Mongolian President Ukhnaagiin Khurelsukh, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, and Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov.
Putin will sum up the results of his visit by taking questions from Kremlin pool journalists accompanying him on the trip.

====================================================================================================

What to Watch from Trump’s US Space Academy Commission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
01:27:30 UTC
10:27:30 KST

President Donald Trump on Aug. 28 announced plans to establish a U.S. Space Academy to bolster the country’s workforce and educate “the next generation” of space experts.
The announcement quickly drew comparisons to existing military academies—in a speech at NASA’s Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, Trump himself likened it to the Army’s United States Military Academy at West Point. But the White House executive order issued in conjunction with the president’s announcement indicates the vision is for a new kind of federal service academy, one led by NASA and designed to train space operators and engineers across the civil, military, and commercial sectors.
“To continue to lead the world in space exploration and technology, while securing and defending our national interests in space, the Nation must prepare the next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers, operators, entrepreneurs, civil servants, and warfighters and ensure that they are capable of advancing American interests in space,” the order states. “It is my administration’s policy to strengthen the nation’s space workforce by expanding opportunities to educate and develop the next generation of leaders across the space domain.”
The President doesn’t have the authority to create the academy on his own—that would require an act of Congress—but his order establishes a commission to explore questions around the academy’s structure, potential military or civil service requirements, location, funding, and eligibility requirements. The group will be led by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, and other commissioners will include leaders from the White House and the Pentagon, including the Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of the Air Force. The commission is meant to issue a report with recommendations by late December.
As those recommendations take shape in the coming weeks and months, experts say they’ll be watching for more detail on the academy’s mission and scope as well as efforts to garner feedback from members of Congress. They’ll also be tracking the U.S. military’s role in the organization and how it might impact the U.S. Air Force Academy, whose 2026 class included 93 Guardians. A Department of the Air Force spokesperson declined to comment for this story. In a statement, USAFA’s Association and Foundation, its alumni organization, said it will “closely monitor developments” and share relevant information with graduates.
Charles Galbreath, director of the Mitchell Institute’s Spacepower Advantage Center of Excellence, said the concept of a NASA-led “space center of excellence” makes sense given NASA’s deep knowledge and legacy operating in the domain.
“For decades, NASA has been the repository of knowledge when it comes to space operations,” Galbreath said. “It stands to reason that it would be useful to codify that, to create an academy where NASA experts could pass on that knowledge to the next generation.”
While the President’s order doesn’t specify the primary audience for the new academy, Galbreath said there’s an opportunity to reach a wide swath of the space community—from undergraduates to mid-career operators—with programming that ranges from certifications to academic degrees. For the military, the academy could eventually serve as a means for commissioning officers, but Galbreath said that may not be necessary immediately given the Space Force’s small size.
“At some point in the future, it could grow and become a commissioning source, I suppose,” he said. “But we’re still a long way from that.”
Todd Harrison, a space policy expert at the American Enterprise Institute, said that while he agrees there’s a need to expand the space workforce, it’s not clear that a new federally run academy is the right answer. In an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, he cited concerns about operational costs, blurring the line between military and civil space missions, and setting up unnecessary competition with the universities that already exist to train the aerospace workforce.
Harrison suggested that rather than create a separate academy, the administration could start a scholarship program similar to the Reserve Officers’ Training Corps, or ROTC. In this scenario, the government would offer scholarships to students pursuing relevant, space-related degrees in exchange for a period of service in the Space Force, NASA, or another federal agency.
“Instead of competing with our world-class institutions . . . you would let them produce the best and the brightest talent with a commitment to go into the government and work for the government for a period of time,” he said. “Establishing a physical academy is going to take years, whereas if you make it a scholarship program, you could literally start awarding scholarships next school year.”
While a scholarship program is one way to address the government’s workforce pipeline, Galbreath argued there’s also value in creating the consolidated hub of space expertise that would come with the academy model.
“When you have people that are colocated, they’re going to breed new ideas as well,” he said. “If you’re a student and you’re learning about orbital mechanics from a NASA PhD who designed the trajectories for a multi-planetary flyby, you’re getting the best.”
Another key question for the commission is where to locate the academy. Galbreath said it’s worth considering whether the academy should be located in a single campus or dispersed across multiple hubs, adding that cost will be an important factor as the commission considers its footprint.
Harrison cautioned that opening that discussion—which is often loaded with parochial politics—too soon could muddy the process. In fact, some lawmakers have already started to pitch their districts to house the Space Academy, including Rep. Dale Strong, R-Ala., who said on Aug. 31 that Huntsville, Ala., has been floated as a potential location. Although the commission has months to recommend a location, Trump indicated he may select one sooner.
Political headwinds may become a problem for Trump’s Space Academy proposal, especially if Republicans lose their majority in either the House or Senate after midterm elections in November. Harrison said there’s likely not enough time for the commission to complete its work and put the decision to a vote before the end of this legislative session.
But Galbreath noted that creating a new academy could garner bipartisan support, similar to the creation of the Space Force in 2019 during Trump’s first term.
“It’s really going to come down to the cost-benefit—can they make a compelling case that this Space Academy is going to be worth the investment of time and money and personnel,” he said. “If they can, then I think they’ll get bipartisan support. I don’t think this is one of those areas that you can get unilateral support.”
Some Democrats, including Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., have already indicated they’re intrigued by the concept. In an Aug. 28 post on the social media site X, Whitesides said the idea “deserves consideration” but raised concerns about funding and the lack of congressional representation on the commission.
“I am open-minded to hear thoughtful answers to these questions, but I recommend that Congress be engaged quickly and substantively or else this intriguing idea will be stuck on the launch pad,” Whitesides said.

SC: Externment orders cannot be passed routinely, require reasons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
01:26:51 UTC
10:26:51 KST

SC rules externment orders cannot be routine, quashes Raigarh DM order, says multiple criminal cases alone not grounds for such action.
NEW DELHI: Holding that forcing a person to stay out of a city or district affects freedom guaranteed by the Constitution, SC on Monday ruled that a govt cannot pass an externment order routinely and must pass a reasoned order to justify such harsh measures.A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu quashed an externment order passed by Raigarh district magistrate directing a person to remove himself from the district and contiguous districts for one year. The order was passed against him as multiple criminal cases were pending and the district authority apprehended that his presence would create further problems in the area and nearby districts.“An order of externment directly impinges upon valuable fundamental freedoms guaranteed to a citizen and, therefore, cannot be made as a matter of routine. Further, merely because multiple criminal cases have been filed against a person would not, ipso facto, be a ground for ordering externment,” the bench said.Before exercising such power, the DM is required to arrive at a bona fide and informed subjective satisfaction that circumstances warrant such an extreme measure and externment is necessary, it said.
The bench said the authority is not expected to render a judgement as a court of law but the order must nonetheless disclose, at least in broad terms, the reasons for such satisfaction.
“The existence of objective material and a discernible nexus between such material and the conclusion reached are indispensable safeguards against arbitrary exercise of power,” it said.Quashing the order under Chhattisgarh Rajya Suraksha Adhiniyam, SC said the externment order fell short of statutory requirement. “The order does not indicate the material on the basis of which such conclusion was reached. No reasons are forthcoming to demonstrate why the third respondent (Raipur DM) considered the situation grave enough to necessitate the appellant’s externment,” it said.

BREWING FRUSTRATION WITH HEGSETH

Zelensky enacts NSDC decision on regions' preparations for winter
The decision is set out in Decree No. 838/2026, dated August 31 and published on the president's website, according to Ukrinform.
"To enact the decision of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine dated August 5, 2026, 'On the status of implementation of comprehensive resilience plans for individual regions and approval of the Comprehensive Resilience Plan for the Kyiv territorial community'," the decree states.
Under the decision, the authorities took note of the prime minister's information on the implementation of comprehensive resilience plans by regional state (military) administrations and mayors, including the scope of measures already completed and the realistic prospects for implementing them before the start of the 2026/2027 heating season.
Officials were warned of personal responsibility for failure to implement the comprehensive resilience plans, as well as for delays or improper implementation.
The decision also approved the Comprehensive Resilience Plan for the Kyiv territorial community. In addition, the mayor of Kyiv was reminded of personal responsibility for preparations for and the stable operation of the city's 2026/2027 heating season.
The Cabinet of Ministers, for its part, must immediately update the comprehensive resilience plans, taking into account the realistic prospects for completing the measures envisaged before the start of the 2026/2027 heating season. The government must also, together with the Kyiv City Military Administration and the mayor of Kyiv, continue co-financing the city's Comprehensive Resilience Plan and take measures to ensure the resilience of critical infrastructure operators.
Together with Ukrzaliznytsia, the Cabinet of Ministers must also take measures to restore and replenish rolling stock, including locomotives, damaged or lost as a result of Russian aggression. This includes introducing state aid programs, attracting international funding and simplifying public procurement procedures.
Regional and Kyiv city state (military) administrations, together with businesses regardless of ownership, must conduct command-and-staff exercises within a month to prepare for possible emergencies at heating, electricity, gas and water supply facilities. Before the start of the heating season, they must also increase backup power capacity for essential services, including heating and water supply facilities, by 20% in line with the targets set out in the comprehensive resilience plans.
In addition, local authorities must maintain fuel reserves sufficient for at least two weeks, prepare apartment buildings for autonomous operation and equip them with independent backup power supplies. Heat and electricity companies must protect critical components of their facilities and create reserves of equipment, spare parts and materials for emergency repairs before the start of the 2026/2027 heating season. Regional and Kyiv city military administrations will monitor implementation of these measures.
Control over implementation of the decision has been assigned to National Security and Defense Council Secretary Ihor Klymenko.
The decree took effect on the day of its publication.

Sony, Warner Music sue Anthropic over songs used in AI training
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01

Sony, Warner Music sue Anthropic over songs used in AI training
- Sony Music and Warner Music have sued Anthropic for using their copyrighted song lyrics and sheet music to train its AI model, Claude, without permission.
- The lawsuit claims Anthropic pirated works from famous artists like The Beatles and Taylor Swift, and that Claude can reproduce these lyrics exactly.
- Sony and Warner seek damages up to US$150,000 (S$191,000) per infringement and want a court order to stop Anthropic from using their works in AI training.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES – The music publishing branches of Sony Music and Warner Music have sued Anthropic in California federal court for allegedly misusing their copyrighted song compositions to train its Claude AI models.
Sony and Warner said in the complaint, filed on Aug 28, that Anthropic pirated hundreds of song lyrics and sheet music from The Beatles, Taylor Swift, Michael Jackson and hundreds of other artists to train Claude to respond to human prompts.
The lawsuit is the latest in a wave of cases brought against tech companies by copyright owners including authors, publishers, music labels and news outlets over the use of their work to train artificial intelligence systems.
Universal Music Group sued Anthropic in 2023 and earlier in 2026 over the alleged use of copyrighted song lyrics in AI training, in lawsuits that are still ongoing.
Anthropic became the first AI company to settle one of the disputes in 2025, when it paid US$1.5 billion (S$1.91 billion) to resolve a class action from a group of authors.
“Anthropic clearly considers that to be just the cost of doing business given that its entire business model continues to be built on copyright theft,” Sony and Warner said in their complaint.
“And US$1.5 billion is obviously not a large enough settlement to deter infringing conduct by a company that has parlayed such mass infringement into a staggering two-trillion-dollar valuation.”
“This is the third lawsuit from the same lawyers, recycling allegations from cases already before the courts,” an Anthropic spokesperson said on Aug 31.
The spokesperson also said that the company will defend itself “robustly” and that AI training makes fair use of copyrighted material, citing the judge in the authors’ case against it.
Spokespeople and an attorney for Sony Music and Warner Music did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the case on Aug 31.
The complaint alleges Anthropic illegally obtained the publishers’ lyrics and sheet music through torrent downloads to train Claude, and that Claude can reproduce copyrighted lyrics “verbatim” when prompted.
Sony and Warner also said Anthropic used their lyrics to teach Claude to “generate vast quantities of purportedly ‘new’ AI-generated song lyrics, which compete with Music Publishers’ legitimate copyrighted works as harmful market substitutes”.
The labels are seeking damages of up to US$150,000 for each infringed copyright and a court order barring Anthropic from using their works. REUTERS
