Farhad Ibragimov: Türkiye is one missile deal away from crossing Russia’s red line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:36:54 UTC
05:36:54 KST

Farhad Ibragimov: Türkiye is one missile deal away from crossing Russia’s red line
Recently, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said that Moscow was still waiting for clarification from the US and Türkiye regarding possible arms supplies to Ukraine. Russia expects a response, as this matter directly affects not only bilateral relations but also the prospects for resolving the Ukraine crisis.
The issue goes far beyond the scope of yet another military-technical deal. In July, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan called for preventing the spread of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to the Black Sea region and advocated for the continuation of Ankara-mediated negotiations between Moscow and Kiev within the framework of the so-called Istanbul format. Türkiye emphasized that the security of shipping and energy infrastructure is of fundamental importance to it.
The Russian side, in turn, points out an obvious contradiction. According to Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Ankara and Washington, in their contacts with Moscow, stated that they sent Kiev signals about the unacceptability of attacks in the Black Sea. However, Moscow has not received a public or equally strong response from Türkiye and the US concerning Ukrainian drone strikes on commercial vessels and the infrastructure of the Caspian Pipeline Consortium near Novorossiysk. The Russian Foreign Ministry also warned that strikes on infrastructure and vessels used for delivering Western weapons to Ukraine would continue until the security threats in the region of the Azov and Black seas are eliminated.
Leaving diplomatic language aside, the question is very simple: can Türkiye simultaneously supply Kiev with weapons capable of being used against Russian targets and demand that Moscow continue to consider it a neutral intermediary?
What do the American documents actually state?
The US Congressional Record, published on August 6, shows two notifications about the proposed permanent transfer of American weapons from Turkish stockpiles to Ukraine. The first package includes 12 M270 MLRS launchers, 2,524 M26 unguided rockets with cluster munitions, and 47,000 M509A1 203mm cluster artillery shells. Their initial procurement price is listed at $255.9 million.
The second notification concerns 70 M39 ATACMS tactical ballistic missiles with an initial procurement price of approximately $28 million. In total this amounts to approximately $283.9 million. However, it would be incorrect to automatically assume that this is the price of the current contract since the terms of the potential deal between Ankara and Kiev have not been publicly disclosed.
Another point is equally important. The documents do not prove that the weapons have already been transferred to Kiev. They only confirm that the Turkish government proposed re-export, and the US Department of State notified Congress of its readiness to approve it after the statutory review period. Ankara cites the desire to get rid of outdated weapons and redirect funds toward modernizing its armed forces as the reason for the re-export. Kiev, according to the documents, intends to use these systems to enhance its offensive and defensive firepower.
This formulation makes the situation particularly serious. This isn’t about armored vehicles, communications equipment, or individual commercial drones; M39 ATACMS missiles are capable of engaging targets at ranges of up to 165 km and carry cluster munitions. Combined with M270 launchers and thousands of rocket and artillery munitions, this constitutes a comprehensive package of enhanced long-range firepower systems. Its possible use will inevitably entail losses among Russian troops and the risk of strikes deep into Russian territory.
Between mediation and participation
Russian-Turkish relations have never been an alliance in the strict sense of the word. Moscow and Ankara supported opposing sides in Syria and Libya; they hold different views on the status of Crimea, and compete for influence in various corners of Eurasia. Türkiye supplied Ukraine with drones, developed military-technical cooperation with it and consistently supported it. Yet, none of this prevented Russia and Türkiye from building gas pipelines, a nuclear power plant, developing trade, and reaching agreements in areas where their interests coincided.
This format was based on an unspoken rule that competition should not escalate into direct, critical damage to the other side. Strong disagreements could arise, but they remained manageable and were offset by cooperation in other areas.
The proposed transfer of ATACMS missiles, M270 launchers, and tens of thousands of cluster munitions brings Ankara dangerously close to the limits of this model of interaction. This is not a matter of one weapons system, but its purpose, the scale of the package, and the political context.
Türkiye isn’t simply offering to sell Kiev a batch of its own military equipment; it intends to transfer a large stockpile of American weapons intended to enhance Kiev’s firepower in the ongoing conflict with Russia, and is doing so with Washington’s approval.
Against this backdrop, Türkiye’s peacemaking rhetoric is starting to look increasingly unconvincing. Clearly, a mediator doesn’t have to be completely equidistant from the parties, but both sides should be able to trust it, at least on a minimum level. A mediator can’t call for a moratorium on strikes in the Black Sea while simultaneously helping one of the sides expand its weapons stockpiles; it can’t propose Istanbul as a platform for negotiations while strengthening Kiev’s military potential under the pretext of getting rid of outdated weapons.
Ankara risks overestimating Moscow’s patience
A familiar argument is being voiced by Turkish experts: Russian-Turkish relations are so deep and multifaceted, they argue, that a single deal can’t destroy them. There’s certainly some truth to that. Neither Russia nor Türkiye want to replay the scenario of the 2015 crisis. Severing ties would be detrimental to both sides.
However, Ankara is drawing an all-too-convenient conclusion that economic interdependence guarantees impunity for any foreign policy maneuver; and this is a dangerous fallacy. The Turkish leadership apparently confuses freedom of maneuver with the absence of a price to be paid for that maneuver.
Russia indeed benefits from the Turkish market, transit routes, and bilateral trade, and this is apparent to all. Türkiye remains an important economic and regional partner for Moscow. However, the dependence of the parties is not symmetrical across all sectors. In recent years, the Russian economy has demonstrated its ability to redirect raw material flows, restructure logistics, and seek new markets. Russia’s size allows it to do this quite well. For Türkiye, however, a sudden reduction in Russian energy supplies, tourism, investment, or access to the Russian market creates a more immediate and concentrated effect.
In 2025, trade between the two countries exceeded $50 billion. Russia retained a significant advantage in the trade structure: Türkiye primarily imports Russian energy resources and raw materials. That same year, it received approximately 22 billion cubic meters of gas from Russia; despite diversification, the share of Russian gas in Türkiye’s supply remained around 37%. Nearly seven million Russians visited Türkiye in 2025, securing Russia as the top source market for Türkiye’s tourism industry.
Finally, Russia is financing and constructing the Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant at a cost of over $20 billion. Once operational, it is expected to supply up to 10% of Türkiye’s total electricity demand. At the end of 2025, Ankara announced an additional $9 billion in Russian financing for the project, part of which is expected to arrive in 2026–2027.
For an economy with an annual inflation rate of nearly 32% (as of July 2026), high borrowing costs, and chronic sensitivity to the price of imported energy, the loss of even a portion of these advantages will not be trivial. It will hit foreign exchange earnings, production costs, the balance of payments, and employment in tourism. The Turkish economy may not collapse overnight, but a significant reduction in ties with Russia will deprive it of several key pillars: stable energy supplies, millions of tourists, foreign exchange earnings, a market, and funding for strategic projects.
For a country already experiencing chronic inflation, pressure on the national currency, and high borrowing costs, this will mean not another temporary downturn, but the risk of a protracted systemic crisis. Ankara will not be able to maintain economic stability for long under such conditions. And this isn’t a theoretical forecast. It didn’t take long for Türkiye to feel the consequences of the 2015 crisis, provoked by Ankara after the downing of the Russian Su-24 aircraft. The crisis brought about a collapse in Russian tourist flows, restrictions on agricultural exports, and business losses, even though the economic interdependence between the two countries was significantly lower then than it is today.
Russia, for its part, is not interested in dismantling relations, but if the delivery of the weapons is confirmed, it has ample tools for selective pressure, from revising trade preferences and tourist flows to tightening the terms of energy cooperation and a tougher stance on issues in which Türkiye requires Russian assistance.
Logistics is also of particular importance. The Russian Foreign Ministry has already stated that Russian forces are striking infrastructure and ships used for delivering weapons to Kiev. If Turkish companies and transport chains are directly involved in the transfer of missiles and ammunition, Ankara will not be able to pretend that this is a purely commercial operation unrelated to Russian security.
Where is the red line?
Moscow will not react emotionally to Türkiye’s maneuver; that is not its style. A complete rupture in relations would only benefit those who have long sought to eliminate the independent Russian-Turkish communication channel and return Ankara to a disciplined, ‘Western’ line of conduct. The response must be consistent and proportionate.
Until the transfer is officially confirmed, Russia will seek a direct answer from Türkiye regarding several points: whether a final political decision has been made; on the terms and conditions of the re-export; and on the existence of any restrictions on the use of these systems to strike Russian territory. But if the weapons reach Kiev, it would no longer be possible to maintain the previous level of trust. Moscow will cease to perceive Ankara as an acceptable intermediary, will become less willing to consider Turkish interests in regional issues, and bilateral relations will become more rigid and purely pragmatic.
Russia has long assumed that Ankara is playing its own game. However, should Türkiye’s multi-vector approach turn into direct and large-scale support of the military capabilities of a state that attacks Russian territory, its civilian vessels, and critical infrastructure, this would be unacceptable for Russia. The Russian-Turkish partnership can withstand competition, mutual grievances, and even acute regional crises; but it cannot indefinitely tolerate a situation in which one side derives economic and political advantages from cooperation with Russia while simultaneously arming Russia’s adversary and posing as a mediator.
It’s time for Ankara to soberly assess the balance of risks. Russia is interested in cooperation with Türkiye but it is not irrevocably dependent on it. Moscow will find other routes, markets, and forms of regional cooperation, although such a restructuring will require time and money. For Türkiye, the Russian factor is embedded in several of its most sensitive sectors: energy, tourism, the nuclear project, trade, and regional security. Given the current state of the Turkish economy, the cost of a strategic reassessment of its own capabilities could prove significantly higher than the expected benefits of a deal with Kiev and political rapprochement with Washington.
This is precisely why the possible transfer of ATACMS missiles isn’t a matter that can be solved by another meeting between the presidents; it’s a test of the entire structure of the Russia-Türkiye relationship. If Ankara crosses the line, Russia doesn’t have to declare Türkiye an adversary – it would suffice to stop treating it as a privileged partner whose actions can always be attributed to regular political balancing.

how architecture has made space for animals across history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:35:24 UTC
05:35:24 KST

the nonhuman client was there before multispecies design
Long before architects began adding bird bricks, bee hotels and wildlife corridors to contemporary buildings, animals were already helping determine the shape of architecture. Across Europe, Asia and the Middle East, buildings were designed to accommodate pigeons, silkworms, horses, cattle and wild birds as part of systems that connected shelter, agriculture, religion, labor and power. The history of these structures suggests that the idea of multispecies architecture is a rediscovery of an older condition, as human buildings have always been influenced by nonhuman bodies.
A pigeon tower in Safavid Iran could turn the free movement of birds into agricultural fertilizer; a farmhouse in Edo-period Japan could use the heat generated by a household fire to sustain silkworm production; an Ottoman mosque might incorporate small sanctuaries for birds into its facade. Elsewhere, animal architecture expressed feudal privilege or increasingly industrial systems of extraction. Seen together, these buildings complicate the contemporary image of architecture as a purely human domain, asking, when architecture makes room for animals, who ultimately benefits from that space?
Mardavij Pigeon Tower walls | image by Գարվիք, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
pigeon towers turn animal behavior into infrastructure
Across the agricultural landscape around Isfahan, Safavid pigeon towers, or kabootar khaneh, housed large colonies of pigeons while serving a practical role in agriculture. The mudbrick structures provided protected nesting spaces, while the birds continued to fly out and forage across the surrounding landscape. Inside, rows of nesting niches filled the thick cylindrical walls. The towers protected the birds from predators and made it possible to collect their droppings, which were used as fertilizer and, in some cases, as a source of saltpeter.
The architecture was closely tied to the behavior of the pigeons. The size and arrangement of the nesting spaces, along with openings for birds to enter and ventilation through the tower, were all part of keeping the colonies healthy and productive. At the same time, the birds connected the building to the surrounding farmland, where they fed before returning to roost. The pigeons were given a protected place to nest because their presence produced something useful: fertilizer and other agricultural resources.
Shirakawa-go | image by lumoplank, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
in japan, the farmhouse becomes a thermal system for silkworms
The gasshō-zukuri farmhouses of Shirakawa-gō and Gokayama are large timber houses built in the snowy mountains of central Japan, where domestic life and silkworm farming took place under the same roof. Their steep thatched roofs are perhaps their most recognizable feature, but the upper floors were also important for sericulture. Silkworms were raised in the attic spaces, while the hearth on the floor below provided heat that rose through the house.
Cooking, heating and silk production were therefore closely connected. The arrangement made the farmhouse a home and a place of production. The household relied on sericulture for income, while the layout of the building helped create the conditions needed to raise the silkworms.
Shirakawa-go | image by lumoplank, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
birdhouses turn the facade into shared urban space
The Ottoman kuş evleri, or birdhouses, offer a different approach to accommodating animals in the city. Built into the walls of mosques, fountains, libraries and other public buildings across Istanbul and other Ottoman cities, these small structures provided nesting spaces for birds. Some were designed as miniature versions of the buildings they were attached to, with tiny arches, roofs, ledges and other architectural details.
Builders deliberately incorporated nesting spaces into the architecture. Unlike dovecotes built for agriculture, these birdhouses were not primarily intended to produce meat or collect manure. Their presence was connected instead to religious and charitable traditions that encouraged care for animals. The small structures brought animal life into prominent public spaces, making birds a visible part of the city.
In Ahmedabad and elsewhere in Gujarat, the chabutro offers a different way of making space for animals in the city. These elevated bird-feeding structures are found within residential neighborhoods, providing food, water and shelter for wild birds. Their raised platforms help protect the birds from predators while keeping them close to the center of daily urban life.
Carved timber and stone, shaded platforms and projecting roofs give the structures a distinct presence within the neighborhood. The chabutro is notable for placing space for birds directly within the city, making feeding and caring for birds part of the shared public environment, a tradition also connected to Jain ideas of ahiṃsā, or non-violence, and compassion toward living beings.
Ayazma Mosque birdhouse | image by R Prazeres, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
ANIMAL ARCHITECTURE AND ARISTOCRATIC POWER
The French colombier and the Grandes Écuries at the Château de Chantilly show how animal buildings could also express wealth and social status. In early modern France, dovecotes were closely tied to seigneurial power and the droit de colombier, which gave certain landowners the right to keep pigeons. Their circular walls contained rows of nesting niches, while rotating ladders allowed keepers to reach the birds. Openings connected the pigeons to the surrounding fields, where they could forage before returning to the estate. Their meat and droppings then became part of the landowner’s economy.
The colombier at the Manoir d’Ango in Normandy makes this relationship particularly visible. Its elaborate construction served the practical needs of pigeon keeping, but its scale and ornament also reflected the status of its owner. The building was part of the estate’s architecture and its system of land ownership.
At Chantilly, this relationship takes on a much larger scale. Designed by Jean Aubert between 1719 and 1735 for Louis-Henri de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, the Grandes Écuries gave horses an architectural setting more commonly associated with palaces and monumental buildings than agricultural structures. Its vaulted interiors and extensive stone construction reflected the importance of horses to aristocratic life.
Colombier du manoir d’Ango | image by Louistisserand, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
the model farm turns animals into measurable units
By the nineteenth century, animal housing was becoming more standardized. The British Model Farm movement focused on ventilation, sanitation and making farm work more efficient. John Claudius Loudon’s writings helped establish a more systematic approach to farm buildings, with cattle, pigs and other livestock housed in spaces designed around feeding, waste removal, ventilation and productivity. This was a shift from the more integrated arrangement of earlier buildings. In the gasshō-zukuri farmhouse, domestic life and silkworm production were closely connected. Model Farms instead treated animals as things that could be measured and managed. The buildings were designed to control the conditions around the animals. Ventilation regulated the air, drainage removed waste, and feeding systems reduced the amount of labor needed to care for livestock. Materials and construction methods could also be used to control temperature. The animal was increasingly treated as part of a system of inputs and outputs: feed, heat, space and labor were calculated against the amount of meat, milk or other products produced. This approach helped establish the spatial logic of modern industrial agriculture, in which animal production became increasingly separated from everyday urban life.
Grandes Écuries, Château de Chantilly, France | P.poschadel, CC BY-SA 2.0 FR, via Wikimedia Commons
MULTISPECIES ARCHITECTURE AS A RETURN TO AN OLDER IDEA
Seen against this history, today’s interest in multispecies architecture begins to look less like a new idea and more like a return to a relationship that modern architecture has largely left behind. For centuries, animals were part of the spaces people lived and worked in, whether they were producing food and materials, contributing to household economies, protected for religious reasons, or serving as markers of wealth and status. Industrialization changed that relationship, moving animal production into increasingly controlled spaces and separating it from everyday urban life.
Looking at these buildings as animal habitats complicates the idea that multispecies architecture begins with contemporary ecological design. Some shelter birds without extracting anything from them, others depend on animals for food or agricultural production, while others turn animal housing into an expression of wealth and power. What they share is a recognition that architecture can create conditions for another species to live. The question contemporary architecture inherits is what those habitats are designed to do and what kind of relationship they establish with the animals that occupy them.
Chabutra in Ahmedabad | image by Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
This article is part of designboom’s MODES OF HABITATION chapter, exploring how the spaces we inhabit can reshape the ways we live together. Discover more stories rethinking domesticity, shared living, and the many forms a home can take here.

France takes aim at ultra-fast fashion with new levy

France takes aim at ultra-fast fashion with new levy
- France will impose a levy from Sept 1 on ultra-fast fashion items, targeting Asian e-commerce platforms like Shein with fees up to €19.50 per garment by 2030.
- The levy is based on clothing volume and repair cost, aiming to reduce environmental and economic harm caused by ultra-fast fashion.
- The measure excludes some European retailers, faces criticism and trade tension with China, but is supported by French officials and cleared by the EU Commission.
AI generated
PARIS – France will from Sept 1 impose a fee on ultra-fast fashion items that will eventually reach almost €20 (S$30) per garment, as the government targets major Asian e-commerce platforms including Shein.
The levy follows legislation passed by the French Parliament in June to regulate so-called “ultra-fast fashion” companies, known for selling large volumes of lower quality clothing at rock-bottom prices.
It is part of a push to rein in Asian e-commerce giants including Shein, Temu and AliExpress, which have exploded in popularity in France in recent years.
“The harmful effects of ultra-fast fashion on our environment and our economy are well known and documented,” said Mathieu Lefevre, the minister for ecological transition on Aug 28, as details of the measure were published.
Under the legislation, ultra-fast fashion will be determined according to two criteria: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price.
The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both these standards.
In 2026, companies will pay fines such as a €0.50 levy on underwear falling into the ultra-fast fashion category, rising to €2 for T-shirts, €9 for jeans and €12 for a jacket.
The levy could reach up to €19.50 per item by 2030, though the cap remains at 50 per cent of the product’s pre-tax price.
A tool to collect data independently, rather than relying solely on companies’ own declarations, is under development, Lefevre’s office said.
Shein – which on Aug 31 was valued at US$26.3 billion in its long-awaited Hong Kong initial public offering – declined to comment when contacted by AFP.
Temu and AliExpress did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The measure has faced criticism over which retailers it will affect.
In July, Lefevre’s office said the levy would not apply to retailers such as H&M or Zara, prompting some to say that the measure appeared to spare European and French companies.
French officials have made repeated statements that they view Shein, Temu and AliExpress as driving the surge in ultra-fast fashion.
The European Commission had also raised questions over whether the legislation complied with EU law, but Lefevre’s office said those concerns had been “dispelled” and the measure was not expected to be blocked.
China, meanwhile, warned in July of potential retaliation over the French law, slamming the regulation as “discriminatory” and in violation of trade principles.
Imports of small parcels from China into the EU have already fallen by around 30 per cent to 40 per cent since a separate €3 EU levy on such shipments came into force on July 1, according to the French government. AFP

Ukrainians turn anger on Kiev for storing explosives near their homes

Ukrainians turn anger on Kiev for storing explosives near their homes
Residents of the Kiev suburb of Milaya have accused Ukrainian officials of placing an ammunition depot dangerously close to civilian homes, according to interviews published by The Guardian on Monday.
The military storage site was hit last week during a Russian barrage. The Russian Defense Ministry said the attack targeted a warehouse complex storing components for Ukrainian long-range kamikaze drones used in strikes on logistics and e-commerce facilities in Russia.
Secondary explosions continued for hours after the strike, scattering stored military ordnance around homes just hundreds of meters from the depot, local residents told the British newspaper.
“Those who set up the depot here are to blame. There are people here, this is a village. You can’t keep something like that here,” Vera, 65, reportedly said.
She and her son Sergey spent hours sheltering in a small bunker beside their home as dozens of secondary explosions rocked the area.
“I thought it was humanitarian aid that was stored there,” Sergey told the newspaper.
The incident killed at least 38 people and damaged more than 200 private homes and 14 apartment buildings, the Kiev military administration said on Sunday. Thirty of those killed were residents of a care home located close to the ammunition depot, according to The Guardian.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky said an investigation had been launched into the “terrible negligence” that allowed munitions to be stored so close to civilians.
“Another such crime – after what happened in Vishnevoe – is absolutely unacceptable,” he wrote on X on Saturday.
A Russian strike on an ammunition depot in the Kiev suburb of Vishnevoe on July 6 also triggered massive secondary explosions, damaging hundreds of civilian buildings and causing civilian casualties. Following that incident, Zelensky and other senior Ukrainian officials vowed to prevent munitions from being stored near residential areas.
Storing ammunition near civilian housing could contravene international humanitarian law. Under Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, parties to a conflict must, “to the maximum extent feasible,” avoid locating military objectives within or near densely populated areas.

How Great Power Rivalry Is Fracturing the Pacific Islands Forum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:25:00 UTC
05:25:00 KST

The 55th Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Leaders’ Meeting opened on August 31 under a banner of unity, but it can’t escape the reality that outside powers are competing for influence in the Pacific. The question now facing the PIF is whether the forum’s consensus model, once a safeguard for small-state sovereignty, has become the very mechanism through which that influence reshapes regional outcomes.
The official theme of this year’s PIF Leaders’ Meeting, held in Palau, is B.E.L.A.U., or Building Economies, Life, Action, Unity, an acronym that doubles as a tribute to the host nation’s indigenous name. It was meant to signal collective resolve. Instead, the gathering has been defined by conspicuous absences and blocked consensus. Given the return of Taiwan as a development partner after last year’s exclusion, some see this year’s PIF as proof of Beijing’s growing capacity to paralyze the region’s most important multilateral institution from within.
At least five Pacific leaders chose not to attend. The leaders of Kiribati, Samoa, and Vanuatu dispatched deputies, while Fiji’s Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka stayed home to manage domestic affairs. The most dramatic absence was that of Solomon Islands’ Prime Minister Matthew Wale, who landed in Palau only to leave hours later after a no-confidence motion was filed against him back in Honiara. Wale had served as prime minister for barely three months and as outgoing PIF chair, was meant to hand the gavel to Palau’s President Surangel Whipps Jr. Instead, he left Foreign Minister Rick Hou to represent his country at the summit.
Kiribati’s case is particularly revealing. President Taneti Maamau dispatched not a cabinet minister but David Teaabo, his director of foreign service and a former ambassador to China. In an organization where decisions require consensus at the level of heads of state, sending a lower-ranking delegate who cannot commit to communique language with full authority is itself a political statement.
Kiribati’s posture becomes clearer against the backdrop of the missile crisis that preceded the summit. On July 6, China conducted a submarine-launched ballistic missile test in the Pacific, firing what Taiwan identified as a JL-2 from the South China Sea. The missile, carrying a dummy warhead, transited the exclusive economic zones of the Federated States of Micronesia, Naoero (formerly Nauru), and Kiribati before landing near Tuvalu’s maritime boundary. Beijing provided only a few hours’ notice to the affected Pacific Island nations.
The reaction was swift – at least from those countries that did respond. Papua New Guinea’s Prime Minister James Marape invoked the region’s traumatic history of nuclear testing, insisting that Pacific nations “do not want history repeated.” Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called the test “provocative” and “destabilizing.” Yet when Pacific foreign ministers gathered in Fiji in early August, Kiribati and Naoero blocked the consensus needed to issue a joint condemnation.
The PIF has historically operated on the principle of unanimity, a practice rooted in what Pacific leaders call the “Pacific Way,” designed to ensure that no island nation, however small, could be overruled by its larger neighbors. But the model assumed that external pressures would remain at the margins of PIF deliberations. When a member state with deep ties to the power responsible for a security event deploys its consensus rights to shield that power from collective criticism, the model risks becoming a means of undermining collective action.
New Zealand’s Foreign Minister Winston Peters made the frustration explicit, noting that two countries “were seeking to use the need for consensus as a veto provision.” Peters said that he had “made it very clear that we didn’t think outsiders should be telling insiders” what positions to take.
Kiribati’s alignment with Beijing extends beyond the blocking of a PIF statement. In late August, its parliament passed the first reading of a constitutional amendment that would restrict diplomatic recognition to states holding U.N. membership or permanent observer status, effectively locking future governments into recognizing Beijing. Graeme Smith of the Australian National University characterized the move as “almost entirely about sending a message to Beijing.”
With that in mind, Taiwan’s return to the PIF may also have contributed to Kiribati’s lack of top-level representation.
Last year, when the Solomon Islands hosted the 54th PIF Leaders’ Meeting, all external partners were excluded. The stated reason was a review of partnership arrangements, but the practical effect was to remove Taiwan from a gathering it had attended as a development partner since 1992. This year, with Palau – which has official diplomatic ties with Taiwan – as host, the dynamics reversed.
Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung arrived in Koror leading a delegation that included representatives from energy, technology, construction, and agriculture, and he met with Whipps, Palau’s president, to strengthen bilateral ties before participating in the Taiwan/Republic of China-Forum Countries Dialogue.
Only three PIF members still maintain formal ties with Taipei, but Taiwan’s development programs extend well beyond those allies. Just in July 2026, Taiwan donated $2 million to the Forum Secretariat and in 2025 it pledged $3 million to the Pacific Resilience Facility.
Beijing, however, doesn’t take kindly to Taiwan’s inclusion in any form. China’s special envoy Qian Bo confronted Whipps directly at the Forum Troika meeting in Fiji, demanding Taiwan’s exclusion and warning that Beijing would “have to retaliate.” He dismissed Palau as “a small country.” Whipps was unfazed: “It doesn’t matter. We’re a country.” He later characterized Qian’s conduct as inappropriate, remarking that “if you want somebody to love you, usually you come with chocolates and nice cards.”
China made good on Qian’s threat on August 19, when Beijing’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism issued a travel advisory for Palau, warning of alleged theft and dangerous marine conditions and portraying one of the Pacific’s safest destinations as a place to avoid. The U.S. Embassy rejected the advisory, stating that “the United States opposes any attempts by China to weaponize tourism to coerce Palau.”
Tourism accounts for roughly 40 percent of Palau’s gross domestic product, and Beijing has used this lever before. After Palau refused to break ties with Taiwan, China banned package tours in 2017 and visitor numbers collapsed, but the country absorbed the shock and the weapon’s effectiveness has diminished with repeated use.
Whipps has been characteristically blunt about the situation “China continues to try to influence us, whether its threatening us with weaponizing tourism or attacking us personally,” he told reporters. “We’ve made it very clear from the beginning [that] nobody is going to tell us who our friends can be.”
Palau, with a population of roughly 18,000, has held its ground on Taiwan. Other Pacific Island states haven’t. Solomon Islands switched recognition to Beijing in 2019; Kiribati followed within weeks. Naoero switched in January 2024. Taiwan’s Pacific footprint has halved, going from six diplomatic partners in 2019 to just three today: the Marshall Islands, Palau, and Tuvalu.
The PIF Leaders’ Meeting, of course, is about much more than Taiwan, or even China. The summit’s agenda includes a climate declaration ahead of COP31 and a new maritime anti-smuggling initiative called Waqa Moana. The Pacific Resilience Facility, with $173 million in pledges toward a $500 million target, represents a genuine institutional innovation as a Pacific-owned climate finance mechanism.
But the credibility of a regional body rests on its capacity to address threats as well as opportunities. A forum that can mobilize around climate finance but cannot issue a statement when a nuclear-armed power tests a ballistic missile in its own members’ waters with barely any warning faces a fundamental question about what regional solidarity actually means.
The empty chairs in Palau are symptoms of a regional order under pressure, one in which the line between domestic sovereignty and external manipulation grows harder to draw with each passing year.

Trump strikes new drug pricing deals with nine midsized drugmakers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:20:24 UTC
05:20:24 KST

President Donald Trump on Monday said he struck new drug pricing deals with nine drugmakers to voluntarily sell their medications for less, building on his push to link the nation's pharmaceutical prices to cheaper ones abroad.
The drugmakers signing the new deals are Alcon, Astellas Pharma, BeOne Medicines, BridgeBio, CSL, Kyowa Kirin, Sun Pharma, Teva Pharmaceuticals and UCB, according to the White House. Shares of most of those companies closed relatively flat on Monday, while Teva and BeOne fell around 1%.
Under the new deals, the nine companies agreed to provide discounts on outpatient drugs to every state Medicaid program so that prices states pay align with what companies charge in foreign countries. The agreements impact drugs that treat several chronic and rare diseases, such as hemophilia, liver disease, skin conditions and certain forms of cancer.
The companies committed to invest at least $19.6 billion collectively in U.S. manufacturing in the near term, according to the White House.
Astellas, Sun Pharma, Teva and UCB also agreed to donate active pharmaceutical ingredients for key products to the federal government's strategic reserve of those ingredients, which aims to reduce reliance on foreign supply and ensure the U.S. is prepared in the event of an emergency. For example, UCB will contribute 163 tons of levetiracetam, an anticonvulsant used to control and prevent certain types of seizures.
The new agreements bring the Trump administration's total number of drug pricing deals to 26 companies, which the president said represents 90% of the domestic pharmaceutical market. He said the other 10% of the industry is "also coming in" and "have no choice."
Over the past year, the Trump administration reached drug pricing deals with 17 other pharmaceutical companies, including Pfizer, Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk, as part of its "most favored nation" policy. Trump signed an executive order in May 2025 to revive that policy, calling for prices to be increased outside of the U.S. and to "end global freeloading."
The deals add to the White House's efforts to spotlight healthcare affordability ahead of the midterm elections.
The "most favored nation" deals that have been signed with the Trump administration have already impacted the commercial strategies, bottom lines and manufacturing pipelines of major pharmaceutical companies.
To insulate themselves from future tariff threats, drugmakers are spending billions of dollars to bring manufacturing capabilities back to the U.S. Companies are also drastically expanding direct-to-consumer channels for their products, including by offering their medicines on the president's TrumpRx portal. Lower prices in the U.S. are weighing on bottom lines, with manufacturers like Novo Nordisk saying that it will take time for prescription volumes to offset the revenue dip.
U.S. prescription drug prices on average are nearly three times higher than they are overseas, according to a 2024 study by Rand Corp. Prices for branded drugs were more than four times higher, the report found.
The trade association PhRMA, which represents many major pharma companies, has previously said that most-favored nation pricing isn't the best way to lower drug costs for Americans and instead blamed pharmacy benefit managers for the price disparity.
The U.S. is the single most important market for many drugmakers, regardless of their home country. Despite being based across the Atlantic, European pharma companies are heavily exposed to the U.S. market, with half of the 10 largest companies on the continent generating a majority of their sales in the U.S.

Russian War Criminal Yan Petrovsky Gets 12-Year Prison Term — Previously Given Life Sentence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:17:10 UTC
05:17:10 KST

The Helsinki Court of Appeals has handed down a ruling in the war crimes case involving Russian national Yan Petrovsky, also known as Vojislav Torden.
This was reported by YLE.
The court sentenced Petrovsky to 12.5 years in prison for three war crimes, although he had previously faced a life sentence.
In March of last year, the Helsinki District Court sentenced the Russian man to life in prison for four war crimes committed in 2014 during an ambush in eastern Ukraine. According to the court, the most serious of these was the murder of a Ukrainian soldier.
In the appeals court, Petrovsky demanded that the charges be dismissed or, at the very least, that his sentence be reduced. Meanwhile, the prosecutor demanded that the Russian be convicted on five counts.
The Court of Appeals concluded that Petrovsky was not liable as a leader for organizing the ambush, which was carried out on September 5, 2014, using a Ukrainian flag.
The ambush against the Aidar battalion in the Luhansk region resulted in the deaths of 22 Ukrainian soldiers and injuries to four others. The Court of Appeals determined that at least four of the deceased had sustained injuries during the attack.
The court recognized that Petrovsky served as deputy commander of the Rusich group. In addition to the commander and his deputy, at least two other members of the group participated in the ambush.
The Russian national denied his role in the group and his participation in the ambush. At the same time, the court established that Petrovsky fired a light machine gun at Ukrainian servicemen, which was classified as a war crime.
However, according to the appeals court, there was insufficient evidence in the case to prove that Petrovsky himself or the two other members of the Rusich group fired at the wounded Ukrainian servicemen.
The appellate court also determined that Petrovsky, as a leader, is not liable for the shooting at wounded Ukrainian servicemen and therefore dismissed the charges on this count.
At the same time, the court recognized that, by participating in joint military operations with others, Petrovsky bears partial responsibility for the killing and wounding of Ukrainian servicemen.
Furthermore, the court ruled that the Russian did not commit a war crime by carving the Rusich group’s symbol into the cheek of a Ukrainian serviceman.
In the court’s view, the wound was superficial, did not cause bleeding, and the damage to the cheek was temporary. Therefore, these actions “did not cause severe physical or mental suffering, which is necessary for classification as a war crime.”
The Court of Appeals also ordered Petrovsky to pay compensation to the soldiers wounded during the ambush and to the relatives of those killed.
Petrovsky was detained in August 2023.

Supreme Court, in 5-4 vote, rules for Trump on new ballroom, dismissing challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:12:17 UTC
05:12:17 KST

Supreme Court, in 5-4 vote, clears way for Trump’s new ballroom
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Supreme Court, 5-4, clears way for Trump to finish a privately funded $400-million White House ballroom, overturning lower-court rulings that said he needed congressional approval.
- Conservative majority tossed the National Trust for Historic Preservation’s lawsuit on standing grounds, saying preservationists weren’t personally harmed.
- In a dissent, Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. said the construction project was ‘likely unlawful’ and should not be allowed to continue.
WASHINGTON — A divided Supreme Court has cleared the way for President Trump to finish building his new White House ballroom with mostly private money and without approval from Congress.
By a 5-4 vote, the justices granted an emergency appeal from Trump and his lawyers on Monday, setting aside a judge’s order that would stop the construction.
But Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. dissented, along with the court’s three liberals.
Roberts said the construction project was “likely unlawful” and should not be allowed to continue.
“The White House is not just any building ... when it comes to historic preservation,” Roberts wrote. “Winston Churchill once remarked that ‘[w]e shape our buildings, and afterwards our buildings shape us.’ All the more reason to ensure that those responsible follow the rules in deciding what to tear down and what to build up at the People’s House.”
The outcome turned on the standing of the plaintiffs, the National Trust for Historic Preservation and its members.
The conservative majority pointed to Alison Hoagland, one of its members, who said she lives in Washington, walks by the White House about once a month and said she found the “scale,” “height” and “massing” of the huge ballroom to be distasteful.
“This court has not found standing in circumstances like these before. To the contrary, we have repeatedly held that mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury,” the unsigned order said.
Trump has responded to growing legal and political obstacles to his ballroom, arch and other projects by attempting to force approvals through faster than opponents can challenge them.
It is a major victory for Trump, whose ballroom project has become a signature effort of his second term and a political lightning rod in Washington, where Republicans have refused to fund it with public money.
Trump celebrated the victory with a post on social media, declaring the venue would now be built “without any further contingency, doubt, or threat.”
“We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C.,” Trump wrote. “When completed in the Summer of 2028, the magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex will be something that the entire Country is very proud of.”
The massive new structure, set to dwarf the historic White House mansion, is the president’s singular vision — one of a string of aesthetic projects Trump has pursued in a feverish effort to cement his legacy by putting his personal stamp on the nation’s capital.
But preservationists and architects have criticized the proposed ballroom as a garish, rushed project that ignored the input of experts. The president has personally overruled his own chosen architects after being told the building would overwhelm the executive complex.
Democrats have seized on the president’s fixation on the ballroom as a symbol of vanity and detachment from the concerns of everyday Americans heading into November’s midterm elections.
According to recent polls, a bipartisan majority of voters disapprove of the president’s handling of the economy and say the country is facing an affordability crisis. The ballroom is projected to cost more than $400 million, excluding the undisclosed cost of underground security upgrades.
Trump’s three appointees — Justices Neil M. Gorsuch, Brett M. Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — joined conservative Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel A. Alito in an unsigned opinion ruling for the president.
The conservative majority also said Trump and his appointees had stressed the new ballroom was needed for national security and said the lower courts judges should not have interfered.
California officials stressed that the court’s ruling does not allow final implementation of the new rules requested by Trump.
Administration officials have argued that an underground “integrated military complex” was the heart of the project and that the ballroom would merely be sit top of the facility “vitally required by national security.”
The decision is not a final ruling, but it gives a green light to Trump’s go-it-alone approach, which is in keeping with his history as a hotel builder.
He believed the White House needed a grand ballroom that could seat hundreds of dignitaries. Acting on his own, he ordered the East Wing torn down in October to make room of his larger ballroom.
He also said most of the project would be paid for by private donations.
But the Constitution gave Congress the power to manage property belonging to the United States. A 1912 law says new buildings “shall not erected ... on public grounds within the District of Columbia without express authority of Congress.”
Trump chose to ignore the law and did not seek approval from Congress, which is led by Republicans.
The Republican president’s lawyers had asked the justices to reconsider their refusal to hear his appeal. The court denied Trump’s petition along with several others.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued in December, contending Trump was a “temporary tenant, not the owner” of the White House.
U.S. District Judge Richard Leon ruled Trump had no authority to build a ballroom on the White House grounds without the approval of Congress, and he ordered a halt to the above-ground construction.
The District of Columbia Circuit Court affirmed his decision by a 2-1 vote.
“Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House — the People’s House — to fit a particular President’s desires,” wrote Judge Patricia Millett for the appeals court.
Trump’s lawyers sent a fast-track appeal to the Supreme Court on Aug. 14.
The court’s majority allowed Trump to fend off the legal challenge by concluding the historic preservationists could not show they were harmed by the huge new ballroom.

Computers once threatened to take over jobs. Is history repeating with AI?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:08:42 UTC
05:08:42 KST

Sixty years ago, 'metal boxes' threatened to take over jobs. Now AI is
In March 1968, in a rich, British accent typical of Australian news reporters of the time, Four Corners journalist Jim Downes asked the country: "When this circuit learns your job, what are you going to do?"
By "circuit", Mr Downes was referring to the computer — a technological innovation at once revered and feared by a 1960s Australian society already living through massive social, political and cultural change.
Mr Downes, a brilliant wordsmith, described computers as "metal boxes of salmon-pink, beige or deep blue, trimmed in stainless steel or aluminium", which "promise or threaten the mind with what the industrial revolution did to the muscles".
"Computers fracture time into billions of a second — nanoseconds — the time taken for a calculation," he explained, over slightly grainy black-and-white video of men dressed in white lab coats working in rooms filled with bulky machinery and flashing buttons.
"The human operator is one bottle-neck, another is translation of the machine's work into language we can understand.
"To a computer, a man is a number, a pattern of holes in a punch card, a recorded symbol on magnetic tape or disk."
The Four Corners report, unearthed from the ABC's vast digitised archive, aired at a tipping point in the computer's rapid evolution in Australia.
There were fewer than 600 computers in the country at the time, but already the machines had advanced from huge contraptions built in universities, to, as Mr Downes put it, "new models, many times smaller, many times cheaper, and a thousand times more efficient".
"The disciples of the computer can see the prospect that a man's rise to the top may depend on his ability to commune with a machine, to turn computer power to personal power, and not the meek, but the systems analyst shall inherit the earth," he stated.
"With near religious fervour, some promote their machines as the cure for the world's ills, economic liberator of the impoverished, even bringer of international peace.
"But they don't say how."
Almost six decades later, a similar conversation is being had about the computer's protégé, artificial intelligence.
Inquiries — at both a state and federal level — are underway, new laws have been introduced, and unions keep a watchful gaze, as the AI horse bolts through Australian workplaces and homes, influencing the way people think, learn and go about their everyday lives.
"The use of artificial intelligence is an exciting opportunity to advance the cause of humanity," South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas said last month, when announcing a royal commission into the technology.
"It is also true that, unchecked, artificial intelligence does represent a material risk to the way our society operates and a risk to the future of work if not thought through carefully."
Disrupting the workforce
Months before Four Corners aired its report, South Australian high school students started to learn how to use computers.
The lessons were an experiment orchestrated by University of Adelaide professor John Ovenstone, a leading computer scientist of his time.
Asked by Mr Downes why he felt it necessary to teach teenagers computing, Mr Ovenstone replied: "If we don't educate our people so that they can use computers properly, our standards of living will have to drop".
"We're faced with a situation and there's no way out of it."
While Mr Ovenstone considered the rise of the computer as an inevitability that would ultimately benefit humanity, others interviewed by Four Corners in 1968 were more cautious.
Computing lecturer Frank Linton-Simpkins predicted computers could wipe out entire professions.
"Most clerk officers are practically unskilled labourers who can read and write and this is about it," he (rather bluntly) said.
"Their jobs are in danger and they have about five years to run at the most."
Council of Salaried and Professional Associations Victorian secretary John Sanders was equally concerned about workforce disruption.
"In certain overseas countries and the United States for instance, it's been formulated that possibly by the year 1980, only 10 per cent of the present workforce would be required to maintain the output of goods and services for the community," he said.
"But, in a developing country like Australia, this is much further ahead I would say."
Leading computer scientist Trevor Pearcey offered (arguably) the most accurate prediction.
"Although some people will become redundant, I feel pretty certain that there will always be new things they can do, even if it means a certain amount of re-training," he said.
"I think the real future lies not so much in the application of computers to automation of industry, but of computers being applied to what are currently semi-intelligent functions of the human brain."
'The conversation seems to be repeating itself'
Watching the Four Corners report in the present day, University of New South Wales AI Institute chief scientist Toby Walsh was struck by how similar the debate was to today's discussion on artificial intelligence.
"Strangely enough, what they [the people interviewed by Four Corners] were saying seems very topical for today as much as it was back then," Professor Walsh said.
"The conversation seems to be repeating itself."
Public anxiety about AI and employment has reached a crescendo in recent times.
Earlier this year, thousands of Australian tech workers were laid off in cuts linked to the technology.
But a first-of-its-kind report from the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations found Australia's job market remains strong, despite some early signs of weakening around jobs predicted to be most affected by AI, such as telemarketers.
Asked what Australians could learn from past debates on how new technologies could impact the workforce, Professor Walsh replied: "I think the heartening news is that it often takes longer for a technology to have the impact it can because it has to deal with human institutions".
"Many of the changes that they were talking about in that Four Corners piece back in 1968 took a bit longer to happen than I think the experts were predicting back then," he said.
"I suspect the same will be true this time, in that we might have technologies like artificial intelligence that could be quickly used and quickly replacing people, but it will actually take longer than we expect."
University of Melbourne computer science Justin Zobel said there was "no doubt" that the way in which people work would change with the rise of AI, but there was also "no line of sight of what the new possibilities are".
"There were very serious reports three years ago now, characterising how a whole range of professions were going to be washed away or diminished by use of AI and how quickly that was going to happen," Professor Zobel said.
"That report has largely has not borne out, but this sense, I think for the first time, that difficult knowledge work could be done by a machine, has really set out the kinds of things that might change."
Professor Zobel said the "big lesson" to be taken from earlier debates was an understanding of the speed at which technology could result in workplace changes.
"The internet really took a long time to arrive — we connected in 1989 and broadband didn't become widespread until the late-2000s, nearly 20 years later," he said.
"But a really sudden change could be tremendously disruptive."
In 2026, the time could be overdue for Australia to consider, as a national question, when AI learns your job, what are you going to do?

Living in a democracy is linked to better mental health through personal autonomy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:00:26 UTC
05:00:26 KST

Living in a democracy is linked to better mental health, and recent research reveals this happens primarily when citizens feel a genuine sense of personal freedom. The research suggests that the subjective experience of democratic governance, rather than official institutional structures alone, shapes human well-being by fulfilling a basic psychological need for autonomy. These findings were published in the journal Political Psychology.
Researchers wanted to understand the psychological mechanisms connecting political systems to mental health. They drew upon Self-Determination Theory, a framework proposing that all humans share fundamental psychological needs required for growth and well-being. One of these primary needs is autonomy, which is defined as feeling that one’s actions are voluntary, authentic, and free from external coercion. Prior investigations into this psychological framework focused largely on immediate environments like schools, workplaces, and families.
Societal structures like governments can also act as broad environments that either support or suppress these basic human needs. Economists and social theorists have proposed that expanding real freedoms, such as political voice and civil rights, enhances a person’s capability to pursue a fulfilling life. Standardized indices can measure a country’s institutional democracy, tracking metrics like civil liberties and free elections. However, official records might not perfectly match how citizens actually experience their political reality on a daily basis.
Joachim Waterschoot, a researcher at Ghent University, and Richard M. Ryan, a psychologist at the Australian Catholic University, led an effort to untangle these objective and subjective layers. They wanted to see if the psychological benefits of living in a democracy depend on a person’s subjective interpretation of their political environment. The researchers designed a multi-step analysis spanning one preliminary evaluation and three large cross-national datasets.
Before analyzing the large global datasets, the researchers conducted a preliminary study to validate their measurement tools. They surveyed 535 English-speaking adults in the United States. The goal was to ensure that the brief, one- or two-question surveys used in international databases accurately reflected complex psychological concepts.
The researchers found that the short survey questions closely matched the results of comprehensive, standardized psychological evaluations. In this initial phase, they also discovered that specific democratic principles related differently to mental health. Perceptions of strong civil rights and opportunities for political participation were the strongest predictors of personal autonomy and well-being. This early step confirmed that their chosen variables were reliable for the larger global analysis.
In the first main analysis, the researchers examined data from a large survey of 54,673 individuals across 28 European countries. They analyzed responses regarding how democratic participants perceived their country to be, alongside measures of their personal autonomy. The researchers also tracked overall happiness and life satisfaction, as well as symptoms of psychological distress, such as anxiety and depression. To isolate the effects of political perception, they controlled for demographic factors like age, gender, and household income.
Waterschoot and Ryan found that people who perceived their country as highly democratic reported better mental health and fewer psychological issues. This relationship was largely explained by higher reported levels of autonomy. The perception of living in a democratic society was consistently tied to people feeling they had a voice and choice in their lives. This enhanced sense of personal freedom then correlated with greater overall happiness and meaning in life across all 28 countries.
The second analysis shifted focus to compare different nations rather than just individuals. The researchers used a different large dataset encompassing 36,831 individuals across 33 countries. In this phase, they incorporated an objective measurement called the Democracy Index. The Democracy Index is a standardized score created by external experts that evaluates a country’s electoral process, civil liberties, functioning of government, and political culture.
The researchers found that a country’s objective Democracy Index score strongly predicted how democratic its citizens felt their society was. This subjective perception then linked to higher autonomy and well-being. The objective institutional score alone did not capture the full picture of a population’s mental health. The official index scores only related to personal well-being when citizens actually perceived their government as legitimately democratic and functioning well.
For the final analysis, the researchers expanded their scope to a global level and observed changes over time. They examined data from 111,909 people across 92 countries on six continents. This data spanned multiple survey waves collected between 2005 and 2022. By looking at information from different time periods, the researchers could track whether shifts in a nation’s objective democratic conditions corresponded to shifts in the population’s mental health.
The results mirrored the previous analyses on a global scale. As a country’s objective democratic conditions improved over time, citizens reported stronger perceptions of democratic functioning. These heightened perceptions corresponded to increases in autonomy, which again correlated with gains in happiness, general health, and life satisfaction. The researchers observed that while the structural conditions of a nation matter, the subjective experience of those conditions most directly supports a person’s psychological needs.
The researchers noted several caveats regarding their findings. These studies relied heavily on observational survey data, meaning the results do not definitively prove that democratic perceptions cause changes in well-being. The relationship might work in both directions over time. Societies composed of individuals who already feel high levels of personal autonomy might be more likely to establish and maintain democratic systems. A lack of autonomy might equally breed support for authoritarian regimes or restrictive political movements.
Another limitation involves the way some psychological concepts were measured in the international surveys. The available datasets often relied on single-question measures to assess complex feelings of autonomy and perceived democracy. Future investigations will need to use more robust, multi-item psychological surveys to capture the complete scope of human autonomy. The current studies also did not measure autonomy frustration, which is the active feeling of being controlled or coerced by outside forces.
Future research could examine how political systems affect other basic psychological needs. Aside from autonomy, people also require a sense of competence and a need to feel connected to others. Democratic environments might support these needs by fostering social trust and allowing citizens to feel capable of influencing societal outcomes. Evaluating how democratic backsliding or national crises impact these psychological metrics remains an open question for future analysis.
The study, “The impact of democracy on people’s well-being through enhanced autonomy: Findings from three cross-national surveys,” was authored by Joachim Waterschoot and Richard M. Ryan.

Migraine drugs are getting more precise. Choosing the right one is still tricky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

Migraine drugs are getting more precise. Choosing the right one is still tricky
New guidelines give patients and doctors more options for migraine prevention
For the first time in 14 years, doctors have updated guidelines for preventing migraine attacks.
The new recommendations from the American Academy of Neurology and American Headache Society, published August 31 in Neurology, incorporate evidence on treatments that weren’t available when the guidelines were last updated. That includes drugs that target calcitonin gene-related peptide, or CGRP. These drugs, like Aimovig and Ajovy, have been a game changer for some, reducing migraines in up to 70 percent of the people who take them.
Some come in tablet form, while others are injected under the skin or infused into a vein. Because the previous guidelines were written before these drugs were developed, they had recommended beta-blockers, like Propranolol and Metoprolol, as well as certain antiseizure medications for migraine prevention. These drugs also appear in the updated guidelines as options for patients who want a medication with a longer track record or a lower cost than CGRP-targeted drugs.
The latest guidelines recommend offering preventive treatment to people with frequent migraine attacks or whose migraine significantly interferes with work or daily activities; that’s roughly 8 million adults in the United States. The previous guidelines did not include explicit criteria for patients eligible for preventive treatment.
“My hope is that this guideline helps clinicians feel more comfortable prescribing preventive treatments for people with migraine,” Rebecca Burch, a headache medicine specialist at the University of Vermont Medical Center in Burlington, said during an Aug. 26 news briefing.
Science News spoke with Amaal Starling, a neurologist specializing in headache at the Mayo Clinic in Phoenix, about the advances reshaping migraine prevention and the challenges that remain. Starling was not involved in creating the guideline updates. This conversation has been edited for clarity and length.
SN: What’s the biggest change in migraine treatment since the last guidelines came out in 2012?
Starling: The biggest scientific shift in how we treat migraine now compared to five to 10 years ago is specifically with migraine prevention. The goal of migraine prevention is to reduce the frequency and severity of migraine attacks.
For the first time, we have disease-specific, mechanism-based, targeted treatment options for migraine prevention, and these are the CGRP-targeted treatment options. CGRP is a protein that is involved in migraine. Levels of CGRP rise during a migraine attack and fall when a migraine attack has been well-treated or resolved. Because these medications are disease-specific, mechanism-based and targeted, they have high rates of efficacy and high rates of tolerability meaning very minimal side effects. Patients are able to stay on these medications for longer periods of time.
All these factors have led to a paradigm shift in prioritizing these medications when medically appropriate. In fact, the American Headache Society has a position statement that indicates that CGRP-targeted treatment options for the prevention of migraine should be considered as first-line treatment options for patients living with migraine.
SN: What guides how you decide on a preventive treatment?
Starling: Currently, we will look at patient preference on the delivery of the medication and their comorbidities. When patients ask me what medication is best for them, I will often say, “the one that you will take.” If the patient has difficulty taking a daily pill or they have a fear of needles, I will try to identify a treatment option that will suit the patient’s preferences to increase adherence and persistence of a treatment regimen.
In addition, many patients with migraine have comorbidities, like anxiety, depression, insomnia, obesity, hypertension or other conditions. There are medications that could be beneficial not only for migraine prevention but also for one of those comorbidities. There are multiple factors in evidence-based guidelines, individual medical history and patient preferences that we take into consideration when identifying the optimal treatment regimen for an individual patient.
SN: If newer drugs target migraine biology more precisely, why can’t doctors yet predict which treatment will work best for a particular patient?
Starling: Migraine is a genetic neurologic disease. However, the most common type of migraine is not based off a single mutation but rather multiple genetic variants that have led to vulnerability of developing migraine disease and migraine attacks. To date, there have been over 100 different genes and over 200 different genetic variants or mutations that have been identified as potentially leading to vulnerability to migraine.
Migraine is not a one-size-fits-all disease, and it cannot be treated with a one-size-fits-all treatment because of this genetic and clinical heterogeneity. We hope that soon we will be able to practice individualized, personalized medicine, where based on biomarkers like lab work or imaging or clinical characteristics, we can predict whose migraine disease may benefit from one medication versus another.
SN: What are researchers learning from people who don’t respond to CGRP-targeting drugs?
Starling: We know that CGRP is one of the mediators of migraine, however, we also know that there are multiple other mediators and mechanisms that may be involved and may vary from one person to another.
If there is an individual or patient who does not respond to CGRP targeted therapies, it tells me that they may not have as much of CGRP-related pathophysiology in their underlying migraine disease. This is why we continue to investigate other novel mediators of migraine including another pain signaling neuropathic tied called pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide, or PACAP, which is currently undergoing clinical trials. In addition, there are many other novel targets that are currently under investigation for the treatment of migraine.
SN: Are there any developments coming down the pike that excite you?
Starling: What excites me most isn’t one single drug that is in the pipeline, but rather the fact that the paradigm has shifted from nonspecific preventive therapies to disease-specific, mechanism-based, targeted preventive treatment options, that have improved efficacy, better tolerability, decreased disability and improved patient-reported outcomes.
