Asus ProArt 27 QD-OLED (PA279cdv) Review: HDR for All
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:48:26 UTC
04:48:26 KST

I wouldn’t call it cheap, but this monitor from Asus brings proper HDR-capable video editing to creators who couldn’t previously afford an OLED display.
Attractive, thin design. Stand comes with lots of adjustability. Forward-facing buttons are convenient. Solid HDR performance for the price. 120-Hz refresh rate is a nice bonus. Great port selection.
TIRED
Not very bright in SDR. Some quirks when connected to macOS.
OLED is common in gaming monitors these days. But for those of us who don’t need gaming gear? Well, home-office and content-creation monitors have been much slower to adopt the exciting and more capable display technology. That’s unfortunate because having an OLED monitor is every bit as useful as having an OLED TV if you ever use your monitor for entertainment purposes. OLED displays are also helpful for photo editors, videographers, game developers, and other creators who might want to work in high dynamic range (HDR) for a broader range of brightness, contrast, and color.
The PA279CDV is Asus’ attempt to bring that OLED goodness to a wider demographic, at a retail price of $699, which is competitive for the technology. This monitor makes a few compromises to hit that price, but it does so without losing what makes owning a high-end OLED display feel unique.
Unique, Ergonomic, and Easy to Use
Asus is one of the few manufacturers releasing OLED monitors precisely for this non-gamer demographic, and the PA279CDV is the cheapest it's ever had in its lineup. In fact, the monitor only has one major competitor: the Dell 32 Plus QD-OLED (9/10 WIRED Recommends). The main difference between the two is the size. Dell’s model is 31.6 inches, compared to Asus’ 27 inches. Being larger gives you more screen to work with, but it's also less sharp and takes up more desk space. The Samsung 32-inch Smart Monitor M90SF (7/10 WIRED Recommends) is the only other non-gaming OLED monitor option, but that's far more expensive.
As far as the Asus’ appearance goes, the side bezels are a bit large, and the top and bottom bezels aren’t the same size, which I find visually off-putting. Nicely, though, the amount of adjustability is impressive. This stand can swivel, tilt, rotate into portrait mode, and the height can shift 5 inches. The stand has some very basic built-in cable management, with down-firing ports that help keep cords organized. Also, the flat base doesn't require much space on my desk.
Each of the two back USB-C ports has a specific purpose. One is USB-C 3.2 with DP Alt Mode, which provides 96 watts of power delivery for your laptop. The other is a USB-C 3.2 port for the KVM switch, enabling you to connect two PCs to the monitor and switch between them seamlessly. Fortunately, Asus clearly labels each port, so you know which to use for your intended purpose. The monitor also comes with two USB-A ports for accessories, a headphone jack, HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4, and a DisplayPort Out for daisy-chaining monitors together. This is a solid array of port selection that gives you just about everything you need to use the ProArt PA279cdv as a workstation.
Meanwhile, the controls for the onscreen display and menu are on the right side of the front panel. I tend to prefer just a single joystick for simplicity's sake, but like the other Asus ProArt monitors, this one gives you five control buttons, plus a power button, in addition to a joystick. Once you know how to use it, though, the buttons give you quick access to switching inputs or changing brightness.
There are quite a lot of features to dig through in the menu, including a number of color modes and detailed picture-quality tweaks. There's also a Display Widget app to handle all these settings, available in Windows 11 or macOS.
The monitor includes speakers, but they sound pretty bad, which is unfortunate for a monitor designed at least partially for entertainment purposes. Keep this in mind if you plan to watch a movie on the monitor, since you’ll only want to use the speakers for basic notifications. By contrast, the Dell 32 Plus QD-OLED has a really nice set of speakers.
OLED, Oh My!
Brightness—both measured in standard dynamic range (SDR) and HDR content—is the key feature of an OLED monitor, as it determines how good at HDR the device in question truly is. OLED displays can switch off individual pixels, a capability that provides the absolute blacks this class of display is known for. But if the pixels aren't bright enough, the display still won’t produce a strong HDR performance.
Using an HDR test pattern, I was able to record 1,038 nits in a 1 percent window and 917 nits in a 4 percent window. These strong results deliver a greater sense of visual fidelity when watching movies or playing games than what you’d get with dimmer displays. Compared to the current ultimate HDR monitor, the Apple Studio Display XDR (7/10, WIRED Recommends), though, these results aren’t stunning. On the Apple monitor, I got to 1,905 nits of brightness in a 25 percent window. Even so, comparing these two monitors is hardly fair, given that the Apple costs more than $3,000 and should provide a premium quality to match. I’m providing these results to demonstrate the broad HDR landscape in monitors.
I tested the Asus visuals in a few scenarios, including HDR video test footage, Netflix streaming, and some games. Dark scenes in Cyberpunk 2077 really come to life, aided by the deep blacks and brighter highlights. The effect isn't mind-blowing, but it's definitely noticeable.
In SDR content, though—which is where you’ll spend most of your time—the results are even less stellar. According to my meter, it maxed out in SDR at 240 nits at full-screen brightness. While that's bright enough for most days, if you sit next to a window, you might find yourself wishing for an extra 100 nits. The Dell 32 Plus 4K QD-OLED has the same issue. The good news is that while the PA279CDV has a glossy display, it’s surprisingly good at resisting reflections and glare.
I also tested the color performance, as that's one of the features that Asus claims distinguishes the PA279CDV from its more expensive OLED options, such as the ProArt PA27ucdmr ($1,401). The color gamut was fantastic across the board, meaning the panel is capable of producing great color, covering 91 percent of Adobe RGB and 98 percent in Display P3. When plugged into a Windows machine, the Spyder Pro I used measured excellent color accuracy as well—far beyond what Asus claimed.
However, when plugged into a MacBook Pro, I was unable to get that same color accuracy. For whatever reason, the best I could measure was a Delta-E of around 2.0. That's not terrible, but it's not quite pro-level. Speaking of Mac compatibility, the PA279CDV has a number of features to entice Mac users. Once you install the Display Widget app, it'll match up color temperature with your MacBook and even allow you to control screen brightness from your keyboard. (It can’t control volume, though, which is a miss.) A lot of this is very similar to what BenQ offers in its own Mac-focused line of monitors, such as the BenQ 5K MA270S that I recently tested.
This doesn't solve the problem of scaling. MacOS still doesn't love the 4K resolution, so you'll need to play around with different resolutions and decide which suits your needs best. When you plug it in, it defaults to a 2560 x 1440 resolution in macOS. This doesn’t yield the same sharpness as running a native 1440p on a Windows machine, but it still looks quite sharp. If you upgrade to a 5K monitor, you won't have to deal with this, but those tend to be more expensive and often aren't available in OLED. The other macOS quirk I ran into was that I could only turn on HDR if I changed the refresh rate to 60 Hz.
Despite the macOS hiccups, the 120-Hz refresh rate is a nice touch in the PA279CDV. It's increasingly common in cheaper monitors, even appearing in the Dell 27 Plus 4K, which is often on sale for less than $300. But it nicely matches the refresh rate of the MacBook Pro and gives the screen smoother animation and motion. And while serious gamers will certainly desire a faster display, 120 Hz at least allows games to look fluid at frame rates over 60 frames per second (fps).
Hope for HDR
There's a lot to like about the PA279CDV and very few reasons for frustration. I'm thrilled to see the category of non-OLED gaming monitors grow, especially in the direction of affordability. The vast majority of laptop screens and monitors lack any meaningful HDR support. So, as these HDR-capable monitors become more accessible, the hope is that we'll see more high-quality HDR content available online. Heck, most browsers and streaming services don't even support HDR at this point. The PA279CDV is exactly what we need more of to improve the situation, and the monitor’s strong port selection makes it a solid option for a home-office workstation in its own right.
Luke Larsen is a product writer and reviewer at WIRED, covering laptops, PCs, Macs, monitors, and the wider PC peripheral ecosystem. He’s been reporting on tech for over a decade, previously at Digital Trends as the senior editor in computing, where he spent seven years leading the publication’s daily coverage. ... Read More

The Ukrainian National Guard received its first 10 Protector unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) with financial support from the German government.
The company Ukrainian Armor reported that 100 such UGVs have been contracted for the National Guard.
On Brave1 Market, one such UGV costs nearly UAH 3.9 million.
The first batch was distributed among four National Guard units.
The Protector is designed to perform logistical and evacuation tasks in combat zones.
The system enables the delivery of ammunition, food, fuel and lubricants, engineering equipment, and other supplies, as well as the evacuation of the wounded, thereby reducing risks to personnel.
The Protector has a payload capacity of 1,480 kg — one of the highest figures among modern robotic logistics systems.
This makes it possible to transport significant volumes of essential supplies in a single trip.
In addition, the system is capable of towing a trailer weighing up to 4 metric tons, which further increases the amount of cargo that can be delivered in a single trip.
“Our partners have contracted for 100 of our systems for the National Guard. The automation of logistics allows important tasks to be carried out without unnecessary risk to personnel,” noted the company’s CEO, Vladislav Belbas.
In particular, the system is already in operation with a separate artillery brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine and will be deployed in the Dobropillia sector.
Previously, Ukrainian Armor delivered the Protector to the UGV Training School based at the KILLHOUSE Academy, as well as to soldiers of the 3rd Army Corps.

Markets see Warsh endorsing a rate hike in September. Not everyone is convinced
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:38:38 UTC
04:38:38 KST

Just a few carefully chosen words from Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh convinced markets that he was serious about inflation and ready to recommend an interest rate hike in just a few weeks.
The path in that direction, though, still looks cluttered, with plenty of incentive left to convince Warsh and his fellow central bank policymakers that a move isn't necessary yet.
Following Warsh's keynote speech Friday at the Fed's annual Jackson Hole, Wyoming symposium, markets flipped on rate expectations. Prior, they expected little likelihood of a rate increase until at least December; after that changed to a high probability of one when the Federal Open Market Committee meets in a little more than two weeks.
However, some observers warned that hype for a hike is unjustified.
"It is my belief that we've seen a supply shock, and traditionally you don't raise into a supply shock unless you see second- or third-order effects," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC on Monday in an interview from the G20 summit in Asheville, N.C. "And we are seeing the core inflation has remained very, very restrained."
Warsh, though acknowledging that inflation numbers have been soft lately, said the progress isn't enough and does "not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved."
"We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do," he added.
Switch in expectations
The sum of his remarks caused a sharp repricing in hike probabilities. Odds for a move at the Sept. 15-16 meeting jumped to 66.1% on Monday, nearly double where they were before Warsh spoke, according to the CME Group's FedWatch.
But Warsh has spoken sternly on the Fed's inflation mandate before, if with less direction about what he considers the proper response. At a July news conference, he pledged the Fed "will not waver" in its pursuit of 2% inflation. Yet markets took his commitment as less than full-throated, bidding up Treasury yields and lowering the probability of a hike.
Indeed, the chairman's comments Friday were "relatively uncontroversial and have been restated by Warsh each time he has spoken," Citigroup economist Andrew Hollenhorst wrote in a client note.
Hollenhorst characterized Warsh's comments as more hawkish than usual "but only marginally so" and coming amid economic data that indicates no particular urgent need for tighter monetary policy.
"At the July FOMC meeting there was not a consensus to raise rates," the economist predicted. "Data since that time have shown cooler inflation and softer hiring. There will not be a consensus to hike rates in September. Our expectation for cooler inflation data to continue make rate hikes unlikely this year."
The Fed will have several key data points to consider before its next meeting.
This week will see important jobs reports, with questions mounting over a labor market that has shown three straight weak nonfarm payrolls numbers. The following week, just before the Fed meeting, will see the consumer and producer price indexes, both of which feed into the central bank's primary inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures price index.
The July PCE inflation reading showed the headline rate at 3.7%, with core at 3.3%. A Dallas Fed measure that strips out extremes on either end held at 2.3%, much closer to the Fed's goal.
Jobs in focus
There also will be several housing reports, along with retail sales figures released the day of the Fed rate decision.
Of those, the most important will the employment picture, which could dissuade the Fed from hikes, said David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management. Recent data indicates "the economy doesn't have quite as much momentum as Kevin Warsh suggested in his Jackson Hole speech," Kelly wrote in his weekly market note.
"Given this, markets may have been premature in now assigning a 60% probability to a September rate hike ... While investors should be prepared for possible policy mistakes, there is little in the labor market to suggest inflationary trouble ahead," he added.
Markets, though, showed confidence that the Warsh Fed is ready to move following a July meeting that saw three of 12 FOMC voters supporting a hike.
Bank of America, meanwhile, is holding to its call for three increases ahead, saying Warsh's Jackson Hole speech showed markets "a more credible Fed."
"For us, the key takeaway is that Warsh has raised the bar for standing pat by arguing that the Fed should focus on trends rather than 'isolated data points' and that underlying inflation hasn't 'meaningfully improved,'" Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave said in a note.
"Absent a material downside surprise, the onus is now on Warsh to deliver a [September] hike," he added. "Otherwise, he risks undermining some of the credibility he gained on Friday, in our view."

Kalshi permanently bans George Santos over State of the Union speech bets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:30:42 UTC
04:30:42 KST

Prediction market company Kalshi said on Monday it imposed a penalty of more than $71,000 on former US Congressman George Santos and permanently banned him from its platform for betting on his own attendance at US President Donald Trump's State of the Union address.
Santos, who was expelled from the House of Representatives in 2023, was also fined by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission a month ago for alleged market manipulation over the incident.
Kalshi also said on Monday it was imposing penalties and temporary suspensions on three current and former candidates for political office in Maine, California, and North Carolina who had allegedly bet on their own races.
US regulators previously fined former White House teleprompter operator Gabriel Perez for allegedly wagering on information about Trump's speeches. Attempts to reach Perez on Monday were unsuccessful.
According to Kalshi and the CFTC, Santos made false statements on social media that benefited his wagers and then did not attend the address, earning him nearly $18,000.
Santos 'never intended to manipulate any market'
Joe Murray, a lawyer for Santos, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In July, Murray said Santos denied the CFTC's allegations and settled them only to avoid drawn-out litigation, asserting that Santos never intended to deceive anyone or manipulate any market.
Trump commuted Santos' seven-year prison sentence for fraud and identity theft last year following his guilty plea for inflating fundraising figures and falsifying donor names to secure Republican Party financial support during the 2022 election cycle.
Laurie Buckhout, the current Republican nominee for North Carolina's 1st congressional district, said in an email that wagering on herself had been "a dumb mistake" that she had quickly worked to correct upon learning that it was improper.
Kalshi imposed a fine of about $2,600 and three-year suspension on Buckhout.
Efforts to contact Stephen Cloobeck and Ben Midgley, former candidates for governor in California and Maine, respectively, who were also penalized by Kalshi, were unsuccessful.
The boom in election betting is likely to test the ability of prediction markets such as Kalshi to police insider trading, according to experts and data shared with Reuters. Kalshi and rival Polymarket have said that they are equipped to identify and block suspicious activity and protect market integrity.

New pressure on PM to allow telehealth for voluntary assisted dying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:30:16 UTC
04:30:16 KST

South Australian government defies Albanese, urges change to voluntary assisted dying telehealth laws
In short:
South Australia's Labor government has openly defied the prime minister's position on telehealth in voluntary assisted dying (VAD), calling for urgent change to a federal law.
It comes weeks after the ALP national conference endorsed a motion committing Labor to removing telehealth restrictions, despite Anthony Albanese's own personal opposition.
The state government has called on the Commonwealth to amend the definition of "suicide" in the criminal code to exclude VAD care.
South Australia has become the first state to formally urge the Commonwealth to change a federal law preventing doctors from using telehealth in voluntary assisted dying (VAD), openly defying the prime minister.
In a letter to federal Attorney-General Michelle Rowland, senior ministers in the Malinauskas government have "implored" the Commonwealth to "take immediate action", arguing the restrictions disadvantage terminally ill people in regional, rural and remote Australia.
"I doubt that I will be the only health minister advocating for this change," SA Health Minister Blair Boyer told ABC News.
The SA ministers' letter said a provision in the Commonwealth criminal code was preventing doctors from using telehealth for VAD and forcing patients to travel long distances to attend appointments, with some dying before being able to access the care.
The intervention puts the SA government at odds with Anthony Albanese, who has expressed personal opposition to changing the law, concerned about the risk of coercion and elder abuse if telehealth replaced compulsory face-to-face consultations.
The letter comes just weeks after the ALP national conference endorsed a motion committing Labor to removing telehealth restrictions, despite Ms Rowland — the highest law officer in Australia — voicing strong concerns on the conference floor.
Penned by Mr Boyer and state Attorney-General Kyam Maher, and co-signed by VAD practitioners, clinicians and advocates, the letter calls for the Commonwealth criminal code to be amended so VAD care is not treated as "suicide" under federal law.
Some states and territories permit limited use of telehealth in VAD, but the federal code overrides those provisions by prohibiting the use of a "carriage service" to counsel or promote suicide.
It means doctors risk $220,000 fines and a criminal record for using phone, email or video to discuss the self-administration of VAD medication.
VAD at a glance
Read more
- Each jurisdiction has its own VAD laws, but all require at least some face-to-face consultations as part of the assessment and approval process.
- There are also safeguards, including restrictions on when doctors can provide information about VAD and making it an offence to induce someone to request or access the care.
- Anthony Albanese has argued safeguards could be weakened if more consultations were conducted via telehealth.
"We suggest a targeted amendment to the definition of 'suicide' under the criminal code such that the definition explicitly excludes conduct authorised under a state or territory VAD law," the letter said.
"We now implore the Federal Government to address this issue and amend the criminal code to better reflect contemporary healthcare practice and to reduce unnecessary disparities between jurisdictions."
The move fits a pattern of the Malinauskas government pursuing its own agenda on contentious national policy debates.
In recent years, South Australia has outlawed political donations, established a royal commission into artificial intelligence and spearheaded the development of a teen social media ban, an initiative followed by the federal government.
Mr Boyer predicted other states would soon join the push to change the criminal code, signalling broader pressure could build.
"This is not an attempt to water down safeguards that were put in place. It is simply an attempt to make good on the commitment that was made," he said.
"This is something that should be available to people regardless of where they live."
The federal government recently blocked debate of a VAD telehealth bill pushed by independent MP Kate Chaney, with Health Minister Mark Butler telling parliament he was "not convinced" telehealth was "well suited to VAD right now".
Doctors divided
Views on telehealth in VAD care are also divided within the medical community.
While the Australian Medical Association (AMA) has backed calls to change the federal law, some doctors remain opposed.
Ballarat geriatrician Mark Yates argued the risks of elder abuse and coercion outweighed the benefits of expanding telehealth access.
Professor Yates said data showed rural, regional and remote Australians were accessing VAD at rates proportional to the population, suggesting there was no widespread access problem, and that individual cases of people missing out highlighted broader failures in regional health services.
"I think [those cases] are an argument for jurisdictions to get their acts together and provide better support and services, whether it's wider-based VAD services or better palliative care,"
Professor Yates said telehealth made it harder to detect coercion or abuse and argued the risk was compounded by the small number of doctors providing VAD.
"When we started the VAD debate, the idea was that it would be your friendly GP who's known you for 30 years who would help you with this. That's clearly not the case. There are one or two practitioners that have [overseen] 300 people with VAD in the short time we've had it.
"To appreciate where coercion or abuse sits without being face-to-face, I think is incredibly difficult. That is where the risk lies."

Iraq sentences militia member for kidnapping American journalist, in rare move against Iran proxies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:30:08 UTC
04:30:08 KST

Iraq has sentenced a man to 15 years in prison for kidnapping Shelly Kittelson, an American journalist, in late March.
Kittelson was kidnapped on March 31, released in early April, and targeted by Iranian-backed militias.
She posted on X/Twitter that “Iraq’s Central Criminal Court has sentenced Amir Rahim Jabar Lazim to 15 years in prison under the Anti-terrorism Law after convicting him of being one of several armed men who took me hostage in Baghdad on March 31.”
She added, “I am grateful to the Iraqi judiciary for its attention to my case, as well as to all those who helped get me out alive. And, of course, to those who love Iraq as much as I do and try to build a better future for it. Thank you from the very depths of my being.”
Rudaw Media in Iraq added that “an Iraqi court has sentenced a key suspect to 15 years in prison under the country’s Anti-terrorism Law in connection with the abduction of American journalist Shelly Kittleson in Baghdad earlier this year, a case the US linked to the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah armed group.”
Rare prosecution of Iranian-backed militia member
The development is important because Iraq rarely prosecutes members of the Iranian-backed militias. In the past, members of the militias have sometimes been detained by authorities, but are often released. There is now pressure in Iraq for the government to rein in the militias. The US has encouraged Baghdad to make progress toward disarming the groups.
The militias have been involved in acts of kidnapping and murder for years. In 2020, Dr. Hisham al-Hashimi was assassinated by gunmen outside his home in the Zayouna neighborhood of Baghdad. He was a journalist and security expert.
Kataib Hezbollah was also behind the kidnapping of Princeton researcher Elizabeth Tsurkov in March 2023. She was released in September 2025.
According to Rudaw, “The Central Criminal Court in Baghdad on Sunday sentenced ‘the convict – Amir Rahim Jabbar Lazem – to 15 years in prison’ pursuant to Iraq’s Anti-terrorism Law ‘for the crime of kidnapping the complainant – Shelly Renee Kittleson of American nationality – on March 31, 2026, in the al-Saadoun area’ in the Iraqi capital, read a copy of the ruling obtained by Rudaw.”
Jabbar Lazem has been detained since April for the kidnapping, and according to a video shown at the time, other men were involved in it. An eyewitness at the scene told Rudaw that “three people surrounded her [Kittleson] and one of them grabbed her from behind.”
Kataib Hezbollah suspected to be behind kidnapping
Kataib Hezbollah, believed to have been behind the kidnapping, is one of the most powerful of the Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. The US has sanctioned it as a terrorist organization, and it is part of the paramilitary Popular Mobilization Forces.
Its former leader, Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, was killed in a US drone strike in January 2020. He was driving in a vehicle alongside IRGC Quds Force head Qasem Soleimani, who was the target of the strike – and who was also killed. The fact that Muhandis and Soleimani were in the same vehicle illustrates the close ties between the IRGC and Iranian-backed militias.
It does not appear Iraq will hold Kataib Hezbollah responsible for the kidnapping or other crimes. Kataib Hezbollah was also likely behind a drone attack that killed three American service members in Jordan in January 2024. It has also been behind attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Former French PM Balladur dies at 97
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:25:36 UTC
04:25:36 KST

Former French PM Balladur dies at 97
PARIS, Aug 31 - Edouard Balladur, who was France's prime minister from 1993 to 1995, has died at 97, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on X on Monday.
A leading figure of France's centre-right, Balladur was the architect of a sweeping privatisation drive that saw the sale of some of France's most prominent companies, including banks Société Générale and Paribas — later part of BNP Paribas — as well as broadcaster TF1. He also pushed through a reform of France's politically sensitive pension system in 1993.
"Edouard Balladur is closely associated with fifty years of the history of the Fifth Republic. From his early days working alongside Georges Pompidou to his appointment as Prime Minister, he was a leading figure in our public life," Lecornu said on X.
"Edouard Balladur was a statesman with a reformist spirit and will remain a role model for many men and women in his political family," he added.
A stiff technocrat, Balladur was often portrayed by his critics as aloof and disconnected. Plantu, a press cartoonist, sketched him as an aristocrat wearing a wig and seated in a sedan chair. The satirical weekly Le Canard enchaîné renamed him "His Courteous Smugness".
Balladur served as prime minister under Socialist President Francois Mitterrand. REUTERS

Details: Prokudin added that the situation in Kherson is particularly difficult because of the Russians' proximity. Quote: "That is why I am asking you to do the most important thing – do not ignore the danger. If there is a recommendation to evacuate, evacuate. Do not listen to those who try to portray such decisions as some kind of 'betrayal' or an attempt to 'drive' people out of Kherson Oblast."
Details: He added that authorities are currently considering options for accommodating residents of the region in boarding houses and other facilities in safer regions.

US targets China’s global trade surplus at G20 meeting ahead of Xi-Trump summit
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent raises concerns over China’s ‘excessive imbalances’ just weeks before crucial bilateral meeting
4-MIN READ4-MIN
25
 Listen
Nayan Sethin Washington
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday targeted China’s global trade surplus, raising concerns over “excessive imbalances,” weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to arrive in Washington for a bilateral summit with US President Donald Trump.
“We are confronting persistent global imbalances that undermine prosperity,” Bessent said in his opening address at the G20 Finance Ministers’ meeting in Asheville, North Carolina. The United States holds the G20 presidency in 2026, leading a forum of the world’s major advanced and emerging economies.
Without naming China, Bessent said that the grouping’s finance ministers and central bank governors “have broadly concurred that it is in the interests of both surplus and deficit countries to address excessive imbalances”.
“We have seen how distorted policies that privileged countries’ own exports have harmed many of the economies represented here today,” he said, adding that a “durable global economy cannot rest on beggar-thy-neighbour acts that stifle fair market-based competition.”
Washington has made trade imbalances a key theme of the G20 ministerial – part of decades-long complaints about Beijing’s high trade surpluses – as a surge in Chinese exports of major products such as automobiles, solar panels and batteries has raised concerns in many countries over Beijing’s alleged “overcapacity”.
